No one, not even the most punctual soul with a watch-chain taut across his waistcoat, ever truly begins at the beginning. We choose a point—any point—like a cook laying down the first board upon the trestles and calling it the start of the feast, though the fire has been banked since dawn and the broth has been murmuring long before the ladle ever touched it. So it was that Daniel Deronda’s first fixed moment with her came not in an English drawing-room with tea and buttered toast, but in a room where the air itself seemed over-reduced—breath upon breath cooked down to a visible haze, thick with gas and perfumes that had lost their innocence under heat.

It was near four o’clock on a September day, when sunlight outside is still clean and the world ought to smell of stone warmed by noon; but here there was only the casino’s enclosed atmosphere, brewed and stale, gilding and velvet acting like a lidded pot that kept every exhalation in. The place had a hush that was not peace, rather the strained quiet one hears when a household has stopped speaking at table: broken only by the small hard acoustics of chance—the light rattle of ivory, the chink of coin, the soft sweep of metal across cloth, and, floating over all, an occasional French phrase from the croupier, level and mechanical, like a clock that has forgotten what time means and still insists on striking.

Two long tables drew their crowds as hearths draw hands in winter. Faces were bent down as if toward a dish that must not be missed in its crucial moment; eyes fixed with the same narrow appetite. All but one: a melancholy little boy, bare-kneed and bare-calfed, the skin of him his only honest garment, while the rest was fancy-dress finery. He stood close behind a lady at the roulette-table, staring toward the doorway with the blank patience of a child made into an ornament—like a sweetmeat figure on a cake that no one is allowed to eat.

Around the roulette-table there were ranks—players pressed close, spectators behind them deposited and removed like extra chairs at a noisy family supper. Now and then a new-comer, often a woman, would lay down a five-franc piece with a little simper, as if tasting a forbidden sauce and wanting to be seen tasting it. Those who had swallowed the thing whole were every variety of European type—Livonian and Spanish, Graeco-Italian and mixed German; English aristocratic near English plebeian—shoulders brushing, hands almost touching. Equality here was bought with the price of appetite.

Deronda’s eye noted the odd intimacy: the white, jeweled fingers of an English countess near the bony yellow hand of a creature that looked as if it had been made for clutching—wrist bare, knuckles sharp, the whole hand crab-like and hungry, and easy to match with the gaunt square face, deep-set eyes, grizzled brows, and scanty ill-combed hair that suggested a vulture in a bad disguise. Near them, too, a dry-lipped woman prematurely withered, as though she had bloomed briefly like forced flowers and then dried, holding a shabby velvet reticule; she now and then put into her mouth the point with which she pricked her card—an action as sharp and joyless as biting a pin.

There was a respectable London tradesman—soft-handed, fair, his sleek hair parted with scrupulous care both behind and before—who carried on him the invisible paper of circulars addressed to “the nobility and gentry,” as if that printed flattery might follow him even here. He did not have the gambler’s fever that kills appetite; his was the well-fed leisure of a man who, between making money and spending it showily, found no better entertainment than to win a little and spend it more showily still. In his mind Providence disapproved of nothing that left him warm and undisturbed. To lose was the vice; to win was, apparently, a blessing.

Standing close behind that tradesman’s chair was a handsome Italian with a calm, carved composure, reaching across to place a first pile of napoleons from a new bag just brought by an envoy with a scrolled mustache. The pile slid away almost at once to an old bewigged woman with eye-glasses pinching her nose; she showed only the faintest gleam, a mumbling smile. The Italian remained impassive, as if his system were a recipe that never failed, and began another pile. Elsewhere an emaciated beau—or a worn-out libertine—looked at life through a single eye-glass, held out his hand trembling for change, driven not by method but by some private superstition as thin and fierce as hunger.

And yet, for all their differences, a sameness lay on them, a mask of uniform negation—as if each had chewed some bitter root that for an hour narrowed the mind to one repetitive motion. Deronda, feeling the room’s dull, gas-poisoned absorption, had the sudden thought that the gambling of Spanish shepherd-boys in open air—tossing coppers on a ruined wall, the wind clean, the smell of earth and sheep and sun-baked stone—had seemed more enviable than this gilded stew of breath and coin. Here even the soundscape was wrong: not the varied music of living, but the petty percussion of money and the monotonous voice that kept time for it, a kind of industrial rhythm disguised as amusement.

Then, as often happens when a quiet dish suddenly turns in the pot and releases a stronger scent, the moment sharpened. His attention was arrested by a young lady standing at an angle not far from him, the last person his eyes would have traveled to if they had been merely wandering. She had been bending to speak English to a middle-aged lady seated beside her at play; then she returned to the table and showed the full height of a graceful figure, and a face that might possibly be looked at without admiration, but could hardly be passed without a second look.

Was she beautiful? Deronda’s mind asked it as one might ask what gives a certain fruit its bite—why one peach is mere sweetness and another has that keen edge that compels you to taste again. What was it in the form or the expression that made her glance dynamic, not soothing? Did the good genius or the evil dominate in those beams? Probably the evil—if evil can be named as that which disturbs rather than charms. The wish to look again felt coercive, not consenting; like hearing a note that is not quite in tune, which one cannot ignore, which sets the teeth on edge and fixes the ear.

He watched her movements—her arms and hands as she bent forward to place a stake with an air of firm choice. The hands were taper, delicately gloved in pale-gray, touching the coins with the precision of someone accustomed to being obeyed by objects; as her winnings were pushed toward her and she adjusted them to send them back again to the winning point, she looked round with a survey too cold and neutral not to be an art concealing exultation. But in that survey her eyes met Deronda’s.

She would have wished, it seemed, to avert them. Instead she was unpleasantly conscious that they were arrested. How long? Long enough for a thought to sting her into feeling: that he was measuring her; that he looked down on her as inferior; that he was of a different quality than the human dross around her; that he held himself outside and above and examined her as a specimen of a lower order.

Resentment pricked her quick and sharp. It did not redden her cheeks; it sent the blood away from her lips, leaving them paler, as if the heat of her had withdrawn into herself to keep her pride from spilling out. She controlled her face with an inward defiance and turned back to the game.

But Deronda’s gaze—so she felt it, without looking—worked on her like an evil eye. Her stake was swept away. No matter. She had been winning since she first put down a few napoleons, and she had reserve enough. Luck had begun to feel like something that belonged to her, like a well-stocked larder to a confident housekeeper; others had begun to believe in it too. She had even let herself imagine the ridiculous triumphs that pride will cook up from nothing: a little court of watchers, a cortège, worshiping her as a goddess of luck, waiting for her hand to dictate their auguries. Men had been treated so; why should a woman not command it?

Her friend and chaperon—the middle-aged lady—had not wished her to play at first. Now she began to approve, only offering prudent counsel: stop in time and carry money back to England. Gwendolen had answered that she cared for the excitement, not the winnings. If that were true, this should have been the flood-tide of delight.

Yet when the next stake was swept away, Gwendolen felt the orbits of her eyes grow hot, as if the air itself had turned into pepper. And the certainty she had—without looking—that the man was still watching her pressed like a finger on a bruise, beginning to torture. All the more reason, she told herself, not to flinch. She would go on as if loss and gain were nothing. She would not give him the satisfaction of seeing her turn from the table like a scolded child.

Her friend touched her elbow, proposing they should quit. In reply Gwendolen laid ten louis on the same spot. She was in that defiant mood where the mind forgets ends and lives only for the satisfaction of resistance; and with the puerile stupidity of a dominant impulse, she included luck itself among the things to be defied. If she could not win strikingly, she would lose strikingly.

She kept her muscles obedient; no tremor showed in mouth or hands. Each time her stake was swept off, she doubled it. The watchers increased; their attention was a new layer of heat in the room. But she was conscious of one observation only—Deronda’s. She did not look at him; she did not need to. She was sure he had not moved away.

The drama did not take long; catastrophe can be counted by the moment-hand, swift as a sauce turning when you have stepped away. “Faites votre jeu, mesdames et messieurs,” said the automaton voice, destiny speaking from between the mustache and imperial of the croupier. Gwendolen’s arm stretched out with her last poor heap of napoleons.

“Le jeu ne va plus,” said destiny.

In five seconds she turned from the table—turned resolutely with her face toward Deronda and looked at him.

There was a smile of irony in his eyes as their glances met. Yet that was better, in her swift calculation, than to be disregarded as part of an insect swarm with no individual physiognomy. Besides, in spite of what she read as superciliousness, it was hard to believe he did not admire her—her spirit as well as her person. He was young, handsome, distinguished-looking; not one of those dowdy, ridiculous Philistines who passed a gaming-table with a sour air of protest, as if virtue were a duty they performed with their faces.

Her mind, trained in a certain easy vanity, had lived on the assumption that she knew what was admirable and that she herself was admired. That foundation had been jarred. It reeled but did not fall. Vanity, when met with a cold reception, rarely yields; it often insists that a little more performance will win the dissident.

In the evening the same room was hotter, more stifling, brilliant with gas and with ladies’ costumes—satins and feathers and ornaments that glittered like sugar-work under lamps. The air held more perfume, as if the night’s finery were meant to drown the day’s breath, though it only made a richer suffocation. The soundscape was fuller too: not silence now, but a hum of voices, a rustle of trains, the clink still present like a persistent utensil dropped on stone.

Gwendolen Harleth had dressed as a Nereid in sea-green robes with silver ornaments; a pale sea-green feather fastened in silver fell backward over her green hat and light-brown hair. She moved under the wing—or rather, she soared by the shoulder—of the same lady who had sat by her at roulette, Madame von Langen. With them walked a gentleman with a white mustache and clipped hair, stiff and German, his brow solid as a lintel.

As they passed seated groups, Gwendolen was much observed.

“A striking girl—that Miss Harleth—unlike others.”

“Yes, she has got herself up as a sort of serpent now—all green and silver, and winds her neck about a little more than usual.”

“Oh, she must always be doing something extraordinary. She is that kind of girl, I fancy. Do you think her pretty, Mr. Vandernoodt?”

“Very. A man might risk hanging for her—I mean a fool might.”

“You like a nez retroussé, then, and long narrow eyes?”

“When they go with such an ensemble.”

“The ensemble du serpent?”

“If you will. Woman was tempted by a serpent; why not man?”

“She is certainly very graceful; but she wants a tinge of color in her cheeks. It is a sort of Lamia beauty she has.”

“On the contrary, I think her complexion one of her chief charms. It is a warm paleness; it looks thoroughly healthy. And that delicate nose with its gradual little upward curve is distracting. And then her mouth—there never was a prettier mouth, the lips curled backward so finely, eh, Mackworth?”

“Think so? I cannot endure that sort of mouth. It looks so self-complacent, as if it knew its own beauty—the curves are too immovable. I like a mouth that trembles more.”

“For my part, I think her odious,” said a dowager. “It is wonderful what unpleasant girls get into vogue. Who are these Langens? Does anybody know them?”

“They are quite comme il faut. I have dined with them several times at the Russie. The baroness is English. Miss Harleth calls her cousin. The girl herself is thoroughly well-bred, and as clever as possible.”

“Dear me! and the baron?”

“A very good furniture picture.”

“Your baroness is always at the roulette-table,” said Mackworth. “I fancy she has taught the girl to gamble.”

“Oh, the old woman plays a very sober game; drops a ten-franc piece here and there. The girl is more headlong. But it is only a freak.”

“I hear she has lost all her winnings to-day. Are they rich? Who knows?”

“Ah, who knows? Who knows that about anybody?” said Mr. Vandernoodt, moving off to join the Langens.

The remark about Gwendolen winding her neck more than usual was true, but not from zeal for the serpent-idea. She watched for Deronda. The measuring gaze she had felt in the afternoon still smarted in her like a taste that would not leave the mouth. It was not merely that she wanted to conquer his opinion; it was that she could not bear an unspoken judgment fixed on her from a man whose silence seemed to claim a higher language than the room’s bright chatter. There are dominions, she felt dimly, in which some people are native and others are foreign; and she hated the notion that she might be a foreigner without knowing why.

At last she had her chance. Mr. Vandernoodt drifted near, that easy man-about-hotel who seemed to have acquaintances as other men have loose change.

“Mr. Vandernoodt, you know everybody,” Gwendolen said—not too eagerly, but with the languid utterance she could summon at will, like a clear soprano made indolent for effect. “Who is that near the door?”

“There are half a dozen near the door. Do you mean that old Adonis in the George the Fourth wig?”

“No, no; the dark-haired young man on the right with the dreadful expression.”

“Dreadful, do you call it? I think he is an uncommonly fine fellow.”

“But who is he?”

“He is lately come to our hotel with Sir Hugo Mallinger.”

“Sir Hugo Mallinger?”

“Yes. Do you know him?”

“No.” Gwendolen colored slightly, and the warmth rose into that warm paleness the critics had praised, as if her blood resented being mentioned aloud. “He has a place near us, but he never comes to it. What did you say was the name of that gentleman near the door?”

“Deronda—Mr. Deronda.”

“What a delightful name! Is he an Englishman?”

“Yes. He is reported to be rather closely related to the baronet. You are interested in him?”

“Yes. I think he is not like young men in general.”

“And you don’t admire young men in general?”

“Not in the least. I always know what they will say. I can’t at all guess what this Mr. Deronda would say. What does he say?”

“Nothing, chiefly. I sat with his party for a good hour last night on the terrace, and he never spoke—and was not smoking either. He looked bored.”

“Another reason why I should like to know him. I am always bored.”

“I should think he would be charmed to have an introduction. Shall I bring it about? Will you allow it, baroness?”

“Why not?—since he is related to Sir Hugo Mallinger. It is a new rôle of yours, Gwendolen, to be always bored,” Madame von Langen continued, when Mr. Vandernoodt had moved away. “Until now you have always seemed eager about something from morning till night.”

“That is just because I am bored to death. If I am to leave off play I must break my arm or my collar-bone. I must make something happen; unless you will go into Switzerland and take me up the Matterhorn.”

“Perhaps this Mr. Deronda’s acquaintance will do instead of the Matterhorn.”

“Perhaps.”

But that evening, for all her watching and for all the cloying heat and the talk that rose and fell like the boil of a crowded kitchen, she did not make Mr. Deronda’s acquaintance. Mr. Vandernoodt did not succeed in bringing him up to her; introductions failed like a sauce that separates at the last moment.

And when Gwendolen re-entered her own room, the air at last cooler and quieter, the sudden hush of privacy ringing in her ears like a relief from machinery, she found a letter waiting—its paper and ink carrying her back to England more sharply than any lecture could have done, recalling her home as inevitably as the smell of a familiar loaf can summon an entire childhood.

“This man contrives a secret ’twixt us two,
That he may quell me with his meeting eyes
Like one who quells a lioness at bay.”

The letter lay on Gwendolen Harleth’s table as if it had been set there by a hand that understood how paper can weigh more than silver. She broke the seal, and the room—its pale curtains, its bright appointments, the faint perfume clinging to her traveling things—seemed to draw in its breath while she read.

“DEAREST CHILD.—I have been expecting to hear from you for a week….”

Her mother’s words hurried on, anxious, practical, trembling with the effort to keep steady. The Langens might be leaving; how could Gwendolen have let her address be uncertain? And then, the change of key—no longer a domestic fret, but the crack of a great thing broken: Grapnell & Co. had failed for a million; they were ruined, all of them. Offendene must be given up. There would be no money to send. There must be no borrowing. There was talk of tradesmen unpaid, servants’ wages, a “hut or other” to shelter them; a life, in short, suddenly pared down to bare necessity, like a household forced to live on crusts after banquets. There was even—sharpest of all—a name for the cause: Mr. Lassman’s wicked recklessness.

“Summon up your fortitude… resign ourselves… it rends my heart… it is hard…”

The signature—FANNY DAVILOW—looked like a familiar hand shaken by cold.

For a little while the first effect was not tears, not any flooding grief, but a kind of stunned resistance, as if her mind refused to admit the new texture of the world. The certainty she had carried like a birthright—that her destiny must be cushioned, that even trouble would come draped and mannered, well-fed and kept in its place—stood for an instant staring at its own eviction.

She remained motionless. Then, with a movement that was almost automatic, she tossed off her hat and looked into the glass.

Her hair was still coiled smooth and exact—ball-room perfection surviving midnight and agitation. On other nights she would have lingered over the image with that innocent pleasure youth takes in its own bloom; but now she stared past her reflection as if some ugly noise had jarred her and she waited, rigid, for its source to show itself.

She dropped into the corner of the red velvet sofa and read the letter again—then a third time, slower, deliberate, as if by pressing each sentence she might wring out its falsehood. At last it slid from her fingers to the carpet. She sat with clasped hands on her lap, very still, dry-eyed.

Her impulse was not to wail. It was to measure, to defy, to look for leverage.

“Poor mamma” did not rise in her with any tender cry. Her mother, in Gwendolen’s view, had always seemed made for anxious endurance rather than enjoyment; and self-pity—hot, immediate—had the first claim. Was she not the chief object of her mother’s dread? Was not this calamity, in its most intolerable form, aimed at her?

And then came anger—anger with a gambler’s sting in it. She had lost at roulette. If only luck had held for this one day she might have gone home with a handsome sum; she might even have stayed and won enough to keep them all. The thought flared—half hope, half rebellion. Even now, was it impossible?

In her purse were four napoleons. But there were ornaments: things that could be turned to money as easily, in these watering-places, as a ribbon is changed. It was common enough—no need to speak of shame. She had an Etruscan necklace she was not wearing; she could sell it and feel, perversely, that she had escaped the dullness of ordinary necessity by living “intensely.” With ten louis—more, perhaps—and the return of that earlier luck which had seemed so natural to her, what could be wiser than to play a few days more, and come home not helpless but triumphant? Let the rectory, the aunts, the moralists at home disapprove of the manner of getting it: the money would be there.

Yet her imagination, though it dwelt on this course and made it glitter with agreeable consequences, did not gather the blind heat of mania. She had gone to the roulette-table not because passion drove her, but because she wished to be driven—to feel what she had been told of, that intoxicating compulsion. Her mind could still set the scales even while it wished to tip them: the chance of winning allured her, and the chance of losing rose up and chilled her pride with an image of herself—stripped of resource, exposed, dependent.

For she was resolved on one point as firmly as if it were written in her bones: she would not tell the Langens of any family disaster, and she would not be beholden to their pity. If she began to part with her jewelry in a way they could observe, there would be questions, interferences, tedious compassion.

The least intolerable course—the one with the smallest risk of humiliation—was swift and simple: raise money early, tell the Langens only that her mother required her return at once, and take the train for Brussels that same evening.

So instead of going to bed she made as brilliant a light as she could, and began packing. She worked with quick diligence, folding and placing each garment as if order itself might be a kind of defense. All the while her mind was haunted by tomorrow’s scenes—explanations and farewells, then the whirling journey toward a home changed into something meaner; and, like an alternative devil whispering at her elbow, the picture of “just one more day,” and her standing again at the roulette-table.

But in that latter scene, always, inevitably, there was Deronda—present as a watcher, his look seeming to weigh and measure her with an exasperating irony. And with him came the other keen experience, welded to his presence: the moment of forsaken luck, the turn of the wheel, the sense of eyes seeing her defeated. That image helped drive her toward departure, helped her pack until changing her mind would be inconvenient.

It was past midnight when she had entered her room. Before she finished, a faint dawn stole through the white blinds, paling the candle-flames, making the gilt edges of her little possessions look suddenly cheap.

What was the use of lying down? A cold bath was refreshment enough; and if there were a slight fatigue about her eyes, she could tell herself it made her face only more touching, more interesting—like a heroine on the edge of some splendid trouble.

Before six she was completely equipped in her gray traveling dress, even to her felt hat. She meant to walk out as soon as she could be sure other ladies would be on their way to the springs. She sat sideways before the long strip of mirror between the windows and looked at herself—elbow on the chair-back, an attitude fit for a portrait.

She had a strong self-love, and it carried no inward torment with it. It was a simple delight in her fortunate self, fed daily by flattering voices and by the looking-glass’s faithful praise. And even now—at the very beginning of what she called “troubles”—she gazed until the growing light seemed to cheer her into complacency. Her lips curled into a smile that deepened, softened, asserted itself; and at last she took off her hat, leaned forward, and kissed the cold glass that had looked so warm.

How could she believe in sorrow? If it attacked her, she would crush it, defy it, or run away from it—as she had done already. Anything seemed more possible than a long, patient bearing of misery.

Madame von Langen never went out before breakfast. Gwendolen could safely end her early walk by going through the Obere Strasse where the needed shop was, sure to be open after seven. At that hour, the few eyes she might care about would be elsewhere—near the springs—or still behind bedroom doors.

And yet there was one grand hotel—the Czarina—where eyes might follow her up to Mr. Wiener’s door. Deronda’s hotel.

It was a chance to be risked. Might she not be going to buy some trifle that had struck her fancy? The implicit falsehood glided through her mind like a thin veil held up to the world. She walked on with her usual floating movement, her figure and drapery falling in those soft curves that drew attention without asking for it. She looked neither right nor left, and when she entered the shop she transacted her business with cool composure.

Little Mr. Wiener had nothing to remark—nothing he would have dared to remark—except the proud grace of her manner, and the superior size and quality of the three central turquoises in the necklace she offered him. They had belonged once to a chain that was her father’s; she had never known her father, and the ornament, in every sense, was the one she could most conveniently surrender.

It is not impossible to be superstitious and rationalizing at once. Roulette had encouraged in her a romantic superstition about chances, and at the same time a practical hardness about the sentiments that obstruct the raising of money. Her dominant regret, as the dealer counted out her sum, was that she had only nine louis to add to the four napoleons already in her purse. These jewelry men—so ready to profit by a Christian’s bad luck at play!

But she was the Langens’ guest; she had nothing to pay in their hired apartment. Thirteen louis would do more than take her home. Even if she risked three—if she yielded to the temptation of one last trial—the remaining ten would suffice, for she meant to travel on, day and night.

When she turned homeward, when she entered and seated herself in the salon to wait for the Langens and breakfast, she still wavered. She had decided to say only that her mother desired her immediate return—and to keep the moment of departure, for the present, hovering.

It was already the usual breakfast-time. She leaned back, tired and hungry, eyes shut for a moment, listening for footsteps that would be familiar. The words she might speak—words that could permit her to linger another day—were ready in her throat.

The door opened.

Not Madame or Herr von Langen, but the servant, bringing a small packet left at the door for Miss Harleth.

Gwendolen took it and, with a sudden inward start, hurried into her own room. Her face was paler now than it had been over her mother’s letter; her agitation had a new quality, sharper, personal, as if her pride had been touched by a finger.

She never quite knew what it was that foretold the contents before she opened it. She only knew that when her fingers began to tear the paper, her heart sank with certainty.

Underneath the wrapping lay the necklace—her necklace—folded in a cambric handkerchief. Inside was a scrap of torn note-paper, with penciled words in clear but rapid handwriting:

“A stranger who has found Miss Harleth’s necklace returns it to her with the hope that she will not again risk the loss of it.”

The blood rushed to her face with the heat of wounded pride. The handkerchief had a corner torn off—recklessly torn, as if to destroy a mark. And at once, without argument, the first image of “the stranger” rose and occupied her mind like a tyrant: Deronda.

He must have seen her enter the shop. He must have followed, repurchased the necklace, and sent it back. The liberty of it! The insolence! He had dared to place her in a position she loathed—helpless, obliged, preached at. And if she sent it back to him, she would have to risk being mistaken; even if she were right, she would be letting him know she had divined him, would have to meet him again with that recognition alive between them.

He knew perfectly what he was doing: entangling her in humiliation, smiling again with that quiet superiority, taking the tone of mentor over her as if she were a child caught stealing sugar.

Bitter tears of mortification rose and rolled down her cheeks. No one had ever before dared to treat her with irony and contempt.

One thing became instantly clear, as if the room itself had spoken it: she must leave this place at once. She could not go back into the public salon; she could not—above all—stand again at the gaming-table with the risk of encountering Deronda’s eyes.

A knock came at her door—importunate. Breakfast was ready.

With a passionate movement she thrust necklace, cambric, scrap of paper and all into her nécessaire, pressed her handkerchief against her face, and waited a minute, summoning back her proud self-control as one summons a servant who must not see one disordered.

When she joined the Langens, the traces of tears and fatigue that remained seemed easily accounted for by what she said at once—that she had sat up packing rather than wait for help from her friend’s maid. There were protests, as she expected: she must not travel alone; there must be some arrangement, some escort, some propriety observed.

She refused them all with quiet peremptoriness. She would be put into the ladies’ compartment and go right on. She could rest perfectly well in the train. She was afraid of nothing.

And so it happened that Gwendolen never reappeared at the roulette-table. That Thursday evening she left Leubronn for Brussels; and on Saturday morning she arrived at Offendene—the home to which she and her family were soon to say a last good-bye.

Pity that Offendene had not clung to Miss Harleth from the beginning, as flavors cling to a childhood tongue—some first sweetness of milk, some crust of home-baked bread, some herb-smell rising whenever the wind turns a hedge. A life, if it is to have any steadiness, should be planted deep in one patch of native earth: not merely so the eyes know the shape of the hills, but so the ears learn the right hush of evening and the particular morning racket of rooks; so the very air—smoke from damp logs, turned soil, bruised apple—becomes a private language the heart understands without translating. It is a cruel thing to ask a child to be “of the world,” as if the world were not first given to us in the narrow compass of a kitchen-sound and a garden-scent, in a dialect spoken by familiar mouths.

But that anchoring had been missing in Gwendolen’s life. Only a year before the summons home from Leubronn, Offendene had been chosen as her mamma’s house—chosen for convenience, because it lay near Pennicote Rectory. Mrs. Davilow, Gwendolen, and the four half-sisters, with governess and maid following, had first come down the avenue on a late October afternoon when the rooks were loud overhead and the elm leaves—yellow as old saffron—went spinning in the draught of their wheels.

The season flattered the old red-brick house, oblong and self-conscious in its stone trimming—stone at every line as if it needed insisting upon, even at the double row of narrow windows and the square portico. The stone had gathered greenish lichen; the brick had dulled to a powdery grey, so that rigidity softened into something like age’s indulgence. Old plantation trees circled the immediate grounds, and the house looked out by its three cut avenues—east, west, and south—across flat pastures. One wished it stood on a knoll, so its windows might command thatched villages, church towers, and scattered homesteads; but from behind its shelter it had at least, on one side, a glimpse of the chalk downs, those steadfast pale curves that took light and shadow like slow-breathing creatures.

It was barely large enough to deserve “mansion,” and only moderately rented, with no manor attached and furniture so sombre and upholstery so faded that tenants were scarce. Yet it had the one advantage that mattered to Mrs. Davilow’s pride: it could not be mistaken for the refuge of retired tradespeople. That negative distinction was worth discomfort to those who lived on the borderland of rank, where one’s name and one’s rooms are forever being measured by the world. To step into a house that had been thought good enough for dowager countesses gave Mrs. Davilow a visible lift—made her seem, for moments, less worn.

How it had suddenly become possible, after the death of Captain Davilow, was a mystery Gwendolen did not care to solve. She cared for the fact: that the roving life—foreign watering-places, Paris apartments, new hired furniture that never smelled like “theirs,” introductions that kept her feeling unimportant—was ended. Even the two showy years at school, where she had always been placed foremost on days of display, had only sharpened her conviction that she could not be meant for ordinary circumstances. Now, with an establishment of her mamma’s own, she felt sheltered from the dread of social meanness. On questions of birth she was easy; her maternal grandfather had been a West Indian—which to her mind was a sort of locked cupboard that one did not open; and her father’s family was “so high” they took no notice of her mamma, who nevertheless kept with pride a miniature of some Lady Molly to prove connection.

She might have asked more about her father, but for an old incident. When she was twelve, Mrs. Davilow had taken out—rarely, and with ceremony—memorials of her first husband, and, showing his miniature, spoke with a fervor that demanded a particular filial response: dear papa had died when his little daughter was in long clothes. Gwendolen, thinking immediately of the unloved stepfather who had occupied her short-frock years, blurted—

“Why did you marry again, mamma? It would have been nicer if you had not.”

Mrs. Davilow colored, a convulsive movement passed over her face, and she shut the memorials away as if shutting a wound.

“You have no feeling, child!” she said, with a violence quite unlike her.

Gwendolen, fond of her mamma and newly ashamed, had never since dared to question her father’s story.

That was not the only time she had pricked herself on the hidden tenderness of others. It was always arranged, when possible, that she should have a small bed in her mamma’s room; Mrs. Davilow’s motherly devotion clung most to the eldest girl, born in happier days. One night, under an attack of pain, she found the medicine meant to stand by her bed had been forgotten, and she begged Gwendolen to rise and fetch it. The young lady, warm as a child in her little nest, objected to stepping into the cold. She lay stubbornly still, and refused with a grumble. Mrs. Davilow went without, and never reproached her; but next day Gwendolen, with that quick inward sting which can come even to the spoiled, knew what her mamma must have felt. She made amends by caresses that cost little.

Having been the household’s pet and pride—waited on by mother, sisters, governess, maids, as if she were a princess in exile—she found it hard to imagine that other pleasures could outweigh her own. When they did, she felt a surprised resentment which, in her cruder days, had flared into sudden acts that seemed to contradict her general nature. She was not thoughtlessly cruel; she would rescue drowning insects and watch them recover. Yet there was the disagreeable memory—like a sharp note in silence—of having strangled her sister’s canary in a final exasperation at its shrill, piercing singing that had again and again broken into her own. She had bought her sister a white mouse by way of reparation; and though she excused herself inwardly by calling it “sensitiveness,” a mark of superiority, the thought of that infelonious murder always made her wince. Her nature was not remorseless—only she preferred penances that did not humiliate. Now that she was twenty and more, her force had hardened into self-control; the show of fire and will was stronger than ever, but calculation lay beneath it like a hidden hand on the reins.

On the day of arrival at Offendene—new even to Mrs. Davilow, for the place had been taken by her brother-in-law, Mr. Gascoigne—the carriage stopped under the porch before the open door. They all stood there, with a glimpse into a stone hall and staircase hung with sombre pictures; the one cheer was the bright wood-fire that snapped and settled with domestic confidence, as if the house had kept a little heart beating while it waited for tenants. No one spoke. Mrs. Davilow, the four sisters, and the governess all looked at Gwendolen, as if her opinion would flavor everything that followed—sweeten it or sour it.

Alice at sixteen and Isabel at ten were simply girlish at first glance, their black dresses already shabby. Miss Merry, elderly, wore neutrality like a shawl. Mrs. Davilow’s worn beauty looked the more touching for the complete appeal in her eyes. Gwendolen glanced round—the house, the landscape, the entrance hall—with rapid judgment, like a young racehorse among patient hacks.

“Well, dear, what do you think of the place?” Mrs. Davilow asked at last, gently, as if asking permission to breathe.

“I think it is charming,” Gwendolen said quickly. “A romantic place; anything delightful may happen in it; it would be a good background for anything. No one need be ashamed of living here.”

“There is certainly nothing common about it.”

“Oh, it would do for fallen royalty, or any sort of grand poverty. We ought properly to have been living in splendor and have come down to this. That would have been romantic indeed.” Then her tone sharpened. “But I thought my uncle and aunt Gascoigne would be here to meet us—and my cousin Anna.”

“We are early,” said Mrs. Davilow, and as they entered the hall she spoke to the housekeeper who came forward briskly. “You expect Mr. and Mrs. Gascoigne?”

“Yes, madam. They were here yesterday to give particular orders about the fires and the dinner. As to fires, I’ve had them in all the rooms for the last week, and everything is well aired. I could wish some of the furniture paid better for all the cleaning it’s had, but I think you’ll see the brasses have been done justice to. I think when Mr. and Mrs. Gascoigne come, they’ll tell you nothing has been neglected. They’ll be here at five, for certain.”

That promise of their arrival soothed Gwendolen at once; she was not prepared to have them treated as negligible. She tripped partway up the matted stone stairs to survey the landing, then came down, and with the girls behind her peeped into the rooms opening from the hall: the dining-room, all dark oak and worn red satin damask, with a copy of snarling, worrying dogs above the sideboard, and a Christ breaking bread above the mantel—bread one could almost imagine smelling faintly in the varnished air; the library with its brown-leather scent, dry and old as pressed leaves; and lastly the drawing-room, reached through a little antechamber crowded with venerable knick-knacks.

“Mamma, mamma, pray come here!” Gwendolen called, for Mrs. Davilow had lagged behind with the housekeeper. “Here is an organ. I will be Saint Cecilia: someone shall paint me as Saint Cecilia. Jocosa—let down my hair. See, mamma?”

She had flung off hat and gloves, seated herself at the organ, and lifted her face in an admirable pose, eyes upward. Miss Merry—whom Gwendolen called Jocosa—obediently drew out the comb that held the coil, and shook the mass free till it fell in a smooth light-brown stream far below its owner’s slim waist.

Mrs. Davilow smiled. “A charming picture, my dear!”—not indifferent to the display of her pet even under a servant’s eye.

Gwendolen rose and laughed, delighted, as if the house had already offered her its proper stage. “What a queer, quaint, picturesque room! I like these old embroidered chairs, and the garlands on the wainscot, and the pictures that may be anything. That one with the ribs—nothing but ribs and darkness—I should think that is Spanish, mamma.”

“Oh, Gwendolen!” cried little Isabel, astonished, her thin voice lifting like a sudden squeak of a door. She had pushed open a hinged panel of the wainscot at the far end of the room.

They all went to look, Gwendolen first. The panel disclosed a painting: an upturned dead face, pallid in gloom, and an obscure figure fleeing with outstretched arms.

“How horrible!” said Mrs. Davilow, with plain disgust.

Gwendolen did not cry out; she shuddered, the chill striking through her quick vanity like a draught through silk. Isabel, plain and inconvenient—one of those children who remember everything and speak it at the worst moment—said with alarming certainty, “You will never stay in this room by yourself, Gwendolen.”

“How dare you open things which were meant to be shut up, you perverse little creature?” Gwendolen snapped, anger rising in reaction against her own fear. She snatched the panel from Isabel and closed it hastily. “There is a lock—where is the key? Let the key be found, or else let one be made, and let nobody open it again; or rather, let the key be brought to me.”

With her cheeks flushed, she turned away as if shaking off a cold touch. “Let us go up to our own room, mamma.”

The housekeeper searched, found the key in a drawer of the cabinet near the panel, and presently handed it to Bugle, the lady’s-maid, with a significant nod. “Give it to her Royal Highness,” Mrs. Startin said.

“I don’t know what you mean, Mrs. Startin,” Bugle returned stiffly. She had been busy upstairs and resented irony from a new servant.

“I mean the young lady that’s to command us all—and well worthy for looks and figure,” Mrs. Startin added, mollified. “She’ll know what key it is.”

Upstairs, in the black-and-yellow bedroom, the best bed stood like a catafalque under its heavy hangings, while by its side a pretty little white couch waited for Gwendolen.

“If you have laid out what we want, go and see to the others, Bugle,” Gwendolen said as she entered with her mamma. “I will help mamma.”

But her first movement was to the tall mirror between the windows, which caught the whole room and her own figure in one obedient frame. Mrs. Davilow sat down and looked too, as mothers will, measuring their own hopes and losses in their child’s reflection.

“That is a becoming glass, Gwendolen; or is it the black and gold that sets you off?” she said.

Gwendolen stood obliquely, three-quarter face turned, brushing back her loosened hair with her left hand, intent as an artist on her own effect. “I should make a tolerable St. Cecilia with some white roses on my head—only how about my nose, mamma? I think saints’ noses never in the least turn up. I wish you had given me your perfectly straight nose; it would have done for any sort of character—a nose of all work. Mine is only a happy nose; it would not do so well for tragedy.”

“Oh, my dear, any nose will do to be miserable with in this world,” Mrs. Davilow said, and sighed heavily as she set her black bonnet down, weariness settling on her like dust.

“Now, mamma,” Gwendolen protested, vexed, turning from the mirror as if it had shown her something disagreeable. “Don’t begin to be dull here. It spoils all my pleasure, and everything may be so happy now. What have you to be gloomy about now?”

“Nothing, dear,” Mrs. Davilow said, rousing herself and beginning to unfasten her dress. “It is always enough for me to see you happy.”

“But you should be happy yourself,” Gwendolen insisted, discontent still in her voice though her hands grew caressing as she helped. “Can nobody be happy after they are quite young? You have made me feel sometimes as if nothing were of any use. With the girls so troublesome, and Jocosa so dreadfully wooden and ugly, and everything make-shift about us—and you looking so dull—what was the use of my being anything? But now you might be happy.”

“So I shall, dear,” said Mrs. Davilow, patting the cheek near hers.

“Yes, but really. Not with a sort of make-believe.” Gwendolen’s persistence was resolute. “See what a hand and arm!—much more beautiful than mine. Anyone can see you were altogether more beautiful.”

“No, no, dear; I was always heavier. Never half so charming as you are.”

“Well, but what is the use of my being charming, if it is to end in my being dull and not minding anything? Is that what marriage always comes to?”

“No, child, certainly not. Marriage is the only happy state for a woman, as I trust you will prove.”

“I will not put up with it if it is not a happy state.” Gwendolen’s chin lifted. “I am determined to be happy—at least not to go on muddling away my life as other people do, being and doing nothing remarkable. I have made up my mind not to let other people interfere with me as they have done. Here is some warm water ready for you, mamma.” She began to undress herself, then waited for her mamma to wind up her hair.

Silence fell while Mrs. Davilow coiled the long strands—quiet, methodical work, the kind that almost convinces the heart the world can be managed if only one keeps one’s hands busy. At last Mrs. Davilow said softly, “I am sure I have never crossed you, Gwendolen.”

“You often want me to do what I don’t like.”

“You mean, to give Alice lessons?”

“Yes. And I have done it because you asked me. But I don’t see why I should, else. It bores me to death, she is so slow. She has no ear for music, or language, or anything else. It would be much better for her to be ignorant, mamma: it is her rôle, she would do it well.”

“That is a hard thing to say of your poor sister, Gwendolen, who is so good to you, and waits on you hand and foot.”

“I don’t see why it is hard to call things by their right names, and put them in their proper places. The hardship is for me to have to waste my time on her. Now let me fasten up your hair, mamma.”

“We must make haste; your uncle and aunt will be here soon.” Mrs. Davilow’s voice took on its pleading note. “For heaven’s sake, don’t be scornful to them, my dear child! or to your cousin Anna, whom you will always be going out with. Do promise me, Gwendolen. You know, you can’t expect Anna to be equal to you.”

“I don’t want her to be equal,” said Gwendolen, tossing her head with a smile, and the matter ended as such matters did—with her will unshaken and her mamma soothed by the appearance of affection.

When Mr. and Mrs. Gascoigne and their daughter arrived, Gwendolen was not scornful. She was all grace—prettily attentive, as if kindness were a natural perfume she could pour out at pleasure. These were relatives who had not seen her since she was sixteen and unfinished; she was resolved that they should admire her.

Mrs. Gascoigne had the family likeness to her sister, but darker, slighter; her face unworn by grief, her movements brisker, her expression more alert and critical—the expression of a rector’s wife who feels bound to a beneficent authority. Their closest resemblance was a non-resistant disposition inclined to imitation and obedience; but in different lives such pliancy hardens into different shapes. The younger sister had been indiscreet, or at least unfortunate, in marriage; the elder believed herself enviable, and her pliancy had ended in opinions surprisingly definite. On church government, on the character of Archbishop Laud, her convictions seemed to remain equally decided through every alteration, as if arrived at less by inquiry than by receptive loyalty to her husband.

And there was much to encourage trust in Mr. Gascoigne. He had agreeable virtues, striking advantages, and even the failings imputed to him leaned toward success. One advantage was his fine person—perhaps more impressive at fifty-seven than earlier. There were no distinctively clerical lines in his face, no professional starchiness or affected ease. In his Inverness cape he could have passed for any gentleman: handsome dark features, a nose that began to be aquiline and then, as if thinking better of itself, became straight; iron-grey hair. He owed that freedom from clerical make-up—skin-deep and gesture-deep—to the fact that he had once been Captain Gaskin, taking orders and a diphthong only shortly before his engagement to Miss Armyn. If anyone questioned the adequacy of his preparation, friends might ask who made a better figure in the parish, who preached better, who carried more weight? He had a native gift for administration, tolerant of opinion and conduct because he felt himself able to overrule both, and free from the irritations of conscious weakness. He smiled at foibles he did not share—floriculture, antiquarianism, so dear to fellow clergy—preferring campaign histories, or divining from his knowledge of Nesselrode how policy would have shifted if our cabinet had chosen differently. His thinking had settled into what he would have called sound English—ecclesiastical rather than theological—national religion seen in daylight and in relation to other things. No clerical magistrate had greater weight at sessions, or less mischievous impracticableness about worldly affairs. The worst charge against him was worldliness: it could not be proved he forsook the unfortunate, yet his friendships were undeniably useful to a father of six sons and two daughters; and sour observers—Wessex had them, not long ago, in a bitterness that now may seem incredible—remarked that the color of his opinions changed with that principle. But cheerful, successful worldliness has a false look of selfishness beside the acrid, unsuccessful kind whose whole history is contained in the words: “Sold, but not paid for.”

Gwendolen wondered she had not remembered how fine a man her uncle was; at sixteen she had been a duller judge. Now it thrilled her to have, at last, the near presence of a dignified male relative—family life no longer entirely, insipidly feminine. She did not intend he should control her; but she saw at once how agreeable it would be for him to be proud of introducing her as his niece. And every sign said he was likely to feel that pride.

“You have outgrown Anna, my dear,” he said, putting his arm tenderly round his daughter and drawing her forward. Anna’s shy face was a tiny copy of his own. “She is not so old as you by a year, but her growing days are certainly over. I hope you will be excellent companions.”

His glance compared them; if he saw Anna’s inferiority, he likely saw too that her timid air and miniature figure would appeal to a different taste than Gwendolen’s vivid, commanding beauty. Gwendolen knew it, and kissed her cousin with real cordiality as well as practiced grace.

“A companion is just what I want,” she said. “I am so glad we are come to live here. And mamma will be much happier now she is near you, aunt.”

It would have been cruelly unfair to charge the rector of Pennicote with any singular worldliness because, as he turned a matter over and over in his mind like a conscientious housekeeper testing a loaf for hollowness, he concluded that Gwendolen Harleth was a girl meant for a brilliant marriage. He lived among people who weighed daughters as they weighed acres, and thought themselves benevolent in hoping the best price should be offered. Why should he be required, alone of his time and station, to wish his niece a fate less applauded than the common ideal?

Besides, Mr. Gascoigne’s feeling in the matter was kindly—kindly as a well-ordered table is kind, where every dish has its proper hour and the servants know their steps. He was not for fantastical recipes. He did not advise that Gwendolen should dress in meek rags like some sainted Griselda, as if a marquis were to be hooked by the bait of shabbiness; nor did he propose that she should hide herself away, as if a fair fruit kept in a dark pantry grew sweeter by neglect. His calculations were those of a man who believed in rational management: show the best goods in the best light, and the neighborhood’s best society would do its part. He did not so much as imagine contriving melodramatic accidents—no acquiring of frisky horses in order that a gentleman of property might be forced into heroism by saving her from a fall. He wished her well, and meant her to be seen to advantage.

In that, his intention chimed exactly with Gwendolen’s own desire—yet not in the plain way everybody assumed. If you had asked her, she would have admitted, with the air of one granting a tiresome point in conversation, that she must be married some day; and she would have been quietly sure—sure as a woman is sure of the salt in a well-kept cellar—that her marriage could never be of the middling kind most girls were content to serve up as their life’s portion. But her imagination did not dwell on marriage as the end of her drama. In the plays she staged within herself, she was a heroine long before any last act of wedding bells. To be much sued, to have hopeless sighs spent on her as if she were a rarity no one could afford—this was an agreeable proof of power, like the power to lift a whole room’s attention with a single clear word. Yet to become a wife—tied into the daily harness, hemmed in by a domestic “must,” burdened with more children than were desirable, and drowned at last in humdrum—seemed, on the whole, a vexatious necessity.

Her own observation of matrimony had left her with the taste of something over-boiled: nourishment perhaps, but dulled, without savor, and served in portions one could not choose. Marriage was undeniably a social promotion; she could not picture for herself a single life. But promotions have their bitter herbs. A title will not satisfy the man who meant to lead; and this delicate-limbed creature of twenty meant to lead. Such passions do not belong to men only.

In Gwendolen they dwelt amid entirely feminine furniture. They had no relation to learning, to public good, to constitutions balanced and nations improved. Her knowledge was the brisk schooling that lays down rules like hard crackers—dry but making ignorance feel less limp—and the rest of the world she felt she had tasted sufficiently through novels, plays, and poems. Her French and her music—those approved accomplishments that were supposed to give a young lady the right bouquet—did not trouble her. Add to these the native, happy confidence that some people are born with, so that whatever subject they turn to seems immediately to prove their own talent for judging it, and it is not strange that Gwendolen felt ready to manage destiny as another woman manages a household, making everything come when she chooses and in the form that pleases her.

There were, of course, many subjects in which she took no interest—because they were stupid. Subjects often look stupid to the young, as light looks dull to the old. Yet she never felt helpless before them; if they rose in conversation, she could meet them as she met any ordinary dish set before her—touch it, taste it, pronounce upon it with an air of having always known.

No one had ever disputed her power. From the moment of their settling at Offendene, and indeed always, the first thought in the house had been, What will Gwendolen think? If the footman’s boots creaked too heavily along the boards, or if the laundress’s work showed a clumsy seam, the maid’s dismay took the form of prophecy: “This will never do for Miss Harleth.” If the wood smoked in the bedroom grate, Mrs. Davilow—whose own eyes suffered most—apologized to Gwendolen, as if smoke were a personal affront to her daughter’s fastidiousness rather than a common misery to them all.

Even under the small violences of traveling, if Gwendolen did not appear to breakfast until everyone else had finished, the only question became how her coffee and toast might still arrive as if they had just come from the fire—hot, crisp, and fragrant with that clean, comforting smell of browned bread which can make a shabby room feel momentarily civilized. And when she did come in, her light-brown hair freshly brushed and streaming back, waiting for her mother’s hand to coil it up, her large brown eyes flashing—dark and bright as a polished stone washed by a wave—she was the one expected to be tolerant. It was she who must beg Alice, sitting ready to serve, not to hunch her shoulders into that frightful posture, and insist that Isabel should stop pressing close with questions and go away to Miss Merry.

Always she was treated like a princess in exile. If famine came, her breakfast-roll would be made of the finest-bolted flour gleaned, by miracle, from the seven thin ears; if there were a general packing up, her silver fork was to be kept out of the baggage as if it were a relic no rough hand might risk. One might say the reason lay plainly on the surface: her beauty, and something uncommon in her; her decided will making itself felt in the way she moved—graceful, certain—and in the tone of her voice, clear and unhesitating. If she entered a room on a rainy day when everyone else seemed softened and slackened by damp, when the very purpose of things felt blurred, her presence was like a sudden command that life should keep its forms. The very air seemed to tighten; and even hotel-waiters, who can be sluggish as if their ears were clogged with stale clatter, would show quicker alacrity—whisking away crumbs, smoothing creases, clearing the dregs where flies struggled, as if her notice were a kind of judgment.

Add to this that she was the eldest daughter, and her mother had long lived in an apologetic tenderness toward her for the evils a step-father had brought. Surely that might seem explanation enough—sunlight enough to account for daylight.

And yet—beware of conclusions that have not been tested by comparison.

I have seen the same trembling, assiduous service offered to people who were not beautiful, not uncommon, not melodious, not even daughters at all. Some were, in truth, very ordinary men. What they shared with Gwendolen was not charm but a fierce, undisguised determination to have what pleased them, and an entire fearlessness about becoming disagreeable—becoming even dangerous—when they were crossed. Who is so coaxed and waited on, so anxiously soothed, as the unscrupulous creature in a household—especially the male—of whom it is said with a shiver that, if he is not given his way at home, he will go and do worse elsewhere? That fear, like the continual grinding hum of a bad machine, can force even tender hands into obedience.

So it is difficult not to suspect that, even without her beauty and her special place as eldest child, Gwendolen might still have ruled like a queen in exile, simply by virtue of her inborn energy of egoistic desire and her power of inspiring apprehension about what she might say or do. Only—she had the charm as well; and those who feared her were also fond of her, the fear and fondness heightened by that shifting, many-colored quality in her—an iridescence of character, where contrary tendencies played over each other like light over the surface of a changing sea.

For the impossibility of being opposite things “in the same moment” belongs to the clumsy necessities of action, not to the finer, more secret possibilities of feeling. We cannot speak a loyal word and remain meanly silent in the same breath; we cannot kill and not kill at once. But a moment is wide enough for the loyal desire and the mean desire together—for the lash-out of a murderous thought, and the sharp backward stroke of repentance that follows as quickly as a knife drawn back from the board.

Gwendolen’s first weeks in the neighborhood fell in with her uncle’s forecasts as neatly as pastry fits the tin it is baked in. From Brackenshaw Castle to the Firs at Wanchester—where Mr. Quallon the banker kept his table as carefully stocked as his ledgers—doors opened to her with a readiness that was less friendship than appetite: society, like a large household, must be fed with novelty, and a striking young woman was a new dish to set down without obliging the hostess to swallow any guest she disliked.

Besides, to ask for Gwendolen did not mean enduring a tedious train. Mrs. Davilow, her mother, sat by with that quiet, watered-color grace which never clamors for attention yet somehow improves a room, like a vase of pale flowers set where the lamplight warms their scent. And Mr. Gascoigne, the clergyman-uncle, was welcomed for his own sake everywhere—like good bread: never too rich, always wanted.

Among the houses where Gwendolen was not quite liked, yet invited all the same, was Quetcham Hall. One of her earliest summonses was to a large dinner-party there, a sort of general introduction—thirty guests arranged with the deliberation of courses, so that hardly any “visitable” family could be left out without making a gap in the composition. It was an evening of long rooms and many lights: the kind of house where one seems to walk through a succession of air—cool at the first doorway, then warmer, then warmest—each chamber carrying its own bouquet of wax, flowers, and fine linen.

Gwendolen had never made that ceremonial promenade before. She floated forward in white drapery, passing under arch after arch into fuller illumination, and felt with a sudden, exulting certainty that this was her element, as if her life had always been measured by galleries and footmen and the soft friction of silk on polished floors. Any one seeing her for the first time might have believed she had been bred among such lights. Her cousin Anna, who had in fact seen more of it, looked as startled and shy as a rabbit set down in an open, lamp-lit square.

“Who is that with Gascoigne?” said the archdeacon, breaking off a discussion of military manoeuvres as if the sight of her had fired a more immediate curiosity.

And his son—young Clintock, the classical scholar who was already at the stage of proposing “not less elegant than ingenious” alterations in Greek texts—uttered, almost in the same breath from the other side of the room, “By George! who is that girl with the awfully well-set head and jolly figure?”

To any mind disposed to wish every one their fair share, it was vexing to see how Gwendolen eclipsed the other young faces, as a bright flame makes even good candles look dull. The handsome Miss Lawe—daughter of Lady Lawe—seemed suddenly broader, heavier, less alive. And Miss Arrowpoint, unhappily in white too, had the air of a small photograph where one imagines the price was mostly for the skirt.

Miss Arrowpoint, Catherine, was generally liked. She wore her great fortune with an amiable absence of ostentation, and served as a soft screen for her mother’s oddities. It struck more than one observer as unfitting that Gwendolen should look, at first glance, the more important person.

“She is not really so handsome if you come to examine her features,” Mrs. Arrowpoint said later to Mrs. Vulcany with the confidential relish of a woman who prides herself on discernment. “It is a certain style she has—very effective at first—but afterwards she is less agreeable.”

For Gwendolen, who could be keenly alive to absurdity in others, was also kindly disposed toward any one who could make life agreeable to her, and she meant to win Mrs. Arrowpoint by giving her an attention beyond what others were likely to show. But self-confidence has its own clumsiness: it talks down to the person it assumes to be dull. Because Mrs. Arrowpoint’s figure was squat, her voice harsh and parrot-like, her head-dress systematically high, it slipped into Gwendolen’s unreflecting mind that ridicule must go with want of penetration. So she played her little scene of pretty deference without suspecting that every shade of her manner was being tasted and judged, like seasoning in a dish by a palate quick to detect mockery.

After dinner, when the company had broken into drawing-room groups and the air had shifted—less savory now, more sweet with hot wax and crushed flowers—Mrs. Arrowpoint approached her for a tête-à-tête.

“You are fond of books as well as of music, riding, and archery, I hear,” she said. In another woman the remark might have come with a low, melodious kindness; in Mrs. Arrowpoint it arrived on a loud twang. “Catherine will be very glad to have so sympathetic a neighbor.”

“It is I who am fortunate,” Gwendolen answered with graceful readiness, the very tone of a girl giving alms of admiration. “Miss Arrowpoint will teach me what good music is. I shall be entirely a learner. I hear she is a thorough musician.”

“Catherine has certainly had every advantage. We have a first-rate musician in the house now—Herr Klesmer; perhaps you know all his compositions. You must allow me to introduce him to you. You sing, I believe. Catherine plays three instruments, but she does not sing. I hope you will let us hear you. I understand you are an accomplished singer.”

“Oh no!—‘die Kraft ist schwach, allein die Lust ist gross,’ as Mephistopheles says.”

“Ah—you are a student of Goethe. Young ladies are so advanced now. I suppose you have read everything.”

“No, really. I shall be so glad if you will tell me what to read. I have been looking into all the books in the library at Offendene, but there is nothing readable. The leaves all stick together and smell musty.” As she spoke she had, in her imagination, the close scent of long-shut bindings—dust, glue, and time—so unlike the clean, appetizing openness of a newly laid table. “I wish I could write books to amuse myself, as you can! How delightful it must be to write books after one’s own taste instead of reading other people’s! Home-made books must be so nice.”

For an instant Mrs. Arrowpoint’s glance sharpened, as if a knife had been laid on the tongue to test whether it was really sweet. But the last phrase could be taken for girlish simplicity, and Gwendolen looked so candid.

“And why should you not?” Mrs. Arrowpoint returned, encouraged. “You have but to begin as I did. Pen, ink, and paper are at everybody’s command. But I will send you all I have written with pleasure.”

“Thanks. I shall be so glad to read your writings.” Gwendolen went on, with the airy eagerness of a child proposing to taste everything on the sideboard. “Being acquainted with authors must give a peculiar understanding of their books: one would be able to tell then which parts were funny and which serious. I am sure I often laugh in the wrong place.”

She felt, even as she spoke, that she had ventured too far, as if she had sprinkled spice into a dish without measuring it; and she added quickly, “In Shakespeare, you know, and other great writers that we can never see. But I always want to know more than there is in the books.”

“If you are interested in any of my subjects I can lend you many extra sheets in manuscript,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint; and Gwendolen had the disagreeable inward consciousness of a young lady who has declared herself fond of potted sprats and is immediately offered a whole jar. “These are things I dare say I shall publish eventually: several friends have urged me to do so, and one doesn’t like to be obstinate. My Tasso, for example—I could have made it twice the size.”

“I dote on Tasso,” said Gwendolen, promptly.

“Well, you shall have all my papers, if you like. So many, you know, have written about Tasso; but they are all wrong. As to the particular nature of his madness, and his feelings for Leonora, and the real cause of his imprisonment, and the character of Leonora—who, in my opinion, was a cold-hearted woman, else she would have married him in spite of her brother—they are all wrong. I differ from everybody.”

“How very interesting!” said Gwendolen. “I like to differ from everybody. I think it is so stupid to agree. That is the worst of writing your opinions; you make people agree with you.”

Again the hostess’s eye took on that momentary, pricking attention; but Gwendolen’s face wore innocence as easily as her dress.

“I know nothing of Tasso except the Gerusalemme Liberata,” she added in a docile tone, “which we read and learned by heart at school.”

“Ah, his life is more interesting than his poetry. I have constructed the early part of his life as a sort of romance. When one thinks of his father Bernardo, and so on, there is much that must be true.”

“Imagination is often truer than fact,” said Gwendolen decisively—words she could not have interpreted any more than if she had spoken them in Etruscan, yet she uttered them with the ease of a singer striking a note she has heard praised. “I shall be so glad to learn all about Tasso—and his madness especially. I suppose poets are always a little mad.”

“To be sure—‘the poet’s eye in a fine frenzy rolling’; and somebody says of Marlowe, ‘For that fine madness still he did maintain, Which always should possess the poet’s brain.’”

“But it was not always found out, was it?” said Gwendolen, with an ingenuous lift of her brows. “I suppose some of them rolled their eyes in private. Mad people are often very cunning.”

A faint shadow passed over Mrs. Arrowpoint’s face, as if she had heard, under the music of the words, an odd, dissonant note. But at that moment the gentlemen entered, and the small, dangerous duet was broken off.

“Ah, here comes Herr Klesmer,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint, rising; and presently she brought him to Gwendolen and left them together.

Herr Klesmer had the kind of presence that seems to bring its own climate: grand features, brown hair floating in an artist’s fashion, and brown eyes behind spectacles—an unlikely veil for brilliance. His English was fluent and scarcely foreign at all; yet there was in him that mingled origin—German, Sclave, Semite—which made his very accent feel like a history. He had, too, the disarming softness that will sometimes come over genius in the act of wishing to be agreeable to beauty; as if the great instrument had, for a moment, played a lighter tune to please the ear nearest it.

Music began.

Miss Arrowpoint and Herr Klesmer played a four-handed piece on two pianos. To the company in general it proved chiefly that the piece was long; to Gwendolen it proved something sharper—that Catherine, with her neutral, placid face, held the instrument under her fingers with a mastery that made Gwendolen’s own much-praised touch and style look like a pretty household trick.

Afterward every one became anxious to hear Gwendolen sing—especially Mr. Arrowpoint, who was the very pattern of an easy, well-bred host, and of whom no one had anything to report except that he had married Miss Cuttler and imported the best cigars. He led her to the piano with a politeness as smooth as well-aged wine.

Herr Klesmer closed the instrument in readiness and smiled as she approached, then placed himself a few feet away so he could see her face as she sang.

Gwendolen was never nervous. What she undertook she did without trembling, and singing was an enjoyment to her, as natural as drawing breath. Her voice was a moderately powerful soprano—some one had compared it to Jenny Lind’s—her ear was good, and she kept in tune. Ordinary hearers were pleased, and she had been used to applause that came like a warm dish set down promptly, with no suspicion of criticism in the aroma. She had even the advantage—rare and enviable—of looking almost prettier when she sang.

Her chosen song was a favorite aria of Bellini’s, one she felt sure of. She sang it through with full confidence, and when she ended Mr. Arrowpoint murmured “Charming!” while the word ran round the room in friendly echoes.

But Herr Klesmer stood mute—statuesque, if a statue can be imagined in spectacles.

Gwendolen was pressed to keep her seat and repeat the general pleasure. She did not wish to refuse; yet before she committed herself she leaned a little toward Herr Klesmer with a smile of appeal.

“It would be too cruel to a great musician. You cannot like to hear poor amateur singing.”

“No, truly; but that makes nothing,” said Herr Klesmer suddenly, and with the words his English changed. The staccato endings came out—an odious German fashion that had not shown itself before, as if his temper had plucked a hidden string and made it sound. “That makes nothing. It is always acceptable to see you sing.”

The sentence struck like a draught of cold air in a warm room: an unexpected assertion of superiority, all the more startling because it was so calmly spoken. Color rushed into Gwendolen’s face; but she had presence of mind enough not to betray resentment by abrupt movement.

Miss Arrowpoint, who had been near enough to overhear—and also to notice that Herr Klesmer’s open admiration of Gwendolen was too conspicuous to be quite in taste—came to her with tact and kindness.

“Imagine what I have to go through with this professor! He can hardly tolerate anything we English do in music. We can only put up with his severity, and make use of it to find out the worst that can be said of us. It is a little comfort to know that; and one can bear it when every one else is admiring.”

“I should be very much obliged to him for telling me the worst,” said Gwendolen, recovering her poise. “I dare say I have been extremely ill taught, in addition to having no talent—only liking for music.”

It was admirably phrased, considering that such a thought had never visited her before.

“Yes, it is true: you have not been well taught,” Herr Klesmer replied quietly. Woman was dear to him, but music dearer. “Still, you are not quite without gifts. You sing in tune, and you have a pretty fair organ. But you produce your notes badly; and that music which you sing is beneath you. It is a form of melody which expresses a puerile state of culture—a dawdling, canting, see-saw kind of stuff—the passion and thought of people without any breadth of horizon. There is a sort of self-satisfied folly about every phrase of such melody; no cries of deep, mysterious passion—no conflict—no sense of the universal. It makes men small as they listen to it. Sing now something larger. And I shall see.”

“Oh, not now—by-and-by,” said Gwendolen. Her heart sank, as if she had been made to taste, in one mouthful, the difference between a sugared confection and a strong, bitter draught whose after-flavor widens the throat. For a girl who meant to lead, this first collision in her campaign was a shock.

Miss Arrowpoint helped her.

“Yes, by-and-by. I always require half an hour to get up my courage after being criticised by Herr Klesmer. We will ask him to play to us now: he is bound to show us what is good music.”

To be quite safe on that point, Herr Klesmer sat down and played a composition of his own—a fantasia called Freudvoll, Leidvoll, Gedankenvoll. It was as if the piano, that moderate instrument of drawing-rooms, had suddenly been made to speak in a language older than parlors and their pretty decorums: a speech of joy and grief and thought braided together. Under his fingers the ivory and wood seemed to acquire nerves; the strings answered in lingering, quivering phrases, as though compelled to confess what they knew of passion.

Gwendolen, wounded in pride, still had nature enough to feel the power of it. Gradually her inward sob of mortification was turned into an excitement that lifted her for a moment into a reckless indifference about her own performance—or rather into a determination to rise above it by laughing at it as if it belonged to some other girl. Her eyes brightened; color stayed in her cheeks; her tongue grew ready for mischief.

“I wish you would sing to us again, Miss Harleth,” said young Clintock, who had had the good fortune to take her down to dinner and now came up eagerly as soon as the playing ended. “That is the style of music for me. I never can make anything of this tip-top playing. It is like a jar of leeches, where you can never tell either beginnings or endings. I could listen to your singing all day.”

“Yes, we should be glad of something popular now—another song from you would be a relaxation,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint, who had come nearer with a careful politeness.

“That must be because you are in a puerile state of culture, and have no breadth of horizon,” Gwendolen said, turning her bright smile up to Clintock and taking no notice of Mrs. Arrowpoint. “I have just learned that. I have been taught how bad my taste is, and am feeling growing pains. They are never pleasant.”

Mrs. Arrowpoint was not insensible to the rudeness—she heard it as plainly as a sour note sounding under a chord—but she merely said, “Well, we will not press anything disagreeably.” Conversation in the room began to bubble up as if a lid had been lifted; guests moved to seek one another; and she stayed seated with the relief of a hostess suddenly unneeded.

“I am glad you like this neighborhood,” Clintock went on, pleased with his position before Gwendolen.

“Exceedingly. There seems to be a little of everything and not much of anything.”

“That is rather equivocal praise.”

“Not with me. I like a little of everything; a little absurdity, for example, is very amusing. I am thankful for a few queer people; but much of them is a bore.”

Mrs. Arrowpoint, hearing, found her earlier doubt revive: this girl’s tone had changed as easily as a mask is shifted, and the suspicion of a satirical doubleness returned like a remembered bad taste.

“I think there should be more croquet, for one thing,” said Clintock. “I am usually away, but if I were more here I should go in for a croquet club. You are one of the archers, I think. But depend upon it croquet is the game of the future. It wants writing up, though. One of our best men has written a poem on it, in four cantos—as good as Pope. I want him to publish it—You never read anything better.”

“I shall study croquet to-morrow,” said Gwendolen. “I shall take to it instead of singing.”

“No, no, not that; but do take to croquet. I will send you Jenning’s poem if you like. I have a manuscript copy.”

“Is he a great friend of yours?”

“Well—rather.”

“Oh, if he is only rather, I think I will decline. Or, if you send it to me, will you promise not to catechise me upon it and ask me which part I like best? Because it is not so easy to know a poem without reading it as to know a sermon without listening.”

“Decidedly,” Mrs. Arrowpoint said to herself, “this girl is double and satirical. I shall be on my guard against her.”

Yet, guarded or not, the Arrowpoints continued to show Gwendolen polite attentions afterward—not merely because invitations and visits have larger foundations than personal liking, but because the little trying scene at the piano had stirred in Miss Arrowpoint a gentle solicitude.
