Catherine, who managed the invitations and calls while her mother was occupied elsewhere, could not help being touched by the sight of a girl so sure of her charms meeting, for once, a judgment that did not flatter—and by the strange, sharp music of Herr Klesmer’s truth sounding through a room trained to softer harmonies.

That high-handed judgment from Herr Klesmer had left Gwendolen with a bruise she could not show. She would not have owned—not even to the looking-glass—that she envied Miss Arrowpoint for anything so unromantic as disciplined practice: the slow, daily surrender to scales, the sure ear trained by patient correction, the confidence that comes from having learned a language of sound thoroughly enough to dispute a master’s taste. Yet it stung her that this pale, slight young woman—no one’s notion of a triumph to look at, with a sallow skin and small, tidy features that seemed made for economy rather than conquest—should possess an authority that could not be laughed away: a certainty in music, a fineness of choice, a quiet refusal to be bullied into admiration. And the worst cruelty was that it never declared itself; it stayed wrapped in perfect kindness, as if superiority could afford to be gentle.

Gwendolen’s mind, when it was hurt, did not like to sit still with the hurt. She pushed it aside as one brushes crumbs from a dress—lightly, decisively, without examining what it means to be eating on the wrong occasion. Herr Klesmer, that sudden magician who had widened her horizon with a word, was not always there; his coming and going between London and Quetcham itself became a sort of promise. A man who moved could be intercepted. A judgment that had once been severe might, with the right performance, be lured into admiration.

Besides, her singing was applauded everywhere the neighborhood had any notion of brilliance—at Brackenshaw, at the Firs, at the little assemblies where tea steamed and candles made every cheek look younger. Praise was warm, immediate, and—she preferred to think—trustworthy. She was not one of those thirsting spirits who must have a perfection no one asks of them; she could live on approval as comfortably as on well-made broth, without demanding that it be clarified to the last impurity.

And yet, for all her pride in being unlike the “ordinary young ladies,” her rebellion had no daring map. It was a hunger for supremacy that wore the ornaments of breeding: it could not consent to look like the sordid struggle for income, could not admit itself as mere appetite. She mocked “theoretical women” and would have separated herself with laughter from anything that smelled of reform; still, she resented the wirework of family obligation as if she had built a whole philosophy against it. Her dreams were the dreams of genteel romance—souls in journals, power in vague phrases, a satin shoe wandering into a swamp and making the tragedy doubly refined.

Offendene, in that first winter, began to feel like a handsome backdrop waiting for an event that would not arrive. She knew, with a sharp clarity, what she did not want: the smooth, predictable days of other girls. What she could not find was the door into a different life, or the particular act that would feel like freedom instead of mere caprice. The neighborhood, on the whole, was too well behaved to supply a plot.

After the earliest invitations had exhausted their small stock of novelty, she returned from these little social raids with a few bright arrows of satire—some of which had already offended Mrs. Arrowpoint—and then filled the long, wet days with devices so girlish that they were almost pathetic in their ingenuity. Her strongest assertion of personal empire was to neglect Alice’s lessons—on the principle that Alice might achieve distinction by not knowing what everyone else knew—and to set Miss Merry, along with the maid who attended “all the ladies,” to work with her on a wardrobe of dramatic costumes. There were Greek draperies, Oriental folds, odd composite inventions that borrowed from everywhere without submitting to any one law; there was the smell of starched linen warmed near the fire, of lavender tucked into drawers, of paste and paint, of candle-grease and the faint metallic tang from pins held between lips. The house became a little workshop where domestic routine—tea-trays, sewing-baskets, the crackle of logs—was threaded through with the stagey labor of hemming and fastening, as if the making of an illusion were as ordinary as mending.

Gwendolen, who had never acted beyond posing in school tableaux, was certain she could act well; certainty rose in her like yeast without requiring proof. She had seen the Théâtre Français once or twice, had heard her mother speak of Rachel, and at times her mind played with the thought of becoming an actress—because the world would be compelled to look. She believed herself more beautiful than that thin Jewess; beauty, in her private creed, was a kind of destiny.

One afternoon, when rain was drawing grey lines down the window and the room smelled of wool drying near the hearth, she stood in her Greek dress before Anna and declaimed scraps with a tragic intention that made the common furniture look like properties.

“Do I look as well as Rachel, mamma?” she asked, turning her arms a little, letting the lamplight skim them as if skin were a material to be displayed like satin.

“You have better arms than Rachel,” Mrs. Davilow said, lazily kind. “Your arms would do for anything, Gwen. But your voice is not so tragic as hers; it is not so deep.”

“I can make it deeper, if I like,” said Gwendolen, as if voice were merely a ribbon to be chosen. Then, with the swift obstinacy of a girl arranging the world to her taste, she added, “I think a higher voice is more tragic. It is more feminine; and the more feminine a woman is, the more tragic it seems when she does desperate actions.”

“There may be something in that,” Mrs. Davilow returned, half amused, half indifferent. “But I don’t know what good there is in making one’s blood creep. And if there is anything horrible to be done, I should like it to be left to the men.”

“Oh, mamma, you are so dreadfully prosaic! As if all the great poetic criminals were not women! I think the men are poor cautious creatures.”

“Well, dear—and you, who are afraid to be alone in the night—I don’t think you would be very bold in crime, thank God.”

“I am not talking about reality, mamma,” Gwendolen said, impatient, as if reality were an ill-bred intruder. And when her mother was called out, she turned instantly to Anna, seizing the moment like a cook snatching the exact second to lift a soufflé before it falls.

“Anna, do ask my uncle to let us get up some charades at the rectory. Mr. Middleton and Warham could act with us—just for practice. Mamma says it will not do to have Mr. Middleton consulting and rehearsing here. He is a stick, but we could give him suitable parts. Do ask, or else I will.”

“Oh, not till Rex comes,” Anna pleaded, brightening. “He is so clever, and such a dear old thing, and he will act Napoleon looking over the sea. He looks just like Napoleon. Rex can do anything.”

“I don’t in the least believe in your Rex, Anna,” Gwendolen laughed, pinching at Anna’s worship with a light cruelty. “He will turn out to be like those wretched blue and yellow water-colors of his which you hang up in your bedroom and adore.”

“Very well, you will see,” Anna said stoutly. “It is not that I know what is clever, but he has got a scholarship already, and papa says he will get a fellowship, and nobody is better at games. He is cleverer than Mr. Middleton—and everybody but you call Mr. Middleton clever.”

“So he may be—in a dark-lantern sort of way. But he is a stick. If he had to say, ‘Perdition catch my soul, but I do love her,’ he would say it in just the same tone as, ‘Here endeth the second lesson.’”

“Oh, Gwendolen!” Anna cried, shocked by the way Gwen’s irreverence threw sacred and profane into the same pan. “And it is very unkind of you to speak so of him, for he admires you very much. I heard Warham say one day to mamma, ‘Middleton is regularly spooney upon Gwendolen.’ She was very angry with him; but I know what it means. It is what they say at college for being in love.”

“How can I help it?” said Gwendolen, with contempt that covered a flicker of triumph. “Perdition catch my soul if I love him.”

“No, of course; papa, I think, would not wish it. And he is to go away soon. But it makes me sorry when you ridicule him.”

“What shall you do to me when I ridicule Rex?” Gwendolen said, wickedly, tasting the power of making Anna tremble.

“Now, Gwendolen, dear, you will not?” Anna’s eyes filled. “I could not bear it. But there really is nothing in him to ridicule. Only you may find out things. For no one ever thought of laughing at Mr. Middleton before you. Every one said he was nice-looking, and his manners perfect. I am sure I have always been frightened at him because of his learning and his square-cut coat, and his being a nephew of the bishop’s, and all that. But you will not ridicule Rex—promise me.”

The beseeching look, so simple and so loyal, touched Gwendolen like a soft hand on a bruise.

“You are a dear little coz,” she said, lifting Anna’s chin with thumb and forefinger. “I don’t ever want to do anything that will vex you. Especially if Rex is to make everything come off—charades and everything.”

When Rex came at last, he brought an immediate stir as fresh as opening a window onto fields after too many days of indoor air. Offendene and the rectory felt suddenly peopled; plans had a partner. Rex was open-hearted, handsome in the same family fashion as his father and Anna—only softer than the one and larger than the other—healthy as if he had been made out of sunlight and good appetite. Life pleased him so naturally that vice lay outside his path like some foul ditch he had no need to step into; “what some fellows did” seemed to him “stupid stuff,” scarcely worth noticing.

His affection for Anna was full and easy; but he had never known a stronger love than the one that took him, almost at once, for Gwendolen. Within a fortnight it had settled into him like a fate. He did not so much observe her as receive her: the sound of her voice, the sway of her movement, the very air of the room shifting when she entered—his senses were her servants. The back of his head seemed enough to tell him whether she was near. He could not imagine obstacles; his love itself felt like a guarantee of hers. It never occurred to him that perfection might demand a grand match; he was without conceit except that small necessary firmness that lets a man call his own life real. He took Gwendolen’s beauty as part of the world’s goodness, as if it were as natural as ripening fruit.

She, for her part, liked him. She sang and played when he wished—music thickening the rooms like warm scent from a kitchen where something sweet is baking—she rode with him willingly, though his borrowed horses were sometimes comical, and she was ready for any sport that amused him. She showed the proper appreciation of Anna. No mark of sympathy seemed absent. And Rex, poor boy, read every kindness as devotion.

They were continually together, more often at Offendene where there was a freer reign—meaning, chiefly, that Gwendolen’s wishes took the place of law. The charades were arranged as she meant, and rehearsals began; even little scenes outside the planned ones occurred, in which Gwendolen’s acting was quicker than her design.

Mrs. Davilow, seeing no great objection now that Rex was there, allowed even Mr. Middleton to be asked and pressed into service. Warham, who was preparing for India under a Wanchester coach, had little time; he moved about as if packed with facts and yet starving for any joy not required by the coming examination, which threatened to prove that the welfare of the Empire depended on the ability to quote Browne’s _Pastorals_ on demand. Mr. Middleton, persuaded to take grave parts, did them well chiefly by not attempting to be amusing. Gwendolen flattered him on his enviable immobility of countenance, and he, who had at first felt a jealous pinch at her easy comradeship with Rex, began to soothe himself with the notion that cousinly familiarity excluded serious passion. Indeed, her more formal manner with himself sometimes seemed like favor; he felt encouraged to think he might speak before leaving Pennicote, though he had meant to wait until his position was surer.

Gwendolen knew, perfectly, that this pale-whiskered curate in his square collar adored her; she felt only that she had no objection to being adored. She looked at him with calm mercilessness and gave him mild hopes by avoiding any direct dramatic contact—as if distance were meaning. For meanings, after all, depend on who translates them, and in what dialect of desire.

If anyone had reasoned beforehand, they might have concluded that a young man with Anglican leanings—scrupulous about small sacrednesses, seldom laughing except from politeness, shrinking from naked names as if they were indecent—would not choose a bride so daring in ridicule, so little shaped into the special softness expected in a clergyman’s wife. Or they might have thought that a young man trained by theological reading would foresee his taste would not suit a restless girl like Miss Harleth. But love, when it comes, does not ask permission from other people’s logic.

Rex, absorbed, would have been sorry for Middleton if he had known of the curate’s inward conflict; but Rex saw nothing except what belonged to Gwendolen. His passion made the whole household’s soundscape—the clink of teacups, the rustle of scripts, the piano’s scales, laughter in the hall—feel like accompaniment to one central melody: her presence. And, sensitive though he was to noise and rhythm in the ordinary way of the young, he had no defense against the sharper noises that sometimes lacerate the mind: a slammed door, an unexpected cry, a chord struck too hard. Those sounds, which later would matter, were not yet part of his foresight.

At last, after much rehearsal, it was decided that a select party should be invited to Offendene. The actors were pleased with themselves; the audience would be chosen to be indulgent. Anna surprised everyone by the neatness of her playing; there was something almost sly in how well she managed her small parts, as if her simplicity had been listening and storing away. Mr. Middleton answered perfectly by remaining solemn.

The chief delay had been caused by Gwendolen’s insistence on appearing in her Greek dress. She could find no charade-word—waking or dreaming—that would justify her favorite costume and its statuesque possibility. Racine was no use; the others could not declaim French verse, and improvised speeches would drop the scene into burlesque. Besides, Mr. Gascoigne prohibited acting scenes from plays. He usually protested against the idea that what was fit amusement for others was unfit for a clergyman; but in this matter he would not step beyond the decorum of that part of Wessex. Charades in his sister-in-law’s house were one thing; private theatricals, fully so called, were another.

Since everyone wished to satisfy Gwendolen, Rex proposed a tableau at the end, where her “majesty” could be presented without speech to mar it. This delighted her; only the choice remained.

“Something pleasant, children, I beseech you,” Mrs. Davilow said. “I can’t have any Greek wickedness.”

“It is no worse than Christian wickedness, mamma,” said Gwendolen, remembering her earlier talk of poetic criminals.

“And less scandalous,” Rex added. “One thinks of it as all gone by and done with. What do you say to Briseis being led away? I would be Achilles, and you would be looking round at me—after the print we have at the rectory.”

“That would be a good attitude for me,” Gwendolen said, accepting the thought of her own posture as the primary argument. But then, later, she rejected it. “No. It will not do. There must be three men in proper costume, else it will be ridiculous.”

“I have it,” Rex said after a pause. “Hermione as the statue in _The Winter’s Tale_. I will be Leontes, and Miss Merry Paulina, one on each side. Our dress won’t signify,” he added, laughing; “it will be more Shakespearian and romantic if Leontes looks like Napoleon, and Paulina like a modern spinster.”

Hermione was chosen; everyone agreed that age did not matter. But Gwendolen insisted there should be just enough acting to introduce the moment: the cue, the music, her stepping down and advancing. Leontes, instead of embracing her, was to kneel and kiss the hem of her garment, and then the curtain would fall. The antechamber with folding doors made an admirable stage; the whole household, with Jarrett the village carpenter added like another instrument to the orchestra of labor, was absorbed in preparations. Paint, wax, wood, cloth—all the homely materials took on that peculiar excitement of becoming something else. Wax-lights were tested and set; their smell—honeyed and faintly animal—mixed with the sharper odor of tallow and the dust disturbed by moving furniture. Boards creaked under hurried feet; someone’s hammer tapped; the piano was opened and shut. The house, which on other days held its silence like a well-bred person, now hummed with purposeful sound.

Gwendolen had a special exultation, for she knew Herr Klesmer was again at Quetcham, and she had made sure to include him among the invited. His presence would be the true audience: not the friendly faces that applauded out of habit, but the one ear she feared and wanted.

Klesmer came. He was in one of his quiet moods, placid and mostly silent, replying with benignant syllables more or less articulate, as if he were meekly bearing a cross in a world overgrown with amateurs—or as if, being a lion among mice, he must take care where he set his paws.

The evening went smoothly—so smoothly that the small accidental things seemed part of the plan, as they often do when people want to believe in success. The charades were received with polite laughter; Anna was praised; Mr. Middleton managed his gravity. The air of the room thickened with warmth from bodies and lamps; the rustle of dresses and whispering of little comments made a soft, continuous undertone. And then the tableau of Hermione came, striking in its stillness after the earlier movement. It answered perfectly. A murmur of applause had begun and was gradually suppressed as Leontes gave permission that Paulina should exercise her utmost art and make the statue move.

Hermione—Gwendolen—stood with her arm resting on a pillar, elevated by about six inches, chosen with care so that her foot and instep would show when she advanced and descended. The wax-lights, placed to flatter her, made her white drapery glow; her hair and eyes looked darker by contrast. She waited for the cue with a triumphant inward steadiness.

“Music, awake her, strike!” said Paulina—Mrs. Davilow, who by special entreaty had consented, wrapped in a white burnous and hood, looking like a gentle specter.

Herr Klesmer, seated at the piano, struck a thunderous chord.

In that same instant—before Hermione had put forth her foot—the movable panel on a line with the piano flew open to the right, opposite the stage, and revealed, in the pale definiteness of the candlelight, a picture: a dead face, and a fleeing figure. The effect was like a wound suddenly uncovered. A startled movement ran through the company; eyes turned toward the opening.

But in the act of turning, all eyes were jerked back by a piercing cry from Gwendolen.

She had not changed her attitude; only her expression had transformed, and the transformation was terrifying in its terror. She looked like a statue into which a soul of Fear had entered: lips gone pallid and parted, eyes—usually narrowed under long lashes—dilated and fixed, as if the sight before her had broken some inner barrier. Her mother, less surprised than alarmed, rushed toward her; Rex, too, was at her side instantly.

Mrs. Davilow’s touch had the effect of an electric shock. Gwendolen dropped to her knees and covered her face with her hands. Her whole body trembled, but no sound came after that first cry. Even in that collapse there was self-consciousness; she seemed to be trying to control the signs of what had mastered her. Presently she allowed herself to be raised, and she was led away while the company, relieved to have something else to do with their fear, began to explain.

“A magnificent bit of plastik that!” Klesmer said to Miss Arrowpoint, his voice almost approving, as if the shock were part of art.

A quick fire of undertoned question and answer ran round, like crackling brushwood.

“Was it part of the play?”

“Oh, no—surely not. Miss Harleth was too much affected. A sensitive creature!”

“Dear me! I was not aware there was a painting behind that panel; were you?”

“No; how should I? Some eccentricity in one of the Earl’s family long ago, I suppose.”

“How very painful! Pray shut it up.”

“Was the door locked? It is very mysterious. It must be the spirits.”

“But there is no medium present.”

“How do you know that? We must conclude that there is, when such things happen.”

“Oh—the door was not locked; it was probably the sudden vibration from the piano that sent it open.”

This last conclusion came from Mr. Gascoigne, who asked Miss Merry, if possible, to fetch the key. His readiness to explain was thought by Mrs. Vulcany unbecomingly rational for a clergyman; she observed in an undertone that Mr. Gascoigne was always a little too worldly for her taste. But the key was produced. The rector turned it in the lock with an emphasis that seemed to say, “it will not fly open again,” and he put the key in his pocket as a security.

The panel was shut; the room’s ordinary noises—small laughs, chair-legs shifting, the soft tap of a fan against fingers—returned cautiously, as if testing whether the air was safe again.

Before long Gwendolen reappeared. She showed her usual spirits with a visible effort, determined to ignore, as far as she could, the terrible interruption she had made in her own Hermione. Her cheeks had color again; her mouth curved; she spoke as if nothing had happened. But there was a strained brightness in it, like music played a little too fast to outrun a memory.

When Klesmer said to her, “We have to thank you for devising a perfect climax: you could not have chosen a finer bit of plastik,” she flushed with pleasure. It was easier to accept his words as belief than to face them as the delicate feigning they were. He had divined that her betrayal into fear must be mortifying to her, and he offered her an escape: he would treat it as acting. Gwendolen, hungry for his admiration, cherished the idea that now he was struck with her talent as well as her beauty, and the uneasiness his earlier criticism had planted in her was half turned to complacency.

But too many knew what had been rehearsed and what had not. No one besides Klesmer took the trouble to soothe her imagined humiliation. The general instinct was to let the incident drop—like a dish that has spilled, wiped away quickly so the meal may go on, while the stain remains in the mind long after the cloth looks clean.

The first warning of the snow that would come was no more than a whitening in the far air—like breath on glass—making the blue beyond look cleaner by contrast. In the rectory the morning sounded as it always did before the house fully woke: the low clink of a spoon against a cup in the nursery, the soft rasp of a coal being coaxed into flame, the brief hush that followed when someone opened an outer door and the cold came in like a living thing. Nothing in those familiar noises told of the private storm that had already begun in two young hearts.

Anna knew Rex’s secret, though for the first time in all their brother-and-sister history he had never once spoken it aloud to her. He had only carried it with a careless confidence, as if she must know what he knew because she had always known him. And for the first time, too, Anna could not say the thing that pressed on her continually, because to speak it would be to stab him with it.

She admired her cousin with the docile reverence that had been bred into her. She would have said, sincerely, “Gwendolen is always very good to me,” and thought it natural that she should be entirely under Gwendolen’s law. Yet she looked at her with a fear she could not explain, as one watches a splendid creature whose beauty is undeniable and whose hunger is unreadable—as if Gwendolen might, without meaning to be cruel, swallow up whatever small, tender things belonged to Anna’s keeping. And now a heavier conviction sat in her: Gwendolen would never care for Rex.

It was not that Anna had any sharp judgment; it was rather that she had a sense for what was fed and what was starved. She watched how certain words—words that meant reverence and home and steady affection—fell dead when they touched Gwendolen, like good seed cast on stone. Gwendolen’s mind always ran toward something extraordinary, as if ordinary love were a dish too plainly seasoned for her palate. And poor Rex—Papa would be angry if he knew. And Rex, of course, was too young to be in love in that grown way; it ought to have been years off; Anna had imagined herself his housekeeper for ever so long, ordering his shirts and keeping his keys, as if that were her marriage. But what heart could refuse him? In her dread of his pain she began, for the first time, to feel a faint, ashamed dislike of the cousin who charmed them all.

To Rex and Anna those weeks at Pennicote had seemed to throb with a life that must be visible to everyone; and yet the elders—over their newspapers, over the rustle of the Guardian and the Clerical Gazette—were as blind to it as they were to the busy arguments of ants in a gravel-walk. The young ones acted out their drama in pantomime, utterly clear to themselves, and missed by those who had learned to look past what did not threaten the day’s propriety.

It was on a gray morning, after Mr. Gascoigne had driven off to the sessions with Mrs. Gascoigne, that Anna noticed Rex coming down the stairs in his antigropelos—his nearest approach to hunting finery—and with that air of purposeful ease which in him always meant a plan that was not to be discussed.

“Where are you going, Rex?” she said, and the question came out too quickly, as if it had been waiting behind her teeth.

“Going to see the hounds throw off at the Three Barns.”

Anna’s heart gave a little thud, as if the house itself had knocked.

“Are you going to take Gwendolen?” she asked, timidly, as though she were asking whether he meant to take fire into the hayloft.

“She told you, did she?”

“No,” said Anna, and her cheeks warmed. “But I thought—Does papa know you are going?”

“Not that I am aware of. I don’t suppose he would trouble himself about the matter.”

“You are going to use his horse?”

“He knows I do that whenever I can.”

Anna’s mind filled with pictures she could not bear—of flying hooves, of hedges, of sudden falls, of her father’s face.

“Don’t let Gwendolen ride after the hounds, Rex,” she said, and fear sharpened her voice into something like second sight.

Rex smiled—half amused, half provoked. “Why not?”

“Papa and mamma and aunt Davilow all wish her not to. They think it is not right for her.”

“Why should you suppose she is going to do what is not right?”

“Gwendolen minds nobody sometimes,” Anna said, gaining boldness from a surge of anger.

“Then she would not mind me,” Rex returned, perversely turning her distress into play.

“Oh, Rex, I cannot bear it.” Her throat tightened; the words came out with a sob. “You will make yourself very unhappy.” And then she cried outright, the child’s helpless crying that seems all the more unreasonable because it is true.

“Nannie, Nannie—what on earth is the matter with you?” Rex said, impatient because he was already delayed—hat on, whip in hand, the whole of him leaning toward the door.

“She will not care for you one bit—I know she never will!” Anna whispered, brokenly. “I know she never will.”

A flush sprang up in Rex’s face, and he turned away as if her words had been a slap he would not acknowledge. He went out through the hall door quickly, leaving Anna with the sick feeling of having been disagreeable—and still useless.

As he rode, her sentence clung to him with that peculiar unpleasantness which any prophecy of ill fortune has, even when one laughs at it. Yet he explained it away as only Anna’s tenderness, her frightened exaggeration. And then he was sorry he had left her so. But the stronger movement in him was a stubborn belief in the opposite—an urgent need to prove her wrong. His certainty had just enough kinship to doubt to drive him toward confession; a secure man can wait, but a man with a tremor in him wants an answer.

Gwendolen was already mounted and riding up and down the avenue when Rex appeared at the gate. She had, with her usual foresight against inconvenience, kept a groom ready behind her so that she need not be made ridiculous by waiting. But Rex came in time; the groom was dismissed; and they rode off together with the delicious lightness of being unchaperoned, as if the whole world were a lane made for them alone.

She was in her highest spirits, and Rex, looking at her, felt that she had never before been so entirely—herself. Her riding dress, compact and severe, made a frame for the long white throat and the proud line from cheek to chin; everything in her seemed finished and decisive, as if nature had not merely formed her but signed her. Rex could not conceive a more perfect girl. And to a young lover the good, the true, and the beautiful appear not as separate virtues to be weighed, but as one substance shining in the beloved.

It was a mild winter morning—January in name, but not in cruelty. The sky was gray, not menacing but calm, and the landscape beneath it had that subdued richness which makes even bareness look nourished: grass borders damp and green, hedgerows hung with red berries, elms standing purple in their leafless strength, furrows of earth as brown as crust. Their horses’ hooves rang a musical chime along the road, and the sound of it—clean, hollow, rhythmic—seemed to steady the air, so that even their laughter had a place to rest. In that acoustical comfort, the mind grows more daring; the young feel as if happiness were a natural law.

Gwendolen laughed at Rex’s equipment—for he was no dandy, and his antigropelos and practical air made him look as if he had ridden out of a schoolbook illustration. Rex loved her laughter; it was like bright water poured over him. The freshness of the morning mingled with the freshness of their youth; each glance, each careless word, seemed to bubble up without effort. It was morning for them, within and without.

“Anna had got it into her head that you would want to ride after the hounds this morning,” Rex said at last, because Anna’s frightened prophecy made this remark feel dangerously close to the real thing he wanted to say.

“Did she?” Gwendolen answered, laughing. “What a little clairvoyant she is!”

“Shall you?” Rex asked, not quite believing she would do what everyone had objected to, trusting in her having good reasons for whatever she chose.

“I don’t know. I can’t tell what I shall do till I get there. Clairvoyants are often wrong: they foresee what is likely. I am not fond of what is likely: it is always dull. I do what is unlikely.”

“Ah—there you tell me a secret,” Rex said, eager, trying to turn her banter toward the point where his heart was waiting. “When once I knew what people in general would be likely to do, I should know you would do the opposite. So you would have come round to a likelihood of your own sort. I shall be able to calculate on you. You couldn’t surprise me.”

“Yes, I could. I should turn round and do what was likely for people in general,” she replied, her laugh like bells in clear air.

“You see you can’t escape some sort of likelihood. And contradictoriness makes the strongest likelihood of all. You must give up a plan.”

“No, I shall not. My plan is to do what pleases me.”

In another girl the words might have sounded hard, like a plate set down sharply. But her head and neck had that sovereign poise which made audacity seem only a kind of grace. Rex, who was hungry for any entrance into her real feeling, only smiled, anxious to lead her on.

“Can you manage to feel only what pleases you?” he asked.

“Of course not; that comes from what other people do. But if the world were pleasanter, one would only feel what was pleasant. Girls’ lives are so stupid: they never do what they like.”

“I thought that was more the case of the men,” Rex said, honestly. “They are forced to do hard things, and are often dreadfully bored—and knocked to pieces too. And then, if we love a girl very dearly, we want to do as she likes—so after all you have your own way.”

“I don’t believe it. I never saw a married woman who had her own way.”

“What should you like to do?” Rex asked, with real anxiety under his simplicity, as if the answer might show him the path to her happiness.

“Oh, I don’t know—go to the North Pole, or ride steeple-chases, or go to be a queen in the East like Lady Hester Stanhope,” Gwendolen said, lightly. The words were born on her lips; deeper reasons, if they existed, did not come with them.

“You don’t mean you would never be married?”

“No; I didn’t say that. Only when I married, I should not do as other women do.”

“You might do just as you liked if you married a man who loved you more dearly than anything else in the world,” Rex said, poor youth, stumbling into a lesson he had never been taught and yet was ready to recite with his life. “I know one who does.”

“Don’t talk of Mr. Middleton, for heaven’s sake,” she said hastily, and a quick blush spread over her face and neck like a sudden warmth under pale skin. “That is Anna’s chant. I hear the hounds. Let us go on.”

She put her chestnut into a canter. The sound changed at once: the brisker beat of hooves, the faint creak of leather, the breath of the horse coming warmer into the cold air. Rex had no choice but to follow, and yet he felt encouraged. That blush—was it annoyance, was it shame, was it something nearer to what he longed for? He took it as hope.

Gwendolen knew perfectly well that Rex loved her. But love, to her, was as yet a pretty story that filled the gaps in time; she had never suffered it, never been scorched by it, never had her pride made helpless by it. She wanted the small romance of Rex’s devotion to be a pleasant ornament to his stay at Pennicote, and she wished to avoid any explanation that would end it too soon. Besides, she had an almost physical repulsion to being directly made love to. She liked adoration as she liked music heard from a little distance—delightful, but not to be pressed close against her skin. There was, in her, a fierce maiden reserve that could turn suddenly into resistance.

All other thoughts were soon swept away for her by the scene at the Three Barns. Here the countryside gathered into color and sound: horses stamping, bits clinking, men’s voices calling across one another, and beneath it all the restless, thrilling undercurrent of the hounds—an eager, breathing music that seemed to make the ground itself impatient. It was the kind of soundscape that intoxicates: it draws the blood forward and makes caution feel like a dull custom. Even the air had a different smell—damp earth, leather warmed by bodies, a faint animal tang, and, somewhere, the sharp sweetness of crushed hedge leaves.

Several gentlemen of the hunt knew Gwendolen, and she exchanged greetings easily, with that air of belonging to any scene she entered. Rex could not get another word with her. The field took possession of her, and it did so with a strength not due to habit—for she had never yet ridden after the hounds. She had only said she wished to, and had been forbidden. Her mother dreaded danger; her uncle declared the violent exercise unseemly in a woman, and insisted that whatever might be done elsewhere, no lady of good position followed the Wessex hunt. No one but Mrs. Gadsby, the yeomanry captain’s wife—who had been a kitchenmaid, and still spoke like one.

That last argument had weighed with Gwendolen more than the first two. She was torn between the desire to assert her freedom and the horror of being classed with Mrs. Gadsby. Yet today none of the unexceptionable women were present to abstain and so make abstaining the right thing, and Mrs. Gadsby herself was not visible to render following vulgar. So the check of social sound—those little murmurs and pauses by which a neighborhood governs itself—was absent. In that lack of restraining voices, the raw, animal stimulus of the hounds and horses rose unchecked.

“Glad to see you here this fine morning, Miss Harleth,” said Lord Brackenshaw, a middle-aged peer with aristocratic seediness in stained pink, as if grandeur had been worn too often without careful brushing. His manner was easy, as if the threatened deluge would be only a change of weather. “We shall have a first-rate run. A pity you didn’t go with us. Have you ever tried your little chestnut at a ditch? you wouldn’t be afraid, eh?”

“Not the least in the world,” said Gwendolen—truthfully, for fear did not readily enter her in action or companionship. “I have often taken him at some rails and a ditch too, near—”

“Ah, by Jove!” said his lordship, in that quiet notation with which men break off talk when something more exciting begins; and as he reined away, Rex was bringing up his sober mount to Gwendolen’s side when—suddenly—the hounds gave tongue.

It was as if the world had been struck like a bell. The whole field moved at once. No one looked to see who followed. The roar and yelp, the cries of men, the thunder of hooves—sound became command. Gwendolen went with everything, borne by the rush, and Rex without a second thought went too. Could he let her go alone? Under other circumstances he would have enjoyed the run, but now he was perturbed—the confession pressing on him and being checked again and again, like breath held under water. And he was on his father’s gray nag, a good horse enough in his way but of sober years and ecclesiastical habits, a creature bred for decent roads and measured paces, not for flying recklessness.

Gwendolen on her spirited chestnut was up with the best and felt as secure as an immortal, because at her core was the confidence that ill luck did not happen to her. Indeed, she did not think of risk at all—certainly not of risk for Rex. If she had thought of him, she might have laughed at the image of him searching for gates, a fine lithe youth with the heart of a beagle trapped, as if by a spell, on a stiff clerical hackney. But Gwendolen was apt to think more of those who saw her than of those she could not see; and soon Rex was so far behind that even if she had looked, she would not have found him.

For in the search for a gate along a lane lately mended—earth still raw where it had been packed and trodden—Primrose stumbled. There was a moment of sickening tilt, the sudden violent give of a body losing its certainty, then the crack of knees against ground. The horse went down. Rex, pitched forward, was thrown over Primrose’s head.

Pain returned to him as sensation, like an ugly guest arriving late but insisting on being noticed. His shoulder burned and sickened; the world rang in his ears with a dull, far-off roar, as if the hunt were happening inside a shell.

A blacksmith’s son, Joel Dagge, who followed the hounds on foot—one of those rear-guard hunters whose very method some frivolous minds judged immoral—had been naturally in the rear and saw Rex go down. He ran up and was of immediate use in that particular way which belongs to people whose knowledge is not ornamental but fitted to emergencies. He knew what was wrong with the horse, how far they were from the nearest public-house, and exactly how to talk about a dislocated shoulder as if it were no more than a button off a coat.

He looked Rex over with the brisk pity of a practised witness.

“Lord, sir, let me shove it in again for you! I’s seen Nash, the bone-setter, do it, and done it myself for our little Sally twice over. It’s all one and the same, shoulders is. If you’ll trusten to me and tighten your mind up a bit, I’ll do it for you in no time.”

“Come then, old fellow,” Rex said, because he could tighten his mind better than he could keep his seat.

Joel set his hands with the confident precision of someone who has watched a thing done and repeated it until it became his own craft. The pain was sharp enough to whiten Rex’s face to the lips; his breath drew in with a thin, involuntary sound. He did not cry out, but his eyes filled in spite of him, and he hated himself for it.

“Ah, sir, you aren’t used to it—that’s how it is,” Joel observed, not unkindly. “I’s see lots and lots o’ joints out. I see a man with his eye pushed out once—that was a rum go as ever I see. You can’t have a bit o’ fun wi’out such sort o’ things. But it went in again. I’s swallowed three teeth mysen, as sure as I’m alive. Now, sirrey”—this to Primrose—“come alonk—you musn’t make believe as you can’t.”

Joel helped Rex as quickly as possible toward home. There was no other course, for Primrose was injured and Rex battered. Yet all the while Rex’s mind was not on himself but on Gwendolen, on the possibility—unthinkable—that she too might have fallen. That misery was worse than his bruises, worse even than the dread of his father’s anger. He tried to comfort himself with the thought that she rode well, that there would be men around her eager to take care of her, that some acquaintance would see her home. Still the uncertainty gnawed like a bad taste that will not be rinsed away.

Mr. Gascoigne was already back, writing letters in his study, when the interruption came: poor Rex entering with a face not less handsome for its pallor and distress. Rex was, secretly, the favorite son and looked like a young portrait of his father; but Mr. Gascoigne never allowed his feeling to soften his rule—rather he was stricter, as if he must guard himself against indulgence.

He did not at first lay down his pen.

“What is the matter?” he asked, hastily.

“I’m very sorry, sir; Primrose has fallen down and broken his knees.”

“Where have you been with him?” Mr. Gascoigne said, and though he rarely gave way to temper, the severity came like an edge in the voice.

“To the Three Barns to see the hounds throw off.”

“And you were fool enough to follow?”

“Yes, sir. I didn’t go at any fences, but the horse got his leg into a hole.”

“And you got hurt yourself, I hope, eh!”

“I got my shoulder put out, but a young blacksmith put it in again for me. I’m just a little battered, that’s all.”

Mr. Gascoigne laid down his pen. “Well, sit down.”

“I’m very sorry about the horse, sir; I knew it would be a vexation to you.”

“And what has become of Gwendolen?” Mr. Gascoigne asked abruptly.

Rex had not imagined his father had made inquiries about her. He flushed—an awkward, sudden blush against the pallor.

“I am anxious to know—I should like to go or send at once to Offendene—but she rides so well, and I think she would keep up—there would most likely be many round her.”

“I suppose it was she who led you on, eh?” Mr. Gascoigne said, leaning back and examining him more closely.

“It was natural for her to want to go: she didn’t intend it beforehand—she was led away by the spirit of the thing. And, of course, I went when she went.”

There was a short silence; it had the charged stillness of a room after a sound has been cut off. Then Mr. Gascoigne spoke with quiet irony.

“But now you observe, young gentleman, that you are not furnished with a horse which will enable you to play the squire to your cousin. You must give up that amusement. You have spoiled my nag for me, and that is enough mischief for one vacation. I shall beg you to get ready to start for Southampton to-morrow and join Stilfox, till you go up to Oxford with him. That will be good for your bruises as well as your studies.”

Rex felt his heart swell in his throat, behaving, as he would have bitterly said, like a girl’s—tears ready, unbidden.

“I hope you will not insist on my going immediately, sir.”

“Do you feel too ill?”

“No, not that—but—” He bit his lip hard, angry with himself as he felt the tears spring; then he forced the words out more firmly. “I want to go to Offendene, but I can go this evening.”

“I am going there myself. I can bring word about Gwendolen, if that is what you want.”

That calm arrangement, that shutting of doors with a sentence, broke him. He read in it—not merely authority, but an intention fatal to him. He had always believed in his father’s penetration; now he feared it had seen everything.

“Father,” he said, and his voice shook in spite of his effort, “I can’t go away without telling her that I love her, and knowing that she loves me.”

Mr. Gascoigne felt a quick inward rebuke that he had not been more wary; he was sorry for the lad. Yet he put all tenderness under what he judged to be wisdom, and answered quietly, as if stating a plain case.

“My dear boy, you are too young to be taking momentous, decisive steps of that sort. This is a fancy which you have got into your head during an idle week or two: you must set to work at something and dismiss it. There is every reason against it. An engagement at your age would be totally rash and unjustifiable; and moreover, alliances between first cousins are undesirable. Make up your mind to a brief disappointment. Life is full of them. We have all got to be broken in; and this is a mild beginning for you.”

“No—not mild. I can’t bear it. I shall be good for nothing. I shouldn’t mind anything, if it were settled between us. I could do anything then,” Rex cried, impetuously, as if the very air had become too tight for him. “But it’s of no use to pretend that I will obey you. I can’t do it. If I said I would, I should be sure to break my word. I should see Gwendolen again.”

“Well, wait till to-morrow morning, that we may talk of the matter again—you will promise me that,” Mr. Gascoigne said, still quietly.

And Rex—beaten not by argument but by the tone which had governed him all his life—did not, could not, refuse.

At the rectory the trouble did not end with a burst of tears and an apology, the way a childish quarrel might be mended over the supper-table. It settled instead like a cold that would not lift—a long, lingering chill that crept through passages and under doors, till even the ordinary house-sounds seemed hushed into caution.

Rex had come home only to fling himself on his bed and lie there in a dull, obstinate stillness, as if he had taken a vow against comfort. When at last the apathy broke, it broke into feverishness and aching that made his mother’s hand hover helplessly above him, and made Anna’s little footsteps go and return on tiptoe with the nervous rhythm of a kitchen clock when the cook is waiting for water to boil. No one spoke now of Southampton. The only thought was how to tend a patient who did not wish to mend—how to coax him to broth, to drink, to rest—how to smooth the pillow without being met by that low, weary murmur, “Let me alone.”

Mrs. Gascoigne tried every homely ministry she knew, as if she could warm him back into himself by the old domestic arts: a cup brought up with the faint steam of beef-tea, bread toasted just enough to give a scent of comfort without roughness, arrowroot stirred till it shone, not lumpy, not thin. Yet the very odors that usually carried peace through a house seemed to offend him by their normality, and the tray came back hardly touched. The bright, thankful spirit who used to come in hungry from the air and praise everything—watercress, pudding, even yesterday’s cold meat if it were cut thin—had been changed into a creature with a blank brow and a dulled eye, as if appetite itself had been struck and left senseless.

His father looked beyond the crisis, believing it the shortest way out of an unlucky affair; but he was sorry for the suffering which must be paid before the boy could stand upright again. Now and then the rector went to sit by the bed a few minutes in silence, bringing with him the subdued murmur of the study—paper, pen, and the small creak of a chair that seems, in a quiet house, to have a conscience. He would leave Rex with only a gentle pressure of the hand on that unresponsive forehead and a low “God bless you, my boy,” as if the blessing could travel where argument could not.

Warham and the younger children would peer round the door, half frightened, half incredulous that the lively brother who made them laugh at table and whistled in the passage could lie so. But fingers were shaken at them at once and they were driven back, as if their common noise might bruise him.

Anna was always there. Her small hand was allowed to rest within Rex’s, though he never returned the pressure that used to answer hers. Her heart was divided—anguish for him, and a hard, hot reproach against Gwendolen that would not cool, do what she could. It kept returning, like a refrain she could not stop humming in her mind: perhaps it was wicked, but she thought she never could love her again.

Even Mrs. Gascoigne, who had been trained by habit and duty to take the charitable view, could not help letting some anger escape her, though she tried to clothe it in apology when she spoke to her husband.

“I know of course it is better—yes, we ought to be thankful—that she is not in love with the poor boy. But really, Henry, I think she is hard. She has the heart of a coquette. I cannot help thinking she must have made him believe something, or else disappointment would never have taken hold of him in this way. And some blame attaches to poor Fanny—she is quite blind about that girl.”

“The less said on that point the better, Nancy,” the rector answered, with the imperative quiet which meant his resolve was already made. “I ought to have been more awake myself. As for the boy—be thankful if nothing worse ever happens to him. Let the thing die out as quickly as possible; and with regard to Gwendolen especially—let it be as if it had never been.”

His dominant feeling was that there had been a great escape. A mutual attachment would have been a knot not to be loosened by mere command or distance, and might have drawn consequences out of his hands altogether.

Still, there was more difficulty to be borne.

One fine morning—fine with that winter clearness that makes every small sound distinct—Rex asked for his bath and made his toilet as usual. It was so sudden a turn toward ordinary life that Anna, full of trembling hope, could do nothing but listen for his step. The boards on the stairs gave their familiar speech under his weight, and she ran down to meet him at the foot.

For the first time he gave her a faint smile; but it sat sadly on his pale face, the way sunshine looks on hoar-frost—light without warmth—so that the tears rushed up in her throat.

“Nannie,” he said gently, taking her hand, and leading her slowly as if each movement had to be learned anew.

Mrs. Gascoigne was in the drawing-room. She came forward to kiss him, and he said, with a weariness that tried to make a jest of itself, “What a plague I am!”

Then he sat still and looked out of the bow-window on the lawn and shrubs coated with hoar-frost, while the sun sent faint, fitful gleams, like a shy guest that cannot make up its mind to stay. Anna thought the light looked like the melancholy smile on Rex’s face—something present and yet not belonging.

He had the sensation of having risen into a new world, where the old desires lay on the other side of some invisible boundary. Anna sat near him, pretending to work, but her needle hardly moved; her eyes were the ones busy, feeding on every change in his expression as if watching could keep him from slipping away again.

Beyond the garden hedge ran the road where wagons and carts went sometimes on field-work. There was a railed opening because the upland, with its bordering wood and a clump of ash-trees against the sky, pleased the eye even in winter. Presently a wagon came along laden with timber; the horses strained, their muscles swelling and shifting under the hide, and the driver cracked his whip—not in cruelty, but in that sharp, anxious way men do when weight and slope and responsibility press at once. He ran alongside to guide the leader’s head, fearing a swerve.

Rex seemed shaken into attention, rose, and looked until the last quivering trunk disappeared. Then he walked once or twice along the room, as if he were trying out his will in the open air of movement. Mrs. Gascoigne had left them; the house behind the drawing-room door was full of softened sounds—somebody stirring the fire, somebody setting down a pan in the kitchen, the faint clang of a lid—those reassuring domestic notes that say life continues and will insist on being fed.

When Rex sat down again, Anna saw a return of speech in his eyes. She could not resist. She brought a little stool and placed herself against his knee, looking up at him with that pleading simplicity which says, without words, Do not shut me out.

He did not shut her out.

“I’ll tell you what I’m thinking of, Nannie,” he said. “I will go to Canada, or somewhere of that sort.”

“Oh, Rex—not for always!”

“Yes—for good. To get my bread there. I should like to build a hut, and work hard at clearing, and have everything wild about me, and a great wide quiet.”

“And not take me with you?” Anna’s voice broke, the tears gathering large and sudden.

“How could I?”

“I should like it better than anything,” she cried, urgent now with the practical fervor of a child who believes love is proved by usefulness. “Settlers go with their families. I would sooner go there than stay here in England. I could make the fires, and mend the clothes, and cook the food—and I could learn how to make the bread before we went. It would be nicer than anything—like playing at life over again, as we used to do when we made our tent with the drugget, and had our little plates and dishes.”

The picture rose between them with a vividness that had the taste of comfort: a small hearth, flour measured and mixed with care, yeast kept alive like a cherished secret, the warm smell of loaves rising in some rough oven while the world outside lay wide and still. To Anna, it was not exile—it was a new household, a restored intimacy, a language of daily acts that could not betray you the way fine words could.

“Father and mother would not let you go,” Rex said, but without conviction, as if he wanted to hear her plead.

“Yes, I think they would when I explained everything,” she insisted. “It would save money; and papa would have more to bring up the boys with.”

They talked so at intervals, in that earnest, matter-of-fact way which is often only the heart disguising itself in housekeeping and accounts. At last Rex was obliged to consent that Anna should go with him when he spoke to his father. He seemed to need her there—as if her presence could soften the rector’s authority, as a hand laid on a kneading-board steadies the bowl.

Of course they chose a time when Mr. Gascoigne was alone in his study. To bring it first to their mother would have been to lay the blade on her nerves. She would have reconciled herself afterward to whatever her husband decided; but the first blow would have been hers to feel.

“Well, my children!” said the rector cheerfully when they entered. It was a comfort to see Rex up again, clothed and steady on his feet.

“May we sit down with you a little, papa?” Anna said. “Rex has something to say.”

“With all my heart.”

It was a noticeable group, those three, even before a word of the petition was made: the same structural family stamp—straight brow; a nose that had started with an intention of being aquiline but had been persuaded into straightness; a short upper lip; a short, strong, well-hung chin. There was the same tone of complexion, the same set of eye, as if heredity had been a dialect spoken in bone and skin. The gray-haired father looked at once massive and keen. A perpendicular line in his brow deepened whenever he spoke with force of interest, and the habit of ruling gave him an air of reserved authoritativeness. Rex, in his paleness and uncertainty, might have been a vision of his father’s youth—if one could imagine Mr. Gascoigne without plans, without command, smitten with heart-sorrow and as incapable of concealment as a wounded creature. Anna was a tiny copy of Rex, her hair drawn back and knotted, her face changing as his changed, as if they shared one soul between them.

“You know all about what has upset me, father,” Rex began.

The rector nodded.

“I am quite done up for life in this part of the world. I am sure it will be no use my going back to Oxford. I couldn’t do any reading. I should fail, and cause you expense for nothing. I want to have your consent to take another course, sir.”

Mr. Gascoigne’s nod this time was slower; the line on his brow grew deeper. Anna’s tremor increased as if she felt her brother’s words as blows falling.

“If you would allow me a small outfit, I should like to go to the colonies and work on the land there.” Rex kept the phrase broad, as if vagueness might pass more easily through opposition than a named destination.

“Oh—and with me, papa,” Anna put in quickly, not bearing to be excluded even for a moment. “Rex would want some one to take care of him—you know, some one to keep house. And we shall never, either of us, be married. And I should cost nothing, and I should be so happy. I know it would be hard to leave you and mamma; but there are all the others to bring up, and we two should be no trouble to you any more.”

She had risen and moved closer, using that argument of nearness which belongs to the young and the tender—her voice and body both pleading. The rector did not smile, but he drew her on his knee and held her there, as if gently removing her from the field while he spoke to Rex.

“You will admit that my experience gives me some power of judging for you,” he said, “and that I can probably guide you in practical matters better than you can guide yourself?”

Rex was obliged to answer, “Yes, sir.”

“And perhaps you will admit—though I don’t wish to press that point—that you are bound in duty to consider my judgment and wishes?”

“I have never yet placed myself in opposition to you, sir.” Rex could not, in the secrecy of his feeling, grant that duty bound him not to go away, but to go back to Oxford—that was the core of the dispute.

“But you will do so,” Mr. Gascoigne continued, “if you persist in setting your mind toward a rash and foolish procedure, and deafening yourself to considerations which my experience assures me of. You think, I suppose, that you have had a shock which has changed all your inclinations—stupefied your brains—unfitted you for anything but manual labor—and given you a dislike to society? Is that what you believe?”

“Something like that,” Rex said. “I shall never be up to the sort of work I must do to live in this part of the world. I have not the spirit for it. I shall never be the same again. And without any disrespect to you, father, I think a young fellow should be allowed to choose his way of life, if he does nobody any harm. There are plenty to stay at home, and those who like might be allowed to go where there are empty places.”

“But suppose I am convinced on good evidence—as I am—that this state of mind of yours is transient,” said the rector, “and that if you went off as you propose, you would by-and-by repent, and feel that you had let yourself slip back from the point you have been gaining by your education till now? Have you not strength of mind enough to see that you had better act on my assurance for a time, and test it? In my opinion—so far from agreeing with you that you should be free to turn yourself into a colonist and work in your shirt-sleeves with spade and hatchet—in my opinion you have no right whatever to expatriate yourself until you have honestly endeavored to turn to account the education you have received here. I say nothing of the grief to your mother and me.”

“I’m very sorry; but what can I do? I can’t study—that’s certain,” Rex said, with the helplessness of one who feels his own mind like a locked pantry.

“Not just now, perhaps. You will have to miss a term. I have made arrangements for you—how you are to spend the next two months. But I confess I am disappointed in you, Rex. I thought you had more sense than to take up such ideas—to suppose that because you have fallen into a very common trouble, such as most men have to go through, you are loosened from all bonds of duty—just as if your brain had softened and you were no longer a responsible being.”

Rex had no arguments ready against his father’s. He felt rebellion coiled within him—hot, ashamed, powerless. Even while he thought, with a stubborn longing that would not reason, that he would like to set off for “the colonies” to-morrow, there lay deep in him, folded away like an old family saying he could not quite forget, the sense that he ought—if he had been better—if he had had more manliness—he ought to feel more for the old ties. It is a strange faith that lives on in us in such sickness: the belief that there exists somewhere a truer self that would behave more nobly than this suffering one.

Rex rose, as if to end the conference.

“You assent to my arrangement, then?” Mr. Gascoigne said, in the tone that closes like a vise.

There was a pause before Rex answered. “I’ll try what I can do, sir. I can’t promise.” And his thought was that trying would be useless.

The rector kept Anna fast on his knee though she wanted to follow her brother.

“Oh, papa,” she said when the door had closed and Rex’s step had faded, “it is very hard for him. Doesn’t he look ill?”

“Yes. But he will soon be better. It will all blow over. And now, Anna—be as quiet as a mouse about it all. Never let it be mentioned when he is gone.”

“No, papa.” Then, as if she needed to save the world from such pain by a private vow, she added, “But I would not be like Gwendolen for anything—to have people fall in love with me so. It is very dreadful.”

She dared not say what else lay stinging under her obedience: that she had wanted—oh, fiercely—to go with Rex, to be his household in a wide quiet place where the day’s labor would end in food you had made with your own hands, and where love might speak in the plain dialect of usefulness—fire lit, clothes mended, bread baked—without the cruel, fashionable language that could toy with hearts and call it nothing. That desire remained her secret, and she went over the whole affair afterward in her mind, thinking with a guilty relish: how she would have done with going out, and gloves, and crinoline, and having to talk when she was taken to dinner—and all that.

And indeed it was just then, in that particular season of the world, that skirts were widening as if the very fashion of cloth demanded more room in churches, ball-rooms, and vehicles—a broadening that made the ordinary life of women noisier and more encumbered, rustling through rooms like a constant reminder of display. But Anna Gascoigne’s figure would only allow the size manufactured for young ladies of fourteen; and perhaps that was fitting, since her longing was not for more space to be seen in, but for a quieter world in which the simplest sounds—the crackle of a hearth, the soft thud of dough on a board, the hush after a kettle’s singing—might be enough to hold a heart together.

Eight months after the Davilows had settled at Offendene, when June had ripened into that late sweetness which makes even hedgerows seem lavish, a rumor began to run—soft at first, like a cart-wheel heard far off on a chalk road, then louder as it passed from market to alehouse, from rectory parlor to dairy-yard. It was not the sort of rumor that came stamped with the red wax of war and Parliament. It was domestic, local, and yet it put a stir into every calling as surely as the first smell of new-mown hay wakes hunger in a village street.

Diplow Hall—Sir Hugo Mallinger’s great place—had been standing for two years with its white shutters closed in a way that made the windows look blind and out of humor with the sun. The deer had grazed as if the lawns were made for them alone; the lilies had opened and shut on the pool without reflection from any passing ribbon or parasol. Now the shutters were to be thrown back; the stables to be aired; the house to be inhabited “in a fitting style,” as if a house itself could taste the difference between neglect and ceremony.

The tenant would not be Sir Hugo. It would be his nephew, Mr. Mallinger Grandcourt—“young Grandcourt,” people called him with that comfortable intimacy which the world allows itself toward other people’s wealth. He was the presumptive heir to the baronetcy, Sir Hugo having daughters and no son; and fortune, never content with a single hook, had more than one to catch admiration with. Through his mother there ran a baronial streak—so that, should certain figures in the middle distance obligingly vanish, he might one day be a peer, and then, by the old conjuring of English custom, any wife he chose would find herself lifted too.

The thought of that unchosen wife rose in minds with the same inevitability as the thought of dinner rises in a kitchen at noon. It was not spoken of openly—not in a neighborhood that could flatter itself on “good taste” and visiting terms with persons of rank. Yet the speculation moved everywhere, threading itself into talk about corn-prices and colts, just as the smell of baking bread will creep into the driest discourse.

Corn-factors, brewers, horse-dealers, saddlers—men who measured life by barley and leather—approved on principle. A landlord in residence meant horses in the stable, mouths at the table, wages paid, ale drawn, shoes hammered; it meant that money would circulate like broth in a large house, flavoring even the poorest crust. The blacksmith at Diplow heard the tidings with a grin that showed his teeth white against soot: there would be hooves to nail, chains to mend, perhaps even an idle gentleman’s whim for a new set of bright fittings. Laborers’ wives thought of their nimble boys in livery, small hands promoted from dung-fork to brush, from hedging to harness. Farmers admitted, with a stiffness that could not quite conceal hope, that straw and hay might find a better market if the Hall were full and hunters were to be fed through the season.

And if those were the practical anticipations of people “not in society,” one could guess the sort of satisfaction among their betters—satisfaction less bluntly spoken, more prettily disguised, and often more hungry. Marriage belongs to both worlds: it is at once a private drama and a public transaction, with servants to hire and dinners to give. So the rumor sent, like a loose feather on a current, an indeterminate vision into more than one well-bred imagination.

At Quetcham, in the beautiful Arrowpoint place, the matter was contemplated from a height at which money does not need to look eager. No one could accuse Mr. and Mrs. Arrowpoint of sordid designs: they could leave their Catherine at least half a million, and fortune makes a virtuous face more readily when it is not pinched. Yet affectionate anxieties are not abolished by a large income. Catherine had refused Lord Slogan—an unimpeachable Irish peer with an estate that wanted nothing but drainage and population—and her parents, without wishing anybody dead (for decent people must always add that clause), could not help thinking it would be agreeable if the intervening persons between Grandcourt and the title were obliging enough to be removed by time. They wondered what sort of man he was: handsome? sound? “reformed,” if there had been anything to reform? and, since politics can be seasoning or poison at a dinner-table, was he liberal-conservative without being too liberal-conservative?

If the Arrowpoints had their private ruminations, it was not surprising that Mr. Gascoigne’s were stirred. Being a clergyman did not exempt him from the parental uneasiness of a man who feels himself responsible for young creatures with wills like unbroken colts. Yet even to his wife he did not speak plainly of matrimonial conjectures. On such subjects, people are as cautious as if they were discussing a new acid or the fixed stars: either your neighbor will seize on your idea and forestall you, or he will take a different view and think the worse of you. Besides, Grandcourt’s past—whatever it was—did not invite in Mr. Gascoigne the suspicious curiosity he might have felt toward a man applying to be butler. A young gentleman of birth and money is forgiven many things as naturally as a rich sauce is forgiven its fat. “Whatever he has done,” the world says, “he has not ruined himself,” and that is the convenient test by which reformation is pronounced genuine.

Mrs. Gascoigne, however, had said to her sister with that interjectional sigh which tries to sound like piety and cannot help sounding like impatience, “It would be a mercy, Fanny, if that girl were well married!” Mrs. Davilow, who could be mild in everything except where her child was touched, made no audible reply; but inwardly the thought rose quick and sharp: You will not get her to marry for your pleasure. The gentle mother could grow saucy in defense of Gwendolen, just as a quiet hen will peck if her chick is threatened.

Then, with her husband, Mrs. Gascoigne said, “I hear Mr. Grandcourt has got two places of his own, but he comes to Diplow for the hunting. It is to be hoped he will set a good example in the neighborhood. Have you heard what sort of a young man he is, Henry?”

Mr. Gascoigne said that he had not heard—at least not in any shape he was disposed to repeat. He carried within him that comfortable doctrine which makes the moral life of a rich man seem a different species of thing from the moral life of the poor. In any case, it was the present—what Grandcourt actually was—that would matter, not the stories men told for want of better talk.

Mrs. Davilow, too, could not be indifferent. The mere mention of an unknown person sets the mind to sketching, as a cook, hearing of a guest, begins to imagine what he likes to eat. Mrs. Davilow’s first picture of Mr. Grandcourt was inevitably flattering: handsome, accomplished, excellent—a man she could be satisfied with as husband for her daughter. But the next thought came like a chill draft under a door: would Gwendolen be satisfied? That girl’s taste was a mystery: excellence might not be her bait. The mother’s image of perfection wavered, dissolved, re-formed into a less certain combination—something that might, by some strange chemistry, touch Gwendolen’s affections. And in the end, pressed by her own anxious love, Mrs. Davilow let herself think what, for her, was almost a hard thought: It would not signify about her being in love, if she would only accept the right person.

Yet she dared not dwell on marriage with her daughter, not since that scene after Rex’s farewell, which had made her feel as if touching Gwendolen’s heart were like touching a wound that might bleed afresh at the lightest pressure. She was ashamed even of her own airy castle-building; for she knew how easily a hint of desire in a mother becomes, in such a daughter, an instant repugnance. With Gwendolen, to recommend a thing was often to condemn it.

The safe subject was dress—the immediate, sensible business of how a girl should appear at the coming Archery Meeting. There was comfort in it: cloth and color are manageable; you can lay them out and decide. They agreed that on her white cashmere, nothing suited her complexion like a touch of pale green. A feather tried in the hat before the glass settled it. The room was quiet except for the small domestic sounds—the brush of fabric, the faint crackle as a ribbon was tightened, the distant clink from below where some spoon or pan was being put away after tea. Even those little noises, regular and known, seemed to steady Mrs. Davilow’s thoughts; the house had its own harmless music.

But then Gwendolen, turning suddenly, flung herself into the attitude of drawing a bow—her whole body alive with that quick, theatrical grace which made play look like power. Her eyes glittered with comic enjoyment.

“How I pity all the other girls at the Archery Meeting—all thinking of Mr. Grandcourt! And they have not a shadow of a chance.”

Mrs. Davilow felt her ears tingle, as if the words had stung them. Before she could answer, Gwendolen wheeled round, wicked with perception.

“Now you know they have not, mamma. You and my uncle and aunt—you all intend him to fall in love with me.”

Mrs. Davilow, piqued into a little stratagem—her timid conscience borrowing a moment’s slyness—said, “Oh, my dear, that is not so certain. Miss Arrowpoint has charms which you have not.”

“I know,” said Gwendolen lightly, “but they demand thought. My arrow will pierce him before he has time for thought.” Her voice had that bright ring which could make cruelty sound like wit. “He will declare himself my slave—I shall send him round the world to bring me back the wedding ring of a happy woman—in the meantime all the men who are between him and the title will die of different diseases—he will come back Lord Grandcourt—but without the ring—and fall at my feet. I shall laugh at him—he will rise in resentment—I shall laugh more—he will call for his steed and ride to Quetcham, where he will find Miss Arrowpoint just married to a needy musician, Mrs. Arrowpoint tearing her cap off, and Mr. Arrowpoint standing by. Exit Lord Grandcourt, who returns to Diplow, and, like M. Jabot, change de linge.”

It was impossible not to feel that she saw too much—saw it with the same instinct by which birds know weather. You could hide a secret as you might sit on a purse and pretend innocence; she would know by the corner of your eye the exact sum you were pressing down. Mrs. Davilow had the uneasy fancy that by sheer divination Gwendolen already knew more about Mr. Grandcourt than anyone else did.

And that fancy, as such fancies will, pushed her into a question that seemed to come merely because she had a tongue and did not know what else to do with it.

“Why, what kind of a man do you imagine him to be, Gwendolen?”

“Let me see!” Gwendolen put her forefinger to her lips, frowning as if in solemn invention, then stretched out the finger with decision. “Short—just above my shoulder—trying to make himself tall by turning up his mustache and keeping his beard long—a glass in his right eye to give him an air of distinction—a strong opinion about his waistcoat, but uncertain and trimming about the weather, on which he will try to draw me out. He will stare at me all the while, and the glass in his eye will cause him to make horrible faces, especially when he smiles in a flattering way. I shall cast down my eyes in consequence, and he will perceive that I am not indifferent to his attentions. I shall dream that night that I am looking at the extraordinary face of a magnified insect—and the next morning he will make an offer of his hand; the sequel as before.”

“That is a portrait of some one you have seen already, Gwen,” said Mrs. Davilow, trying to keep her voice steady. “Mr. Grandcourt may be a delightful young man for what you know.”

“Oh, yes,” Gwendolen returned, with a careless assent pitched high, taking off her hat and turning it round on her hand as if it were a dish she meant to judge from every angle. “I wonder what sort of behavior a delightful young man would have? I know he would have hunters and racers, and a London house and two country-houses—one with battlements and another with a veranda. And I feel sure that with a little murdering he might get a title.”

The jest was of the kind that carries a grain of belief like pepper hidden in sweetness. It left a sharpness. Mrs. Davilow’s brow drew together in distress.

“Don’t talk in that way, child, for heaven’s sake! you do read such books—they give you such ideas of everything. I declare when your aunt and I were your age we knew nothing about wickedness. I think it was better so.”

“Why did you not bring me up in that way, mamma?” said Gwendolen.

The words were quick; their cruelty was quicker than she meant. She saw at once the crushed look, the sob rising like a wave that can’t be held back. The sound of it changed the room—made every small domestic noise beyond the door seem suddenly too loud, too indifferent, as if the world went on clattering its cups while a heart broke.

Gwendolen tossed down her hat and knelt, catching her mother’s hands.

“Mamma, mamma! I was only speaking in fun. I meant nothing.”

“How could I, Gwendolen?” Mrs. Davilow sobbed, the effort to speak making her voice broken. “Your will was always too strong for me—if everything else had been different.”

The logic was disjoined, but the meaning struck home. Gwendolen understood with that swift, uncomfortable clarity that was her nearest approach to self-distrust.

“Dear mamma, I don’t find fault with you—I love you,” she said, truly compunctious. “How can you help what I am? Besides, I am very charming. Come, now.”

With her handkerchief she dabbed and rubbed gently at her mother’s tears, as if soothing could be done by the same careful touch with which one wipes a misted glass. And then, to bring back the ordinary world, she added with coaxing mischief, “Really—I am contented with myself. I like myself better than I should have liked my aunt and you. How dreadfully dull you must have been!”

That blend—tenderness made into a little comedy—quieted Mrs. Davilow as it had often done after collisions. The collisions were rarely repeated on precisely the same spot; both of them carried away from such moments a dread of the topics that had kindled them. Gwendolen dreaded the unpleasant compunction she felt toward her mother; Mrs. Davilow dreaded any hint that she had been reproached. So, by tacit agreement, Mr. Grandcourt’s name was shut out of their talk as one shuts a door against a draft.

When Mr. Gascoigne referred to Grandcourt once or twice, Mrs. Davilow listened with a fearful attention lest Gwendolen’s dangerous perspicacity should betray what might be in her uncle’s mind. But she was not betrayed. Gwendolen knew differences of character with an instinct as sure as an ear that distinguishes woodsong from the thin metallic rasp of a distant machine. And precisely because she meant to evade her uncle’s control, she meant also not to clash with him. She prized the shelter of his indulgence.

Their good understanding was helped by archery. Mr. Gascoigne, being one of the best bowmen in Wessex, was pleased to find in his niece the same elements of skill: the poised elbow, the steadiness of aim, the pleasure in the clean flight of an arrow through air that, on such June days, carried every sound—birdcall, footstep, faint laughter—so distinctly that the world seemed held together by its own hearing. Gwendolen, too, was careful not to forfeit the fatherly kindness that made her freer.

For since Rex’s trouble, both Mrs. Gascoigne and Anna could not hide what Gwendolen felt—unreasonable—alienation. Toward Anna, Gwendolen made efforts at a regretful affectionateness.
