But neither dared to mention Rex’s name; and Anna, for whom the thought of him was as constant as breath, was constrained beside the cousin whose lightness had ruined his happiness. She tried dutifully to repress all sign; but pain cannot mimic the glance and hand-touch of pleasure. That dumb change, unfair as it was, hardened Gwendolen, and she grew more defiant in secret.

Sometimes she felt as if she were being trained like a performer, expected always to please—mother, aunt, uncle, the whole circle of approving and disapproving eyes. And one day, with that sudden leap from thought to speech which made her so difficult to guard against, she said, “Mamma, I see now why girls are glad to be married—to escape being expected to please everybody but themselves.”

Happily, Mr. Middleton was gone without any avowal. And though admiration for the handsome Miss Harleth spread over thirty square miles—among families that included several disengaged young men, each glad to sit near the lively girl who made conversation as easy as breathing—the fact remained: there had been no explicit offers. Providence, or nature, or whatever name one gives the order that keeps the world from burning itself out in universal passion, had taken care that admiration should not always become love, and love should not always declare itself. Many hidden conditions—some as coarse as the price of corn—help to decide why a girl, perfect in person, accomplishment, and costume, is not besieged by proposals.

It was only eight months since Gwendolen had come to Offendene. Some inclinations grow slowly, like plants edging sunward day by day. And if none of the eligible young men already near at hand had spoken, why should Mr. Grandcourt be expected to do what they had left undone? Perhaps because he was thought still more eligible; and a great deal of what passes for likelihood in the world is only a wish turned into prophecy.

The Arrowpoints, having no anxiety that Miss Harleth should make a brilliant marriage, formed their “likelihoods” differently. But in the quiet rooms at Offendene, where pale-green feathers were chosen and tears were wiped away, the rumor of Diplow Hall being opened again continued to hover—like the scent from a kitchen window that promises something rich without telling you whether it will nourish or poison.

“What woman should be?” one gentleman drawled, as if he were tasting the phrase before swallowing it. “Sir, consult the appetite of marriageable men. The world’s store—iron, cotton, wool, and all the rest—gets hammered and spun into whatever the market wants. So with our daughters. They must be wives; and to be wives they must be what men will choose. Men’s taste is woman’s test. You mark the phrasing? The little click of t’s and s’s—excellent.”

“Nay,” said another, amused, “turn it round. Give us the test of taste. A fine menu—does it mean to-day what Roman epicures meant when they insisted a gentleman must know how to eat before he could pretend to dine?”

Their talk ran on with the lightness of champagne bubbles, while Brackenshaw Park spread itself under a July sky like a great green table laid for company. From the gentle heights the view fell away over the neighboring valley to the eastern downs, and westward the cultivated country rose broad and slow, like a curtain hung in folds of wheat, hedgerow, and pale road-dust. The castle, rough-hewn of limestone, held the sun in pits and angles where rain and lichen had worked their patient stains; beech and fir sheltered it on the north, and slid down the slopes in dark masses that looked, at a distance, like flocks moving toward the glitter of water.

At the far end of the park the archery-ground lay as carefully tended as a kitchen garden before a fête-day: the gravel walk combed smooth, the turf newly shorn, the targets set out with the punctuality of plates. Tall elms and a dense screen of hollies threw an agreeable afternoon shade—shade that softened everything, even vanity. The Archery Hall, white with an arcade in front, showed like a small temple against the green; and before it the ladies moved in flower-groups, bowing and turning their necks with that leisurely grace lilies might have, if lilies decided to stroll.

The soundscape was as carefully composed as the scene. When the military band from Wanchester paused, the air did not collapse into emptiness; it filled instead with bright, layered laughter, with speech that rose now into mild excitement, now sank to a contented murmur. There were no coarse roars, no pushing crowd, none of the harsh modern din that makes pleasure feel like an engine-room. Here the human voices kept their musical proportion to the birds in the trees and the soft, periodic thud of arrows finding their mark. Even the tenants admitted as spectators—Lord Brackenshaw’s own people with their families—seemed to keep a natural hush, as if the place itself required a certain gentleness of sound.

The men among the tenants made sport for themselves with imaginative betting—“anything you like” laid down on their favorite archer—while the young maidens, ruled by another kind of hunger, chose silently which sweetly-dressed lady they would like to be if the choice were offered. Perhaps their rustic fancy would have picked a face with more pink and hair of a more fashionable yellow than Gwendolen Harleth’s; but the male judges pressed nearest her were unusually unanimous: she was, to them, the finest girl present.

No wonder she enjoyed her existence that day. Pre-eminence is sweet to those who love it. And for complete enjoyment the outward must answer to the inward: the body’s ease must match the mind’s bright certainty. That concurrence was happening for Gwendolen, as if everything—light, air, eyes upon her—had been prepared like a well-timed course.

Bows and arrows, too, are among the prettiest weapons for a feminine figure to play with: they demand grace, and that fine concentration seen in all marksmanship, but without the associations of blood and powder. Archery carried no acrid breath of brimstone on it; it broke nobody’s shins, bred no hulking athletic monsters. Its only danger was failure—and for generous blood that danger is enough to mould skill.

At Brackenshaw the prizes were of the symbolic kind, not something to wrap and carry home like a joint from market. The gold arrow and the silver, the gold star and the silver, were to be worn awhile in sign of victory and then passed on to the next who deserved them. Like wreaths, only without the inconvenience of wilting in a ballroom. The whole institution had been framed with good taste so that, by necessity, it need not admit ridiculous incidents.

And to-day everything incalculable was in its favor. The warmth was mild; there was no wind to disturb hair, drapery, or the arrow’s course. Skill had fair play. When all marched together to extract the arrows, the movement of bright young creatures toward a common object—light speech, quick laughter, the swish of skirts, the subdued tap of shoes on gravel—made a kind of ritual, pleasant to the eye and, in its gentle rhythm, soothing to the ear.

Here Gwendolen seemed a Calypso among her nymphs. It was in her attitudes and movements that all were obliged to admit her surpassing charm.

“That girl is like a high-mettled racer,” said Lord Brackenshaw to young Clintock, one of the invited spectators.

“First chop! tremendously pretty too,” said the elegant Grecian, who had been paying her assiduous attention. “I never saw her look better.”

Perhaps she had never looked so well. Her face beamed with young pleasure without that stray ray of discontent which can spoil even beauty. Satisfied with her own chances, she felt kindly toward everybody and, for the hour, toward the universe.

Not to have the highest distinction in rank, not to be marked out as an heiress like Miss Arrowpoint, gave an added triumph to her eclipse of such advantages. She would not have exchanged her own accompanying group for any other: her mother’s appearance might have suited an amiable duchess; her uncle and aunt Gascoigne with Anna made equally gratifying figures in their way. And she was too full of joyous belief in herself to feel jealousy though Miss Arrowpoint was one of the best archeresses.

Even the reappearance of the formidable Herr Klesmer—which caused surprise through the company—fell in with Gwendolen’s appetite for amusement. Short of Apollo himself, what great musical maestro could be anything but a comic contrast at an archery meeting?

There was a satirical light in her eyes when she looked toward the Arrowpoint party at their entrance. The contrast between Klesmer and the average group of English country people was at its utmost, set close by his hosts—or patrons, as Mrs. Arrowpoint would have liked to hear them called, that she might deny the possibility of patronizing genius now that its royalty was, in her imagination, universally acknowledged.

We English are a miscellaneous people; any chance fifty will show varieties of face and figure. But our prevailing expression is not that of a lively, impassioned race carrying the real as mere make-weight. The strong point of the English gentleman pure is his easy style; he objects to marked ins and outs of costume, and he objects to looking inspired.

Now imagine those ordinary well-bred men watching the entrance of Herr Klesmer: his mane of hair floating backward in massive inconsistency with the chimney-pot hat perched above pronounced, well-modeled features; the powerful clear-shaven mouth and chin; the tall thin figure clothed in a way which, not being strictly English, was all the worse for its apparent emphasis of intention. Draped in some loose Florentine grace with a berretta on his head, he might have stood beside Leonardo; but here the trousers were not what English feeling demanded at the knees; and the fire in his glances, the quick movement of his head as he looked round with curiosity, became comedy under a hat that proclaimed mankind should have well-cropped hair and a staid demeanor. Some present laughed; others felt a mild disgust at what they called the Arrowpoints’ want of judgment in presenting such a figure, unexpectedly, on a July afternoon in exclusive society.

“What extreme guys those artistic fellows usually are!” Clintock said to Gwendolen. “Do look at the figure he cuts, bowing with his hand on his heart to Lady Brackenshaw—and Mrs. Arrowpoint’s feather just reaching his shoulder.”

“You are one of the profane,” said Gwendolen. “You are blind to the majesty of genius. Herr Klesmer smites me with awe; I feel crushed in his presence; my courage all oozes from me.”

“Ah—you understand all about his music.”

“No, indeed,” said Gwendolen, laughing lightly. “It is he who understands all about mine and thinks it pitiable.”

Klesmer’s verdict on her singing had been an easier joke since he had been struck by her plastik.

“It is not addressed to the ears of the future, I suppose. I’m glad of that: it suits mine.”

“Oh, you are very kind. But how remarkably well Miss Arrowpoint looks to-day! She would make quite a fine picture in that gold-colored dress.”

“Too splendid, don’t you think?”

“Well, perhaps a little too symbolical—too much like the figure of Wealth in an allegory.”

The malice of it was only surface—one of those bubbles of fun that sparkle and burst, leaving no bitterness. Gwendolen did not wish Miss Arrowpoint, or any one else, out of the way; she believed in her own luck even more than in her skill. And as the shooting went on, belief in both rose together. She promised a score among the best—astonishing in a new member—and to her temperament one success prepared the next. She trod on air; all pleasant things seemed possible. The hour was enough for her: she did not need to ask herself what she should do next to keep life at the due pitch.

“How does the scoring stand, I wonder?” said Lady Brackenshaw. A gracious personage, adorned with two little girls and a stout boy, she sat as lady paramount while her lord came up during an interval.

“It seems to me Miss Harleth is likely to win the gold arrow,” Lady Brackenshaw added.

“Gad, I think she will, if she carries it on! She’s running Juliet Fenn hard,” said Lord Brackenshaw. “Wonderful for one in her first year. Catherine is not up to her usual mark,” he continued, turning to the heiress’s mother who sat near. “But she got the gold arrow last time. There’s a luck even in these games of skill. That’s better. Gives the hinder ones a chance.”

“Catherine will be very glad for others to win,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint, with the smooth emphasis of a woman serving virtue as if it were a dish she had invented. “She is so magnanimous. It was entirely her considerateness that made us bring Herr Klesmer instead of Canon Stopley, who had expressed a wish to come. For her own pleasure, I am sure she would rather have brought the Canon; but she is always thinking of others. I told her it was not quite en règle to bring one so far out of our own set; but she said, ‘Genius itself is not en règle; it comes into the world to make new rules.’ And one must admit that.”

“Ay, to be sure,” said Lord Brackenshaw carelessly, dismissing the subject with the ease of a man who prefers his entertainment without lectures. “For my part, I am not magnanimous; I should like to win. But, confound it! I never have the chance now. I’m getting old and idle. The young ones beat me. As old Nestor says—the gods don’t give us everything at one time: I was a young fellow once, and now I am getting an old and wise one. Old, at any rate; which is a gift that comes to everybody if they live long enough—so it raises no jealousy.”

He smiled comfortably at his wife.

“Oh, my lord, people who have been neighbors twenty years must not talk to each other about age,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint. “Years, as the Tuscans say, are made for the letting of houses. But where is our new neighbor? I thought Mr. Grandcourt was to be here to-day.”

“Ah, by the way, so he was. The time’s getting on too,” said his lordship, looking at his watch. “But he only got to Diplow the other day. He came to us on Tuesday and said he had been a little bothered. He may have been pulled in another direction. Why, Gascoigne!”—the rector was just then crossing at a little distance with Gwendolen on his arm and turned at the call—“this is a little too bad; you not only beat us yourself, but you bring up your niece to beat all the archeresses.”

“It is rather scandalous in her to get the better of elder members,” said Mr. Gascoigne, with inward satisfaction curling his short upper lip. “But it is not my doing, my lord. I only meant her to make a tolerable figure, without surpassing any one.”

“It is not my fault either,” said Gwendolen, with pretty archness. “If I am to aim, I can’t help hitting.”

“Ay, ay, that may be a fatal business for some people,” said Lord Brackenshaw good-humoredly; then, watch still in hand, he looked again toward Mrs. Arrowpoint. “The time’s getting on, as you say. But Grandcourt is always late. In town he’s always late—and he’s no bowman, understands nothing about it. But I told him he must come; he would see the flower of the neighborhood here. He asked about you—had seen Arrowpoint’s card. I think you had not made his acquaintance in town. He has been a good deal abroad. People don’t know him much.”

“No; we are strangers,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint. “But that is not what might have been expected. For his uncle Sir Hugo Mallinger and I are great friends when we meet.”

“I don’t know; uncles and nephews are not so likely to be seen together as uncles and nieces,” said Lord Brackenshaw, smiling toward the rector. “But just come with me one instant, Gascoigne, will you? I want to speak a word about the clout-shooting.”

Gwendolen chose to go too and be deposited in the same group with her mother and aunt until she had to shoot again. And there—beneath her saucy satire, provoked chiefly by the divination that her friends thought Grandcourt a desirable match for her—there stirred something not at all indifferent: a quick, secret concern as to the impression she would make.

True, she told herself he was to have not the slightest power over her. He would be one of those complimentary, assiduously admiring men whom even her narrow experience had supplied in several specimens: various-colored beards, various styles of bearing, all obedient to her charm. The fact that her friends wanted her to think him delightful gave her a resisting impulse to presuppose him ridiculous. But that was no reason to spare his presence. Even a passing prevision of trouble—if she despised and refused him—raised not the least wish that he should save her the trouble by keeping away. Mr. Grandcourt scarcely noticing her, and shortly becoming engaged to Miss Arrowpoint, was no picture to flatter her imagination.

So she had been all ear to Lord Brackenshaw’s accounting for Grandcourt’s non-appearance; and when he did arrive, no consciousness—not even Mrs. Arrowpoint’s or Mr. Gascoigne’s—was more awake to it than hers. Yet she steadily avoided looking toward any point where he was likely to stand. She would not let the smallest shift of angle betray that it mattered to her whether the much-talked-of Mr. Mallinger Grandcourt appeared or not.

She became absorbed again in shooting, and abstained so resolutely from any observant glance that even if he took a conspicuous place among the spectators it would be clear she was unaware. All the while, the certainty that he was there ran like a distinct thread through her consciousness. Perhaps her shooting was the better for it: it gained in precision; and at last she raised a storm of clapping and applause by three hits running in the gold. Among the Brackenshaw archers the feat had no vulgar reward of coin, but a special gold star to be worn on the breast.

The moment was happy to herself—and it was exactly what her mother and uncle would have chosen. People fell back, giving her space to advance conspicuously and receive the gold star from Lady Brackenshaw. The movement of her fine form in the clear afternoon light—shadows long and still—made her the center of a pretty picture; everyone must gaze at her. That was enough. She was determined to see nobody in particular, to turn her eyes no way except toward Lady Brackenshaw. But thoughts are not bridled like eyes.

It entered into her pleasure that Herr Klesmer must be observing her at a moment when music was out of the question and his superiority far in the background. Vanity, like tenderness, cannot rest easily under a gaze it cannot govern; and the unconquered Klesmer threw a trace of his malign power even across her pleasant certainty that Mr. Grandcourt was seeing her to the utmost advantage and was likely to admire without criticism. She did not expect to admire him; that was not necessary to her peace of mind.

Gwendolen met Lady Brackenshaw’s gracious smile without blushing—blushes came to her only when surprise took her—and bent with easy grace while the star was fixed near her shoulder. The little ceremony ended; she exchanged playful speeches, received congratulations, drifted among the groups now intent on the scoring. Presently she stood outside them, examining the point of an arrow with an absent air, when Lord Brackenshaw came up.

“Miss Harleth,” he said, “here is a gentleman who is not willing to wait any longer for an introduction. He has been getting Mrs. Davilow to send me with him. Will you allow me to introduce Mr. Mallinger Grandcourt?”

The beginning of any acquaintance—whether it is with a person, or with a place, or with a dish you have never tasted—is only this: you get, at last, a clean outline for what had been ignorance, a shape you can turn over in the mind as you would a loaf newly drawn from the oven, judging its crust before you ever cut it.

Mr. Grandcourt’s desire to be introduced had not come upon Gwendolen as a thunderclap; it had been in the air all day, like the distant tuning of strings before dancing begins. Yet when Lord Brackenshaw shifted aside and the prefigured gentleman became the real one advancing toward her, she felt the small shock that betrays itself in the body before pride can intercept it. Heat rose to her cheeks—annoying heat, as if she had been caught too plainly alive.

For this man was not at all the creature her fancy had been cooking up in secret: no extravagant ornament, no theatrical flourish. He was only a little taller than herself, so that their eyes met on a level that made her feel as if there were no shelter in looking down or up. He raised his hat with an ease that had neither vanity nor hesitation in it. The hat-lift disclosed a wide baldness with a mere reddish-blonde fringe, and at the same instant a hand so perfectly cared for it might have belonged to some fastidious cutter of truffles who could not bear the least grit beneath a nail. His face—clean-shaven—was handsome in a narrow, measured way, the lines running almost straight, the whisker too cut in a perpendicular that seemed less a choice than a law. There was no smile: not the faintest twitch, not the smallest grimace that might be pleaded as friendliness. Nor was there that stiff, correct drilling into which many an Englishman draws himself, hinting at some imprisoned liveliness that will leap out when parade is over. Grandcourt’s bearing was not rigid; it was rather slack with assured possession, as if he had never needed to brace himself against anything. His fairness was faded, like a stage face when the paint is washed off; his long gray eyes gave nothing away—neither anger nor pleasure—only a cool indifference that could observe without seeming to care.

It is stupid work, trying to describe a human creature as if he could be captured at once in words. We learn the alphabet quickly enough; we do not, for that, know the language. Gwendolen had only this first impression to seize on, and it condensed itself into one private sentence that steadied her: He is not ridiculous.

Then Lord Brackenshaw had moved away, and what is called conversation began—yet with a curious rhythm. Grandcourt looked at her persistently, a slow, exploring gaze without any change of expression, while she, who hated to be mastered by surprise, only returned the look now and then in quick flashes—observation softened with that habitual coquetry which was, in her, as instinctive as throwing a pinch of salt to wake the taste. And after each answer she gave, there fell a pause—sometimes long, sometimes brief—as if he let the words lie between them like a card placed down, to be considered before the next was played.

“I used to think archery was a great bore,” he began. His voice had the fine accent of a man bred to have his tones received; yet it came with a broken drawl, as if some distinguished cold sat in his chest and refused to be hurried.

“Are you converted to-day?” said Gwendolen.

And while he paused, she imagined, with rapid irritation, the different degrees and species of opinion he might be forming about her—how far admiration went, where contempt began.

“Yes,” he said at last, “since I saw you shooting. One generally sees people missing and simpering.”

“I suppose you are a first-rate shot with a rifle,” she returned.

Again that pause—during which she had time to sketch him for herself as if she were telling an unseen listener: bald crown, perfect hand, lifeless eyes, the air of a man who has never once needed to ask pardon.

“I have left off shooting.”

“Oh, then you are formidable,” she said, letting a lightness play over her words as a cook might scatter herbs over something meant to bite. “People who have done things once and left them off make one feel contemptible—as if one were wearing cast-off fashions. I hope you have not left off all follies, because I practise a great many.”

He waited again, as if he tasted her speech and found it neither sweet nor sour enough to show reaction.

“What do you call follies?”

“Well—whatever is agreeable is called a folly, I think. But you have not left off hunting, I hear.”

Pause: and in it she recollected the things said of him—his position, his fortune—and decided, unwillingly, that he had the most aristocratic look she had ever met with: not by flourish, but by a quiet assumption that the world was arranged for him like a well-served table.

“One must do something,” he answered.

“And do you care about the turf?—or is that among the things you have left off?”

“I run a horse now and then; but I don’t go in for the thing as some men do. Are you fond of horses?”

“Yes, indeed. I never like my life so well as when I am on horseback, having a great gallop. I think of nothing. I only feel myself strong and happy.”

And as she spoke it, there ran through her a bodily memory: the tightness of glove leather, the clean animal heat rising through the saddle, the keen air cutting the face, the thud of hooves that makes the blood answer like a drum. It was not thought; it was sensation—and she would not pretend otherwise for any man.

“Do you like danger?” he said.

“I don’t know. When I am on horseback I never think of danger. It seems to me that if I broke my bones I should not feel it. I should go at anything that came in my way.”

He listened as he had listened to everything—without showing the smallest quickening; yet his gaze never slackened.

“You would perhaps like tiger-hunting or pig-sticking. I saw some of that for a season or two in the East. Everything here is poor stuff after that.”

“You are fond of danger, then?” she asked.

“One must have something or other. But one gets used to it.”

“I begin to think I am very fortunate,” she said, leaning a little on her own frankness as on a rail, “because everything is new to me: it is only that I can’t get enough of it. I am not used to anything except being dull—which I should like to leave off, as you have left off shooting.”

“How are you dull?”

“This is a dreadful neighbourhood. There is nothing to be done in it. That is why I practised my archery.”

And underneath her complaint lay another, more secret: the dullness of being an unmarried girl, shut in by proprieties like a larder locked against the hungry; allowed to taste, perhaps, but never to choose the meal.

“You have made yourself queen of it,” he said. “I imagine you will carry the first prize.”

“I don’t know that. I have great rivals. Did you not observe how well Miss Arrowpoint shot?”

“Miss Arrowpoint. No—that is, yes.”

“Shall we go now and hear what the scoring says? Every one is going to the other end now—shall we join them? I think my uncle is looking toward me. He perhaps wants me.”

She found relief in the movement, in breaking the sealed little room of the tête-à-tête. It was not that the talk had been wholly disagreeable; rather that the unwonted flush would not go, and she hated the feeling of not being entirely mistress of herself. Besides, this Mr. Grandcourt—who seemed to feel his own importance more than he felt hers—must not imagine she held herself ready at his whistle because the world found him a desirable match. Few unreasonablenesses are harder to endure than being taken for granted.

“You have just missed the gold arrow, Gwendolen,” said Mr. Gascoigne as she came up. “Miss Juliet Fenn scores eight above you.”

“I am very glad to hear it. I should have felt that I was making myself too disagreeable—taking the best of everything,” she said easily.

It was impossible to be jealous of Juliet Fenn, a girl as plain and middling as a market noon—serviceable, unadorned—save for that one bright skill with the bow. There are men who speak of daughters as if beauty were a moral duty imposed upon them; yet those same “intending bridegrooms” might do well to consider what faces they contribute to the future before they bargain for loveliness as if it were a fruit one buys by the pound.

Now the groups mingled more briskly, voices crossing and recrossing like swallows. Gwendolen, choosing at last to look outward rather than inward, saw Grandcourt having Herr Klesmer presented to him by a stranger unknown to her—a middle-aged man with a dark full face and fat hands, on easy terms with both. Soon the stranger led the way to the Arrowpoints, whose acquaintance he and Grandcourt already possessed. She did not care to know his name; she wanted rather to watch Grandcourt with other people, to see if he had reserved some warmer manner for them.

But no: precisely the same bearing and tone. Only he looked little at Miss Arrowpoint; his attention lay more on Klesmer, who spoke with animation—hands stretched out, forefinger pointing down, arms folded then flung open again, the mane of hair tossed as if the very air should obey his argument. Grandcourt listened with narrow eyes, impassive, his left forefinger lodged in his waistcoat-pocket, his right lightly touching his thin whisker—a man who seemed to keep even his gestures on a short leash.

“I wonder which style Miss Arrowpoint admires most,” flickered through Gwendolen’s mind, and the thought gathered a mocking curve about her mouth. Yet she refused to linger in looking as if curious. She turned her brightness on those near her, determined not to care whether Grandcourt sought her again.

He did, however, at the moment of leaving, when he could offer his arm to conduct Mrs. Davilow to her carriage.

“Shall we meet again in the ball-room?” Gwendolen said as he raised his hat.

“Yes,” he returned, in that same drawl, with perfect gravity.

“You were wrong for once, Gwendolen,” her mother said in the brief drive back to the castle.

“In what, mamma?”

“About Mr. Grandcourt’s appearance and manners. You can’t find anything ridiculous in him.”

“I suppose I could if I tried, but I don’t want to do it,” said Gwendolen, a little pettishly; and her mother, accustomed to the shifting weather of her daughter’s mood, feared to press further.

On such occasions it was the rule that ladies and gentlemen dined apart, the separation being counted a mercy to both—rest for the women from the demand to smile, rest for the men from the demand to attend. The gentlemen, indeed, kept alive a set of archery tales about the ladies’ epicurism—stories told with mock horror, as if it were a scandal that a woman should have a palate, as if taste were a masculine monopoly like certain offices or estates. Lord Brackenshaw, who prided himself on being something of a gourmet, would each year repeat Byron’s opinion that a woman should never be seen eating—introducing it with a confidential, “The fact is,” as if he were admitting a difficult truth. Yet even as he said it, the house rang with the gentler acoustics of old prosperity: cutlery not clattering but chiming; voices kept to civilized distances; servants gliding rather than stamping—sounds that were part of comfort, as the faint fragrance of soup and baked meats was part of it. In such a place, the mind could breathe. It is the brutal modern world—its needless racket, its metal shrieks and hammering—where one’s inner life is battered thin; here, the very noise had a measure.

In the ladies’ dining-room it was plain that Gwendolen was not a general favourite with her own sex. No beginnings of intimacy sprang up around her. The other girls noticed what she said rather than spoke to her in free exchange, as if they were listening to a performer they did not mean to applaud. Perhaps she was not much interested in them; perhaps, when left among them, she felt something like empty benches—an audience that would not warm. Mrs. Vulcany once remarked that Miss Harleth was too fond of the gentlemen; yet Gwendolen was not fond of them in the least—she was fond of their homage, and women did not offer it. The single exception, quiet but persistent, was Miss Arrowpoint, who often managed to be beside her without display and talked with a mild friendliness, as if goodwill were a habit of the blood.

“She knows, as I do,” Gwendolen thought, “that our friends are ready to quarrel over a husband for us—and she is determined not to enter into the quarrel.”

“I think Miss Arrowpoint has the best manners I ever saw,” Mrs. Davilow said later, when they were in a dressing-room with Mrs. Gascoigne and Anna, but a little apart, where their voices could have privacy.

“I wish I were like her,” said Gwendolen.

“Why? Are you getting discontented with yourself, Gwen?”

“No. But I am discontented with things. She seems contented.”

“You ought to be satisfied to-day. You must have enjoyed the shooting. I saw you did.”

“Oh, that is over now, and I don’t know what will come next,” Gwendolen said, stretching herself with a sort of moan and flinging up her arms.

Her arms were bare now; it was the fashion to dance in the archery dress, the jacket thrown off. The simplicity of her white cashmere, bordered with pale green, set off her form to the utmost. A thin line of gold lay about her neck; the gold star on her breast was her only other ornament. Her smooth soft hair, piled high into a grand crown, drew a clear line around her brow. One could imagine a painter loving that steadied moment and fastening it—never mind that life is not paint and never holds still.

“The dancing will come next,” said Mrs. Davilow. “You are sure to enjoy that.”

“I shall only dance in the quadrille,” said Gwendolen. “I told Mr. Clintock so. I shall not waltz or polk with any one.”

“Why in the world do you say that all on a sudden?”

“I can’t bear having ugly people so near me.”

“Whom do you mean by ugly people?”

“Oh—plenty.”

“Mr. Clintock, for example, is not ugly.” Mrs. Davilow dared not name Grandcourt, though the name fluttered unspoken between them like a moth near flame.

“Well—I hate woollen cloth touching me.”

“Fancy!” Mrs. Davilow said to her sister, who had now come up. “Gwendolen says she will not waltz or polk.”

“She is rather given to whims, I think,” Mrs. Gascoigne replied gravely. “It would be more becoming in her to behave as other young ladies do on such an occasion as this; especially when she has had the advantage of first-rate dancing lessons.”

“Why should I dance if I don’t like it, aunt? It is not in the catechism.”

“My dear!” Mrs. Gascoigne said, sharply checking her; and Anna looked frightened at Gwendolen’s daring. But they passed on without more.

Something had altered in Gwendolen’s mood since the hour of exultation on the archery-ground, as if a shadow had crossed the sun and made her restless. Still, she did not look worse for it under the chandeliers when the ball-room filled. The soft splendour—light caught in glass and satin, flowers breathing out their damp sweetness from the conservatory—had a soothing power, like the first warm waft when the lid is lifted from a tureen: a promise that the senses will be cared for. And alongside that came the steadier, more dangerous comfort—the consciousness of being sought. Hardly a dancing man but was eager to have her for a partner, and each whom she accepted complained, half-laughing and half-wounded, that she would not waltz or polk.

“Are you under a vow, Miss Harleth?”—“Why are you so cruel to us all?”—“You waltzed with me in February.”—“And you who waltz so perfectly!” The exclamations pricked her vanity pleasantly. The ladies who waltzed told themselves that Miss Harleth only wished to seem particular. Her uncle, overhearing one refusal, supported her at once.

“Gwendolen has usually good reasons.”

He thought her more distinguished in not waltzing, and he wanted her distinguished. This archery ball was meant to keep a subdued pitch suited to dignities clerical and secular; it was not an outlet for violent youth. He himself considered the fashionable dances too much of a romp. Even the sound of the evening followed this intention: no stamping, no drunken roar of fiddles, but a regulated pulse—music that did not tyrannize the room, and talk that could still be heard as human talk, not shouted against noise. In such measured sound, people’s tempers were less frayed; one could almost believe manners were bred in the ear.

Among the remonstrant dancing men, however, Mr. Grandcourt was not numbered. After standing up for a quadrille with Miss Arrowpoint, he seemed disposed to ask no other partner. Gwendolen observed him frequently with the Arrowpoints, but he never took an opportunity to approach her. Mr. Gascoigne spoke to him sometimes—Mr. Gascoigne being everywhere, like a well-meaning bell whose sound reaches every corner—but Grandcourt remained apart.

It entered Gwendolen’s mind that she would, after all, have no trouble about him. Perhaps he had looked at her without admiration and was too used to everything in the world to consider her more than one of the girls invited in that neighbourhood. Very likely the elders were ridiculous to weave romances about what a man would do, without having seen him even through a telescope. Perhaps he meant to marry Miss Arrowpoint. Whatever happened, she told herself, she would not be disappointed. She had never committed herself—not even in silent confidence—to anything he might do. Still, she noticed that he did sometimes, quietly, gradually, change his position according to hers, so that he could see her when she was dancing. And if he did not admire her—so much the worse for him.

Late in the evening, when she had accepted Herr Klesmer as a partner, Grandcourt’s movement for sight of her became more direct. Klesmer, whose wide glance seemed to seize everything and nothing by turns, said as they walked, “Mr. Grandcourt is a man of taste. He likes to see you dancing.”

“Perhaps he likes to look at what is against his taste,” said Gwendolen, with a light laugh. She felt courageous with Klesmer. “He may be so tired of admiring that he likes disgust for variety.”

“Those words are not suitable to your lips,” Klesmer said quickly, with one of his grand frowns, shaking his hand as if to banish the discordant phrase from the air. “I should require your words to be what your face and form are—always among the meanings of a noble music.”

“That is a compliment as well as a correction,” said Gwendolen. “I am obliged for both. But do you know, I am bold enough to wish to correct you, and require you to understand a joke?”

“One may understand jokes without liking them,” Klesmer returned, terrible in his sincerity. “I have had opera books sent me full of jokes; it was just because I understood them that I did not like them. The comic people are ready to challenge a man because he looks grave. ‘You don’t see the witticism, sir?’ ‘No, sir, but I see what you meant.’ Then I am ticketed as a fellow without esprit. But in fact”—here he dropped suddenly from rapid narrative into reflective tone, and the frown became impressive—“I am very sensible to wit and humor.”

“I am glad you tell me that,” said Gwendolen, and she had a little wickedness to herself because his thoughts had already flown off on the wings of his own statement. “Pray, who is that standing near the card-room door? He is a friend of yours, I think.”

“No, no; an amateur I have seen in town. Lush—a Mr. Lush—too fond of Meyerbeer and Scribe—too fond of the mechanical-dramatic.”

“Thanks. I wanted to know whether you thought his face and form required that his words should be among the meanings of noble music?”

Klesmer was conquered; a delightful smile flashed out, and they were friendly from that moment until she begged to be deposited beside her mamma.

Three minutes afterward, all Gwendolen’s preparations for Grandcourt’s indifference were cancelled. She had turned her head after some remark to her mother, and there he was: he had made his way up to her.

“May I ask if you are tired of dancing, Miss Harleth?” he began, looking down with that same unperturbed expression.

“Not in the least.”

“Will you do me the honor—the next—or another quadrille?”

“I should have been very happy,” said Gwendolen, glancing at her card, “but I am engaged for the next to Mr. Clintock—and indeed I perceive that I am doomed for every quadrille; I have not one to dispose of.”

She was not sorry to punish Mr. Grandcourt’s tardiness; yet she would have liked to dance with him. She looked up, giving him a charming smile—one that seemed to offer sweetness as plainly as a dish set forward on the table. He stood still, looking down at her with no smile at all.

“I am unfortunate in being too late,” he said, after a moment.

“It seemed to me you did not care for dancing,” said Gwendolen. “I thought it might be one of the things you had left off.”

“Yes. But I have not begun to dance with you,” he answered—always that pause, as if each sentence were measured out with a spoon. “You make dancing a new thing, as you make archery.”

“Is novelty always agreeable?”

“No, no—not always.”

“Then I don’t know whether to feel flattered or not. When you had once danced with me there would be no more novelty in it.”

“On the contrary, there would probably be much more.”

“That is deep. I don’t understand.”

“It is difficult to make Miss Harleth understand her power?”

He had turned, while saying this, to Mrs. Davilow; and she, smiling gently at her daughter, replied, “I think she does not generally strike people as slow to understand.”

“Mamma,” said Gwendolen, in a deprecating tone, “I am adorably stupid, and want everything explained to me—when the meaning is pleasant.”

“If you are stupid, I admit that stupidity is adorable,” said Grandcourt—after the usual pause, without change of tone; but plainly he knew how to place the words where they would have effect.

“I begin to think my cavalier has forgotten me,” Gwendolen said presently. “I see the quadrille is being formed.”

“He deserves to be renounced,” said Grandcourt.

“I think he is very pardonable,” Gwendolen returned.

“There must have been some misunderstanding,” said Mrs. Davilow. “Mr. Clintock was too anxious about the engagement to have forgotten it.”

Then Lady Brackenshaw came up.

“Miss Harleth, Mr. Clintock has charged me to express to you his deep regret that he was obliged to leave without having the pleasure of dancing with you again. An express came from his father, the archdeacon; something important; he was to go. He was au désespoir.”

“Oh, he was very good to remember the engagement under the circumstances,” said Gwendolen. “I am sorry he was called away.”

It was easy to be politely sorrowful on so felicitous an occasion—like expressing regret that the dish you did not want has been removed.

“Then I can profit by Mr. Clintock’s misfortune?” said Grandcourt. “May I hope that you will let me take his place?”

“I shall be very happy to dance the next quadrille with you,” said Gwendolen.

On the second morning after the archery meeting, Mr. Henleigh Mallinger Grandcourt sat at breakfast with Mr. Lush in a room so perfectly ordered it seemed to hold its breath. Through the open windows the summer air came in unbidden—warm as milk, scented with mown grass and the faint resin of the bordering wood—and the lawn lay close and green as a table-cloth spread for a feast. Even the park beyond had that bruised purple softness which makes distant trees look like fruit left to darken on the bough.

The hush inside was not the hush of peace, but the hush of well-bred furniture that had learned not to creak, not to complain, not to betray what it had witnessed. Outside, the world spoke in gentler tongues: the far combing of leaves, a bird’s punctual call, the padded scuff of paws on turf. It was a soundscape that could have steadied a more honest mind; here it merely framed a kind of domestic theatre.

Half-a-dozen dogs drifted in and out, making languid circuits between table and window as if appetite were an amusement rather than a need. They were the sort of creatures who had been offered delicacies so often that they could afford to sniff and decline, turning hunger into a game of manners. Only Fetch—the liver-colored water-spaniel with the dark, expressive eyes—watched Grandcourt with a devotion that had no play in it.

Grandcourt had drawn his chair aside to face the lawn. One leg was flung over another chair, his right elbow rested on the table, and he smoked a large cigar as if his breakfast were the smoke itself. In his lap he held a tiny Maltese dog, Fluff, warm and silken as a hand-muff, its small silver collar and bell catching the light whenever his fingers moved. When his hand was free of cigar or coffee-cup, it lay on that small parcel of animal heat with an absent ownership.

Fetch bore it as long as she could, then set her broad paw—so soft it might have been a piece of velvet—on his leg. Her head lifted, her nose quivered, and the plea in her eyes was as plain as a child’s who has watched another child be fed sweets.

Grandcourt looked at her without change for half a minute, letting the moment sour. Then, with a deliberate leisure, he laid down his cigar, raised Fluff close to his chin, and patted it with a demonstrative tenderness, his gaze gravely fixed on Fetch as if the point were not affection but discipline.

Fetch whimpered, trying to swallow her complaint—making little broken sounds like someone choking back words that have no permitted language. At last she rested her head beside that outstretched paw and looked up with a beseeching that any creature with a pulse might have understood.

It held until it didn’t. The ache broke into a howl—sharp, raw, too honest for the room. Grandcourt pushed Fetch down without speaking. Fluff was set carelessly on the table, where its black nose dominated the salt-cellar as if it meant to season the world. Grandcourt turned back to his cigar and found—annoyed, as though Fetch had personally spoiled his comfort—that it needed relighting.

Fetch, having begun, could not stop. The second howl was louder. The third followed it, as if grief had found its own refrain and would not be silenced by manners.

“Turn out that brute, will you?” Grandcourt said to Lush, not raising his voice, not even looking at him—merely dropping the words like a command that expected the air itself to obey.

Lush rose at once. He lifted Fetch—heavy with muscle and unhappy loyalty—and carried her out, taking longer than he liked, for he was not fond of stooping and Fetch did not go as a docile parcel. When he returned, he lit a cigar, angled himself so he could see Grandcourt’s face without seeming to stare, and after a moment said, “Shall you ride or drive to Quetcham to-day?”

“I am not going to Quetcham.”

“You did not go yesterday.”

Grandcourt smoked in silence, letting the pause thicken. Then he said, “I suppose you sent my card and inquiries.”

“I went myself at four, and said you were sure to be there shortly. They will suppose some accident prevented you from fulfilling the intention. Especially if you go to-day.”

Another stretch of silence lay between them, filled only by the soft crackle of tobacco and the distant, steadier music of the park. Then Grandcourt said, “What men are invited here with their wives?”

Lush drew out a note-book, the small ledger of other people’s convenience. “The Captain and Mrs. Torrington come next week. Then there are Mr. Hollis and Lady Flora, and the Cushats and the Gogoffs.”

“Rather a ragged lot,” Grandcourt said after a while, with that lazy distaste which treated human company like ill-matched plate. “Why did you ask the Gogoffs? When you write invitations in my name, be good enough to give me a list, instead of bringing down a giantess on me without my knowledge. She spoils the look of the room.”

“You invited the Gogoffs yourself when you met them in Paris.”

“What has my meeting them in Paris to do with it? I told you to give me a list.”

The words were not louder than before, but something in them shifted—no longer the drawling languor that made his speech seem half asleep, but a low, inward distinctness that carried the weight of a peremptory will. It had the same effect as a knife laid quietly on the table: no gesture, yet every motion afterward must take account of it.

“Are there any other couples you would like to invite?” Lush asked.

“Yes. Think of some decent people, with a daughter or two. And one of your damned musicians. But not a comic fellow.”

Lush spoke with a careless air, though his attention sharpened. “I wonder if Klesmer would consent to come to us when he leaves Quetcham. Nothing but first-class music will go down with Miss Arrowpoint.”

Grandcourt turned his eyes toward Lush for the first time, slowly, as if granting a favor. He took two long luxuriant puffs before he said, in a tone lower than ever yet edged with contempt, “What in the name of nonsense have I to do with Miss Arrowpoint and her music?”

“Well, something,” Lush said, jocosely—too jocosely, as if sugar could disguise a dose. “You need not give yourself much trouble, perhaps. But some forms must be gone through before a man can marry a million.”

“Very likely. But I am not going to marry a million.”

“That’s a pity—to fling away an opportunity of this sort, and knock down your own plans.”

“Your plans, I suppose you mean.”

“You have some debts, you know, and things may turn out inconveniently, after all. The heirship is not absolutely certain.”

Grandcourt did not answer. He sipped his coffee—dark, bitter, perfectly served—and the simple domestic act had in it the cold steadiness of someone who believed he could drink while the house burned. Lush went on, his voice tightening with the urgency of a man who had lived too long on borrowed ease.

“It really is a fine opportunity. The father and mother ask for nothing better, I can see, and the daughter’s looks and manners require no allowances, any more than if she hadn’t a sixpence. She is not beautiful; but equal to carrying any rank. And she is not likely to refuse such prospects as you can offer her.”

“Perhaps not.”

“The father and mother would let you do anything you like with them.”

“But I should not like to do anything with them.”

Lush paused, set down his cigar, and thrust his hands into his side pockets as if bracing himself against an irritant he dared not strike. When he spoke again, the remonstrance came up from deeper, from that old residue of conscience or calculation which men keep even when they have mislaid their scruples.

“Good God, Grandcourt! after your experience, will you let a whim interfere with your comfortable settlement in life?”

“Spare your oratory. I know what I am going to do.”

“What?” Lush’s impatience broke through. He meant to keep his temper, and the effort showed.

“I am going to marry the other girl.”

“Have you fallen in love?” Lush’s question carried a sneer that tried to turn feeling into a joke before it could command respect.

“I am going to marry her.”

“You have made her an offer already, then?”

“No.”

“She is a young lady with a will of her own, I fancy. Extremely well fitted to make a rumpus. She would know what she liked.”

“She doesn’t like you,” Grandcourt said, and there was the faintest ghost of a smile, as if dislike were a private entertainment.

“Perfectly true,” Lush returned, and the sneer came back, sharpened. “However, if you and she are devoted to each other, that will be enough.”

Grandcourt took no notice. He finished his coffee, rose, and strolled out onto the lawn as if the matter were as light as the ash he tapped from his cigar. All the dogs followed him at once, their nails ticking briefly on stone before the turf swallowed the sound. The morning’s gentle acoustics—leaf-hush, bird-call, distant insect hum—closed around him like a cloak that did not warm.

Lush watched him a moment. Then he resumed his cigar and lit it again, smoking slowly while his eyes and fingers consulted his beard in that habitual way of his—as if the face he presented to the world were a text he might still edit. At last, stroking the beard as though concluding a calculation, he said under his breath, “Check, old boy!”

He had not known Grandcourt fifteen years without learning which measures were useless—though which might be useful was another matter, always uncertain. Long ago he had held a fellowship and come near taking orders for the sake of a college living; but he had not loved that future, with its dutiful restraints and plain dinners, and had accepted instead the post of travelling companion to a marquess, and afterward to young Grandcourt, who had lost his father early and found Lush so convenient that he let him become prime minister in all his more personal affairs.

Fifteen years of that arrangement had made Grandcourt more dependent on Lush’s handiness, and Lush more dependent on the lazy luxury that required only adroit management—no honest labor, no loud exertion. Grandcourt’s want of respect for his companion had been absolute from the beginning; time had not intensified it so much as confirmed his sense that he might kick Lush if he chose—only he never chose to kick any animal himself. Kicking, after all, was an attitude that compromised a gentleman. A gentleman’s dogs should be kicked for him.

Lush was not unconscious of being held kickable. He preferred to count that estimate among Grandcourt’s peculiarities, one more incalculable mood to be weathered for the sake of soft chairs, good horses, and dinners chosen with discrimination. What son of a vicar—sent to Oxford at the cost of his mother’s and sisters’ calico—keeps an independent spirit when he is bent on dining well and living in luxuriant honey-blossomed clover without working? He had passed for a scholar once, and retained the odor of scholarship as one keeps a scent on a glove long after the flower is gone. The bachelor’s arts that soften manners had served him as a preparation for sinecures; and his present provision was as good a sinecure as a man could want, requiring no more than tact, memory, and the ability to turn away disagreeable noises at the right moment.

He told himself he had never done a bad action; and so he had never needed to ask whether he might do one if ease demanded it. Ease demanded very little beyond that he should take what was handed to him and swallow it without choking. If puddings rolled toward him through dust, he took the inside bits and found them relishing.

That morning, for example, though he had been more annoyed than usual, he went to his private sitting-room and played a good hour on the violoncello—drawing from the strings a rich, human voice that filled the quiet house with something better than cigar-smoke and command: a sound that remembered feeling even when the men who lived among such sounds had forgotten how to translate it into life.

Grandcourt, having once determined that Miss Harleth should be his wife, displayed that grave, unsmiling talent of his for fitting acts to an end. Scarce a day passed, through that fortnight of ripening fields and shortening evenings, in which he did not contrive to be near her, or at least to let her feel his nearness as one feels a presence in a room before one has turned one’s head. His cousin, Mrs. Torrington, now presided at Diplow; and thus Mrs. Davilow and Gwendolen were invited among a large company, where there were abundant eyes to take note how the master of the house singled out the portionless beauty, and wore an air of indifference toward the heiress.

All that world within visiting distance of Pennicote—Mr. Gascoigne and the families worth naming—began to speak as if the thing were already sealed, and the rector’s assurance hardened quickly into a resolve that he must “do his duty” by his niece and see that the settlements were such as became the position. Even to Mrs. Davilow, the wonder was less that Grandcourt meant it than that he had not yet said it; and to Grandcourt himself there was a faint, irritated surprise that a matter so clear in his intention still hung on a formality undischarged. More than once he had risen with the quiet promise to himself that before night he would put Gwendolen into the position of accepting him; and more than once the evening came and he had not done it. This delay, instead of cooling him, acted as an acrid spice: it sharpened determination, as a too-sweet dish asks for salt.

He asked leave that a beautiful horse should be brought for her to ride. Mrs. Davilow was to follow in the carriage; they were to go to Diplow for luncheon, Grandcourt conducting them. It was mid-harvest—days when the land seems to give forth its very meaning in smell and sound: the dry, warm breath from stubble where the cut straw prickles under foot; the greener, milk-sweet damp by a hedge-bottom; the faint metallic tang where iron has fretted in a gate; and everywhere that soft, incessant language of the season—finches ticking in the thorn, a far scythe’s whisper, the creak of a loaded wain, and, underneath all, the steady hush of corn-heads shifting their multitude as the breeze moved through them like a sociable spirit. Poppies flamed along the field-borders; here sheaves stood in ranks; there horses strained under the last load from a broad expanse of gray-brown stubble; and beyond, the downs lay in their tender, cloud-shadowed pallor. The road ran for a time through a country of dairy-farms that had kept the old look—low barns, quiet yards, slow cattle under wide boughs—so that one might believe peace had found a refuge away from the railway’s distant rush, that new harsh note in the landscape’s ear.

But peace does not always pass, like a cool hand, over the fevered forehead. It did not soothe Mrs. Davilow. The sight before her—Gwendolen and Grandcourt cantering, then slackening to a walk till the carriage overtook them—was precisely what a mother’s hopes had hung upon; yet it only fed that inward conflict of longing and foreboding which had become her habit. If Grandcourt spoke to-day, the uncertainty would end. If he spoke and Gwendolen refused—what then? If he spoke and Gwendolen accepted—would that be safety or another kind of peril? Mrs. Davilow, who could not imagine her daughter content in what are traditionally called “mean circumstances,” tried to quiet herself with the thought, “Perhaps she will be as happy as she could be with any one—or as most other women are.” Yet the question returned, like a refrain one cannot silence: Is he a man she would be happy with?

Grandcourt, too, wanted the uncertainty ended—the uncertainty of not having spoken. Other uncertainty—he would not name it—had no reasonable foundation; it was merely like an irritant in the air.

Gwendolen enjoyed the ride—the measured lift of the horse beneath her, the clean clink of bit and curb, the warm animal smell rising from a glossy neck, the little drum of hoofs on firm ground. But her pleasure did not overflow into that unpremeditated girlish chatter and laughter which had come so easily with Rex. Her words were few, her laughs light as an echo heard from far off. There was for her also “something in the air,” though she would have denied that it was any subjugation of her will. She desired—oh, keenly—that this dignified gentleman, and every one else, should understand she meant to do as she liked. If she chose to take him, he must know she would not be managed into the pattern of other women. She would not renounce her freedom.

Grandcourt spoke, as usual, in that brief manner which makes a man appear to have depths by merely not using them. His sentences ended as if he had clipped them with shears; he left pauses that might have contained meaning, and which others filled with conjecture.

“How do you like Criterion’s paces?” he said, when they had entered the park and fallen from canter to walk.

“He is delightful to ride. I should like to have a leap with him, if it would not frighten mamma. There was a good wide channel we passed five minutes ago. I should like to gallop back and take it.”

“Pray do. We can take it together.”

“No, thanks. Mamma is so timid—if she saw me it might make her ill.”

“Let me go and explain. Criterion would take it without fail.”

“No—indeed—you are very kind—but it would alarm her too much. I dare take any leap when she is not by; but I do it and don’t tell her about it.”

“We can let the carriage pass and then set off.”

“No, no—pray don’t think of it any more: I spoke quite randomly.” Even as she said it, she felt a strange recoil from her own proposal, as if some inner caution had pulled the rein.

“But Mrs. Davilow knows I shall take care of you.”

“Yes, but she would think of you as having to take care of my broken neck.”

A pause lengthened between them; the carriage wheels were a soft, regular murmur behind, and the park’s air had that faint scent of damp earth under grass, as if water were stored somewhere in the ground. Grandcourt looked toward her and said at last, as if he were remarking on the weather,

“I should like to have the right always to take care of you.”

Gwendolen did not turn her eyes on him. She felt, in that moment, blood rush and retreat—first the heat of a blush, then a pallor that seemed to take away breath; yet she answered quickly enough, in the lightest flute-tone, with a careless movement of her head.

“Oh, I am not sure that I want to be taken care of: if I chose to risk breaking my neck, I should like to be at liberty to do it.”

As she spoke she checked her horse and turned in her saddle, looking toward the advancing carriage. Her eyes swept over Grandcourt in the movement, but there was no language in them to correct the carelessness of her words. She knew—keenly—that she was risking something, not her neck but the forward course of this courtship; and she was not content with that risk, even while she made it.

“Damn her!” thought Grandcourt, checking his horse. He was not given to running his thoughts into speech, even inwardly; the phrase stood for a whole press of irritation and resolve. Was she trying to force him into protestations—to make him perform the lover with kneelings and vows? That was not the gate by which she would enter on the privileges he could give. Did she expect a letter, a written proposal? Equally absurd. He would not put himself in any posture that could be definitely rejected. Besides, had she not already accepted him in accepting his attentions? Any rupture would be understood to her disadvantage. It was coquetry, then—nothing else.

The carriage came up; the moment of solitude was broken, and there could be no more _tête-à-tête_ until they reached the house, where a crowd made a moving screen of faces and voices. There, Gwendolen—still in her riding-dress, her hat laid aside—came into the bright pressure of observation. The talk, the laughter, the clink of glass, the shifting of chairs, the flutter of skirts, made a kind of domestic music in which she could hide a little from her own inward tumult; and since Mr. Lush was not there to look at her with that offensive familiarity, the admiring attention acted like wine on her spirits, dispersing for the time the uneasy consciousness of divided impulses. Whether Grandcourt had been offended she could not tell; his manners did not change. Yet her quickness had not reached the delusion that his manners were any clue: because they were unchanged, she was not the less afraid of him.

She had not been at Diplow before except to dine; and when luncheon was over and some guests had departed, Lady Flora Hollis proposed that the remaining party should explore the grounds, since certain views from windows and garden were worth showing in the sloping afternoon light. There were opportunities enough for Grandcourt to draw Gwendolen aside and speak unheard; but he did not. He spoke to no one else; yet what he said to her was no more eager than in their first interview. He looked at her not less than usual; and a fresh return of defiance rose in her—she met his eyes fully, not caring, rather preferring, that they seemed to have no expression.

At last it seemed as if he had contrived his moment. The party stopped by the pool, amused with Fetch’s accomplishment of bringing a water-lily to the bank, like Cowper’s Beau; the dog, having failed once, insisted on trying again, plunging and snorting, sending little rings of sound across the water so that even the rushes seemed to listen.

Grandcourt stood with Gwendolen a little outside the group. He turned deliberately, fixed his eyes on a knoll planted with American shrubs, with a winding path up it, and said languidly,

“This is a bore. Shall we go up there?”

“Oh, certainly—since we are exploring,” said Gwendolen. She was pleased, and yet afraid: pleased with being chosen out of the crowd, afraid of what might be said when there were no ears to hear it.

The path was too narrow for him to offer his arm. They went up in silence. At the small platform at the top, Grandcourt said,

“There is nothing to be seen here: the thing was not worth climbing.”

How was it that she did not laugh? She stood perfectly still, holding up the folds of her skirt like a statue, tightening her grasp on the handle of her whip—which she had snatched up automatically with her hat when they set out.

“What sort of a place do you prefer?” Grandcourt asked.

“Different places are agreeable in their way. On the whole, I think I prefer places that are open and cheerful. I am not fond of anything sombre.”

“Your place of Offendene is too sombre....”

“It is, rather.”

“You will not remain there long, I hope.”

“Oh, yes, I think so. Mamma likes to be near her sister.”

A silence, brief but heavy.

“It is not to be supposed that _you_ will always live there, though Mrs. Davilow may.”

“I don’t know. We women can’t go in search of adventures—to find out the North-West Passage or the source of the Nile, or to hunt tigers in the East. We must stay where we grow, or where the gardeners like to transplant us. We are brought up like the flowers, to look as pretty as we can, and be dull without complaining. That is my notion about the plants; they are often bored, and that is the reason why some of them have got poisonous. What do you think?” She ran on with a nervous quickness, lightly whipping the rhododendron bush before her, as if the glossy leaves could take her agitation in their leathery patience.

“I quite agree. Most things are bores,” said Grandcourt, as if her talk had pushed his mind into an easy current away from the track he meant to follow. Then, after a pause, he went on in his refined, broken drawl: “But a woman can be married.”

“Some women can.”

“You, certainly, unless you are obstinately cruel.”

“I am not sure that I am not both cruel and obstinate.” Suddenly she turned her head and looked full at him. She was less concerned with the effect on him than with what that steady regard might do within herself.

He stood perfectly still, half a yard away. It flashed through her mind that a kind of lotus-eater’s stupor had begun in him and was stealing over her too: a languor that dulled resistance, that made will seem like something far off. Then he said,

“Are you as uncertain about yourself as you make others about you?”

“I am quite uncertain about myself; I don’t know how uncertain others may be.”

“And you wish them to understand that you don’t care?” There was a touch of hardness now.

“I did not say that,” she answered, hesitating, turning her eyes away and whipping the rhododendron again. She wished she were on horseback—she could have fled in a canter. One cannot canter down a knoll.

“You do care, then,” said Grandcourt, not more quickly, but softened again into that drawl which seemed to caress without warmth.

“Ha! my whip!” Gwendolen cried, with a little scream of distress. She had let it go—nothing more natural in agitation—and it had sprung away with an odd force, lodging in the branches of an azalea half-way down the knoll. Here was escape, neatly offered by accident. She ran down, laughing prettily, and Grandcourt was obliged to follow; but she rescued the whip before he could reach it, and went on to the level ground. There she paused and looked at him with an exasperating brightness and heightened colour, as if she had carried off a small triumph and still wore the signs of it.

These signs were still visible to Mrs. Davilow when they joined the rest of the party.

“It is all coquetting,” thought Grandcourt. “The next time I beckon she will come down.”

It seemed likely enough to him that the beckoning might occur the very next day, at the picnic and archery meeting in Cardell Chase, planned on the evening of the ball.

In Gwendolen’s mind, too, that result presented itself as one of two alternating likelihoods—as if she were being hurried toward a boundary-line and did not know on which side she would fall. This subjection to a possible self, a self she could not absolutely predict, filled her with astonishment and a kind of terror. Her favourite key to life—doing as she liked—seemed to fail her. She could not foresee what, at a given moment, she might like.

The prospect of marrying Grandcourt had become more alluring than she had ever believed marriage could be. Dignities and luxuries, the power to do a great deal of what she liked—these were no longer airy imaginings but close, palpable, like a rich scent suddenly brought under one’s very senses: the thought of fine rooms, bright with firelight; of table-linen smooth as water under the hand; of silver that caught and returned the candle’s flame; of a life where the very daily bread should be chosen rather than endured. And Grandcourt himself? He seemed as little of a flaw in his fortunes as lover and husband could be. She wanted, in her fancy, to mount the chariot and drive the plunging horses herself, with a spouse beside her who would fold his arms, lend his countenance, and never look ridiculous. He had been everywhere, seen everything—an enviable preamble to his supreme preference for Gwendolen Harleth. He did not appear to enjoy anything much. That, she told herself, was not necessary; indeed, the fewer tastes and ardours he had, the freer his wife might be to follow her own. With all her perspicacity, with all the reading that seemed to her mamma dangerously instructive, her judgement was curiously at fault before him. He was adorably quiet, free from absurdities—he would be a husband with whom a woman could make the best appearance.

And yet—why this constraint? Why did her talk with him lack the daring playfulness she had shown with other admirers? The very absence of demonstrativeness she was glad of worked on her like a charm that numbed as well as attracted. Grandcourt was formidable—like a handsome lizard of some unknown species, not one of the quick bright darting kind. But Gwendolen knew hardly anything about lizards; and ignorance offers a wide pasture to probability. This splendid creature might be gentle, suitable even as a boudoir pet: what might not a lizard be, if one had never been bitten? Her acquaintance with Grandcourt was such that no accomplishment suddenly revealed in him would have surprised her; yet he was so little suggestive of drama that it scarcely occurred to her to picture, in any detail, how his six-and-thirty years had been spent. She imagined him always cold and dignified, never committed. He had hunted the tiger—had he ever been in love? Had he ever made love? Those experiences seemed as remote from the Grandcourt of Diplow as a far country’s language heard through a wall—one catches cadence without meaning.

On the whole she wished to marry him; he suited her purpose. Her prevailing, deliberate intention was to accept him.

But was she going to fulfil that intention? Already, her evasions had gone farther than necessary. She began to be afraid of herself—of that caprice she had always treated as a royal prerogative.

On the drive home she sat, as was her habit, with her back to the horses; and thus she lay open to her mother’s constant observation. Mrs. Davilow saw the excitement and changefulness in her eyes, her unwonted silence, her absence of mind, and took them for sure signs that something unprecedented had occurred. Anxiety urged her at last into speech. The Gascoignes were to dine at Offendene; perhaps there was reason to consult the rector. She did not expect influence over Gwendolen—neither the rector nor herself had much hope of that—but she longed to disburden her mind.

“Something has happened, dear?” she began, in a tender, questioning tone.

Gwendolen turned, as if roused suddenly to the sense of her own body, and took off her gloves, then her hat, letting the soft moving air touch her head as if it could cool thought itself. They were in a retired part of the road, long afternoon shadows lying across it from bordering trees; there were no eyes on them. Gwendolen met her mother’s look and said nothing.

“Mr. Grandcourt has been saying something?—Tell me, dear.” The last words were a beseeching.

“What am I to tell you, mamma?” Gwendolen returned perversely.

“I am sure something has agitated you. You ought to confide in me, Gwen. You ought not to leave me in doubt and anxiety.” Mrs. Davilow’s eyes filled with tears.

“Mamma, dear, please don’t be miserable,” said Gwendolen with pettish remonstrance. “It only makes me more so. I am in doubt myself.”

“About Mr. Grandcourt’s intentions?” Mrs. Davilow asked, gathering courage from fear.

“No; not at all,” said Gwendolen curtly, with a pretty little toss as she put on her hat again.

“About whether you will accept him, then?”

“Precisely.”

“Have you given him a doubtful answer?”

“I have given him no answer at all.”

“He _has_ spoken so that you could not misunderstand him?”

“As far as I would let him speak.”

“You expect him to persevere?” Mrs. Davilow asked anxiously, and, receiving no reply, ventured on: “You don’t consider that you have discouraged him?”

“I dare say not.”

“I thought you liked him, dear,” her mother said timidly.

“So I do, mamma, as liking goes. There is less to dislike about him than about most men. He is quiet and _distingué_.” Gwendolen spoke with a pouting gravity; but suddenly mischief returned, and her face broke into a smile as she added, “Indeed he has all the qualities that would make a husband tolerable—battlement, veranda, stable, etc., no grins and no glass in his eye.”

“Do be serious with me for a moment, dear. Am I to understand that you mean to accept him?”

“Oh, pray, mamma, leave me to myself,” Gwendolen said, with a pettish distress that was near a sob.

And Mrs. Davilow said no more.

When they reached home, Gwendolen declared she would not dine. She was tired; she would come down in the evening, after rest. The likelihood that her uncle would hear something did not trouble her. Whatever he said would be on the side of accepting Grandcourt; and she wished to accept him—if she could. At that moment she would willingly have had weights hung upon her own caprice.

Mr. Gascoigne did hear—not Gwendolen’s words repeated exactly, but a softened, generalized account. Mrs. Davilow conveyed—so vaguely as the rector’s keen questions would allow—that Gwendolen was uncertain of her own mind, yet inclined on the whole toward acceptance. The result was inevitable: the uncle felt called upon to interfere. He did not believe he could do his duty by withholding direction from his niece at such a crisis. Mrs. Davilow ventured a hesitating opinion that it might be safer to say nothing—Gwendolen was so sensitive (she did not like to say wilful). But the rector’s mind was firm: it held to first judgements tenaciously and acted on them promptly; counter-judgements, to him, were no more than shadows passing over solid ground.

Gwendolen came down late to breakfast the next morning with that fresh firmness which sometimes follows a night’s tossing—as if sleep had kneaded yesterday’s misgiving into something smooth, and she could rise again, tall and white and vigorous, like a lily opened by the first heat. The day promised Cardell Chase, roving archery, shifting shade, voices among the leaves; and she had already dressed her fancy in green boughs and sunlight, moving through the beeches as if she belonged to them. Grandcourt’s attentions, too, fell into their places in her mind with an air of being manageable—no lyric shepherd, certainly, but that suited her. She had foreseen him edging, by those slow approaches he made as if he were feeling the weight of his own words, toward what must end in a declaration; and she had foreseen herself receiving it with the composed encouragement she had resolved on with her uncle.

Only Mrs. Davilow remained at the table when Gwendolen entered. Letters lay on her plate. She broke one open, and her smile gathered as she read—one of those smiles that take the mother’s heart by surprise and make it believe in ease again. She handed the note across.

Mrs. Davilow read it and smiled too, as if her daughter’s brightness were a coal warmed into life.

“You don’t feel inclined to go a thousand miles away?” she said, folding the paper back.

“Not exactly so far.”

“It was a sad omission not to have written again before this. Can’t you write now—before we set out this morning?”

“It is not so pressing. To-morrow will do. They leave town to-day. I must write to Dover. They will be there till Monday.”

“Shall I write for you, dear—if it teases you?”

Gwendolen’s cup touched her lip; she sipped, set it down, and answered with a brusqueness that was like a little slap given to prevent tenderness from clinging. “Oh no. Let it be; I will write to-morrow.” Then, as if she disliked even her own harshness, she looked up with sudden playful softness. “Dear, old, beautiful mamma!”

“Old, child, truly.”

“Please don’t, mamma! I meant old for darling. You are hardly twenty-five years older than I am. When you talk in that way my life shrivels up before me.”

“One can have a great deal of happiness in twenty-five years, my dear.”

“I must lose no time in beginning,” said Gwendolen, merrily. “The sooner I get my palaces and coaches the better.”

“And a good husband who adores you, Gwen,” Mrs. Davilow added, as if to coax Fate into kindness by naming it.

Gwendolen only pushed out her lips in saucy silence.

One small cloud lay on the morning: the rector was detained by magistrate’s business and would likely not reach Cardell Chase. She did not greatly care that Mrs. Gascoigne and Anna stayed behind, but she missed her uncle’s presence as a kind of seal upon the decision she had almost taken. To decide had begun to look like stepping into a mould—this unhoped-for fullness rounding itself too neatly. When one begins to wish largely for one’s self, whatever arrives soon seems a fence, shutting out all the other imaginable lives. Still, she told herself, marriage was a gate into a larger freedom.

They met at Green Arbor—a grassy hollow where a hanging wood made an amphitheatre, the leaves roofing it so that the light fell in sifted coins. A coachful of servants had gone before with provisions; the warden of the Chase was to guide the archers along a curve marked by familiar points—the double Oak, the Whispering Stones, the High Cross—so that the roving should not become mere wandering. They would stroll first, and keep the longer expedition for the afternoon when shadows lengthened and the forest put on its richest colour.

The assembling was quick enough to prevent dulness. Soon groups scattered through beech shade and open oak-light, and the whole scene had that composed gayety in which it seems as if even footsteps take care not to jar. Roving archery, prettiest of sports, is also a capricious one: the marks shift, distances deceive, the bow answers differently when the air cools under thicker leaves.
