Gwendolen, though graceful as ever, did not win great credit in those first tries—perhaps because her mind was not wholly in the aim, and because she wished her mind not to be seen elsewhere. Yet she made even her failures look like choice, laughing them off with a charm that asked pardon of no one.

She wore white and green as she had worn it on the former day—the day that had become an epoch because it had brought her Grandcourt. He was continually beside her now; but to an eye watching only looks and manners, their relation might have seemed scarcely changed. Still, people read what they want to read; and there were enough glances, enough nearness and quiet understanding, to make most conclude that if they were not engaged already, they stood on the lip of it. Gwendolen believed it herself.

As they returned toward Green Arbor in divergent little knots, talking more than aiming, words passed that seemed to be the first clear turning of the lock.

“Do you know how long it is since I first saw you in this dress?” Grandcourt said.

“The archery meeting was on the 25th, and this is the 13th,” Gwendolen answered with a light laugh. “I am not good at calculating, but I will venture to say it must be nearly three weeks.”

A pause. Then, in his slow way, “That is a great loss of time.”

“That your knowing me has caused you? Pray don’t be uncomplimentary; I don’t like it.”

Pause again. “It is because of the gain that I feel the loss.”

Gwendolen herself let silence stand, amused and watchful. She thought, with a kind of complacent surprise, He is really very ingenious. He never speaks stupidly. Her unusual quietness seemed to him a yielding, and he went on.

“The gain of knowing you makes me feel the time I lose in uncertainty. Do you like uncertainty?”

“I think I do, rather,” she said, suddenly beaming on him, playful. “There is more in it.”

He met her laughing eyes with that steady, slow gaze of his, as if he looked, not at her, but through her—as if the act of seeing were separate from any warmth. “Do you mean more torment for me?”

Something in the moment—his look, his tone, the sudden closeness of his meaning—shook her out of her usual self-possession. She blushed, turned her eyes away, and said, “No—that would make me sorry.”

He might have pressed on; her changed manner seemed decisive. But they were now descending into Green Arbor where the slope became inconveniently steep. The very ground offered him an excuse; he put out his hand to help her. She took it, and they came down in silence, plainly observed by those already below—Mrs. Arrowpoint among them, standing near Mrs. Davilow.

That lady, having long settled that Grandcourt’s merits would never have satisfied Catherine, looked on him without romance. She spoke with a clear voice that carried farther than she meant.

“Mr. Grandcourt is not equal as a man to his uncle, Sir Hugo Mallinger—too languid. To be sure, Mr. Grandcourt is much younger; but I shouldn’t wonder if Sir Hugo outlived him, notwithstanding the difference of years. It is ill calculating on successions,” she concluded.

“It is indeed,” said Mrs. Davilow; and she could say it with quiet cheerfulness, so content had she become with the visible promise of things.

There was a feast laid in that green refectory—cold meats, pastries, fruit with bloom still on it, bottles drawn from cool shade, baskets opened and closed with brisk hands. The talk and laughter, too, were of the well-bred kind that takes its good fortune as if it were a matter of course. The forest beyond made large pictures—glades opening like windows, distant trunks standing in ordered ranks, the light changing without hurry, as if time itself had softened in the leaves. Yet for Gwendolen the beauty entered only by narrow oblique inlets; her mind was busy with its small drama, as self-absorbed as a puppet-show.

After luncheon some gentlemen strolled and smoked. Strange to say, Grandcourt was among them; but Lush was not. Lush, in fact, threw himself into service—ordering, fetching, attending—so active and obliging that he became more than ever a blot in Gwendolen’s sense of the scene, though he kept himself amiably at a distance and never stared.

When the general move began for setting out again, it appeared that the bows were all under the charge of Lord Brackenshaw’s valet, and that Lush was saving ladies the trouble of fetching theirs from the carriage where they were propped. He did not mean to bring Gwendolen’s; but she, fearing even the approach of that officious figure, hurried to fetch it herself.

The valet, seeing her, met her bow—and with it handed her a letter addressed to her. She asked no question. At once she saw the handwriting was a lady’s: delicate, formed for small confidences, of a kind now less common. She moved away with her bow in hand, and as she did so she saw Lush coming to fetch other bows. To avoid him she turned so that her back was toward the line of carriages and opened the letter as she walked.

It said:

If Miss Harleth is in doubt whether she should accept Mr. Grandcourt, let her break from her party after they have passed the Whispering Stones and return to that spot. She will then hear something to decide her; but she can only hear it by keeping this letter a strict secret from every one. If she does not act according to this letter, she will repent, as the woman who writes it has repented. The secrecy Miss Harleth will feel herself bound in honor to guard.

A shock went through her, swift and cold; yet her first thought was: It is come in time. Youth, eager for revelations, made her mind rush to the imagined disclosure. She had not a moment’s suspicion of contrivance that might justify showing the letter. At once she resolved she would manage to reach the Whispering Stones unseen. She thrust the paper into her pocket with that bracing sense of concealment which, for her nature, strengthened rather than weakened self-command.

It surprised everyone that Grandcourt was not, like the other smokers, ready to set out roving with the rest.

“We shall alight on him by-and-by,” Lord Brackenshaw said. “He can’t be gone far. At any rate, no man can be waited for.”

His apparent forgetfulness might have been read as the lover’s distraction; and the Earl, good-natured, threw Gwendolen a distant hint to that effect. She received it with fitting quiet. But she thought: Can he too be starting away from a decision? The thought was not pleasant—yet it was near the truth. Not “starting away” by any energetic flight; rather that numb languor which sometimes seized Grandcourt when an end came within easy reach: to desist at the very moment when all expected him to advance became another gratification of mere will, independent of motive. He had begun a second large cigar with a vague obstinacy that, if any mortal whom he could insult with impunity had tried to coax him back, would have been met only with a slow removal of the cigar and an undertone: “You’ll be kind enough to go to the devil, will you?”

No one interrupted him. The rovers set out without visible dampening of spirits, leaving behind a few less vigorous ladies—Mrs. Davilow among them—who preferred a quiet stroll free from the obligation of keeping pace. Soon the day rose to its highest pitch: the sport grew livelier; the forest opened and closed around them in changing rooms of shade; and the lengthening afternoon mellowed everything, making voices softer, footsteps more distinct, and the small sounds of the Chase—bird-calls, creaking leather, the thud of arrows, faint laughter carried and lost—compose themselves into a kind of music. Someone said they were acting an extemporized As You Like It; and when a compliment was turned on Gwendolen, naming her Rosalind, she felt the more obliged to be surpassing in loveliness. Her excitement helped her: what had happened to-day had set a restless energy in her, not fear exactly but adventure, and a strained attention to the instant when she might slip away without being hindered.

Nearly an hour had passed when they reached the Whispering Stones—two tall conical blocks leaning toward each other like gigantic figures wrapped in grey mantles. They were glanced at, admired, passed; someone said they would make good ghosts on a starlit night. But soft sunlight lay on them now, and Gwendolen felt bold.

They stood near a fine grove of beeches where the archers found plenty of marks. Gwendolen got in front for a moment beside the warden.

“How far are we from Green Arbor now?” she asked.

“Oh, not more than half a mile, taking along the avenue we’re going to cross up there; but I shall take round a couple of miles, by the High Cross.”

She began to fall back among the others. Then she noticed that the whole party seemed to hurry obliquely forward under Mr. Lush’s guidance. Linger a little—only a little—and the chance would be hers. She let them go on. In a moment she was out of sight.

She did not run; yet she seemed to herself to fly, the ground sliding under her feet like something unreal. She counted the moments as nothing, except for one sharp dread: if there were nothing after all—nothing behind the stones but her own foolishness, and she must go back puzzled. That was her only fear now. Coming close, she walked straight round the right-hand stone; and there, at a foot’s distance, she found herself fronting a woman.

Large dark eyes met hers. For all her expectation she started and shrank back; but in that recoil she took in the stranger’s whole figure—unmistakably a lady, and one who must once have been strikingly handsome. A few yards away two children sat on the grass.

“Miss Harleth?” the lady said.

“Yes.” Wonder filled Gwendolen’s consciousness like a sudden fog.

“Have you accepted Mr. Grandcourt?”

“No.”

“I promised to tell you something. And you will promise to keep my secret. However you may decide, you will not tell Mr. Grandcourt, or any one else, that you have seen me?”

“I promise.”

“My name is Lydia Glasher. Mr. Grandcourt ought not to marry any one but me. I left my husband and child for him nine years ago. Those two children are his, and we have two others—girls—who are older. My husband is dead now, and Mr. Grandcourt ought to marry me. He ought to make that boy his heir.”

As she spoke she looked at the boy, and Gwendolen’s eyes followed. The handsome little fellow puffed out his cheeks, trying to blow a tiny trumpet which remained dumb. His hat hung backward by a string; brown curls caught the sunlight like fine threads. He was as pretty as a painted cherub, and the silence of his toy made the scene more uncanny—as if even play had been deprived of its proper voice.

The two women looked at each other again. Gwendolen, pale-lipped, shivering as if cold had seized her under the warm leaves, said with pride, “I will not interfere with your wishes.”

“You are very attractive, Miss Harleth. But when he first knew me, I too was young. Since then my life has been broken up and embittered. It is not fair that he should be happy and I miserable, and my boy thrust out of sight for another.”

The words came with a biting accent, yet she held herself—no violence, no theatrics—only a determined restraint that made the threat of passion more dreadful. Watching her face, Gwendolen felt a terror that was like seeing, in waking daylight, a vision one expects only in nightmare: I am a woman’s life.

“Have you anything more to say to me?” Gwendolen asked in a low voice, still proud, still cold. The revulsion within her did not soften her; it made everything hateful.

“Nothing. You know what I wished you to know. You can inquire about me if you like. My husband was Colonel Glasher.”

“Then I will go,” said Gwendolen, moving away with a ceremonious inclination. The other returned it with equal grace.

In a few minutes Gwendolen was back among the beeches; but her party had gone out of sight, and no one seemed to have sought her. Solitude lay thick, broken only by distant, muffled cries of sport. She reached the avenue the warden had pointed out and took it toward Green Arbor. Rapid movement was, just then, her only way of keeping thought from rising up and choking her. And as she went she had already made up her mind what step she would take.

At Green Arbor, Mrs. Davilow was astonished to see her return alone, and uneasiness pressed hard—yet other ladies stood near, and she could not show it. Gwendolen answered her mother’s surprised questions with an ease that was almost too ready.

“Oh, I have been rather silly. I lingered behind to look at the Whispering Stones, and the rest hurried on after something, so I lost sight of them. I thought it best to come home by the short way—the avenue the warden told me of. I’m not sorry after all. I had had enough walking.”

“Your party did not meet Mr. Grandcourt, I presume,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint, with intention under her smoothness.

“No,” said Gwendolen, with a flash of defiance and a light laugh. “And we didn’t see any carvings on the trees, either. Where can he be? I should think he has fallen into the pool or had an apoplectic fit.”

She meant not to betray agitation, yet her tone rang too high and hard, like metal struck. Her mother felt at once that something unpropitious had happened.

Mrs. Arrowpoint, thinking only of ordinary pique, concluded that the self-confident young lady was smarting, and that Mr. Grandcourt might be cooling into change.

“If you have no objection, mamma, I will order the carriage,” Gwendolen said. “I am tired. And every one will be going soon.”

Mrs. Davilow assented. There was delay—horses had to be fetched from the warden’s stables—and by the time the carriage was announced ready, the roving party reappeared. With them was Mr. Grandcourt.

“Ah, there you are!” Lord Brackenshaw said to Gwendolen, who was arranging her mother’s shawl for the drive. “We thought at first you had alighted on Grandcourt and he had taken you home. Lush said so. But after that we met Grandcourt. However, we didn’t suppose you could be in any danger. The warden said he had told you a near way back.”

“You are going?” Grandcourt said, coming up with his usual air, as if he could not imagine any omission on his own part. Lord Brackenshaw gave place and moved away.

“Yes, we are going,” Gwendolen answered, looking busily at her scarf as she arranged it across her shoulders Scotch fashion.

“May I call at Offendene to-morrow?”

“Oh yes, if you like,” she said, sweeping him at a distance with her eyelashes. Her voice had the light sharpness of the first touch of frost.

Mrs. Davilow took his arm to be led to the carriage. But while that happened, Gwendolen, with incredible swiftness, got in advance of them and sprang into the carriage alone.

“I got in, mamma, because I wished to be on this side,” she said apologetically when her mother followed. But she had avoided Grandcourt’s touch. He only lifted his hat and walked away, with the not unsatisfactory impression that she meant to show herself offended by his neglect.

For five minutes mother and daughter drove in silence. Then Gwendolen spoke, her voice set hard as if she were pressing it into a mould.

“I intend to join the Langens at Dover, mamma. I shall pack up immediately on getting home, and set off by the early train. I shall be at Dover almost as soon as they are. We can let them know by telegraph.”

“Good heavens, child! what can be your reason for saying so?”

“My reason for saying it, mamma, is that I mean to do it.”

“But why do you mean to do it?”

“I wish to go away.”

“Is it because you are offended with Mr. Grandcourt’s odd behavior in walking off to-day?”

“It is useless to enter into such questions. I am not going in any case to marry Mr. Grandcourt. Don’t interest yourself further about it.”

“What can I say to your uncle, Gwendolen? Consider the position you place me in. You led him to believe only last night that you had made up your mind in favor of Mr. Grandcourt.”

“I am very sorry to cause you annoyance, mamma, dear, but I can’t help it,” Gwendolen said; and the tenderness of the words only made the resistance in her tone more stubborn. “Whatever you or my uncle may think or do, I shall not alter my resolve, and I shall not tell my reason. I don’t care what comes of it. I don’t care if I never marry any one. There is nothing worth caring for. I believe all men are bad, and I hate them.”

“But need you set off in this way, Gwendolen?” Mrs. Davilow pleaded, miserable and helpless.

“Now mamma, don’t interfere with me. If you have ever had any trouble in your own life, remember it and don’t interfere with me. If I am to be miserable, let it be by my own choice.”

Mrs. Davilow could only tremble into silence, feeling dimly that, whatever this trouble was, it might indeed be easier borne—less made a public spectacle—if Gwendolen went away.

Gwendolen had gone abroad and, like a child loosed into a fair, learned too quickly the bright trick of chance. The saloons with their green tables had become her new drawing-room; the sharp click of ivory, the thin metallic rustle of gold, the murmurs broken by sudden cries—these were the household sounds she carried in her blood. There were hours when she fancied herself crowned by luck, as if Fate were a lady-in-waiting obliged to smile and hand her winnings; and with that intoxication there crept in a blurred, perilous notion—an idea that in this muddled world nothing mattered so long as one was amused.

Yet the world has its hidden creditors. While she played at reigning, other hands—mysteriously summarized, like a firm-name stamped on a bill, as Grapnell & Co.—had also chosen their amusement, and the cost fell where it was easiest to bruise: on her home. So she returned to England, carrying against her will the visible emblem of her own entanglement: a necklace she had pawned and that another had redeemed, lying on her like a cold chain that refused to become ornament.

As she travelled back, Grandcourt set out to find her—after his fashion. He did not fly with the ardor of a lover who cannot sleep for missing a woman’s face. He drifted. He let Baden-Baden detain him with Russian acquaintances, appointments made and broken with the languid irresponsibility of a man to whom even intention is a kind of pastime. His passions were of that intermittent sort that flicker rather than burn—enough to light a cigar, not enough to warm a house. The common business of living goes on very well without a blazing soul: cravats are tied with scrupulous care, dinners are attended, speeches made to august healths, all at a low expenditure of inward fire. Grandcourt could be persistent too on the same economy—stubborn not from intensity, but from the mere absence of any channel that would carry his will into generous habit. Under pressure such a nature does not rise like a spring; it oozes, then spurts.

Oddly, he had not been displeased by Gwendolen’s sudden flight from the splendid chance he had held out to her. It had piqued him. It pleased him to think she had resented his coolness at Cardell Chase—his having drawn her to the edge of an admission and then walked away, as if consent were a trifle he could postpone. A girl worth mastering ought to have spirit; and if she meant him to follow, it was what he meant too. But for a whole week he did nothing—not even the small act of inquiring where Miss Harleth had gone.

Mr. Lush, watching him, tasted a triumph with his suspicion, like a sauce too rich to trust. Grandcourt said nothing; his face might have belonged to an alligator that has no need to move. Still, delay meant waste—Grandcourt’s slow-churning mind losing momentum, as water loses force in a marsh.

At Diplow the guests were more curious than the host. Was it credible that Miss Harleth had refused Grandcourt? Lady Flora Hollis, lively and inquisitive, found a reason to make a round of calls with Mrs. Torrington—rectory, Offendene, Quetcham—so that she might collect and distribute, twice over, the newest morsels of report. By then Mrs. Davilow and the Gascoignes, after their first sharp agitation, had resolved to prefer any interpretation that did not paint Gwendolen as eccentric or secretive; they wanted her absence to sound as ordinary as a visit, as harmless as a change of air.

The rector’s mind—practical, yet crusted with maxims as a baking-stone with old flour—still entertained the notion that the marriage might only be deferred. He did not know the bitter firmness with which Gwendolen had spoken at home. He could quote to himself that Amaryllis flees only wishing her hiding-place known; and that love, even now, finds its way “over the mountain and over the wave,” steam and timetables making the old hyperbole almost literal. He conceived Gwendolen an Amaryllis with excellent sense and coquettish daring; the question was whether she had dared too much.

Lady Flora, returning from her visits with the news that Miss Harleth had gone to Leubronn with old friends, the Baron and Baroness von Langen, could not resist trying to electrify Grandcourt by dropping the fact at table with a few artful hints that rumor had him for a disappointed adorer. Grandcourt received it quietly—quietly, but not blankly. The next day he ordered Lush to contrive a decent reason for breaking up the Diplow party within another week: he meant to go yachting to the Baltic or somewhere. It was impossible, he implied, to remain at Diplow as if on parole among people he had never wanted.

Lush needed no clearer notice that the yacht would, by some leisurely tacking, drift toward Leubronn. His fear was only that Grandcourt might adhere to his plan with the manner of a creeping billiard-ball and stick on the way. Lush, however, had his own plan: to make himself indispensable and thus accompany him. He succeeded. Gwendolen’s repulsion to Lush was a fact that amused Grandcourt, who liked his creatures obedient and disliked the idea of any creature being outside his reach.

And so it happened that Grandcourt arrived at the Czarina on the fifth day after Gwendolen had left Leubronn, and found there, by one of those crossings that feel like ill-timed repetitions in the long story of families, his uncle, Sir Hugo Mallinger, with his household, including Deronda.

It is not necessarily a pleasure either to the reigning power or to the heir presumptive when their separate affairs—gout in one, willfulness in the other—bring them to the same watering-place. Sir Hugo was easy-tempered and tolerant; he could bear many differences, many defects. But one difference fretted him more than any debate on Church discipline or ballots: the settlement of the family estates. Faults, too, are less venial when they belong to the person whose existence inconveniences you.

Grandcourt had never been a nephew after Sir Hugo’s heart; but as presumptive heir to the Mallinger lands he was the sign and embodiment of Sir Hugo’s chief grievance—the lack of a son to inherit an estate in which Sir Hugo had only life-interest. Sir Francis had made an ill-advised will: even Diplow, with its modest acres, had been tied up under the same conditions as the ancient wider inheritance of the two Toppings—Diplow, where Sir Hugo had lived and hunted in his younger years, and where his wife and daughters ought to have been able to retire. The grievance had thickened with time. Lady Mallinger had borne three daughters quickly, and then eight silent years had followed; she was now over forty. Sir Hugo, nearly twenty years older, was in that stage when hope wears thin unless some second childhood refreshes it. He had begun to despair of a son; and that made Grandcourt’s interest feel more like a personal affront.

Yet the very pressure of that fact made Sir Hugo careful to keep politeness between them. For he had a plan—grown like a graft alongside his disappointment—to secure Diplow as a future home for Lady Mallinger and the girls. He meant, if he could, to buy off Grandcourt’s prospective interest in Diplow and its attached land with a good lump sum of ready money. If, by some miracle, a son appeared at last, the money would have been wasted; Grandcourt would have been paid to surrender an interest that would have turned to nothing. But Sir Hugo set that risk at nil. He had husbanded his fortune well of late—mines working, leases sold—so that he was prepared for the outlay. The plan required that he should not quarrel with Grandcourt.

Some years earlier, when he wanted Grandcourt’s concurrence to fell an obstructive mass of timber on the demesne, he had congratulated himself on finding no active spite in his nephew’s peculiar mind. Since then nothing had occurred to make them hate each other beyond the limits of perfect politeness, or beyond what was compatible with any strictly mutual accommodation.

Grandcourt, for his part, thought Sir Hugo superfluous and tiresome, and felt the world would be improved when Sir Hugo could be expunged. But he had been made aware through Lush—always a useful medium—of the baronet’s inclinations regarding Diplow, and was secretly gratified to have the alternative of money in his thoughts. Even if he never meant to accept it, there was a pleasure in being able to refuse what Sir Hugo desired. That hinted transaction had counted among the motives which made him ask for a year’s tenancy of Diplow—a request that had annoyed Sir Hugo to grant, because the excellent hunting might tempt Grandcourt to keep his future grasp on the place. A man who already has two houses, one with worse hunting, might naturally covet a third with better. And Lush had thrown out to Sir Hugo a probability that Grandcourt would woo and win Miss Arrowpoint; in that case, ready money might tempt him less. Thus, meeting unexpectedly at Leubronn, Sir Hugo was full of curiosity to learn how things had gone at Diplow, bent on being civil, and looking forward to a private talk with Lush.

Between Deronda and Grandcourt there was also a relation—fainter in its outward marks, but peculiar—depending on circumstances not yet spoken. Still, at the first meeting in the table d’hôte, an hour after Grandcourt’s arrival, no one showed suppressed chagrin. Later, when the four gentlemen met on the terrace without Lady Mallinger, they drifted together through the rooms, Sir Hugo saying as they entered the large saal, “Did you play much at Baden, Grandcourt?”

“No; I looked on and betted a little with some Russians.”

“Had you luck?”

“What did I win, Lush?”

“You brought away about two hundred,” Lush answered.

“You are not here for the sake of play, then?” Sir Hugo asked.

“No; I don’t care about play now. It’s a confounded strain,” said Grandcourt, his diamond ring catching the light as he moved, his fingers idly at his whisker while rouged foreign faces turned to stare at the new milord.

“The fact is, somebody should invent a mill to do amusements for you, my dear fellow,” said Sir Hugo, “as the Tartars get their praying done. But I agree with you; I never cared for play. It’s monotonous—knits the brain up into meshes. And it knocks me up to watch it now. I suppose one gets poisoned with the bad air. I never stay here more than ten minutes. But where’s your gambling beauty, Deronda? Have you seen her lately?”

“She’s gone,” said Deronda, curtly.

“An uncommonly fine girl—a perfect Diana,” Sir Hugo went on, turning again toward Grandcourt. “Really worth a little straining to look at. I saw her winning, and she took it as coolly as if she had known it all beforehand. The same day Deronda happened to see her losing like wildfire, and she bore it with immense pluck. I suppose she was cleaned out, or was wise enough to stop in time. How do you know she’s gone?”

Deronda’s answer came with a slight shrug, as if he would have shut the subject into a drawer. “Oh—by the Visitor-list. Vandernoodt told me her name was Harleth, and she was with the Baron and Baroness von Langen. I saw by the list that Miss Harleth was no longer there.”

To Lush this added nothing beyond the fact that Gwendolen had been gambling—something he had already inferred. He too had looked at the list and learned she was gone, but had no intention of forcing that knowledge on Grandcourt before Grandcourt chose to ask for it. Grandcourt had not asked. It had been enough, apparently, to believe that the object of search would turn up somewhere sooner or later.

Now, though, something piquant had been said, and Grandcourt did not miss a syllable. After a pause he turned to Deronda. “Do you know those people—the Langens?”

“I have talked with them a little since Miss Harleth went away. I knew nothing of them before.”

“Where is she gone—do you know?”

“She is gone home,” Deronda answered, coldly, as if drawing a line.

But another impulse crossed him—sharp, inexplicable even to himself. He turned and looked markedly at Grandcourt, adding, “But it is possible you know her. Her home is not far from Diplow: Offendene, near Winchester.”

The sudden directness of Deronda’s gaze could make silence seem like speech. There was in his face a calm intensity, a richness of tint and life, that startled attention as if something had been uttered. It irritated Grandcourt—not enough to show more than a slight movement of eyelids—that Deronda should turn on him with such intentness when no more was demanded than a simple exchange of information.

“Yes, I know her,” Grandcourt drawled, and with his shoulder toward Deronda paused to look again at the gambling as if that were a better conversation.

Sir Hugo, as the three moved on a little, turned to Lush. “What of her, eh? She must be a new-comer at Offendene. Old Blenny lived there after the dowager died.”

“A little too much of her,” Lush said in a low, significant tone, not sorry to let Sir Hugo smell the truth of it.

“Why—how?” Sir Hugo asked.

They passed out of the salon into an airy promenade, where footsteps fell with that hollow politeness particular to such places, and the music from within thinned into a distant, constant tremor.

“He has been on the brink of marrying her,” Lush went on. “But I hope it’s off now. She’s a niece of the clergyman—Gascoigne—at Pennicote. Her mother is a widow with a brood of daughters. This girl will have nothing, and is as dangerous as gunpowder. It would be a foolish marriage. But she has taken a freak against him; she ran off here without notice when he had agreed to call the next day. The fact is, he’s here after her; but he was in no great hurry, and between his caprice and hers they are likely enough not to get together again. But of course he has lost his chance with the heiress.”

Grandcourt joined them, cutting the thread of confidence. “What a beastly den this is!—a worse hole than Baden. I shall go back to the hotel.”

When Sir Hugo and Deronda were alone, the baronet began again, his tone half amused, half calculating. “Rather a pretty story. That girl has something in her. She must be worth running after—has de l’imprévu. I think her appearance on the scene has bettered my chance of getting Diplow, whether the marriage comes off or not.”

“I should hope a marriage like that would not come off,” Deronda said, with a note of disgust that was more than mere disapproval; it was as if he heard, behind the words “marriage” and “like that,” an unwholesome noise in the world’s soundscape, a harsh grinding where something living ought to breathe.

“What! are you a little touched with the sublime lash?” Sir Hugo said, lifting his glasses to make out Deronda’s expression more clearly.

“On the contrary,” said Deronda, “I should rather be inclined to run away from her.”

“Why, you would easily cut out Grandcourt. A girl with her spirit would think you the finer match of the two,” Sir Hugo persisted, enjoying his own impossible counsel, the way a man enjoys a jest that costs him nothing.

“I suppose pedigree and land belong to a fine match,” Deronda returned, coldly.

“The best horse will win in spite of pedigree, my boy. You remember Napoleon’s mot—Je suis un ancêtre.”

“I am not sure that I want to be an ancestor,” said Deronda. “It doesn’t seem to me the rarest sort of origination.”

“You won’t run after the pretty gambler, then?” Sir Hugo asked, letting the glasses drop.

“Decidedly not.”

He spoke truth. And yet the truth had a shadow. Deronda knew—because he could not quite prevent knowing—that under other circumstances he might have given way to the interest this girl had stirred in him and tried to learn what lay beneath her daring, beneath that quick ear for the world’s applause and that reckless deafness to the world’s warning. But his own history, still unspoken, had biased him strongly in another direction. He felt himself in no sense free.

Men, like seasoned soups, keep two histories at once: the surface you can skim with a spoon, bright with fat and garnish; and the depth that holds its long-simmered bones, its bitter herbs, its secret salt. If you would truly account for a human action, you must do what the careful cook does—follow the hidden stages: the first heat that wakes scent from cold flesh, the slow bubbling where what was separate begins to belong together, the sudden boil-over of feeling that seems itself an act, like a cry flung out so fiercely it changes the air that hears it.

For Daniel Deronda, one instant—no larger than a mouthful and yet impossible to swallow—became the chief epoch of his early life. It came in July, when the sun had the frank warmth of ripe fruit, and the last petals of great pink roses were letting go, one by one, onto a lawn within a grassy court. Three sides were enclosed by a Gothic cloister whose stone held coolness as a pantry holds the night. The place had its own small acoustic: a hush salted with birdsong, the dry tick of petals landing, the far, softened rumor of a household moving behind thick walls—sounds that never struck like iron, never rasped like London wheels, but soothed the mind into a belief that the world was ordered.

There lay a boy of thirteen stretched prone where the grass was in shadow, his curly head propped on his arms above an open book, while his tutor—an able young Scotchman who served as secretary to Sir Hugo Mallinger—sat under shelter on a camp-stool with his own reading. Daniel’s book was Sismondi’s history of the Italian republics. He loved history with an appetite like hunger: he wanted to know how time had been filled since the Flood, what men did in the dull stretches when no one seems to happen, and by what recipes nations kept themselves alive.

All at once, in the unguarded, boyish tone that can sound as pure as a treble note sung in a still room, he let his left arm drop and said, without looking away from the page,

“Mr. Fraser, how was it that the popes and cardinals always had so many nephews?”

Mr. Fraser, roused unwillingly from his political economy as from a lukewarm bowl, answered in that clear-cut Scotch chant which can make blunt truth ring twice as hard.

“Their own children were called nephews.”

“Why?” Daniel asked.

“It was for the propriety of the thing,” said Mr. Fraser, giving the last words their emphatic edge, impatient to return to his book. “Because, as you know, priests don’t marry, and the children were illegitimate.”

He had already turned his eyes back to his page when Daniel—stung as if the rose had suddenly shown a thorn—started upright with his back to the tutor and sat perfectly still.

He had always called Sir Hugo Mallinger his uncle. Once, when it had occurred to him to ask of father and mother, Sir Hugo had said, with that easy cheerfulness which made even sorrow sound like a story long finished, “You lost your father and mother when you were quite a little one; that is why I take care of you.” Daniel, trying to see back into that earliest twilight, could catch only a dim sense: too many kisses, a cloudy softness like scented drapery close to his face, and then his fingers snagging on something hard that hurt him into crying. After that, all memory belonged to the world he lived in now.

And that world had been so complete, so kindly set, that until this moment he had not hungered for any other. Sir Hugo was indulgent and bright—a fine man in the noon of life. Diplow, Sir Hugo’s place, was one of the finest in England: historical, romantic, and yet as habitable as a well-run kitchen where everything has its hook and shelf. The house was an architectural outgrowth from an abbey; remnants of the monastic trunk remained, as if old stone still remembered the murmur of Latin, even when the living tongues had changed. The Mallingers had their grant of Monk’s Topping from Henry the Eighth, and before that had held neighboring lands of King’s Topping, tracing themselves back—so it was said—to a Hugues le Malingre who came in with the Conqueror. The portraits in the gallery above the cloisters looked down in rows upon Daniel as he walked: men in armor with pointed beards and arched brows; pinched ladies in hoops and ruffs whose faces seemed all law and little flesh; grave gentlemen in black velvet and stuffed hips; fair frightened women holding boys by the hand; later, smiling politicians swelling in magnificent perruques; ladies painted like prize animals, rosebud mouths and heavy lids; then Kneller’s revised faces, and Reynolds and Romney smoothing types into refinement, until the line ended at Sir Hugo and his younger brother Henleigh—who had married Miss Grandcourt, taken her name and estates, and made that junction of old families which now gave promise to their son, Henleigh Mallinger Grandcourt.

Sir Thomas Lawrence, in Sir Hugo’s youthful portrait, had done justice to his agreeable alacrity, and more than justice to his nose, which he obligingly lengthened. The Mallinger nose reappeared in refined regularity in Sir Hugo’s younger brother, and in the nephew Grandcourt. But in Daniel Deronda there was no reflex of those family faces. He was handsomer than any of them; at thirteen his face might have served any painter wanting the most memorable of boys—one of those countenances that make you believe mankind has done nobly and might do more nobly yet, and that make you shudder freshly at the thought of grossness and basely wrought griefs, as if such things were smoke that might drift into a clean room and taint it.

But on this July grass, among the rose-petals, Daniel was meeting griefs at close quarters. An idea had entered him as swiftly as a sharp smell can enter a kitchen and change every breath. He sat with his back to Mr. Fraser, and his face went through rapid inward transitions. The deep blush that had risen at the first shock subsided; but his features held that look of subdued activity that comes when the mind is suddenly compelled to re-measure familiar facts.

He had been kept apart from other boys. His ignorance and his knowledge were oddly mingled, as often happens in bright children who read more than they talk. He had Shakespeare and histories in him; he knew how men born out of wedlock were held unfortunate, as if they carried an invisible stain that required them to become heroes merely to stand where their lawful brothers stood by right. But he had never let that knowledge touch his own life. It had been a story about other people, like Pericles or Columbus, a way of filling blank places before fame began.

Until now.

Now, with the magic of quick comparison, there darted into him the possibility that the secret of his own birth lay here: that the uncle he loved might in truth be his father. The thought came not as a reasoned conclusion but as a taste that will not leave the mouth. With it came other imaginings—dim, dreaded revelations carried by a veiled guest entering the tender chambers of his life and refusing to be sent away.

What had become of his mother? Had he been taken from her? Was there wrong—yes, wrong—done him? The ardor that usually ran into the worlds of books rushed upon his own history and spent its pictorial energy there. Sir Hugo, in a moment, took on a double aspect: still beloved, still the center of morning happiness with his watch-chain and seals and the rightness of his voice; but also possibly a man who held secrets, a man who had done him injury. And to speak of it, to ask, seemed like uttering something that would fall through his imagination like flakes of fire.

Those who have known impassioned childhood know that dread: shame connected with parents is felt as if it were a brand laid on the child’s own skin. Daniel could not at once reflect that he might be trembling at a fiction of his own. Feeling and the fear of betraying it collided within him until at last the pressure found relief in big, slow tears, falling without restraint.

Then Mr. Fraser’s voice reached him, as practical as the clink of a spoon on china.

“Daniel, do you see that you are sitting on the bent pages of your book?”

Daniel moved the book without turning. He held it before him a moment, then rose and walked away into the open grounds where he could dry his tears unseen.

Once the first shock had passed, he could tell himself there was no certainty—only conjecture. He had often invented motives for dead men to fill blank places; perhaps he was doing it now with himself. Yet certain facts returned with obstinate reality, like fragments of a broken bridge that still show where the arches must have been. At other times he would recoil from his own conjectures as from an offense, as if he were prying meanly after what he was not meant to know; for there was scarcely a delicacy of feeling the boy was not capable of.

But in sum, a secret impression had come to him, giving him something like a new sense. The idea that others might know what they would not mention planted in him a premature reserve. His ear became newly awake to words that before would have passed him like harmless kitchen clatter. Trifles that imagination could fasten to his suspicion began to gather feeling round them, as a plain broth takes on richness when some strong essence is added.

One such incident, a month later, sank deep.

Daniel had a thrilling boy-voice—one of those voices that seem to bring an idyllic heaven and earth before the mind—together with a fine musical instinct. Early, he had found accompaniments for himself at the piano while he sang from memory; later he had had some teaching. Sir Hugo delighted in him and liked to ask for his singing before guests.

One rainy morning, after Daniel had been singing “Sweet Echo” for a small party of gentlemen detained indoors, Sir Hugo—passing from a smiling remark to his neighbor—called out,

“Come here, Dan!”

Daniel came forward with unusual reluctance. He wore an embroidered holland blouse that set off the rich coloring of his head and throat. There was a resistant gravity about his mouth and eyes as he stood under admiration, and that very resistance made his beauty more striking, like fine fruit that is not yet to be plucked.

Sir Hugo spoke as if in play, but play can have a blade.

“What do you say to being a great singer? Should you like to be adored by the world and take the house by storm, like Mario and Tamberlik?”

Daniel reddened at once. There was a perceptible pause—no more than the moment before a knife comes down—then he answered with angry decision,

“No; I should hate it!”

“Well, well, well!” Sir Hugo said, surprised but kindly, intending to soothe. Yet Daniel turned quickly away, left the room, and went to his own chamber. He flung himself on the broad window-sill, a favorite perch when there was nothing demanded of him.

From there he watched the rain slacken, and gleams split the clouds to light a great reach of parkland. Old oaks stood apart like elders in a field, each with its own authority. Beyond them the bordering wood was pierced by a green glade meeting the eastern sky. The scene was part of his home—part of the dignified ease he had taken as naturally as bread at breakfast. His ardent clinging nature had claimed it all with affection. He knew much of what it was to be a gentleman by inheritance, not by thinking about himself but by living in a world where certain sounds—the quiet orders, the respectful footfall, the absence of harsh mechanical din—said, without words, You belong.

It had never occurred to him that he might be shut out from such a lot. True, some people choose poverty like a bride, preferring scoured deal and whitewash to splendor; some run away from privilege to bind themselves to hard-handed labor. But Daniel’s tastes matched his nurture: he did not rebel against habitual ease; he loved it, as one loves the familiar loaf, the known orchard, the pantry whose scents mean safety. And now he had been stung by the idea that Sir Hugo—perhaps his father—could imagine a career for him utterly unlike his own: to be dressed up and made to sing before fine people who would care for him only as they care for a clever toy, applauded and then put away.

He had been to the opera with Sir Hugo, who indulged the boy’s ear. The image of taking the house by storm was vivid; he could almost hear the roar that sweeps over a singer like wind over corn. But with that sound came another—a more cruel undertone—like coins clinking, like wheels, like the grind of commerce where art becomes wares. The thought of being set up for admiration in that way made his stomach turn as if at something too sweet, too perfumed, meant to hide what was coarse beneath.

And Sir Hugo’s question felt to Daniel like proof: something about his birth cast him out from the class of gentlemen. Would it ever be spoken? Would a day come when Sir Hugo would tell him everything? He shrank from it; his imagination preferred ignorance. If his father—he used strong words in his inward hurt—if his father had done wrong, he wished it might never be spoken. It was cutting enough to think such knowledge might live in other minds.

Was it in Mr. Fraser’s? Probably not, or he would not have spoken so freely about the pope’s nephews. Yet Daniel, like older people, fancied everyone’s consciousness must be as busy as his on what was vital to him. Did Turvey the valet know? Old Mrs. French the housekeeper? Banks the bailiff, with whom Daniel had ridden on his pony over the farms where cows chewed and whey steamed faintly sour-sweet in the dairy? And then memory pricked him with a small sharpness: years ago, drinking Mrs. Banks’s whey—cool, thin, and alive with the clean tang of milk turned—he had heard Banks say to his wife with a wink and a cunning laugh, “He features the mother, eh?” At the time little Daniel had only thought Banks made a silly face, like common farming men laughing at what was not laughable; he had resented being winked at as if he did not understand. Now that trifling moment became information to be weighed.

How could he be like his mother and not like his father? His mother must have been a Mallinger if Sir Hugo were his uncle. But no—his father might have been Sir Hugo’s brother and changed his name, as Henleigh Mallinger had taken Grandcourt. But then why had Sir Hugo never spoken of a brother Deronda, as he spoke of brother Grandcourt?

Before, Daniel had not cared about the family tree, except for the ancestor who killed three Saracens in one encounter. Now his mind turned to a cabinet of estate-maps in the library, where he had once seen an illuminated parchment hanging out, which Sir Hugo had called the family tree. The phrase had seemed odd then. Now he longed to examine that parchment, to trace names as if they were ingredients in a dish whose true flavor depended on what had been added and what omitted. He imagined the cabinet always locked. He even felt the urge to try it.

Then he checked himself. He might be seen. And he would not bring himself near even a silent admission of the sore opened in him.

It is in such experiences—while elders debate whether education is science or literature—that the main lines of character are often set. If Daniel had been less ardently affectionate, his reserve and the sense that others held something against him might have hardened into proud antagonism. But his inborn lovingness kept level with resentment. He was fond of almost every creature in his habitual world, teasing them now and then as happy children do—everyone except that he did not tease Sir Hugo, whom he called “Nunc,” as Sir Hugo had taught him; the baronet was not strait-laced and let his dignity take care of itself.

Daniel loved him with that deep-rooted filial love that makes children happier merely to be in the same room with father or mother, even while doing nothing together. Sir Hugo’s handwriting, his way of smoking, his tone in speaking to dogs and horses—each had a charm and rightness that mixed with the happiness of morning and breakfast. Sir Hugo’s politics—he had always been a Whig—made Tories and Radicals equally opponents of what seemed to Daniel the truest and best. Sir Hugo’s writings, whether travels in brilliant style, or articles on everything, or pamphlets on political crises, were all consecrated in the boy’s belief: what was his had a rightness that could test other men’s knowledge.

And so the bitterness of suspecting something not quite right in this object of complete love was like tasting spoilage in what you have always trusted as wholesome. Children demand their heroes fleckless; the first discovery of a possible stain can feel like the ground shifting.

Some time after Daniel’s renewed agitation, it appeared that Sir Hugo’s question about singing had been only a playful experiment. He sent for Daniel into the library. When the boy entered, Sir Hugo looked up from his writing and threw himself sideways in his arm-chair.

“Ah, Dan!” he said, drawing one of the old embroidered stools close. “Come and sit down here.”

Daniel obeyed. Sir Hugo laid a gentle hand on his shoulder and looked at him affectionately.

“What is it, my boy? Have you heard anything that has put you out of spirits lately?”

Daniel was determined not to let tears come, but his throat closed; he could not speak.

“All changes are painful when people have been happy, you know,” Sir Hugo went on, lifting his hand to rub the boy’s dark curls. “You can’t be educated exactly as I wish you to be without our parting. And I think you will find a great deal to like at school.”

This was not what Daniel expected, and the relief came like a draught of fresh air after smoke. He found voice.

“Am I to go to school?”

“Yes. I mean you to go to Eton. I wish you to have the education of an English gentleman; and for that it is necessary you should go to a public school in preparation for the university. Cambridge I mean you to go to; it was my own university.”

Daniel’s color came and went.

“What do you say, Sirrah?” Sir Hugo asked, smiling.

“I should like to be a gentleman,” Daniel said, with firm distinctness, “and go to school, if that is what a gentleman’s son must do.”

Sir Hugo watched him a moment in silence, thinking he understood now why the lad had bristled at the idea of being a singer. Then he said, tenderly,

“And so you won’t mind about leaving your old Nunc?”

“Yes, I shall,” Daniel said, clasping Sir Hugo’s caressing arm with both hands as if holding to something warm and certain. “But sha’n’t I come home and be with you in the holidays?”

“Oh yes, generally,” said Sir Hugo. “But now I mean you to go at once to a new tutor, to break the change for you before you go to Eton.”

After this, Daniel’s spirits rose again. He was meant to be a gentleman; perhaps—by some unguessed arrangement—his conjectures were wrong. His very keenness taught him to find comfort in ignorance: while he had been constructing possibilities, it became plain there must be possibilities of which he knew nothing. He stopped brooding. Youthful joy and the spirit of adventure are not easily quenched; and in the interval before leaving, he sang about the house, danced among the old servants, made them parting gifts, and repeated his injunctions to the groom about the care of the black pony, as if love could be packed into instructions and carried forward intact.

“Do you think I shall know much less than the other boys, Mr. Fraser?” Daniel asked. He was always inclined to think strangers would be surprised by his ignorance.

“There are dunces to be found everywhere,” Fraser replied, judiciously. “You’ll not be the biggest; but you’ve not the makings of a Porson in you, or a Leibnitz either.”

“I don’t want to be a Porson or a Leibnitz,” Daniel said. “I would rather be a greater leader, like Pericles or Washington.”

“Ay, ay,” said Fraser, “you’ve a notion they did with little parsing, and less algebra.” But in truth he thought his pupil remarkable, able to take up anything easily, if only he cared.

Things went well enough for Daniel in his new world—except in one point that left a lasting taste. A boy he was at once inclined to love as a close friend talked to him much of his own home and parents, and seemed to expect the same openness in return. At once Daniel shrank into reserve, as if a door had been quietly shut. That experience stayed with him, checking his natural bent toward intimate friendship. Everyone—even his tutor—called him reserved, though he was good-humored, unassuming, quick at study and sport; no one found his reserve disagreeable.

And certainly his face had much to do with that favorable judgment. In him, the beauty of closed lips told no falsehood.

On a clear evening near the end of July, Daniel Deronda took his skiff out from Putney and let the Thames have him as it would. The river was his truest holiday—more faithful than drawing-rooms, more honest than books read out of obedience. In town with the Mallingers, where talk thickened like over-salted soup and a man’s hours were portioned out by other people’s appetites, he could find nowhere the same clean emptiness as he found between two reaches of water.

He had returned to England more than a year ago with the convenient understanding that his education was complete, and that now he would step, without stumble or protest, into the place prepared for him in English society. Sir Hugo—excellent, worldly, and satisfied with the world because it had been satisfied with him—had pressed law upon Daniel as one presses a steadying draught into a reluctant hand: not because it delighted, but because it filled time. Daniel had taken it up, and the pages had done what dry bread does to a mouth already parched—made him more conscious of thirst. The more he tried to fix himself to a profession, the more his uncertainty rooted itself, not like a weed you can pull, but like an old tree that has chosen its soil.

So he rowed. It was labor enough to be wholesome, solitary enough to be sweet, and its music—water lipping the blade, the hollow knock of oar against thole-pin, the far-off clink of chain and creak of timber—made a kind of acoustic shelter. Even the city’s noises came to him softened: wheels were muffled into a distant sigh; the sharp cries of boys and vendors became mere bright flecks on the air, like birds crossing a wide sky. He had often thought, without putting it into any learned phrase, how much a man’s courage is governed by what he hears. There are sounds that press the mind down—hammering, grinding, unrelenting iron—and there are sounds that give it room. The river, at least, did not bully.

As he pulled steadily, his own voice—half unconsciously—fell into subdued snatches of a melody that had clung to him all day, as a scent clings to the cuff of a coat after passing a garden wall. It was the gondolier’s song in Rossini’s *Otello*, carrying Dante’s words—those words that taste bitter on the tongue like burnt sugar: *Nessun maggior dolore che ricordarsi del tempo felice nella miseria*. He sang under his breath, not from any fashionable sentimentality, but because the cadence matched the stroke of the oars, and because the line itself had that terrible exactness which makes sorrow feel as if it were being named for the first time.

Near Kew Bridge, between six and seven, the Thames was no hermitage. There were saunterers on the towing-path; a few boats moved with slow purpose; and a great barge came pushing its heavy way, making the water thicken and lift in broad ridges. Daniel guided his boat aside, rested on his oar within a couple of yards of the river-brink, and let the barge go past.

His voice, continuing without his will, fell to a pianissimo on the last words—*nella miseria*—and the wail died into the river’s breath.

Then, close by, on the bank, he saw a figure that seemed like the bodily shape of the very misery he had been uttering.

A girl—hardly more than eighteen—slight, low in stature, with a face so small and fine it might have been carved out of some pale stone. Dark curls were pushed behind her ears under a large black hat; a long woollen cloak hung on her shoulders. Her hands were clasped before her and hung down as if she had forgotten they could do anything else. She stared at the river with a despair so still it was like an image set there for warning.

The shock of her presence made him stop singing at once. At the sudden silence she changed her attitude, as if the broken thread of sound had snapped inside her, and she turned with a frightened glance—then met his face. For a moment they looked straight at each other, longer than seemed possible between strangers. Her look had the timid directness of some gentle animal caught and not yet decided whether to flee—no blush, no appeal, only that startled watchfulness which is more moving than any confession.

Something in him sprang forward—pity, yes, but also a quick reverence, as if he had come upon a sacred distress. Yet she turned away almost at once and walked to a bench under a tree.

Poorly dressed, melancholy women were not rare along London’s edges; and the very delicacy that made her striking made it impossible for him to intrude. He turned his boat and rowed on, as fast as if he could put distance between himself and the ache her face had planted in him.

He could not. Again and again, as the water carried him, her image rose as distinctly as if it were pressed into a dark gem: brown-black drapery, white face, small features, the long lashes shadowing eyes too heavy with unshed tears. He found himself weaving possible histories behind her—then checked himself with a half-smile at his own romantic prejudice that beauty must have romance attached to it like a ribbon. And yet he could not quite scold himself down. There are sorrows that the world will not notice unless a delicate face bears them—like a rare dish left untouched because it is served in coarse ware; the hunger is the same, but the eye is bribed into attention only by a finer vessel.

He slackened his rowing, let the tide begin to take him back. The evening light lengthened; thought and feeling slid together in him as smoothly as water over weed. The river, widening and darkening, drew him into that solemn passivity which can feel like wisdom because it is quiet. As he drifted, he heard the day’s sounds thinning: fewer voices from the shore, fewer oars, the distant rumble of London held off by the broad coolness of the stream. The world’s industrial roar seemed, from here, like an impertinence—an endless grinding that pretended to be progress while it simply drowned the subtler lives beneath it.

By the time he came with the tide past Richmond Bridge the sun was near setting—his favourite hour, when tree and building mass into darkness against the double glow of sky and river, and every sound seems chosen, not accidental. He searched for a solitary spot to lodge his boat against the bank, one where he could lie back on the cushions and watch the light go out and the first stars answer, one by one, that ancient call of evening.

He found it on the bend opposite Kew Gardens: broad water before him taking the sky’s gold and rose, while he lay in shadow. He stretched himself on his back, hands behind his head, his face turned to the open west. So placed, he could see all round without being readily seen—an odd comfort to a man who had always disliked the notion that his mere appearance had power over other people’s attention.

He was beginning to lose himself in that half-speculative fancy of shifting one’s centre until the self feels as external as the landscape—when he became aware of movement on the opposite bank, where willow bushes made a low wavering line.

He turned his eyes, and in the first instant felt a darting presentiment—like the recognition of a flavour before you can name the herb.

It was the girl again.

The dying sunlight struck her small face so that it seemed lit from within, while everything around her sank into dusk. Daniel held himself motionless, afraid that any sudden stir might startle her away. She looked round, but the apparent emptiness seemed to reassure her. She slipped her hat among the willows, took off her woollen cloak, and sat down with a deliberateness that made his throat tighten. Then she dipped the cloak in the water and held it there a little while; drew it up with effort; rose.

The meaning was clear—terribly clear. She meant to wrap that soaked weight around herself as a drowning shroud, to make the river’s work swift and certain.

There was no time to hesitate about frightening her.

He rose, seized his oars, and drove across. Her place lay a little below him; the current helped. At the first sign of movement from the opposite bank, she sank down again, clutching the cloak half out of the water. She crouched and covered her face, as if hoping she had not truly been seen—as if the boatman might be merely crossing by accident.

But soon he was close, steadying his boat against the bank. He spoke gently, with the softness one uses toward a creature in pain.

“Don’t be afraid. You are unhappy. Pray, trust me. Tell me what I can do to help you.”

She lifted her head. The light was behind him now, so his face was clearer to her than hers was to him, and he saw recognition in her gaze. They looked at each other again—those same long moments in which speech seems too blunt.

At last she said, in a low sweet voice, her accent distinct in a way that suggested foreignness and yet could not be called foreign, “I saw you before,” and then, as if her mind were moving by music rather than by sense, she added, “*nella miseria*.”

He could not at first follow. He had a fear—strong and shameful—that her distress had loosened the mind’s hold on reality.

“It was you, singing?” she went on hesitatingly. “*Nessun maggior dolore*.”

The words, uttered in that soft undertone, seemed to carry their melody back into his ear.

“Ah, yes,” he said, understanding. “I am often singing them. But I fear you will injure yourself staying here. Pray let me take you in my boat to some place of safety. And that wet cloak—let me take it.”

He did not touch it without her permission. Even as he spoke he thought she shrank, clasping it more tenaciously; then her eyes held his with a question.

“You look good,” she said. “Perhaps it is God’s command.”

“Do trust me. Let me help you. I will die before I will let any harm come to you.”

She rose from her crouching posture, dragged the saturated cloak, then let it drop—too heavy for her tired arms. She stood with her delicate chilled hands laid one over the other at her waist, stepping back as if to keep a space, leaning her head forward as though she dared not lose sight of his face.

“Great God!” escaped him—so low, so solemn, it was like a prayer that had found a voice without intending it.

The cry was not only for her. A deep old wondering in him—about the unseen person to whom his own face must be like a sign—stirred as if it had been touched with fire. *Perhaps my mother was like this one.* The thought, long held back, rose now with a force that made it tremble through him.

The low words seemed to reassure her; she came close to the boat’s side. Daniel put out his hand. She had already slipped her tiny hand into his—his fingers closed around it—when some new terror struck her. She drew back and whispered, “I have nowhere to go—nobody belonging to me in all this land.”

“I will take you to a lady who has daughters,” he said at once. The answer sprang up because it promised a home-like safety: women’s shelter, women’s hands, women’s voices.

She hesitated still, and then, more timidly than ever, asked, “Do you belong to the theatre?”

“No,” he said, decisively. “I have nothing to do with the theatre.”

Then, with a quiet urgency, “I will put you in perfect safety at once; with a lady—a good woman. I am sure she will be kind. Let us lose no time: you will make yourself ill. Life may still become sweet to you. There are good people—there are good women who will take care of you.”

She drew back no more. She stepped into the boat easily, as if she were used to such movements, and sat on the cushions.

“You had a covering for your head,” he said.

“My hat?” She lifted her hands to her hair. “It is quite hidden in the bush.”

“I will find it,” he said, holding out his hand in a small restraining gesture as she tried to rise. “The boat is fixed.”

He jumped out, found the hat among the willows, lifted the wet cloak, wrung it as well as he could, and threw it into the bottom of the boat. The cloak had that heavy, sodden smell wool takes on when it has drunk river-water—cold, animal, earthy, as if the fleece remembered the rain and the field.

“We must carry the cloak away,” he said, forcing a cheerfulness into his voice, “to prevent any one who may have noticed you from thinking you have been drowned.”

He got in again and handed her the hat.

“I wish I had any other garment than my coat to offer you,” he went on. “But shall you mind throwing it over your shoulders while we are on the water? It is quite an ordinary thing to do, when people return late and are not enough provided with wraps.”

He held out the coat with a smile. She answered with the faintest melancholy smile—so slight it was like a ghost of courtesy—and put it on with a neat quickness that spoke of former habits, of a life in which one had learned to arrange oneself properly even when the heart was breaking.

“I have some biscuits—should you like them?” he asked.

“No; I cannot eat,” she said. “I had still some money left to buy bread.”

He began to row. For many minutes they went swiftly in silence. She did not look at him; she watched the oar. The dip and lift, the dripping, the clean creak, the small splash and hush—she seemed to cling to it as to a lullaby. The twilight deepened; the red flush died; little stars came out and held their places. The moon began to rise but was still caught among trees and building like a pale lamp behind lattices.

Daniel could not see her expression distinctly, and yet her face was present to him with a strange definiteness, as if distress itself had sharpened the lines. One anxiety troubled him: the possibility that her mind was disordered. The attempt on her life was unmistakable, and it coloured every other sign with dread. He longed to speak, to draw her into some steadying common talk—bread, a bed, warmth—but he held back. He did not want to claim the harsh authority of a benefactor, nor to speak to her as if distress gave him rights.

At last she spoke herself, quietly, as if the oar had taught her to begin.

“I like to listen to the oar.”

“So do I,” he said.

“If you had not come, I should have been dead now.”

“I cannot bear you to speak of that. I hope you will never be sorry that I came.”

“I cannot see how I shall be glad to live,” she answered, and the words had a weary exactness. “The *maggior dolore* and the *miseria* have lasted longer than the *tempo felice*.” After a pause she added dreamily, “*Dolore—miseria*—I think those words are alive.”

He was silent. To question her felt like an intrusion, as if he would be putting his hands into a wound to learn its depth. He felt the untranslatability of her inward suffering—how the very words she used were only a thin crust over something private and burning. Even the borrowed Italian, beautiful as it was, seemed a cloak that could not fit the exact shape of her despair.

She went on, still in that musing tone, as if speaking not to him but to some inward judge.

“I thought it was not wicked. Death and life are one before the Eternal. I know our fathers slew their children and then slew themselves, to keep their souls pure. I meant it so. But now I am commanded to live. I cannot see how I shall live.”

“You will find friends,” he said. “I will find them for you.”

She shook her head. “Not my mother and brother. I cannot find them.”

“You are English?” he said at last—clinging to any simple certainty. “You must be—speaking English so perfectly.”

She did not answer at once. She looked at him again, straining to see him in the mixed light, as if she were trying to decide whether he belonged to dream or waking. Sorrowful isolation had benumbed her sense of reality; one could see that the border between inner and outer had worn thin.

“You want to know if I am English?” she said at last.

“I want to know nothing except what you like to tell me,” he answered quickly. Then, still uneasy, “Perhaps it is not good for you to talk.”

“Yes,” she said, as if choosing. “I will tell you. I am English-born. But I am a Jewess.”

He was silent, with an inward start—less surprise than a sudden sense that something he ought to have understood had been waiting there plainly. The cast of her features, the delicate darkness, the way her voice held its music, might have led another to guess Spain; but her words placed her within a history deeper than geography, a people marked and named by others for centuries.

After a little while she asked, very low, and with a sadness that was like the cry of a small dumb creature, “Do you despise me for it?”

“Why should I?” he said. “I am not so foolish.”

“I know many Jews are bad.”

“So are many Christians,” he answered. “But I should not think it fair for you to despise me because of that.”

“My mother and brother were good,” she said. “But I shall never find them. I am come a long way—from abroad. I ran away; but I cannot tell you—I cannot speak of it.” Her voice broke, then steadied again with a stubborn gentleness. “I thought I might find my mother again—God would guide me. But then I despaired. This morning when the light came, I felt as if one word kept sounding within me—Never! never! But now—I begin—to think—” The words dissolved into rising sobs. “I am commanded to live—perhaps we are going to her.”

With that, her restraint gave way. She bent forward, buried her head on her knees, and wept—deeply, helplessly, as if the tears had been waiting for permission.

Daniel rowed on, his arms moving with the steady necessity of the stroke, his mind working in anxious turns. He had first thought to take her straight to Park Lane, to Lady Mallinger; and Lady Mallinger was kindness itself. But he saw, with a shiver of practical dread, the likelihood of Lady Mallinger not being at home; of footmen’s eyes resting on this wet-cloaked, delicate stranger; of bright stairs and hard questions; of the chill authority of a housekeeper or maid who would measure distress by its respectability and find it wanting. A mind already trembling might be frightened into flight—or into a second attempt.

He could not risk that.

Another refuge rose before him—small, safe, warm with the quiet decencies of poverty: Mrs. Meyrick’s little house at Chelsea. He had been there often since his return from abroad. He could see Mrs. Meyrick’s Quakerish neatness, the order that smelled faintly of clean linen and tea-leaves; the three girls with their unspoiled eagerness; the household’s gentle reverence for Hans Meyrick, away in Italy, which would make them ready to do anything asked by Deronda, Hans’s friend and idol. Those girls, with their innocent romance, would see at once in a lovely Jewess the echo of some tale they had cherished—Rebecca, perhaps—and would not begin by suspecting sin.

The vision steadied him. Once decided, he felt no more wavering.

The rumble of the cab toward Chelsea, after the river’s hush, was like being thrust back into a harsher world. Wheels clattered; hoofs struck sparks of sound from the stones; voices were sharpened by streets. The city’s noise, indifferent and incessant, seemed to press on the very skin—an oppression that made him more fiercely determined to win this girl into a pocket of quiet where she could breathe.

She was silent now, spent after weeping. In the cab she set down her hat and tried to rest her head, but the jolting would not let it settle. Still she dozed, and her sweet head hung helplessly from side to side like a tired child’s. Daniel watched her with a protection that felt both urgent and unearned. Her very presence—her voice, her careful English, her fragile beauty—was an appeal that made disbelief seem cruel.

And yet what had brought her to that riverbank?

He thought of an old story Plutarch tells: Delphic women, Maenads, who after torch-lit wandering lay down asleep in a market-place; and how the matrons came and stood silently round them to guard their slumber, and when they woke ministered to them tenderly and saw them safely to their own borders. He clung to that image as to a promise. He could trust the women he was going to—trust them not to let suspicion speak louder than pity.

As the cab jolted on, he had the strange sensation of growing older within the hour, as if this one act of drawing a stranger back from death had shifted the whole weight of his life. He had been questioning whether to take part in the world’s battle; but now the world had thrust a life into his hands, and the question was no longer abstract. Rescue—yes: but how to make sure that snatching someone from death would not be only the beginning of a different misery?

The moment of finding a fellow-creature can be like the moment of finding an idea—full of doubt and exultation, and heavy with consequences that cannot yet be named.

Life, which can sweep down marble staircases with plumes and jewels or huddle in back alleys with hot gin and a hoarse scream, came this night to the Meyricks like a thrifty matron with clean hands—quiet, nimble, and intent on making much of little.

Their house, narrow as a slice cut from London soot, held its peace. The front parlor faced the river, the back looked on gardens; so even with a lamp and two candles burning, a window could be left ajar, letting in air that tasted faintly of water and damp leaves instead of coal-smoke. Mrs. Meyrick sat in the small double room reading aloud in French, her voice clipping consonants neatly, bright as a sharp knife that makes daylight in whatever it divides. On a side table, two candles pooled steady light over Kate’s drawing—publisher’s work, exact and patient. The lamp on the center table served the reader and the two younger girls, Amy and Mab, who were stitching satin cushions intended for “the great world,” though no world could seem much greater than the one contained between their old prints and their faithful furniture.

The place had that rare cleanliness poverty can enforce when display is out of reach and vanity has nothing to spend itself upon. Everything stayed where it had always stayed. Those engravings—saved for by stinting in other matters—were not ornaments but ancestral voices; scenes and heads the children had learned like prayers, the way a family learns its own dialect long before it can explain it. The chairs and tables were old friends, their worn edges known to the fingers. No broker would have coveted much besides the prints and the piano, and yet there was room here for the finest things: music that could make the river outside seem to listen, poetry that could make the lamp-flame steady itself, painting that trained the eye to tenderness.

If there had been seasons when the scarcity was so great that even a servant to light fires and sweep floors was doubtful, still the Meyricks remained fastidious where it mattered to them. They could not quite believe the fashionable world was as coarse and slangy as “literary photographs” pretended. Their oddities—those unexpected recesses and crooked stairways in the mind—came from both parents; but all four women were bound by three cords twisted tight: family love, reverence for the best work and best action, and habitual industry.

Hans, their brother, had longed to spend his money in turning their modest life into something more luxurious. He had been resisted—by all of them, including himself, saved from that triumph of appetite for art which would, later, force him to give up his fellowship. They could laugh at his Gavarni caricatures and still let him be blameless in following a bent their independence did not hinder. A grand treat of opera-going—up in the gallery—when Hans came home: that was enough.

Tonight, as they made their compact little group, one could hardly wish them different. They were all small, suited to their miniature rooms—Mrs. Meyrick scarcely five feet, half French and half Scotch, rippling hair mostly gray under a quakerish net cap, brown brows and bright eyes, black dress buttoned like a priest’s cassock. The daughters matched her in scale and firmness: hair coiled tight and fastened back à la Chinoise, gray skirts worn in Puritan dissent from the then-fashion that demanded skirts to swell like architecture. Their faces looked as if the minds behind them had been shelled like horse-chestnuts—bright, ready, full of speech.

The only creature in the room who might be called large was Hafiz, the Persian cat, enthroned on the brown leather back of a chair, opening his wide eyes now and then to assure himself the lower animals were not plotting disorder.

Mrs. Meyrick had been reading Erckmann-Chatrian’s *Histoire d’un Conscrit*. When she closed the book, Mab—who had let her embroidery slip to the floor so she could lean toward the voice, hungry for it—cried out, “I think that is the finest story in the world.”

“Of course, Mab,” said Amy without lifting her needle. “It is the last you have heard. Whatever pleases you is always the best in its turn.”

“It’s hardly to be called a story,” Kate said, drawing back a little to judge her lines. “It’s history brought near with a strong telescope. We can see the soldiers’ faces—no, more than that—we can hear everything. We can almost hear their hearts beat.”

“I don’t care what you call it,” Mab said, flinging her thimble with a click. “Call it a chapter in Revelations. It makes me want to do something good—something grand. It makes me so sorry for everybody. It makes me like Schiller. I want to take the world in my arms and kiss it. I must kiss you instead, little mother!” And she threw herself about Mrs. Meyrick’s neck.

“Whenever you are in that mood, Mab, down goes your work,” Amy remarked. “It would be doing something good to finish your cushion without soiling it.”

Mab groaned theatrically as she stooped for her satin and thimble. “I wish I had three wounded conscripts to take care of.”

“You would spill their beef tea while you were talking,” said Amy.

“Poor Mab, don’t be hard on her,” Mrs. Meyrick returned. “Give me the embroidery now, child. You go on with your enthusiasm, and I will go on with the pink and white poppy.”

“Well, ma, I think you are more caustic than Amy,” Kate said, still at her drawing.

“Oh—oh—oh!” Mab cried again, standing and stretching her arms as if to push the ceiling higher. “I wish something wonderful would happen. I feel like the deluge—the waters of the great deep are broken up, and the windows of heaven are opened. I must sit down and play the scales.”
