She was lifting the piano lid while the others laughed at her climax, when the hush of the house was cut by the soft, heavy stop of a cab and then a quick rap on the knocker—sharp in that quiet street, a small violence against their peace.

“Dear me!” Mrs. Meyrick started up. “It is after ten, and Phœbe is gone to bed.” She hurried out, leaving the parlor door ajar.

The girls heard her exclamation, half astonishment, half welcome: “Mr. Deronda!”

Mab clasped her hands and whispered loudly, as if afraid her own wish had called something down: “There now! something *is* going to happen.”

Kate and Amy set down pencil and needle, their surprise turning them suddenly still. Deronda’s reply was too low to catch; then Mrs. Meyrick closed the parlor door.

“I know I am trusting to your goodness in a most extraordinary way,” Deronda said, after his brief narrative, his voice held under as if the cab and the night were listening. “But you can imagine how helpless I feel with a young creature like this on my hands. I could not go with her among strangers; and in her nervous state I should dread taking her into a house full of servants. I have trusted to your mercy. I hope you will not think my act unwarrantable.”

“On the contrary,” Mrs. Meyrick answered at once—no hesitation, only that neat, practical compassion which is itself a kind of courage. “You have honored me by trusting me. I see your difficulty. Pray bring her in. I will go and prepare the girls.”

Deronda went back to the cab. Mrs. Meyrick returned to the parlor and spoke quickly, so the matter should be met as simply as one meets a sudden need at table.

“Here is somebody to take care of instead of your wounded conscripts, Mab: a poor girl who was going to drown herself in despair. Mr. Deronda found her only just in time to save her. He brought her along in his boat, and did not know what else it would be safe to do with her, so he has trusted us and brought her here. It seems she is a Jewess, but quite refined, he says—knowing Italian and music.”

The three girls came forward and stood close together, their confidence in one another showing itself in the very way their shoulders aligned. Mab looked almost afraid, as if the marvelous, asked for in jest, had answered in earnest and therefore must be approached with reverence.

At the cab door the pale face now gazing out had a roused, startled look, like a bird that has been handled and still expects the hand to close again. Deronda, keeping his voice gentle and distinct, said, “I have brought you to some of the kindest people in the world: there are daughters like you. It is a happy home. Will you let me take you to them?”

She stepped down obediently, slipping her hand into his as if the act had become her only remaining certainty, and forgetting her hat. When he led her into the full light of the parlor, where the four little women waited, she made a picture that would have touched dulled sensibilities: the darkness of her curls against the pallor of her face, the delicate exhaustion in her posture, the way her eyes struggled to focus as if the world kept shifting under her.

Deronda, inwardly relieved that the Meyricks were so small—the stranger’s head was the highest among them—put her hand at once into Mrs. Meyrick’s. There was no towering, no threatening space: only gentle faces near enough to be read.

“You must be weary, poor child,” Mrs. Meyrick said.

“We will take care of you—we will comfort you—we will love you,” cried Mab, unable to hold back, taking the small right hand between both her own with the eager softness of someone who has longed to give, not merely to feel.

Warmth, human and immediate, worked its way through the bewildered girl. She hung back a fraction—not in refusal but in the instinct to see clearly—letting her eyes move from one face to another. The good-will in them began to reflect in her, not as a smile, but as that subtle easing which tells you fear is loosening its grip. For an instant she looked up at Deronda, as if the mercy in this room must have its source in him; then she turned again to Mrs. Meyrick and said in a sweet tone now steadier than it had been on the river,

“I am a stranger. I am a Jewess. You might have thought I was wicked.”

“No, we are sure you are good,” Mab burst out, as if the very idea were an insult to the trembling hand in hers.

“We think no evil of you, poor child,” Mrs. Meyrick said. “You shall be safe with us. Come now and sit down. You must have some food, and then you must go to rest.”

Kate moved a chair forward with quiet decision; Amy ran to fetch tea—already thinking of water boiled to the right point, the leaf not scalded into bitterness, the small comforts that are more persuasive than speeches. The room filled with familiar domestic sounds: the clink of china, the whisper of fabric as someone shifted, the cat’s soft leap to the floor. Outside, the city’s distant rumble was kept at bay by their thick old walls and the river’s steady hush—an acoustic shelter that made the stranger’s breathing easier, as if the air itself were less harsh when not scored by shouting and wheels.

The girl yielded at last and sat with perfect grace, crossing her small feet, laying her hands one over the other in her lap, looking at her new friends with a kind of placid reverence, as if their faces were icons she dared not touch. Hafiz, having watched restlessly, came forward with tail erect and rubbed himself against her ankles, offering the silent treaty animals offer when they decide you belong.

Deronda felt the hour and the strain of the day gather on him; it was time to go before his presence made this refuge seem less purely theirs.

“Will you allow me to come again and inquire—perhaps at five to-morrow?” he asked Mrs. Meyrick.

“Yes, pray; we shall have had time to make acquaintance then.”

He turned to the girl. “Good-bye,” he said, and held out his hand.

She rose as she took it, and the motion brought back to both of them—sharp, immediate—the earlier moment when she had first grasped that offered hand out of darkness and water. Her eyes lifted to his with reverential fervor.

“The God of our fathers bless you and deliver you from all evil as you have delivered me,” she said. “I did not believe there was any man so good. None before have thought me worthy of the best. You found me poor and miserable, yet you have given me the best.”

Deronda could not answer. The words, the look, the small hand in his—everything pressed at the place in him where speech becomes inadequate. With silent adieux to the Meyricks, he hurried away, leaving behind him, in that small room by the river, the beginning of a sheltering bond.

CHAPTER XIX.

“I pity the man who can travel from Dan to Beersheba, and say, ‘’Tis all barren’: and so it is: and so is all the world to him who will not cultivate the fruits it offers.”—STERNE: _Sentimental Journey_.

No one would have called Deronda romantic without doing violence to the quiet composure he wore as carefully as a well-cut coat. Yet beneath it there burned a heat that answered to ordinary life as a kitchen fire answers to plain ingredients—making fragrance out of what looked like mere necessity. Some minds pass through the world as if everything were tasteless, and then complain there is no savor; but poetry, like good broth, is not rare—it is only lost on those whose senses have been dulled by habit, by hurry, by the ceaseless clatter of surfaces.

He felt it that night with a vividness that would not let him lie down inside himself. London, even at its latest hours, has its own soundscape: the far, iron-shod roll of wheels along the main streets; the occasional shout that rises and breaks like a gull’s cry; a door slammed too hard; a watchman’s measured step; and, in the spaces between, that uneasy urban hush which is never truly silence, only a thinner veil over the city’s restless breathing. Deronda lay listening, but it was not the external noises that kept him awake. His mind replayed, with the clean sharpness of remembered taste, the moments since he had first discerned Mirah on the river-brink.

The Thames, too, has its voice—lap and suck against the stones, the sly whispering along timbers, the sudden hollow slap under an oar. He heard it again as if the water still ran under his bed. And with that voice came her own: not loud, not showy, but carrying an accent like a spice you cannot mistake once you have known it. He took up a book to force his thoughts into the narrow channel of printed lines; the words were only a mesh, and through it his inward sight kept seeing her—her look of resolved despair, the wet chill of the river air clinging about her, the tremor in her speech that made every sentence feel as if it had cost her breath.

For him, the finding of Mirah had the kind of stirring inevitableness that ancient stories ascribe to fateful meetings—only it had happened in a very modern way, among common garments and common dangers, with no witnesses but the river and the city. Yet the mythic and the domestic can share the same room, as easily as a microscope can sit on the same table with a loaf newly cut. What drives them out is not science or railways, but the deadening clang of minds that cannot be moved by awe, tenderness, or fellowship—minds that hear the world’s music as mere noise.

Mirah’s search for her mother gripped him with a peculiar force, because some chord in his own life answered to it. The first movement of his sympathy was practical: if certain persons were indeed alive somewhere in London, there were ways—quiet, methodical, almost experimental—of setting the right machinery in motion until a hidden fact surfaced. There are men who can trace a family as a food-historian traces an ingredient through markets and mouths: by small evidence, by the residue of habit, by the scent of a dialect clinging to a name. It was possible.

But his sympathy did not come alone; it brought with it a dread he knew too well—the dread that to find what one longs for may be to meet calamity. In the boat she had said her mother and brother were good. Yet goodness, he knew, can be a thing preserved in the amber of a child’s memory—pure because the child was pure, and because longing will sweeten what it cannot verify. Ten or twelve years are time enough for harsh changes. A pot left unattended does not keep its flavor; it scorches, turns, breeds bitterness. Time does its work on souls as on provisions.

And there were other forebodings, less fair and more humiliating to his pride in justice. Deronda’s nature was strongly inclined to take the side of those who bore inherited disadvantages; scorn flung at a man for the mere name of his people would always rouse him to indignant pity. Yet he had never been drawn, in any close and daily way, toward existing Jews. What he knew of them was chiefly a collection of facts and rumors—some true, some swollen by prejudice—which had gathered in his mind like rancid tales passed from mouth to mouth until they seem to have the authority of experience. Of the learned and accomplished among them, he had assumed—without having cared enough to examine—that they must have dropped their religion, wished to be merged and absorbed, and so to escape the old mark.

He hated, in theory, the severance of past from present; he had often protested against that cheap forgetting which refuses to see history moving in living bodies. Yet in practice he had been like many who protest nobly and inquire little. He had been content with generalities: a long-oppressed race must have its virtues and its vices—endurance, acuteness, clannishness, suspicion, and whatever else the world’s cruelty has kneaded into human nature when it keeps it always under the hand.

Now, because Mirah’s yearning had made the question immediate—because it was no longer an “idea” but a life that might be broken—his mind, to his own discomfort, began to crowd itself with disagreeable images of what the finding might mean. It was as if he stood at the door of some kitchen whose air might, at the first opening, either welcome him with the warm clean smell of bread, or strike him sick with the sourness of neglect. He could not yet know. Perhaps, through Mrs. Meyrick, he might gather more exact hints from Mirah’s own lips—names, places, scraps of remembered speech. Her voice and accent were themselves clues, belonging to no fashionable smoothing-out of utterance, but to a native cadence carrying history inside it—something that could not be translated away without loss. And her very refinement, her delicacy of manner, the purity that seemed to clothe her like a consecrating garment, made him shrink the more from associating her—either in imagination or in fact—with anything he dreaded as coarse, contaminating, or shameless.

Fine words can be used like perfumes to hide what is unpleasant; but the mind, when it is afraid, thinks in naked pictures. Deronda’s thoughts would not remain decorous. They went on, swift and involuntary, showing him scenes as if they were thrust upon his sight. He saw himself led—by some official guide with indifferent eyes—into a dingy street where the air was thick with stale damp and cheap fried food, where drains and soot had their own bitter taste on the tongue. He entered through a dim doorway and found a hawk-eyed woman, rough-haired, unwashed, bargaining with hard rapidity, pinching a hungry girl’s last poor finery between fingers that had no gentleness in them. Or else—in some quarter only the more hideous for being smarter, where bright shop-lights made vice look respectable—he found himself under the too-close breath of a young man talkative and familiar, eager to show acquaintance with “gentlemen’s tastes,” speaking in a slippery lingua franca of commerce, that dominant lexicon which smooths over shame and calls it business. He imagined that voice—oily, incessant—filling the air like a machine that cannot be silenced; and he felt, with physical repugnance, how such sounds can invade the mind, scraping at it until one’s better feelings are worn down.

It would be easy, perhaps, to blame him for the unlovely drift of these images. Yet they sprang less from any natural delight in insult than from the governance of dread; and if Mirah’s parents had been Christian, the chief difference might have been only that his forebodings would have fed on a wider acquaintance. The habit of connecting unknown parentage with peril was already rooted in him. His own life had made the link seem reasonable; his own withheld knowledge had taught him how a family history can be like a language half-lost—words missing, meanings guessed at, the whole story liable to be distorted by the louder voices that dominate a household and a society.

But the practical question pressed: what was to be done with Mirah now? She needed shelter—shelter of the body and of the spirit; protection not as alms, but as a human right owed to her by the mere fact that she was vulnerable and alone. In him, every instinct of chivalry rose up, not as a flourish but as a duty: the sooner and the more firmly he could engage the interest of others besides himself, the more safely he would fulfill her claim upon him. He had no right to make her dependent on him alone, though he might have the means. Indeed, the depth of the impression she had made on him sharpened his resolve that she should understand herself to be entirely independent of him—free from any chain that gratitude might fasten, free from any suspicion that could poison what he meant to keep clean.

And there was another anxiety, more inward. Vague visions of the future—visions he tried to dismiss as mere fantastic vapor—still left their influence behind like an after-taste: he felt an urgent need that those who watched him closely should know, from the first, the true history of his relation to Mirah. He had learned to hate secrecy in the great ties and obligations of life—hated it the more because he himself was ensnared in a secrecy he could not simply cast off. He had made a vow that, since the truths which disgrace mortals are not all of their own making, the truth should never be made a disgrace to another by his act. The vow was like a steady tone in his ear, a sustaining note he feared to lose amid the city’s discord. He was not without terror lest, by some weakness, he should break it and slide into that apologetic philosophy which explains the world into meaning that nothing better exists than one’s own conduct.

Once, in the thick of the night, he resolved that he would tell the whole of his adventure to Sir Hugo and Lady Mallinger at breakfast the next morning—plainly, at once, so that no shadow could grow by concealment. But then another possibility checked him: his next visit to Mrs. Meyrick’s might reveal something quite new—some detail from Mirah, some name, some remembered phrase in her own tongue, something that would change what he ought to say and how. He wavered, weighing openness against premature disclosure, until at last he went to sleep on one conclusion: he would wait until that visit had been made.

Mirah said she had slept well; and when she came down in Mab’s black dress, her dark hair still loosening itself into fresh curls from its heavy washing, there was already a softer bloom stealing back under the faint pallor, as if rest had stirred warmth again in the blood. Mab, with the solemn pride of a small priestess serving at a new altar, had carried the breakfast-tray upstairs, and now ushered her down as if conducting a rescued princess—pausing, in the very doorway of the little parlor, to show off a triumph.

For want of shoes small enough, Mab had rushed out and returned with a pair of tiny felt slippers; and in them Mirah’s feet looked the more delicately finished because the borrowed dress ended short, showing the cheap under-skirt and the slim ankles above those farthing buckles which Mab, in her rapture, treated as jewels.

“Oh, if you please, mamma,” Mab cried, clasping her hands and dropping toward Mirah’s feet as if to worship them, “look at the slippers—how beautiful they fit! I declare she is like Queen Budoor—‘two delicate feet, the work of the protecting and all-recompensing Creator, support her; and I wonder how they can sustain what is above them.’”

Mirah, with a child’s startled obedience to the attention, looked down at her own feet and then up again with a shy smile that went straight to Mrs. Meyrick’s heart. The mother, neat and composed as ever, felt the familiar inward check of prudence—one could hardly imagine evil in this creature; but wise people would bid her be cautious. Yet the smile asked for nothing except leave to be grateful.

“I fear the feet have had to sustain their burden a little too often lately,” Mrs. Meyrick said gently. “But to-day she will rest and be my companion.”

“And she will tell you so many things, and I shall not hear them,” Mab grumbled, feeling herself put into the very first volume of a romance and obliged to miss whole chapters because she had pupils.

Kate was already gone down the river to sketch, and Amy had errands: it was what Mrs. Meyrick wished. If this young creature had come washed up, as it were, on the threshold of their quiet life, there must be sorrow behind her; and sorrow, if it was to be borne with decency, needed privacy, not a chorus.

The small front parlor had a hush in it that morning which made even the commonest movements feel like part of a rite. The window stood open on the mild air; the river, sunlit, seemed to breathe. On the walls the black-and-white prints—Virgins and sibyls, prophets, the School of Athens, the Last Supper, faces out of Holbein and Rembrandt, tragic muses and last-century children—hung like a silent company gathered to listen. Hafiz purred on the sill, answering the outside world with his small domestic thunder; the clock ticked without haste, and when wheels passed in the street their sound fell away again as if the house itself were a sheltering hand laid over the ears. Mrs. Meyrick, sorting colored wools for her embroidery, was more aware than usual of how the health of a mind lies partly in the sounds it lives among—how merciful it is that there are still rooms where the day is not clattered into pieces, where no harsh din insists on ruling the heart’s pace.

Mirah sat opposite, hands clasped on her lap, ankles crossed, the new slippers planted with a quietness that made Mab’s rapture seem less absurd. At first her eyes traveled slowly over the room, taking in the prints, the little domestic order, the soft moving of light on wools; then they settled on Mrs. Meyrick with a kind of reverent dependence, as if the older woman’s very stillness promised safety. Mrs. Meyrick, thinking it best to let the quiet itself invite speech, did not disturb it.

At length Mirah began, softly, as if she feared loudness might break the thin glass of peace.

“I remember my mother’s face better than anything; yet I was not seven when I was taken away, and I am nineteen now.”

“I can understand that,” Mrs. Meyrick said. “There are earliest things that last the longest.”

“Oh yes—it was the earliest. I think my life began with waking up and loving my mother’s face. It was so near to me, and her arms were round me, and she sang to me.” Mirah’s voice grew steadier as it moved into remembrance, like a hand finding a familiar tool. “One hymn she sang so often—so often—and then she taught me to sing it with her; it was the first I ever sang. They were always Hebrew hymns she sang; and because I never knew the meaning of the words, they seemed full of nothing but our love and happiness.

“When I lay in my little bed and it was all white above me, she used to bend over me—between me and the white—and sing in a sweet, low voice. I can dream myself back into that time when I am awake; and it often comes back to me in my sleep—my hand is very little, I put it up to her face and she kisses it. Sometimes in my dreams I begin to tremble and think that we are both dead; but then I wake up and my hand lies like this, and for a moment I hardly know myself. But if I could see my mother again I should know her.”

“You must expect some change after twelve years,” said Mrs. Meyrick. “See my grey hair: ten years ago it was bright brown. The days and months pace over us like restless little birds, and leave the marks of their feet backward and forward; especially when they are like birds with heavy hearts—then they tread heavily.”

“Ah, I am sure her heart has been heavy for want of me. But to feel her joy if we could meet again—if I could make her know I love her, and give her deep comfort after all her mourning! If that could be, I should mind nothing. I should be glad that I have lived through my trouble. I did despair. The world seemed miserable and wicked; none helped me so that I could bear their looks and words; I felt that my mother was dead, and death was the only way to her.

“But then—in the last moment—yesterday, when I longed for the water to close over me, and I thought that death was the best image of mercy—then goodness came to me living, and I felt trust in the living. And—it is strange—but I began to hope she was living too. And now, I with you—here—this morning, peace and hope have come into me like a flood. I want nothing; I can wait; because I hope and believe and am grateful—oh, so grateful! You have not thought evil of me—you have not despised me.”

She spoke with low-toned fervor, never moving her hands, as if she feared any gesture might betray her into sobbing. Mrs. Meyrick felt her eyes moisten; she bent over her sorted wools, though she had ceased to see the colors.

“Many others would have felt as we do, my dear,” she said.

“But I did not meet them—they did not come to me.”

“How was it that you were taken from your mother?”

Mirah drew a breath, and the sound of it was like a door opening into a colder passage.

“Ah, I am a long while coming to that. It is dreadful to speak of—yet I must tell you. I must tell you everything. My father—it was he that took me away. I thought we were only going on a little journey; and I was pleased. There was a box with all my little things in. But we went on board a ship, and got farther and farther away from the land. Then I was ill; and I thought it would never end—it was the first misery, and it seemed endless. But at last we landed. I knew nothing then, and believed what my father said. He comforted me, and told me I should go back to my mother. But it was America we had reached, and it was long years before we came back to Europe.

“At first I often asked my father when we were going back; and I tried to learn writing fast, because I wanted to write to my mother; but one day when he found me trying to write a letter, he took me on his knee and told me my mother and brother were dead—that was why we did not go back. I remember my brother a little; he carried me once; but he was not always at home. I believed my father when he said they were dead. I saw them under the earth when he said they were there, with their eyes forever closed. I never thought of its not being true; and I used to cry every night in my bed for a long while.

“Then when she came so often to me, in my sleep, I thought she must be living about me though I could not always see her, and that comforted me. I was never afraid in the dark because of that; and very often in the day I used to shut my eyes and bury my face and try to see her and to hear her singing. I came to do that at last without shutting my eyes.”

She paused, and her face took on a sweet stillness, as if the remembered sound had filled her ears. The river’s hush seemed to lean toward her, holding its breath. Mrs. Meyrick waited a moment, then spoke, anxious not to let Mirah drift away into that inward refuge where no help could follow.

“Still your father was not unkind to you, I hope?”

“No; he petted me, and took pains to teach me. He was an actor; and I found out, after, that the ‘Coburg’ I used to hear of his going to at home was a theatre. But he had more to do with the theatre than acting. He had not always been an actor; he had been a teacher, and knew many languages. His acting was not very good, I think; but he managed the stage, and wrote and translated plays.

“An Italian lady—a singer—lived with us a long time. They both taught me; and I had a master besides, who made me learn by heart and recite. I worked quite hard, though I was so little; and I was not nine when I first went on the stage. I could easily learn things, and I was not afraid.

“But then and ever since I hated our way of life. My father had money, and we had finery about us in a disorderly way; always there were men and women coming and going; there was loud laughing and disputing—strutting, snapping of fingers, jeering—faces I did not like to look at, though many petted and caressed me. All those noises—those sudden shrieks of laughter, those sharp claps and calls—went through me as if they were meant to drive out the quieter voice I remembered. But then I remembered my mother.

“Even at first, when I understood nothing, I shrank away from all those things outside me into companionship with thoughts that were not like them; and I gathered thoughts very fast, because I read many things—plays and poetry, Shakespeare and Schiller—and learned evil and good.

“My father began to believe that I might be a great singer: my voice was considered wonderful for a child; and he had the best teaching for me. But it was painful that he boasted of me, and set me to sing for show at any minute, as if I had been a musical box. Once when I was nine years old, I played the part of a little girl who had been forsaken and did not know it, and sat singing to herself while she played with flowers. I did it without any trouble; but the clapping and all the sounds of the theatre were hateful to me; and I never liked the praise I had, because it all seemed very hard and unloving. I missed the love and trust I had been born into.

“I made a life in my own thoughts quite different from everything about me. I chose what seemed to me beautiful out of the plays and everything, and made my world out of it; and it was like a sharp knife always grazing me that we had two sorts of life which jarred so with each other—women looking good and gentle on the stage, and saying good things as if they felt them, and directly after I saw them with coarse, ugly manners. My father sometimes noticed my shrinking ways; and Signora said one day, when I had been rehearsing, ‘She will never be an artist: she has no notion of being anybody but herself. That does very well now, but by-and-by you will see—she will have no more face and action than a singing-bird.’ My father was angry, and they quarrelled. I sat alone and cried, because what she had said was like a long unhappy future unrolled before me.

“I did not want to be an artist; but this was what my father expected of me. After a while Signora left us, and a governess used to come and give me lessons in different things, because my father began to be afraid of my singing too much; but I still acted from time to time.

“Rebellious feelings grew stronger in me, and I wished to get away from this life; but I could not tell where to go, and I dreaded the world. Besides, I felt it would be wrong to leave my father: I dreaded doing wrong, for I thought I might get wicked and hateful to myself, in the same way that many others seemed hateful to me. For so long, so long I had never felt my outside world happy; and if I got wicked I should lose my world of happy thoughts where my mother lived with me. That was my childish notion all through those years. Oh, how long they were!”

Her eyes wandered again toward the river, as if she listened for the old lullaby in its steady movement. Mrs. Meyrick—who had been brought up to think of duty in certain familiar English words—felt herself fumbling, and yet would not be false by using phrases that might strike Mirah’s experience as foreign, or as the speech of those who take the largest matters and make them small by misnaming.

“Had you no teaching about what was your duty?” she asked.

“No—only that I ought to do what my father wished. He did not follow our religion at New York, and I think he wanted me not to know much about it. But because my mother used to take me to the synagogue, and I remembered sitting on her knee and looking through the railing and hearing the chanting and singing, I longed to go. One day when I was quite small I slipped out and tried to find the synagogue, but I lost myself a long while till a pedlar questioned me and took me home. My father, missing me, had been much in fear, and was very angry. I too had been so frightened at losing myself that it was long before I thought of venturing out again.

“But after Signora left us we went to rooms where our landlady was a Jewess and observed her religion. I asked her to take me with her to the synagogue; and I read in her prayer-books and Bible, and when I had money enough I asked her to buy me books of my own, for these books seemed a closer companionship with my mother: I knew that she must have looked at the very words and said them. In that way I have come to know a little of our religion, and the history of our people, besides piecing together what I read in plays and other books about Jews and Jewesses; because I was sure my mother obeyed her religion.

“I had left off asking my father about her. It is very dreadful to say it, but I began to disbelieve him. I had found that he did not always tell the truth, and made promises without meaning to keep them; and that raised my suspicion that my mother and brother were still alive though he had told me they were dead. For in going over the past again as I got older and knew more, I felt sure my mother had been deceived, and had expected to see us back again after a very little while; and my father taking me on his knee and telling me that my mother and brother were both dead seemed to me now but a bit of acting, to set my mind at rest. The cruelty of that falsehood sank into me, and I hated all untruth because of it.

“I wrote to my mother secretly: I knew the street—Colman Street—where we lived, and that it was not Blackfriars Bridge and the Coburg, and that our name was Cohen then, though my father called us Lapidoth, because, he said, it was a name of his forefathers in Poland. I sent my letter secretly; but no answer came, and I thought there was no hope for me.

“Our life in America did not last much longer. My father suddenly told me we were to pack up and go to Hamburg, and I was rather glad. I hoped we might get among a different sort of people, and I knew German quite well—some German plays almost all by heart. My father spoke it better than he spoke English. I was thirteen then, and I seemed to myself quite old—I knew so much, and yet so little. I think other children cannot feel as I did. I had often wished that I had been drowned when I was going away from my mother. But I set myself to obey and suffer: what else could I do?”

She stopped, and in the stillness the small household sounds—the cat’s purr, the clock, the faint far-off traffic—seemed to arrange themselves around her words, as if the room were taking care not to interrupt.

“One day when we were on our voyage, a new thought came into my mind. I was not very ill that time, and I kept on deck a good deal. My father acted and sang and joked to amuse people on board, and I used often to hear remarks about him. One day, when I was looking at the sea and nobody took notice of me, I overheard a gentleman say, ‘Oh, he is one of those clever Jews—a rascal, I shouldn’t wonder. There’s no race like them for cunning in the men and beauty in the women. I wonder what market he means that daughter for.’

“When I heard this it darted into my mind that the unhappiness in my life came from my being a Jewess, and that always to the end the world would think slightly of me and that I must bear it, for I should be judged by that name; and it comforted me to believe that my suffering was part of the affliction of my people—my part in the long song of mourning that has been going on through ages and ages. For if many of our race were wicked and made merry in their wickedness—what was that but part of the affliction borne by the just among them, who were despised for the sins of their brethren?”

Her voice faltered, and she looked suddenly afraid, as if a word might be a chain.

“But you have not rejected me,” she added quickly, with a change into gratitude, clinging to the one fact that saved the whole narrative from ending in bitterness.

“And we will try to save you from being judged unjustly by others, my poor child,” Mrs. Meyrick said. She had laid down her work now, her hands folded; her listening face was scarcely less eager than Mab’s would have been. “Go on—go on. Tell me all.”

“After that we lived in different towns—Hamburg and Vienna the longest. I began to study singing again; and my father always got money about the theatres. I think he brought a good deal of money from America, I never knew why we left. For some time he was in great spirits about my singing, and he made me rehearse parts and act continually. He looked forward to my coming out in the opera.

“But by-and-by it seemed that my voice would never be strong enough—it did not fulfil its promise. My master at Vienna said, ‘Don’t strain it further: it will never do for the public:—it is gold, but a thread of gold dust.’ My father was bitterly disappointed. We were not so well off at that time.

“I think I have not quite told you what I felt about my father. I knew he was fond of me and meant to indulge me, and that made me afraid of hurting him; but he always mistook what would please me and give me happiness. It was his nature to take everything lightly; and I soon left off asking him any questions about things that I cared for much, because he always turned them off with a joke. He would even ridicule our own people; and once when he had been imitating their movements and their tones in praying, only to make others laugh, I could not restrain myself—for I always had an anger in my heart about my mother—and when we were alone, I said, ‘Father, you ought not to mimic our own people before Christians who mock them: would it not be bad if I mimicked you, that they might mock you?’

“But he only shrugged his shoulders and laughed and pinched my chin, and said, ‘You couldn’t do it, my dear.’

“It was this way of turning off everything that made a great wall between me and my father, and whatever I felt most I took the most care to hide from him. For there were some things—when they were laughed at I could not bear it: the world seemed like a hell to me. Is this world and all the life upon it only like a farce or a vaudeville, where you find no great meanings? Why then are there tragedies and grand operas, where men do difficult things and choose to suffer? I think it is silly to speak of all things as a joke.

“And I saw that his wishing me to sing the greatest music, and parts in grand operas, was only wishing for what would fetch the greatest price. That hemmed in my gratitude for his affectionateness, and the tenderest feeling I had toward him was pity. Yes, I did sometimes pity him.

“He had aged and changed. Now he was no longer so lively. I thought he seemed worse—less good to others than to me. Every now and then in the latter years his gaiety went away suddenly, and he would sit at home silent and gloomy; or he would come in and fling himself down and sob, just as I have done myself when I have been in trouble. If I put my hand on his knee and say, ‘What is the matter, father?’ he would make no answer, but would draw my arm round his neck and put his arm round me and go on crying.

“There never came any confidence between us; but oh, I was sorry for him. At those moments I knew he must feel his life bitter, and I pressed my cheek against his head and prayed. Those moments were what most bound me to him; and I used to think how much my mother once loved him, else she would not have married him.

“But soon there came the dreadful time. We had been at Pesth and we came back to Vienna. In spite of what my master Leo had said, my father got me an engagement—not at the opera, but to take singing parts at a suburb theatre in Vienna. He had nothing to do with the theatre then; I did not understand what he did, but I think he was continually at a gambling house, though he was careful always about taking me to the theatre.

“I was very miserable. The plays I acted in were detestable to me. Men came about us and wanted to talk to me; women and men seemed to look at me with a sneering smile. It was no better than a fiery furnace. Perhaps I make it worse than it was—you don’t know that life: but the glare and the faces, and my having to go on and act and sing what I hated, and then see people who came to stare at me behind the scenes—it was all so much worse than when I was a little girl.

“I went through with it; I did it; I had set my mind to obey my father and work, for I saw nothing better that I could do. But I felt that my voice was getting weaker, and I knew that my acting was not good except when it was not really acting, but the part was one that I could be myself in, and some feeling within me carried me along. That was seldom.”

People repeat, with an air of finality, that knowledge is power. They forget how swiftly ignorance can unmake what patience took centuries to cure and season. Knowledge keeps its stores like a careful housekeeper—records stacked as neatly as jars of preserved fruit in a cool pantry, each label a promise to the future. Ignorance, hungry for the day’s heat and unwilling to walk to the woodpile, will tear down the shelves and feed the fire with the very labels—burning the names, the dates, the old dialect words no one thought to save, just to give a moment’s sharp flavor to one careless roast. Knowledge raises a slow, scrupulous architecture; ignorance—great, blind, noisy—lumbers in and, for sport, shakes the pillars, leaving only soot and a ringing emptiness where there used to be rooms full of remembered voices.

And in a single life, too, one may watch it happen: the dull, fatal ignorance of how one event binds itself to another, the wilful belief that consequences can be forced like a sauce rushed on too fierce a flame—boiling over, scalding, spoiling everything with haste. There are days when the smallest, most contemptible detail—an ugly station, a sour smell, a voice that grates—tips a mind toward ruin as surely as a stone tips a cart into a ditch.

It was half-past ten when Gwendolen Harleth, after her leaden journey from Leubronn, arrived at the station from which she must drive to Offendene. No carriage waited; no familiar face lifted a hand. From Dover she had telegraphed naming a later train, and in her impatience—her hatred of being kept under the station roof and the eyes of strangers—she had come on without imagining what it would be to arrive alone at that desolate point of rail that seemed chosen because it belonged to no place in particular, being equally far from everywhere.

So she was set down a solitary woman with her large trunks, and the waiting-room received her like an insult: dirty paint flaking under her gaze, a dusty decanter of water that looked as though it had stood there since last winter, and great printed texts calling on her to repent—texts that felt, to her, like the cracked voice of a preacher heard through a wall. She fled out to the door that looked toward the lane and fields, yet even there the day offered no comfort. Autumn sunlight fell with a kind of tired pity; the leaves and grass shivered under a wind that worried at everything—turning up the feathers of a cock and two croaking hens that seemed, in their lonely fussing, to have lost their whole brood and not know what to do with the remainder of life. The very air had a thin, raw scent, as if the earth had been rinsed and left to dry in draught.

The railway official hovered, resource-less and incurious, watching her and her luggage with an innocent stare made unbearable by a cast in his eye. He was new; he did not know her; and in his not knowing her there lay the humiliation that he must class her with any other stranded traveller, not “high in the world,” not guarded by attendance. That ignorance in him—mere blankness—had power enough to sting her.

At last the vehicle came within sight: a dirty old barouche, slowly being made ready by an elderly laborer. Such details look wretchedly small beside the word “history”; yet most turns in life cannot be accounted for without just these specks of annoyance that lodge, accumulate, and harden into motive. A soul will take its theory of the world from a draught, a stain, a look; and to be dropped alone at an irrelevant place, with the new gnawing consciousness of no income, might prompt even a thinker to bitterness about the origin of things. How much more must such trifles tell on a young woman with fastidious taste, an Indian shawl over her arm, twenty cubic feet of trunks by her side, and a mortal dread of the poverty that was suddenly giving her imagination a thousand disagreeables to chew upon like grit between teeth.

They told heavily on Gwendolen. Her spirit, which had set itself up in resistance all through the journey, began to droop under this first sample of “home.” What was the good of living if the future meant ugliness, hardship, humiliation? The drive in the uneasy barouche made those questions repeat themselves like the clatter of wheels over ruts. One trunk squeezed the meek driver; another was lashed with rope on the seat in front of her. The old leather smelled stale and damp; the road’s dust rose and settled, tasting of chalk. And there was sound—too much sound—iron-shod hooves striking flint, a loose panel rattling, the wind worrying the hedges, the barouche groaning as if it complained aloud of the task of carrying her.

All the way from Leubronn her ruling vision had been of going abroad again. Surely, surely, there must be some little income left—her mother could not have meant they would literally have nothing. The picture she had accustomed herself to was dreary but bearable: some dull place on the Continent, living poorly; and she had seen poor English people abroad—pale, pinched, trying to make a little gentility out of thin soup and worn gloves—and she imagined herself plunged among them, despised and bored, with Alice and Bertha and Fanny and Isabel all growing up in tediousness around her while she drifted toward thirty and her mother sank deeper into melancholy. She did not mean to submit. She had not quite believed in the misfortune.

Yet weariness and disgust, fed by this miserable arrival, began to act on her like an uncomfortable waking—worse, even, than uneasy dreams, because now the air was cold and the dust real. The self-delight with which she had once kissed her image in the glass had faded. What was the good of being charming, clever, resolute, if events could turn out anyhow? Men were hateful—yes, hateful. And in these last hours, hatred had shifted its object: she was beginning to be angry with Grandcourt not only as a man to be feared, but as the man whose existence—whose hideous flaw—had hindered her from marrying him and escaping this very lot. It is one thing to despise a thing in itself, and another to despise it the more because it blocks your way.

The barouche lumbered into the avenue; the windows of Offendene showed themselves. Then under the portico a figure appeared, and the hard selfishness in Gwendolen’s breast gave way as quickly as a crust breaks when a warm knife presses it. She sprang from the carriage; she saw the dear beautiful face—her mother’s—now with fresh lines of sadness traced upon it as if grief had been doing needlework in the skin. Gwendolen flung her arms round Mrs. Davilow’s neck, and for the moment all sorrow existed only as something that touched her mother.

Behind were the four “superfluous girls,” the sad, quiet faces; each had her own hidden world, important to herself and to no one else, and all of them felt—poor things—that where Gwendolen was, something interesting might happen, some decisive movement would be made. Even her hurried submission to their kisses, even her “Now go away, girls,” carried that harsh comfort which weakness takes from decision in another.

Miss Merry, with her meek depressed air—which had once been puzzling in a governess attached to the family—was now only on a level with the rest of the circumstances. She did not expect greeting; she busied herself with trunks and coachman’s pay. Mrs. Davilow and Gwendolen hastened upstairs and shut themselves in the black-and-yellow bedroom.

“Never mind, mamma dear,” Gwendolen said, tenderly pressing her handkerchief where tears rolled down Mrs. Davilow’s cheeks. “Never mind. I don’t mind. I will do something. I will be something. Things will come right. It seemed worse because I was away. Come now—you must be glad because I am here.”

She felt every word. Compassion stirred in her like sudden heat, and the vague projects that had glanced through her mind on the journey gathered into a sharper shape, as if now she could see how to become “something.” It was one of her best moments—one of those moments when even self-love turns into a kind of brave devotion—and her fond mother, forgetting everything below that high tide mark, looked at her with something like adoration.

“Bless you, my good, good darling!” Mrs. Davilow said. “I can be happy, if you can!”

But the tide ebbed later. Misfortune ceased to be a telegram and began to sit down in the house like a tyrannical inmate, breathing its cold breath into corners. At first, it was still Offendene: the large solid rooms; the quiet; the familiar order that secured her ease. Her toilet luxuries were still there, still ministered to without her lifting a finger. A little tray with her favorite food was brought to her in private, because she had said, “Keep them all away from us to-day, mamma. Let you and me be alone together.”

When she came down into the drawing-room, fresh as a newly-dipped swan, and leaned against the cushions of the settee beside her mother, the worst had not yet fully struck her. She felt prepared; she began with deliberate intention.

“What have you thought of doing, exactly, mamma?”

“Oh, my dear, the next thing is to move away from this house. Mr. Haynes is most fortunately as glad to have it now as he would have been when we took it. Lord Brackenshaw’s agent is to arrange everything with him to the best advantage for us—Bazley, you know; not at all an ill-natured man.”

“I cannot help thinking Lord Brackenshaw would let you stay here rent-free, mamma,” said Gwendolen. Her mind, trained more in reading admiration than in reading accounts, moved naturally to that sort of hope.

“My dear child, Lord Brackenshaw is in Scotland, and knows nothing about us. Neither your uncle nor I would choose to apply to him. Besides, what could we do in this house without servants, and without money to warm it? The sooner we are out the better. We have nothing to carry but our clothes, you know.”

“I suppose you mean to go abroad, then?” Gwendolen said. At least that future had been rehearsed.

“Oh no, dear—no. How could we travel? You never did learn anything about income and expenses.” Mrs. Davilow tried to smile, and laid her hand on Gwendolen’s, adding more mournfully, “That makes it so much harder for you, my pet.”

“But where are we to go?” The question came sharp, as if fear had edged her voice.

“It is all decided. A little furniture is to be got in from the rectory—all that can be spared.” Mrs. Davilow hesitated, dreading less for herself than for the shock she must give. “It is Sawyer’s Cottage we are to go to.”

At first Gwendolen said nothing. She paled; anger rose in her throat like something bitter. Then she spoke with haughtiness.

“That is impossible. Something else ought to have been thought of. My uncle ought not to allow that. I will not submit to it.”

“My sweet child, what else could have been thought of? Your uncle is as kind as he can be—but he is suffering himself; he has his family to bring up. And do you quite understand? We have nothing—absolutely nothing except what he and my sister give us.” Mrs. Davilow spoke timidly, yet forced herself on, because how else to make the fact real? “They have been as wise and active as possible, and we must try to earn something. I and the girls are going to work a table-cloth border for the Ladies’ Charity at Winchester, and a communion cloth the parishioners are to present to Pennicote Church.”

She offered details as one offers a thin broth—hoping it will go down, knowing it is poor nourishment. Gwendolen, caught as in a nightmare by the image of that house where an exciseman had lived, persisted.

“But surely somewhere else than Sawyer’s Cottage might have been found.”

“No indeed, dear. Houses are scarce, and we may be thankful to get anything so private. It is not so very bad. There are two little parlors and four bedrooms. You shall sit alone whenever you like.”

But the sympathetic care for her mother had gone low; the sound of “two little parlors” came to her like the clink of a cheap spoon against a tin cup. She did not answer the tenderness.

“I cannot conceive that all your property is gone at once, mamma. How can you be sure in so short a time? It is not a week since you wrote to me.”

“The first news came much earlier, dear. But I would not spoil your pleasure till it was quite necessary.”

“Oh, how vexatious!” Gwendolen colored with fresh anger. “If I had known, I could have brought home the money I had won; and for want of knowing, I stayed and lost it. I had nearly two hundred pounds, and it would have done for us to live on a little while till I could carry out some plan.” She paused, and then broke out more impetuously. “Everything has gone against me. People have come near me only to blight me.”

Among those “people” her mind included Deronda. If he had not interfered—if his voice, his look, his insistence had not stood between her and the gaming-table—she might have gone again with a few napoleons and won back her losses. Even now, the memory of that moment brought a strange soreness, as if a word had been taken from her mouth and she could not translate the feeling into any language that would make others see it as she saw it.

“We must resign ourselves to the will of Providence, my child,” said Mrs. Davilow. The confession of gambling startled her; but she dared not rebuke. She believed “people” meant Grandcourt, and on that subject her lips were sealed.

“But I don’t resign myself,” Gwendolen returned quickly. “I shall do what I can against it. What is the good of calling the people’s wickedness Providence? You said in your letter it was Mr. Lassman’s fault we had lost our money. Has he run away with it all?”

“No, dear, you don’t understand. There were great speculations: he meant to gain. It was all about mines and things of that sort. He risked too much.”

“I don’t call that Providence. It was his improvidence with our money, and he ought to be punished. Can’t we go to law and recover our fortune? My uncle ought to take measures and not sit down by such wrongs. We ought to go to law.”

“My dear child, law can never bring back money lost in that way. Your uncle says it is milk spilled upon the ground. Besides, one must have a fortune to get any law: there is no law for people who are ruined. And our money has only gone along with other people’s. We are not the only sufferers: others have to resign themselves besides us.”

“But I don’t resign myself to live at Sawyer’s Cottage and see you working for sixpences and shillings because of that. I shall not do it. I shall do what is more befitting our rank and education.”

“I am sure your uncle and all of us will approve of that, dear, and admire you the more for it,” Mrs. Davilow said, grateful for an opening. “I didn’t mean that you should resign yourself to worse when anything better offered itself. Both your uncle and aunt feel that your abilities and education are a fortune for you, and they have already heard of something within your reach.”

“What is that, mamma?” Interest softened some of Gwendolen’s sharpness, and imagination stirred—always ready to gild any possible exit.

“There are two situations. One is in a bishop’s family—three daughters—and the other is in quite a high class of school. In both, your French, and music, and dancing—and then your manners and habits as a lady—are exactly what is wanted. Each is a hundred a year—and—just for the present”—Mrs. Davilow grew frightened and hesitating—“to save you from the petty, common way of living that we must go to—you would perhaps accept one of the two.”

“What! Be like Miss Graves at Madame Meunier’s? No.”

“I think, myself, Dr. Monpert’s would be more suitable. There could be no hardship in a bishop’s family.”

“Excuse me, mamma. There are hardships everywhere for a governess. I don’t see that it would be pleasanter to be looked down on in a bishop’s family than in any other. Besides, you know very well I hate teaching. Fancy me shut up with three awkward girls something like Alice! I would rather emigrate than be a governess.”

Mrs. Davilow fell silent, seeing no outlet, thinking with dread of the collision that might come when Gwendolen met her uncle and aunt. There was something withheld in Gwendolen’s resistance—as if she had a plan in reserve. And though Gwendolen’s ignorance of practical life showed itself at every step, the mother’s faith in her force remained: that daring will which had mastered her so often must surely find a way.

“I have some ornaments, mamma, and I could sell them,” Gwendolen said. “They would make a sum. I want a little sum—just to go on with. I dare say Marshall at Wanchester would take them. I know he showed me some bracelets once that he said he had bought from a lady. Jocosa might go and ask him. Jocosa is going to leave us, of course—but she might do that first.”

“She would do anything she could, poor dear soul. I have not told you yet—she wanted me to take all her savings—her three hundred pounds. I tell her to set up a little school. It will be hard for her to go into a new family now she has been so long with us.”

“Oh, recommend her for the bishop’s daughters,” Gwendolen said, and for a moment a gleam of laughter lit her face. “I am sure she will do better than I should.”

“Do take care not to say such things to your uncle,” Mrs. Davilow begged. “He will be hurt at your despising what he has exerted himself about. But I dare say you have something else in your mind that he might not disapprove, if you consulted him.”

“There is some one else I want to consult first. Are the Arrowpoints at Quetcham still, and is Herr Klesmer there? But I daresay you know nothing about it, poor dear mamma. Can Jeffries go on horseback with a note?”

“Oh, my dear, Jeffries is not here, and the dealer has taken the horses. But some one could go for us from Leek’s farm. The Arrowpoints are at Quetcham, I know. Miss Arrowpoint left her card the other day: I could not see her. But I don’t know about Herr Klesmer. Do you want to send before to-morrow?”

“Yes—as soon as possible. I will write a note,” said Gwendolen, rising with sudden alacrity.

“What can you be thinking of, Gwen?” Mrs. Davilow asked, relieved despite her wonder, because energy and better humor were like a window opened.

“Don’t mind what—there’s a dear, good mamma,” Gwendolen said, reseating herself to give atoning caresses. “I mean to do something. Never mind what until it is all settled. And then you shall be comforted. The dear face—it is ten years older in these three weeks. Now, now, now—don’t cry.” Holding her mother’s head with both hands, she kissed the trembling eyelids. “But mind you don’t contradict me or put hindrances in my way. I must decide for myself. I cannot be dictated to by my uncle or any one else. My life is my own affair. And I think”—her tone sharpened with scorn—“I think I can do better for you than let you live in Sawyer’s Cottage.”

She rose and went to a desk. The room was quiet in the way country rooms can be quiet, with a softness of distant sounds—the faint tick of a clock, a far door closing—so that the scratch of her pen seemed loud, like a small animal worrying at wood. She wrote to Klesmer:

Miss Harleth presents her compliments to Herr Klesmer, and ventures to request of him the very great favor that he will call upon her, if possible, to-morrow. Her reason for presuming so far on his kindness is of a very serious nature. Unfortunate family circumstances have obliged her to take a course in which she can only turn for advice to the great knowledge and judgment of Herr Klesmer.

“Pray get this sent to Quetcham at once, mamma,” she said as she addressed the letter. “The man must be told to wait for an answer. Let no time be lost.”

For the moment, sending the letter absorbed her like a fixed hunger: as if, if she could only get it into the right hands quickly enough, her life might yet be saved from the mean, thin fare of humiliation. But once she had been assured it would go, another anxiety rose and set her nerves jangling.

If Klesmer happened not to be at Quetcham—what then?

Her belief in her star had been bruised. A splendid marriage, shining within reach, had shown its hideous flaw. Roulette had refused to arrange itself to her deserts. A man of whom she knew nothing had thrust himself between her and her own intentions, stopping her with a look and a few words that still seemed to sound in her memory with an intolerable distinctness. The conduct of those dull people who managed the world’s business had been culpable precisely in the points most injurious to her. Now, for the first time, the conditions of this world felt to her like a hurrying, roaring crowd—too loud, too indifferent—where she had got astray and no one cared to shelter her more than any other girl, though to her it seemed a peculiar cruelty.

If Klesmer were absent, it would be all of a piece with the rest. The negative pressed itself on her imagination, and her mind began to dart toward desperate alternatives—anything that would save her from Sawyer’s Cottage, from the phrase “taking a situation,” which summed up for her the whole bitterness of being ranked, spoken to, and listened to in a diminished key, as if her very voice must be translated into smaller meanings.

And yet—Klesmer might be there. The thought of that possibility brought a hopefulness that threw a strange light even over her trouble, as if this misery were only the necessary dark background for the biography of the remarkable. For Gwendolen, with all her beauty and conscious force, could not imagine herself unremarkable; and if any one she knew had been cross-examined as to whether she was “remarkable,” the first who said “No” would have astonished her like a word spoken in a dialect she had never learned.

Gwendolen’s little note came to Herr Klesmer as he was stepping into his carriage at Quetcham—one of those messages that arrive with the neatness of a well-timed course at dinner, neither raw with haste nor over-kept with delay. To answer it meant discomfort and rearrangement; he must sleep at Wanchester, though every hour he lingered under the Arrowpoints’ roof had begun to scald him. The house was too splendid, too full—hot with other people’s expectations, as kitchens grow close when too many hands crowd the hearth.

Quetcham that season held, as it always did, an abundant company; and among them Mrs. Arrowpoint had already distinguished a fresh claimant for Catherine’s fortune, as neatly as she might have pinned a card to an entrée. Mr. Bult came of good family, spoke as if a peerage were waiting in the sideboard drawer, and carried about him the wholesome pink solidity of a man who believed the world’s business to be done, like carving, with a steady wrist and no need of finer senses. He had strong opinions on distant rivers and remoter islands, and the air of one who could talk through a whole dinner without once hearing the room. To Mrs. Arrowpoint he had the flavor of suitability; to Catherine he was merely tiresome—dull as bread baked without salt.

Catherine had long disturbed her parents by the simple trouble of being clear-headed. She did not accept the creed—held by those who had money and meant to keep their rank—that an heiress must marry where her fortune ought to be lodged, as if she herself were but the silver dish beneath it. The Arrowpoints had been uneasy at her repeated refusals; but they were not uneasy about Klesmer. That blindness, so common in households as in politics, was ready at hand: people are amazed when the consequence arrives that their own arrangements have been preparing all along.

For a year Klesmer had been in and out of their lives—town and country—no more restricted than the seasons. It began, as such things often do, with an engagement that looked innocent under the light of money: Catherine’s musical talent asked for the best instruction; wealth could buy a great musician’s presence as it bought a conservatory or a tapestry. Mr. Arrowpoint’s large cheque seemed to make Klesmer safe, as if he were a splendid instrument locked in its case between lessons. Where marriage is “inconceivable,” people think a girl’s feelings are insured against risk.

But life does not take its pattern from what is conceivable to parents.

Klesmer was a man of honor; and yet love seldom begins with a formal proposal any more than a sauce begins with the last stir. It begins earlier—quietly—when heat and time do their work. Catherine’s mind and ear were so finely true, her judgment so quick and unpretending, that intimacy with her had the charm of finding, day by day, a new herb in familiar ground—a fragrance not shouted from a distance, but rising when you bruise the leaf. She was not an acknowledged beauty; and yet the strongest beauty is often that which appears only after sympathy has taught the eye what to look for: the play of meaning that gathers in a smile that never comes wrongly; the dignity that settles in a face where perception is alive. Klesmer, with all his susceptibility to obvious loveliness, was won by that deeper charm—by the sense that no intention would be wasted on her, that her understanding met his like a hand that knows the right pressure in kneading, neither slack nor brutal.

Between them there had been, at first, a safety of full cups: each feeling enough to be silent, and silent enough to pretend nothing overflowed. Klesmer could not imagine that an heiress would think of him as a lover; Catherine was not used to thinking herself capable of rousing more than friendship, or of receiving any passion that was not tied to her fortune like a label. Yet he knew—he knew as surely as a man knows the difference between hunger and appetite—that if she had been poor he would have spoken out long ago, instead of flinging storms through the piano or folding his arms and firing off a tirade on some impersonal pole of the earth. And she knew—quietly, with a kind of steady wonder—that if it had been possible for him to wish for her hand, she would have found reasons strong enough to take it.

Of late, the hidden fire had altered its color. Klesmer’s brusquerie grew more frequent, and Catherine, though naturally kind, was firm enough to resent it: she saw in it an unnecessary stamping of superiority, as if he must keep proving himself master even where he was already obeyed. And in this visit to Quetcham he had begun to taste departure—had begun to tell himself he would not come again.

Then Mr. Bult arrived, like a joint set down at table with the certainty of being eaten. He was all amiable confidence. He could not feel counterpoint; he could not be made to hear it; and he did not conceive that such insensibility could count against him. He regarded Klesmer as a clever foreign appendage—hardly a serious human creature with claims beyond entertainment—and Miss Arrowpoint’s devotion to music seemed to him a harmless feminine expense, like antique lace.

At dinner one evening, something in the talk—English politics, markets, distant races treated as ledgers—set Klesmer alight. His words burst out like fireworks lit by accident: he spoke of the lack of idealism, of the meanness of treating mutuality between peoples as mere buying and selling, of how even the crusades had at least carried a banner of sentiment that could rally generous feeling—scoundrels too, yes, but the generous had something to gather round, unlike the modern van shouting “Buy cheap, sell dear.” He flamed for a few moments; then, as suddenly, he sank into a silence as immovable as stone.

Mr. Bult was not surprised that a musician should be flighty; what amazed him was Klesmer’s command of English idiom—his power to point a sentence so it might have told at a constituents’ dinner. He explained it to himself as he explained most foreign phenomena: fermenting refugeeism.

Later in the drawing-room, Klesmer at the piano and Catherine near, Mr. Bult approached with a large good-nature, as if condescending to taste a dish he suspected was not nourishing.

“I had no idea before that you were a political man,” he said.

Klesmer folded his arms, thrust out his lower lip, and stared at him.

“You must have been used to public speaking. You speak uncommonly well, though I don’t agree with you. From what you said about sentiment, I fancy you are a Panslavist.”

“No; my name is Elijah. I am the Wandering Jew,” Klesmer answered, and flashed a smile at Catherine—then ran his hands in a swift, wind-like rush over the keys, a sound like something passing through reeds at night.

Mr. Bult found the buffoonery offensive, and, to his mind, suitably Polish; but Catherine’s presence kept him rooted.

“Herr Klesmer has cosmopolitan ideas,” Catherine said, gently, trying to lay a cloth over the awkwardness. “He looks forward to a fusion of races.”

“With all my heart,” said Mr. Bult, ready to be gracious. “I was sure he had too much talent to be a mere musician.”

Klesmer’s temper sprang as if struck on flint.

“Ah, sir, you are under some mistake there. No man has too much talent to be a musician. Most men have too little. A creative artist is no more a mere musician than a great statesman is a mere politician. We are not ingenious puppets, sir, who live in a box and look out on the world only when it gapes for amusement. We help to rule the nations and make the age as much as any other public men. We count ourselves on level benches with legislators. And a man who speaks effectively through music is compelled to something more difficult than parliamentary eloquence.”

With that he turned from the piano and walked away.

Catherine colored. Mr. Bult, with his heavy stolidity, observed, “Your pianist does not think small beer of himself.”

“Herr Klesmer is something more than a pianist,” Catherine said, with apology in her tone, as if smoothing a wrinkled napkin. “He is a great musician in the fullest sense. He will rank with Schubert and Mendelssohn.”

“Ah, you ladies understand these things,” Mr. Bult replied, none the less confirmed that such things were frivolous—especially when they came with vanity.

The next day Catherine found Klesmer alone in the music-room, scores spread before him like a cook’s clean mise en place: ordered, precise, ready to be transformed by heat and touch. Outside, Quetcham’s life went on with its muffled comforts—the far wheels on gravel, the faint tap of a door, the soft rustle of gowns. Within, the room held that particular hush that belongs to places where sound is made deliberately. Catherine, who always felt the air of a room as much as she heard it, had been thinking how violently his outburst had struck the household’s acoustics: the dinner-table noise had swallowed his passion as a busy dining-room swallows the fine crackle of a small flame.

“Why were you so heated last night with Mr. Bult?” she asked. “He meant no harm.”

“You wish me to be complaisant to him?” Klesmer said, fiercely.

“I think it is hardly worth your while to be other than civil.”

“You find no difficulty in tolerating him, then?—you have a respect for a political platitudinarian as insensible as an ox to everything he can’t turn into political capital. You think his monumental obtuseness suited to the dignity of the English gentleman.”

“I did not say that.”

“You mean that I acted without dignity, and you are offended with me.”

“Now you are slightly nearer the truth,” Catherine said, smiling—a small smile that tried to keep the room gentle.

“Then I had better put my burial-clothes in my portmanteau and set off at once.”

“I don’t see that. If I have to bear your criticism of my operetta, you should not mind my criticism of your impatience.”

“But I do mind it. You would have wished me to take his ignorant impertinence about a ‘mere musician’ without letting him know his place. I am to hear my gods blasphemed as well as myself insulted. But I beg pardon. It is impossible you should see the matter as I do. Even you can’t understand the wrath of the artist: he is of another caste for you.”

“That is true,” Catherine said, and the words came out with a tremor she could not keep from them. “He is of a caste to which I look up—a caste above mine.”

Klesmer, who had been seated, started up as if something in him had been struck awake. He walked away a little, then spoke from that distance—like a man who must place his heart across the room before he dares touch it.

“That is finely felt—I am grateful. But I had better go, all the same. I have made up my mind to go, for good and all. You can get on exceedingly well without me: your operetta is on wheels—it will go of itself. And your Mr. Bull’s company fits me wie die Faust ins Auge. I am neglecting my engagements. I must go off to St. Petersburg.”

Catherine made no answer.

“You agree with me that I had better go?” he said, irritation sharpening him, because silence is sometimes louder than speech.

“Certainly; if that is what your business and feeling prompt,” she replied at last, coolness returning as a defense. “I have only to wonder that you have consented to give us so much of your time in the last year. There must be treble the interest to you anywhere else. I have never thought of you consenting to come here as anything else than a sacrifice.”

“Why should I make the sacrifice?” Klesmer said. He sat down at the piano and, with the delicacy of something heard as if from a far room, touched out a melody he had set to Heine—Ich hab’ dich geliebet und liebe dich noch—each note like a taste remembered when the dish is gone.

“That is the mystery,” Catherine said. She would not pretend; but agitation made her hands seek refuge in a childish action. She began tearing a piece of paper into the smallest morsels, as if some cruel fairy had set her the task of making infinity from a single sheet.

“You can conceive no motive?” Klesmer asked, folding his arms again.

“None that seems in the least probable.”

“Then I shall tell you. It is because you are to me the chief woman in the world—the throned lady whose colors I carry between my heart and my armor.”

Her fingers trembled so that the paper would no longer tear. Her lips could not form a word. The room seemed full of sound though nothing moved but his breath.

“This would be the last impertinence in me,” he went on, “if I meant to found anything upon it. That is out of the question. I meant no such thing. But you once said it was your doom to suspect every man who courted you of being an adventurer, and what made you angriest was men’s imputing to you the folly of believing that they courted you for your own sake. Did you not say so?”

“Very likely,” Catherine murmured.

“It was a bitter word. Well, at least one man—who has seen women as plenty as flowers in May—has lingered about you for your own sake. And since he is one whom you can never marry, you will believe him. There is an argument in favor of some other man. But don’t give yourself for a meal to a minotaur like Bult. I shall go now and pack. I shall make my excuses to Mrs. Arrowpoint.”

He rose and moved quickly toward the door, as if flight were the only honorable way to keep from taking what he desired.

“You must take this heap of manuscript,” Catherine said suddenly—desperate, practical, snatching at the only thing that could detain him. She had risen and brought the folio sheets from the other table. When he came back, the thick papers lay between them like a barrier and a bridge at once.

“Why should I not marry the man who loves me, if I love him?” Catherine said. The words were a leap—like a woman springing from a deck into the lifeboat, not knowing whether the water will strike like stone.

“It would be too hard—impossible—you could not carry it through,” Klesmer answered at once. “I am not worth what you would have to encounter. I will not accept the sacrifice. It would be thought a mésalliance for you, and I should be liable to the worst accusations.”

“Is it the accusations you are afraid of?” Catherine said. Her voice steadied on the truth she had been circling. “I am afraid of nothing but that we should miss the passing of our lives together.”

After that decisive word, there was no longer doubt about what each willed. Only the road remained; and Catherine, who in music preferred the plain right progression to any affected flourish, chose the straightest course. She went to the library where her father and mother were, and told them she had promised to marry Klesmer.

Mrs. Arrowpoint’s mind, under the shock, was a spectacle of ruined self-consistency. She who had written with lofty indignation of the arts and their corruptions—she who had safely admired tragic lovers on paper—found the admired defiance stepping, alive and unmanageable, on to her own carpet. It is one thing to serve sentiment as a garnish in literature, another to swallow it as a daily food. She wanted the best of everything—fine feeling and fine position; it pleased her to be above her circle in eloquence, but not to be below it in “consideration.” While Klesmer was a patronized musician his oddities were picturesque, like spices used sparingly; to see him suddenly as a son-in-law was to smell the whole jar overturned, and with it the imagined cries of society.

Anger, pure and immediate, seized her like a fit.

“If Klesmer has presumed to offer himself to you, your father shall horsewhip him off the premises. Pray, speak, Mr. Arrowpoint.”

Mr. Arrowpoint took his cigar from his mouth and stood up, roused with difficulty to a proper paternal emphasis.

“This will never do, Cath.”

“Do!” Mrs. Arrowpoint cried. “Who in their senses ever thought it would do? You might as well say poisoning and strangling will not do. It is a comedy you have got up, Catherine. Else you are mad.”

“I am quite sane and serious, mamma, and Herr Klesmer is not to blame,” Catherine said, as steadily as she could. “He never thought of my marrying him. I found out that he loved me, and loving him, I told him I would marry him.”

“Leave that unsaid, Catherine,” Mrs. Arrowpoint said, bitterly. “Every one else will say that for you. You will be a public fable. Every one will say that you must have made an offer to a man who has been paid to come to the house—who is nobody knows what—a gypsy, a Jew, a mere bubble of the earth.”

“Never mind, mamma,” Catherine said, indignation warming her. “We all know he is a genius—as Tasso was.”

“Those times were not these, nor is Klesmer Tasso,” Mrs. Arrowpoint retorted, the heat rising. “There is no sting in that sarcasm, except the sting of undutifulness.”

“I am sorry to hurt you, mamma. But I will not give up the happiness of my life to ideas that I don’t believe in and customs I have no respect for.”

“You have lost all sense of duty, then? You have forgotten that you are our only child—that it lies with you to place a great property in the right hands?”

“What are the right hands?” Catherine said. “My grandfather gained the property in trade.”

“Mr. Arrowpoint, will you sit by and hear this without speaking?”

Mr. Arrowpoint, who disliked scenes as he disliked sour wine, made his effort.

“I am a gentleman, Cath. We expect you to marry a gentleman.”

“And a man connected with the institutions of this country,” Mrs. Arrowpoint added quickly, seizing the larger phrase as if it were a stronger weapon. “A woman in your position has serious duties. Where duty and inclination clash, she must follow duty.”

“I don’t deny that,” Catherine said, growing colder as her mother grew hotter, as if she must cool herself to keep from breaking. “But one may say very true things and apply them falsely. People can easily take the sacred word duty as a name for what they desire any one else to do.”

“Your parent’s desire makes no duty for you, then?”

“Yes, within reason. But before I give up the happiness of my life—”

“Catherine, Catherine, it will not be your happiness,” Mrs. Arrowpoint said, in a tone like a croak of prophecy.

“Well, what seems to me my happiness—before I give it up, I must see some better reason than the wish that I should marry a nobleman, or a man who votes with a party that he may be turned into a nobleman. I feel at liberty to marry the man I love and think worthy, unless some higher duty forbids.”
