“And so it does, Catherine, though you are blinded and cannot see it. It is a woman’s duty not to lower herself. You are lowering yourself. Mr. Arrowpoint, will you tell your daughter what is her duty?”

“You must see, Catherine, that Klesmer is not the man for you,” Mr. Arrowpoint said. “He won’t do at the head of estates. He has a deuced foreign look—is an unpractical man.”

“I really can’t see what that has to do with it, papa,” Catherine answered. “The land of England has often passed into the hands of foreigners—Dutch soldiers, sons of foreign women of bad character:—if our land were sold to-morrow it would very likely pass into the hands of some foreign merchant on ’Change. It is in everybody’s mouth that successful swindlers may buy up half the land in the country. How can I stem that tide?”

In every household that has ever hung a print of Apollo over the mantel or kept a cracked gilt frame for the sake of what it once held, there is a quiet superstition: that Art is a kind of inheritance. You are “born to it,” people say, as if genius were a field you might walk into at will, with a deed in your pocket and a gate that will open because you are handsome, or well-bred, or praised at dinner.

But Art is not a landed estate. It is more like a bread you do not get by wanting it, nor by imagining its taste, but by hard daily work at the kneading-trough—by learning the exact temper of water and yeast, the stubbornness of flour that will not be bullied into smoothness, the discipline of heat that gives nothing to vanity. It is prophecy without possession until you have earned the loaf with burned fingers and a watchful ear.

The beliefs we carry most obstinately are often those we have never tested—beliefs that live in us like a pulse, self-fed, asking no evidence beyond our own pleasure in feeling them. And there are young creatures, especially, who have been so consistently applauded for being themselves that they cannot imagine the world asking for anything else.

The next morning was Sunday, and the air had the clean, mild edge of autumn—sunlight thinned by a veil of melancholy, lying in slanting bars on the half-strewn grass and entering the drawing-room like a benediction that had no words. The house was quiet in that particular way country houses are quiet on a Sunday: not silence, but a soft arrangement of sounds—the distant rustle of skirts, a door cushioned in its closing, the small click of china somewhere far off, and then the faint, steady hush that comes when a family is preparing itself to be seen as orderly.

“Pray go to church, mamma,” Gwendolen said, with that tone which made a request a decree. “I prefer seeing Herr Klesmer alone.”

Mrs. Davilow’s anxious face took on the look of one who hears an instrument slightly out of tune and cannot bear it. “That is hardly correct, I think.”

“Our affairs are too serious for us to think of such nonsensical rules,” said Gwendolen, and her contempt fell like salt on a wound. “They are insulting as well as ridiculous.”

“You would not mind Isabel sitting with you? She would be reading in a corner.”

“No; she could not. She would bite her nails and stare. It would be too irritating. Trust my judgment, mamma—I must be alone. Take them all to church.”

She had her way, of course. Yet decorum—like a cook who cannot help saving the drippings—found a compromise: Miss Merry and two of the girls remained at home, planted as if by design at the dining-room windows, to give the place the look of habitation.

Gwendolen stayed in the drawing-room where so many of her triumphs had been staged in miniature. The old furniture received the sun as if it had known it longer than any living face: tapestried chairs with their faded flower-wreaths; dark pictures that looked back with an enigmatic patience; that superannuated organ at which she had once pleased herself with acting Saint Cecilia, making religion into applause; and, through open doors, the pale, dusty knick-knacks of the antechamber—witnesses of her earlier play at being Hermione in a Greek dress. That memory was busy now, not for its own charm but because Herr Klesmer had been struck then, had admired her pose and expression. Whatever he had said, and whatever she had decided he must have thought, was now sharpened into importance, like a remembered aroma which one believes will decide whether a dish succeeds or fails.

For perhaps she had never before been so inwardly dependent—so consciously in need of another person’s opinion. Something had altered in her self-estimate: a new fluttering, a new deliberation, as if the easy certainty with which she had always judged herself were no longer sufficient. Yet the refrain within her was still that he had seen so little of her; any unfavorable conclusion must rest on too narrow a base. She felt clever enough for anything. She only needed the world to agree.

To occupy the minutes before eleven, she gathered her volumes and pieces of music, and laid them in a neat heap on the piano, setting herself to classify them with an air of method, as if order on a polished surface could command order in a life. And then, catching her own image in the glass panel that reflected the room, she was drawn toward it—as many women are drawn, not by vanity but by the hunger for confirmation.

She wore black, without ornament. The warm whiteness of her skin was set like cream against a tawny crust—between her light-brown coronet of hair and the square-cut bodice. The effect was severe and antique: a statue in black, white, and tawny marble. Watching the reflection advance, she thought, “I am beautiful”—not with a laugh, not even with exultation, but with a grave decision. Beauty was the one claim she needed others to attest. If anyone objected to the turn of her nose or the line of her chin, she could not answer as she might answer any criticism of skill by showing she could learn; there is no practice that reshapes bone.

The sound of wheels came at last, then the loud ring, and the opening doors—each noise distinctly placed in the house’s acoustic map, each a signal that her privacy was about to be entered. The arrival slightly increased her flutter. For all her confidence, she dreaded Herr Klesmer as one dreads a strong acid: something of the world that does not melt away because you smile at it, that burns in spite of your will. Poor Gwendolen—she was at a higher crisis of her woman’s fate than in that last experience which had revolved around Grandcourt. Then, the question had been whether she would take a particular man as husband. Now, more deeply folded within her, was the question whether she need take a husband at all—whether ambition might be satisfied without bondage, whether she might win bread and praise by herself.

Herr Klesmer entered with his most deferential bow in the wide doorway of the antechamber—deference conveyed not only by manner but by the perfect gloves and finest gray kerseymere trousers, as if even genius knew the value of exact finish. Gwendolen met him with unusual gravity, holding out her hand.

“It is most kind of you to come, Herr Klesmer. I hope you have not thought me presumptuous.”

“I took your wish as a command that did me honor,” he said. His gravity answered hers, yet there was in his tone a slight edge, as if his own feelings—quickened by yesterday—had not yet settled into repose.

For once, Gwendolen was too strained to remember social flourishes. She remained standing near the piano; he took his stand at the other end, his back to the light, his terribly omniscient eyes on her. There was no use in prettiness now, no room for charade. She began at once.

“I wish to consult you, Herr Klesmer. We have lost all our fortune; we have nothing. I must get my own bread, and I desire to provide for my mamma, so as to save her from any hardship. The only way I can think of—and I should like it better than anything—is to be an actress—to go on the stage. But, of course, I should like to take a high position, and I thought—if you thought I could”—her voice faltered, not from timidity but from the effort of holding herself steady—“it would be better for me to be a singer—to study singing also.”

He set his hat down on the piano and folded his arms as if to compress his attention into a smaller space.

“I know,” she continued, cheeks flushing and paling in turns, “I know that my method of singing is very defective; but I have been ill taught. I could be better taught; I could study. And you will understand my wish—to sing and act too, like Grisi, is a much higher position. Naturally, I should wish to take as high rank as I can. And I can rely on your judgment. I am sure you will tell me the truth.”

She had always believed truth, when solemnly requested, would come dressed in favor.

But he did not speak. He drew off his gloves quickly, tossed them into his hat, rested his hands on his hips, and walked to the other end of the room. Compassion was in him—more than she could imagine—yet he needed to lay a guard on his speech, as a careful cook guards heat from scorching what is delicate. Turning again, he looked at her with a mild frown of inquiry.

“You have never seen anything, I think, of artists and their lives?—I mean of musicians, actors, artists of that kind?”

“Oh, no,” said Gwendolen, not abashed by the bareness of the fact. She had been well provided for; ignorance was one of the luxuries of her condition.

“You are—pardon me,” he said, pausing again near the piano, “in coming to a conclusion on such a matter as this, everything must be taken into consideration—you are perhaps twenty?”

“I am twenty-one,” she answered quickly. A small fear rose like a sudden cold draught. “Do you think I am too old?”

He pouted his under lip and shook his long fingers upward in a gesture that was enigmatic as a foreign idiom one cannot translate.

“Many persons begin later than others,” Gwendolen said, instinctively offering information as if she were still in a room where her thoughts were welcomed for their own sake.

He took no notice. His gentleness became studied, as if he were choosing words that might not bruise.

“You have probably not thought of an artistic career until now: you did not entertain the notion, the longing—what shall I say?—you did not wish yourself an actress, or anything of that sort, till the present trouble?”

“Not exactly: but I was fond of acting. I have acted; you saw me, if you remember—you saw me here in charades, and as Hermione.” Her anxiety clung to that moment when she had felt herself most vivid, most applauded.

“Yes, yes,” he said quickly, “I remember—I remember perfectly.” And again he moved away, as if his body must pace while his mind argued.

She felt she was being weighed, and the delay was like the long pause before a dish is tasted by a judge. Yet she did not conceive the verdict could be truly against her. To seem graceful, she said, “I shall be very much obliged to you for taking the trouble to give me your advice, whatever it may be.”

“Miss Harleth,” he began at last, and there was a solemnity in him that made the room feel colder, “I will veil nothing from you in this matter. I should reckon myself guilty if I put a false visage on things—made them too black or too white. The gods have a curse for him who willingly tells another the wrong road. And if I misled one who is so young, so beautiful—who, I trust, will find her happiness along the right road—I should regard myself as a—Bösewicht.”

The German word fell with a loud whisper, heavy with meaning that was not quite hers; and she felt, in that moment, how much of experience remains untranslatable—how a single foreign syllable can carry a whole cultural weight that an English equivalent cannot lift.

Her heart sank under the unexpected gravity. She watched his face as one watches a knife that will either slice bread or cut flesh.

“You are a beautiful young lady,” he went on, “you have been brought up in ease—you have done what you would—you have not said to yourself, ‘I must know this exactly,’ ‘I must understand this exactly,’ ‘I must do this exactly,’”—with each terrible must he lifted a long finger in succession, like marks on a ledger. “In sum, you have not been called upon to be anything but a charming young lady, whom it is an impoliteness to find fault with.”

He paused only an instant, then thrust out his powerful chin.

“Well, then, with that preparation, you wish to try the life of an artist; you wish to try a life of arduous, unceasing work, and—uncertain praise. Your praise would have to be earned, like your bread; and both would come slowly, scantily—what do I say?—they may hardly come at all.”

The discouragement pricked her into resistance. She turned her head slightly away, with an air of pique.

“I thought that you, being an artist, would consider the life one of the most honorable and delightful. And if I can do nothing better?—I suppose I can put up with the same risks as other people do.”

“Do nothing better?” His voice sharpened with sudden fire. “No, my dear Miss Harleth, you could do nothing better—neither man nor woman could do anything better—if you could do what was best or good of its kind. I am not decrying the life of the true artist. I am exalting it. I say, it is out of the reach of any but choice organizations—natures framed to love perfection and to labor for it; ready, like all true lovers, to endure, to wait, to say, I am not yet worthy, but she—Art, my mistress—is worthy, and I will live to merit her. An honorable life? Yes. But the honor comes from the inward vocation and the hard-won achievement: there is no honor in donning the life as a livery.”

His fervor, which might have seemed like a halo over the subject to another girl, did not yet strike Gwendolen as exclusion. She heard only that excellence existed and that honor belonged to it; she did not quite hear him saying she was not made for it. Besides, she had always believed herself able to learn whatever she chose, and the notion that she could simply step upon a public stage and produce the effect she produced in drawing-rooms was in her like blood: you could not draw it out without pain.

“I am quite prepared to bear hardships at first,” she said, insisting. “Of course no one can become celebrated all at once. And it is not necessary that every one should be first-rate—either actresses or singers. If you would be so kind as to tell me what steps I should take, I shall have the courage to take them. I don’t mind going up hill. It will be easier than the dead level of being a governess. I will take any steps you recommend.”

He understood then that delicacy would only leave her with false hopes. His plainness came as a knife comes when one must cut away what is rotten.

“I will tell you the steps,” he said, “not that I recommend, but that will be forced upon you. It is all one, so far, what your goal will be—excellence, celebrity, second, third rateness—it is all one. You must go to town under the protection of your mother. You must put yourself under training—musical, dramatic, theatrical: whatever you desire to do you have to learn”—she looked as if she would interrupt, but he lifted his hand decisively—“I know. You have exercised your talents—you recite—you sing—from the drawing-room Standpunkt. My dear Fräulein, you must unlearn all that. You have not yet conceived what excellence is: you must unlearn your mistaken admirations. You must know what you have to strive for, and then you must subdue your mind and body to unbroken discipline. Your mind, I say. For you must not be thinking of celebrity: put that candle out of your eyes, and look only at excellence. You would of course earn nothing—you could get no engagement for a long while. You would need money for yourself and your family. But that”—here his frown deepened as if to dismiss a trifling ingredient in a larger recipe—“that could perhaps be found.”

Her pride winced as if the edge had been set deliberately against it. The last sentence stung worst, because it hinted at dependence—at charity disguised as practicality. She felt herself flushing and paling again, and hated being seen moved. Seeking refuge, she walked suddenly to a seat and pointed out a chair to him.

He did not sit. He turned slightly to face her and leaned against the piano, a posture of firmness, as if he meant to keep the weight of his counsel steady.

In that instant she wished she had never sent for him. In all her life, she had rarely been met on any ground but rank and beauty; now she was being handled like an incompetent apprentice, and the bitterness rose to her throat.

“Now,” he went on, still with that grave, unaltered tone, “what sort of issue might be fairly expected from all this self-denial? You would ask that. It is right that your eyes should be open to it. I will tell you truthfully. This issue would be uncertain, and, most probably, would not be worth much.”

He looked at her through his spectacles with a monstrous impartiality, as if beauty were a thing as irrelevant as gilt on a cracked plate.

Her eyes began to burn, but dread of weakness drove her into harder self-control. She forced herself to speak in a dry tone.

“You think I want talent, or am too old to begin.”

He made a sort of hum, then came down emphatically.

“Yes! The desire and the training should have begun seven years ago—or a good deal earlier. A mountebank’s child who helps her father to earn shillings when she is six years old—a child that inherits a singing throat from a long line of choristers and learns to sing as it learns to talk, has a likelier beginning. Any great achievement in acting or in music grows with the growth. Whenever an artist has been able to say, ‘I came, I saw, I conquered,’ it has been at the end of patient practice. Genius at first is little more than a great capacity for receiving discipline. Singing and acting, like the fine dexterity of the juggler with his cups and balls, require a shaping of the organs toward a finer and finer certainty of effect. Your muscles—your whole frame—must go like a watch, true, true to a hair. That is the work of spring-time, before habits have been determined.”

“I did not pretend to genius,” she said, still clinging to the belief that some opening must remain. “I only suppose that I might have a little talent—enough to improve.”

“I don’t deny that,” he answered. “If you had been put in the right track some years ago and had worked well you might now have made a public singer, though I don’t think your voice would have counted for much in public. For the stage your personal charms and intelligence might then have told without the present drawback of inexperience—lack of discipline—lack of instruction.”

He sounded cruel; but his impulse was compassion, sharpened by knowledge. He saw, with a painful definiteness, the humiliations, the long rehearsals, the cheap lodgings, the harsh voices of drill and correction, the auditory assaults of a world that makes its living amid din and judgement—the clang of modern life that leaves no quiet corner for a young woman’s pride to recover in. He could not convey those details to her; she had lived too sheltered, her ear accustomed to praise and the muffled sounds of comfort.

And she was not convinced. Her self-opinion rallied, as it always did when opposed. She began to think his judgement fallible—perhaps biased. It struck her that she might have done better to write directly to a London theatre manager and demand an appointment; she might have obtained at once what Herr Klesmer was denying her. She would say no more about singing—he had set himself against that. But she felt able to argue about acting.

“I understood, of course, that no one can be a finished actress at once,” she said, resistance in her tone. “It may be impossible to tell beforehand whether I should succeed; but that seems to me a reason why I should try. I should have thought that I might have taken an engagement at a theatre meanwhile, so as to earn money and study at the same time.”

“Can’t be done, my dear Miss Harleth—I speak plainly—it can’t be done. I must clear your mind of these notions which have no more resemblance to reality than a pantomime. Ladies and gentlemen think that when they have made their toilet and drawn on their gloves they are as presentable on the stage as in a drawing-room. No manager thinks that. With all your grace and charm, if you were to present yourself as an aspirant to the stage, a manager would either require you to pay as an amateur for being allowed to perform or he would tell you to go and be taught—trained to bear yourself on the stage, as a horse, however beautiful, must be trained for the circus; to say nothing of that study which would enable you to personate a character consistently, and animate it with the natural language of face, gesture, and tone. For you to get an engagement fit for you straight away is out of the question.”

“I really cannot understand that,” she said, haughtiness returning like a stiff collar. Then she checked herself and altered her tone, striving for reasonableness. “I shall be obliged to you if you will explain how it is that such poor actresses get engaged. I have been to the theatre several times, and I am sure there were actresses who seemed to me to act not at all well and who were quite plain.”

“Ah, my dear Miss Harleth,” he said, and there was a weary patience in him, “that is the easy criticism of the buyer. We who buy slippers toss away this pair and the other as clumsy; but there went an apprenticeship to the making of them. Excuse me; you could not at present teach one of those actresses; but there is certainly much that she could teach you. For example, she can pitch her voice so as to be heard: ten to one you could not do it till after many trials. Merely to stand and move on the stage is an art—requires practice. It is understood that we are not now talking of a comparse in a petty theatre who earns the wages of a needle-woman. That is out of the question for you.”

“Of course I must earn more than that,” said Gwendolen, with a sense of wincing rather than being answered. “But I think I could soon learn to do tolerably well all those little things you have mentioned. I am not so very stupid. And even in Paris, I am sure, I saw two actresses playing important ladies’ parts who were not at all ladies and quite ugly. I suppose I have no particular talent, but I must think it is an advantage, even on the stage, to be a lady and not a perfect fright.”

“Ah, let us understand each other,” he said, and something new flashed out, as if he had at last found the exact word in a language both could grasp. “I was speaking of what you would have to go through if you aimed at becoming a real artist—if you took music and the drama as a higher vocation in which you would strive after excellence. On that head, what I have said stands fast. You would find—after your education in doing things slackly for one-and-twenty years—great difficulties in study; you would find mortifications in the treatment you would get when you presented yourself on the footing of skill. You would be subjected to tests; people would no longer feign not to see your blunders. You would at first only be accepted on trial. You would have to bear what I may call a glaring insignificance: any success must be won by the utmost patience. You would have to keep your place in a crowd, and after all it is likely you would lose it and get out of sight. If you determine to face these hardships and still try, you will have the dignity of a high purpose, even though you may have chosen unfortunately. You will have some merit, though you may win no prize. You have asked my judgment on your chances of winning. I don’t pretend to speak absolutely; but measuring probabilities, my judgment is: you will hardly achieve more than mediocrity.”

The words fell like cold water. She sat motionless, looking down at her hands lying one over the other in her lap, as if she could read her future there. The room’s quiet pressed on her; outside, even the Sunday soundscape seemed to mock her—those distant wheels, that faint stir of leaves—nature going on in its old rhythms while her imagined life was being unmade.

Then the deep-toned, long-drawn “But—” startled her, as a sudden chord startles one out of reverie, and she looked up again.

“But—there are certainly other ideas, other dispositions with which a young lady may take up an art that will bring her before the public. She may rely on the unquestioned power of her beauty as a passport. She may desire to exhibit herself to an admiration which dispenses with skill. This goes a certain way on the stage: not in music: but on the stage, beauty is taken when there is nothing more commanding to be had. Not without some drilling, however: as I have said before, technicalities have in any case to be mastered. But these excepted, we have here nothing to do with art. The woman who takes up this career is not an artist: she is usually one who thinks of entering on a luxurious life by a short and easy road—perhaps by marriage—that is her most brilliant chance, and the rarest. Still, her career will not be luxurious to begin with: she can hardly earn her own poor bread independently at once, and the indignities she will be liable to are such as I will not speak of.”

Every sentence struck her with a confused sting. She heard, beneath his careful restraint, a contempt for the very course she had half-imagined as her salvation; and she felt, too, the pressure of his vocabulary—how his terms separated “artist” from “woman who exhibits herself,” as if language itself were a gate guarded by those who possessed the right words. She, who had always ruled by ease of speech, suddenly felt the power of a lexicon that could exclude.

“I desire to be independent,” she said, and her voice trembled with wounded pride. “That was my reason for asking whether I could not get an immediate engagement. Of course I cannot know how things go on about theatres. But I thought that I could have made myself independent. I have no money, and I will not accept help from any one.”

She could not bear that he should imagine she had sent for him to solicit anything but counsel. If she must be denied her dreams, she would at least keep her pride upright, like a table set with nothing on it yet kept spotless for the sake of dignity.

Gwendolen was thankful she had already endured Klesmer’s keen, musician’s scrutiny before she faced her uncle and aunt. That earlier interview had scraped her pride raw; it left her with a grim, clenched composure, as if she had swallowed something too hot and meant to show no sign of pain. Whatever came next, she told herself, would be disagreeable; and she would meet it with a kind of stubborn stillness, letting humiliation spend itself against a face that would not change.

The meeting waited until Monday. She went with her mother to the rectory; and on the way they stopped at Sawyer’s Cottage—her mother’s coming refuge—because arrangements had to be made, because a new life insisted on being measured in inches and corners. They saw every cranny in a hard, midday light that made no allowances. Bare boards, bare plaster, the small garden with cabbage-stalks like spent torches, and a yew arbor powdered with dust and hung with cobwebs as if even shade had become miserly. The air had that faint, cold smell of emptiness—old lime-wash, dry wood, and the sour echo of neglect—like a pantry after the last jar has been taken down and the shelves wiped too clean.

Gwendolen had been silent while they looked; her silence was a sort of pride, refusing to give the place the honor of a complaint. But when they walked away, the words broke out of her as if her throat could no longer bear the taste of them.

“How shall you endure it, mamma?” she said. “You and the four girls all in that closet of a room, with the green and yellow paper pressing on your eyes? And without me?”

“It will be some comfort that you have not to bear it too, dear.”

“If it were not that I must get some money, I would rather be there than go to be a governess.”

“Don’t set yourself against it beforehand, Gwendolen. If you go to the palace you will have every luxury about you. And you know how much you have always cared for that. You will not find it so hard as going up and down those steep narrow stairs, and hearing the crockery rattle through the house, and the dear girls talking.”

The very mention of crockery made Gwendolen’s mind flash with the homely acoustics she was being sentenced to: thin walls carrying every clink, every scrape, every rattling argument of plates that had outlived their glaze. The cottage seemed already to ring with it, as if poverty had its own ceaseless soundtrack—no soft curtains to drink it in, no thick carpets to hush it. A house can be cruel with noise when it is small.

“It is like a bad dream,” she said, fiercely. “I cannot believe my uncle will let you go to such a place. He ought to have taken some other steps.”

“Don’t be unreasonable, dear child. What could he have done?”

“That was for him to find out. It seems to me a very extraordinary world if people in our position must sink in this way all at once,” she said—because her inner world had always been arranged for her, like a table set with the right glass for every course, and nothing placed there that was not meant to please her.

It was her temper speaking, sharpened under this new pressure; she could have been wise enough about other people’s calamities, and even eloquent, if it had been her choice. But she had never aimed at virtue so much as brilliancy. Her words were often worse than she was.

And yet, when she reached the rectory and her uncle and aunt met her with a tenderness deeper than they had ever shown before, something in her tightened and then slackened with compunction. There was a dignified cheerfulness in them—no parade of martyrdom, no whimpering over lost comforts. It was as if, when fortune had been taken away, character began to show its clean grain. Her uncle in particular—whose worth had been half hidden by his usual clerical habits and smooth securities—stood out now with a new distinctness, like a good figure in plain clothes.

Already, with prompt, methodical decision, he had begun the little economies that are at once humiliating and oddly bracing: the carriage must go; old suits must be considered and made to serve; meat was to be banished from breakfast; periodicals dismissed; Edwy fetched from school; the boys’ hours arranged under their father’s own eye; the whole household brought to the sparest footing. There is even a pleasure in such paring down, when one’s body is healthy and one’s spirit not spoiled; it gives a sense of mastery, like trimming fat from a joint with a sure hand. The rector’s temper spread through the house. Mrs. Gascoigne and Anna, who always took papa for their pattern, truly did not miss much they cared for; their sorrow was chiefly for Mrs. Davilow and the girls.

Anna, for the first time, let her resentment on Rex’s behalf soften into sympathy for Gwendolen. Mrs. Gascoigne hoped—without duty-bound severity—that trouble might do her niece good. They had been busy devising blinds and curtains for the cottage out of the rectory’s stores, as careful women contrive meals out of remnants; but with a delicacy that refused to make charity sound like a lecture, they kept such matters back at first. They spoke instead of Gwendolen’s journey, and of the comfort her return had been to her mother.

There was, in truth, nothing in the manner of the rectory people that gave Gwendolen a plausible excuse for flinging her bitterness at them. It shook her into a sharper attention, as if everyone else had heard a command and fallen into order. Then her uncle, in a voice that had firm kindness for its tone—as if he were both comforting her and bracing her—began to speak of what he had been doing for her.

“I felt that there was no time to be lost, Gwendolen; for a position in a good family where you will have some consideration is not to be had at a moment’s notice. And however long we waited we could hardly find one where you would be better off than at Bishop Mompert’s. I am known to both him and Mrs. Mompert, and that of course is an advantage to you. Our correspondence has gone on favorably; but I cannot be surprised that Mrs. Mompert wishes to see you before making an absolute engagement. She thinks of arranging for you to meet her at Wanchester when she is on her way to town. I dare say you will feel the interview rather trying for you, my dear; but you will have a little time to prepare your mind.”

Gwendolen’s imagination—quick as a hand snatching at a knife—had already cut out a dozen disagreeable reasons why a strange lady would want to inspect her: daughters to guard, manners to judge, defects to scent out as if she were meat brought to market. The very word “see” felt like a cold finger under her chin, turning her face toward a harsh light.

“Do you know why she wants to see me, uncle?” she asked.

He smiled, trying to ease her. “Don’t be alarmed, my dear. She would like to have a more precise idea of you than my report can give. And a mother is naturally scrupulous about a companion for her daughters. I have told her you are very young. But she herself exercises a close supervision over her daughters’ education, and that makes her less anxious as to age. She is a woman of taste and also of strict principle, and objects to having a French person in the house. I feel sure that she will think your manners and accomplishments as good as she is likely to find; and over the religious and moral tone of the education she, and indeed the bishop himself, will preside.”

Gwendolen dared not answer. She felt the blood surge up—an angry, humiliating flush over face and neck—and fall away again, leaving her chilled. Anna, frightened by that sudden change she did not understand, slid her small hand into Gwendolen’s. Mr. Gascoigne, too kind not to feel the weight of what he was asking, pressed on with a cheerful tone, as if he were not arguing against objections but simply setting out advantages that any sensible mind would taste and approve.

“I think so highly of the position, that I should have been tempted to try and get it for Anna, if she had been at all likely to meet Mrs. Mompert’s wants. It is really a home, with a continuance of education in the highest sense: ‘governess’ is a misnomer. The bishop’s views are of a more decidedly Low Church color than my own—he is a close friend of Lord Grampian’s; but, though privately strict, he is not by any means narrow in public matters. Indeed, he has created as little dislike in his diocese as any bishop on the bench. He has always remained friendly to me, though before his promotion, when he was an incumbent of this diocese, we had a little controversy about the Bible Society.”

To him these were solid, reassuring morsels of information—sound, nourishing, plain. To Gwendolen they were like things alive and cold set loose at her feet: “continuance of education,” “privately strict,” “religious and moral tone,” “Bible Society”—phrases that hissed in her mind. She did not hear a home: she heard supervision, examinations, a life where her very silence would be judged; and, behind all, the oppressive hush of a great house where sound carries, where footsteps are measured, where a girl’s laughter might be taken for frivolity. It was as if her uncle had proposed to cure her by shutting her in a room whose air was scented with sermons.

She made a desperate reach for any other outlet.

“There was another situation, I think mamma spoke of?” she said, with a rigid control that made her voice sound almost calm.

“Yes,” her uncle answered, with reluctance. “But that is in a school. I should not have the same satisfaction in your taking that. It would be much harder work, you are aware, and not so good in any other respect. Besides, you have not an equal chance of getting it.”

“Oh dear no,” said Mrs. Gascoigne, “it would be much harder for you, my dear—it would be much less appropriate. You might not have a bedroom to yourself.”

Gwendolen’s school memories rose with their stale odors and relentless noises: the close air of dormitories, the mingled smell of soap and damp wool, the scraping of benches, the incessant human friction that made even silence noisy. This alternative brought no relief. She turned again to her uncle, and the words came out with the outward air of submission, as if she were accepting medicine she despised.

“When is Mrs. Mompert likely to send for me?”

“That is rather uncertain, but she has promised not to entertain any other proposal till she has seen you. She has entered with much feeling into your position. It will be within the next fortnight, probably. But I must be off now. I am going to let part of my glebe uncommonly well.”

He rose, ending with hearty cheerfulness, carrying away the conviction that he had done his part and that Gwendolen would do hers—adapt herself, sensibly, as people ought. Used to being asked to “speak to” refractory persons with the notion that words from authority have a coercive virtue, he naturally expected appropriate effects from appropriate counsel.

“What a stay Henry is to us all!” Mrs. Gascoigne said when he had gone.

“He is indeed,” Mrs. Davilow answered warmly. “I think cheerfulness is a fortune in itself. I wish I had it.”

“And Rex is just like him,” Mrs. Gascoigne said. “I must tell you the comfort we have had in a letter from him. I must read you a little bit.” She put her hand in her pocket to draw it out, while Anna looked suddenly timid, as if an old rule—never mention Rex before Gwendolen—had the power of a charm that might be broken at their peril.

Mrs. Gascoigne ran her eyes over the page, searching for safe sentences. But she seemed to find it thick with nearer allusions than she wished; she folded it again and spoke instead, her voice bright with a mother’s proud relief.

“However, he tells us that our trouble has made a man of him; he sees a reason for any amount of work: he means to get a fellowship, to take pupils, to set one of his brothers going, to be everything that is most remarkable. The letter is full of fun—just like him. He says, ‘Tell mother she has put out an advertisement for a jolly good hard-working son, in time to hinder me from taking ship; and I offer myself for the place.’ The letter came on Friday. I never saw my husband so much moved by anything since Rex was born. It seemed a gain to balance our loss.”

This letter was, in fact, what helped both mother and daughter at the rectory to be kind to Gwendolen without mixture. And Gwendolen, who had no gratuitous delight in other people’s pain, felt amiable about it. She smiled at Anna and pinched her chin, as if to say, There—nothing is wrong now. She only objected intensely to other people making her miserable.

But when the talk slipped back to blinds and curtains for the cottage, to what could be spared from the rectory, and how to contrive comfort out of scant means, Gwendolen’s spirit sank again. She could not rouse even a languid interest in the practical details. She felt she had already done enough merely by sitting there, by holding her face, by not bursting out. Inside her, a struggle went on without words, like teeth grinding in sleep.

For the recoil from the one definite prospect allowed her was stronger than she had imagined. The idea of presenting herself to Mrs. Mompert for approval or rejection pressed on her like a hand on a bruise. Even now, when she had done the violence of consenting to go, she was still to be judged—her looks, her voice, her very manner of being silent. And if accepted, the judgment would not end: it would become the air she breathed. Mrs. Mompert’s supervision always; expectations always; tasks she had no desire to do, performed under a gaze that would never quite be absent. Perhaps the bishop himself would examine her—on serious topics—like a magistrate questioning a culprit. Only a few weeks ago, she had moved in drawing-rooms where a handsome girl’s daring talk passed for wit and was rewarded with smiling attention. Then she might have pitied a bishop’s dulness. Now she saw the coming life as a penitentiary where every day would be an effort at self-constraint.

Wild thoughts came—running away, becoming an actress, shaking off all this—thoughts with the lure of freedom like a sudden gust at a window. But Klesmer’s words hung on her, heavy as a hand at the back of her neck. He had alarmed her pride and her maidenly dignity. She saw, dimly, the coarse glare of vulgar company, the rude familiarity of men who would grin and smirk without the strong bars of polite custom between. Her daring was not that of the adventuress. The demand to be treated as a lady was in her very marrow. Even when she had dreamed herself a heroine of the gaming-table, it was with the condition that no one should presume, no one should look at her with an irony like Deronda’s. She had always been protected and petted; her susceptibilities consulted as naturally as her hunger was fed. To be flung into solitary dependence on strangers’ doubtful civility was no attractive liberty. The episcopal penitentiary was less repulsive than that. Yet there, too, she would not be petted.

As hour followed hour, rebellion grew rather than diminished. It seemed to her the family trouble was easier for everyone than for her—even for her poor dear mother, because her mother had never been trained to expect enjoyment. Hope—hope that things might get better if she went and was patient—seemed to Gwendolen a foolish luxury she could not afford. Her talents, it appeared, would never be recognized as remarkable; no probability flattered her wishes. Romance might have offered a pretty picture to some girls—governesses becoming centers of attraction, rescued into marriage—but Gwendolen’s mind could not project itself far. The past and the immediate future pressed too close. She had a nausea of the world, and no reason, she thought, for living through a whole life in a way she hated.

No religious view came to help her; she felt her troubles had been caused by other people’s disagreeable or wicked conduct. She had heard phrases about discipline and blessing, but they were only phrases; she had never found them delicious enough to take into herself. Talk of the sweetness of labor, the fulfilled claim, the inward activity that makes life discovery—such things would have been faint doctrines to her even if preached with eloquence. The fact she knew, because she had always observed it, was that for a lady to “take a situation” was to descend and to be treated, at best, with a patronizing compassion. Happiness, for her, had never been divorced from personal pre-eminence and éclat. That she should now find life hardly worth having when these were threatened, made her pitiable rather than monstrous: a young creature facing the labyrinth with no clue, struck suddenly by distrust in herself and her fortune, as if the smooth path had split open under her feet.

Her healthy body did not save her from the physical effect of this inward repugnance. She felt numb, inert, as if her limbs belonged to another person. The slightest urgency—even being called to meals—irritated her. Other people’s speech on any subject felt unreasonable, because it ignored what she felt; it made a claim on her as if she were obliged to answer a world that did not include her. She did not busy herself with those dramatic fancies of suicide that fill some young minds; what tormented her was the sense that she must go on living, but only in a way she detested.

She avoided the rectory. It was intolerable to look and talk as if she were compliant, and she could not bring herself to pretend an interest in furnishing that dreadful cottage. Miss Merry was staying on purpose to help; Jocosa would like such bustle and contrivance, the cheerful clatter of domestic plans. Gwendolen could not. Her mother had to make excuses for her even when Anna came. The dogged calm Gwendolen had promised herself had turned into a sick, motiveless inaction. “I suppose I shall begin to pretend by-and-by,” she thought; “but why should I do it now?”

Her mother watched her in silent distress; and, falling back into the habit of indulgent tenderness, she began to imagine the thoughts behind that altered face and to wish that everything might yield to making her darling less miserable.

One day, when Gwendolen lay in the black and yellow bedroom and Mrs. Davilow lingered there under the pretext of arranging her clothes, Gwendolen suddenly roused herself, as if some practical thought had stung her out of stupor. She rose, fetched the casket that held her ornaments, and brought it back with a decisive movement.

“Mamma,” she began, lifting the lid and glancing at the upper layer, “I had forgotten these things. Why didn’t you remind me of them? Do see about getting them sold. You will not mind about parting with them. You gave them all to me long ago.”

She lifted the upper tray and looked below.

“If we can do without them, darling, I would rather keep them for you,” Mrs. Davilow said, seating herself beside her with a relief that Gwendolen was speaking of anything that could be handled and done. Their old relation was reversed now: the mother tried to cheer the daughter. “Why, how came you to put that pocket handkerchief in here?”

It was the handkerchief with the corner torn off—the one Gwendolen had thrust in hurriedly with the turquoise necklace.

“It happened to be with the necklace—I was in a hurry,” Gwendolen said. She took the handkerchief away and put it in her pocket. Then, as if a new warmth had come over her about that rescued trinket which once had stung her pride, she added quickly, “Don’t sell the necklace, mamma.”

“No, dear, no; it was made out of your dear father’s chain. And I should prefer not selling the other things. None of them are of any great value. All my best ornaments were taken from me long ago.”

Mrs. Davilow colored. She usually avoided such facts about Gwendolen’s step-father—how he had carried off his wife’s jewelry and disposed of it. After a moment she went on, softly, “And these things have not been reckoned on for any expenses. Carry them with you.”

“That would be quite useless, mamma,” Gwendolen said, cold and scornful, as if she were speaking of a dish set before her when she was already sick. “Governesses don’t wear ornaments. You had better get me a gray frieze livery and a straw poke, such as my aunt’s charity children wear.”

“No, dear, no; don’t take that view of it. I feel sure the Momperts will like you the better for being graceful and elegant.”

“I am not at all sure what the Momperts will like me to be. It is enough that I am expected to be what they like,” Gwendolen said bitterly. The bitterness was like something burnt at the bottom of a pan: it tainted everything.

“If there is anything you would object to less—anything that could be done—instead of your going to the bishop’s, do say so, Gwendolen. Tell me what is in your heart. I will try for anything you wish,” her mother pleaded. “Don’t keep things away from me. Let us bear them together.”

“Oh, mamma, there is nothing to tell,” Gwendolen answered. “I can’t do anything better. I must think myself fortunate if they will have me. I shall get some money for you. That is the only thing I have to think of. I shall not spend any money this year: you will have all the eighty pounds. I don’t know how far that will go in housekeeping; but you need not stitch your poor fingers to the bone, and stare away all the sight that the tears have left in your dear eyes.”

Her words held tenderness, but they did not caress; she did not even look at her mother. She kept turning the turquoise necklace in her fingers, as if the smooth stones could steady her more than any human touch.

“Bless you for your tenderness, my good darling!” Mrs. Davilow said, tears rising. “Don’t despair because there are clouds now. You are so young. There may be great happiness in store for you yet.”

“I don’t see any reason for expecting it, mamma,” Gwendolen said, hard; and her mother fell silent, thinking the question she had thought too often—what had happened between Gwendolen and Mr. Grandcourt?

“I will keep this necklace, mamma,” Gwendolen said at last. She laid it apart and closed the casket with a decisive click. “But do get the other things sold, even if they will not bring much. Ask my uncle what to do with them. I shall certainly not use them again. I am going to take the veil. I wonder if all the poor wretches who have ever taken it felt as I do.”

“Don’t exaggerate evils, dear.”

“How can any one know that I exaggerate, when I am speaking of my own feeling? I did not say what any one else felt.”

She drew out the torn handkerchief again and, with a deliberate care that was almost ceremonial, wrapped it round the turquoise necklace. Mrs. Davilow watched the act with surprise; but Gwendolen’s tone, like a door shut fast, discouraged any question.

How is one to map the motives of a man whose inner country has been grazed to stubble by fastidious self-regard—where wanting is no longer a clean hunger but a finicky loitering before a larder that never quite tempts? A life left too long to “as you like” grows rank with impulses that sprout and die without bearing. And there are people—men of breeding, men of means—whose intentions are declared not by generous speech but by a small, cruel alteration of tone, as if they were tasting a sauce and deciding, without complaint, that it shall be thrown away.

So it was that when Grandcourt, hearing that Gwendolen Harleth had quitted Leubronn, let fall—incidentally, with the same languid certainty with which he might pronounce a cut of meat overdone—that the place was a beastly hole, worse than Baden, Mr. Lush took it for a settled menu: they were going back to Diplow. The resolve, of course, would be executed with the leisurely dawdle that was Grandcourt’s way of giving power its full savor.

He loitered through another day, giving no distinct order. He lingered over his toilet as if the choosing of linen and the exacting brush of a sleeve were a kind of private cookery—an art of reduction, taking the wholesome blood out of life until only a pale essence remained, refined and faint. He came down with that faded distinction which makes fresh hands—hands that have kneaded dough or cut herbs in the garden—seem, by contrast, raw and common. He lingered on the terrace, in the gambling-rooms, in the reading-room; he occupied himself in a deliberate indifference, as if indifference were an expensive dish served cold and meant to be admired for its chill.

Yet even the chilled can be made to speak when society approaches with its spoon and expects a taste.

When he met Lady Mallinger, he raised his hat, paused, and listened just long enough that she might feel she had been heard. She recommended the waters, with that amiable faith which tries to sweeten bitterness by insisting it is tonic.

“Yes,” he said, “I heard somebody say how providential it was that there always happened to be springs at gambling places.”

“Oh, that was a joke,” Lady Mallinger answered, innocent as milk just drawn and still warm with the cow’s breath—misled by his languid seriousness. “In imitation of the old one about the towns and the rivers, you know.”

“Ah, perhaps,” said Grandcourt, with no more change of expression than a face of stone in rain.

Lady Mallinger carried this to Sir Hugo as something curious—like an odd flavor one cannot name. Sir Hugo, who liked his scandal and his wit as he liked his claret: not too harsh, not allowed to turn sour in bad company, said, “My dear, he is not a fool. Don’t suppose he can’t see a joke. He can play his cards as well as most of us.”

“He has never seemed to me a very sensible man,” she said, and beneath her excuse there lay a more secret smart: Grandcourt was a great living reminder of what she called, in her own mind, her failure as a wife—the absence of a son for Sir Hugo. It is a quiet grief, like bread that will not rise no matter how patiently you keep it warm; and the thought that a husband might fairly regret his choice, might have dealt harshly if he were less good, haunted her with a timorous gratitude.

Grandcourt also gave Deronda a recognition. Deronda answered with perfect civility—and felt no gratitude. Old feelings, rooted as early tastes are rooted—those first strong impressions of sweetness and shame—do not yield to later reasoning. He could not unmake, by any argument about custom, the sense that his birth had been attended by an injury for which his father was to blame. He knew, too, that but for that injury Grandcourt’s prospects might have been his. And because he saw how easily such knowledge can turn into a mean relish—triumphing over another’s good fortune, or nursing rancor at one’s own lack—he was proud enough to refuse the dish. He turned his back on that ugly pit, and held to kindlier affections as a man holds to honest food when he might cheaply gorge on poison.

Pride served him well here: the pride that will not let a vulgar mind dictate what counts as disadvantage. He would not have Grandcourt imagine envy in him, as a coarse eater imagines everyone covets his heavy supper. But there is no guarding against another man’s interpretation. Grandcourt was quite capable of believing that Deronda, poor devil, inwardly winced under their mutual position; and the thought of envy—imaginary envy—was one of those sweet meats egoism likes to keep by. Grandcourt’s pet dogs were not the only creatures he enjoyed making jealous.

So he was civil enough to exchange a few words with Deronda on the terrace about the hunting round Diplow, and even said, “You had better come over for a run or two when the season begins.”

Lush, who was never displeased by delay when delay promised him comfort, amused himself with lounging promenades, gossiping with Sir Hugo, answering questions about Grandcourt’s affairs so far as they touched the baronet’s willingness to part with his interest in Diplow. Sir Hugo had a taste for good-humored scandal—he called it, with a little air, traits de mœurs—yet he kept it from listeners who might let it turn into moral hysteria. Whatever he knew of his nephew’s secrets, he had never offered it to Deronda. Deronda, for his part, found Grandcourt a pale-blooded mortal, and had no desire to hear in what way the red had been washed out.

Lush’s policy, when he had no reason to the contrary, was to gratify. He had the knack of being agreeable, like a dish that suits many palates precisely because it is not too strong. Sir Hugo treated him well: one of those handy, second-best articles a gentleman uses without anxiety. And Lush, being used to a world that took him for apt and pleasant, liked to be of use—liked, too, the sense of being needed.

“Well, you will let me know the turn of events,” Sir Hugo said, “if this marriage seems likely to come off after all, or if anything else happens to make the want of money pressing. My plan would be much better for him than burdening Ryelands.”

“That’s true,” said Lush, “only it mustn’t be urged on him—just placed in his way that the scent may tickle him. Grandcourt isn’t a man to be always led by what makes for his own interest—especially if you let him see that it makes for your interest too. I’m attached to him, of course. I’ve given up everything else for the sake of keeping by him, and it’s lasted a good fifteen years now. He wouldn’t easily get anyone else to fill my place. He’s a peculiar character, is Henleigh Grandcourt, and it has been growing on him of late years. However, I’m of a constant disposition, and I’ve been a sort of guardian to him since he was twenty; an uncommonly fascinating fellow he was then, to be sure—and could be now, if he liked. I’m attached to him; and it would be a good deal worse for him if he missed me at his elbow.”

Sir Hugo did not trouble himself with sympathy. He knew how much of any man’s speech is a kind of verbal dressing-gown, put on decently for company; and he could allow for such necessities as a member of Parliament allows for the tailor’s bill.

But Lush’s easy expectation of procrastination was cut short the next morning. Grandcourt, as if deciding on a journey with the same small motion with which he taps ash from a cigar, said, “Are you making all the arrangements for our starting by the Paris train?”

“I didn’t know you meant to start,” Lush answered—more accurately, he had not been told.

“You might have known,” said Grandcourt, looking at the burned length of his cigar and speaking in that lowered tone he used when he meant to be peremptory and let disgust do the work of passion. “Just see to everything, will you? and mind no brute gets into the same carriage with us. And leave my P.P.C. at the Mallingers’.”

So they were at Paris the next day. There Lush was gratified—commanded, rather—into going straight on to Diplow and seeing everything right, while Grandcourt and the valet remained behind. It was not until several days later that Lush received the telegram ordering the carriage to the Wanchester station.

During the interval, Lush was active: he carried out orders about stud and household, but he also did what was habitual to him—he gathered information like a man tasting as he goes, knowing that one spice too many can ruin the whole dish. He learned all he could about Gwendolen, about Offendene, about the family misfortunes that had fallen like a sudden blight on harvest.

What would such news do to Grandcourt’s fitful obstinacy? Lush could not calculate it. Poverty might make acceptance more likely; and the thought of being accepted—without the delicious risk of a repulse—might, perversely, be just the thing to send Grandcourt fluttering away like a moth from a candle too steadily lit. Lush had watched him for years. To know Grandcourt was to doubt him.

It might happen—Lush was not blind to theatrical possibilities—that Grandcourt would step, for once, into a sort of moral splendor, like a modern French stage-hero who suddenly grows noble at the curtain, leaving you no confidence in what he’d do in Act Two. What more honorable final pose than to decline an heiress and marry the attractive girl who had none? But Lush held to one general certainty: of all inward movements, generosity was least likely in Grandcourt. And yet what use is it to know an insect never walks head-first backwards, when you must predict which twist of stimulus will send it down a particular thread in the web?

Lush wanted, above all, to be confident that Grandcourt and Gwendolen would never marry. He could have tolerated an heiress. He could even have tolerated Mrs. Glasher; there, at least, was gratitude, security, a wife dependent and therefore manageable—and if society refused her, it would not disturb Lush’s private comfort. He could have tolerated no marriage. But a marriage with Gwendolen—young, proud, likely to bring trouble—threatened the ease he felt he had earned by living, for years, a dog’s life: a dog well fed, to be sure, with music and luxury, but still a dog at heel.

He was not conscious of wishing harm to anyone—except, perhaps, just now, a little harm to the inconvenient and impertinent Gwendolen. Even the easiest-humored of toad-eaters has nerves; even a palate accustomed to rich sauces may revolt at being forced to swallow insult.

So, with a half-formed war-policy, he waited for Grandcourt’s arrival, mostly wondering how the campaign would begin.

The first day, Grandcourt was much occupied with the stables. Among other things he ordered a groom to put a side-saddle on Criterion and let him review the horse’s paces. That one order was like the smell of a particular dish from a kitchen door: it told Lush what was intended, more certainly than a declaration. It set him reconsidering whether he should risk speaking first, while he was still sure no compromising step had been taken.

He rose the next morning nearly resolved that if Grandcourt appeared in any talkative humor, he would drop—casually, as if letting fall a crumb—those facts about Gwendolen and her family, to see how they worked and to get some guidance. But Grandcourt did not enter into talk. In answer to a question even about convenience, he kept a silence no fish could have bettered.

After reading his letters, he gave various orders to be executed or transmitted by Lush, then thrust his shoulder toward that useful person—the dismissal. Lush rose to go. But before he reached the door, Grandcourt turned his head slightly and gave a broken, languid “Oh.”

“What is it?” said Lush.

“Shut the door, will you? I can’t speak into the corridor.”

Lush shut it, came forward, and chose to sit down—choice being his small rebellion.

After a pause, Grandcourt said, “Is Miss Harleth at Offendene?”

He was quite certain Lush had made it his business to know; and he tasted, in advance, the displeasure of forcing Lush to speak what Lush would rather keep seasoned for later.

“Well, I hardly know,” said Lush carelessly. “The family’s utterly done up. They and the Gascoignes too have lost all their money. It’s owing to some rascally banking business. The poor mother hasn’t a sou, it seems. She and the girls have to huddle themselves into a little cottage like a laborer’s.”

“Don’t lie to me, if you please,” said Grandcourt, in his lowest audible tone. “It’s not amusing, and it answers no other purpose.”

“What do you mean?” Lush asked, nettled beyond his habit; the future was disturbing him, and irritation makes a man careless of his own recipe for pleasing. “Just tell me the truth, will you? It’s no invention of mine. I’ve heard the story from several—Bazley, Brackenshaw’s man, for one. He is getting a new tenant for Offendene.”

“I don’t mean that. Is Miss Harleth there, or is she not?” Grandcourt said, as if he were asking for a single ingredient, not a whole stew of circumstances.

“Upon my soul, I can’t tell,” said Lush, sulkily. “She may have left yesterday. I heard she had taken a situation as governess; she may be gone to it for what I know. But if you wanted to see her no doubt the mother would send for her back.”

The sneer slipped out with the words, unbidden.

“Send Hutchins to inquire whether she will be there to-morrow.”

Lush did not move. He had thought over beforehand what he might say, and now an unexpected irritation shoved those prearranged warnings onto his tongue. The scrape Grandcourt might get into was too tremendous to watch in silence while the first step was taken. He kept a tone of rational friendliness, but he felt his own value and was ready to be bold.

“It would be as well for you to remember, Grandcourt, that you are coming under closer fire now. There can be none of the ordinary flirting done, which may mean everything or nothing. You must make up your mind whether you wish to be accepted; and more than that, how you would like being refused. Either one or the other. You can’t be philandering after her again for six weeks.”

Grandcourt said nothing. He pressed the newspaper down on his knees and began to light another cigar—as calmly as a man in a noisy city might seal his ears by attending only to the scratch of his match, choosing that small clean sound over the world’s coarse clamor. Lush, catching at the sign of permission, went on; he wanted to learn which hesitation would be stronger—fear of refusal or distaste for certain acceptance.

“Everything has a more serious look now than it had before. There is her family to be provided for. You could not let your wife’s mother live in beggary. It will be a confoundedly hampering affair. Marriage will pin you down in a way you haven’t been used to; and in point of money you have not too much elbow-room. And after all, what will you get by it? You are master over your estates, present or future, as far as choosing your heir goes; it’s a pity to go on encumbering them for a mere whim, which you may repent of in a twelvemonth. I should be sorry to see you making a mess of your life in that way. If there were anything solid to be gained by the marriage, that would be a different affair.”

His voice grew more and more unctuous, like oil poured in hopes of making a hard morsel slide down. He had nearly forgotten that he was gambling in argument.

When he stopped, Grandcourt took the cigar from his mouth and looked steadily at its moist end while he adjusted the leaf with delicate fingertips, as if the whole matter were merely a question of tidiness.

“I knew before that you had an objection to my marrying Miss Harleth.” He paused, letting the sentence cool. “But I never considered that a reason against it.”

“I never supposed you did,” Lush answered, dryly. “It was not that I urged as a reason. I should have thought it might have been a reason against it, after all your experience, that you would be acting like the hero of a ballad, and making yourself absurd—and all for what? You know you couldn’t make up your mind before. It’s impossible you can care much about her. And as for the tricks she is likely to play, you may judge of that from what you heard at Leubronn. However, what I wished to point out to you was, that there can be no shilly-shally now.”

“Perfectly,” said Grandcourt. He looked round at Lush and fixed him with narrow eyes. “I don’t intend that there should be. I dare say it’s disagreeable to you. But if you suppose I care a damn for that you are most stupendously mistaken.”

“Oh, well,” said Lush, rising, hands in pockets, venom still warm in him, “if you have made up your mind!—only there’s another aspect of the affair. I have been speaking on the supposition that it was absolutely certain she would accept you, and that destitution would have no choice. But I am not so sure that the young lady is to be counted on. She is kittle cattle to shoe, I think. And she had her reasons for running away before.”

He moved a step or two, standing nearly in front of Grandcourt, not much restrained by consequences. He knew his hold was serviceableness; even after a quarrel the need of him would return like appetite. He foresaw Gwendolen would oust him for a time, and his temper urged him to risk the rupture.

“She had her reasons,” he repeated, more significantly.

“I had come to that conclusion before,” said Grandcourt, with contemptuous irony.

“Yes, but I hardly think you know what her reasons were.”

“You do, apparently,” said Grandcourt, betraying by no eyelash that he cared.

“Yes—and you had better know too, that you may judge of the influence you have over her if she swallows her reasons and accepts you. For my own part I would take odds against it. She saw Lydia in Cardell Chase and heard the whole story.”

Grandcourt made no immediate answer. He went on smoking, as if the only thing in the room worth attending to were the faint crackle of the leaf and the soft exhale—private sounds, controlled, unlike the loud machinery of other people’s feelings. He waited so long that Lush began to move about and look out of the window, unwilling to leave without seeing some effect. He had expected Grandcourt to accuse him of contriving the interview, since Mrs. Glasher was then living at Gadsmere a hundred miles away, and he was ready to admit it. What mattered was that Grandcourt should feel he must approach a girl who had that knowledge and had been frightened by it.

At last Grandcourt looked at Lush again and said, with the same contempt as if discussing a trivial point of stable-management, “What follows?”

It was a neat mate to Lush’s check. However exasperated he was, it would have been idiocy to pretend that another move could do good. He gave a slight shrug and was turning away when Grandcourt—turning on his seat toward the table—said, as quietly as if nothing sharp had passed between them, “Oblige me by pushing that pen and paper here, will you?”

No blustering tyrant could have exercised the spell Grandcourt did in such moments. Men who would never call him master still found themselves moving at his smallest sign, as if his will were a dominant language their bodies understood even when their minds resented it.

Lush pushed the pen and paper. Grandcourt took them and said, “Just wait for this letter.”

He scrawled with ease; a brief note, quickly addressed.

“Let Hutchins go with it at once, will you?” Grandcourt said, pushing it away.

As Lush expected, it was directed to Miss Harleth, Offendene.

When Lush’s irritation cooled, he was glad there had been no explosive quarrel. Yet he felt a notch had been cut against him, and that somehow he was meant to pay. It was clear, too, that his revelation had not softened Grandcourt but hardened him, like sugar boiled too far into brittle. And as to what inward motions had made that hardening—what secret appetite, what resistance to being mastered by another’s knowledge—Lush could only lift his chin in despair of any theory.

Mr. Gascoigne came to Offendene with news he believed would steady a tottering household: Mrs. Mompert had fixed the following Tuesday for Gwendolen’s interview at Wanchester. He delivered it with the air of a man setting a stone into place—firmly, as if the wall would stand because one must.

He did not mention that Mr. Grandcourt was again at Diplow. He knew nothing of Leubronn as the end of that journey, and he judged it both needless and unkind to rake up a glittering possibility now that their circumstances had gone grey and tight as overboiled linen. In his private mind he regretted his niece’s caprice—unintelligible still—yet he excused it by remembering Grandcourt’s own strange withdrawal when admiration might have ripened into avowal. The rector’s sense of duty, trained to parish weather and human frailty, urged only this: she must be helped to meet what could not be avoided.

“You will find an interest in varied experience, my dear,” he said, arranging his words as if laying out cutlery in its proper order. “And I have no doubt you will be a more valuable woman for having sustained such a part as you are called to.”

“I cannot pretend to believe that I shall like it,” Gwendolen answered. For the first time there was a sharpness, like the quick crack of a crust split too soon. “But I am quite aware that I am obliged to bear it.”

“And your good sense will teach you to behave suitably under it,” he returned, with a shade more gravity. “Mrs. Mompert will be pleased with you. You will know how to conduct yourself to a woman who holds—in all senses—the relation of a superior to you. This trouble has come on you young; that makes it in some respects easier. There is a benefit in all chastisement if we adjust our minds to it.”

But her mind would not adjust. It was not a joint that could be coaxed into place by patience and pressure; it resisted like a lid warped by heat. When her uncle was gone, she sat alone and the tears came—slowly, bitterly, as if each drop had to be forced out from some depth where pride had kept it sealed. Young? Easier? Her heart denied it. If happiness did not come while she was young, when was it to come at all?

Her old visions of ease and triumph had already begun to sour: she could no longer believe that life’s fruits might be bitten without meeting some hard kernel, some bruising truth. Yet that very disenchantment, that new suspicion of herself—of her not being fashioned for effortless pre-eminence—only widened the sterile distance around her, hemming her in with a blank horizon. She could see the path at her feet and it looked dreary; it took courage merely to put one foot before another.

She was in that first fierce rebellion of youth, not so much against pain as against the absence of joy—the rage of a morning that ought to be bright and is instead a cold drizzle of duties. Later, when years have taught us to think of calamity as a common risk, we grow impatient with the amazement that this blow should be mine. And yet—many who afterward have stood between another and hurt, keeping their own wound quiet, began by raging like this when the world refused their desire. Gwendolen’s proud nature, trained from childhood to care most for what happened to her, could not swallow the thought that she must submit: Klesmer’s verdict that she could not command fortune by mere will; Mrs. Mompert’s expected rigours; the forced cheerfulness with three Miss Momperts; the perpetual demand to be agreeable and yet silent inside. The descent from a throne is nothing beside the discovery that one’s imagined divinity cannot summon a miracle.

The drawing-room held its accustomed gentility, but it felt airless, as if all the windows had been painted shut. She rose from the low ottoman where she had been sitting without purpose and walked up and down, her elbow planted on one palm, her cheek leaning on the other. A tear slipped down with the slow insistence of something that will not be denied.

“I have always—ever since I was little—felt that mamma was not a happy woman,” she thought. “And now I dare say I shall be more unhappy than she has been.”

For a moment she pictured herself losing her youth, ceasing to care, moving through days like a shadow that no longer startles at its own outline. But the image would not stay hers alone; it pulled her mother into it. “Poor mamma! It will be still worse for her now. I can get a little money for her—that is all I shall care about now.”

Then something in her imagination shifted, as if a door opened that had never opened before. She saw her mother old, hair gone white; she saw herself no longer young, faded and dulled. And she felt, with a sudden tenderness that pierced the armour of self-absorption, the moment when their faces might meet and memory would pass between them without words—her mother thinking, Poor Gwen too is sad and faded now. For the first time she sobbed not in anger, but with a grief that had love in it.

Her face was toward the door. She saw her mother enter—barely, because her eyes were flooded and she pressed her handkerchief against them in haste, ashamed of the evidence of weakness. Before she could compose herself, her mother’s arms were round her. The touch came like the completion of her own inward picture, and it undid her resolve to be reticent. The sobbing rose again in spite of her; cheeks pressed together, warmth against her trembling skin.

Mrs. Davilow had come in holding something—paper, folded, white against her fingers—and with it an agitation that made her look paler than usual, a tremor in her mouth. But she dared not speak until her darling was calmer.

Gwendolen, to whom weeping had always been a humiliating betrayal, pressed the handkerchief hard against her eyes again, drew a deep breath, and pulled back to look at her mother.

“It was nothing, mamma,” she said, thinking her mother’s alarm was only the sight of tears. “It is all over now.”

But Mrs. Davilow had already loosened her hold, and Gwendolen saw the letter.

“What is that letter?—worse news still?” she asked, with bitterness that flared like salt on a cut.

“I don’t know what you will think it, dear,” said Mrs. Davilow, keeping the letter in her hand as if it were hot. “You will hardly guess where it comes from.”

“Don’t ask me to guess anything,” said Gwendolen impatiently, as if her bruised feeling were being pressed upon.

“It is addressed to you, dear.”

A tiny toss of the head—an old motion of pride.

“It comes from Diplow,” said Mrs. Davilow, and gave it her.

Gwendolen knew the indistinct handwriting. The colour rushed into her face—deeply, quickly—then, as she read, it drained away as if some invisible hand had turned a tap. Even her lips went pale. She held out the open note without speaking.

The words were few, formal, edged like cold metal: Mr. Grandcourt presents his compliments to Miss Harleth, and begs to know whether he may be permitted to call at Offendene to-morrow after two and to see her alone. Mr. Grandcourt has just returned from Leubronn, where he had hoped to find Miss Harleth.

Mrs. Davilow read and looked up, questioning. Gwendolen let the note fall to the floor and turned away.

“It must be answered, darling,” Mrs. Davilow said timidly. “The man waits.”

Gwendolen sank on the settee, clasped her hands, and stared straight before her, as if listening for what follows a sudden sound in the night. A few minutes earlier she had been trapped in the dull corridor of necessity; now—without warning—a door stood open. A moment of choice had come.

Triumph, yes: it stirred in her like a remembered taste of power at the very instant she had begun to learn the bitterness of insignificance. Again, someone’s will bent toward hers; again, her life seemed to turn on her own decision. But with the triumph came terror—an inward recoil that had nothing to do with modesty and everything to do with what she knew.

Quickly, like pages forced open by a hurried thumb, there flashed back what she had been through with Grandcourt: the first allurements; her vacillations; her near assent; the final repulsion; and, cutting through all, the dark-eyed lady with the lovely boy—an image that had become a symbol of her new disbelief in the worth of men’s admiration and promises. Had she pledged herself—had she, in her soul, sworn never? The memory was unalterable; it made a shape in the mind that her native dread shrank from. What good was choice, if choice only meant facing that shape again?

And yet, deep beneath fear, a new wish began to germinate—blind, urgent, unreasoning: I wish I had never known it. If something, anything, could save her from letting Grandcourt come.

Mrs. Davilow waited—too long, it seemed, though it could only have been moments—before she said gently, “It will be necessary for you to write, dear. Or shall I write an answer for you—which you will dictate?”

“No, mamma,” said Gwendolen, drawing a deep breath. “But please lay me out the pen and paper.”

That was a way of gaining time, of bringing hands into play so that thought might hide behind a small ceremony. Was she to refuse? To shut the shutters on possibility? To keep herself safe in the same narrow future she had just been railing against?

Something restless in her—the young current that could not bear stagnation—ran warm under the fear and pushed toward an event, toward the chance to speak, to look, to act with her former effectiveness. The morrow was no longer a dead wall.

“There is really no reason on earth why you should be so alarmed at the man’s waiting a few minutes, mamma,” she said, with a remonstrant lift of tone as her mother set the writing materials and then looked toward her. “Servants expect nothing else than to wait. It is not to be supposed that I must write on the instant.”

“No, dear,” said Mrs. Davilow, corrected and quiet, turning to sit down and take up a piece of work lying near. “He can wait another quarter of an hour, if you like.”

The simplicity of it—needlework resumed, time allowed—had the effect of something subtly chosen. Gwendolen felt a contradictory wish to be hurried. Hurry would rescue her from deliberation; it would let her act without feeling the full weight of deciding.

“I did not mean him to wait long enough for that needlework to be finished,” she said, lifting her hands to smooth the backward curves of her hair, then standing still as if motion might shake loose a conclusion she could not yet bear.

“But if you don’t feel able to decide?” said her mother, with sympathy that made the question gentle.
