“I must decide,” said Gwendolen, and walked to the writing-table and sat down.

All the while, her mind ran a busy under-current, like someone keeping up a conversation while searching for a way to slip out of a room. Why not let him come? It bound her to nothing. He had gone to Leubronn after her; of course he meant to renew his suit plainly now. And then? She could refuse him. Why deny herself the freedom of doing what she wanted—to refuse him, to feel the old mastery in her voice?

“If Mr. Grandcourt has only just returned from Leubronn,” Mrs. Davilow said, seeing Gwendolen lean back with the pen in her hand, “I wonder whether he has heard of our misfortunes?”

“That could make no difference to a man in his position,” Gwendolen answered, with a contempt that tried to sound like certainty.

“It would to some men,” said Mrs. Davilow. “They would not like to take a wife from a family in a state of beggary almost, as we are. Here we are at Offendene with a great shell over us, as usual. But just imagine his finding us at Sawyer’s Cottage. Most men are afraid of being bored or taxed by a wife’s family. If Mr. Grandcourt did know, I think it a strong proof of his attachment to you.”

She spoke with an emphasis unusual for her—hesitant courage breaking through long reserve. And the words, meant as nothing more than a possibility, struck Gwendolen with a force her mother could not measure. They raised a fresh vision: what he might do for her mother if she—if she did what she was not going to do. The thought did not settle into resolve; it only set her blood moving with a sudden rush, as if a new flavour—dangerous and compelling—had touched her tongue.

The pressure of those ideas made her feel she must finish the immediate thing quickly, before she was overwhelmed by all that might follow. After all, she did what she had wanted: she acted in haste, and haste became a reason for postponing an absolute inward answer. She wrote:

“Miss Harleth presents her compliments to Mr. Grandcourt. She will be at home after two o’clock to-morrow.”

Before addressing the note, she said, “Pray ring the bell, mamma, if there is any one to answer it.” She truly did not know who did the work of the house now—what hands moved behind the scenes, quiet as breath, keeping their gentility from collapsing.

When the letter had been taken away, Gwendolen rose and stretched out one arm, then rested it on her head, letting out a low moan that held something like relief. Only then did Mrs. Davilow dare ask, “What did you say, Gwen?”

“I said that I should be at home,” Gwendolen answered, with a loftiness that tried to settle the matter. Then, after a pause, as if warning her mother against hope: “You must not expect, because Mr. Grandcourt is coming, that anything is going to happen, mamma.”

“I don’t allow myself to expect anything, dear. I desire you to follow your own feeling. You have never told me what that was.”

“What is the use of telling?” said Gwendolen, hearing a reproach in the truth. “When I have anything pleasant to tell, you may be sure I will tell you.”

“But Mr. Grandcourt will consider that you have already accepted him, in allowing him to come,” said Mrs. Davilow. “His note tells you plainly enough that he is coming to make you an offer.”

“Very well; and I wish to have the pleasure of refusing him.”

Mrs. Davilow looked up, amazed. But Gwendolen, as if the air itself were suddenly too thick to breathe, cut off further questioning.

“Put down that detestable needlework, and let us walk in the avenue. I am stifled.”

Desire, like a careful hand with a sail, had been trimming and trimming in the dark; and now circumstance, as if it had been waiting outside the window, brought the exact breath to fill the cloth.

While Grandcourt, splendid on his black Yarico, rode from Diplow toward Offendene with the groom behind on Criterion, Gwendolen sat before the glass in her mother’s room, and the long pale-brown hair—brushed until it lay like silken flax—was being gathered up by Mrs. Davilow with fingers that trembled a little from long practice and a recent anxiety.

“Only gather it up easily, mamma—make a coil,” Gwendolen said; and her voice, which had been thin and fretful of late, had a steadier warmth in it, like a stove newly coaxed into a clearer draught.

Mrs. Davilow’s eyes went from her daughter’s hair to the face in the mirror. The eyes were brighter; the shadow that had sat across the young cheeks seemed lifted, and the old placid lines were there again, as if some harsh sound had stopped in the house and left the air breathable. She spoke with a cheerfulness she could not quite account for.

“Let me bring you some earrings, Gwen.”

“No, mamma. I shall not wear any ornaments. I shall put on my black silk. Black is the only wear when one is going to refuse an offer.”

She smiled one of those old smiles that had always had the power of turning a poor room into a stage and her mother into an audience who must consent to be amused.

“Suppose the offer is not made after all,” said Mrs. Davilow, with a little slyness meant to coax out what her daughter meant.

“Then it will be because I refuse it beforehand,” Gwendolen returned. “It comes to the same thing.”

There was a proud toss of the head, and when she went down-stairs in the long black robe, the poise and elasticity that had lately failed her were back—as if a plant that had drooped in heat had felt water in the soil again.

Mrs. Davilow, watching, had the thought she would not dare to utter: She is quite herself again. It must be pleasure in his coming. Can she really be fixed against him?

Gwendolen would have flamed at that suspicion, perhaps because for nearly twenty-four hours her mind had been a perpetual seesaw—images and arguments dipping and rising—until the resolution she had clung to felt like a dried pressed flower: the shape remained, but life had been sucked from it. She had meant to refuse Grandcourt from the moment his letter came; yet the very act of meaning it had forced her to look full into the unwelcome reasons, to stare them down until they seemed less aweful; and then imagination, that busy cook of the mind who can make twenty dishes out of one doubtful ingredient, had begun to season and transform what she knew.

Her earlier hesitation before the Whispering Stones counted for nothing now: everything had merged in the final repulsion she had felt that day in Cardell Chase. It was not a neat weighing of motives; it had been an impulse like a gust that takes the reins for you. Pride and jealousy, yes; the shock of another woman’s calamity pushed suddenly close, yes; but behind these, stronger than she liked to confess, was dread of wrong-doing—vague, not tied to any daily habit of hers, yet as real as the chill that runs through you when some deep note sounds in an empty church. “Disgraceful,” “wrong,” “guilty”—she shrank from those words as from a harsh foreign tongue that could name her and command her. And apart from shame, deliberate injury of another fell for her into that region called guilt.

But did she know exactly—exactly—what Mrs. Glasher’s claim was? She had said, “I will not interfere with your wishes.” But would another woman’s marrying Grandcourt really be the decisive obstacle to those wishes—really a new injury? Might it not even be better that he should marry? What could not a wife do, if she knew how to assert herself? Here she built castles, and the mortar was ignorance. Marriage, to her, was as little understood as the law of storms; she had seen one household shipwreck and concluded, with a young captain’s arrogance, that it was the navigator’s fault. “Mamma managed badly”—that was her summary. She would manage differently.

And yet she wondered, in a flash that had more fear in it than curiosity, what her mother and her uncle would say if they knew about Mrs. Glasher. She could not imagine telling them—promise or no promise. “What would anybody say?” she asked herself, taking refuge in that great anonymous tribunal which saves one the pain of judging. And her memory answered: “anybody” looked shyly on illegitimate children as if they were the ones to be punished, while fathers went on in ease. “Anybody,” that is, the dominant lexicon of her world, made the boy and the mother the lower word in the sentence, the disposable clause. It would be, by that ruling, absurd for her to trouble herself.

But there was another sting: indignation, loathing, that she should be asked to unite herself to a life already worn and secret, a past that must have been more keenly real to him than any new association with her. Love, on her side, had hardly entered the question; marriage had always appeared to her as a means—of freedom, of power, of escape from humiliations. To be enamored was the man’s part. She had not objected to Grandcourt’s enamored manner until she had seen that glimpse of what lay behind him—resenting it as if he had deliberately insulted her by having lived before she met him. His advances had been deliberate; her disgust went backward over them.

Perhaps, she thought in her darker moment, other men’s lives were like this—full of secrets that made women’s ignorant suppositions a kind of farce. That disgust had sunk deep; though later troubles had dulled it from flame into a steady heat, it still kept her firm to the old understanding with herself: she was not going to accept him. She was not forming a new determination—only considering what would be said. If anything could have bribed her into yielding, it would have been “poor mamma.” To make everything easy for her mother—that temptation had a taste as sweet as warm bread when one has been hungry too long. But no: she was going to refuse him.

And yet—this was the treachery of her spirits—there was a kind of exhilaration in knowing he was coming to be refused. The situation restored to her the sensation of holding reins again. After the beaten-down helplessness left by Klesmer’s judgment, she was not to crave any opinion; she was to exercise power. That, perhaps, was why her heart beat so uncomfortably when she heard the hoofs on the gravel—when Miss Merry, who had opened the door, came to say that Mr. Grandcourt was in the drawing-room.

All her hours of preparation seemed suddenly useless; she might have been caught unawares in her worst dejection. Walking toward the room, she had to gather her self-command as one gathers a shawl close in a cold gust—so that she entered gravely gracious, gave her hand, and answered his hope that she was well in a voice as low and languid as his own.

A moment later they were seated on two wreath-painted chairs: Gwendolen upright, eyelids lowered; Grandcourt two yards distant, one arm thrown over the chair-back, hat in his left hand, his long narrow eyes fixed on her with that impenetrable attention which felt like a hand laid on the nape of the neck. As a picture, they would have seemed in the suspended stage of love-making.

And indeed the wooing had begun. He was seated at an agreeable distance, but the subtle atmosphere of attar of roses clung about him, as if his very leisure had been perfumed. She already felt herself being pursued—not by eagerness, but by a silent persistence that made every pause a net.

“I was disappointed not to find you at Leubronn,” he began, his broken drawl softened by a shade of amorous languor. “The place was intolerable without you. A mere kennel of a place. Don’t you think so?”

“I can’t judge what it would be without myself,” Gwendolen said, and lifted her eyes with a spark of recovered mischief. “With myself I like it well enough to have stayed longer, if I could. But I was obliged to come home on account of family troubles.”

“It was very cruel of you to go to Leubronn,” said Grandcourt, taking no notice of troubles—precisely what made her wish, she hardly knew why, to have them understood. “You must have known it would spoil everything. You knew you were the heart and soul of everything that went on. Are you quite reckless about me?”

To say “yes” seriously was impossible; to say “no” was no easier. In her difficulty she lowered her lids and felt the heat of a blush steal over face and neck, as if some inner oven-door had opened. Grandcourt watched her, reading inclination in what was only embarrassment, and he was not a man to let uncertainty remain as mere air; he liked it shaped into something he could hold.

“Perhaps there is some deeper interest?” he went on. “Some attraction—some engagement—which it would have been only fair to make me aware of? Is there any man who stands between us?”

The instant answer sprang up: No; but there is a woman. Yet she could not utter it. Even without her promise to silence, she could not have spoken of Mrs. Glasher to him. And how could she stop his approach by beginning a formal rejection? A fish honestly invited to be eaten has a clear refusal; but what if the water itself is a net?

Grandcourt waited only long enough to make her silence a confession.

“Am I to understand that some one else is preferred?”

Now impatience with her own faltering seized her. She raised her eyes with something of her old clearness.

“No,” she said—meaning, There is no one else; but that does not mean I am ready for you.

He understood at once whatever touched his own pride.

“The last thing I would do is to importune you,” he replied. “I should not hope to win you by making myself a bore. If there were no hope for me, I would ask you to tell me so at once, that I might just ride away to—no matter where.”

The image of him riding away struck her with a sudden alarm—like a door shutting on music. What would be left then? The old dreariness, the small economies, the prospect of Sawyer’s Cottage and being “inspected” by Mrs. Mompert—those domestic humiliations with their perpetual small sounds: the scrape of a mean grate, the thin clink of a cheap teacup, the relentless whisper of money-counting. She liked him there. She seized on the subject that would postpone a decisive answer.

“I fear you are not aware of what has happened to us,” she said. “I have lately had to think so much of my mamma’s troubles that other subjects have been quite thrown into the background. She has lost all her fortune, and we are going to leave this place. I must ask you to excuse my seeming preoccupied.”

As she spoke, she recovered dignity—stood straighter, looked at him steadily. His eyes met hers and held them with a strange arrest; and in that held gaze there was the whole unspoken drama, untranslatable into the neat dominoes of words. Love was too small a word for what passed between them—too generalized, too commercial, like a label slapped on a jar without naming what spice lies within.

Grandcourt’s strongest wish at that moment was mastery: this creature—maidenly and mischievous, with some knowledge that had made her start away—was the very thing to conquer. Her repugnance was an affront to his triumph. And she, equal in the piteous need to dominate, felt drawn as the thirsty are drawn toward seeming water in a desert—drawn by the sense that in his homage lay rescue from helplessness, from an oppressive lot.

He spoke slowly, languidly, as if matters were already settled and this were a mere arrangement.

“You will tell me now, I hope, that Mrs. Davilow’s loss of fortune will not trouble you further. You will trust me to prevent it from weighing upon her. You will give me the claim to provide against that.”

The pauses gave her time to live a whole dream. His words went into her like wine: the world softened; desirable things seemed less wrong; people in general less disagreeable. In a swift phantasm she loved him—loved the way he chose his phrases, the way he offered relief as if it were a natural right he could confer. Repugnance, dread, scruple fell back like pains remembered after a dose has begun to work. She saw herself running to her mother, playful again; saw Sawyer’s Cottage as something that belonged to another life.

“You are very generous,” she said, gently, her eyes not moving.

“You accept what will make such things a matter of course?” he asked.

Then the question came plain.

“You consent to become my wife?”

This time she did not blush; she went quite pale. Something in her rose and made her stand up and move away, as if her body knew it stood at a dangerous turn. She walked a little distance, then turned and stood with hands folded before her, silent.

Grandcourt rose too, resting his hat on the chair but still holding it. Her hesitation—this hesitation in a girl with no fortune, offered his splendid security—stung him into a keenness he had not felt for years. He attributed it wholly to what she knew about Mrs. Glasher; and her very silence became to him a kind of defiance.

In that poised moment he said, “Do you command me to go?”

No familiar spirit could have put into his mouth words more effective. Command him to go? The phrase gave her the taste of power at the very edge of losing it. She could not bear the shut door, the emptied air.

“No,” she said.

That “no” was a clutch—her hand closing on the last strong rope before she was swept back into the small, grinding noises of her new poverty.

“You accept my devotion?” he said, standing still, hat at his side, looking straight into her eyes.

Their eyes meeting in that way seemed to create a pause without measure; but however long she waited, how could she contradict herself? What had she detained him for? He had shut out explanation as if he had quietly turned a key.

“Yes,” came from her lips, gravely, as if she were answering to her name in a court where the verdict would bind her life.

He received it with the same gravity, and for an instant they were still—an engagement sealed without the usual smiles and fluttered phrases. At length he laid down his hat, advanced, took her hand, pressed his lips upon it, and let it go again.

She found his manner perfect: it imposed no immediate claim, and in that she felt almost free. Her “Yes” seemed, at the moment, to entail very little beyond an opening door. Her mind filled with release: no more the Momperts; no more Sawyer’s Cottage. It was as if a harsh language had been silenced and she could speak again in her own key.

With a happier curl of the lip she said, “Will you not see mamma? I will fetch her.”

“Let us wait a little,” said Grandcourt, assuming his favorite attitude—left forefinger and thumb in his waistcoat pocket, right hand caressing his whisker—standing near her and looking as if he had made a felicitous entrance at an evening party. “Have you anything else to say to me?”

“Yes—” Gwendolen’s tone turned playful, warmed by her sense of power returned. “Have you anything else to say to me?”

“Yes—I know having things said to you is a great bore,” he answered, with a faint sympathy.

“Not when they are things I like to hear.”

“Will it bother you to be asked how soon we can be married?”

“I think it will—to-day,” she said, lifting her chin saucily.

“Not to-day, then, but to-morrow. Think of it before I come to-morrow. In a fortnight—or three weeks—as soon as possible.”

“Ah, you think you will be tired of my company,” she laughed, and the laugh sounded like a bright spoon on fine china after weeks of tin. “I notice when people are married the husband is not so much with his wife as when they are engaged. But perhaps I shall like that better, too.”

“You shall have whatever you like,” he said.

“And nothing that I don’t like?—please say that; because I think I dislike what I don’t like more than I like what I like.”

She was in that woman’s paradise where nonsense becomes adorable. Grandcourt paused; he had experience of subtleties and of the power in yielding to them with a half-mocking patience.

“I don’t know. This is such a brute of a world—things are always turning up that one doesn’t like. I can’t always hinder your being bored. If you like to ride Criterion, I can’t hinder his coming down by some chance or other.”

“Ah, my friend Criterion—how is he?”

“He is outside. I made the groom ride him, that you might see him. He had the side-saddle on for an hour or two yesterday. Come to the window and look at him.”

They went, and through the glass saw the two horses led slowly round the sweep. Their coats had that deep, brushed gloss that holds the light like polished fruit; their steps made a measured, living music on the gravel—the clean, rhythmic crunch and click that seemed to quiet something in Gwendolen’s nerves, as if a healthy soundscape could wash away inner clamor. The horses’ breathing was faintly visible, and the jingle of harness came with the small wind like a promise.

A thrill of exultation went through her. They were symbols—command, luxury, motion—everything opposite to the ugliness of humiliation and the thin, scraping economies of poverty.

“Will you ride Criterion to-morrow?” said Grandcourt. “If you will, everything shall be arranged.”

“I should like it of all things,” she said. “I want to lose myself in a gallop again. But now I must go and fetch mamma.”

“Take my arm to the door, then,” he said.

She accepted. Their faces were near, almost level; he looked at her, and she found his lover-like manners more agreeable than any she remembered in books. There was no alarm that he meant to kiss her; he kept within a ceremonial distance that made her feel safe, even triumphant.

Halfway across the room she paused, suddenly remembering something that, in her new confidence, she could name without shame.

“Oh—while I think of it—there is something I dislike that you can save me from. I do not like Mr. Lush’s company.”

“You shall not have it. I’ll get rid of him.”

“You are not fond of him yourself?”

“Not in the least. I let him hang on me because he has always been a poor devil,” Grandcourt said, in an adagio of utter indifference. “They got him to travel with me when I was a lad. He was always that coarse-haired kind of brute—sort of cross between a hog and a dilettante.”

Gwendolen laughed. It seemed kind and natural enough; his fastidiousness even enhanced the kindness. And when he opened the door for her, the easy homage of the act had the grace of a well-trained hand in a well-ordered house.

Really, she thought, he was likely to be the least disagreeable of husbands.

Mrs. Davilow was waiting anxiously in her bedroom. At the sight of her mother’s strained face, Gwendolen’s heart gave a small inward twist; but she stepped quickly forward, kissed her on both cheeks, and said in a low tone, as if the words were hot and must be spoken at once:

“Come down, mamma, and see Mr. Grandcourt. I am engaged to him.”

“My darling child,” Mrs. Davilow murmured, with a surprise that was more solemn than glad—like a bell sounded softly in a church when the air is full of prayers.

“Yes,” said Gwendolen, with a quickness that denied questions. “Everything is settled. You are not going to Sawyer’s Cottage, I am not going to be inspected by Mrs. Mompert, and everything is to be as I like. So come down with me immediately.”

An hour after Grandcourt had ridden away from Offendene, the air of the rectory seemed to change—like a kitchen when the first word goes round that there is to be a wedding feast. By evening, Mr. and Mrs. Gascoigne arrived with Anna, and the house filled itself with voices and the small domestic rustlings that make even great news feel like it must submit to cups of tea and a decent fire.

“My dear,” said the rector, taking Gwendolen’s hand with an approving gentleness, “let me congratulate you. You look grave—and no wonder. A life-long union is solemn. But from the way Mr. Grandcourt has acted, I think we already see good rising out of our adversity. It has enabled you to observe your future husband’s—hm—delicate liberality.”

He alluded, with the calm satisfaction of a man quoting a comforting text, to Grandcourt’s manner of letting it be understood that Mrs. Davilow would be provided for—an item of the courtship which Gwendolen had repeated to her mother with exactness, as if she were copying down a recipe that must not fail.

“But I have no doubt he would have behaved handsomely even if you had never gone away to Germany,” Mrs. Gascoigne put in, feeling the need to salt the sweetness with duty. “And now there is no more room for caprice. I trust you have no inclination to any. A woman owes a debt of gratitude to a man who perseveres in making her such an offer. No doubt you feel properly.”

“I’m not at all sure I do, aunt,” said Gwendolen, with that saucy gravity which let her mock propriety while seeming to ask for it. “I don’t know everything it is proper to feel on being engaged.”

The rector patted her shoulder, smiling as if she were merely a child who had spilt sugar and made it pretty. Mrs. Gascoigne, watching his indulgence, allowed herself not to be offended. Anna kissed Gwendolen and murmured, “I do hope you will be happy,” and then, as if her own breath would betray her, withdrew into stillness and struggled with tears.

For Anna, lately, had been nursing a shy romance of her own—imagining Rex’s longing enduring, and trouble softening Gwendolen at last into a love that would make amends. That romance had dwindled into a prayer—only that she might rejoice like a good sister, and, if Rex was not rich, still be useful. And now she had to find grace to rejoice in something else altogether.

Miss Merry and the four girls were there too—Alice with her high shoulders; Bertha and Fanny whispering; Isabel listening with that devout attention which makes listeners seem wiser than speakers. It was as if the household had arranged itself, without a word said, into an audience for a heroine whose life had taken on the splendid interest of a novel, and every cup and chair was merely a prop for “the honor and glory of Gwendolen.”

The evening went chiefly in Mr. Gascoigne’s decisive remarks, answering the conjectures of the elder ladies. On the question of settlements—those domestic contracts that can make love sound like law—he declared the case was not one in which he could think it his duty to mention them: all must, and doubtless would, be safely left to Mr. Grandcourt.

“I should like to know exactly what sort of places Ryelands and Gadsmere are,” said Mrs. Davilow.

“Gadsmere, I believe, is a secondary place,” the rector replied; “but Ryelands I know to be one of our finest seats. The park is extensive; the woods valuable. The house was built by Inigo Jones, and the ceilings are painted in the Italian style. The estate is said to be worth twelve thousand a year, and there are two livings—one a rectory—in the gift of the Grandcourts. There may be burdens on the land. Still, Mr. Grandcourt was an only child.”

“It would be most remarkable,” said Mrs. Gascoigne, counting the grandeur on her fingers as if she were portioning out fruit at a dessert-table, “if he were to become Lord Stannery in addition to everything else. Only think—there is the Grandcourt estate, the Mallinger estate, and the baronetcy, and the peerage—though they say there will be no land coming with the peerage.” She paused on the fourth finger, as if regretting that providence provided no fifth.

“The peerage,” said the rector, smoothing the matter as one smooths dough that threatens to crack, “must be regarded as a remote chance. There are two cousins between the present peer and Mr. Grandcourt. It is a serious reflection how death and other causes sometimes concentrate inheritances on one man. But excess is to be deprecated. To be Sir Mallinger Grandcourt Mallinger, I suppose that will be his style, with corresponding properties, is talent enough for any man to have committed to him. Let us hope it will be well used.”

“And what a position for the wife, Gwendolen!” Mrs. Gascoigne said. “A great responsibility. But you must lose no time in writing to Mrs. Mompert, Henry. It is a good thing you have an engagement to offer as an excuse, else she might feel offended. She is rather a high woman.”

“I am rid of that horror,” thought Gwendolen, for the name Mompert had become to her like a conjuring-word—one of those noises that make the mind recoil before it even attaches meaning.

She had been very silent, and that night, in her little white bed, she could hardly sleep at all. Wakefulness was rare for her robust youth; rarer still was this care—almost stealthy—that her mother should not know she lay staring into the dark. But everything within her was new. She, who had always felt sure of herself, always ready to manage others, had taken a decisive step she had beforehand believed she would not take—nay, perhaps, must not.

There was no retreat now. She liked much of what lay before her; and behind her there seemed nothing to like—only the dull humiliation of insignificance and servitude. Yet the resolution she had just made was dogged by the shadow of her former resolve, when her whole being had first started back from Grandcourt with repugnance.

Lying with wide-open eyes—“looking on darkness which the blind do see”—she was appalled by the notion that she was going to do what she had once turned from as wrong. It was new to her that the question of right or wrong should rouse terror; she had been used to little stings of conscience being soothed by caresses, gifts, distractions—like a bitterness covered over with sugar. But now some other consciousness had awakened, raw and importunate. It was as if she stood on the verge of adopting, deliberately, for all her life, the bitter sentence she had flung out when her discovery had driven her to Leubronn—that it did not signify what she did; she had only to amuse herself as best she could.

That lawlessness—that casting away of the need for justification—suddenly frightened her. It came with a shadowy array of calamities behind it; and calamity had ceased to be a mere word. The old, half-forgotten influences of religious teaching she had disregarded, and the deeper impression that something inexorable might wrap itself round her, gathered into the vague idea of avenging power.

The brilliant position she had longed for, the freedom she imagined marriage would grant her, the deliverance from the flatness of girlhood—all stood close, ready. And yet they came to her hunger like food tainted with sacrilege: something she must snatch with trembling, and then pretend it nourished her without poisoning her.

In that loneliness, her resistant self could not rise against the first onslaught of dread after her irrevocable decision. The unhappy-faced woman and her children—Grandcourt and his relations with her—returned and returned, sticking in her imagination like the taste of smoke that clings after a kitchen fire has been put out. Gradually they blotted out all other thought, leaving only one consciousness: she had taken those scenes into her life.

Her long wakefulness became like fever. A faint light crept in beside the curtain; the chill increased. She could bear it no longer.

“Mamma!” she cried.

“Yes, dear,” Mrs. Davilow answered at once, in a voice that had not slept.

“Let me come to you.”

She went, and soon fell asleep on her mother’s shoulder, as if that familiar warmth could quiet all the unseen terror. She slept late; and when she opened her eyes again she was dreaming of a lit ball-room, only to find her mother standing by the bed with a small packet in her hand.

“I am sorry to wake you, darling, but I thought it better you should have this at once. The groom has brought Criterion—he has come on another horse, and says he is to stay here.”

Gwendolen sat up and broke the packet. Inside was a delicate enamelled casket; inside that, a splendid diamond ring. There was a letter too, with a folded slip of colored paper, and these words:

Pray wear this ring when I come at twelve in sign of our betrothal. I enclose a check drawn in the name of Mr. Gascoigne, for immediate expenses. Of course Mrs. Davilow will remain at Offendene, at least for some time. I hope, when I come, you will have granted me an early day, when you may begin to command me at a shorter distance.—Yours devotedly,

H. M. GRANDCOURT.

The check was for five hundred pounds. Gwendolen turned it toward her mother with the letter.

“How very kind and delicate!” said Mrs. Davilow, with real feeling. “But I should like better not to be dependent on a son-in-law. I and the girls could get along very well.”

“Mamma, if you say that again, I will not marry him,” Gwendolen said, sharply—anger rushing up like heat from a stove someone has opened too suddenly.

“My dear child, I trust you are not going to marry only for my sake,” Mrs. Davilow said, deprecatingly.

Gwendolen tossed her head away on the pillow and let the ring lie untouched. She was irritated at her mother’s attempt to take away a motive—as if someone had moved the very board on which she meant to play her game. Perhaps the deeper cause was the knowledge that she was not marrying solely for her mother’s sake—that she was drawn toward it by other forces, and that even her mother’s renunciation was not strong enough to stop them.

She had woken to the signs that she was irrevocably engaged; and the ugly visions, alarms, arguments of the night had to be met in daylight, where they would likely seem feeble—like ghosts that are bold only in dark corners.

“What I long for is your happiness, dear,” Mrs. Davilow continued, pleading. “I will not say anything to vex you. Will you not put on the ring?”

Gwendolen did not answer at once; but thoughts moved quickly in her as hands move when a cook, resolved not to fail, begins again with fresh precision after a moment’s discouragement. At last she raised herself with a sudden determination—like one who, having started on horseback, will go on with spirit whatever wild fancies gallop beside her.

“I thought the lover always put on the betrothal ring himself,” she said, laughing as she slipped it on and turned her head with a charming movement to see its fire. “I know why he has sent it,” she added, nodding at her mother.

“Why?”

“He would rather make me put it on than ask me to let him do it. Aha! he is very proud. But so am I. We shall match each other. I should hate a man who went down on his knees and came fawning on me. He really is not disgusting.”

“That is very moderate praise, Gwen.”

“No, it is not—for a man,” Gwendolen said gaily. Then, with the swift change of a girl who can turn from defiance to caress as if it were the same motion: “But now I must get up and dress. Will you come and do my hair, mamma dear,” she coaxed, drawing her mother’s face down and rubbing cheek to cheek, “and not be so naughty any more as to talk of living in poverty? You must bear to be made comfortable even if you don’t like it. And Mr. Grandcourt behaves perfectly now, does he not?”

“Certainly he does,” said Mrs. Davilow, encouraged, and persuading herself—as mothers do—that her daughter must be fond of her betrothed. She herself judged Grandcourt as many judge suitors: by the figure they make in society, by the look of their attentions, by the quiet authority of their wealth. Her anxiety lay less in his character than in Gwendolen’s mood—whether it would hold steady.

That mood necessarily shifted this morning. Even while she made her toilet, she drew on all the knowledge she had—like a housewife searching her shelves—to find grounds that would justify her marriage. What she dwelt on most was a determination: when she was Grandcourt’s wife she would urge him to liberal conduct toward Mrs. Glasher’s children.

“Of what use would it be to her that I should not marry him? He could have married her if he liked; but he did not like. Perhaps she is to blame for that. There must be a great deal about her I know nothing of. And he must have been good to her in many ways, else she would not have wanted to marry him.”

But that last argument began at once to taste doubtful—like a sauce that turns on the tongue. Mrs. Glasher naturally wished to exclude other children who would stand between Grandcourt and her own; and Gwendolen’s comprehension of that feeling opened another way of reconciling claims.

“Perhaps we shall have no children. I hope we shall not. And he might leave the estate to the pretty little boy. My uncle said Mr. Grandcourt could do as he liked with the estates. Only when Sir Hugo Mallinger dies there will be enough for two.”

Then Mrs. Glasher appeared unreasonable in demanding that her boy should be sole heir; and the double property seemed a sort of safety—proof that Grandcourt’s marriage need do her no wrong, when the wife was Gwendolen Harleth, armed with proud resolution not to be fairly accused. She had been accustomed to regard herself as blameless: it was other people who were faulty.

Strikingly, as this argument took hold—that she was doing no wrong—her repugnance toward the idea of Grandcourt’s past sank into something secondary. The terror of overstepping the border of wickedness dulled her emotions about his conduct. She thought of him now, whatever he might be, as a man she was going to have indefinite power over; and since loving him had never been a question, any agreeableness he had was so much gain.

Poor Gwendolen had no awe of unmanageable forces in marriage. She regarded it as a matter of management, and believed she knew how to act. As to Grandcourt’s past, she encouraged herself with doubts—perhaps he differed little from other men; perhaps men in general were expected to have such histories. She even devised little schemes for learning, without seeming to ask, what was allowed by the dominant language of “the world”—that language which can turn suffering into a mere “indiscretion,” and make a woman’s life into an unspeakable footnote.

But whatever else might be true, her hair was dressed suitably for riding, and she went down in her habit so that there might be no delay before mounting. She wanted her blood stirred again with the intoxication of youth; she wanted to recover the daring with which she had always imagined her course in life. A load already seemed lifted: in daylight and movement, it was less oppressive to have doubts than to have no choice but insignificance.

As she went down-stairs she turned suddenly.

“Go back and make yourself look like a duchess, mamma. Put your point-lace over your head. I must have you look like a duchess. You must not take things humbly.”

At twelve Grandcourt came. When he raised her left hand gently and looked at the ring, she said gravely, “It was very good of you to think of everything and send me that packet.”

“You will tell me if there is anything I forget?” he said, still keeping her hand softly within his own. “I will do anything you wish.”

“But I am very unreasonable in my wishes,” said Gwendolen, smiling.

“Yes, I expect that. Women always are.”

“Then I will not be unreasonable,” she retorted, taking her hand away and tossing her head. “I will not be told I am what women always are.”

“I did not say that,” Grandcourt answered, looking at her with his usual gravity. “You are what no other woman is.”

“And what is that, pray?” Gwendolen moved a little away, with an air of pretty menace.

He paused before answering, as he always did, as if even tenderness must submit to his measure. “You are the woman I love.”

“Oh, what nice speeches!” she laughed, letting his words fall on her like music she did not mean to believe in, yet liked to hear. The sense of that love he must once have given another woman under strange conditions had begun to feel familiar—as if the mind, like a household, can grow used to any sound that repeats often enough.

“Give me a nice speech in return. Say when we are to be married.”

“Not yet. Not till we have had a gallop over the downs. I am so thirsty for that I can think of nothing else. I wish the hunting had begun. Sunday the twentieth, twenty-seventh, Monday, Tuesday—” She counted on her fingers, nodding prettily as she looked at him, then swept one palm over the other with triumph. “It will begin in ten days!”

“Let us be married in ten days, then,” said Grandcourt, “and we shall not be bored about the stables.”

“What do women always say in answer to that?” she asked, mischievously.

“They agree to it,” he said, a little off his guard.

“Then I will not!” She took up her gauntlets and began to draw them on, her eyes on him with gathering fun.

The scene pleased them both. A cruder lover would have spoiled it with heavy caresses, breaking the fine surface of her play; but Grandcourt preferred the drama, and she, left at ease, felt her spirits rise as she played at reigning. There was in her—when she was not trying, when she was simply alive—a kind of unconscious acting, more persuasive than any theatrical effort.

After they had had their gallop—a glorious one, with the clean rush of air and the ground sounding under hoof like a deep drumbeat in the open world—she was exhilarated into thinking well of hastening the marriage that would make her life all of a piece with this splendid enjoyment. She would not debate any more about an act she had committed herself to; and she consented to fix the wedding for that day three weeks, despite the difficulty of fulfilling the customary laws of the trousseau.

Lush, of course, read the engagement in a hundred signs without being formally told: the altered movements in the house, the brief orders, the new silences, the sense of a door closing on old habits. He expected communication as a consequence, and after a few days grew impatient under Grandcourt’s quiet. He was sure the change must affect his own prospects and wanted to know precisely how.

His tactics no longer included opposition; he did not love it for its own sake. He could annoy Grandcourt, certainly—but it would injure himself, and mere annoyance was not his motive. Miss Gwendolen he would not have been sorry to thwart a little; but one never knew what might come. Grandcourt’s perverse wilfulness was not new, yet in this freak about the girl he struck Lush as something like a man who was fey—led on by an ominous fatality. That one born to fortune should make worse business of his life than was necessary seemed, to Lush, genuinely pitiable.

Grandcourt had even taken pains to write letters and give orders himself instead of employing Lush; he appeared to ignore his usefulness, and, against the habit of years, chose sometimes to breakfast alone in his dressing-room. But in a house empty of guests a tête-à-tête cannot be wholly avoided. One day after dinner—difficult enough, since Grandcourt did not regularly dine at Offendene—Lush seized his chance.

“And when is the marriage to take place?”

Grandcourt, who drank little, had left the table and lounged near the hearth, smoking in an easy chair while a fire of oak boughs gaped into glowing depths and edged itself with delicate ash. The chair’s red-brown velvet brocade set off the pale, well-cut features and the exquisite long hands. Without the cigar he might have been a portrait by Moroni—impenetrable gaze, air of distinction; and such a portrait would have been as lively a companion as Grandcourt was disposed to be. But he answered without unusual delay.

“On the tenth.”

“I suppose you intend to remain here.”

“We shall go to Ryelands for a little while; but we shall return here for the sake of the hunting.”

There was that languid inarticulate sound Grandcourt often made when he meant to continue. Lush waited, hearing in that faint noise the promise of his own future. Nothing followed. Lush was about to question again when the inarticulate sound began once more and introduced, mildly uttered:

“You had better make some new arrangement for yourself.”

“What! I am to cut and run?” said Lush, prepared to be good-tempered.

“Something of that kind.”

“The bride objects to me. I hope she will make up to you for the want of my services.”

“I can’t help your being so damnably disagreeable to women,” Grandcourt said, by way of apology, as if soothing a horse he was turning out.

“To one woman, if you please.”

“It makes no difference since she is the one in question.”

“I suppose I am not to be turned adrift after fifteen years without some provision.”

“You must have saved something out of me.”

“Deuced little. I have often saved something for you.”

“You can have three hundred a year. But you must live in town and be ready to look after things when I want you. I shall be rather hard up.”

“If you are not going to be at Ryelands this winter, I might run down there and let you know how Swinton goes on.”

“If you like. I don’t care a toss where you are, so that you keep out of sight.”

“Much obliged,” said Lush; the terms were easier than he had feared. Underneath, he nursed a secret belief that by-and-by he would be wanted as much as ever.

“Perhaps you will not object to packing up as soon as possible,” Grandcourt added. “The Torringtons are coming, and Miss Harleth will be riding over here.”

“With all my heart. Can’t I be of use in going to Gadsmere?”

“No. I am going myself.”

“About your being rather hard up. Have you thought of that plan—”

“Just leave me alone, will you?” Grandcourt said in his lowest audible tone, tossing his cigar into the fire and rising to walk away.

He spent the evening in solitude in the smaller drawing-room. Various new publications lay on the table—political, comic, cynical, romantic—the sort a gentleman likes to have in view without touching, as if the presence of books could stand in for the trouble of reading. He employed himself in sitting meditatively on the sofa and abstaining from literature. In this way hours pass surprisingly soon—not from love of thought but from hatred of effort: a premature inward age, where the need for action lapses into a mere image of what has been, is, and might be; where impulse is born and dies in a phantasmal world, rejecting even shadowy fulfilment.

That condition often comes with whitening hair; and sometimes with it comes an intense obstinacy and tenacity of rule—an exorbitant egoism standing out more starkly as the susceptibilities of youth are stripped away.

But Grandcourt’s hair, though not abundant, was of a fine sunny blond; and his moods could not be explained solely by ebbing energy. There is a strange chemistry within us: a lazy stagnation, even a cottony milkiness, may be preparing—one knows not what—biting or explosive material. The navvy who wakes and without malice crushes his sleeping comrade is understood to lack trained motive; yet by roundabout courses even a gentleman may make of himself a chancy personage—raising, in those who live near him, an uncertainty as to what he may do next, which spoils companionship as surely as any harsh sound spoils a quiet room.

“Now my cousins are at Diplow,” Grandcourt said, as if he were speaking of weather that could be altered by raising an eyebrow. “Will you go there—to-morrow? The carriage shall come for Mrs. Davilow. You can tell me what you would like done in the rooms. Things must be put in decent order while we are away at Ryelands. And to-morrow is the only day.”

Rain made a thin, steady music on the panes at Offendene—no harsh battering, only that small, persistent tapping which turns a house inward and magnifies each footfall, each rustle of silk, each drawn breath into something audible and intimate. The hearth answered with its low crackle, the coals shifting like a creature settling itself; yet beyond these domestic sounds there was the duller, more modern undertone: the far wheel on the road, the distant hammering that had become the countryside’s new pulse, reminding one how noise creeps outward from towns as surely as smoke.

Grandcourt sat sideways on the sofa, arranged as if ease were a commandment. One arm lay along the back; the other hand was thrust between his crossed knees, a posture meant to suggest attention without yielding any of his own repose. He watched Gwendolen as if she were a spectacle he had paid for and meant to enjoy without interruption.

She had taken up embroidery since her engagement—an occupation that pretended to patience and purity. The white cloth lay like an altar-piece across her lap, and the thread shone, obedient; but the stitches, were anyone to study them closely, betrayed hurry and little acts of rebellion—false turns, uneven tensions, the secret signature of a hand that did not love submission. Still, she made a show of application, and that show had its own advantage: it gave her something to do with her fingers while her mind ran on other tracks.

The last eight or nine days had been chiefly horseback—wind, leather, the living heat of a horse under you, and the clean, fluting whistle of air past the ears. Even now, kept indoors by rain, she could feel that remembered canter in her blood. Yet there had always been, between rides, this other companionship—harder, more delicate, and in some ways more dangerous.

She had been well satisfied with Grandcourt, as one is satisfied with a dish that is rich, costly, and never surprises the palate. He answered her lively questions with a drawl that seemed, in his mouth, not dullness but mastery: the leisure of a man for whom time had always waited. From the first she had felt that he knew how to speak—how to make his knowledge a kind of possession, and his contempt a kind of gift. He implied, without saying it, that folly belonged to other people, those who busied themselves, exerted themselves, wanted things too openly. A man who had always been served the best could, with a slight movement of tone, make the best seem a thing too common to care about. And his homage as a lover had hovered near her rather than pressed upon her: inobtrusive as the scent of roses carried in from another room—pleasant, flattering, and leaving her vanity warmed.

Once only he had startled her: not a kiss on the cheek, which would have been a familiar courtesy, but on the neck, just below the ear. The touch had been like a sudden cold drop on the skin. She started up, heart leaping, and he rose too with a smoothness that had nothing of apology’s clumsiness.

“I beg your pardon—did I annoy you?”

“Oh, it was nothing,” she had said, trying to laugh away what she could not name without confessing too much. “Only I cannot bear—to be kissed under my ear.”

She sat down again, playful on the surface; but inside she felt the pulse of fear. With Rex she had been free to flout, to toy, to withdraw; with this man—this engagement—there was no such liberty. The agitation had seemed to please him; he did not transgress again.

To-day, the rain kept them from riding; but a package had come up from London, and Mrs. Davilow had just left the room after bringing in the beautiful things Grandcourt had ordered—soft fabrics, pale gleams of jewelry, all the shining apparatus of a new life laid out like confections on the tables. Gwendolen enjoyed, for a moment, the scenery of her own existence as if she were looking at it from a height: the wealth, the attention, the inevitability.

She let her hands fall on her lap and said, with a pretty perversity that tasted sweet on her tongue,

“Why is to-morrow the only day?”

“Because the next day is the first with the hounds,” said Grandcourt.

“And after that?”

“After that I must go away for a couple of days—it’s a bore—but I shall go one day and come back the next.”

A slight change crossed her face—quick as a shadow when a cloud passes the sun. He noticed it; he always noticed what touched his possession. He released his hand from under his knees and laid it over hers, the pressure cool and certain.

“You object to my going away?”

“It’s no use objecting,” Gwendolen said coldly. The answer was true, but not in the way she meant. She was holding back—by a force that was half pride and half terror—from saying she suspected where he went, and to whom.

“Yes it is,” he said, folding her hand as if it belonged there. “I will put off going. And I will travel at night, so as only to be away one day.”

He thought he knew the reason of her temper; and because he thought he knew, it amused him. And because it amused him, it pleased him—she was more fascinating in her resistance than in her assent.

“Then don’t put off going, but travel at night,” she said, tasting the small pleasure of command. The peremptoriness was a vent; it let out a little of the bitter heat in her.

“Then you will go to Diplow to-morrow?”

“Oh yes, if you wish it,” she said, in a high, careless tone. Her attention was so knotted in other feelings that she had hardly taken in that her hand was being held.

“How you treat us poor devils of men!” said Grandcourt, lowering his voice, shaping complaint into compliment. “We are always getting the worst of it.”

“Are you?” Gwendolen asked, with a note of inquiry. She looked at him more naively than usual, because she longed to believe this easy jest as a deep truth. If men always had the worst, then her own uneasiness could pass for virtue. Then Mrs. Glasher—dark, suffering, unmanageable in memory—might be made more to blame than he.

“Are you always getting the worst?”

“Yes. Are you as kind to me as I am to you?” he asked, and his narrow gaze held hers with the steadiness of a man who expects surrender.

She felt struck, as if a string inside her had been snapped and another tightened in its place. She was conscious—painfully—of how much she had received: gifts, deference, the weight of a name bending toward her. Her sense of command faltered. It was as if she had mounted a chariot and discovered, too late, that another held the reins. She could not leap down in sight of the world; she would not. She had not consented in ignorance. Anything she said now would be a confession that she had known enough to be guilty. Her right to demand explanations was gone; she had spent it when she accepted.

A little shiver ran through her mind, and she changed her inner posture as one changes a pin that pricks. There was a pause; she did not look away. Then she broke into a smile, sudden as the turning of a page.

“If I were as kind to you as you are to me, that would spoil your generosity,” she said lightly. “It would no longer be as great as it could be—and it is that now.”

“Then I am not to ask for one kiss,” Grandcourt returned, content to pay a large price for this new softness that carried marriage in its perfume.

“Not one?” She nodded at him, saucy and defiant.

He lifted her left hand to his lips and released it—an act that was respectful enough to be almost tender, and restrained enough to be powerful. If it was faint praise to say he was not disgusting, it was also true that he could be—at moments—almost charming. She had a swift sense that she might never have loved another man better than this one. His reticence created in her an inexplicable, delicious consciousness—as if something were being withheld, and in being withheld became precious.

“Apropos,” she said, taking up her work again, “is there any one besides Captain and Mrs. Torrington at Diplow?—or do you leave them tête-à-tête? I suppose he converses in cigars, and she answers with her chignon.”

“She has a sister with her,” said Grandcourt, the shadow of a smile passing, “and there are two men besides—one of them you know, I believe.”

“Ah, then I have a poor opinion of him,” Gwendolen said, shaking her head.

“You saw him at Leubronn—young Deronda—a young fellow with the Mallingers.”

At the name her heart made a sudden, involuntary leap, like a fish breaking water. Her fingers, trying to keep their hold on the thread, went cold.

“I never spoke to him,” she said, fearing her own face. “Is he not disagreeable?”

“No, not particularly,” Grandcourt replied in his languid way. “He thinks a little too much of himself. I thought he had been introduced to you.”

“No. Some one told me his name the evening before I came away. That was all. What is he?”

“A sort of ward of Sir Hugo Mallinger’s. Nothing of any consequence.”

“Oh, poor creature! How very unpleasant for him!” She spoke without sarcasm; it sounded like pity and meant, in a strange way, admiration—the pity one gives to a fine dish served without a proper plate. “I wonder if it has left off raining!” she added, rising to the window.

The next day, happily, was dry. Gwendolen rode to Diplow on Criterion, as she had ridden before, and the riding-dress made her bolder, as armor does: it gave her a sense of competence and beauty at once, like a well-made crust that holds its filling without spilling. She believed she looked as well as possible in it, and that belief was sustaining.

Her anger toward Deronda had changed. It was no longer heat; it was dread—superstitious, intimate, as if the first sharp interference of his glance had planted a seed of future power. Such forebodings are brewed from intense self-feeling: they make the evening star seem to look back with threat, and a beggar’s blessing sound like prophecy. And then, because we carry them, we enact them; superstition becomes fate by our own hands.

Before luncheon she went through the rooms with Mrs. Torrington and Mrs. Davilow, attending to arrangements, order, the visible domestic stage on which the great life must appear. She thought that if she saw Deronda, a mere bow would be all; she meant to notice him as little as possible.

But from the first moment they were in the same room, she seemed to herself to do nothing but notice him. Everything else became automatic: her smile, her words, the turning of her head. She was a practiced actress, yet felt the audience had changed into a single pair of eyes.

At lunch, as Deronda took his place, Grandcourt said, “Deronda, Miss Harleth tells me you were not introduced to her at Leubronn?”

“Miss Harleth hardly remembers me, I imagine,” Deronda said, looking at her simply as they bowed. “She was intensely occupied when I saw her.”

Did he suppose she had not suspected him—the man who had redeemed her necklace? The thought pricked her like a needle through too-thin fabric.

“On the contrary. I remember you very well,” she said, nervous but governing herself, studying him with a fresh, hungry scrutiny. “You did not approve of my playing at roulette.”

“How did you come to that conclusion?” he asked gravely.

“Oh, you cast an evil eye on my play.” She turned her head with a smile, trying to make jest a shield. “I began to lose as soon as you came to look on. I had always been winning till then.”

“Roulette in such a kennel as Leubronn is a horrid bore,” said Grandcourt.

“I found it a bore when I began to lose,” Gwendolen returned. She faced Grandcourt as she spoke, but cut a sidelong glance at Deronda—and met his eyes fixed on her with a grave penetration that had a keener edge than irony, keener even than Klesmer’s judgments. She wheeled her neck, pretending to listen to others, while in truth she listened inwardly to the disturbance Deronda made.

His face had that corrective power—form and expression that threaten to alter one’s standard, as if one had been living with a false measure. She had known such faces: they chastise without speaking. Often they lose their power by some foolish word; but his silence, his steadiness, maintained it. And his voice—heard now for the first time—fell into the room like deeper strings among thin clucking treble: to Grandcourt’s toneless drawl, so familiar now, it was like the violoncello under the broken discourse of poultry in sun.

Grandcourt, she thought, might be right in saying Deronda thought too much of himself—an easy way to explain any superiority that humiliates.

The talk moved on—rinderpest and Jamaica—light darts of opinion shot across the table. Grandcourt spoke of the Jamaica negro as a beastly baptist Caliban; Deronda said he had always felt a little with Caliban, who naturally had his own point of view and could sing a good song. Mrs. Davilow mentioned her father’s estate in Barbadoes and her own ignorance of the West Indies; Mrs. Torrington declared she would never sleep in her bed among blacks; Captain Torrington corrected her by saying the blacks would be manageable enough if it were not for the half-breeds; and Deronda quietly remarked that the whites had to thank themselves for the half-breeds.

While this polite pea-shooting went on, Gwendolen trifled with her jelly. Its tremor under the spoon, the sweet cold on her tongue, seemed absurdly out of keeping with the inward strain. She looked from speaker to speaker, as if to make it natural that she should look at Deronda.

All the while questions ran under her thoughts like an underground stream you hear but cannot see.

What did he think of her—really? He must have been interested in her, or he would not have sent back the necklace. What did he think of her marriage? Why was he so grave about everything? Why was he here at Diplow?

And why did she care so much about the opinion of this man who was “nothing of any consequence”? She had no leisure to answer; she was too busy caring.

In the drawing-room afterward, when something called Grandcourt away, she found herself moving—without forethought—toward Deronda, who stood at a table apart turning over prints. The room had its own hush: the soft brush of skirts, the paper’s faint rasp beneath his fingers, the clock’s measured insistence. Compared with the coarse roaring of public places—railways, streets, the new iron life—this quiet was like a chapel for the ear, each sound distinct and therefore meaningful.

“Shall you hunt to-morrow, Mr. Deronda?” she asked.

“Yes, I believe so.”

“You don’t object to hunting, then?”

“I find excuses for it. It is a sin I am inclined to—when I can’t get boating or cricketing.”

“Do you object to my hunting?” she said, lifting her chin saucily, as if daring him to judge.

“I have no right to object to anything you choose to do.”

“You thought you had a right to object to my gambling,” she persisted.

“I was sorry for it. I am not aware that I told you of my objection,” he replied, meeting her with that directness of gaze—large-eyed gravity, without any visible intention to wound. His eyes had the dark mild intensity that seems, to those it rests on, like a special interest; and such seeming invites claims, as beggars make a reason out of another’s goodness.

“You hindered me from gambling again,” she said.

The words were out—and instantly she blushed, heat rushing over face and neck. Deronda blushed too, as if struck by the memory of the questionable freedom he had taken in the affair of the necklace.

No further words could follow. She turned away to the window, feeling she had said what she had not meant to say—yet oddly happy that she had plunged into mutual understanding. It was as if a secret ingredient had been named aloud; the dish could never again taste as it had before.

Deronda, too, did not dislike it. Gwendolen seemed more decidedly attractive than before; and in truth, changes had been going on within her since Leubronn. Struggle, and the knowledge of error, had wakened something like a new soul in her—one with better possibilities, but also worse. Among the forces she had come to dread was something within herself that disturbed satisfaction.

That evening, in the quieter part of the house—when the sounds had settled into night’s economy, the servants moving with muffled steps, the wind sounding in the trees—Mrs. Davilow said, gently curious,

“Was it really so, or only a joke of yours, about Mr. Deronda’s spoiling your play, Gwen?”

“It merely happened that he was looking on when I began to lose,” Gwendolen said carelessly. “I noticed him.”

“I don’t wonder at that: he is a striking young man,” Mrs. Davilow went on, pleased with her own impression. “He puts me in mind of Italian paintings. One would guess, without being told, that there was foreign blood in his veins.”

“Is there?” Gwendolen asked.

“Mrs. Torrington says so. I asked particularly who he was, and she told me that his mother was some foreigner of high rank.”

“His mother?” Gwendolen said sharply, as if the word itself were a knife turned. “Then who was his father?”

“Well—every one says he is the son of Sir Hugo Mallinger, who brought him up; though he passes for a ward. She says, if Sir Hugo Mallinger could have done as he liked with his estates, he would have left them to this Mr. Deronda, since he has no legitimate son.”

Gwendolen was silent. Her mother saw the effect in her face—too marked to miss—and regretted having repeated gossip. It was knowledge of the world, the kind she disliked for her daughter; and she wished, suddenly, that she herself had never been forced to learn such things, never had them pressed into her mind by the dominant tongues that decide which lives may be spoken of openly and which must be murmured, half-erased.

In Gwendolen’s imagination, an image had risen at once: the unknown mother—a dark-eyed woman, surely—perhaps sad, perhaps silenced. Hardly any face could be less like Deronda’s than Sir Hugo’s crayon portrait at Diplow. A dark-eyed woman, no longer young, became “stuff o’ the conscience” to Gwendolen.

That night, when she had got into her little bed and only a dim light burned, she lay listening to the house—the settling beams, the faint creak of a stair as if the building itself had a memory and shifted in its sleep. Then she said, abruptly,

“Mamma, have men generally children before they are married?”

“No, dear, no,” Mrs. Davilow answered quickly. “Why do you ask such a question?” But her heart, like a hand, began to grope for the reason.

“If it were so, I ought to know,” Gwendolen said, indignation lending her voice a sharpness.

“You are thinking of what I said about Mr. Deronda and Sir Hugo Mallinger. That is a very unusual case, dear.”

“Does Lady Mallinger know?”

“She knows enough to satisfy her. That is quite clear, because Mr. Deronda has lived with them.”

“And people think no worse of him?”

“Well, of course he is under some disadvantage: it is not as if he were Lady Mallinger’s son. He does not inherit the property, and he is not of any consequence in the world. But people are not obliged to know anything about his birth; you see, he is very well received.”

“I wonder whether he knows about it,” Gwendolen said, “and whether he is angry with his father?”

“My dear child, why should you think of that?”

“Why?” Gwendolen burst out, sitting up. “Haven’t children reason to be angry with their parents? How can they help their parents marrying or not marrying?”

But at once another consciousness rushed over her, and she fell back upon the pillow. It was not only the old, half-formed fear she once would have had—that she might seem to reproach her mother for her second marriage. What seized her now was the sense that she had been led into condemning something that made her own marriage look forbidden. A word spoken about another life had turned, like an echo in a cavern, and struck her back.

There was no more talk. She lay, long, arguing within herself against the reasons that pressed on her now with new force—reasons mirrored unexpectedly in the story of a man whose slight relation to her had bitten deep into the most permanent layers of feeling. Yet, characteristic of her crude debating, she was never troubled by the question whether the indefensibleness of her marriage included the fact that she accepted Grandcourt simply because it was convenient, not because she meant to bind herself in duty to him. Her ideas were raw; but life often thrusts its grand difficulties upon us when we are rawest, and we feel them with a simple pain that wiser people disguise.

Morning brought a double excitement. She was going to hunt—scruples about propriety had threatened to stop her until it was found that Mrs. Torrington was horsewoman enough to accompany her. It would be her first hunt since the escapade with Rex. And she was going to see Deronda again, in whom her interest had gathered during the night until she expected—like those who meet a revealed celebrity—to find something new in his face, some sign she had missed before.

What was he going to be? What sort of life had he before him—he being nothing of any consequence? With only a little difference in events he might have been as important as Grandcourt; indeed her imagination, inevitably, went further: he might have held the very estates Grandcourt was to have. Yet now Deronda would likely, someday, see her as mistress of the Abbey at Topping, bearing the title that might have been his wife’s. These futile thoughts of what might have been made a new epoch in her. She, who had always taken the best that came to her as less than her claim, now saw the position that tempted her in a new light—as a hard exclusion of others. What she had heard about Deronda threw him, in her mind, into one group with Mrs. Glasher and her children—before whom she felt herself apologetic, she who had hitherto been surrounded by people she thought needed to apologize to her.

Perhaps Deronda knew of Mrs. Glasher. If he knew that she knew, he would despise her; but he could not know that. Would he, without that, despise her for marrying Grandcourt? His possible judgment pressed on her as importunately as Klesmer’s judgment of her powers; but she found more room to resist disapproval of her conduct than disapproval of her talent. Conduct can always plead, How can I help it? Incompetence cannot. And she said to herself, fiercely,

“How can I help what other people have done? Things would not come right if I were to turn round now and declare I would not marry Mr. Grandcourt.”

Turning round was impossible. The horses in the chariot she had mounted were going at full speed.

This mood—youthful, elated, desperate—returned like a tide. She could dare anything ahead sooner than go backward into humiliation; and it was almost soothing to think there would be ill-doing either way. But the immediate, exquisite fact was the hunt—wind on her face, the cry, the drum of hooves on turf—and there Deronda would see her as she would see him.

For a long while, the hunt absorbed everything. Deronda was there, often within sight, and that only sharpened the pleasure. It was a delight she had tasted only once before and felt would always renew itself, independent of crosses except those that stole the chance of riding. No accident threw them together. The run kept them within reach of home, and under the agreeable sombreness of the gray November afternoon—where a long stratum of yellow light lay in the west like a slow-burning ember—Gwendolen returned with the company from Diplow, attended on her way to Offendene.

Now that the glorious excitement was spent, irritation took its place. She was disappointed—childishly, fiercely—that she had had no opportunity to speak to Deronda. She would not see him again; he was to go away in a couple of days. What did she want to say? She did not quite know. But she wanted to hear him answer; she wanted the sound of his voice shaped toward her.

Grandcourt rode by her side; Mrs. Torrington, her husband, and another gentleman were a little in advance; and behind, she could hear Deronda’s horse—hoofs soft on the path, nearer than the voices ahead, like a persistent thought. They had lately come out of a wood of pines and beeches where twilight stillness had pressed down on impatience, and each sound had stood out—the birds’ last thin notes, the horses’ breathing, the creak of leather—making the world feel hushed enough for conscience to be audible.

The hoofbeats behind grew into a torment. Gwendolen reined in and looked back. Grandcourt, after a few paces, paused too. Then, waving her whip and nodding sideways with playful imperiousness, she said,

“Go on! I want to speak to Mr. Deronda.”

No penitence and no confessional, no priest to allot the penance—only the long compelled sitting amid the gray ash of what has burned down, while life still asks for breakfast and lessons and the small decencies of an afternoon.

Gadsmere had that look of old country comfort which, in another county, might have been praised as picturesque: the best of it built in sober gray stone, with a red-tiled roof softened by years of rain; a round tower thrusting itself out at one corner, capped with a conical darkness where a weathercock turned, not bravely, but with the patient compliance of metal submitted to wind. Great trees laid their shade over gravel and grass; a broken bank showed the naked grip of roots where Scotch firs clung; beyond, a rookery kept its harsh parliament. On the other side, a pool lay under bushes, and waterfowl made their sudden flutters and screams—sharp, living cries that cut across the November hush like a knife across crust.

But outside the gate, the country had been darkened into another element. What had once been hedgerow and pasture now wore coal like mourning: black roads, black mounds, and men emerging with candles fixed in their hats, their faces so stained that children, honest in their instincts, called them devils and drew close to nursemaids’ skirts. The new world sounded different too: the distant clank of iron, the low continuous grind, the occasional whistle that seemed to split the air for the sake of commerce—no birds’ music there, only industry insisting upon itself. At Gadsmere, the seclusion purchased by ugliness was exact to Mrs. Glasher’s taste. No carriages of neighboring gentry met her waggonet; no eyes at church were charged with old knowledge. The curate and his wife, whether ignorant or politely incurious, received her as a widow tenant. In that district, Grandcourt was a name less vital than Fletcher and Gawcome, lessees of the collieries—names spoken with the respect given to whoever makes the ground profitable, even if it must first be wounded.

It had been ten years since the elopement that had rippled through drawing-rooms like gossip stirred into tea: an Irish officer’s beautiful wife running away with young Grandcourt, and afterwards a duel in which the bullets found only air. Those who still remembered the affair, remembered it as they remembered a tragedy that had happened to other people at some foreign resort—interesting while the sound of it was fresh, then folded away. They supposed, naturally, that Grandcourt had tired of the woman; and they supposed, just as naturally, that a woman who had left child and husband had fallen lower. Grandcourt, in their imagining, lay safe in harbor—colors flying, seaworthy, ready for a suitable marriage with a noble daughter. Mrs. Glasher was a wreck no one sent out boats to find.

Yet the truth had never been so neat. He had not disentangled himself; he had merely let passion crack and sour like a flute whose music can no longer be trusted, leaving behind a dull habit of return. When her husband died three years ago, that habit had even prompted him now and then toward the old understanding spoken in the days when his ardor had been a religion—that he would marry her if the way were free. Once, in that early heat, he would have paid for a divorce; but the husband would not. He did not desire a second marriage, and he did not wish the evidence of his domestic habits paraded as print.

Time had altered Lydia in the opposite fashion from Grandcourt. At first, marriage had mattered to her less than escape and the intoxication of being loved with youth’s extravagance: to be out of a rough husband’s reach, to be clasped by a handsome lover who lived in the best style—equipage, talk, the easy insolence of men who have seen everything and are bored by most of it. She had wanted adoration; she had been made raw by five years of marital rudeness; and relief itself was so strong that it quieted anxiety about the future. An equivocal position, then, had seemed a small price for such sweetness. She did not envy the dull honors of a disregarded wife.

Only one bruise had lain under the velvet: the boy she had left, three years old, who died two years after; and in her memory the first tones of “mamma” from his lips kept a difference no later child could repeat—a dialect of tenderness now extinct. But as years went on, her cheek and throat changed; and with them changed the whole meaning of her life. Marriage with Grandcourt became not a romance but an urgent necessity—less for herself than for the children who sat at her knees like a debt she must pay back with interest. The shame that had once seemed hers alone now struck them. If he married her, the past could be folded, the children could stand in the world without disadvantage; her son could be made heir. That hope hardened into a single purpose so intense it could bear the look of tragic calm. She asked for nothing less. Grandcourt kept all gifts voluntary; he had said he would settle nothing except by will. Sometimes—when she forced herself to look at ugly alternatives—she thought: even if he never married her, he might die without a legitimate son; her boy might yet be named heir to the best of his estates. The child had, at that early age, too much of his father’s physique to be overlooked.

Lush had even believed the marriage possible; and when he fancied Grandcourt meant to win Miss Arrowpoint at Diplow, he had fanned that project as a tacit renunciation of Lydia. But Gwendolen Harleth’s appearance had altered all those airy calculations; and it had been easy for Lydia, with passion stored like venom, to enter into Lush’s plan of frightening the girl away by setting a barrier in her mind.

After that, Lydia heard from Lush that Gwendolen had gone, and danger was likely over; but no one wrote to tell her that danger had returned and hardened into certainty. Lydia, as she did habitually, had written to Grandcourt; he had delayed his answer longer than usual. She guessed he might come to Gadsmere; she could not help hoping—hope, that stubborn cook, will season any scrap into a feast—that a disgust from frustrated courtship might make him slide back into the old intention as into a familiar chair.

Grandcourt, when he came, carried two grave purposes with him: to deliver news of his approaching marriage in person, making the first difficulty final; and to retrieve his mother’s diamonds, confided long ago to Lydia and worn by her with an effect he had liked—diamonds that, on her, looked as if they were worth the money paid. They were not mountains of light: peas and little haricots for ears, neck, and hair; but worth thousands, and he meant them for his wife. Once, asking for them back on the pretext of safety and a bank, he had been refused with Lydia’s quiet absolutism. “If you ever marry another woman I will give them up to her: are you going to marry another woman?” At that time he had not persisted. In him there was a peculiar forbearance toward Lydia: the old power she had had over him did not die, it merely changed its form, leaving him disinclined to provoke her. A harder interpreter might say that her dependence was a standing banquet to his love of domination; but even he had kept that propensity oddly asleep in her presence. Now, however, novelty had taken hold of him, and urged him toward its own completion.

Mrs. Glasher sat in the room where she spent her mornings, the children gathered as naturally as crumbs gather birds. A square projecting window looked on broad gravel and grass that sloped toward a little brook running into the pool. The top of a low black cabinet, an old oak table, chairs in tawny leather, were all littered with toys, books, and the small garments of garden and play. On the wall a maternal lady in pastel smiled down as if indulgence were an inherited property.

The children were all there. The three girls sat near their mother by the window—dark-eyed, delicate-featured little brunettes with rich bloom on their cheeks, their tiny nostrils and brows finished with the precision of miniatures.
