The eldest, Josephine, was barely nine. The boy, Henleigh, sat on the carpet at some distance, bending his fair head over the animals from a Noah’s ark, admonishing them with fierce little commands, then licking the spotted ones to see whether the colors would hold—testing the world with his tongue, as if truth were always, in some degree, a taste.

Josephine was at her French lesson; the two younger girls, dolls in their laps, had the demure stillness of Madonnas painted small. Mrs. Glasher’s dress had been made with care. Each day now she said to herself that Grandcourt might come. Her head—emaciation notwithstanding—kept a beauty that could not be effaced: fine profile, crisp curves of hair, eyebrows clearly marked as if drawn with resolve. Above bronze-colored silk and velvet, the gold necklace he had clasped round her years ago lay against the hollowness at her throat like a memory that would not melt.

She did not take pleasure in her toilet. The mirror offered her one recurring sentence: How changed. Yet the remnant of good in life—what could be held—she would hold. If her chief wish were fulfilled, she could imagine taking on again the comeliness of a matron fit for the highest rank. The little faces beside her, almost exact reductions of her own, told of blooming curves where her pallor now was. But they kissed her cheeks and found no deficiency. Their love—warm, unquestioning, hungry as young mouths—was the one end of her life.

Suddenly she turned her head from Josephine’s book and listened. Sound at Gadsmere was intimate: you could tell footsteps by the way gravel yielded, could hear a gate-latch’s complaint, could distinguish the soft scramble of dogs from the heavier tread of a stranger. Even the distant collieries had their own bass note, like a far organ held down.

“Hush, dear,” she whispered. “I think some one is coming.”

Henleigh sprang up. “Mamma, is it the miller with my donkey?”

He repeated the question, insistent, at her knee. She did not answer. The door opened, and the servant announced Mr. Grandcourt.

Mrs. Glasher rose, agitated as if her blood had received an order. Henleigh frowned at the disappointment of no donkey; the little girls lifted timid eyes to the visitor. They had never loved this friend of mamma’s. When Grandcourt took Lydia’s hand and then reached to lay his other hand on Henleigh’s head, the boy beat his arm away with small fists, indignant at being touched without consent. The girls submitted bashfully to being patted beneath the chin and kissed, but there was relief when Lydia sent them into the garden. Soon they were out on the gravel, dancing, chatting, the dogs leaping and circling—light sounds and quick breaths making a brief music against the November barrenness.

“How far are you come?” Lydia asked, as Grandcourt put away hat and overcoat.

“From Diplow,” he said slowly, seating himself opposite her. He looked at her with a gaze so unnoting that she felt the omission like a pinch.

“You are tired, then.”

“No. I rested at the Junction—a hideous hole. These railway journeys are always a confounded bore. But I had coffee and smoked.”

He drew out his handkerchief, rubbed his face, and when he returned it to his pocket he glanced down at his crossed knee and blameless boot, as if any stranger sat opposite rather than a woman quivering with suspense. Yet he was not absent; he was measuring, arranging, anticipating—the way a man does who means to pass through disagreeable business with the least possible stain.

“I expected to see you,” Lydia said. “It was so long since I had heard from you. I suppose the weeks seem longer at Gadsmere than they do at Diplow.” Her speech had a quick incisive edge, like the bright strain of a violin whose body is shaped for sharpness.

“Yes,” Grandcourt drawled. “But you found the money paid into the bank.”

“Oh, yes,” she said curtly, tingling. Always before—at least she believed it—he had noticed her and the children more than he did today.

“Yes,” he went on, playing with his whisker, not looking at her at first. “The time has gone on at rather a rattling pace with me; generally it’s slow enough. But there has been a good deal happening, as you know.” He turned his eyes on her then.

“What do I know?” she said sharply.

He paused, then said without change of manner, “That I was thinking of marrying. You saw Miss Harleth?”

“She told you that?” Lydia’s cheeks whitened further; the fierce brightness in her eyes made the pallor look lit from within.

“No. Lush told me.”

It was like watching the tools of torture laid out—thumb-screw and iron boot—by hands that moved with careful patience.

“Good God! say at once that you are going to marry her,” Lydia burst out. Her knees shook; her hands clasped tight as if to keep her bones from coming apart.

“Of course, this kind of thing must happen some time or other, Lydia,” he said, and there was even a shade of unwillingness to drive the screw too fast. “I see it now.”

In those few undertoned words she felt resistance as absolute as iron. She knew how useless beseeching was with him: crying into a dead ear, clinging to dead knees, only to meet an immovable face and rigid limbs. She did not weep. She did not speak. The certainty came with a chill sickness that made thought and feeling swim together. Hope, defeated, left her with a horrible bodily sensation—like a clutching hand suddenly empty.

At last she rose with a spasmodic effort and pressed her forehead against the window-glass, hard and cold. In the garden the children saw and mistook: running forward, sweet faces upturned, they stood expectant as if called. The sight roused her. She shook her head, waved them away, and with the painful exertion sank into the nearest chair.

Grandcourt had risen too, leaning against the corner of the fireplace. He was annoyed—by the scene, and by the fact that no imperiousness could save him from it. Still, the business had to be done, and he must arrange matters for future quiet.

Lydia looked up at him and said bitterly, “All this is of no consequence to you. I and the children are importunate creatures. You wish to get away again and be with Miss Harleth.”

“Don’t make the affair more disagreeable than it need be, Lydia. It’s of no use to harp on things that can’t be altered. Of course, it’s deucedly disagreeable to me to see you making yourself miserable. I’ve taken this journey to tell you what you must make up your mind to—you and the children will be provided for as usual—and there’s an end of it.”

Silence. She dared not answer. Mother’s anguish had put iron into her soul, and sometimes it enabled a repression harder than shrieking. But under the silence there sprang hatred, vindictiveness: she wanted the marriage to bring wretchedness on others too, not only herself. Presently he continued, slow and administrative:

“It’ll be better for you. You may go on living here. But I think of by-and-by settling a good sum on you and the children, and you can live where you like. There’ll be nothing for you to complain of then. Whatever happens, you’ll feel secure. Nothing could be done beforehand. Everything has gone on in a hurry.”

He stopped, as if that were a reasonable conclusion. He did not expect thanks, but he thought she might be contented—if contentment were possible for Lydia. She did not change. After a minute he said,

“You’ve never had any reason to fear that I should be illiberal. I don’t care a curse about the money.”

“If you did care about it, I suppose you would not give it us,” Lydia said, and the sarcasm came out like a spasm.

“That’s a devilishly unfair thing to say,” he answered, voice lowered. “And I advise you not to say that sort of thing again.”

“Should you punish me by leaving the children in beggary?” The one outlet of venom had opened the other.

“There is no question about leaving the children in beggary,” he said, still low. “I advise you not to say things that you will repent of.”

“I am used to repenting,” she said bitterly. “Perhaps you will repent. You have already repented of loving me.”

“All this will only make it uncommonly difficult for us to meet again. What friend have you besides me?”

“Quite true.”

The words fell like a low moan. And in the same instant, like a flash that shows a landscape only to make it darker after, she imagined him miserable and lonely with his new wife, driven back to her by emptiness, craving some memory of being young, glad, hopeful. But no—he would go scathless. It was she who must bear the ash.

After that, the scorching words ended, not because the fire was out, but because both knew speech only widened the wound. Grandcourt had meant to stay until evening; he wished to curtail the visit, but there was no earlier train than the one he had arranged. Hours had to pass. There was eating to be done; the children came in and out; servants moved with the careful deafness of good training. All that mechanism of life went on with the dreary constraint felt in household quarrels, when the teacups clink too loud and the ticking clock seems like mockery.

To Lydia it was a slight relief to have the children present: their loveliness rose in her like a savage pride, as if their faces could taunt him with what he was throwing away. She watched him watch them, hungry for some sign—any softening, any hesitation. He acquitted himself with the ease of a man whose grace has been molded by long practice in boredom. He nursed little Antonia, who sat with hands crossed and eyes upturned at his bald head with solemn curiosity; and he propitiated Henleigh by promising a beautiful saddle and bridle. Only the two eldest girls had known him as a continual presence; now intervening years had covered their infant memory with bashfulness that his bearing would never dissolve.

He and Lydia, when servants were near, exchanged occasional conventional remarks, as if words were merely furniture to fill an emptiness. Otherwise they did not speak. In Grandcourt’s mind all the while lay a stagnant irritation: his own folly in giving her those diamonds, which now obliged him to ask for them back. He had a deep care for what belonged to his caste; about property he liked to be lordly. And he hated the consciousness of needing to ask anyone for anything. Yet, whatever independence he asserted, he had forged for himself a past that pulled harder than any yoke he could fasten on others. He had promised the diamonds to Gwendolen. He must have them.

At last they were alone again, candles lit above them, facing each other with the room’s dim corners pressing inward. Grandcourt looked at his watch, then said in a tone made indifferent by practice, “There is one thing I had to mention, Lydia. My diamonds—you have them.”

“Yes, I have them,” she answered promptly, rising. She stood with her arms thrust down, fingers threaded tight, while he sat still. She had expected this; during the long hours she had shaped her resolve, and now she meant—if possible—to carry it out without exasperating him. She was aching to take back her earlier words, not from softness but from strategy: they had only widened the breach.

“They are in this house, I suppose?” he said.

“No; not in this house.”

“I thought you said you kept them by you.”

On the morning when Gwendolen Harleth was married and became Mrs. Grandcourt, the air had that clean, biting sweetness which comes when the sun is bright but the earth is still frosted—leaves crisping underfoot like thin wafers, and every sound in the village sharpened as if the cold had tuned it: boots on the path, a cough held back in a sleeve, the low murmur of bodies gathered close.

Half Pennicote made a lane to the church. They stood as they might on a harvest day when the last cart comes in—eager to see what the year has yielded, eager to measure fortune as if it were a sheaf you could count with your eyes. An old friend of the rector’s read the service; the rector himself, for the great advantage of the procession, stood in the place of father. Faces leaned forward. Whispered judgments ran like small currents under the respectable stillness.

It was observed that only two faces looked clouded—Mrs. Davilow’s and Anna’s. Mrs. Davilow’s delicate eyelids were pink, as if she had spent half the night in tears; and no one wondered. A mother may watch the finest prize carried from her hands and still feel only the ache of empty arms. But why Anna should be troubled—when she was being so well set off by her bridesmaid’s dress—was less understood.

The others reflected the brilliancy of the occasion as a polished tray throws back candlelight; and the bride most of all. It was agreed that for figure and carriage she was worthy of being “a lady o’ title.” As for her face, some thought a title asked for something rosier; but since the bridegroom himself was not fresh-coloured—indeed, as the miller’s wife observed, he had much the complexion of her own husband—the match looked the more complete. And if he was taking her, surely he must be fond; and one could only hope he would never cast it up to her that she had gone out to service as a governess, nor to her mother that she had lived at Sawyer’s Cottage—those vicissitudes the village had chewed over as steadily as it chewed its Sunday dinners.

The miller’s daughter of fourteen could not believe high gentry behaved badly to their wives, but her mother had her lore, handed down like an old recipe whose bitterness is in the memory as much as on the tongue.

“Oh, child, men’s men: gentle or simple, they’re much of a muchness. I’ve heard my mother say Squire Pelton used to take his dogs and a long whip into his wife’s room, and flog ’em there to frighten her; and my mother was lady’s-maid there at the very time.”

“That’s unlucky talk for a wedding, Mrs. Girdle,” said the tailor. “A quarrel may end wi’ the whip, but it begins wi’ the tongue, and it’s the women have got the most o’ that.”

“The Lord gave it ’em to use, I suppose,” said Mrs. Girdle. “He never meant you to have it all your own way.”

“By what I can make out from the gentleman as attends to the grooming at Offendene,” said the tailor, “this Mr. Grandcourt has wonderful little tongue. Everything must be done dummy-like without his ordering.”

“Then he’s the more whip, I doubt,” said Mrs. Girdle. “She’s got tongue enough, I warrant her. See, there they come out together!”

“What wonderful long corners she’s got to her eyes!” said the tailor. “She makes you feel comical when she looks at you.”

Gwendolen, in truth, had never shown more elasticity in her bearing, more lustre in her long brown glance. She shone with that fierce, brilliant life which sometimes comes of pain—yet it was not pain she felt. She had worked herself into much the same state as that in which she had stood at the gambling-table while Deronda watched her and she began to lose: a hot, perilous enjoyment, an inward daring that tastes its own sharpness as if it were wine.

Whatever uneasiness a growing conscience had brewed in her was flung aside like a sudden qualm amidst a feast. The ambitious vanity within her—the hunger for luxury, for the visible proofs of being “somebody”—was too ravenous to be killed except by long poisoning. This morning she could not have said truly that she repented her acceptance of Grandcourt, or that any fears, still misty on the far horizon, could dim the immediate scene where all eyes confirmed her importance.

That she was doing something wrong—that punishment might be hanging over her—that the woman to whom she had given a promise and broken it was thinking of her with bitterness and misery, with a just reproach—that Deronda, with his way of looking into things, very likely despised her for marrying Grandcourt, as he had despised her for gambling—above all, that the cord she had once held in her own hand was now being flung over her neck—these things had been fermenting in her through the weeks of engagement: a yeasty mixture of half-understood facts, deep impressions, images at once real and fantastic. But were they nullified this morning? No: they were thrust down and trodden under with an exulting defiance. She felt herself at the great game of life with many eyes upon her, daring everything to win much—or, if she must lose, to lose with éclat, with a sense of having mattered.

Yet a losing destiny did not press on her as fear. She believed she was entering a fuller power of managing circumstances—with all the official strength of marriage, which some women made so poor a use of. The youthful egoism that trouble, humiliation, and culpability had shaken had returned, newly fed, with the old fumes stronger for the draught. She did not present any ideal of the tremulous, tearful bride. With erect head and elastic footstep she walked among illusions; and beneath it all there was a dim under-consciousness that she was a little intoxicated.

“Thank God you bear it so well, my darling!” said Mrs. Davilow when she had helped Gwendolen doff the bridal white and put on her travelling dress. All the trembling had belonged to the mother; and her agitation urged Gwendolen doubly to take the morning as a triumph.

“Why, you might have said that if I had been going to Mrs. Mompert’s, you dear, sad, incorrigible mamma!” said Gwendolen, putting her hands to her mother’s cheeks with laughing tenderness—then retreating and spreading out her arms as if to show herself: “Here am I—Mrs. Grandcourt! what else would you have me, but what I am sure to be? You know you were ready to die with vexation when you thought that I would not be Mrs. Grandcourt.”

“Hush, hush, my child, for heaven’s sake!” Mrs. Davilow almost whispered. “How can I help feeling it when I am parting from you. But I can bear anything willingly if you are happy.”

“Not gladly, mamma, no!” said Gwendolen, shaking her head, bright smile playing as if it could charm away the ache. “Willingly you would bear it, but always sorrowfully. Sorrowing is your sauce; you can take nothing without it.”

Then, clasping her mother’s shoulders and raining kisses, first on one cheek then on the other between her words, she said gaily, “And you shall sorrow over my having everything at my beck—and enjoying everything glorious—splendid houses—and horses—and diamonds, I shall have diamonds—and going to court—and being Lady Certainly—and Lady Perhaps—and grand here—and tantivy there—and always loving you better than anybody else in the world.”

“My sweet child!—But I shall not be jealous if you love your husband better; and he will expect to be first.”

Gwendolen thrust out her lips and chin with a pretty grimace. “Rather a ridiculous expectation. However, I don’t mean to treat him ill—unless he deserves it.”

Then the two clung to each other, and Gwendolen could not hinder the small rising sob when she said, “I wish you were going with me, mamma.” But the slight dew on her long eyelashes only made her the more charming when, a moment later, she gave her hand to Grandcourt to be led to the carriage.

The rector looked in on her for a final blessing—“Good-bye; God bless you; we shall see you again before long”—and then returned to Mrs. Davilow, half cheerful, half solemn. “Let us be thankful, Fanny. She is in a position well suited to her, and beyond what I should have dared to hope for. And few women can have been chosen more entirely for their own sake. You should feel yourself a happy mother.”

There was a railway journey of some fifty miles before husband and wife reached the station near Ryelands. The sky, which had begun so clear, had veiled itself; and by the time their carriage rolled through the park-gates it was hardly more than twilight. Yet even in that dimness Gwendolen, looking from the window, could see enough to feel her heart beat to a new measure: the long winding drive bordered with evergreens backed by huge gray stems; then the widening of grassy spaces and undulations, studded with dark clumps; till at last a wide level where the white house showed itself, with a hanging wood behind, and in front the terrace balustrade rising and sinking like the calm line of a wave.

During the journey she had been at her liveliest—chatting incessantly, as if determined to ignore any change in their mutual position since yesterday. Grandcourt had been rather ecstatically quiescent; and when he took her hand she made his gentle seizure into a grasp of his hand with both hers, with a kittenish vivacity that refused quiet petting. She was growing febrile in her excitement; and now, on this drive through the park, her usual susceptibility to changes of light and scenery made her heart palpitate with the almost incredible fulfilment of girlish dreams.

Was it only novelty—this nearing of her own corridors, her own ceilings out of sight for loftiness, where her own painted Spring shed painted flowers and her own foreshortened Zephyrs blew painted trumpets; where her own servants—lackeys in clothing but men in bulk and shape—were as nothing in her presence, reverencing even the propriety of her insolence; where she could be the heroine of an admired play without the pains of art? Or was there some dim forecast, an insistent penetration from what she had suppressed—mixing triumph with the dread of a crisis? In her nature exultation always carried an infusion of dread, ready to curdle. In spite of herself she fell silent as they drew nearer; and when her husband said, “Here we are at home!” and for the first time kissed her on the lips, she scarcely knew it had happened. It was like a greeting passively accepted while the eyes are held by a spectacle.

After the half-willful excitement of the day, a numbness had come over her. Yet the hall struck her at once with its brilliant warmth: carpets and matting muffling footsteps, full-length portraits looking down with composed indifference, statues with an Olympian coldness, servants moving with assiduous noiselessness, as if trained to keep the house’s own hush. There were not many extra hands—only a few from Diplow in addition to those in constant charge; and Gwendolen’s new maid, who had come with her, was taken under the housekeeper’s guidance.

Gwendolen felt herself led by Grandcourt along a corridor subtly scented—polish, old wood, something like dried lavender kept in drawers—into an anteroom where an open doorway sent out a rich glow of light and colour.

“These are our dens,” said Grandcourt. “You will like to be quiet here till dinner. We shall dine early.” He pressed her hand to his lips and moved away—more in love than he had ever expected to be.

She let her hat and mantle be taken, and then threw herself into a chair near the glowing hearth. Glass panels repeated her figure again and again amid faint-green satin surroundings, as if the house itself were rehearsing her new title, multiplying her into a chorus of mistresses.

The housekeeper had passed in from the adjoining dressing-room and seemed disposed to linger. Gwendolen, impatient for solitude, said, “Will you tell Hudson, when she has put out my dress, to leave everything? I shall not want her again unless I ring.”

The housekeeper, coming forward, said, “Here is a packet, madam, which I was ordered to give into nobody’s hands but yours, when you were alone. The person who brought it said it was a present particularly ordered by Mr. Grandcourt; but he was not to know of its arrival till he saw you wear it. Excuse me, madam; I felt it right to obey orders.”

Gwendolen took the packet and let it lie on her lap until she heard the doors close. In her confused feeling and creeping luxurious languor she welcomed the diversion. It came into her mind at once: the diamonds Grandcourt had spoken of, deposited somewhere and to be given her on her marriage. Her own diamonds to try on—cold fire to set against skin, hard brightness to answer her own sense of having prevailed.

Within the sealed paper coverings was a box; within the box a jewel-case. Her fingers, suddenly eager, flipped it open.

The gleam met her eyes—and at the same instant she saw the letter lying above the jewels.

She knew the handwriting on the address.

It was as if an adder had lain coiled among the glitter. Her heart leaped so violently it seemed to spend her strength in one stroke; and when she took up the thin paper it shook between her fingers. Yet the words were legible as print; they thrust themselves on her sight, and would not let her look away.

These diamonds, which were once given with ardent love to Lydia Glasher, she passes on to you. You have broken your word to her, that you might possess what was hers. Perhaps you think of being happy, as she once was, and of having beautiful children such as hers, who will thrust hers aside. God is too just for that. The man you have married has a withered heart. His best young love was mine: you could not take that from me when you took the rest. It is dead: but I am the grave in which your chance of happiness is buried as well as mine. You had your warning. You have chosen to injure me and my children. He had meant to marry me. He would have married me at last, if you had not broken your word. You will have your punishment. I desire it with all my soul. Will you give him this letter to set him against me and ruin us more—me and my children? Shall you like to stand before your husband with these diamonds on you, and these words of mine in his thoughts and yours? Will he think you have any right to complain when he has made you miserable? You took him with your eyes open. The willing wrong you have done me will be your curse.

At first Gwendolen’s eyes seemed spell-bound, reading the horrible lines again and again as if repetition could make them less real, as if she were sentenced to a penance that must be fulfilled by staring. Then a new spasm of terror seized her—terror not only of the curse but of the words existing where other eyes might meet them. She leaned forward and stretched out the paper toward the fire, as if she could undo time with flame.

It flew from her trembling fingers like a feather and was caught by a great draught of heat. The letter flared—thin paper turning to light and black ash with a swift, hungry sound, as if the hearth had been waiting for it.

In the movement the casket fell, and the diamonds rolled out across the floor, scattering their cold points of fire like spilled hailstones on polished wood. She did not notice. She fell back in her chair helpless.

The reflections in the glass panels, which had so lately mocked and multiplied her, became only pale shapes—women petrified white. But close to her you would have seen the tremor in her lips, the shake that ran through her hands as if her whole body had become an instrument struck too sharply. She sat a long while, knowing little more than that she felt ill, and that those written words—burned and gone—went on repeating themselves inside her, untranslatable into anything softer, inexhaustible as an echo in a vaulted place.

Truly here were poisoned gems, and the poison had entered into her.

After that long while there came a tap at the door, and Grandcourt entered dressed for dinner.

The sight of him brought a new nervous shock. Gwendolen screamed—again and again—with hysterical violence.

He had expected to find her dressed and smiling, ready to be led down. Instead he saw her pallid, shrieking as if in terror, and the jewels scattered about her on the floor. Was it a fit of madness? In some form or other, the Furies had crossed his threshold.

Love is often spoken of as if it were a lightning-struck fate, severed from all habit and judgment—a madness that would laugh at doctrines and proofs, whether the lover had Heraclitus on his tongue, or scholastic subtleties in his head, or a map of the heavens in his pocket. Yet there is another kind of potent love, no less consuming, that does not isolate itself like fever, but enters every chamber of the mind and makes common days shine with borrowed meaning. It can take the most ordinary act—an offered book, a door held open, a voice heard through thin walls—and set it ringing with larger histories, as if the heart had suddenly learned to keep time with remoter ages.

When Daniel Deronda came back to town, he could at least give Sir Hugo an intelligible account of what had been done. Grandcourt, he believed, now understood distinctly that he might secure fifty thousand pounds by relinquishing a prospect that was both distant and uncertain; but beyond that there was no further sign, except the colder sign of a man choosing to keep the channel open—friendly words, future convenience, no promise.

“And what did you think of the future bride on a nearer survey?” Sir Hugo asked, with that air of a man tasting gossip as lightly as he tasted a good claret.

“I thought better of her than I did in Leubronn,” Deronda said. “Roulette was a bad setting; it brought out something—something demoniac. At Diplow she seemed more womanly—more attractive; less hard, less self-possessed. Her mouth and eyes had another expression.”

“Don’t flirt with her too much, Dan,” Sir Hugo returned, amused with his own warning. “If you make Grandcourt savage when they come to the Abbey at Christmas, it will interfere with my affairs.”

“I can stay in town, sir.”

“No, no. Lady Mallinger and the children can’t do without you at Christmas. Only don’t make mischief—unless you can get up a duel, and manage to shoot Grandcourt, which might be worth a little inconvenience.”

“I don’t think you ever saw me flirt,” Deronda said, with a quietness that was not the same thing as being pleased.

“Oh, haven’t I, though?” Sir Hugo persisted, enjoying his own perversity. “You’re always looking tenderly at the women, and talking to them in a Jesuitical way. You are a dangerous young fellow—a kind of Lovelace who’ll make the Clarissas run after you, instead of you running after them.”

There are jokes that leave a smear, however lightly they are thrown, because they inform you—confidently—of a habit you do not possess and would not choose. Deronda, who had never knowingly flirted, felt the familiar irritation come first and the uselessness afterward. He was thankful, at least, that Sir Hugo knew nothing of the necklace he had repurchased for Gwendolen; the baronet would have seasoned that act with precisely this kind of raillery, and it would have soured the memory of it.

So he resolved to be watchful of himself—especially at the Meyricks’, where he was going for the first time since his return from Leubronn; for Mirah, by the mere fineness of her gratitude and the quiet tremor of her feeling, made it difficult not to show tenderness even in the simplest words.

Mrs. Meyrick had already written to him, and her letter, with its homely warmth, had been like a hearth-scent after travel. “We are getting fonder of her every day,” she said. “At breakfast-time we all look toward the door with expectation to see her come in; and we watch her and listen to her as if she were a native from a new country. I have not heard a word from her lips that gives me a doubt about her. She is quite contented and full of gratitude. My daughters are learning from her, and they hope to get her other pupils; for she is anxious not to eat the bread of idleness, but to work, like my girls. Mab says our life has become like a fairy tale, and all she is afraid of is that Mirah will turn into a nightingale again and fly away from us. Her voice is just perfect: not loud and strong, but searching and melting, like the thoughts of what has been. That is the way old people like me feel a beautiful voice.”

Mrs. Meyrick, with her delicacy, did not enlarge upon the little shocks Amy and Mab had received on accompanying Mirah to the synagogue—shocks not of piety, but of arrangement and custom. They were too loyal to Mirah to handle her faith as if it were a specimen to be criticized; still, curiosity, that innocent cousin of sympathy, will sometimes push a question between people who mean only kindness.

“Excuse me, Mirah,” Amy had ventured at last, “but does it seem quite right to you that the women should sit behind rails in a gallery apart?”

Mirah’s mild surprise was like a soft light thrown on their ignorance. “Yes—I never thought of anything else.”

“And you like better to see the men with their hats on?” Mab asked, with the caution of one touching a sacred thing by the smallest edge.

“Oh, yes. I like what I have always seen there, because it brings back to me the same feelings—the feelings I would not part with for anything else in the world.”

After that, criticism—of doctrine or practice—would have seemed to those generous girls like thrusting a cold hand into a warm nest. Mirah’s religion was not an argument she possessed: it was a texture of memory and love, and any rougher handling would have frayed it.

“She says herself she is a very bad Jewess, and does not half know her people’s religion,” Amy said one night, when Mirah had gone to bed. “Perhaps it would gradually melt away from her, and she would pass into Christianity like the rest of the world, if she got to love us very much, and never found her mother. It is so strange to be of the Jews’ religion now.”

“Oh, oh, oh!” Mab cried. “I wish I were not such a hideous Christian. How can an ugly Christian, who is always dropping her work, convert a beautiful Jewess, who has not a fault?”

“It may be wicked of me,” Kate said, with her sharper seeing, “but I cannot help wishing that her mother may not be found. There might be something unpleasant.”

“I don’t think it, my dear,” said Mrs. Meyrick. “I believe Mirah is cut out after the pattern of her mother. And what a joy it would be to her to have such a daughter brought back again! But a mother’s feelings are not worth reckoning, I suppose”—she threw a mischievous glance at her daughters—“and a dead mother is worth more than a living one?”

“Well, and so she may be, little mother,” said Kate; “but we would rather hold you cheaper, and have you alive.”

Not only the Meyricks—clever girls who had gathered knowledge as they could, by irregular foraging—but Deronda himself, with his masculine instruction and his calm competence, had been startled by Mirah into the sense of knowing almost nothing about living Judaism, about the inward story still moving under the surface of modern streets. It had been convenient, in the common way, to treat the Jews as a people “chosen” for the sake of someone else’s lesson; to suppose their thought was an error that ought to have died. To Deronda, as to most of his neighbors, Judaism had been an eccentric fossil; a thing for specialists, not for an accomplished man to trouble his mind with.

Then Mirah—her terrified flight from one parent, her yearning for the other—made the fossil throb. It was not a relic in a cabinet: it was a vesture of the world for actual human lives. And on the idle excursion that followed with Sir Hugo, Deronda found himself looking, with a new kind of attention, for synagogue fronts and for book-titles about Jewish history, as a man begins to listen for a language he has discovered he ought to understand. That sudden shift—from supposing we have right opinions because we have cared little, to caring and finding our opinions were ignorance—can cure ennui better than any physician; Deronda carried that cure with him through weeks that might else have been mere lounging.

It was on that journey that he first entered a synagogue—at Frankfort, where the party rested on a Friday. He had been in the Juden-gasse long before, and had remembered chiefly the picturesque houses. Now his eyes rested on the human types, and his mind connected them with past phases of their race; the old fibre of historic sympathy in him began to stir as if it had heard its name called.

There is a kind of young man whom society lets pass without inquiry: if he has a fine person, no odd manners, the education of a gentleman, and an income, people do not pry into his tastes and thoughts. He may be accepted as agreeable and clever without being examined. Later, when he grows portly and a little slovenly, his peculiarities are easier to see; and it is taken for a mercy if they are not offensive. But anyone who would understand what later events might do with Deronda must know something of what he was at five-and-twenty, which ordinary conversation did not reveal.

The vividness of his impressions had often made him seem enigmatical. His early sensibility and reflectiveness had opened into a many-sided sympathy that threatened to hinder any persistent course: as soon as he took up an antagonism, even in thought, he felt like a man striking at his own flesh. His imagination so habitually showed him how things looked to others that strong partisanship—unless against an immediate oppression—became insincerity for him. Sympathy flowed into analysis, and analysis neutralized sympathy.

He kept himself clear of vices; yet he hated vices mildly, because he was used to tracing them not as abstractions but as parts of mixed natures with individual histories. He was fervidly democratic in his feeling for the multitude, and yet, by affection and imagination, intensely conservative; eager for speculations on government and religion, and yet reluctant to part with long-sanctioned forms that were, for him, quick with memories no argument could kill. He suspected himself of loving too well the losing causes of the world; and since martyrdom changes sides, he was in danger of changing with it—repelled by the clue of success which the order of the world forces on us, and makes it treason against common good to reject. Yet he feared narrow hatred; he apologized for heirs of privilege; he shrank from the bitter tone of the unaccepted innovator.

In him, a too reflective, too diffusive sympathy threatened to paralyze indignation against wrong and the selectness of fellowship which give moral force. Of late he had grown painfully aware of this, and what he longed for—more than knowledge, more than practice—was some outward event or inward light that would urge him into a definite line of action and compress his wandering energy into one channel with his emotions. He dreaded that dead anatomy of culture which makes the universe a ceaseless answer to queries and knows everything about everything—except the scent itself of violets, for which it has no nostril. He wanted his feelings—the true savours of life—to remain substantial against a reflectiveness that would turn all differences into dust.

How and whence was the needed event to come—something that would justify partiality, and make him what he could not make himself: an organic part of social life instead of a yearning, disembodied spirit roaming through it? To make a little difference for the better—that was what he could not consent to live without; yet how to do it? It is one thing to see a road, another to cut it. He saw that his birth and upbringing had laid no special demands on him and given him no fixed relationship except one of doubtful kind; but he did not excuse himself wholly. He knew he had fallen into a meditative numbness, gliding away from the life of practically energetic sentiment which he would have named—if he had been inclined to proclaim anything—as the best life, and for himself the only life worth living.

These currents ran beneath him while he attended to law in a half-hearted way and to polite talk still more imperfectly: not an admirable condition, but a common struggle before daybreak.

He had always had a fervour under his calm, a readiness to feel poetry in daily things; and the Juden-gasse, with its union of the remote and the present, set him musing on two elements of history that this sense makes poetic—the faint beginnings of faiths and institutions, and their obscure lingering decay. Dust and withered remnants may cover them; yet for an awakened perception, the very dust can deepen the impressiveness—whether of the living seed that will become sheltering tree, or of the pathetic inheritance whose grandeur has turned into sorrowing memory.

So, as he turned out of the Juden-gasse in the warm evening air, making his way toward the synagogue, his imaginative stirring neutralized the repulsion of a few ugly incidents. He went into an old bookshop to ask the time of service, and was affectionately directed by a precocious Jewish youth who entered cordially into his wish—not for the fine new Reformed building, but for the old Rabbinical school of the orthodox—and then cheated him, with Teutonic honesty of method and a more amiable face, in the price of a book “nicht so leicht zu bekommen.” At the opposite counter, a deaf and grisly tradesman cast a flinty look at certain cards while a dingy man in a tall coat, a bag in hand, and a broad low hat above his chosen nose shouted proposals to him in Jew-dialect; that dingy man disappeared only for another of the same pattern to emerge from the shop’s shadow and shout in the same dialect. Deronda saw queer-looking Israelites not altogether without guile—just distinguishable from queer-looking Christians of similarly mixed morale.

Lately, because of Mirah’s unknown relatives, he had begun to think of vulgar Jews with a personal alarm; but comparison is a corrective, and that evening he became conscious of unfair exaggerations. He paid his thaler too much without surrendering either his interest in Hebrew destiny or his wish to find the Rabbinische Schule. He reached it by sunset, entered with the men, and took his place.

In his line sat an elderly man whose ample white beard and felt hat framed a profile of such fine contour that it might have been Italian as easily as Hebrew. Deronda glanced at him more than once, and the man returned the notice until their eyes met—an undesirable chance, the sort of accidental intimacy that makes one resolve not to look again. Immediately the man pushed an open prayer-book toward him; Deronda bowed his thanks.

The congregation had mustered. The Reader mounted to the almemor, and the service began. Deronda looked at the German translation enough to know he was hearing chiefly Psalms and phrases of the Old Testament. Then he yielded to that strongest effect of chanted liturgy which does not depend on detailed meaning—like the power of an Allegri Miserere or a Palestrina Magnificat. The deepest movement in a liturgy is often prayer that asks for nothing special: a yearning to escape our cramped weakness and to invoke all Good to enter and abide; or else a self-oblivious lifting of gladness—a Gloria in excelsis that such Good exists. Both yearning and exaltation draw force from communion, from a form that has carried them through long generations of struggling fellow-men.

The Hebrew liturgy, like other liturgies, passes through litany, lyric, proclamation, dry statement, and blessing; but this evening, for Deronda, all of it blended into one. The Chazaris’ wide-ranging chant moved from monotony into sudden cries; sweet boys’ voices rose from the little choir; men swayed backward and forward with devotion; and the very commonness of the building, the shabbiness of the scene where a national faith that had penetrated half the world was now finding a remote, obscure echo—all this was one coherent strain, the utterance of a binding history, tragic and yet glorious. He wondered at the strength of his own feeling. It seemed beyond the occasion, like an influx before any vision had interpreted it.

Then the devotional sound ceased. Faces and figures shifted—indifferent, vulgar, human. A chilling thought darted in: he had probably been alone in his emotion, perhaps the only one for whom the service was more than dulled routine. He had just time for that coldness before he bowed to his civil neighbour and moved away with the rest—when a hand caught his arm.

He turned with the unpleasant start such a claim produces, and saw close to him the white-bearded man, who said in German, “Excuse me, young gentleman—allow me—what is your parentage—your mother’s family—her maiden name?”

Deronda felt a strong recoil. He was inclined to shake off the touch outright; but he slipped his arm away and answered, coldly, “I am an Englishman.”

The man looked at him with lingering doubt, then lifted his hat and turned aside. Whether he felt he had made a mistake, or had been repulsed, Deronda could not tell.

As he walked back to the hotel, he tried to quiet his uneasiness by reasoning with it. He could not have acted differently. How could he tell a total stranger that he did not know his mother’s family name? And the abruptness of the question had been an unwarrantable liberty, probably prompted by some fancy of likeness—one of those momentary delusions that mean nothing. He called it trivial; yet whatever it might signify, his inward shrinking had been too strong for him to regret cutting it short.

It was an additional reason—besides his habitual reserve—not to speak of the synagogue to the Mallingers. Sir Hugo, good-natured as any man and capable of kind acts, especially toward women, never took a romantic view of anything and smiled at motives on a grand scale or reasons lying far off. That was his sharpest difference from Deronda, who could hardly eat breakfast without some silent, discursive flight after grounds for filling up his day in the fashion of his contemporaries.

Frankfort had been only a halt on the journey home. Yet its impressions stayed active in him, made more vivid by his duty toward Mirah. The stranger’s question about parentage—trivial, yes, and yet like a finger pressed on an old bruise—reinforced his anxiety about Mirah’s relatives and his resolve to proceed with caution. If he discovered anything unpleasant, was he bound to disclose it and throw a new net of trouble over her life?

He had written to Mrs. Meyrick to announce his visit at four o’clock. When he arrived, he found Mirah seated at her work, with only Mrs. Meyrick and Mab beside her, the piano open, and the walls peopled by engravings—the “glorious company” that made the little room seem larger and more inhabited than many drawing-rooms. Mirah’s hair was dressed with that dainty neatness which is a sort of modest pride; her dress had the same quiet order; and in her face there was a glow of tranquil happiness that would have asked no alteration from a painter who wished to set her before a chorus singing peace on earth and good-will.

The contrast with his first sight of her by the river was a delight to him; and Mirah herself was thinking of it. Almost as soon as they had greeted one another, she said, with a soft eagerness,

“See how different I am from the miserable creature by the river! all because you found me and brought me to the very best.”

“It was my good chance to find you,” Deronda said. “Any other man would have been glad to do what I did.”

“That is not the right way to be thinking about it,” Mirah answered, shaking her head with a decisive gravity that sat strangely and beautifully on her gentleness. “I think of what really was. It was you, and not another, who found me and were good to me.”

“No man,” a Rabbi had said, setting down his truth as if it were a law of the body as well as of the soul, “may turn the bones of his father and mother into spoons.” The saying had the clean, sudden hardness of a knife laid flat on a board: it stopped a hand in mid-reach. There were economies which would never become common because the only barrier against them was not statute but shudder—an inherited recoil, a taste, a sacredness that could not be melted down and recast for profit. And yet the world, being forever hungry for use, forever inventing new markets, was always tempting some man to ask, “Why not?” as if progress were only a more ingenious grinding of old substance.

Deronda, since Mirah had come like a dropped spark into his guarded life, had taken to a less fashionable exercise than parading a horse among glossy riders. He walked. Not the West End promenades, but the parts of London where the air thickened with human closeness, and shop-signs spoke in strange syllables, and the faces in doorways—women with heavy earrings, men with anxious eyes—carried the stamp of a race that history had battered into a sort of visible endurance. He went when he could to synagogues at the hour of service, standing apart, listening, watching lips move in prayer as if prayer were a language older than breath. He looked into shops, at counters where scales and measures clicked softly like insect wings, at windows where old silver flashed a cold, patient light.

He told himself, more than once, that if he were wise he would go directly to some Rabbi, some trusted man among the Jews, and state simply what he knew: a mother once named Cohen; a son named Ezra; a child, Mirah; a vanishing. He thought of doing so—after Christmas. It was always after something: after the next duty at home, after the next claim from Sir Hugo, after the next day’s fatigue. It was not that he lacked sympathy; it was that reality, when it pressed close and warm, could make even a man who loved common things feel as if his nerves were being rubbed against a coarse cloth. There is an easy enthusiasm that floats above facts—can imagine a beautiful maiden’s kindred in Cordova, can let garlic be medieval perfume, can turn dingy streets into Rhine-border legend, and hear in the modern shout the far-off bay of crusading bloodhounds. But to stand at noon among unbeautiful faces, with the beloved idea made flesh and liable to disappointment—that asks for a different imagination, the kind that can pierce what is solid without fleeing from it.

Now Mirah was not an idea. She was a living, trembling certainty with a voice that had learned fear and a silence that carried the weight of exile. And because she was so delicate in his mind—because she had the sort of inward music that made him listen for the least discord—he began, in spite of himself, to see every common Jew and Jewess under the harsh light of comparison. He could not help forecasting the collision between what she hoped—some mother transfigured by love, some brother purified by remembrance—and what might be found: a life dulled by trade, thickened by years, forgetful, even indifferent. The forecast was sharpened by a faint, suppressed consciousness that somewhere in his own destiny there might lie a similar collision between expectation and discovered fact.

He rambled, telling himself that he looked only to prepare his own mind. He did not want—he almost dared not want—to find anybody in particular. And yet he could not keep from glancing up at shop-fronts as he passed, scanning names as one tastes an unfamiliar dish with caution, hoping it will not be too strange upon the tongue. When his eye met “Cohen,” his heart gave a small, involuntary contraction—then eased if the next word was not “Ezra.” He had even the unreasonable wish that if he ever met an Ezra Cohen, he should not be a shopkeeper. One has these superstitions of fastidious hope, as if fate were a perverse cook who will always add what you most dislike the moment you confess your dislike.

One morning, turning into a little side street away from the grind and clatter of Holborn, he felt tired enough to hail a hansom and let the city roll past without his feet bearing him. He had paused, the cab coming toward him, when something in a window at his right caught his attention: clasps of chased silver, old and finely wrought, lying with a restrained gleam amid other objects whose histories were mute and dubious. The metal looked as if hands long dead had polished it with habit, and the engraving held the delicate sharpness of work done slowly, as if time itself were an artisan.

His first thought—domestic, almost tender in its ordinariness—was of Lady Mallinger, whose strictly Protestant taste had a weakness for Catholic spoils, and how these missal-clasps might be made into a bracelet to clasp her wrist. His eyes moved over the window. It was one of those pawnbrokers’ shops where jewelry led the show and lace and odd relics of gentility lay about like shed skins. In one corner a placard announced: Watches and Jewelry exchanged and repaired.

His looking had been noticed. A figure appeared at the door and, with the cordial push of trade, said, “Good day, sir.”

Deronda needed only that instant to see the face was unmistakably Jewish: a young man, about thirty, with the sleek confidence of a seller who believes in the persuasive power of his own smile. Deronda, shrinking from the coming pressure of attentions, returned the “good day” and crossed quickly to the other side of the street. There, as if he had meant only to avoid the man’s approach, he beckoned the cabman to draw up.

From his safer station he saw the name painted over the window.

EZRA COHEN.

The letters were black and plain, yet they struck him like a sound—like a name called unexpectedly in a crowded room. There might be a hundred Ezra Cohens in London, he reasoned, and he had happened upon one. But he had not seen a hundred; he had seen this. And the man at the door had been about the age one would expect for Mirah’s brother, grown while she was still small.

As the cab carried him away, he worked at his own mind with the obstinacy of one trying to knead a lump of dough into the shape his hands require. There was no warrant, he said; no solid presumption. And even if it should prove that this Ezra was Mirah’s brother, and her mother were dead—then it was not necessarily his duty to tell her. Why should he fling her into sorrow, perhaps into disillusion? He could keep her safe from that shock.

But the thought would not stay quiet under his hand. He had learned, through Mirah’s timid religious earnestness, that she would have a sacred desire to know even of her mother’s death—to mourn in truth, to pray with knowledge. And was he justified in ordering another life by his own notions of tenderness? Was not his secret complaint against the ordering of his own life that he had been denied open daylight—left without the clear claims of primary duty?

The immediate relief was the notion that he had discovered nothing—only a name on glass. Facts would surely dismiss this uneasy fantasy. He resolved to return as soon as he could and buy the clasps for Lady Mallinger; the purchase would be his pretext and his test.

But several days were wasted by Sir Hugo, who, being about to make an after-dinner speech on a burning topic, required Deronda to forage for him on the legal part of the question, and to fence with him daily in arguments that always ended in a draw. They differed, as they often did; Sir Hugo enjoyed opposition as he enjoyed any lively sport, but he also had his impatiences.

“Confound it, Dan!” he said one day, when Deronda had put his point with quiet firmness. “Why don’t you make an opportunity of saying these things in public? You’re wrong, you know. You won’t succeed. You’ve got the massive sentiment—the heavy artillery of the country—against you. But it’s all the better ground for a young man to display himself on. When I was your age, I should have taken it. And it would be quite as well for you to be in opposition to me here and there. It would throw you more into relief. If you would seize an occasion of this sort to make an impression, you might be in Parliament in no time. And you know that would gratify me.”

“I am sorry not to do what would gratify you, sir,” Deronda answered. “But I cannot persuade myself to look at politics as a profession.”

“Why not? If a man is not born into public life by his position in the country, there’s no way for him but to embrace it by his own efforts. The business of the country must be done—her Majesty’s Government carried on, as the old Duke said. And it never could be, my boy, if everybody looked at politics as if they were prophecy, and demanded an inspired vocation. If you are to get into Parliament, it won’t do to sit still and wait for a call either from heaven or constituents.”

“I don’t want to make a living out of opinions,” Deronda said; “especially out of borrowed opinions. Not that I mean to blame other men. I dare say many better fellows than I don’t mind getting on to a platform to praise themselves, and giving their word of honor for a party.”

“I’ll tell you what, Dan,” Sir Hugo returned, “a man who sets his face against every sort of humbug is simply a three-cornered, impracticable fellow. There’s a bad style of humbug, but there is also a good style—one that oils the wheels and makes progress possible. If you are to rule men, you must rule them through their own ideas; and I agree with the Archbishop at Naples who had a St. Januarius procession against the plague. It’s no use having an Order in Council against popular shallowness. There is no action possible without a little acting.”

“One may be obliged to give way to an occasional necessity,” said Deronda. “But it is one thing to say, ‘In this particular case I am forced to put on this foolscap and grin,’ and another to buy a pocket foolscap and practice myself in grinning. I can’t see any real public expediency that does not keep an ideal before it which makes a limit of deviation from the direct path. But if I were to set up for a public man I might mistake my success for public expediency.”

The talk jarred on him. It left a taste, as if a heavy, over-sauced dish had been pressed on his palate when he was craving something plain. It was after this that he set out again toward Ezra Cohen’s, with his pretext of the silver clasps and his deeper reluctance, slower and stickier than any fatigue in his limbs.

He entered the street from the end farthest from Holborn. The roar behind him fell away; here, the sound changed—voices nearer, more distinct, a thinner rattle of carts, the clink of small objects handled, the occasional sharp cry of a child like a bird’s complaint. The sonic air of the place—the way noise nested here in narrow channels rather than spreading—pressed on him with a kind of intimacy. Modern London had its industrial brute sounds, the endless iron grind; but in this street the soundscape had older textures: bargaining voices, coins dropped, doors opened and shut, and under it all the hum of lives kept close to their own necessities.

He found himself turning Sir Hugo’s words inward, translating “public expediency” into the private difficulty that drew him back. Was it wise—was it merciful—to conceal possible kindred? Such decisions, in most lives, are made rough-and-ready; men keep secrets as they keep money, without much scruple, calling it prudence. But Deronda had come to feel concealment as a kind of moral mildew—spreading, spoiling, making even good intentions smell faintly stale. To act under the necessity of concealment was, to him, often the sign of a wrong path.

Still, he hesitated. He paused before shop-windows with the air of a gentleman merely looking, as if he could delay the next step by admiring a tie-pin or a ring. A bare possibility, when it threatens pain, can weigh more than the best-clad likelihood.

One of the windows he paused at belonged to a second-hand bookshop. Outside, on a narrow table, the ages lay in compromise: Homer and railway novels, sermons and scandal, battered histories and bright lies. Deronda’s eye, trained by hunger for meaning rather than for fashion, lit on something he wanted at once: Salomon Maimon’s autobiography. He had heard of it, and the very title had the taste of strong bread—something made of difficult grain, nourishing and austere.

He slipped the book into his hand and entered to pay, expecting to see the usual grimy nonchalance of second-hand trade—the seller who never presses you, as if even he does not believe in the good of what he sells. But behind the counter was a figure that startled him into stillness.

A man in threadbare clothing sat on a stool against shelves that projected beyond the counter. His age was hard to guess; the flesh had the dead, yellowish flatness of old ivory. He was reading yesterday’s Times. When he let the paper rest on his lap and looked up, Deronda had the sudden, absurd sense that he was being looked at by a face that belonged, not to this dim shop, but to some older world—a prophet of exile, or a poet who had made a language burn in the middle ages. It was a fine, typical Jewish face, wrought into intensity by long striving where satisfactions were indirect and far away, and perhaps by bodily suffering that permitted no ease in the present. The features were clear-cut, not large; the brow not high but broad, edged sharply by crisp black hair. It might never have been handsome; it must always have been forcible. The dark gaze, far off and yet piercing, made the shop’s gloom seem like a prison cell.

For a moment they merely looked. The air held the faint odor of old paper and dust—dry, almost edible in its way, like the scent that rises when one breaks a crust of stale bread. Outside, a cart wheel squealed; inside, the silence tightened around their breathing.

Deronda asked at last, “What is the price of this book?”

The man took it and examined the fly-leaves without rising. “There is no mark, and Mr. Ram is not in now. I am keeping the shop while he is gone to dinner. What are you disposed to give for it?” He held the book close on his lap, his hand upon it, and looked examiningly at Deronda.

A disagreeable thought crossed Deronda—was this an attempt to extract more from a stranger? Yet the man’s look seemed less mercantile than hungry, as if he were tasting Deronda’s words for some flavor.

Without weighing further, Deronda said, “Don’t you know how much it is worth?”

“Not its market-price.” The man’s voice was low, dry. “May I ask—have you read it?”

“No. I have read an account of it, which makes me want to buy it.”

“You are a man of learning—you are interested in Jewish history?” The tone deepened, sharpened with eager inquiry, as if something in him had leaped awake at the mention of that book.

“I am certainly interested in Jewish history,” said Deronda, quietly, curiosity overcoming his distaste at being inspected.

The man rose abruptly. A thin hand pressed Deronda’s arm with a tightness that made him flinch, and a hoarse, excited voice—scarce above a loud whisper—said, “You are perhaps of our race?”

Deronda colored deeply. He disliked the grasp, the sudden claim implied by it, the way the question sounded like a gate creaking open—or shutting. He shook his head slightly. “No.”

The hand fell away. The eagerness collapsed into a melancholy indifference, as if a spirit that had rushed up to the eyes and fingers sank back again into some dark inward chamber. The man moved a little off, held out the book, and said with distant civility, “I believe Mr. Ram will be satisfied with half-a-crown, sir.”

Deronda, afterwards, could smile at the odd humiliation of it—as if he had been measured for a robe and found unworthy, dismissed with a curt permission to go. There was nothing to say. He paid his half-crown, took Salomon Maimon’s Lebensgeschichte, and left with a bare “good-morning,” carrying the book like a warm stone that had been in another man’s hand.

He felt vexed at the abrupt closing of the encounter, at the sense that he had been forbidden to know more of a man who was clearly uncommon. The contrast grew sharper as, a little later, he stood before the door of Ezra Cohen’s shop and went in.

Here the air was different—more metallic, more perfumed with cheap sweetness: the faint scent of worn velvet and old lace, of human skin warmed in close rooms, and underneath it the cold, thin smell of silver and plated ware. On the counter lay two plated stoppers and three teaspoons, spread like specimens. Behind the partition Ezra Cohen’s flourishing face hung in negotiation, glistening on its way to fatness.

Seeing Deronda enter, he called out, “Mother! Mother!” and then, with a familiar nod and smile, “Coming, sir—coming directly.”

Deronda’s eyes went anxiously toward the back door. His uneasiness was not soothed when a vigorous woman beyond fifty came in and approached. There was nothing ghastly about her; the worst one could say was that she looked as if she had made her toilet with little water and by twilight—one of those faces on which comfort has left a film and hardship a stain. Her large earrings had the look of having been slept in; rings and necklace sat on her with a sort of permanent assertion, as if she would not be stripped of ornaments even by night.

What caused Deronda’s sinking was not that she was too coarse and ugly to be Mirah’s mother, but that she was not. He did what all men do when they hunt kinship in a stranger’s face: he tried to think away the fat laid on by years, to press back time with his mind until he could glimpse the earlier outlines. The eyebrows vexed him with a similarity of line; and who can decide how far youth may be masked by uncherishing years, thrust onward in the procession where every face is altered and yet remains itself?

The good-humor of her glance shone out, motherly, as she said in a mild guttural tone, “How can I serve you, sir?”

“I should like to look at the silver clasps in the window,” said Deronda. “The larger ones, please, in the corner there.”

They were not quite easy to get at from where she stood. Ezra called out, “I’ll reach ’em, mother; I’ll reach ’em,” and ran forward with alacrity. He handed the clasps to Deronda with a smiling remark that seemed half apology, half performance.

“Mother’s too proud: she wants to do everything herself. That’s why I called her to wait on you, sir. When there’s a particular gentleman customer, sir, I daren’t do any other than call her. But I can’t let her do herself mischief with stretching.”

He made way again for his parent, and she gave a little guttural, amiable laugh, looking at Deronda as if to say, This boy will be at his jokes, but you see he’s the best son in the world. The son plainly enjoyed pleasing her, and yet wanted Deronda to understand that he himself could have served with equal readiness, if only proper ceremony allowed it.

Deronda examined the clasps as if they required long judgment. The silver had a cool, old sheen; the chased work caught the light in tiny ridges like ripples frozen. He thought, absurdly, of hands that had once closed a book with them, of prayers that might have risen while the metal rested against leather, of a language murmured that might now be dead on living tongues.

“They are only three guineas, sir,” said the mother, encouragingly.

“First-rate workmanship, sir—worth twice the money; only I get ’em a bargain from Cologne,” said Ezra, from a little distance, tossing the word “Cologne” into the air like a spice meant to improve the flavor of the sale.

Two new customers came in. Ezra’s repeated call—“Addy! Addy!”—brought from the back a small group that Deronda turned frankly to stare at, sure the stare would be taken as compliment. The group was noisy in its own way: not loud, but full of quick little sounds—the soft thump of a child set down, the rustle of skirts, the brisk inhalations and exclamations of people entering a familiar place.

A black-eyed young woman carried a black-eyed little one, its head already covered with black curls, and set it on the counter, where it looked round with more than the usual intelligence of babies, as if it listened to everything. With her came a robust boy of six and a younger girl—both black-eyed, black-ringed hair close about their faces—looking more Semitic than their parents, like young lion-cubs showing spots from far-off progenitors.

“Addy”—a bright, complacent creature in a vivid blue dress, coral necklace and earrings, her hair built up into a huge bush—looked as lively and unrefined as her husband. Her presence, by difference from the elder woman, deepened Deronda’s unwelcome impression that the mother was not so utterly common as to exclude her being Mirah’s mother.

While that thought passed like a cold draught through him, the boy stamped energetically forward into the shop and set himself about four feet from Deronda, hands deep in the pockets of his miniature knickerbockers, to look at him with a precocious air of survey—as if the child had learned already the commercial habit of measuring a stranger’s worth.

Perhaps to linger, perhaps from a sudden need to touch something innocent amid his own uneasy calculations, Deronda patted the boy’s head and said, “What is your name, sirrah?”

“Jacob Alexander Cohen,” the small man answered, with ease and distinctness.

“You are not named after your father, then?”

“No, after my grandfather; he sells knives and razors and scissors—my grandfather does,” said Jacob, anxious to impress Deronda with the grandeur of that connection. “He gave me this knife.” He drew out a pocket-knife; the small fingers, naturally and artificially dark, opened two blades and a cork-screw with quick, practiced deftness. The metal made a small, keen click that seemed too sharp for such a young hand.

“Is not that a dangerous plaything?” Deronda said, turning to the grandmother.

“_He_’ll never hurt himself, bless you!” she answered, contemplating her grandson with placid rapture.

“Have _you_ got a knife?” said Jacob, edging closer, his small voice hoarse in its glibness, as if it belonged to an aged bargaining soul that had been talking prices through generations.

“Yes. Do you want to see it?” Deronda said, taking a small penknife from his waistcoat-pocket.

When Deronda arrived at five, the shop-front was already shuttered, as if the day’s bargaining were something to be folded away before the Sabbath could be unfolded. A Christian servant admitted him and led him through the dim passage into the room behind, where the family’s private life—so little guessed at by a passer-by—had been set out with a care that was almost ceremonial.

The house was old and stretched far back, and the room he entered must have been heavy with shadow in daylight; but now it was softened and warmed by a fine brass lamp, old enough to have gathered its own patina of years, hanging with seven little oil-flames above a table dressed in snow-white linen. The air carried that mingled household scent which no shop ever quite loses—wax, warmed wood, and the faint metallic tang of handled things—yet over it there floated the richer reassurance of food held ready: a whisper of fried fish, a breath of sweet cake, and that particular clean, yeasty fragrance that rises from newly cut bread.

The surroundings were dark enough to throw the figures into a Venetian glow. The grandmother, in yellowish-brown, wore a thick gold chain instead of a necklace; and in the lamplight her yellow face, with its strongly marked brows and the rolled framing of gray hair, looked almost handsome by mere force of lighting and attitude. Young Mrs. Cohen was vivid in red and black, with large artificial pearls wound again and again round her throat. The baby slept in a cradle under a scarlet counterpane. Adelaide Rebekah, braided amber, stood watchfully near, and Jacob Alexander, in black velveteen with scarlet stockings, seemed braced for some important negotiation. Their black eyes shone such an eager welcome that Deronda felt a small shame at the contemptuous distaste their daylight aspect had stirred in him. Here, under lamplight and linen, they looked like people who knew how to keep a hearth.

He glanced—almost despite himself—at the room’s few dignities: an oaken bureau, a high side-table, a large dish of blue and yellow ware set up like an heirloom, and two old silver vessels flanking it. In front lay a great volume in darkened vellum, ribbed at the back—heavy with some inheritance of words. At the far corner an open door showed another lit room beyond. Deronda took in these details in swift parenthetic looks while Jacob pressed his grave concern about the knife.

Deronda had bought one to order, with the hook and the white handle, and now produced it.

“Is that the sort of thing you want, Jacob?”

Jacob examined it with the severity of a small connoisseur. He opened the blades, tested the hook, drew out the corkscrew from his own knife for comparison.

“Why do you like a hook better than a cork-screw?” Deronda asked.

“’Caush I can get hold of things with a hook. A cork-screw won’t go into anything but corks. But it’s better for you, you can draw corks.”

“You agree to change, then?” Deronda said, aware that the grandmother listened with visible delight, as if this traffic were a little drama in itself.

“What else have you got in your pockets?” Jacob demanded, with deliberative seriousness.

“Hush, hush, Jacob, love,” the grandmother said; and Deronda, mindful that discipline was part of kindness, answered evenly, “I think I must not tell you that. Our business was with the knives.”

Jacob lifted his face and scanned Deronda for a long moment, as if weighing a man by the set of his mouth and the steadiness of his eyes. Then he said, with judicial gravity, “I’ll shwop,” and handed over the cork-screw knife. Deronda pocketed it with corresponding gravity.

Immediately Jacob ran into the inner room, his rapid voice chattering there; then he was back again, and when he saw his father enter, he seized a little velveteen hat from a chair, clapped it on, and advanced as if dressing for an audience. Cohen himself kept on his own hat and, at first, took no notice of the visitor. He stood still while the two children went up and clasped his knees; then he laid his hands on each in turn and uttered the Hebrew benediction. The wife—who had lifted the baby from the cradle—brought it and held it, still sleeping, beneath the father’s outstretched hands to be blessed in its sleep.

For one suspended minute Deronda felt that the pawnbroker, proud of his vocation, was not wholly prosaic. The room’s small sounds—cloth faintly rustling, oil-lights making their tiny, steady murmur, a child’s breath, a woman’s skirt—seemed to arrange themselves into a calm acoustic order, as if even the air were learning to be reverent. Whatever harsh racket the street might carry, here the Sabbath began by quieting the very hearing.

“Well, sir, you found your welcome in my family, I think,” Cohen said, setting down his hat at last and becoming his former self. “And you’ve been punctual. Nothing like a little stress here,” he added, tapping his side pocket as he sat. “It’s good for us all in our turn. I’ve felt it when I’ve had to make up payments. I began to fit every sort of box. It’s bracing to the mind. Now then! let us see, let us see.”

“That is the ring I spoke of,” Deronda said, drawing it from his finger. “I believe it cost a hundred pounds. It will be a sufficient pledge to you for fifty, I think. I shall probably redeem it in a month or so.”

Cohen’s glistening eyes seemed to draw a little nearer together as he met the ingenuous look—so young, so sure of his own good faith—that supposed redemption must be a satisfaction to pawnbrokers. Cohen took the ring, examined it, returned it, and said with studied indifference, “Good, good. We’ll talk of it after our meal. Perhaps you’ll join us, if you’ve no objection. Me and my wife’ll feel honored, and so will mother; won’t you, mother?”

The invitation was echoed warmly; and Deronda accepted with readiness, for the table—with its white cloth and warm scents held in check—seemed to offer him more than food. It offered access.

All now turned and stood round. No dish was yet visible except one covered with a napkin; young Mrs. Cohen set a china bowl by her husband so that he might wash his hands. But after he had put on his hat again, he paused and called in a loud voice, “Mordecai!”

Deronda, ignorant what role might be expected of some ancient hero at such a moment, half wondered whether this were part of the ceremony. He heard a “Yes” from the next room and looked toward the open door. There, to his astonishment, stood the very figure he had met that morning in the book-shop—the enigmatic Jew with the ardent, worn face.

Their eyes met. Mordecai looked as surprised as Deronda; and neither, in the suddenness of it, made any sign of recognition. When Mordecai came forward and seated himself at the end of the table, he bent his head to the guest in a cold distant way, as if the morning’s disappointment still clung to Deronda as an unpleasant association.

Cohen washed his hands, Hebrew words running from him in a practised current. Then he took away the napkin and showed two long flat loaves, besprinkled with seed—bread that bore memory in its very shape, a memorial of manna for wandering forefathers. He broke off small pieces and gave to each—grandmother, wife, children—Adelaide Rebekah standing on a chair at her full little height in amber, her lip compressed so that her small Jewish nose seemed longer in the effort to look properly solemn. After another blessing the men uncovered their heads, all were seated, and the meal began.

Deronda, preoccupied, could hardly have told what he ate. Yet the table made itself felt through the senses even while his mind ran ahead. There was fried fish—crisp at the edges, with that savor of oil that has taken on the flavor of the pan and of repeated Fridays, its thin tails browned and delicate. There was sweet cake, thick with sugar and spice, soft enough to swell a child’s cheek. There were the loaves with their seeded crust, their torn interior steaming faintly when broken, their smell like warm grain and old kitchens. The comfort of it was domestic, physical, unarguable—and it sat oddly beside the questions pressing in him about the man opposite.

Mordecai had no handsome Sabbath garment; but instead of the threadbare rusty black coat of the morning he wore a light drab one, which had once been a handsome loose paletot, now shrunk by washing and poverty. The change sharpened rather than softened the impression of his face—dark-haired, eager, emaciated—like some prophet’s head set down among shopkeepers. Deronda could not help noticing how the thin tails of the fried fish were assigned to Mordecai, and in general how his portion bore that quiet stamp given to a poor relation: a distribution as old as households, done without discussion, almost without awareness.

Cohen kept the conversation lively, choosing subjects “in taste”—royalty and empire. He spoke proudly of the Queen and the Royal Family; of the Emperor and Empress of the French; and the grandmother and wife entered with zest. Young Mrs. Cohen had an accurate memory of distinguished birthdays; the elder helped her son recall what occurred when the Emperor and Empress were in England and visited the City ten years before.

“I dare say you know all about it better than we do, sir,” Cohen said repeatedly, by way of preface to still fuller information.

“Our baby is named _Eu_genie Esther,” the young mother said, with bright emphasis.

“It’s wonderful how the Emperor’s like a cousin of mine in the face,” the grandmother declared. “It struck me like lightning when I caught sight of him. I couldn’t have thought it.”

“Mother and me went to see the Emperor and Empress at the Crystal Palace,” Cohen said. “I had a fine piece of work to take care of, mother; she might have been squeezed flat—though she was pretty near as lusty then as she is now. I said if I had a hundred mothers I’d never take one of ’em to see the Emperor and Empress at the Crystal Palace again; and you may think a man can’t afford it when he’s got but one mother—not if he’d ever so big an insurance on her.”

He stroked his mother’s shoulder and chuckled at his own humor. Deronda, listening, sought a path into what he wished to know.
