“Your mother has been a widow a long while, perhaps,” he said. “That has made your care for her the more needful.”

“Ay, ay, it’s a good many _yore-zeit_ since I had to manage for her and myself,” Cohen answered quickly. “I went early to it. It’s that makes you a sharp knife.”

“What does—what makes a sharp knife, father?” Jacob asked, his cheek swollen with sweet cake.

The father winked at Deronda. “Having your nose put on the grindstone.”

Jacob slipped down from his chair, still holding his cake, and went straight up to Mordecai, who had been totally silent so far.

“What does that mean—putting my nose to the grindstone?” the boy demanded.

Mordecai turned his eyes on the small face close to his and said, with a benign gravity, “It means that you are to bear being hurt without making a noise.”

Jacob, as if moved by a sudden impulse of alliance, pushed the corner of the cake into Mordecai’s mouth—inviting him to bite—saying at the same time, “I shan’t though,” and watching carefully to see how much of the cake disappeared in this act of generosity. Mordecai took a bite and smiled, clearly meaning to please him; and the moment made both seem more lovable.

Deronda, however, felt a vexation: his question had yielded little. He tried another approach, letting it seem general.

“I fancy that is the right quarter for learning,” he said, and then, turning toward Mordecai as if naturally drawn, “You have been a great student, I imagine?”

“I have studied,” Mordecai answered quietly.

“And you?—You know German by the book you were buying.”

“Yes,” Deronda said. “I have studied in Germany. Are you generally engaged in bookselling?”

“No; I only go to Mr. Ram’s shop every day to keep it while he goes to meals,” Mordecai said. He now looked at Deronda with what seemed a revival of his earlier interest, as if something in Deronda’s face drew him and began to counteract the morning’s disappointment. After a slight pause he asked, “Perhaps you know Hebrew?”

“I am sorry to say, not at all.”

Mordecai’s countenance fell. He lowered his eyelids, looked at his hands crossed on the table, and said no more.

Deronda noticed now, more decisively than in the shop, Mordecai’s difficulty in breathing—an effort hidden badly beneath composure, and suggestive of consumption. It gave the man’s silence a weight: as if speech itself were a costly substance he must ration, like a poor household portioning out oil.

“I’ve had something else to do than to get book-learning,” Cohen said, throwing himself into talk with the pride of the practical. “I’ve had to make myself knowing about useful things. I know stones well,”—and he pointed toward Deronda’s ring. “I’m not afraid of taking that ring of yours at my own valuation. But now,” he added, dropping his voice into a more familiar nasal, “what do you want for it?”

“Fifty or sixty pounds,” Deronda answered, rather too carelessly.

Cohen paused, thrust his hands into his pockets, and fixed on Deronda a pair of glistening eyes that suggested a miraculous guinea-pig’s scrutiny—bright, quick, and intent on gain.

“Couldn’t do you that. Happy to oblige, but couldn’t go that lengths. Forty pound—say forty—I’ll let you have forty on it.”

Deronda was aware that Mordecai had looked up again at the sound of money, and was examining him as he replied, “Very well. I shall redeem it in a month or so.”

“Good. I’ll make you out the ticket by-and-by,” Cohen said indifferently, and held up his finger to check further speech.

Then Cohen, Mordecai, and Jacob put on their hats again. Cohen opened a thanksgiving; the others responded. And presently Mordecai delivered himself alone at some length, chanting in a solemn tone, his chin slightly uplifted, his thin hands clasped loosely before him. There was in his voice an eerie purity, a steadiness that seemed to belong to older air than London’s—an acoustic refuge from the day’s clangor. It made Deronda think, with a sudden resentment at modern harshness, how much human well-being depends on the sounds that surround us: how quickly a coarse street can bruise the mind, and how a measured chant can mend it. The words themselves were not Deronda’s; the syllables were foreign to his tongue, and yet their cadence carried a meaning beyond translation—something that could not be rendered without loss, because it lived partly in breath and pitch, in the very way the room listened.

In accent and tone, in the freedom from any glance toward others’ approval, Mordecai was the strongest contrast possible to Cohen at the other end of the table. It was an unaccountable conjunction: among these common, prosperous, shopkeeping types sat a man threadbare and emaciated, imposing on Deronda a certain awe—and an embarrassment, too, as if he were failing some expectation he could not name.

No sooner had Mordecai finished than he rose, bent his head slightly to the stranger, walked back into his room, and shut the door behind him.

“That seems to be rather a remarkable man,” Deronda said, turning to Cohen.

Cohen set up his shoulders, put out his tongue slightly, and tapped his own brow. The gesture made plain enough what standard of sanity Cohen applied.

“Does he belong to your family?” Deronda asked.

The notion seemed ludicrous to the ladies as well as to Cohen; they exchanged amused looks.

“No, no,” Cohen said. “Charity! charity! He worked for me, and when he got weaker and weaker I took him in. He’s an incumbrance; but he brings a blessing down, and he teaches the boy. Besides, he does the repairing at the watches and jewelry.”

Deronda could hardly keep from smiling at the mixture: kindliness needing to be justified as calculation, pity balanced with profit like weights on a scale. But any further attempt to speak of Mordecai was baffled at once. Cohen dismissed the subject by returning to the “accommodation”—which was also, by his account, an act of charity—and proceeded to make out the pawn-ticket, fetch the forty pounds, and hand both over in exchange for the diamond ring.

Deronda felt it would not be delicate to prolong his visit beyond the settlement of the business which had been its pretext. He took his leave with no more decided result than the money and the pawn-ticket in his breast-pocket—a reason to return when he came up to town after Christmas. Yet he left with a stronger resolve than he had entered with: that on his return he would contrive to gain a clearer insight into the character and history of Mordecai—and, through him, perhaps something decisive about the Cohens too: for example, why it seemed forbidden to ask the elder Mrs. Cohen whether she had a daughter.

If conscience were weighed out in due proportion to wrongdoing, the chronicles of our kind would read like a different music altogether: the great architects of hunger and ruin would be the ones kept awake by their own inward knives, and the petty thief would sleep as soundly as a well-fed child. Yet wickedness has its wages; and the terrible secret is that the human creature is rarely made of a single metal. Most men and women are compounded—capable of harm, yet still shadowed by a fear that resembles justice, and a pity that resembles love. Those faint resemblances are enough to spoil the pure serenity of cruelty. They are enough to make even the well-dressed wrong-doer start at his own footsteps in a corridor.

On the twenty-ninth of December, Daniel Deronda knew the Grandcourts had reached the Abbey; but up to the moment he went upstairs to dress for dinner he had not once seen them. The day had brought a splendid fall of snow, deep and unbroken in the park, whitening even the cedar boughs so that they drooped like heavy-laden platters. The children had made a festival of it—snow-balls that burst in soft floury clouds, a fort rising with earnest little hands packing and smoothing as if they were shaping dough, and “cousin” Deronda pressed into service because no game felt complete unless he planned it, judged it, or was pelted by it. Afterward there had been billiards; the click of balls, the muffled swish of the cue, and the subdued laughter—those civilized sounds that never quite become noise in an old house—carried the afternoon away without his dwelling on the evening’s encounter.

But in his room, with the hush that comes before the half-hour bell, the prospect of meeting Gwendolen returned to him and began to work like a spice warmed in the palm—subtle, inevitable. He found himself asking what marriage to Grandcourt would do to her; whether there would be any new shade upon her manner since Diplow, as there had been since that first vision of her at Leubronn, bright as a flame above the roulette-table.

“I fancy there are natures one could see growing—or degenerating—every day, if one watched them,” he thought, fastening a cuff with a patience that did not quiet his mind. “Some of us go on faster than others. And she keeps strong traces of anything that has once impressed her. That business of the necklace—and merely the knowledge that somebody disapproved her play—had bitten in. But an impressible creature may be driven either way: to desperation as readily as to anything better. And whatever fascinations Grandcourt may have for caprice—good heavens! who can believe he would call out tender affection in daily companionship? One might want to strike him only to see if he could show a sign of feeling. I’m afraid she married him from ambition—to escape poverty. Yet she fled him at first… Poor thing! she may have been pressed into it. How can one feel anything else than pity for a young creature like that—full of unused life—hanging blind expectation on that remnant of a human being?”

The harsher his inner phrases for the bridegroom, the more they seemed to wrap and soften the bride in excuse. He had no intimate knowledge of Grandcourt—only that ordinary polite contact which had left the impression of a man whose natural interest in the world had been worn away, as if by long handling, until only the smooth outer surface remained.

And it is a common arrangement in society’s secret ledger: when a marriage of note is made, the men are apt to pity the bride and the women the bridegroom. Each is thought to have done worse than might have been; and if the bride is young and charming, young men on the spot commonly conclude she cannot really love a husband so uninteresting to themselves, but has chosen him for reasons that taste like money or position. Who pities the husband? Even his female friends often take his situation as a kind of reckoning—he might have chosen otherwise.

Deronda, perhaps, was excusable for saving no pity for Grandcourt, who had never struck anyone as likely to take more pain from life than he gave it; but for Gwendolen—young, eager, used to the flattery that makes a lovely girl believe the world owes her obedience—how swiftly might life turn from bright expectancy into the bitter knowledge of what cannot be undone? Deronda would have had to be dull indeed not to feel some interest in her entrance. Yet the honeymoon already lay three weeks behind; she had been enthroned at Ryelands and at Diplow; she was not one to expose helplessly whatever went on within her. She would have learned how to wear her face—what to show, what to hide.

A various party had been invited to meet the new couple. The old aristocracy was there in Lord and Lady Pentreath; the old gentry in young Mr. and Mrs. Fitzadam from the Worcestershire branch; politics and “the public good” as expressed in cider, in Mr. Fenn, member for West Orchards, with his two daughters; Lady Mallinger’s family in her brother, Mr. Raymond, and his wife; and the useful bachelor element in Mr. Sinker, the eminent counsel, and Mr. Vandernoodt—pleasant enough at Leubronn to be adopted by Sir Hugo in England.

They were all assembled in the drawing-room before the Grandcourts appeared. The time was chiefly spent in noticing the children—little Raymonds among Lady Mallinger’s three girls—who were always allowed to make part of this hour. The scene itself had a rich domestic splendour: cedar paneling pierced with full-length portraits set in deep backgrounds; a ceiling glowing with coats of arms ranged between the sockets; pale wax-lights softened and warmed by the great red fire of oak-boughs; the deep-piled carpet swallowing sharp footfalls so that conversation seemed to float without edge or clatter. There was that peculiar acoustic of old rooms well-draped—sound held in gentleness, as if the house itself insisted that voices behave. It was an environment that nourished the nerves: no metallic ringing, no thin modern echo; only the low crackle of wood and the occasional childish murmur checked by breeding.

Lady Mallinger, fair, matronly, in black velvet, moved about with a tiny white dog on her arm as if it were the last flourish of her costume. The children were scattered among the ladies; most of the gentlemen stood a little aloof, making those moderate remarks that bridge the long minutes before dinner.

Deronda was drawn aside by Mr. Vandernoodt, a close-clipped, pale-eyed man, nonchalant and commodious, of good Dutch blood imported at the Revolution—one of those who are nothing in particular, but are understood to have access to everything in particular. He made an excellent foil to Deronda’s vivid gravity, and he was now talking of the bride and bridegroom with the industrious air of a gatherer of personal tidbits.

“Men who have seen a good deal of life don’t always end by choosing their wives so well,” Vandernoodt murmured. “He has had rather an anecdotic history—gone rather deep into pleasures, I fancy, lazy as he is. But, of course, you know all about him.”

“No, really,” Deronda answered, with an indifference that was honest. “I know little more than that he is Sir Hugo’s nephew.”

At that moment the door opened, cutting off further confidences. The room, with its firelight and portraits and hushed voices, was made to set off any figure of distinction; and when Mr. and Mrs. Grandcourt entered, no one could deny they had it.

Grandcourt was exactly as before marriage: neither more nor less perfect in costume, neither more nor less cut and finished in impassibility. A man like that would accept nothing under the best in outward equipment, wife included; and the bride was precisely what he might be expected to choose. “By George, I think she’s handsomer, if anything!” Vandernoodt whispered. Deronda thought so too, though he said nothing.

She wore white silk and diamonds—diamonds at her throat, in her ears, in her hair—sparkling coldly, like frost that has caught the firelight. The new splendour seemed to make her beauty flash into a more unquestionable authority, even if it did not make it more satisfying. Some faces, in their peculiar beauty, are like original works of art: the first encounter brings a question; the second, perhaps, a startled assent. At Diplow he had seen more than he expected of that tender, appealing charm called womanly. Was there a change now? He distrusted his own impressions; yet as he watched her receive greetings with proud, quiet coldness and a superficial smile, it seemed to him that within she carried the same demonic force he had felt at Leubronn—the resolute glance, the turning away as a loser, as if wounded pride could be transmuted into scorn.

There was no time to conclude more. Before Deronda could even approach for a proper greeting, the summons to dinner went round them like a bell of command.

He sat not far from opposite her at table. Sometimes he caught what she said in answer to Sir Hugo, who was at his liveliest with her, glad to show off hospitality as if it were a well-roasted joint offered with a flourish. But though Deronda turned his eyes toward her with the intention of bowing, she gave him no opening for some time—her face always angled away, her attention so precisely managed that recognition seemed postponed by design.

At last Sir Hugo, who might have imagined they had spoken already, said, “Deronda, you will like to hear what Mrs. Grandcourt tells me about your favourite Klesmer.”

Gwendolen’s eyelids had been lowered; Deronda, looking toward her, thought he saw a quivering reluctance as she was obliged to raise them and return his unembarrassed bow and smile. Her own smile moved only her lips, as if the rest of her face refused it. It lasted but an instant; Sir Hugo went on without pause.

“The Arrowpoints have condoned the marriage, and he is spending Christmas with his bride at Quetcham.”

“I suppose he will be glad of it for the sake of his wife,” said Deronda; “else I dare say he would not have minded keeping at a distance.”

“It’s a sort of troubadour story,” said Lady Pentreath, deep-voiced and easy. “I’m glad to find a little romance left among us. Our young people now are getting too worldly wise.”

“It shows the Arrowpoints’ good sense, however, to have adopted the affair after the fuss in the paper,” Sir Hugo added. “Disowning your own child for a _mésalliance_ is something like disowning your one eye: everybody knows it’s yours, and you’ve no other to make an appearance with.”

“As to _mésalliance_, there’s no blood on any side,” said Lady Pentreath. “Old Admiral Arrowpoint was one of Nelson’s men—a doctor’s son. And we all know how the mother’s money came.”

“If there were any _mésalliance_, I should say it was on Klesmer’s side,” said Deronda.

“Ah, you think it’s the immortal marrying the mortal. What is your opinion?” Sir Hugo asked, turning to Gwendolen.

“I have no doubt Herr Klesmer thinks himself immortal,” she said coolly. “But I dare say his wife will burn as much incense before him as he requires.”

“Don’t you approve of a wife burning incense before her husband?” Sir Hugo returned, jocose.

“Oh, yes—if it were only to make others believe in him,” Gwendolen said. Then, with a little lift of gaiety, “When Herr Klesmer admires his own genius, it will take off some of the absurdity if his wife says Amen.”

“Klesmer is no favourite of yours, I see,” Sir Hugo said.

“I think very highly of him, I assure you,” she answered, with sudden seriousness, as if correcting herself. “His genius is quite above my judgment, and I know him to be exceedingly generous.”

Deronda wondered, as he listened, what he should have thought of her had he known nothing of her before—perhaps that she wore hardness and defiance as a shield over painful consciousness. Yet why did she manage her recognition of him with such deliberate chill?

Sir Hugo, changing the subject, turned to the room itself. “Isn’t this a beautiful room? It was part of the refectory of the Abbey. There was a division made by those pillars and the three arches, and afterward they were built up. Else it was half as large again originally. There used to be rows of Benedictines sitting where we are sitting. Suppose we were suddenly to see the lights burning low, and the ghosts of the old monks rising behind all our chairs!”

“Please don’t!” Gwendolen cried, with a playful shudder that had a sharpness in it. “It is very nice to come after ancestors and monks—but they should know their places and keep underground. I should be rather frightened to go about this house all alone. I suppose the old generations must be angry with us because we have altered things so much.”

“Oh, the ghosts must be of all political parties,” Sir Hugo said. “Those fellows who wanted to change things while they lived and couldn’t do it must be on our side. But if you would not like to go over the house alone, you will like to go in company, I hope. You and Grandcourt ought to see it all. And we will ask Deronda to go round with us. He is more learned about it than I am.”

Gwendolen stole a glance toward Deronda. He must have heard; his face was turned in their direction as he helped himself to an entrée, but his look might have been painted—so still, so unreadable. At the thought of Deronda showing her and Grandcourt the place that would be theirs—and that she remembered, with a painful emphasis, might have been his—certain old thoughts rushed in upon her, not new in themselves, but newly placed, newly embarrassing. She felt something furtive in her own glance, something that might betray too much. With her quick resource against betrayal, she said playfully, “You don’t know how much I am afraid of Mr. Deronda.”

“How’s that? Because you think him too learned?” Sir Hugo asked, missing nothing.

“No. Ever since I first saw him at Leubronn. When he came to look on at the roulette-table I began to lose. He cast an evil eye on my play. He didn’t approve it. He has told me so. And now, whatever I do before him, I am afraid he will cast an evil eye on it.”

“Gad! I’m rather afraid of him myself when he doesn’t approve,” Sir Hugo said, and glanced at Deronda. Then, lowering his voice with his chronic facetiousness, he added to Gwendolen, “I don’t think ladies generally object to have his eyes upon them.”

“I object to any eyes that are critical,” she said in a cool, high voice, turning her neck as if to throw off a touch. “Are there many of these old rooms left in the Abbey?”

“Not many. There is a fine cloistered court with a long gallery above it. But the finest bit of all is turned into stables—part of the old church. When I improved the place I made the most of every other bit; but it was out of my reach to change the stables. So the horses have the benefit of the fine old choir. You must go and see it.”

“I shall like to see the horses as well as the building,” said Gwendolen.

“Oh, I have no stud to speak of,” Sir Hugo answered. “Grandcourt will look with contempt at my horses. I’ve given up hunting, and go on in a jog-trot way, as becomes an old gentleman with daughters. The fact is, I went in for doing too much at this place. We all lived at Diplow two years while the alterations were going on. Do you like Diplow?”

“Not particularly,” said Gwendolen, with an indifference that sounded as if she had always had more houses than she could digest.

“Ah! it will not do after Ryelands,” Sir Hugo returned, well pleased. “Grandcourt took it for the hunting. But he found something so much better there,” he added, lowering his voice with a pleased smile, “that he might well prefer it to any other place in the world.”

“It has one attraction for me,” said Gwendolen, passing over the compliment with a chill smile, “that it is within reach of Offendene.”

“I understand that,” Sir Hugo said, and let the subject fall.

An amiable baronet, for all his good humour, is not made of stone; a strong desire for a particular possession will press on his spirits like a thumb on a bruised fruit. Sir Hugo would have been glad that Grandcourt, with or without reason, should prefer any other place to Diplow; and because wishing is so deft at dressing itself as benevolence, he even wished Grandcourt’s disgust for Diplow might not be associated, in his own mind, with this marriage to so charming a bride. Gwendolen was much to his taste; later he observed to Lady Mallinger that he should never have taken her for a young girl who had married beyond her expectations.

Deronda had not caught much of this talk, his attention being elsewhere; but what he did see of Gwendolen—the careful angles of her face, the managed coolness, the sudden sharpenings—deepened his impression that there was something newly artificial in her, as if she had taken up a part and was determined not to let it slip.

Later, in the drawing-room, someone asked Deronda to sing. He sat at the piano and did so. The instrument gave out its sound with that mellow restraint which old rooms breed—no harsh brightness, no jangling reverberation, only a rounded tone that seemed to settle into the velvet and wood as naturally as warmth into bread. Afterward Mrs. Raymond took his place; and when Deronda rose, he observed that Gwendolen had left her seat and come to the far end of the room, as if to listen more fully. She stood with her back to everyone, apparently contemplating a fine cowled head carved in ivory that hung above a small table.

He longed to go to her and speak. Why should he not obey the impulse as he would toward any other woman present? Yet he hesitated, watching the graceful line of her back, the stillness with which she held herself—still as if she were listening not to the music but to the house’s own stored whispers. The fire made a faint, steady undertone; voices came and went like softened birds in a winter thicket.

If you have any reason for not indulging a wish to speak to a fair woman, it is a bad plan to look long at her back. The wish to see what it screens grows stronger. There may be, on the other side, a smile that would undo your scruples.

Deronda went at last to the end of the little table, standing at right angles to her. Before he could begin, she turned—no smile at all, but an appealing look of sadness, so different from the chill effort she had made at table, that his prepared words fell away. For a space of time that felt large to both, though it would have measured as nothing to the room, they looked at each other: she as if taking a deep rest in confession, he answering with a sympathy that, for the moment, neutralized everything else.

“Will you not join in the music?” he said at last, taking refuge in the obvious.

The look of confession had been involuntary; a just perceptible shake and change passed over her, as if she roused herself from a dangerous sleep.

“I join in it by listening,” she replied calmly. “I am fond of music.”

“Are you not a musician?”

“I have given a great deal of time to music. But I have not talent enough to make it worth while. I shall never sing again.”

“But if you are fond of music, it will always be worth while in private—for your own delight. I make it a virtue to be content with my middlingness,” Deronda said, smiling. “It is always pardonable, so long as one does not ask others to take it for superiority.”

“I cannot imitate you,” she said, recovering that tone of artificial vivacity which sat on her like a bright, tight glove. “To be middling with me is another phrase for being dull. And the worst fault I have to find with the world is that it is dull. Do you know, I am going to justify gambling in spite of you. It is a refuge from dullness.”

“I don’t admit the justification,” Deronda answered. “I think what we call the dullness of things is a disease in ourselves. Else how can anyone find an intense interest in life? And many do.”

“Ah, I see! The fault I find in the world is my own fault,” she said, smiling at him as if it were a clever retort and nothing more. Then, after a moment, lifting her eyes again toward the ivory head, she asked, “Do you never find fault with the world—or with others?”

“Oh, yes. When I am in a grumbling mood.”

“And hate people?” she insisted, her voice tightening. “Confess you hate them when they stand in your way—when their gain is your loss. That is your own phrase, you know.”

“We are often standing in each other’s way when we can’t help it,” Deronda said. “I think it is stupid to hate people on that ground.”

“But if they injure you—and could have helped it?” she said, and there was a hard intensity in her words, unaccountable in talk meant to be casual.

A painful impression held back his answer for an instant; then he said, with a graver, deeper intonation, “Why, then, after all, I prefer my place to theirs.”

“There I believe you are right,” she said, with a sudden little laugh that rang too quickly and ended too soon, as if it had been summoned to cover something. And she turned away to rejoin the group at the piano.

Mr. Vandernoodt had a knack of fastening on to a man as if with a buttonhook, and he had fastened on Deronda now—drawing him away from the company with the brisk appetite of one who wanted a sharper walk, a cigar freshly lit, and that other indulgence which makes smoke seem sweeter: gossip.

The winter air outside the Abbey had a clean bite; it carried the thin whir of distant wheels on the road, the caw of rooks stripped bare of leaf-shelter, and, nearer, the faint crunch and scuff of their own steps on gravel. Mr. Vandernoodt’s cigar gave off a warm, resinous smell that clung in the cold like a sauce reduced too fast—strong, a little acrid, with a sweetness that was almost cloying.

“What a washed-out piece of cambric Grandcourt is!” he began, with the confident relish of a man slicing into a joint he expects everyone to find tasteless. “But if he’s a favorite of yours, I withdraw the remark.”

“Not the least in the world,” said Deronda, his voice even.

“I thought not. One wonders how he came to have a great passion again; and he must have had—to marry in this way. Though Lush, his old chum, hints that he married this girl out of obstinacy. By George! it was a very accountable obstinacy. A man might make up his mind to marry her without the stimulus of contradiction. But he must have made himself a pretty large drain of money, eh?”

“I know nothing of his affairs.”

“What! not of the other establishment he keeps up?”

“Diplow? Of course. He took that of Sir Hugo. But merely for the year.”

“No, no; not Diplow: Gadsmere. Sir Hugo knows, I’ll answer for it.”

Deronda kept silence. The words, dropped as if they were crumbs meant for sparrows, stirred an unwilling curiosity in him; yet he would not stoop to peck. Mr. Vandernoodt, satisfied with his own power of producing suspense, took another measured pull at his cigar, nipped the ash, and went on.

“Lush would not altogether own to it, of course. He’s a confident and go-between of Grandcourt’s. But I have it on the best authority. The fact is, there’s another lady with four children at Gadsmere. She has had the upper hand of him these ten years and more, and by what I can understand has it still—left her husband for him, and used to travel with him everywhere. Her husband’s dead now; I found a fellow who was in the same regiment with him, and knew this Mrs. Glasher before she took wing. A fiery dark-eyed woman—a noted beauty at that time—he thought she was dead. They say she has Grandcourt under her thumb still, and it’s a wonder he didn’t marry her, for there’s a very fine boy, and I understand Grandcourt can do absolutely as he pleases with the estates. Lush told me as much as that.”

“What right had he to marry this girl?” Deronda’s disgust broke through, sharp as when the palate meets something tainted under a fair crust.

Mr. Vandernoodt shrugged, his cigar-end lifting with the gesture. “She can know nothing of it,” Deronda added, emphatically—only to have the certainty instantly pricked by a question in himself, like a thorn he couldn’t see: Could she have known anything?

“It’s rather a piquant picture,” said Mr. Vandernoodt, pleased with his own seasoning of the tale—“Grandcourt between two fiery women. For depend upon it this light-haired one has plenty of devil in her. I formed that opinion of her at Leubronn. It’s a sort of Medea and Creüsa business. Fancy the two meeting! Grandcourt is a new kind of Jason: I wonder what sort of a part he’ll make of it. It’s a dog’s part at best. I think I hear Ristori now, saying, ‘Jasone! Jasone!’ These fine women generally get hold of a stick.”

“Grandcourt can bite, I fancy,” said Deronda. “He is no stick.”

“No, no; I meant Jason. I can’t quite make out Grandcourt. But he’s a keen fellow enough—uncommonly well built too. And if he comes into all this property, the estates will bear dividing. This girl, whose friends had come to beggary, I understand, may think herself lucky to get him. I don’t want to be hard on a man because he gets involved in an affair of that sort. But he might make himself more agreeable. I was telling him a capital story last night, and he got up and walked away in the middle. I felt inclined to kick him. Do you suppose that is inattention or insolence, now?”

“Oh, a mixture. He generally observes the forms: but he doesn’t listen much,” said Deronda. Then, after a moment, as if trying to set a lid on what had begun boiling in his mind, he said, “I should think there must be some exaggeration or inaccuracy in what you have heard about this lady at Gadsmere.”

“Not a bit, depend upon it; it has all lain snug of late years. People have forgotten all about it. But there the nest is, and the birds are in it. And I know Grandcourt goes there. I have good evidence that he goes there. However, that’s nobody’s business but his own. The affair has sunk below the surface.”

“I wonder you could have learned so much about it,” said Deronda, drily.

“Oh, there are plenty of people who knew all about it; but such stories get packed away like old letters. They interest me. I like to know the manners of my time—contemporary gossip, not antediluvian. These Dryasdust fellows get a reputation by raking up some small scandal about Semiramis or Nitocris, and then we have a thousand and one poems written upon it by all the warblers big and little. But I don’t care a straw about the faux pas of the mummies. You do, though. You are one of the historical men—more interested in a lady when she’s got a rag face and skeleton toes peeping out. Does that flatter your imagination?”

“Well, if she had any woes in her love, one has the satisfaction of knowing that she’s well out of them.”

“Ah, you are thinking of the Medea, I see.”

Deronda, refusing further seasoning from this kitchen of scandal, pointed to some giant oaks worth looking at in their bareness—dark, rigid limbs lifted against the paling sky. He felt Mr. Vandernoodt had emptied his dish; there would be no more to take.

Yet the story clung. In the quiet that followed—the clean winter hush, broken by a distant door-latch, the low clatter of a pail somewhere in the service-yard, the muffled call of a groom—Deronda’s thoughts began to work as they had not worked for years, weaving and unweaving, laying one thread across another until a pattern started out and then blurred again.

Since those early days when, hungry with the peculiar hunger of the unclaimed, he had tried to build the hidden story of his own birth out of looks, silences, and half-words, his mind had perhaps never been so active in guessing at any private affair as it was now over Gwendolen’s marriage. This unavowed relation of Grandcourt’s—could she have known of it, and had it been that knowledge which made her shrink, shrink again, and then at last go forward under the spur of poverty? Deronda could recall almost every word she had said to him; and in some of those words he now seemed to taste an after-flavor he had missed before, as one recognizes a spice only when told its name. There was a consciousness in her—of wrong done, of injury inflicted. And his own secret ache made him keenly alive to the form of injury that falls on unacknowledged children and their mother.

Was Mrs. Grandcourt, beneath all her determined show of satisfaction, gnawed by a grief with more than one head—self-reproach, disappointment, jealousy? He dwelt especially on the slight signs of self-reproach, and his judgment, which might have hardened, turned instead into tenderness: to excuse, to pity. He thought he held a key now; and the thought of a young creature wedding fresh hopes to old secrets made him see her misery magnified, as if the walls of her life were closing in.

It was easy, too, to understand Sir Hugo’s silence: why no hint had been dropped. And then—suddenly, painfully—this Mrs. Glasher, with her four children, was drawn into association with his own obscurity, his own unspoken origin. The thought of Gwendolen knowing, marrying nevertheless, and wearing content like a jewel would have made her, to Deronda, among the most repulsive of beings. But Gwendolen tasting remorse for contributing to their injury—if that were the truth—brought her near to his fellow-feeling. It would mean she had been pushed down from the fine, sheltered ignorance where women so often sit in easy judgment, into a common plane where one begins to understand the Hagar-and-Ishmael side of life. Precedent, after all, would have offered her an almost comfortable legend: that her husband’s marriage with her was his entrance on the path of virtue, while Mrs. Glasher stood for forsaken sin. Deronda felt, by old instinct, a resentment for those who are cast out and then named in someone else’s language as mere wrongdoing, as if the name were a sentence.

And undeniably his growing solicitude for Gwendolen hung chiefly on her peculiar manner toward him—an appeal, hesitant yet importunate, which would have touched any sensibility not deadened by vanity. One sign that his interest had shifted its footing was that he dismissed any caution against her being a coquette laying snares for a vulgar flirtation. He determined he would not again evade any opportunity of talking to her.

He had shaken off Mr. Vandernoodt and found a solitary corner in the twilight; but half an hour was long enough for those possibilities to press in on him. With his resolution made, he remembered she would likely be at tea with the other ladies.

And so she was. For Gwendolen, having decided she would not go down again for the next four hours, felt at the end of one that by shutting herself up she shut out her chances of seeing and hearing—shut out, too, whatever small power she might snatch from knowledge. Her visit would last only two days more. She adjusted herself—smoothed her hair, gathered her self-possession around her like a cloak, and went down with a resolve to be agreeable, to seem at ease.

Only ladies were assembled, and Lady Pentreath—voice full and seasoned by authority—was amusing them with a description of a drawing-room under the Regency and the figure cut by ladies and gentlemen in 1819, the year she was presented. The room had that domestic hush in which the soft chink of teaspoons against china is almost a kind of music, with the faint whisper of tea being poured and the occasional rustle of silk like dried leaves. When Deronda entered, the little soundscape shifted: a chair-leg slid, someone exhaled a laugh, the kettle-lid trembled faintly on its stand.

“Shall I be acceptable?” he said. “Perhaps I had better go back and look for the others. I suppose they are in the billiard-room.”

“No, no; stay where you are,” said Lady Pentreath. “They were all getting tired of me; let us hear what you have to say.”

“That is rather an embarrassing appeal,” said Deronda, drawing up a chair near Lady Mallinger’s elbow at the tea-table. “I think I had better take the opportunity of mentioning our songstress,” he added, looking at Lady Mallinger—“unless you have done so.”

“Oh, the little Jewess!” said Lady Mallinger. “No, I have not mentioned her. It never entered my head that any one here wanted singing lessons.”

“All ladies know some one else who wants singing lessons,” said Deronda. “I have happened to find an exquisite singer.” He turned toward Lady Pentreath. “She is living with some ladies who are friends of mine—the mother and sisters of a man who was my chum at Cambridge. She was on the stage at Vienna; but she wants to leave that life, and maintain herself by teaching.”

“There are swarms of those people, aren’t there?” said the old lady. “Are her lessons to be very cheap or very expensive? Those are the two baits I know of.”

“There is another bait for those who hear her,” said Deronda. “Her singing is something quite exceptional, I think. She has had such first-rate teaching—or rather first-rate instinct with her teaching—that you might imagine her singing all came by nature.”

“Why did she leave the stage, then?” said Lady Pentreath. “I’m too old to believe in first-rate people giving up first-rate chances.”

“Her voice was too weak. It is a delicious voice for a room. You who put up with my singing of Schubert would be enchanted with hers,” said Deronda, looking at Mrs. Raymond. “And I imagine she would not object to sing at private parties or concerts. Her voice is quite equal to that.”

“I am to have her in my drawing-room when we go up to town,” said Lady Mallinger. “You shall hear her then. I have not heard her myself yet; but I trust Daniel’s recommendation. I mean my girls to have lessons of her.”

“Is it a charitable affair?” said Lady Pentreath. “I can’t bear charitable music.”

Lady Mallinger, helpless in conversation and feeling the constraint of not telling Mirah’s story, smiled with embarrassment and glanced at Deronda.

“It is a charity to those who want to have a good model of feminine singing,” said Deronda. “I think everybody who has ears would benefit by a little improvement on the ordinary style.” And then, letting his attention turn like a hand searching for warmth, he looked at Gwendolen. “If you heard Miss Lapidoth—perhaps you would revoke your resolution to give up singing.”

“I should rather think my resolution would be confirmed,” said Gwendolen. “I don’t feel able to follow your advice of enjoying my own middlingness.”

“For my part,” said Deronda, “people who do anything finely always inspirit me to try. I don’t mean that they make me believe I can do it as well. But they make the thing, whatever it may be, seem worthy to be done. I can bear to think my own music not good for much, but the world would be more dismal if I thought music itself not good for much. Excellence encourages one about life generally; it shows the spiritual wealth of the world.”

“But then, if we can’t imitate it, it only makes our own life seem the tamer,” said Gwendolen, her tone resisting because the truth had already begun to press on her like a garment too tight.

“That depends on the point of view, I think,” said Deronda. “We should have a poor life of it if we were reduced for all our pleasure to our own performances. A little private imitation of what is good is a sort of private devotion to it, and most of us ought to practice art only in the light of private study—preparation to understand and enjoy what the few can do for us. I think Miss Lapidoth is one of the few.”

“She must be a very happy person, don’t you think?” said Gwendolen, with a touch of sarcasm, and a turn of her neck toward Mrs. Raymond.

“I don’t know,” answered the independent lady; “I must hear more of her before I say that.”

“It may have been a bitter disappointment to her that her voice failed her for the stage,” said Juliet Fenn, with gentle sympathy.

“I suppose she’s past her best, though,” said the deep voice of Lady Pentreath.

“On the contrary, she has not reached it,” said Deronda. “She is barely twenty.”

“And very pretty,” interposed Lady Mallinger, eager to help. “And she has very good manners. I’m sorry she’s a bigoted Jewess; I should not like it for anything else, but it doesn’t matter in singing.”

“Well, since her voice is too weak for her to scream much, I’ll tell Lady Clementina to set her on my nine granddaughters,” said Lady Pentreath. “And I hope she’ll convince eight of them that they have not voice enough to sing anywhere but at church. My notion is, that many of our girls nowadays want lessons not to sing.”

“I have had my lessons in that,” said Gwendolen, looking at Deronda. “You see Lady Pentreath is on my side.”

As she spoke, Sir Hugo entered with some of the other gentlemen, including Grandcourt. The sound of heavier footsteps and a low murmur of male voices thickened the air like a draught through a corridor. Sir Hugo, placing himself against the group at the tea-table, said with his easy good-humor,

“What imposition is Deronda putting on you, ladies—slipping in among you by himself?”

“Wanting to pass off an obscurity on us as better than any celebrity,” said Lady Pentreath, “a pretty singing Jewess who is to astonish these young people. You and I, who heard Catalani in her prime, are not so easily astonished.”

Sir Hugo listened smiling as his wife handed him a cup of tea. “Well, you know, a Liberal is bound to think that there have been singers since Catalani’s time.”

“Ah, you are younger than I am. I dare say you are one of the men who ran after Alcharisi. But she married off and left you all in the lurch.”

“Yes, yes; it’s rather too bad when these great singers marry themselves into silence before they have a crack in their voices. And the husband is a public robber. I remember Leroux saying, ‘A man might as well take down a fine peal of church bells and carry them off to the steppes,’” said Sir Hugo, setting down his cup and turning away.

Deronda, who had moved to make room and felt he was not in request, sat down a little apart. The tea-things made their small domestic concert—cup on saucer, spoon on cup—while talk broke into clusters and drifted. Presently Deronda became aware that in the dispersal Gwendolen had extricated herself from Mr. Vandernoodt’s attentions and walked to the piano, where she stood, apparently examining the music on the desk.

Will any one be surprised that Deronda concluded she wished him to join her? Perhaps she meant to soften what had been sharp in her resistance; he had noticed in her that first impulses often spoke in the wrong voice, and afterward she wished to take the words back as one tries to rescue an over-salted dish.

He went to her side. “Are you relenting about the music and looking for something to play or sing?”

“I am not looking for anything, but I am relenting,” said Gwendolen; and there was a submissiveness in her tone, as if she were laying down a weapon.

“May I know the reason?”

“I should like to hear Miss Lapidoth and have lessons from her, since you admire her so much—that is, of course, when we go to town. I mean lessons in rejoicing at her excellence and my own deficiency,” she said, turning on him a sweet, open smile—too sweet, as if sweetness were something she had learned to apply.

“I shall be really glad for you to see and hear her,” said Deronda, returning the smile in kind.

“Is she as perfect in every thing else as in her music?”

“I can’t vouch for that exactly. I have not seen enough of her. But I have seen nothing in her that I could wish to be different. She has had an unhappy life. Her troubles began in early childhood, and she has grown up among very painful surroundings. But I think you will say that no advantages could have given her more grace and truer refinement.”

“I wonder what sort of trouble hers were?”

“I have not any very precise knowledge. But I know that she was on the brink of drowning herself in despair.”

“And what hindered her?” Gwendolen’s question came quickly, and her eyes fixed on his, as if the answer were a draught she needed.

“Some ray or other came—which made her feel that she ought to live—that it was good to live,” he answered quietly. “She is full of piety, and seems capable of submitting to anything when it takes the form of duty.”

“Those people are not to be pitied,” said Gwendolen, impatience flashing like a knife drawn too suddenly. “I have no sympathy with women who are always doing right. I don’t believe in their great sufferings.” Her fingers moved quickly among the edges of the music, as if she could shred what she could not bear.

“It is true,” said Deronda, “that the consciousness of having done wrong is something deeper, more bitter. I suppose we faulty creatures can never feel so much for the irreproachable as for those who are bruised in the struggle with their own faults. It is a very ancient story, that of the lost sheep—but it comes up afresh every day.”

“That is a way of speaking—it is not acted upon, it is not real,” said Gwendolen, bitterness thickening her words. “You admire Miss Lapidoth because you think her blameless, perfect. And you know you would despise a woman who had done something you thought very wrong.”

“That would depend entirely upon her own view of what she had done,” said Deronda.

“You would be satisfied if she were very wretched, I suppose,” said Gwendolen, impetuously, as if trying to force him to pronounce a sentence.

“No, not satisfied—full of sorrow for her. It was not a mere way of speaking. I did not mean to say that the finer nature is not more adorable; I meant that those who would be comparatively uninteresting beforehand may become worthier of sympathy when they do something that awakens in them a keen remorse. Lives are enlarged in different ways. I dare say some would never get their eyes opened if it were not for a violent shock from the consequences of their own actions. And when they are suffering in that way one must care for them more than for the comfortably self-satisfied.”

Deronda forgot everything but his vision of what her experience had probably been; compassion urged him, and his eyes and voice betrayed as much interest as they could.

Gwendolen had slipped on to the music-stool and looked up at him with pain in her long eyes—like a wounded creature that has found, for one instant, someone who might lift the weight off its hurt.

“Are you persuading Mrs. Grandcourt to play to us, Dan?” said Sir Hugo, coming up and laying a hand on Deronda’s shoulder with a gentle, admonitory pinch—kindly, but a reminder.

“I cannot persuade myself,” said Gwendolen, rising at once.

Others followed Sir Hugo; the room filled in, voices crossed, chairs shifted, and the possibility of any confidence ended for that day under the cover of social sound—like a bird’s call drowned by a passing cart.

But the next was New Year’s Eve, and there was to be a grand dance, to which the chief tenants were invited, held in the picture-gallery above the cloister—one of those entertainments where numbers and general movement can, by their very abundance, create privacy.

While Gwendolen dressed, she longed—remembering Leubronn—to put on the old turquoise necklace for her sole ornament. The stones, with their cool sky-color, were a private language to her: a remembrance not translated into anyone else’s approval. But she dared not offend her husband by seeming shabby on an occasion when he would demand her utmost splendor. Determined to wear the memorial somehow, she wound it thrice round her wrist and made a bracelet of it, going to her room to put it on just before she entered the ball-room, as if to hide the act itself from observation.

It was always a beautiful scene, this dance on New Year’s Eve, kept up by family tradition as nearly in the old fashion as inexorable change would allow. Red carpet was laid down; hot-house plants and evergreens were arranged in bowers at the extremities and in every recess of the gallery, and their damp, living scent rose against the chill of stone—earthy, resinous, with a hint of bruised leaf. The old portraits stretched back through generations, even to the pre-portraying period, making a piquant line of spectators—faces that had watched other faces, other alliances, other seasons of hope and defeat, as if time itself were a long room where the same steps were tried again with different shoes.

Neighboring gentry, major and minor, were invited; and it was certainly an occasion when a prospective master and mistress of Abbott’s and King’s Topping might see their future glory in an agreeable light, as a picturesque provincial supremacy with a rent-roll personified by the most prosperous-looking tenants. Sir Hugo expected Grandcourt to feel flattered by being asked to the Abbey at a time which included this festival in honor of the family estate; but he also hoped that his own hale appearance might impress his successor with the probable length of time that would elapse before the succession came, and with the wisdom of preferring a good actual sum to a minor property that must be waited for.

All present, down to the least important farmer’s daughter, knew they were to see “young Grandcourt,” Sir Hugo’s nephew, presumptive heir and future baronet, now visiting the Abbey with his bride after an absence of many years; any coolness between uncle and nephew having, it was understood, given way to friendly warmth. There was a particular rustle in the room—a communal quickening—when such knowledge moved among them; the tenants’ voices, trained by open fields and barns to carry and blend, made a soft roar like wind in winter hedges. The fiddles tuned; the floorboards received testing taps; laughter rose and fell in waves, and above it all the high gallery seemed to hold the sound as a vaulted shell holds the sea.

The bride, opening the ball with Sir Hugo, was necessarily the cynosure of all eyes. Less than a year before, if some magic mirror could have shown Gwendolen her actual position, she would have imagined herself moving in it with a glow of triumphant pleasure, conscious that she held in her hands a life full of favorable chances which her cleverness and spirit would enable her to make the best of. Now she wondered that she could get so little joy out of the exaltation to which she had been suddenly lifted—away from the distasteful petty empire of her girlhood, with its irksome lack of distinction and superfluity of sisters. She would have been glad to be even unreasonably elated, to forget everything but the flattery of the moment; but she was like one courting sleep, in whom thoughts insist like willful tormentors.

And so, wondering at her own dullness, longing all the while for some excitement that would deaden the importunate aches, she passed through files of admiring beholders in the country-dance with which it was traditional to open the ball. Eyes followed her as she moved—women measuring her air, men noting her beauty, girls storing away the picture like a story they would tell in kitchens and parlors. She was generally regarded by her own sex as an enviable woman. It was remarked that she carried herself with a wonderful air, considering she had been nobody in particular and without a farthing to her fortune. If she had been a duke’s daughter, or one of the royal princesses, she could not have taken the honors of the evening more as a matter of course.

Poor Gwendolen! By-and-by it would become a skill, automatically practiced, to bear this last great gambling loss with an air of perfect self-possession.

Deronda’s wish to be in town again had grown roots in more than one soil: the quick, anxious care he could not shake for Mirah, and the restless curiosity that Mordecai had kindled with a few words and a look. Yet his steps were checked by the simplest of hindrances—days slipping away, arrangements never quite made—until Sir Hugo had already gone up before the household, eager to be in readiness for Parliament’s opening on the sixth of February. When Deronda at last took his old quarters in Park Lane, he went in expecting only what was reasonable: that Hans Meyrick had made free with rooms left in friendly trust.

He had made free, indeed—yet not as Deronda had imagined.

The sitting-room had been turned into a painter’s den that looked less like a bachelor’s lodging than the back-room of some small Italian cookshop where everything—tools, scraps, jars, odd treasures—had been pulled out and set near at hand because life was hungry and work must be fed. Two Rome chests had been unpacked to their last wrinkled paper; plaster casts leaned their pale mouths and noses against the wall; the lower halves of the windows were muffled with baize so that the daylight came subdued, like a voice quieted for a sick-room. The very air held a mingled odor—damp wool from the baize, the sweetish bite of oil paint and turpentine, and a faint dustiness of old paper, like spice left too long in a cupboard.

And in the midst of it Hans—blond as ever, but more wildly unfinished, his hair longer, his face more whimsically puckered, his high voice lifted higher by haste and excitement—stood presiding as if the whole clutter were a banquet he had laid for his own ambition.

“I knew you would like to see my casts and antiquities,” he cried, after the first grip of hands and affectionate questions. “So I didn’t scruple to unlade my chests here. But I’ve found two rooms at Chelsea, not many hundred yards from mother and the girls—soon as they’ve scraped the walls and put in some new lights, I shall be ready to hang out there. That’s all I’m waiting for. But you see I don’t wait to begin work: you can’t conceive what a great fellow I’m going to be. The seed of immortality has sprouted within me.”

“Only a fungoid growth, I dare say—a growing disease in the lungs,” said Deronda, with the familiar brotherly irony that had always been their safe bridge.

He had moved toward some drawings propped along the ledge of his bookcases—five quick-sketched heads, all different angles of one face. He took his stand at a distance convenient for judging, and said nothing.

Hans, too, was silent a moment. He picked up palette and pencil and began adding touches to the half-finished work on his easel with that absorbed briskness which made his fingers seem to have their own mind.

“What do you think of them?” he asked at last, without looking round.

“The full face looks too massive; otherwise the likenesses are good,” Deronda returned—more coolly than his habit with Hans.

“No, it is not too massive,” said Hans decisively. “I have noted that. There is always a little surprise when one passes from the profile to the full face. But I shall enlarge her scale for Berenice. I am making a Berenice series—look at the sketches along there—and now I think of it, you are just the model I want for the Agrippa.” Then, as if he felt he had blundered, he added quickly, “No, no—I forgot; you don’t like sitting for your portrait, confound you! However, I’ve picked up a capital Titus. There are to be five in the series. The first is Berenice clasping the knees of Gessius Florus and beseeching him to spare her people; I’ve got that on the easel. Then, this—where she is standing on the Xystus with Agrippa, entreating the people not to injure themselves by resistance.”

“Agrippa’s legs will never do,” said Deronda.

“The legs are good realistically,” Hans insisted, his face creasing with droll gravity. “Public men are often shaky about the legs—‘Their legs, the emblem of their various thought,’ as somebody says in the Rehearsal.”

“But these are as impossible as the legs of Raphael’s Alcibiades.”

“Then they are good ideally,” said Hans, triumphant. “Agrippa’s legs were possibly bad; I idealize that and make them impossibly bad. Art, my Eugenius, must intensify. But never mind the legs now: the third sketch is Berenice exulting in the prospects of being Empress of Rome, when the news has come that Vespasian is declared Emperor and her lover Titus his successor.”

“You must put a scroll in her mouth, else people will not understand that. You can’t tell that in a picture.”

“It will make them feel their ignorance then—an excellent æsthetic effect,” Hans said lightly. “The fourth is Titus sending Berenice away from Rome after she has shared his palace for ten years—both reluctant, both sad—*invitus invitam*, as Suetonius hath it. I’ve found a model for the Roman brute.”

“Shall you make Berenice look fifty? She must have been that.”

“No, no; a few mature touches to show the lapse of time. Dark-eyed beauty wears well—hers particularly. But now, here is the fifth: Berenice seated lonely on the ruins of Jerusalem. That is pure imagination. That is what ought to have been—perhaps was. Now, see how I tell a pathetic negative. Nobody knows what became of her—that is finely indicated by the series coming to a close. There is no sixth picture.”

He spoke as if he were tasting his own conceit and finding it delicious. He even threw his head back with a mock-sublime frown, searching Deronda’s face for admiration.

“I break off in the Homeric style,” he went on, gasping theatrically. “The story is chipped off, so to speak, and passes with a ragged edge into nothing—*le néant*; can anything be more sublime, especially in French? The vulgar would desire to see her corpse and burial—perhaps her will read and her linen distributed. But now come and look at this on the easel. I have made some way there.”

Deronda moved nearer. The figure on the easel—Berenice in supplication—had that poignant bend of the body which is like a prayer made visible: the arms gathered their pleading around another’s knees as if clasping could keep cruelty from happening. It was the kind of posture one remembers with one’s own muscles, as if one had once knelt so.

“That beseeching attitude is really good,” Deronda said, after a moment. “You have been very industrious in the Christmas holidays; for I suppose you have taken up the subject since you came to London.”

Neither had yet spoken Mirah’s name; and Deronda felt the omission like a plate left uncovered on a table.

“No,” said Hans, touching in a line with quick certainty. “I made up my mind to the subject before. I take that lucky chance for an augury that I am going to burst on the world as a great painter. I saw a splendid woman in the Trastevere—the grandest women there are half Jewesses—and she set me hunting for a fine situation of a Jewess at Rome. Like other men of vast learning, I ended by taking what lay on the surface. I’ll show you a sketch of the Trasteverina’s head when I can lay my hands on it.”

“I should think she would be a more suitable model for Berenice,” Deronda answered, choosing his words as if they were knives he did not wish to draw blood with.

“Not a bit of it. The model ought to be the most beautiful Jewess in the world, and I have found her.”

Deronda’s throat tightened. “Have you made yourself sure that she would like to figure in that character? I should think no woman would be more abhorrent to her. Does she quite know what you are doing?”

“Certainly. I got her to throw herself precisely into this attitude. Little mother sat for Gessius Florus, and Mirah clasped her knees.”

Hans stepped back to judge the effect of his last touches, as serene as if he had said, *We had tea*.

“I dare say she knows nothing about Berenice’s history,” Deronda said, indignation rising in him faster than he could justify it.

“Oh, yes, she does—ladies’ edition,” Hans replied, with airy certainty. “Berenice was a fervid patriot, but was beguiled by love and ambition into attaching herself to the arch-enemy of her people. Whence the Nemesis. Mirah takes it as a tragic parable, and cries to think what the penitent Berenice suffered as she wandered back to Jerusalem and sat desolate amidst desolation. That was her own phrase. I couldn’t find it in my heart to tell her I invented that part of the story.”

“Show me your Trasteverina,” Deronda said, mainly to stop himself saying something harsher.

“Shall you mind turning over that folio?” Hans answered. “My studies of heads are all there. But they are in confusion. You will perhaps find her next to a crop-eared undergraduate.”

Deronda began turning the sheets. Paper whispered against paper; charcoal smudged his fingertips with a dry, soot-like stain. Face after face—quickly caught, variously loved—rose from the pages like people met in a crowd and remembered for one striking feature.

“These seem to be all Cambridge heads and bits of country,” he said, after a minute. “Perhaps I had better begin at the other end.”

“No; you’ll find her about the middle. I emptied one folio into another.”

“Is this one of your undergraduates?” Deronda asked, pausing over an unusually agreeable face—an honest brow, a mouth that looked as if it would rather laugh than sneer.

“That! Oh, that’s a man named Gascoigne—Rex Gascoigne. An uncommonly good fellow; his upper lip, too, is good. I coached him before he got his scholarship. He ought to have taken honors last Easter. But he was ill, and has had to stay up another year. I must look him up. I want to know how he’s going on.”

Deronda found the Trasteverina: a bold head, coarse in the way of robust living—strong jaw, frank mouth, a gaze made to meet sun and street noises without flinching.

“Here she is, I suppose.”

“Ah,” said Hans, glancing and shrugging with contempt. “Too coarse. I was unregenerate then.”

Deronda closed the folio. He left the Trasteverina sketch lying outside, like something exiled.

For a moment he only stood there, his hand at his coat-collar, the words he wanted to say gathering and pressing at him. Outside, the street carried its winter London sounds—wheels, hoofbeats, a call—broken and hurried; within, Hans’s brush made a soft rasp, a private industrious sound like a knife sharpening against stone. Deronda felt, with sudden vividness, how much of human peace depends on what reaches the ear: a home can be made by gentle familiar sounds, and unmade by harsh ones. The city’s roar, even muffled, seemed an enemy to the delicate new life being coaxed into safety at Chelsea.

“I dare say my scruples are excessive, Meyrick,” Deronda said at last, “but I must ask you to oblige me by giving up this notion.”

Hans flung himself into a tragic pose as if struck. “What! my series—my immortal Berenice series? Think of what you are saying, man—destroying, as Milton says, not a life but an immortality. Wait before you answer, that I may deposit the implements of my art and be ready to uproot my hair.”

He laid down palette and pencil with ceremonious care, threw himself backward into a great chair, let his long hair fall over his face, lifted his fingers like talons beside his head, and stared up in comic terror at Deronda.

Deronda could not help smiling. “Paint as many Berenices as you like, but I wish you could feel with me—perhaps you will, on reflection—that you should choose another model.”

“Why?” Hans asked, springing up, suddenly serious.

“Because she may get into such a position that her face is likely to be recognized. Mrs. Meyrick and I are anxious for her that she should be known as an admirable singer. It is right—and she wishes it—that she should make herself independent. And she has excellent chances. One good introduction is secured already, and I am going to speak to Klesmer. Her face may come to be very well known, and—well, it is useless to attempt to explain, unless you feel as I do. I believe that if Mirah saw the circumstances clearly, she would strongly object to being exhibited in this way—to allowing herself to be used as a model for a heroine of this sort.”

Hans listened with thumbs hooked in his blouse belt. Surprise spread on his face and melted into amusement, until a laugh broke out; but when he saw Deronda’s grave offence, he checked himself.

“Excuse my laughing, Deronda,” he said. “You never gave me an advantage over you before. If it had been about anything but my own pictures, I should have swallowed every word because you said it. And so you actually believe that I should get my five pictures hung on the line in a conspicuous position, and carefully studied by the public? Zounds, man! cider-cup and conceit never gave me half such a beautiful dream. My pictures are likely to remain as private as the utmost hypersensitiveness could desire.”

He turned back to his easel as if painting could plaster over an awkward pause. Deronda stood still, recognizing his own mistake about publicity and yet feeling no ease; his repugnance had roots deeper than practical fear. He had expected Hans would be trouble; he had not expected the trouble would sting him with a private soreness.

Hans went on, brushing in color, talking as he worked.

“But even supposing I had a public rushing after my pictures as if they were a railway series including nurses, babies, and bonnet-boxes, I can’t see any justice in your objection. Every painter worth remembering has painted the face he admired most, as often as he could. It is a part of his soul that goes out into his pictures. He diffuses its influence in that way. He puts what he hates into a caricature. He puts what he adores into some sacred, heroic form. If a man could paint the woman he loves a thousand times as the *Stella Maris* to put courage into the sailors on board a thousand ships, so much the more honor to her. Isn’t that better than painting a piece of staring immodesty and calling it by a worshipful name?”

“Every objection can be answered if you take broad ground enough, Hans,” Deronda said, with a peremptory edge he did not quite mean. “No special question of conduct can be properly settled in that way. I might admit all your generalities, and yet be right in saying you ought not to publish Mirah’s face as a model for Berenice. But I give up the question of publicity. I was unreasonable there.”

He paused, then went on more slowly, as if feeling his way along a narrow path.

“Still, even as a private affair, there might be good reasons for your not indulging yourself too much in painting her from the point of view you mention. You must feel that her situation at present is a very delicate one; and until she is in more independence, she should be kept as carefully as a bit of Venetian glass, for fear of shaking her out of the safe place she is lodged in. Are you quite sure of your own discretion? Excuse me, Hans. My having found her binds me to watch over her. Do you understand me?”

“Perfectly,” said Hans, turning a good-humored smile on him. “You have the very justifiable opinion of me that I am likely to shatter all the glass in my way, and break my own skull into the bargain. Quite fair. Since I got into the scrape of being born, everything I have liked best has been a scrape either for myself or somebody else. Everything I have taken to heartily has somehow turned into a scrape. My painting is the last scrape; and I shall be all my life getting out of it. You think now I shall get into a scrape at home. No; I am regenerate. You think I must be over head and ears in love with Mirah. Quite right; so I am. But you think I shall scream and plunge and spoil everything. There you are mistaken—excusably, but transcendently mistaken. I have undergone baptism by immersion. Awe takes care of me. Ask the little mother.”

“You don’t reckon a hopeless love among your scrapes, then,” Deronda said; and his voice, without his willing it, sank deeper.

“I don’t mean to call mine hopeless,” Hans returned with provoking calm, laying down his tools and stepping back as if to contemplate his picture.

“My dear fellow, you are only preparing misery for yourself,” said Deronda, decisively. “She would not marry a Christian, even if she loved him. Have you heard her—of course you have—heard her speak of her people and her religion?”

“That can’t last,” said Hans, with a quick shake of the head. “She will see no Jew who is tolerable. Every male of that race is insupportable—‘insupportably advancing’—his nose.”

“She may rejoin her family. That is what she longs for. Her mother and brother are probably strict Jews.”

“I’ll turn proselyte, if she wishes it,” Hans said, with a shrug and laugh.

“Don’t talk nonsense, Hans. I thought you professed a serious love for her,” Deronda answered, heat rising in him.

“So I do. You think it desperate, but I don’t.”

“I know nothing; I can’t tell what has happened. We must be prepared for surprises. But I can hardly imagine a greater surprise to me than that there should have seemed to be anything in Mirah’s sentiments for you to found a romantic hope on.”

He felt the contempt in his own words and disliked himself for it; yet he could not recall them.

“I don’t found my romantic hopes on a woman’s sentiments,” Hans retorted, perversely growing merrier under gravity. “I go to science and philosophy for my romance. Nature designed Mirah to fall in love with me. The amalgamation of races demands it—the mitigation of human ugliness demands it—the affinity of contrasts assures it. I am the utmost contrast to Mirah—a bleached Christian, who can’t sing two notes in tune. Who has a chance against me?”

“I see now; it was all *persiflage*. You don’t mean a word you say, Meyrick,” Deronda said, laying his hand on Hans’s shoulder, relief softening him.

“Upon my honor I do mean it, though,” Hans answered, turning and setting his left hand on Deronda’s shoulder so their eyes were close and level, as if he spoke at a confessional. “I meant to tell you as soon as you came. My mother says you are Mirah’s guardian, and she thinks herself responsible to you for every breath that falls on Mirah in her house. Well, I love her—I worship her—I won’t despair—I mean to deserve her.”

“My dear fellow, you can’t do it,” Deronda said quickly.

“I should have said, I mean to try.”

“You can’t keep your resolve, Hans. You used to resolve what you would do for your mother and sisters.”

“You have a right to reproach me, old fellow,” Hans said gently.

“Perhaps I am ungenerous,” Deronda returned—without apology in his tone. “Yet it can’t be ungenerous to warn you that you are indulging mad, Quixotic expectations.”

“Who will be hurt but myself, then?” said Hans, pushing out his lip like a boy. “I am not going to say anything to her unless I felt sure of the answer. I dare not ask the oracles: I prefer a cheerful caliginosity, as Sir Thomas Browne might say. I would rather run my chance there and lose, than be sure of winning anywhere else. And I don’t mean to swallow the poison of despair, though you are disposed to thrust it on me. I am giving up wine, so let me get a little drunk on hope and vanity.”

“With all my heart, if it will do you any good,” Deronda said, loosening Hans’s shoulder with a little push, forcing kindness into his tone.

But inwardly he was silenced.

There is a peculiar irritation that comes sometimes to the man others trust as mentor: they speak to him as if he were set on a higher shelf, outside the reach of desire and temptation—like a book too clean to have been handled. Deronda had long been indulgent to Hans’s egotism; it had been part of the boy’s charm, and Deronda had been content to be the listener. But now he had felt, with a sting he must not show, Hans’s easy assumption that for any danger of rivalry where Mirah was concerned Deronda was as impossible as an angel. It is one thing to decide to put oneself out of the question; it is another to have others do the excluding for you, without a thought.

And Hans’s hope—however irrational—raised an image of Mirah altered by that hope, changed by the very fact of being hoped for; an image Deronda rejected and yet could not keep from returning. He had expected to have to guard Mirah from the world’s roughness, from accident, from the loud vulgar press of London life; he had not expected to have to guard his own inner quiet from the sound of another man’s longing.

When he went to Chelsea, Mrs. Meyrick’s evident release from anxiety about her beloved but incalculable son ought to have made him feel easy; and in truth the little house had a homely music that always steadied him—the friendly clink of cups, the hush of sewing, the soft footsteps on the stair, the voices that did not strive to outshout one another. It was as if that modest domestic soundscape were a sheltering dialect of kindness, spoken daily without thinking, and therefore all the more powerful.

Mirah, too, seemed livelier than he had yet seen her; and for the first time Deronda saw her laugh. It was when Hans became, as ever, Mrs. Meyrick’s first subject.

Mirah wanted to know whether Deronda had seen Mr. Hans pass through a sort of character-piece without changing his dress.

“He passes from one figure to another as if he were a bit of flame where you fancied the figures without seeing them,” Mirah said, eager in her description; “he is so wonderfully quick. I used never to like comic things on the stage—they were dwelt on too long; but all in one minute Mr. Hans makes himself a blind bard, and then Rienzi addressing the Romans, and then an opera-dancer, and then a desponding young gentleman—I am sorry for them all, and yet I laugh, all in one—”

And then she gave a little laugh that might have been the bright run of a voice in song—light, shy, and suddenly present, like warmth felt through a door that has opened a crack.

“We hardly thought that Mirah could laugh till Hans came,” said Mrs. Meyrick, and Deronda saw that she too was watching the picture—watching it as one watches a hearth flame one fears may go out.

“Hans seems in great force just now,” Deronda said, in a tone meant for congratulation. “I don’t wonder at his enlivening you.”

“He’s been just perfect ever since he came back,” said Mrs. Meyrick; and she kept to herself what her heart added—*if it will but last*.

“It is a great happiness,” Mirah said softly, “to see the son and brother come into this dear home. And I hear them all talk about what they did together when they were little. That seems like heaven, and to have a mother and brother who talk in that way. I have never had it.”

“Nor I,” said Deronda, involuntarily; and the words came out with a plainness that surprised him, as if some older, half-buried part of himself had spoken in its own tongue.

There are lives in which the hardest bondage is not the chain after triumph, but the chain before it—when a hand has almost closed on the narthex of fire and is struck numb by the cold apparatus of “how things are done.” A mind is thrust aside with its unmarketable ardor; a body, pinched by want and illness, becomes the very argument used against it. People pass, their boots beating a steady, indifferent rhythm on the pavement, and do not turn their heads. The visionary—so often mocked as if he were merely a superstition with eyes—may yet be one who thinks in images the way some cook thinks in scents: a future dish appears complete before the first knife touches board; the taste arrives on the tongue before the broth begins to tremble. Such persons are not necessarily less reasoning than the calculators who tally profit; they are often more porous, with a hundred gates for sound, sight, and remembered feeling to pour through. Their danger is not madness, but the loneliness of having too many entrances and too few welcoming rooms.

Mordecai’s figure had lodged itself in Deronda’s mind as a question he meant to return to when he could. Yet Deronda’s interest was still the suspense of a humane observer: the consumptive-looking Jew—fervid, studious, earning his crust by a quiet handicraft—had not, at first, fitted into any of Deronda’s accustomed anticipations of life.

But in Mordecai the meeting had fallen like a spark on hoarded tinder.

For many winters, as he had felt the ebb of physical strength and the widening, draughty solitude of a soul that could not make itself heard, his desire had narrowed and sharpened into a single hunger: to find some young ear into which he might pour his mind as a testament—some spirit kindred enough to receive what his brief, painful life had distilled, and carry it beyond the small room and the dying breath. The hopefulness that illness sometimes lends—an almost childish promise of recovery—had in him been diverted entirely away from his body. He did not imagine lungs newly full of air; he imagined a future in which his thought would walk abroad, no longer coughing in corners, no longer cheapened by the visible stamp of poverty.

At first the need had taken shape by contrast. Mordecai had learned, through rebuff and the coarse economy by which the world prices a man’s ideas according to the cut of his coat and the soundness of his chest, that his own very look—his hollow cheeks, his worn clothing, the labor that kept bread in his mouth—had become a kind of translation error. People read him in the dominant lexicon of the street: “odd Jew,” “poor creature,” “dangerous dreamer,” and the meaning he meant to utter was lost, as if spoken in a dialect that no one had patience to learn.
