So his imagination, urgent and practical in its very exaltation, constructed another man: a Jew too, but one who would not be discounted at sight—cultured, morally fervid, capable of sympathy with Mordecai’s inward fire, yet embodied in strength, beauty, refinement; one whose voice would flow without that occasional hoarse catch, one whose circumstances were free from sordid need; one who would glorify the possibilities of his people, not sit as Mordecai did with waning breath and the visible brand of hardship. He needed—he confessed it to himself with a candor that did not soften the necessity—an executive self, a blooming life that could take what was best in his own and give it room to act.

Because he was sensitive to physical types, he had sought them not only in faces but in pictures. In idle hours, when his fingers were not bent over watch-wheels and trinkets, he had wandered through the National Gallery as if searching a larder in time of famine—hoping, among all those canvases, to find one image that would feed his expectation: a face at once young, grand, and beautiful, where melancholy—if it lay there—did not droop like weakness but gathered itself for heroism. He would stand long, in his cloth cap rimmed with black fur, his dark eyes sunk deep as if the sockets were made too large by thought and sickness. The spectators, hearing only the gallery’s hush broken by the faint scuff of shoes and a distant cough, might take him for a Jew who got money out of pictures, or for one of those impoverished souls who linger where they cannot buy. Mordecai knew exactly what he looked like in other people’s language. That knowledge had become a second sound always in his ear, like an unwanted accompaniment.

His mind worked so constantly in images that his coherent trains of thought had the texture of significant dreams—those dreams that waking invention envies, because they break, without apology, across the boundary between what is known and what is longed for. For a long while the Being he needed appeared to him as a figure against a golden sky, distant, turning away, the outline darkened by light behind it. The gold was not arbitrary. Mordecai, despite his cramped life, was keenly alive to certain poetic aspects of London, and his strength, when it allowed him a luxury of air and distance, carried him to the bridges at sunrise or sunset. There the river’s broad, patient movement—sometimes slate-dark, sometimes with a skin of trembling light—opened his thoughts into wide spaces. The massive shapes of buildings, signs of world-commerce, stood dim and solemn, while barges and boats came on from the haze into sound and color: the dip of oars, the creak of timber, the low calls and answers on the water. It was like a great domestic routine of the city, repeated each day with variations of weather and mood; and in it Mordecai could almost believe that the soul, too, had its tides, its returns, its promise of being borne onward rather than shut in.

He needed, too, the soundscape of it—the river’s breathing against stone, the layered hush that even London could still offer when the modern din had not wholly seized the air. In that gentler acoustic, his nerves were less jangled; his thought could rise without being continually startled back into his body. The bridge was his refuge from the harsh percussion of wheels and shouted commerce, from the cheapened, advertised noise that made even art into a barked commodity.

Gradually, in the inevitable progress of imagination toward fuller detail, the figure ceased to turn its back. It advanced; a face became discernible. Youth, beauty, refinement, Jewish birth, noble gravity—these words became, not a list, but color and contour, gathered from faces he had known among the Jews of Holland and Bohemia, and from the paintings that revived those memories. Reverently, it was akin to the young person’s picturing of a future beloved; but Mordecai’s longing—strained by imminent dissolution—was fiercer, not for possession, but for transmission. The visionary form became a companion and auditor, holding its place not only in waking reverie but in those lighter sleeps where the heart seems to keep watch. The trivial story of yesterday would be charged, in those half-dreams, with the impassioned purpose of years.

Lately, the urgency of irremediable time—measured by the gradual choking of life—had turned trust into an agitated watch. Would the bell toll before his mind had found a bearer? Was the sentence already being written? The deliverer’s footstep must be near—the deliverer who would rescue Mordecai’s travail from oblivion and give it an abiding place in the best inheritance of his people.

Many would have called it an insane exaggeration of his own value. Why not say, nobly, “If not I, then another”? But the fuller nature desires not only to look on; it hungers to bless and act. It cannot be content that the heat in it should die unused, like coals quenched in ash. Mordecai could not surrender the moment’s charge without feeling he had betrayed it.

Yet, with that mingling of inconsequence that belongs to us all—and sometimes saves us from the consequences of our own errors—his confidence in the friend to come did not make him passive. He tried, humbly and pathetically, whatever channels were at hand.

It was now two years since he had lived under Ezra Cohen’s roof. There he was regarded with good-will in a composite, half-comic, half-reverent way: workman, dominie, vessel of charity, inspired idiot, man of piety, and—if anyone pressed inquiry—dangerous heretic. Little Jacob, meanwhile, had advanced into knickerbockers and into that quick apprehension which had already shown itself in all matters of hardware and exchange. He had advanced also in attachment to Mordecai, regarding him as an inferior—yet liking him none the worse for that—and taking his services as he might have taken the obedient cleverness of some enslaved spirit.

Mordecai, who had given Jacob his first lessons, found his habitual tenderness easily turning into a teacher’s fatherhood. He knew perfectly the spiritual distance between the parents and himself; he would never have tried to translate his peculiar world into their hearing, aware how the dominant household lexicon would flatten it into nonsense or danger. But the boy moved him with that idealizing affection which sees, in a child, not merely the individual creature with pockets full of treasures, but childhood itself—its glory, its unspent future.

So he began—at first without premeditation, later with conscious purpose—to pour something of himself into Jacob’s ear. No excellent man of business would have heard it without thinking it wild; but none overheard, when Jacob came up to Mordecai’s small upper room on a day with little work, or at an hour when the work was ended. There, after a brief lesson in English reading or numeration, the boy might be coaxed to stay: standing at his teacher’s knees, or jumping astride them, often to the patient fatigue of the wasted limbs. The inducement might be the mending of a toy—Mordecai’s practiced finger-tips were deft in these small salvations—or some little mechanical device that made Jacob’s eyes brighten with greed for trick and power.

With the boy thus tethered, Mordecai would begin to repeat a Hebrew poem of his own, telling Jacob to say the words after him.

“The boy will get them engraved within him,” Mordecai would think. “It is a way of printing.”

Jacob had the lively delight of imitating unintelligible sounds—rolling them in his mouth as he might roll a sweet, savoring the mere physical play. If no opposing diversion occurred, he would keep at it as long as Mordecai’s breath held out. Mordecai, for his part, threw into each repetition the fervor of a sacred occasion, as if the syllables themselves were seed—hard little grains that must be set into the child’s mind, to sprout after many days.

Jacob’s distractions were those of a boy who lives by touch and mischief. He would reach into his pockets, survey their contents like a small merchant; he would draw down the skin of his cheeks to make his eyes look dreadful and roll his head to complete the effect; he would alternately handle his own nose and Mordecai’s as if testing the relation of their masses. Under all this, Mordecai would not pause. He was satisfied if the young organs of speech would submit themselves at all.

More commonly, a sudden impulse would send Jacob leaping away into some antic, and instead of following the recitation he would return on the words already most ready to his tongue, gabbling them with a see-saw motion suited to his limbs—making a verse on which Mordecai had spent his scant heart’s blood into mere accompaniment to play. Yet Mordecai waited with the patience of one who believes in slow fermentations. “My words may rule him some day,” he would say inwardly. “Their meaning may flash out on him. It is so with a nation—after many days.”

Meanwhile, Jacob’s sense of power increased and his time was enlivened by this store of magical articulation. He made the baby crow with it; he drove the large cat into a dark corner; he promised himself he would frighten any incidental Christian of his own years. One week he had seen a street mountebank, and his muscular imitativeness was carried off into that new channel, to Mordecai’s secret vexation.

It was on a day like that, when Mordecai had arrived at a fresh passage—because new combinations of sound generally held Jacob a few minutes longer—that his voice, usually a strong high baritone, let out its Hebrew with more than usual excitement. The hoarseness in it was like haze among illuminations; now and then there was an incipient gasp, as if the words had to be pushed past a narrowing gate. The verses he intoned held a meaning something like this:

“Away from me the garment of forgetfulness,
Withering the heart;
The oil and wine from presses of the Goyim,
Poisoned with scorn.
Solitude is on the sides of Mount Nebo,
In its heart a tomb:
There the buried ark and golden cherubim
Make hidden light:
There the solemn gaze unchanged,
The wings are spread unbroken:
Shut beneath in silent awful speech
The Law lies graven.
Solitude and darkness are my covering,
And my heart a tomb;
Smite and shatter it, O Gabriel!
Shatter it as the clay of the founder
Around the golden image.”

In the absorbed invocation, Mordecai did not notice that Jacob had stopped echoing him. He had started away; and when Mordecai paused, he saw—like a sudden glare—that the boy had thrown himself on his hands with his feet in the air, mountebank fashion, and was picking up with his lips a bright farthing, a favorite among his pocket treasures.

Mordecai had endured many tricks, but this jarred him horribly at that moment, as if a Satanic grin had been set upon his prayer. Something within him—strained, starved, thwarted—broke its composure.

“Child! child!” he cried out, in a tone so strange that Jacob tumbled to his feet in alarm.

Then Mordecai sank backward with a shudder, closing his eyes.

“What?” Jacob said quickly. Not getting an answer, he pressed Mordecai’s knees with a shaking movement, trying to rouse him—as if to insist the familiar, indulgent companion must return.

Mordecai opened his eyes with a fierce expression, leaned forward, grasped the boy’s shoulders, and whispered rapidly, hoarsely, words that seemed to Jacob like thunder spoken into his face:

“A curse is on your generation, child. They will open the mountain and drag forth the golden wings and coin them into money, and the solemn faces they will break up into earrings for wanton women! And they shall get themselves a new name, but the angel of ignominy, with the fiery brand, shall know them, and their heart shall be the tomb of dead desires that turn their life to rottenness.”

The sunken eyes so close, the thin fingers gripping, the hoarse accents freighted with obscure threat—Jacob felt as if the room itself had become unsafe, as if the house were tumbling in and dinner would never come again. He stood trembling; then, when the terrible speech ended and the pinch relaxed, the shock melted into tears. He lifted his small patriarchal countenance and wept aloud.

The sound of that child’s grief brought Mordecai back as quickly as if a hand had soothed his brow. He could not speak again at once, but with a maternal tenderness he drew the curly head to him and pressed it against his breast.

Jacob, sensing danger nearly over, howled more freely; then, in that common transition from impulse into art, began to imitate his own sobbing and improve upon it, as if practicing a performance. The next day he tried to terrify Adelaide Rebekah in the same manner, and succeeded very well.

But Mordecai suffered long from the check within himself. Sane as well as excitable, he judged his own aberration with severity and felt discredited in his own eyes, as if he had used sacred speech like a blunt instrument. He could not bear the sense of having forced his meaning into a child who did not yet possess the language to receive it—of having made his heart’s dialect into mere noise.

All the more his mind strained toward discerning that friend to come, with whom there would be calm certainty of fellowship and understanding—someone who would not turn his words into mountebank tricks, someone whose inner ear could hear the intended music and not only the syllables.

It was then, in his usual midday guardianship of the old book-shop, that Deronda’s appearance struck him like the sudden accord one has waited years to hear. Mordecai’s glance took on an eager interest because the new-comer’s face and frame seemed to realize the long-conceived type. But when Deronda disclaimed Jewish birth, it was as if the vision had been thrust back with double severity: not only disappointment, but the shake to faith itself.

Yet, when Mordecai found Deronda seated at the Cohens’ table, that disclaimer seemed, for a moment, nullified. The impression returned with added force, as if guaranteed by this second meeting under circumstances more peculiar than the first; and when Mordecai asked if Deronda knew Hebrew, he was so possessed by the inrush of belief that he forgot every other condition he had once insisted on.

Deronda’s “No” struck him down again. The frustration was sharper than before.

After he had turned his back on the visitor that Sabbath evening, Mordecai went through days of deep discouragement—like men on a doomed ship who strain their eyes, behold a sail with rejoicing, then watch it never advance and say at last, “Our sick eyes made it.”

But the figure he had long contemplated was not a casual fancy. It was the emotional sequence of his firmest convictions; it had been wrought from the imagery of his most passionate life. Inevitably it reappeared—more specific, more self-asserting. Deronda’s resemblance to the preconceived type was like that of a finely individual portrait to a generalized memory: it corrects even while it delights. And now Deronda’s face met Mordecai’s inward gaze as if it had always belonged there, bringing with it, in imagination, some of the influence that belongs to breathing flesh.

Little by little, discouragement hardened into obstinacy. The ever-recurrent vision took the force of an outward call, commanding him to disregard counter-evidence and keep expectation awake. It was Deronda now who appeared in those night-watches when one thought clutches the mind; Deronda, never with his back turned, in moments of soothed reverie or soothed dozing—painted on the golden sky that was Mordecai’s doubly blessed symbol of advancing day and approaching rest.

Mordecai knew the nameless stranger would come to redeem his ring; and in spite of contrary chances, his wish to see him again grew into a belief that he would see him.

In the January weeks, he felt an increasing agitation—subdued, hidden, like the tremor that keeps nervous people from steady work on the eve of an anticipated change. He could not go on printing Hebrew on little Jacob’s mind, nor keep up attendance at a weekly club which had been another forlorn attempt at utterance. Something else was coming.

The one thing he longed for was to get as far as the river, which he could do but seldom and with difficulty. He yearned, with a poet’s yearning, for the wide sky, the far-reaching vista of bridges, the tender fluctuating lights on the water that seemed to breathe—shiver and mourn, then be comforted and rejoice—while the living city’s sounds rose and fell around it, and the old, truer music of tide and wind struggled to be heard beneath the coarse modern roar.

Two days after Daniel Deronda had sat in this same small Chelsea house and helped decide the name Mirah should carry into the world, the consequence that mattered most to the Meyricks arrived not as a thought but as a sound.

It was near four o’clock when wheels drew up outside—hansom wheels, quick and light, their iron rims brushing the cobbles with a brief, crisp hiss that died under the larger hush of the street. Then came a knock, not the friendly rap of a neighbor but a measured, authority-laden summons, followed by a ring that trembled a moment in the bell-wire like a bright note held too long. In a neighborhood where the most habitual music was the muffin-man’s cry and the clink of milk-pails, that ring enlarged the house itself—made the little front room feel, for an instant, as if it stood inside some vast social instrument waiting to be played.

All the girls were at home. The two rooms had been thrown into one by pushing back the door and shifting chairs, so that Kate could spread out her drawing things and the long embroidery might lie like a pale river across the space. It was their daily pageant: Mrs. Meyrick bending near one corner, needle dipping and rising with practiced economy; Mab in the middle, quick hands bright as sparrows; Amy at the far end, steadying the work so it would not drag. The satin cushions were gone—no frivolous softness today—this embroidery was their chief dish, their sustaining course, taken up whenever any clever fingers were free.

Mirah, who could hem and mend only with the makeshift neatness of a bird stitching leaves together, had been placed on a camp-stool and given the reader’s office—her voice the warm kettle-singing that kept their labor companionable. She also served Kate as a model for a title-page vignette: a fair public, as Kate had teased, absorbed in the successive volumes that came by way of the family tea-table. Mirah was reading Lamb—“The Praise of Chimney-Sweeps”—with a charming distinctness, and their smiles rose and fell with his “innocent blackness,” when the knock and ring lifted every head as one, like a sudden change in wind over a field.

“Dear me,” said Mrs. Meyrick, pausing with her needle in the air. “Can it be Lady Mallinger? Is there a grand carriage, Amy?”

“No—only a hansom cab,” Amy answered, peering. “It must be a gentleman.”

“The Prime Minister, I should think,” Kate said, dryly, charcoal poised like a weapon. “Hans says the greatest man in London may get into a hansom cab.”

“Oh, oh, oh!” Mab cried. “Suppose it should be Lord Russell!”

The old maid-servant came in with a card and that distracted air which always accompanied the appearance of rank; she even left the parlor-door open, and in the gap there was seen bowing toward Mrs. Meyrick a figure quite unlike any Premier: tall and physically imposing even in kid and kerseymere, massive of face, flamboyant of hair, gold spectacles catching what little light the afternoon offered and throwing it back as if he were already on a stage.

Mrs. Meyrick’s eyes ran to the card: Julius Klesmer.

If embarrassment could have made the little mother awkward, she would have been saved by the speed of her perceptions. Her heart gave a practical leap of satisfaction. He had come here, into their smallness, instead of requiring Mirah to climb into his largeness. That, to her, was the sign of active interest, of kindness with power behind it.

But as Klesmer entered, the rooms seemed to shrink into closets. The cottage piano, which had so often been a hearth of sound, looked to Mab suddenly like a toy set up for dolls. Their whole domestic arrangement—the embroidery, the scattered drawing materials, the Holbein faces pinned on the walls—had the minuteness and privacy of a mouse-establishment beneath palace staircases. Klesmer’s very way of glancing round him suggested multitudinous audiences, vast areas, orchestras warming up beyond the door. It was as if, with him, the air carried the remembered rustle of concert-halls: not the wholesome little ecology of their street—the distant hawker, the sparrows, the occasional laughter of children—but that other louder human weather, where applause comes down like rain and vanity may sprout like weeds.

And yet, in the same glance that enlarged the world, there was a keen, thoroughly kind sensibility taking in their details. He looked at the embroidery as one might look at a dish prepared with care in a small kitchen: not grand, perhaps, but honest and sustaining. He had known a home no larger on the outskirts of Bohemia; he had lived among the romances of small incomes where art and hunger share the same plate. He addressed Mrs. Meyrick with deference.

“I hope I have not taken too great a freedom. Being in the neighborhood, I ventured to save time by calling. Our friend, Mr. Deronda, mentioned to me an understanding that I was to have the honor of becoming acquainted with a young lady here—Miss Lapidoth.”

Though he had discerned Mirah the instant he crossed the threshold, his politeness made him look bowingly at the three sisters as if uncertain which was the young lady in question.

“Those are my daughters: this is Miss Lapidoth,” Mrs. Meyrick said, turning her hand toward Mirah.

“Ah,” Klesmer answered, with a tone of gratified expectation, and he turned on Mirah a radiant smile and deep bow.

Mirah was not startled. There was calm pleasure in her face. She liked the look of him, feeling sure he would scold her as great musicians scold—severely, and for her good. His presence had its own acoustics: even his breathing seemed measured, as if his lungs kept time.

“You will not object to beginning our acquaintance by singing to me,” he said, stripping away ceremony as one peels fruit to reach what matters. “I shall be very glad,” Mirah replied, moving to the piano. “It is good of you to be willing to listen to me. Shall I accompany myself?”

“By all means,” Klesmer said, seating himself where, at Mrs. Meyrick’s invitation, he could see her clearly.

The little mother would not confess it as a weakness, but she said inwardly, with the quick practical instinct of women who have managed households on narrow means: He will like her singing better if he sees her.

All the feminine hearts except Mirah’s beat fast with anxiety. Klesmer sat with a listening frown that made him seem terrific; his spectacles flashed when he shifted his head, and the girls dared only furtive looks, as if the very act of watching might provoke condemnation. If he spoke severely, it would bruise them all.

But Mirah chose her song and began as if she had entered a familiar kitchen and set her hands to a task she must do well: not for show, but because it was necessary. Her voice rose in recitative—Leopardi’s Ode to Italy set to music—words like stone and fire: “O patria mia, vedo le mura e gli archi…” Her tone had the clean edge of something honed, but not metallic; it carried warmth as bread carries warmth from an oven. Then came the mournful melody—“Ma la gloria—non vedo”—a rhythmic plaint, as if grief itself were being kneaded into shape, pressed down and lifted, pressed down again, until it could be borne.

And then, from that sorrow, a devout triumph: an Andante where the subdued adoration seemed to move like a careful hand stirring a pot so it would not scorch—“Beatissimi voi…”—and after it the joyous outburst of an exultant Allegro, “Oh viva, oh viva,” her voice opening like a window flung wide on a clear day, letting light and air rush in.

When she ended, Klesmer held silence a moment, as if tasting what lingered.

“That is old Leo’s music,” he said at last.

“Yes. He was my last master—at Vienna: so fierce and so good,” Mirah answered, with a melancholy smile. “He prophesied that my voice would not do for the stage. And he was right.”

“Con-tinue, if you please,” Klesmer said, putting out his lips and shaking his long fingers; and while he made smothered sounds—words bitten in two and swallowed—none of the listeners could understand. The three girls detested him unanimously for not saying one word of praise. Mrs. Meyrick felt a little alarmed. Mirah, intent on doing what he desired, went on without pause, thinking now he would want German, and she sang Prince Radzivill’s settings for Gretchen in Faust, one after another, not daring to ask a question with her eyes even.

When she finished, Klesmer rose. He paced to the extremity of the small space as if it were a length of stage marked for him; then he walked back to the piano. Mirah had risen and stood looking toward him with her hands crossed before her, meekly awaiting judgment.

Suddenly his brow unknit. His eyes beamed. He stretched out his hand and said abruptly, as if the sentence had been waiting behind his teeth and could no longer be held in: “Let us shake hands: you are a musician.”

Mab felt herself beginning to cry. In the same breath, all three girls held Klesmer adorable. Mrs. Meyrick drew a long, relieved breath, as if the house itself had been granted a better air.

But the frown returned as quickly as if it belonged to his craft. He stretched out his hand again, back uppermost, touching Mirah’s with the finger-tip in a different meaning, and with protruded lip he said, “Not for great tasks. No high roofs. We are no skylarks. We must be modest.”

Mab’s adoration cooled at once. As if Mirah had shown the least conceit.

Mirah stayed silent, understanding that more was coming—something specific. And presently Klesmer went on, measured and practical.

“I would not advise—I would not further your singing in any larger space than a private drawing-room. But you will do there. And here in London that is one of the best careers open. Lessons will follow. Will you come and sing at a private concert at my house on Wednesday?”

“Oh, I shall be grateful,” Mirah said, and her hands came together as if in prayer. “I would rather get my bread in that way than by anything more public. I will try to improve. What should I work at most?”

Klesmer made preliminary answers in noises that were hardly words—his fingers shaking as if he were seasoning a dish by instinct before he gave the recipe aloud—then said clearly, “I shall introduce you to Astorga: he is the foster-father of good singing and will give you advice.”

Then he addressed Mrs. Meyrick. “Mrs. Klesmer will call before Wednesday, with your permission.”

“We shall feel that to be a great kindness,” Mrs. Meyrick said.

“You will sing to her,” Klesmer added, turning again to Mirah. “She is a thorough musician, and has a soul with more ears to it than you will often get in a musician. Your singing will satisfy her: ‘Vor den Wissenden sich stellen;’ you know the rest?”

“Sicher ist’s in allen Fällen,” Mirah replied promptly.

“Schön!” Klesmer said, and put out his hand again in farewell.

He had chosen the most delicate way of praising Mirah, and the Meyrick girls now gave him their entire esteem. But Mab’s amazement was renewed when Klesmer suddenly fixed his eyes on her and said decisively, “That young lady is musical, I see!”

Mab became nothing but a blush and a scorching sense of being exposed.

“Yes,” Mirah said for her, quick as kindness. “And she has a touch.”

“Oh, please, Mirah—a scramble, not a touch,” Mab said, in anguish, with the horrible fear that this dreadful divining personage—Satan in gray trousers—might order her to the piano on the spot. Her heart went soft and hot like wax.

But then her amazement turned to joy when Klesmer said benignantly, turning to Mrs. Meyrick, “Will she like to accompany Miss Lapidoth and hear the music on Wednesday?”

“There could hardly be a greater pleasure for her,” Mrs. Meyrick answered. “She will be most glad and grateful.”

Klesmer bowed round to the three sisters more grandly than they had ever been bowed to. It made an amusing picture: the little room with so much of its diagonal taken up by that magnificent bend, the small feminine figures like images a little less than life-size, and the grave Holbein faces on the walls looking hard at this stranger whose face seemed a dignified contemporary of their own, while his garments seemed, to Kate’s fastidious eye, a lamentable mockery of the human form.

Mrs. Meyrick could not help going out with him and closing the door behind her. The parlor’s hum—thread drawn through cloth, breath, the faint settling creak of the floor—was shut away. In the passage, Klesmer understood her at once, and with a frowning nod said, “She will do: if she doesn’t attempt too much and her voice holds out, she can make an income. I know that is the great point: Deronda told me. You are taking care of her. She looks like a good girl.”

“She is an angel,” Mrs. Meyrick said, warmth breaking through her prudence.

“No,” Klesmer answered, with a playful nod. “She is a pretty Jewess: the angels must not get the credit of her. But I think she has found a guardian angel,” he added, and bowed himself out.

Inside, the four young creatures stared at one another mutely until the front door banged and Mrs. Meyrick re-entered. Then came the explosion—sound returning like water released.

Mab clapped her hands and danced everywhere inconveniently; Mrs. Meyrick kissed Mirah and blessed her; Amy said, with the emphasis of one thinking already of pins and pennies, “We can never get her a new dress before Wednesday!” and Kate exclaimed, “Thank heaven my table is not knocked over!”

Mirah had reseated herself on the music-stool without speaking. Tears rolled down her cheeks as she looked at her friends, as if happiness had overflowed and found no other outlet.

“Now, now, Mab!” Mrs. Meyrick said. “Come and sit down reasonably and let us talk.”

“Yes, let us talk,” Mab cried, returning to her low seat and hugging her knees. “I am beginning to feel large again. Hans said he was coming this afternoon. I wish he had been here—only there would have been no room for him. Mirah, what are you looking sad for?”

“I am too happy,” Mirah said. “I feel so full of gratitude to you all; and he was so very kind.”

“Yes, at last,” Mab said sharply. “But he might have said something encouraging sooner. I thought him dreadfully ugly when he sat frowning and only said, ‘Con-tinue.’ I hated him all the long way from the top of his hair to the toe of his polished boot.”

“Nonsense, Mab; he has a splendid profile,” Kate said.

“Now, but not then. I cannot bear people to keep their minds bottled up for the sake of letting them off with a pop. They seem to grudge making you happy unless they can make you miserable beforehand. However, I forgive him everything,” Mab added with a magnanimous lift of chin, “but he has invited me. I wonder why he fixed on me as the musical one? Was it because I have a bulging forehead, ma, and peep from under it like a newt from under a stone?”

“It was your way of listening to the singing, child,” Mrs. Meyrick said. “He has magic spectacles and sees everything through them, depend upon it. But what was that German quotation you were so ready with, Mirah—you learned puss?”

“Oh, that was not learning,” Mirah said, her tearful face breaking into an amused smile. “I said it so many times for a lesson. It means that it is safer to do anything—singing or anything else—before those who know and understand all about it.”

“That was why you were not one bit frightened, I suppose,” Amy said. “But now, what we have to talk about is a dress for you on Wednesday.”

“I don’t want anything better than this black merino,” Mirah said, rising to show it—simple, serviceable, the cloth already acquainted with their little household smells: tea-steam, warmed wool, the faint iron scent of needles. “Some white gloves and some new bottines.” She put out her little foot, still in the famous felt slipper that had padded so quietly through their days.

“There comes Hans,” Mrs. Meyrick said, as footsteps sounded—boyish, quick, with the particular thud and scrape of someone who brought the outside world in on his boots. “Stand still, and let us hear what he says about the dress. Artists are the best people to consult about such things.”

“You don’t consult me, ma,” Kate said, lifting an eyebrow in playful complaint. “I notice mothers are like the people I deal with—the girls’ doings are always priced low.”

“My dear child,” Mrs. Meyrick replied, “the boys are such a trouble—we could never put up with them, if we didn’t make believe they were worth more,” just as her son entered.

Hans came in with his habitual air of being too large for the room in a different way from Klesmer—youthful largeness, as if he carried future canvases inside him. Mrs. Meyrick wasted no time.

“Hans, we want your opinion about Mirah’s dress. A great event has happened. Klesmer has been here, and she is going to sing at his house on Wednesday among grand people. She thinks this dress will do.”

“Let me see,” Hans said.

Mirah, in her childlike docility, turned toward him to be looked at; and he, stepping back, knelt with one knee on a hassock to survey her as if she were already a figure arranged for a picture.

“This would be thought a very good stage-dress for me,” she said pleadingly, “in a part where I was to come on as a poor Jewess and sing to fashionable Christians.”

“It would be effective,” Hans admitted, with a considering air; “it would stand out well among the fashionable chiffons.”

“But you ought not to claim all the poverty on your side, Mirah,” Amy put in. “There are plenty of poor Christians and dreadfully rich Jews and fashionable Jewesses.”

“I didn’t mean any harm,” Mirah said quickly. “Only I have been used to thinking about my dress for parts in plays. And I almost always had a part with a plain dress.”

“That makes me think it questionable,” Hans said, and in that moment he became as fastidious and conventional as he had thought Deronda had been about the Berenice pictures. “It looks a little too theatrical. We must not make you a rôle of the poor Jewess—or of being a Jewess at all.”

Underneath his words lay something he did not quite know how to confess: a desire to neutralize the Jewess in private life, to stop that name from being a label others might use like a blunt instrument.

But Mirah’s answer came steady, like a truth she had carried across seas and hungers.

“But it is what I am really. I am not pretending anything. I shall never be anything else,” she said. “I always feel myself a Jewess.”

“But we can’t feel that about you,” Hans said, and there was a devout look in him, as if he were trying to lift her out of any harshness the world might throw at her. “What does it signify whether a perfect woman is a Jewess or not?”

“That is your kind way of praising me; I never was praised so before,” Mirah said, smiling—smiling in a way that was rather maddening to Hans because it made his own generosity feel cosmopolitan and incomplete, as if it spoke a language that missed certain native sounds.

“People don’t think of me as a British Christian,” he said, his face creasing merrily. “They think of me as an imperfectly handsome young man and an unpromising painter.”

“But you are wandering from the dress,” Amy insisted. “If that will not do, how are we to get another before Wednesday? and to-morrow Sunday?”

“Indeed this will do,” Mirah said entreatingly; and then, looking at Hans with that misplaced trust which always made his conscience wince, she added, “It is all real, you know—even if it seemed theatrical. Poor Berenice sitting on the ruins—any one might say that was theatrical, but I know that this is just what she would do.”

Hans flinched as if she had put her finger on a bruise.

“I am a scoundrel,” he burst out. “That is my invention. Nobody knows that she did that. Shall you forgive me for not saying so before?”

“Oh, yes,” Mirah said, after a small pause of surprise. “You knew it was what she would be sure to do—a Jewess who had not been faithful—who had done what she did and was penitent. She could have no joy but to afflict herself; and where else would she go? I think it is very beautiful that you should enter so into what a Jewess would feel.”

“The Jewesses of that time sat on ruins,” Hans said, starting up with the sense of being checkmated by her earnestness. “That makes them convenient for pictures.”

“But the dress—the dress,” Amy repeated, not to be drawn into moral histories when there was cloth to be bought. “Is it settled?”

“Yes; is it not?” Mirah asked, looking doubtfully at Mrs. Meyrick.

Mrs. Meyrick looked to her son. “What do you think, Hans?”

“That dress will not do,” Hans said decisively. “She is not going to sit on ruins. You must jump into a cab with her, little mother, and go to Regent Street. It’s plenty of time to get anything you like—a black silk dress such as ladies wear. She must not be taken for an object of charity. She has talents to make people indebted to her.”

“I think it is what Mr. Deronda would like—for her to have a handsome dress,” Mrs. Meyrick said, deliberating. In her mind was Daniel’s quiet care for Mirah’s dignity—care that never rang loud, never made a spectacle of itself.

“Of course it is,” Hans said, with some sharpness. “You may take my word for what a gentleman would feel.”

“I wish to do what Mr. Deronda would like me to do,” Mirah said gravely; and Hans, turning on his heel as if his own feelings needed to be masked by activity, went to Kate’s table and took up one of her drawings, pretending sudden interest.

“Shouldn’t you like to make a study of Klesmer’s head, Hans?” Kate said. “I suppose you have often seen him?”

“Seen him!” Hans exclaimed, and immediately threw back his head and mane, seated himself at the piano, and looked round as if he were surveying an amphitheatre. He held his fingers down perpendicularly toward the keys, his face a swift caricature of Klesmer’s grandeur. The room filled with their brief laughter—the kind of laughter that is a balm after strain, restoring the small domestic soundscape to its usual cheerful measures.

But in another instant he wheeled round on the stool, looked at Mirah, and said half timidly, “Perhaps you don’t like this mimicry; you must always stop my nonsense when you don’t like it.”

Mirah had been smiling at the quickly made image; she smiled still, but now with something gentler and deeper than amusement.

“Thank you. But you have never done anything I did not like,” she said. “I hardly think he could, belonging to you,” she added, looking at Mrs. Meyrick.

Hans took that as food for hope. How could the rose help it when, one after another, several bees came and mistook its sweetness for a message meant only for them?

Deronda came out of the narrow Chelsea house with heat under his skin, as if his blood had been turned with a spoon. The air outside—raw with river damp—took him by the face; yet even that coolness only made him want a harder answer from his body, something honest and muscular to beat the vapor of ill-temper out of him. He was bound toward the City, but the sight of the stairs and the waiting boats decided him. A cab would be a box of jangling idleness. He called for a wherry, dropped in, and took an oar, glad of the first pull that set his shoulders to work and made the world answer him with resistance.

His errand was simple in words and tangled in feeling: Ram’s little book-shop, where he had missed Mordecai yesterday at the midday watch, and where the man was said to return between five and six. Deronda wanted more than directions about the ring; he wanted, for Mirah’s sake, to keep the talk from ending again with that sudden failing of interest—like a drawbridge hauled up, leaving him on the wrong side of a moat. Yet as he rowed, and warmth gathered in him, another thought rose—quiet, reproachful, familiar.

“If I got what I want from him,” he said within himself, “should I not be content to let him close his gate and pass away unseen? I’m in danger of being no better than a recruiting-sergeant—taking what I need, never asking what drama of hunger and hope brings the needful man within reach. And yet—how often do lives go by each other like ships, freighted with exiles who might have known one another if they could have looked out face to face?”

The Thames received these musings and returned them altered. As the wherry neared Blackfriars Bridge it was half-past four; the day—gray for hours—was dying with a kind of grave splendor. Westward, clouds had broken into long, narrowing bands of purple, laid one on another like bruised petals; beneath them spread a clear saffron space, calm as something monumental. On the river the color lived restlessly—caught, chopped, and thrown back by the shiver of ripples; a brown sail, dull a moment ago, flamed suddenly as it crossed the opening; a barge moved from blackness into color as though it had passed under a benediction. Even the water’s small noises—lap and suck along the boat’s side, the hollow knock of oar against thole, the distant rattle of wheels above—made a weaving accompaniment, a river-music which, for those who listened, could soothe or sting. Deronda felt how much of a mind’s health lies in such soundscapes—how a man can be kept feverish by incessant clatter, and healed, almost against his will, by a broader rhythm that leaves room for breath.

He had grown hot with rowing. He gave up the oar, drew his Inverness cape about him, and as he lifted his head to fasten the topmost button his eyes were arrested by a face over the bridge parapet—caught full by the western light and made startlingly distinct. A face he knew: the very emblem of bodily wasting and spiritual hunger, as if some inner flame were burning through too thin a lantern.

It was Mordecai.

Mordecai, too, had seen the advancing boat. At first it was only a moving thing to watch; then impressions recovered—quick, sharp, cumulative—until the nearing figure lifted its face, and to Mordecai it was as if a vision had stepped out of the gold behind the clouds. His white hand rose and beckoned, again and again, with an urgency that was stillness turned into command.

Deronda, anxious to be recognized and not missed, signaled at once. Mordecai answered—lifting his cap, waving it—his whole being flooded with that sense which makes all obstacles melt as if they had never been. It was the triumph of the experimenter who sees the first obedient stir of the thing he has foreseen: this, at least, was real; and because this was, the rest could be.

In three minutes Deronda had landed, paid the boatman, and was beside him. Mordecai stood quite still, as if movement would waste what remained of breath and certainty.

“I was glad to see you standing there,” Deronda said. “I meant to go on to the book-shop and look for you again. I was there yesterday—they may have spoken of it.”

“Yes,” Mordecai answered, with simple gravity. “That was the reason I came to the bridge.”

The words startled Deronda—quiet as they were. Cohen’s hint of mental disorder came back, but with it something else: the sense that there are inward necessities which can mimic madness only because most minds have never known their pressure.

“You knew nothing of my being at Chelsea?” he asked, after a moment.

“No; but I expected you to come down the river. I have been waiting for you these five years.”

Mordecai’s deep-sunk eyes held Deronda’s with a look of affectionate dependence—pathetic and solemn, like one who has lived upon a promise and has suddenly found it walking toward him. Deronda’s own sensitiveness answered, though his judgment whispered illusion.

“It will satisfy me if I can be of any real use to you,” he said, earnestly. “Shall we take a cab? You’ve probably walked enough for—your short breath.”

“Let us go to the book-shop. It will soon be time for me to be there. But now—look up the river.” Mordecai turned again toward the west, and spoke in undertones with an excited calm, as if no barrier existed between their minds. “See the sky, how it is slowly fading. I have always loved this bridge. I stood on it when I was a little boy. It is a meeting-place for the spiritual messengers. The Masters said—each order of things has its angel: that means, the full message of each from what is afar. Here I have listened to earth and sky. When I was stronger I stayed to watch for the stars in the deep heavens. But this time—just about sunset—was always what I loved best. It sank into me and dwelt with me—fading, slowly fading. It was my own decline. It paused—it waited—till at last it brought me my new life—my new self—who will live when this breath is all breathed out.”

Deronda could not speak. Something in the man’s tone—the way the words seemed to ride upon a scant breath like a violin note sustained on a trembling bow—worked upon him strangely. The easy explanation, “madness,” fell away; his mind was too large, too schooled in imagining regions beyond his own experience, to settle at once into contemptuous safety. And in that moment he felt the old legend’s shape: the meanly clothed guide who suddenly drops the disguise and stands forth a power—not by force, but by need that has found its answer. Mordecai’s quietude, born of a persuasion of fulfillment, gave him an authority which no worldly prosperity could have imitated.

After a silence Mordecai said, “Let us go now.” In the cab he added, “We will get down at the end of the street and walk to the shop. You can look at the books; Mr. Ram will soon go away and leave us alone.”

So—this man of visions was cautious, alive to other men’s judgments, measuring the small proprieties of a narrow shop as carefully as any “man of the world.” The cab rattled, and its ironed noise, its hard urban chime, seemed to Deronda like a coarse instrument laid across a fine ear; he thought with sudden irritation of how London’s din bruises thought, and how even art is turned into commodity beneath that perpetual pounding—songs sold like stamped tins, voices made into advertisements—while the true inward music of a people’s speech and memory is allowed to starve.

Yet Mirah’s image stayed with him—her gentleness, her terror, the little domestic facts that meant life: the bread earned, the fires kept, the family’s safety. He foresaw he could not choose his questions; Mordecai would lead. And Deronda, feeling himself slide into a mood that was almost superstitious, said inwardly, “Perhaps I am like a man awaiting a destiny that can interpret an oracle. But if this man feels a strong relation to me, there is something—faith has proved itself potent even when mistaken; expectation has moved the world even when disappointed. Am I to disappoint or fulfill? If it is possible for me to fulfill, I will not disappoint.”

In ten minutes they were alone in Ram’s small gas-lit shop—close air, paper-dust, leather and glue, and that particular smell of old pages, as if dried herbs and human hands had been shut up together. Outside, the street sent in its thin metallic noises; inside, the quiet was dense, and every slight movement—cloth brushing cloth, a breath drawn sharply—had weight. Each of them, as if by a single instinct, bared his head: they wished to see and be seen without veil.

Mordecai leaned back against the little counter; Deronda stood against the opposite wall, hardly four feet away. Mordecai’s face bore the stamp of consumption—brilliant glance under sharply defined features, as if a forsaken temple still held a lamp. He was little above thirty, yet wore that age which suffering adds, stretching time until it feels like a long road walked barefoot. Black hair and beard threw out the yellow pallor; difficult breathing sharpened the mobile nostril; wasted yellow hands lay on folded arms. And there was in the yearning look something like the slowly dying mother’s gaze when the one beloved son comes to her bedside and she flings up a flicker of gladness to say, “My boy!”—for the wish to be spiritually continued in another is a kind of maternal transfer.

Opposite him Deronda’s face held youth and health, with a masculine gravity that made his reverence look like judgment, not mere softness. He did not believe in the validity of Mordecai’s impressions; he did not foresee any clear, effective issue. But he felt, profoundly, a cry from the depths of another being—felt, too, the summons not to resist by easy scorn, but to receive. That receptiveness, rare and massive as fortitude, gave his face a calm, benignant force which fed Mordecai’s confidence and opened the way for his words.

Mordecai began, speaking quietly, as if hoarding strength.

“You cannot know what has guided me to you and brought us together at this moment. You are wondering.”

“I am not impatient,” said Deronda. “I am ready to listen to whatever you wish to disclose.”

“You see some of the reasons why I needed you,” Mordecai said. “You see that I am dying. You see I am as one shut behind bars by the wayside—who, if he speaks, is met only by head-shaking and pity. The day is closing; the light is fading; soon we should not have been able to discern each other. But you have come in time.”

“I rejoice that I am come in time,” Deronda answered, and could not bring himself to utter the word “mistaken,” which lay in ambush on his tongue like cruelty.

“But the hidden reasons began afar off,” Mordecai went on. “In my early years, when I was studying in another land, ideas—beloved ideas—came to me because I was a Jew. They were a trust because I was a Jew. They were an inspiration because I was a Jew and felt the heart of my race beating within me. They were my life; I was not fully born till then. I counted this heart, and this breath, and this right hand—” he pressed his hand on his breast and then held out the wasted fingers—“I counted my sleep and waking, the work that fed my body, the sights that fed my eyes—counted them only as fuel to the divine flame. But I had wandered, engraving my thought in rocky solitudes, and before I could change my course came care and labor and disease, and blocked the way, and bound me with iron that eats into the soul. Then I said, ‘How shall I save the life within me from being stifled with this stifled breath?’”

He paused to rest; the poor lungs took in air with effort, as if every draught were paid for. The silence between the shelves was alive—made audible by the faint hiss of the gas and the muffled city beyond. Deronda dared not break it.

Mordecai went on, checking excitement as if it were a flame that might consume him too fast.

“But you may misunderstand me. I speak not as an ignorant dreamer—one bred in inland valleys, thinking ancient thoughts anew and not knowing them ancient, never standing by the great waters where the world’s knowledge passes to and fro. English is my mother-tongue; England is the native land of this body—only a breaking pot of earth around the fruit-bearing tree whose seed might make the desert rejoice. My true life was nourished in Holland at the feet of my mother’s brother, a Rabbi skilled in special learning. When he died, I went to Hamburg to study, and afterward to Göttingen, that I might take a larger outlook on my people and the Gentile world, and drank knowledge at all sources. I was a youth; I felt free; I saw our chief seats in Germany; I was not then in utter poverty. And I had possessed myself of a handicraft. For I said, I care not if my lot be as Joshua ben Chananja’s: after the last destruction he earned his bread by making needles, but in youth he had been a singer on the Temple steps, and carried a memory of what was before the glory departed. So I said: let my body dwell in poverty and my hands be as the hands of the toiler; but let my soul be a temple of remembrance where the treasures of knowledge enter and the inner sanctuary is hope. I knew what I chose. They said, ‘He feeds himself on visions,’ and I denied not; for visions create and feed the world. I see, I measure the world as it is—which the vision will create anew. You are not listening to one who raves aloof from his fellows’ lives.”

He paused, and Deronda felt the pause asking him to speak.

“Do me the justice to believe,” Deronda said, “that I was not inclined to call your words raving. I listen that I may know, without prejudgment. I have had experience which gives me a keen interest in the story of a spiritual destiny embraced willingly—and embraced in youth.”

“A spiritual destiny—embraced willingly—in youth?” Mordecai repeated, with a kind of correction. “It was the soul fully born within me, and it came in my boyhood. It brought its own world—a mediaeval world—where men made the ancient language live again in new psalms of exile. They had absorbed Gentile philosophy into the faith of the Jew, and still yearned toward a center for our race. One of their souls was born again within me, and awoke amid the memories of their world. It traveled into Spain and Provence; it debated with Aben-Ezra; it took ship with Jehuda ha-Levi; it heard the roar of the Crusaders and the shrieks of tortured Israel. And when its dumb tongue was loosed, it spoke the speech they had made alive with new blood—their ardor, their sorrow, their martyred trust. It sang with the cadence of their strain.”

He stopped again, and then, in a loud hoarse whisper, as if the words must be forced through a narrowed passage:

“While it is imprisoned in me, it will never learn another.”

“Have you written entirely in Hebrew, then?” Deronda asked, remembering with a stir of anxiety his earlier confession.

“Yes—yes,” Mordecai said, deep sadness softening the repetition. “In my youth I wandered toward that solitude, not feeling it was solitude. I had the ranks of the great dead around me; the martyrs gathered and listened. But soon I found the living were deaf. At first I saw my life spread as a long future. I said: part of my Jewish heritage is unbreaking patience; part is skill to seek divers methods and find a rooting-place where planters despair. But there came new messengers from the Eternal. I had to bow under the yoke that presses on the multitude born of woman: family troubles called me; I had to work, to care, not for myself alone. I was left solitary again; but already the angel of death had turned and beckoned, and I felt his skirts continually on my path. I loosed not my effort. I besought hearing and help. I went to men of our people—to the rich in influence or knowledge, to the rich in other wealth. I found none to listen with understanding. I was rebuked for error; I was offered a small sum in charity. No wonder: I looked poor; I carried a bundle of Hebrew manuscript; I said our chief teachers are misleading the hope of our race. Scholar and merchant were both too busy. Scorn stood as interpreter between me and them. One said, ‘The book of Mormon would never have answered in Hebrew; and if you mean to address our learned men, it is not likely you can teach them anything.’ He touched a truth there.”

The last words held a thin edge of irony, sharpened by fatigue.

“But though you have accustomed yourself to write in Hebrew,” Deronda said, wanting to offer some foothold for hope, “few can use English better.”

Mordecai slowly shook his head.

“Too late—too late. I can write no more. My writing would be like this gasping breath. But the breath may wake the fount of pity—the writing not. If I could write now and used English, I should be as one who beats a board to summon those used to no signal but a bell. My soul has an ear to hear the faults of its own speech. New writing of mine would be like this body—” he spread his arms—“within it might be the Ruach-ha-kodesh, the breath of divine thought; but men would smile and say, ‘A poor Jew!’ and the chief smilers would be of my own people.”

His hands fell. His head sank. A darkness, called up by his own words, seemed to hover and eclipse him.

“I feel with you—I feel strongly with you,” Deronda said, and his voice, clear and deep, was a cordial even before the meaning of it reached the ear. “Forgive me if I speak hastily. For what you have written there need be no utter burial. The means of publication are within reach. If you will rely on me, I can assure you of what is necessary to that end.”

“That is not enough,” Mordecai said quickly, lifting his head; memory and confidence flashed back as if a coal had been blown upon. “That is not all my trust in you. You must be not only a hand to me, but a soul—believing my belief—moved by my reasons—hoping my hope—seeing the vision I point to—beholding a glory where I behold it!”

He took a step nearer and laid his hand tightly on Deronda’s arm. His face, a foot away, was like a pale flame; the reliance in it was a claim that would not be denied.

“You will be my life—planted afresh; it will grow. You shall take the inheritance; it has been gathering for ages. Generations crowd on my narrow life as on a bridge: what has been and what is to be are meeting there—and the bridge is breaking. But I have found you. You have come in time. You will take the inheritance which the base son refuses because of the tombs the plow and harrow may not pass over, or the gold-seeker disturb. You will take the sacred inheritance of the Jew.”

Deronda turned as pale as Mordecai. Within him spread a quick alarm—compassionate dread of discouraging this man who prayed as if in his last extremity, and an opposing dread of feeding an illusion and being hurried into a self-committal that might become falsity. Yet the appeal to tenderness overcame the natural recoil from a grasp that would dominate. He could not bear to strike doubt into that ardent suffering creature, crowding too much of his brief being into one moment.

Before he spoke, he laid his palm gently on Mordecai’s straining hand—a touch that was, just then, more than many speeches. Then he said, slowly, without haste, as if aware he might be wrong:

“Do you forget what I told you when we first saw each other? Do you remember I said I was not of your race?”

“It can’t be true,” Mordecai whispered at once, with no sign of shock, as if the denial were not argument but sheer recognition. The warmth of Deronda’s hand upon his seemed to strengthen a certainty older than that statement.

There was a pause. Deronda felt unable to reply, conscious—against his will—that “It can’t be true” weighed on him with a strange pressure.

Mordecai, possessed only by the supreme importance of the relation, followed the whisper with another assertion, as if it were merely the next bead on a long-strung conviction:

“You are not sure of your own origin.”

“How do you know that?” Deronda said, and an habitual shrinking made him draw away his hand. Mordecai loosened his grasp, leaned back again.

“I know it—I know it; what is my life else?” Mordecai cried low, impatient. “Tell me everything: tell me why you deny.”

The evening after he had left Mordecai—left him with that fever of conviction still warming the very air about the bridge—Deronda found that no later hour, no change of coat, no well-lit room, could quite disperse the encounter from his nerves. He dressed for dinner as custom required; the white tie lay cool against his throat like a bandage; the house moved with its usual soft mechanics—doors shutting with cushioned certainty, the subdued clink of glass, the obedient hush that wealth trains into walls. Yet under that cultivated quiet there ran another sound, remembered and sharper: Mordecai’s voice, with its thin insistence, a note that seemed to vibrate in him long after the speaker had been left behind.

Deronda’s mind, always quick to feel and then to question the feeling, turned upon itself with the same persistence as a tongue returns to a flavor it cannot name. He was alarmed—not at Mordecai’s poverty, nor at his cough, nor at the extravagant shape of his hope, but at the fact that he, Deronda, had been half mastered by another man’s certainty. It is easy to be moved and call it compassion; harder to discover, when one is alone again, that something like consent had begun to kindle under the pity, as if the stranger’s need had found a private hollow in him where it could lodge and echo.

Part of him drew back from a cowardice he despised: the fear of being laughed at by the people who took their own shallowness for wit. There were circles in which a grave emotion was a social indiscretion, and any seriousness about one’s own life a kind of vanity. Deronda had always shrunk from that modish obtuseness. Why should he be ashamed because he still lived among men who dined, and talked, and wore faultless linen, as if history were a far-off theatre and the present only a drawing-room? If the same incident were written in an old chronicle—Rome, or Alexandria, or Jerusalem—if some young man, dissatisfied with his neutral existence, had been caught into a new fellowship by a fervent voice, Deronda knew he would have called it natural, even sacred. The centuries lent dignity by mere distance; they did not alter the substance of the human hunger. Was he to treat his own hour as trivial because it was noisy with carriages and trimmed with etiquette?

And yet—another recoil came with equal force. He feared, too, the easy slavery of contagion: to be hurried by reverential pity into a path dimly seen, merely because a suffering soul clutched at him as at a staff. He repeated to himself, deliberately, the plain worldly verdict which Sir Hugo would have delivered with that good-humored sharpness that made skepticism sound like common sense.

“A consumptive Jew,” Sir Hugo would say—Deronda could hear the tone—“possessed by a fanaticism made more intense by obstacles and by the sense of death at his elbow, has fixed on you as the body into which he would pour his own visionary spirit. Odd in form, but not uncommon in substance. There are plenty of men who are sure they have the key of the universe—mathematical, metaphysical, moral. One believes all physicists conspire to keep his discovery locked up; another is certain that with one hair’s-breadth of alteration he has fitted the old wards of philosophy at last. They lie in wait for the man who must hear them; they carry manuscripts no printer wants; they talk as if fate had appointed an audience. It is right to be kind—indulge him a little, ease his last days if you can—but do not imagine his notions are worth what he thinks them.”

Deronda did not refuse those whisperings; he even gave them their clearest wording, as if he must be just to doubt in order to be just to belief. He had been forced before to face that troublesome family-likeness among heirs of enthusiasm—prophets and dreamers, benefactors and deluded inventors. The same heat that makes one man Columbus may make another the pursuer of perpetual motion. If you strip the grandest life down to bare qualities—immovable conviction in face of hissing incredulity—you can put Galileo beside a charlatan and find the statement fit them both. A mind anxious to be fair could not rest satisfied with such tests. The only safeguard against giving the hemlock to the wrong man, or banishing truth as if it were a nuisance, was the difficult faculty of understanding the matter on which conviction fastened, and the still rarer fellowship with human travail that prevents one from scanning deep experience lightly.

“Let the ages judge,” people say—yet the ages are made out of separate breasts making separate judgments, each one a beginning. Even the making of a steam-engine required that kind of justice in some single head before it could become a common thing in the world; Watt’s thought would have remained a thought if no one had trusted it, tested it, suffered for it. Deronda’s thinking, long trained in that direction, saved him from contemptuous prejudgment. Even if Mordecai’s claim had been no more than the plaint of an eager spirit, Deronda’s reverence for the struggles of men would have made him listen. But Mordecai’s claim was not merely, “Understand me.” It was—strangely, urgently—“Be what I need you to be.”

It was that which turned sympathy into a weight on conscience. Deronda’s conscience was not the clean, hard mechanism some men carry, clicking out judgments by a fixed inner law. It was a voice made of many sensibilities, and those sensibilities had been stretched by the habit—begun early and never abandoned—of imagining himself into lives unlike his own. Mordecai, with the rash right of a soul in extremity, demanded more than kindness: “You must believe my beliefs—hope my hopes—see the vision I point to—behold a glory where I behold it.” Taken as an obligation, it was preposterous. To seem to accept it would have been dishonest. Deronda, in remembering the agitation of the moment, felt grateful that even in his pity he had not let himself be driven into false concessions.

And the claim hung upon a supposition which might be, and most likely was, discordant with fact: that he, Deronda, was of Jewish blood. What appeal could be more hypothetical? Yet his whole life had been threaded with one hypothesis that had bitten into him like a secret tooth: since he was thirteen he had associated the deepest experience of affection, resentment, gratitude, and shame with the supposition that Sir Hugo was his father. That unproved belief had taught him passionate self-command; by its light he had learned to subdue feelings and to cherish them; he had lived in suspense with a conscience that could not rest. He was well used to motives that sprang from conceptions which might one day be overturned; well used to waiting for a revelation that would change the duties belonging to him. Suspense, when it stirred scruple and imagination together, was almost his native climate.

Now, then—suppose this other supposition were a foreshadowing of discovery. Suppose Mordecai’s belief about him proved true, and Mordecai’s ideas made a real conquest over his own convictions. It was not impossible that a mind like Mordecai’s—burning, organizing, intense—might give to Deronda the very shape of duty he had long felt as fragments within him, like broken sculpture that certifies beauty without revealing the whole form. That possibility rose before him with a tremulous attraction, and he found himself beginning to defend it against the mockery he could already foresee.

If the influence had come from an honored professor, an accepted philosopher, a man enthroned in a chair of learning with the sanction of printed name and public homage, would receptiveness have been laughed at? Only by those who think it weakness to be obliged for an idea—who prefer to hint that they always held implicitly, and in a better form, whatever another has made explicit. But what was there, after all, but vulgarity in deciding beforehand that a poor Jewish workman met perhaps on the sanded floor of the Hand and Banner could not contain any spiritual force worth discipleship to a white-handed gentleman? The world reads souls by their hands, and is wrong on both sides: an emperor once dismissed the descendants of David because their palms were those of laborers; a rabbi at Rome believed the Messiah would be found among the destitute. Outward signs are treacherous. Poverty is no guarantee of inspiration; neither is comfort. Yet inspiration has often worn poor clothes, and to dismiss it because of them is only another kind of blindness.

A more plausible objection lay in Mordecai’s visionary excitability—his habit of turning wishes into overwhelming impressions, of reading events as fulfillments. Could such a temperament keep that wise estimate of consequences which guards even noble motives from fatal error? And yet—Deronda could not honestly conclude beforehand. There are natures in which a just estimate of consequence is fused within the fire of belief, not melted away by it—belief that does not merely foresee consequences but helps to make them. Even strict science, with all its measurements, has needed a forecasting ardor—a faith in its preconception strong enough to outlast failures of experiment. And where human motives and actions are concerned, passionate belief has an efficacy that can resemble proof: it may happen first in one soul, and later become the habit of many. Mordecai’s excitement might be the mark of delusion; it might also be the fevered edge of a truth struggling to live.

Besides, if he demanded “strict reasoning” as a credential, would that secure safety? The driest argument has its hallucinations. Men dream in demonstrations; they build an illusory world out of axioms and definitions, then shut out fact with a triumphant Q.E.D. No formula will save mortals from mistake about matter imperfectly apprehended. If an unemotional intellect can carry a man into a mathematical dreamland where nothing is but what is not, why may not an emotional intellect absorb into its vision some portion of what will one day be? Perhaps comprehensive life feeds theory with new material, as an artist’s sensibility seizes combinations which science later explains and justifies. Deronda could not trust presumptions, either way. Human thinking is a makeshift, whether in the sum of it or in each separate mind that helps to make the sum.

Columbus had superstitions about himself, and argued poorly in places; yet he held sound physical conceptions and had the passionate patience of genius to make them tell on mankind. The world now speaks contemptuously of those who were deaf to him. Deronda felt the sting of that example. “My contempt for them,” he said inwardly, “binds me to see that I do not adopt their mistake on a small scale—to make myself deaf by assuming there can be no momentous relation between this Jew and me simply because he has clad it in illusory notions.”

For—whatever Mordecai believed about the way they had met, Deronda could trace the visible chain of links. If he had not found Mirah, it is likely he would never have begun to care especially for the Jews; certainly he would not have lingered in that search after an Ezra Cohen which had made him pause at Ram’s book-shop and ask the price of the Maimon. Mordecai, on his side, had long nursed a vision of a disciple; he saw Deronda by that light; Deronda fitted the longing image. Mordecai took him for one of his race. Suppose—against probability—that this impression should be proved true. Suppose Deronda should one day share the ideas to which Mordecai gave his last breath. That was what concerned the shape their meeting might give to his life.

But if the issue should be different—if there were nothing to share, nothing but illusion? Then something painful lay in wait. He would almost inevitably become the active cause of Mordecai’s crushing disappointment. The thought made his chest feel tight, as if the air had thickened. He feared that no tenderness of his could soften that suffering. And he asked himself, with a kind of reluctant honesty, whether the alternative—that he should not disappoint Mordecai—would be less painful to him.

Here he wavered; and he knew why. Lately there had been feelings at work in him that had altered the reluctance he once had to the notion of being a Jew. Call it romance if you will: that young spirit of adventure which has sent generations of youths to seek the hidden tokens of their birth, and with them an inheritance of tasks, began to quiver in him at the bare possibility that his path might suddenly widen into something ancient and appointed—something that joined thought to action, private life to the long memory of a people. Yet he could not let possibility harden into belief. The conviction that his father was an Englishman only grew firmer under the weak assaults of unwarranted doubt; and he would not say, even to himself, “I should be glad” if some hour came when that conviction was declared a delusion. His lifelong affection for Sir Hugo—stronger than his resentment—made him shrink from wishing for any truth that would wound that bond, even if it also freed him.

Which way the truth lay, he repeated to himself what he had said to Mordecai: he could not, without farther reason, undertake to hasten discovery. Indeed, the longer he pondered, the more he was tempted to cherish uncertainty for the present, as one might keep a flame low to prevent the sudden flare that consumes all. If continued intercourse revealed only illusions in what he was expected to share, the lack of valid evidence that he was a Jew might spare Mordecai the worst shock—the shock of a refused fraternity. Perhaps, even, it might be justifiable to use that uncertainty to keep Mordecai in suspense long enough to accept the offices of friendship Deronda yearned to press on him—help more practical than discipleship, kindness that could be given without lying.

These were the thoughts that occupied him through the interval of four days before he could fulfill his promise to call for Mordecai at Ezra Cohen’s. Sir Hugo’s demands on him often lasted so late that each evening expedition to Holborn was put out of the question; and meanwhile Deronda moved through the ordered domestic hours—voices softened by carpets, laughter trained to the right pitch, the faint percussion of knives and forks like a courteous rainfall—carrying within him another sound, the ragged, earnest cadence of a man who spoke as if the last crumb of his life must be made to nourish a future he would not live to see.

Deronda had been reading, only the night before, a passage that clung to his mind with the tenacity of an old refrain—Zunz speaking of a tragedy that had lasted not for one theatre-season but for fifteen centuries, written and acted by its sufferers, carried like a wound from land to land. It came back to him now with a sort of ironical contrast as he walked toward the Cohens’ pawnbroker’s shop; for nothing in that narrow frontage, with its bright little temptations under glass, suggested an aristocracy of sorrow. Ezra Cohen’s prosperity had the self-satisfied sheen of well-rubbed metal; his hands were quick for bargains, his eyes quick for safety, and his life had grown fat in that exasperating way in which greed seems sometimes to flourish most where it has been most condemned.

Yet it was precisely here—among padded counters and the common plenty of a family who talked loud and lived close—that Mordecai’s fragile, burning consciousness had found a nest. The thought had a strange fitness in it, as if history loved to hide its most haunted spirits behind the most ordinary doors.

Their gladness at seeing Deronda again was almost lustrous. Cohen met him with the eager cordiality of a man whose hospitality had the air of being a shrewd investment and yet was not wholly that.

“Why, sir, we’ve done nothing but talk of you since you was here. And as for the ring—let it lie a bit longer, and it would have bred more money, so to speak—but I don’t mind that—not a sixpence—against the pleasure you’ve given the women and the children.”

Young Mrs. Cohen hurried him inward as if the parlour itself were a better proof of affection than the shop.

“Don’t stop here among the tickets and the bundles, Mr. Deronda. Come in—mother and the children are in the parlour. I’m only sorry baby’s asleep—though then again I’m glad, for she’d cry at the door opening. But Adelaide’s up.”

Deronda had come prepared for such welcome. He drew out his little offerings with the quiet pleasure of one who likes to see delight take shape: a packet of paper figures for Adelaide, bright and jointed for dancing; and an ivory cup and ball for Jacob, smooth as bone and cool to the touch.

In the parlour the grandmother sat with a pack of cards before her, making “plates” with the children—little flat constructions that could be tossed and caught in a way that seemed to the young a kind of miracle. One plate had just been flung down and, by a stroke of luck, had kept itself whole.

“Stop!” Jacob cried, darting to Deronda as he entered. “Don’t tread on my plate. Stop and see me throw it up again.”

Deronda paused at once, smiling, and the grandmother gave him a look that said she understood this reverence for a child’s proud moment. Jacob tossed again and again, until the cards at last broke apart and the triumph ended in a crash of paper.

Only then was Deronda allowed to come forward and seat himself. He noticed, with a quick inward note, that the door through which Mordecai had appeared last time was now closed. He let the moment wait. It seemed right first to take his place among these homely affections, to let their warmth reach him before he asked for the man who had drawn him here.

Adelaide, light as a bird, climbed to his knee, and he set up the paper figures on the table, making them bow and turn as if the stiff little dancers had breath. Jacob had seized his ivory toy already and practised, tongue between teeth, the patient rhythm of catching—cup, ball, string taut and slack, his small wrist learning its own precision.

Then, as if speaking only because the room’s merriment could bear it, Deronda said, “Is Mordecai in just now?”

“Where is he, Addy?” Cohen asked, having slipped in from the shop during a lull.

“In the workroom there,” said his wife, nodding toward the closed door.

Cohen’s face altered—business alertness giving place to a perplexed concern.

“The fact is, sir, we don’t know what’s come to him this last day or two. He’s always what I may call a little touched, you know”—he tapped his forehead with an apologetic bluntness—“not quite so rational in all things, like you and me; but mostly he’s wonderful regular and industrious, so far as a poor creature can be. And he takes as much delight in the boy as anybody could. But this last day or two he’s been moving about like a sleep-walker, or else sitting as still as a wax figure.”

“It’s the disease,” said the grandmother, her voice softening like a cloth laid over something fragile. “Poor dear creature. I doubt whether he can stand long against it.”

“No,” said Mrs. Cohen, with the more practical resistance of youth, “I think it’s only something he’s got in his head. He’s been turning over writing continually, and when I speak to him it takes him ever so long to hear and answer.”

“You may think us a little weak ourselves,” Cohen added, half defending himself against an imagined critic. “But my wife and mother wouldn’t part with him if he was a still worse incumbrance. It isn’t that we don’t know the long and short. It’s our principle. There’s fools do business at a loss and don’t know it. I’m not one of ’em.”

“Oh, Mordecai carries a blessing inside him,” the grandmother said, with the obstinate tenderness of an older generation that keeps faith with what it cannot prove.

“He’s got something the matter inside him,” Jacob put in, coming near to correct her with childish exactness. “He said he couldn’t talk to me, and he wouldn’t have a bit o’ bun.”

Deronda’s heart tightened at that small detail—the refusal of a sweet, the turning away from the ordinary bribe of comfort. It meant a mind drawn so far inward that even taste had become distant.
