“So far from wondering at your feeling for him,” Deronda said, “I already feel something of the same sort myself. I have lately talked to him at Ram’s book-shop—in fact, I promised to call for him here, that we might go out together.”

“That’s it, then!” Cohen exclaimed, slapping his knee with the sudden pleasure of explanation. “He’s been expecting you, and it’s taken hold of him. I suppose he talks about his learning to you. It’s uncommonly kind of you, sir; for I don’t suppose there’s much to be got out of it, else it wouldn’t have left him where he is. But there’s the shop.” And he hurried away again, pulled by the tide of customers.

Jacob, always ready to be useful, pushed himself near Deronda’s elbow. “I’ll call Mordecai for you, if you like.”

“No, Jacob,” his mother said quickly. “Open the door for the gentleman and let him go in himself. Hush! Don’t make a noise.”

Jacob entered into the importance of silence as if it were part of a game. He turned the handle with exaggerated care, and Deronda followed, standing on the threshold.

The little workroom beyond was lit only by a fire dying into a red dullness and one candle, shaded. The air held that peculiar mingling of things stored too long: faint metal tang, dusty cloth, a suggestion of oil used for mechanisms. On the board beneath the window lay scattered pieces of jewellery—brooches, chains, a few rings—objects that had once been intimate on someone’s skin and were now coldly awaiting redemption. In the corner, beyond them, a small heap of books leaned in a way that suggested they had been taken up and put down with impatience.

Mordecai sat on a high chair at the board, his back to the door, his hands resting on one another and on the wood. A watch stood propped before him like an idol of measured time. His stillness was not calm; it was strained, as if all his being listened.

Deronda spoke, and the sound seemed to cut through the close room like a breath of fresh air.

“I am come for you. Are you ready?”

Mordecai turned instantly, without a word. He seized his furred cap and moved toward Deronda with the swiftness of a man released from a sentence. In another moment they were back in the parlour, and Jacob, catching the change in Mordecai’s face—some tightening loosened, some pallor stirred—caught his arm with affectionate urgency.

“See my cup and ball!” he cried, sending the ball up close to Mordecai’s cheek, as if skill and play were medicine.

It was a sign of the easing within Mordecai that he could smile.

“Fine, fine!”

“You’ve forgotten your greatcoat and comforter,” said Mrs. Cohen, and Mordecai went back obediently, fetching them as if he had been half-dreaming until that reminder tied him again to the outer world.

“He’s come to life again, do you see?” Cohen whispered when he reappeared, triumph warming his undertone. “I told you so: I’m mostly right.” Then, aloud, with hospitable insistence: “Well, sir, we mustn’t detain you, I suppose; but I hope this isn’t the last time we shall see you.”

“Shall you come again?” Jacob demanded, advancing with the earnestness of a small bargainer. “See, I can catch the ball; I’ll bet I catch it without stopping, if you come again.”

“He has clever hands,” Deronda said, glancing toward the grandmother. “Which side of the family does he get them from?”

The grandmother only nodded toward her son, who answered with prompt vanity.

“My side. My wife’s family are not in that line. But bless your soul! ours is a sort of cleverness as good as gutta percha; you can twist it which way you like. There’s nothing some old gentlemen won’t do if you set ’em to it.”

He winked down at Jacob’s back; but the boy, catching only the words, stamped and gave a nasal whinny of laughter, chanting, “Old gentlemen, old gentlemen,” in a little sing-song that made the room ring.

As Deronda went out with Mordecai, the thought returned, persistent as hunger: he would never know anything decisive about these people until he asked Cohen pointblank whether he had lost a sister named Mirah when she was six years old. Yet the decisive question lodged in him like something too sharp to swallow. He could not find the moment for it—not yet.

His first recoil from the Cohens’ commonness had already begun to yield to a gentler judgment. Their speech was coarse, their manners unpolished; and yet there was a kind of moral fineness in the way they kept this consumptive worker under their roof, not as a profitable tool but as a being they had pledged themselves to shelter—loving him, even while understanding him only as a harmless, silent visionary.

Outside, the street had its usual London sound—wheels over stones, calls that rose and fell, a far clink as if the city’s iron nerves were never at rest. Mordecai’s breathing made a thin, inward counter-music, and Deronda instinctively kept his pace fitted to it.

“The Cohens seem to have an affection for you,” Deronda said.

“And I for them,” Mordecai answered at once. “They have the heart of the Israelite within them, though they are as the horse and the mule, without understanding beyond the narrow path they tread.”

“I have caused you some uneasiness, I fear, by my slowness in fulfilling my promise,” Deronda said. “I wished to come yesterday, but I found it impossible.”

“Yes—yes, I trusted you. But it is true I have been uneasy, for the spirit of my youth has been stirred within me, and this body is not strong enough to bear the beating of its wings. I am as a man bound and imprisoned through long years: behold him brought to speech of his fellow and his limbs set free: he weeps, he totters, the joy within him threatens to break and overthrow the tabernacle of flesh.”

Deronda felt those words of reliance fasten round him with a painful tenderness, like cords that bound because they were made of need.

“You must not speak too much in this evening air,” he said, practical care answering the poet’s rapture. “Cover your mouth with the woollen scarf. We are going to the Hand and Banner, I suppose, and shall be in private there?”

“No—that is my trouble that you did not come yesterday,” Mordecai said. “For this is the evening of the club I spoke of, and we might not have any minutes alone until late, when all the rest are gone. Perhaps we had better seek another place. But I am used to that only. In new places the outer world presses on me and narrows the inward vision. And the people there are familiar with my face.”

“I don’t mind the club if I am allowed to go in,” Deronda answered, and he found he was not sorry for the delay that company would bring. It gave him a breathing-space before the private strain that waited between them. “It is enough that you like this place best. If we have not time, I will come again. What sort of club is it?”

“It is called ‘The Philosophers.’ They are few—like the cedars of Lebanon—poor men given to thought. But none so poor as I am. And sometimes visitors of higher worldly rank have been brought. We are allowed to introduce a friend who is interested in our topics. Each orders beer or some other drink, in payment for the room. Most of them smoke. I have gone when I could, for there are other men of my race who come, and sometimes I have broken silence. I have pleased myself with a faint likeness between these poor philosophers and the Masters who handed down the thought of our race—the great Transmitters, who laboured with their hands for scant bread, but preserved and enlarged for us the heritage of memory, and saved the soul of Israel alive as a seed among the tombs. The heart pleases itself with faint resemblances.”

Deronda listened as they walked. Around them the modern city kept up its ceaseless grinding chorus—too many hard edges, too much haste, as if even sound had been commercialised into mere pressure. He had a sudden sense that the little room Mordecai spoke of, with its human voices and chosen silence, might be a refuge not only from cold air but from the vulgar tyranny of noise.

“I shall be very glad to go and sit among them,” Deronda said, “if that will suit you. It is a sort of meeting I should like to join in.”

In a few minutes they had passed through a glazed door with a red curtain and entered a little parlour hardly more than fifteen feet square. Gaslight shone through a slight haze of smoke, and the air was dense with the smell of burning tobacco—acrid and sweet at once, layered with the damp wool of coats and the faint sourness of beer. The room’s sounds were intimate: the small click of pipes against teeth, a match struck and hissed, a chair leg scraping, the low murmur that swelled into argument and dropped again, like waves in a confined harbour.

Half-a-dozen men sat in a tight semicircle round the fireplace and a small table holding glasses, spare pipes, and tobacco. They were shabbily dressed, but their faces had that sharpened look which comes from minds that have had to bite their knowledge out of scant hours. A broad-chested man in pepper-and-salt, fair-haired with a wide forehead, was speaking, his pipe lifted in his left hand while his right beat time on his knee. He was finishing a quotation from Shelley—his voice thickened a little by smoke but clear with conviction.

“As thought by thought is piled, till some great truth
Is loosened, and the nations echo round.”

The entrance broke the fixity of their attention. Seats shifted; bodies made room in the cramped arc. This was the soberest of clubs; and yet the need to smoke and “take something” asserted itself as the common rite of equality, a way of buying one’s place in talk.

Mordecai was greeted with voices that carried, under their cordiality, a cadence of compassion. But the curious glances went instantly to Deronda.

“I have brought a friend who is interested in our subjects,” Mordecai said. “He has travelled and studied much.”

“Is the gentleman anonymous? Is he a Great Unknown?” the broad man asked, with an amused readiness.

“My name is Daniel Deronda,” Deronda said. “I am unknown, but not in any sense great.”

The smile that broke over his gravity made the company murmur approval in that indistinct way which passes for applause among men who will not cheapen their feeling by noise. The broad man nodded.

“You recommend the name, sir, and are welcome. Here, Mordecai, come to this corner against me,” he added, making the warmest place the sick man’s.

Deronda took a seat opposite, where he could easily include them all in his view. Mordecai remained, even among these sharply marked faces, an object that compelled attention—so thin, so eager, with something in his eyes like a lamp burning too near its end.

Deronda noted, too, how little “pure English blood” declared itself here, if such a thing could ever be measured except by the fictions men like to tell. Miller—the fair, broad man—was a second-hand bookseller of an uncommon sort, one who knew books from within, and whose ancestry, by his own hinting, ran back to Germany and perhaps further to a denied Jewishness. Buchan the saddler had the quick, cool Scotch sound in his speech. Pash the watchmaker was small, dark, and vivid—his Jewishness stamped on him like a seal, his mind triple-fired into sharpness. Gideon, who made optical instruments, had red hair and generous features that might have passed anywhere for English cordiality. Croop the shoemaker, dark-eyed, looked as if Celtic blood had left its restless shadow in him. Only a few would have been recognised anywhere as simply English—Goodwin the wood-inlayer, open-faced and well-built; Marrables, florid, an assistant in a laboratory; and Lily, a pale copying-clerk with neat features and a shirt whose freshness seemed almost a national assertion against seediness.

Deronda did not look for comedy in their departures from polished tone. The room’s talk had an earnestness that made laughter feel beside the point. He ordered whisky and water, and, out of habit and a certain wish not to stand apart like a diagram of virtue, offered the contents of his cigar-case. He rarely smoked himself, for reasons he held to; but he liked to give. Matches flared; smoke thickened, and the talk returned to its thread as if his presence had been quietly absorbed.

“This is what I call one of our touch-and-go nights, sir,” Miller said to Deronda, assuming the role of moderator without offence, and nodding toward each man as he named him. “Sometimes we stick pretty close to the point. But to-night our friend Pash there brought up the law of progress; and we got on statistics; then Lily there saying we knew well enough before counting that in the same state of society the same sort of things would happen, and it was no more wonder that quantities should remain the same than that qualities should remain the same—for in relation to society numbers are qualities—the number of drunkards is a quality in society—the numbers are an index to the qualities, and give us no instruction, only setting us to consider the causes of difference between different social states—Lily saying that, we went off on causes of social change; and when you came in I was going upon the power of ideas, which I hold to be the main transforming cause.”

“I don’t hold with you there, Miller,” said Goodwin, leaning forward with the eagerness of a man more hungry for truth than for deference. “For either you mean so many sorts of things by ideas that I get no knowledge by what you say, any more than if you said light was a cause; or else you mean a particular sort of ideas, and then I go against your meaning as too narrow. Look at it one way, all actions men put a bit of thought into are ideas—sowing seed, making a canoe, baking clay; and such ideas as these work themselves into life and go on growing with it, but they can’t go apart from the material that set them to work and makes a medium for them. It’s the nature of wood and stone yielding to the knife that raises the idea of shaping them, and with plenty of wood and stone the shaping will go on. I look at it that such ideas as are mixed straight away with all the other elements of life are powerful along with ’em. The slower the mixing, the less power they have. And as to the causes of social change, I look at it in this way—ideas are a sort of parliament, but there’s a commonwealth outside, and a good deal of the commonwealth is working at change without knowing what the parliament is doing.”

“But if you take ready mixing as your test of power,” Pash said, eyes glittering as if he enjoyed the click and spring of paradox, “some of the least practical ideas beat everything. They spread without being understood, and enter into the language without being thought of.”

“They may act by changing the distribution of gases,” Marrables put in, half serious, half pleased with his own image. “Instruments are getting so fine now, men may come to register the spread of a theory by observed changes in the atmosphere and corresponding changes in the nerves.”

“Yes,” Pash replied, and his tone had a little impish lightness, “there is the idea of nationalities; I dare say the wild asses are snuffing it, and getting more gregarious.”

Deronda, struck by the incongruity between the sarcasm and the strong racial stamp of Pash’s features, let his curiosity take shape.

“You don’t share that idea?”

“Say, rather, he does not share that spirit,” Mordecai said, turning a melancholy glance on Pash. “Unless nationality is a feeling, what force can it have as an idea?”

“Granted, Mordecai,” Pash answered good-humouredly. “And as the feeling of nationality is dying, I take the idea to be no better than a ghost, already walking to announce the death.”

“A sentiment may seem to be dying and yet revive into strong life,” Deronda said. “Nations have revived. We may live to see a great outburst of force in the Arabs, who are being inspired with a new zeal.”

“Amen, amen,” Mordecai murmured, and his delight in Deronda’s words was visible: he sat more upright, as if energy had flowed back into him from that agreement, as if even his breath had found a fuller measure.

“That may hold with backward nations,” Pash said, “but with us in Europe the sentiment of nationality is destined to die out. It will last a little longer in the quarters where oppression lasts, but nowhere else. The whole current of progress is setting against it.”

“Ay,” Buchan cut in, his Scotch rapidity like a cool draught in the thick air, “ye’ve done well to bring us round to the point. Ye’re all agreed that societies change—not always and everywhere—but on the whole and in the long run. Now, with all deference, I would beg t’ observe that we have got to examine the nature of changes before we have a warrant to call them progress, which word is supposed to include a bettering, though I apprehend it to be ill-chosen for that purpose, since mere motion onward may carry us to a bog or a precipice. And the questions I would put are three: Is all change in the direction of progress? if not, how shall we discern which change is progress and which not? and thirdly, how far and in what way can we act upon the course of change so as to promote it where it is beneficial, and divert it where it is injurious?”

But Buchan’s method could not bridle the talk; it broke and ran in livelier channels at once.

“Change and progress are merged in the idea of development,” Lily said, with the clipped assurance of a clerk who has made certainty out of copied sentences. “The laws of development are being discovered, and changes taking place according to them are necessarily progressive; that is to say, if we have any notion of progress or improvement opposed to them, the notion is a mistake.”

Deronda felt his mind resist, not out of love for contradiction but out of dread of that new superstition which wears the mask of reason and asks men to bow without understanding.

“I really can’t see how you arrive at that sort of certitude about changes by calling them development,” he said. “There will still remain the degrees of inevitableness in relation to our own will and acts, and the degrees of wisdom in hastening or retarding. There will still remain the danger of mistaking a tendency which should be resisted for an inevitable law that we must adjust ourselves to—which seems to me as bad a superstition or false god as any that has been set up without the ceremonies of philosophising.”

“That is a truth,” Mordecai said, and his voice, though low, had the ring of something forged in long inward fire. “Woe to the men who see no place for resistance in this generation! I believe in a growth, a passage, and a new unfolding of life whereof the seed is more perfect, more charged with the elements that are pregnant with diviner form. The life of a people grows, it is knit together and yet expanded, in joy and sorrow, in thought and action; it absorbs the thought of other nations into its own forms, and gives back the thought as new wealth to the world; it is a power and an organ in the great body of the nations. But there may come a check, an arrest; memories may be stifled, and love may be faint for the lack of them; or memories may shrink into withered relics—the soul of a people, whereby they know themselves to be one, may seem to be dying for want of common action. But who shall say, ‘The fountain of their life is dried up, they shall for ever cease to be a nation?’ Who shall say it? Not he who feels the life of his people stirring within his own. Shall he say, ‘That way events are wending, I will not resist?’ His very soul is resistance, and is as a seed of fire that may enkindle the souls of multitudes, and make a new pathway for events.”

The hush came upon the room as if someone had laid a cloth over a simmering pot: not to smother it, but to keep the heat steady. After a few minutes that unwonted stillness penetrated Mordecai’s consciousness; he lifted his eyes to Deronda, not startled, but soothed, with the look of a man whose pain has at last been met by gentleness. Deronda, reading that look, rose and moved his chair nearer—so near that no voice need be raised, and every syllable could fall like a warm crumb into a listening palm. Mordecai felt the motion as an invalid feels a pillow set right: a small mercy that changes the whole body’s burden.

He began to speak low, not as one performing for an audience, but as if he were tasting his own thoughts aloud—slowly, with care, as if the words were costly spices not to be scattered.

“In the doctrine of the Cabbala,” he said, “souls are born again and again in new bodies till they are perfected and purified. And a soul liberated from a worn-out body may join the fellow-soul that needs it, that they may be perfected together, and their earthly work accomplished. Then they depart from the mortal region, and leave place for new souls to be born out of the store in the eternal bosom. It is the lingering imperfection of the souls already born into the mortal region that hinders the birth of new souls and the preparation of the Messianic time: thus the mind has given shape to what is hidden—as the shadow of what is known—and has spoken truth, though it were only in parable. When my long-wandering soul is liberated from this weary body, it will join yours, and its work will be perfected.”

He paused, and the pause had the quality of an offered cup—an appeal that asked to be taken up and answered. Deronda felt the demand of truth and the peril of too much truth. He chose the words that would not deceive, yet would not break what was burning so delicately.

“Everything I can in conscience do to make your life effective,” he said, “I will do.”

“I know it,” Mordecai answered, with a quiet certainty that required no further pledge. “I heard it. You see it all—you are by my side on the mount of vision, and behold the paths of fulfilment which others deny.”

He fell silent again; the room held only the faint sounds of breathing, and beyond that, the far-off murmur of the street—a muffled tide of wheels and footsteps, the modern world’s ceaseless grind that had no reverence for frail lungs or sacred confidences. Deronda, who had lately noticed how noise could thin the mind and fret the nerves as surely as hunger, felt that the soft quiet between them was a kind of shelter, a little pocket of clean air.

Then Mordecai went on, and his tone changed—more inward, as if memory were drawing him back by a strong thread.

“You will take up my life where it was broken. I feel myself back in that day when my life was broken. The bright morning sun was on the quay—it was at Trieste—the garments of men from all nations shone like jewels—the boats were pushing off—the Greek vessel that would land us at Beyrout was to start in an hour. I was going with a merchant as his clerk and companion. I said, I shall behold the lands and people of the East, and I shall speak with a fuller vision.”

As he spoke, the air seemed to fill with that southern brightness, as if sunlight had been stored in the syllables and now released. Deronda saw the quay, smelled the salt and tar and wet rope; heard the slap of water against hulls, the calls in many tongues, each dialect carrying its own cadence—some sharp as cracked pepper, some flowing as oil. And in that imagined soundscape there was already what Mordecai would mourn later: how voices, once rooted in place and kinship, could be drowned by the harsh, indifferent roar of commerce.

“I breathed then as you do,” Mordecai said, “without labor; I had the light step and the endurance of youth. I could fast, I could sleep on the hard ground. I had wedded poverty, and I loved my bride—for poverty to me was freedom. My heart exulted as if it had been the heart of Moses ben Maimon, strong with the strength of three score years, and knowing the work that was to fill them. It was the first time I had been south; the soul within me felt its former sun; and standing on the quay, where the ground I stood on seemed to send forth light, and the shadows had an azure glory as of spirits become visible, I felt myself in the flood of a glorious life, wherein my own small year-counted existence seemed to melt, so that I knew it not; and a great sob arose within me as at the rush of waters that were too strong a bliss.”

He stopped as if he had heard again a particular sound rising above the rest—a voice cutting clean through his vision.

“So I stood there awaiting my companion; and I saw him not till he said: ‘Ezra, I have been to the post and there is your letter.’”

“Ezra!” Deronda cried, unable to hold back the exclamation, as if the name had struck him like a bell.

“Ezra,” Mordecai repeated, affirmatively, and sank deeper into the remembered moment, with no sign that Deronda’s outburst had disturbed him. “I was expecting a letter; for I wrote continually to my mother. And that sound of my name was like the touch of a wand that recalled me to the body wherefrom I had been released, as it were, to mingle with the ocean of human existence, free from the pressure of individual bondage. I opened the letter; and the name came again as a cry that would have disturbed me in the bosom of heaven, and made me yearn to reach where that sorrow was—‘Ezra, my son!’”

Deronda’s mind hung poised, almost breathless. A strange possibility, long hovering at the edge of his thoughts, came nearer and took shape. Mordecai’s eyes were cast down; his face seemed carved by that far-off grief. After a little while he went on, and the words came like drops—slow, heavy, each falling with its own weight.

“She was a mother of whom it might have come—yea, might have come to be said, ‘Her children arise up and call her blessed.’ In her I understood the meaning of that Master who, perceiving the footsteps of his mother, rose up and said, ‘The Majesty of the Eternal cometh near!’ And that letter was her cry from the depths of anguish and desolation—the cry of a mother robbed of her little ones. I was her eldest. Death had taken four babes one after the other. Then came, late, my little sister, who was, more than all the rest, the desire of my mother’s eyes; and the letter was a piercing cry to me—‘Ezra, my son, I am robbed of her. He has taken her away and left disgrace behind. They will never come again.’”

With the last words Mordecai lifted his eyes suddenly, and laid his hand on Deronda’s arm. His touch was light, yet it held the whole urgency of his life.

“Mine was the lot of Israel,” he said. “For the sin of the father my soul must go into exile. For the sin of the father the work was broken, and the day of fulfilment delayed. She who bore me was desolate, disgraced, destitute. I turned back. On the instant I turned—her spirit and the spirit of her fathers, who had worthy Jewish hearts, moved within me, and drew me. God, in whom dwells the universe, was within me as the strength of obedience. I turned and traveled with hardship—to save the scant money which she would need. I left the sunshine, and traveled into freezing cold. In the last stage I spent a night in exposure to cold and snow. And that was the beginning of this slow death.”

He let his eyes wander again and withdrew his hand. Deronda felt questions crowding to his lips—questions that seemed to contain Mirah’s very face and voice—but he forced them down. To press him now would be like shaking a vessel whose contents were already on the point of spilling; and Deronda dreaded his own speech as something too momentous, too capable of wounding by clumsiness. Mordecai’s confidence must come of itself, as naturally as a simmer rises, not by any poking of the fire.

“But I worked,” Mordecai continued. “We were destitute—every thing had been seized. And she was ill: the clutch of anguish was too strong for her, and wrought with some lurking disease. At times she could not stand for the beating of her heart, and the images in her brain became as chambers of terror, where she beheld my sister reared in evil. In the dead of night I heard her crying for her child. Then I rose, and we stretched forth our arms together and prayed. We poured forth our souls in desire that Mirah might be delivered from evil.”

“Mirah?” Deronda repeated, not trusting his own hearing—fearing that imagination had seasoned the sound to its own hunger. “Did you say Mirah?”

“That was my little sister’s name,” Mordecai said. “After we had prayed for her, my mother would rest awhile. It lasted hardly four years, and in the minute before she died, we were praying the same prayer—I aloud, she silently. Her soul went out upon its wings.”

The name—Mirah—stood between them like a lamp suddenly lit. Deronda’s heart beat with a force that made his lips go pale. Now the strange tenderness in his bond with this man took on a new solemnity: this was not only the chosen companion of his mind, but Mirah’s brother—blood of her blood, keeper of her mother’s grief, the one living link to a past she had spoken of as a blank shore.

“Have you never since heard of your sister?” Deronda asked, as quietly as he could manage.

“Never. Never have I heard whether she was delivered according to our prayer. I know not, I know not. Who shall say where the pathways lie? The poisonous will of the wicked is strong. It poisoned my life—it is slowly stifling this breath. Death delivered my mother, and I felt it a blessedness that I was alone in the winters of suffering. But what are the winters now?—they are far off—”

He laid his hand again on Deronda’s arm and looked at him with that joy which sometimes comes upon the fevered, piercing the watcher’s heart with sadness—the flare of a dying fire that dazzles and makes one fear the dark that will follow.

“There is nothing to wail in the withering of my body,” he said. “The work will be the better done. Once I said the work of this beginning was mine, I am born to do it. Well, I shall do it. I shall live in you. I shall live in you.”

His grasp grew convulsive. Deronda, agitated as he had never been—now certain beyond all doubt that this suffering prophet was indeed Mirah’s brother—shrank from any revelation. To tell him now, in this exalted state, might strike him like sudden music too loud for his weakened frame; it might push that fragile spirit into a dangerous ecstasy, and shorten the very time Mirah might still have with him. And yet to keep silence tore at Deronda with its own cruelty: the truth lay ready like bread waiting to be broken and shared, but he dared not offer it while the recipient could scarcely swallow.

His dominant impulse was the same as before—human, immediate, careful. He laid his firm, gentle hand upon the hand that clutched him. Mordecai’s fingers, as if they had a separate will and then were coaxed back into peace, relaxed; the palm turned upward beneath Deronda’s. In that meeting of hands there was more said than either could speak aloud: a promise of steadiness, a vow against abandonment.

Mordecai recovered a sense of the room, of the air that was not Trieste’s sunlit breath but London’s close mixture, and he said, “Let us go now. I cannot talk any longer.”

They went out; at Cohen’s door they parted without further speech—only another pressure of hands, brief and quiet. The street’s noises rushed back upon Deronda as if he had opened a door onto machinery: wheels rasping, voices pitched sharp, some tinny tune from a distant public-house, and beneath it all the steady, indifferent hum that made a man feel how hard it was for any solitary ardor to be heard. He carried away a weight that was half joy, half anxiety.

The joy: that Mirah’s brother, found at last, was not merely worthy of her love, but greater than Deronda had imagined—a nature refined by suffering, fierce with purpose, tender with conscience. Yet even that joy was solemn; the reunion he now foresaw had in it the shadow of farewell. Brother and sister would meet only to begin the last parting—like those kisses where greeting and leave-taking are so entangled that the sweetness hurts.

The anxiety: how to bring them together without a harsh jar; how to prepare both sides, and also how to set Mordecai in a place that would not fight against his breathing and exhaust him with petty indignities. Deronda’s mind, practical in its tenderness, refused to imagine recognition as a bare scene of embraces and cries. Real lives, moving through dim streets and shabby rooms, were always hemmed in by details—by doorways and landladies, by the smell of damp plaster, by the clatter that comes through thin walls. And Deronda, with no snobbery in him—no belief that duty requires fine linen—still felt it right to save Mirah’s first meeting with her brother from every outward discord he could prevent. He knew too well what small abrasions can do to the spirit: how a coarse laugh from a neighbor, or the scraping of boots on a stair, or the too-near din of a club-room, can make a sacred moment feel exposed and cheapened, as if someone had hawked it in the street like a song.

His own sense of release from the dreaded relationship of the other Cohens—kind enough, and yet, to his fastidious pity for Mirah, so certain to bring some unmeant coarseness into delicate grief—made him resolve, if possible, to keep them in the background until Mirah could render gratitude without being forced to endure the whole jangle of their household ways. On every account he wished to give Mordecai surroundings better suited to his frail bodily condition, and less hindering to intimate intercourse—especially in view of what was now almost inevitable: that Mirah would take up her abode with her brother, and tend him through the precious remnant of his life.

In the heroic dramas, recognitions are not encumbered with such things; the stage is cleared, the air is still, and the great names ring out without interruption. Deronda felt toward Mordecai and Mirah with as reverential an interest as if they were the offspring of Agamemnon; but he was caring for destinies not yet among constellations, only moving through London’s soot and noise, and his task presented itself as difficult and delicate—above all in persuading Mordecai to change his abode and habits.

About Mirah’s resolve he had no doubt. There would be a complete union of feeling toward the dead mother; Mirah would understand her brother’s greatness. Yes—greatness: that was the word Deronda deliberately chose now, even in defiance of the colder, more negative spirit that sometimes whispered within him. This man—consumptive Jewish workman in threadbare clothing, lodged by charity, pouring forth his visions to hearers who took them as idly as townsfolk take the ethereal chimes that drift above their market-places—had the chief elements of greatness: a mind consciously, energetically moving with the larger march of human destinies, and yet full of conscience and tender heart for the near footsteps that needed a leaning-place; capable of choosing a life’s task with far-off issues, and yet capable of the unapplauded heroism that turns off the road of achievement at the call of the nearer duty, whose effect lies within the beatings of hearts close to us, as the hunger of a young bird lies close against its parent’s breast.

That night Deronda was stirred with a new sense of guardianship. He had been peculiarly wrought on by what he had seen at the club—the friendly indifference Mordecai must have faced again and again, as if the world’s loudness had no ear for a voice that would not sell itself in easy phrases. Deronda’s own habit of reserve—his dislike of appearing exceptional, his dread of insisting where he might fail—seemed contemptible to him now, when he felt, for the first time as a complete reality, the lives that burn themselves out in solitary enthusiasm: martyrs of obscure circumstance, exiled in the rarity of their own minds, whose deliverances are, in most ears, no more than a long passionate soliloquy—unless, perhaps at the last, when they are nearing invisible shores, some sign of recognition penetrates the cloud of loneliness; or perhaps it is with them as with the dying Copernicus, made to touch the first printed copy of his book when the sense of touch was gone, seeing it only dimly through the deepening dusk.

Deronda had been brought near to one of those spiritual exiles, and it was in his nature to feel such a bond as a chain—strong, and willingly worn. Without sharing Mordecai’s Jewish consciousness, he felt his imagination move without repugnance in the direction of Mordecai’s desire; the lines of their emotional theory touched. The yearning in Deronda—grown stronger from long denial and the grievance of having no avowed ties—answered to Mordecai’s hunger for a chosen inheritor. His feeling was ready for difficult obedience.

So he set about his new task ungrudgingly; and again his thoughts turned to Mrs. Meyrick as his chief helper. To her first he must make known the discovery of Mirah’s brother, and with her consult on the preliminaries of bringing the lost together. Happily, the best quarter for a consumptive patient did not lie too far from the small house at Chelsea; and the first office Deronda had to perform for this Hebrew prophet who claimed him as a spiritual inheritor was to get him a healthier lodging.

Such is the irony of earthly mixtures, that the heroes do not always have carpets and teacups of their own, and may be seen through an open window by a mackerel-vender who, with cheerful hopefulness, invites them to pay three hundred per cent in the form of fourpence. Deronda’s mind, however, was already busy with the homeliest of refinements: the thought of a furnished lodging made gentler by dismantling his own chambers—sending his best old books in vellum, his easiest chair, and the bas-reliefs of Milton and Dante, as one might send bread, broth, and a quiet lamp into a room where a sick man must husband his breath.

But was not Mirah to be there? What furniture can give such finish as the presence of a tender woman? What arrangement of objects can do as much as the mere modulation of her voice, falling like soft water on a fevered ear? Here was one good, at least, Deronda thought—a good born out of Mordecai’s strange election of him—that would come to Mordecai: he had recovered a perfect sister, whose affection was already waiting, like a warmed meal kept back from the table until the one who most needs it can be brought home.

Fairy folk a-listening, they said, can hear the seed split in spring as plainly as a kettle beginning to sing; and the hedgerows, before they show a bud, have their own small chorus—sap rising in measured pulses, a thin, bright music that makes the invisible life feel near enough to touch. There are days when even a household seems to have such under-sounds: the click of a latch, the drawl of a voice, the hush that follows it—each a signal, each a kind of weather.

And Gwendolen—Gwendolen listened most to what was not said.

Deronda’s name moved through her thoughts with the persistence of a remembered flavor, something once tasted and afterward longed for in hours of dryness. She wondered what his mind fed on, what gave it strength. What were his ideas “about things”? How did he fill his days? She imagined him reading, judging, laboring at some noble aim—as if life had for him a recipe written in a clear hand, while she stood helpless before the pantry, proud, hungry, and not knowing how to begin.

“He said I must get more interest in others, and more knowledge, and that I must care about the best things—but how am I to begin?” she asked herself again and again, as if the question could be answered by repetition. She thought of the books he might name to her—those famous authors whose very names had the chill of physic bottles: Descartes, Bacon, Locke, Butler, Burke, Guizot. She carried them up to her own room in a rash armful, like provisions snatched in haste; she dipped into each, expecting that by quick tasting she might learn the whole dish. But the pages were dry on her tongue. They asked for a mind that could sit still and chew slowly, while her own days would not let her sit: constantly she must be on the scene as Mrs. Grandcourt, served up to the world in a glossy sauce of ease and triumph.

At Diplow, through the weeks of new year, her riding, hunting, visiting, and receiving were performed with the exactness of a woman determined not to spill a drop. She moved as if she had mastered all her part; and the neighbors, seeing only the surface, took the surface for the whole.

“She disguises it under an air of taking everything as a matter of course,” said Mrs. Arrowpoint. “A stranger might suppose she had condescended rather than risen. I always noticed that doubleness in her.”

To her mother, most of all, Gwendolen kept the smooth face. Poor Mrs. Davilow, with her worn delicacy and timid brightness, was deceived so far as to imagine that the distance now imposed was only the natural widening that marriage brings. She was fetched to lunch and to dinner with the Gascoignes, driven back soon after breakfast, and allowed brief calls from Gwendolen—calls in which Grandcourt waited outside, either seated in the carriage or on horseback, as if time itself were his to leash.

The second time Gwendolen proposed bringing her mother again with the Gascoignes, Grandcourt had first been silent; then, with that languid cruelty which turned contempt into a sort of indolent music, he drawled, “We can’t be having those people always. Gascoigne talks too much. Country clergy are always bores—with their confounded fuss about everything.”

Those words were like a knife laid quietly on the table: no flourish, only the certainty that it might be used. To have her mother classed under “those people” made Gwendolen’s blood run cold with pride and foreboding. Yet she could not tell the truth—could not say, “He wants to recognize you as little as possible; and besides, it is better you should not see my married life, lest you find out I am miserable.” She waved away every hint with practiced lightness. When Mrs. Davilow timidly spoke again of a house near Ryelands, Gwendolen said, “It would not be so nice for you as being near the rectory here, mamma. We shall perhaps be very little at Ryelands. You would miss my aunt and uncle.”

And all the while, this contemptuous veto, making her shrink from giving her family the look of troublesome pensioners, woke in her a stronger, more aching tenderness toward them. She looked back on her uncle’s cheerful complacency and busy kind management—even when mistaken—as a warmth of hearth and common bread, compared with the cold, high polish that chilled her daily. Perhaps, without knowing it, she was finding the mental enlargement Deronda had urged—not from hard authors that must be approached like tasks, but from that slow recognition of what love and familiar voices had meant to her.

One day, when Mr. and Mrs. Gascoigne were at Offendene, it was a surprise like a sudden shaft of sun through cloud to see Gwendolen ride up without her husband, only the groom behind. All were at lunch—the rector and his wife, the four girls, Miss Merry—and from the dining-room they could see her coming. Even the elder ones felt something of Isabel’s romantic imagination: the beautiful sister on the splendid chestnut, the creature holding its head as if proud to bear her, like a heroine returned out of the printed “happiness ever after.”

Mr. Gascoigne went to the door and gave her his hand. She sprang down with an alacrity that might well confirm their pleasant fancies; for to-day she was resolved to set her mother’s heart at rest, and the unusual freedom of coming alone gave her a momentary lift, as if she had been allowed to breathe.

The seven kisses—mother, aunt, cousins—were not so tiresome as they used to be. They were like small household rituals one submits to, and afterward remembers with a pang.

“Mr. Grandcourt is gone out, so I determined to fill up the time by coming to you, mamma,” said Gwendolen, laying down her hat and seating herself close by her mother. Then, with a playful, warning look, “That is a punishment to you for not wearing better lace on your head. You didn’t think I should come and detect you—you dreadfully careless-about-yourself mamma!” She touched the dear head with a caress, light as a feather, heavy as a blessing.

“Scold me, dear,” said Mrs. Davilow, flushing with delight. “But I wish there was something you could eat after your ride—instead of these scraps. Let Jocosa make you a cup of chocolate in your old way. You used to like that.”

Miss Merry rose at once and went out, though Gwendolen protested, “Oh, no, a piece of bread, or one of those hard biscuits. I can’t think about eating. I am come to say good-bye.”

“What! going to Ryelands again?” said Mr. Gascoigne.

“No, we are going to town,” said Gwendolen. She broke a piece of bread, crumbling it between her fingers, but did not carry it to her mouth, as if appetite had been taken from her by some inward nausea.

“It is rather early to go to town,” said Mrs. Gascoigne, “and Mr. Grandcourt not in Parliament.”

“Oh, there is only one more day’s hunting to be had, and Henleigh has some business in town with lawyers, I think,” said Gwendolen. “I am very glad. I shall like to go to town.”

“You will see your house in Grosvenor Square,” said Mrs. Davilow; and she and the girls watched every movement, as if trying to store it like winter fruit against her absence.

“Yes,” said Gwendolen, giving assent to the interest expected of her. “And there is so much to be seen and done in town.”

“I wish, my dear Gwendolen,” said Mr. Gascoigne, in the tone of a man conscientiously paying his due of counsel, “that you would use your influence with Mr. Grandcourt to induce him to enter Parliament. A man of his position should make his weight felt in politics. The best judges are confident that the ministry will have to appeal to the country on this question of further Reform, and Mr. Grandcourt should be ready for the opportunity. I am not quite sure that his opinions and mine accord entirely; I have not heard him express himself very fully. But I don’t look at the matter from that point of view. I am thinking of your husband’s standing in the country. And he has now come to that stage of life when a man like him should enter into public affairs. A wife has great influence with her husband. Use yours in that direction, my dear.”

To Gwendolen, the speech had the taste of bitter comedy—like being offered a sugared almond when one’s mouth is full of ashes. Grandcourt, “not expressing himself very fully”! Her “influence”! Those general maxims about husbands and wives, once so useful in girlish planning, now seemed like fine printed recipes for a kitchen that did not exist.

“I should be very glad, uncle,” she said, searching for the proper answer, as if politeness were a garment she must keep without stain. “But I think Mr. Grandcourt would not like the trouble of an election—at least, unless it could be without his making speeches. I thought candidates always made speeches.”

“Not necessarily—to any great extent,” said Mr. Gascoigne. “A man of position and weight can get on without much of it. A county member need have very little trouble in that way, and both out of the House and in it is liked the better for not being a speechifier. Tell Mr. Grandcourt that I say so.”

“Here comes Jocosa with my chocolate after all,” said Gwendolen, gladly seizing the interruption as one snatches at a screen. The cup came in with its familiar steam, the thick scent of cocoa rising—sweet, dark, homely, the ghost of old afternoons. Yet to her it was suddenly oppressive, as if comfort itself had turned heavy.

Mr. Gascoigne, pushing his chair aside and crossing his leg, looked satisfied with his own good sense and his duty done. He had decided that Grandcourt was proud, but pride belonged to old families like armor to ancestral portraits; it need not imply real unkindness. Mrs. Gascoigne felt the haughtiness more sharply, as a slight toward her husband, and she could not entirely keep the resentment from touching Gwendolen.

“Your uncle and Anna will very likely be in town about Easter,” she said. “Dear Rex hopes to come out with honors and a fellowship, and he wants his father and Anna to meet him in London, that they may be jolly together, as he says. I shouldn’t wonder if Lord Brackenshaw invited them, he has been so very kind since he came back to the Castle.”

“I hope my uncle will bring Ann to stay in Grosvenor Square,” said Gwendolen, venturing thus far for the sake of the present moment—while inwardly wishing she might never be obliged to bring her family near Grandcourt again. “I am very glad of Rex’s good fortune.”

“We must not be premature, and rejoice too much beforehand,” said the rector, whose pleasure in this topic was pure and permitted. “Not but that I am in correspondence with impartial judges, who have the highest hopes about my son, as a singularly clear-headed young man. And of his excellent disposition and principle I have had the best evidence.”

“We shall have him a great lawyer some time,” said Mrs. Gascoigne.

“How very nice!” said Gwendolen; the word slipped out with a faint edge of secret scepticism as to niceness in general, which could make it apply even to lawyers.

“Talking of Lord Brackenshaw’s kindness,” said Mrs. Davilow, leaning forward with an anxious eagerness to share her bit of good, “you don’t know how delightful he has been, Gwendolen. He has begged me to consider myself his guest in this house till I can get another that I like—he did it in the most graceful way. But now a house has turned up. Old Mr. Jodson is dead, and we can have his house. It is just what I want; small, but with nothing hideous to make you miserable thinking about it. And it is only a mile from the Rectory. You remember the low white house nearly hidden by the trees, as we turn up the lane to the church?”

“Yes, but you have no furniture, poor mamma,” said Gwendolen, and the tenderness in her voice turned at once to a melancholy, because it brought with it the sting of how this comfort had been bought.

“Oh, I am saving money for that. You know who has made me rather rich, dear,” said Mrs. Davilow, laying her hand on Gwendolen’s. “And Jocosa really makes so little do for housekeeping—it is quite wonderful.”

At that, Gwendolen felt her heart swell as if it would break its bounds. The room, with its clatter of plates and easy talk, became suddenly dangerous. She could not trust herself to sit there another moment.

“Oh, please let me go up-stairs with you and arrange my hat, mamma,” she said quickly, lifting her hand to her hair and perhaps making the disarray she pretended to correct.

They went into the black and yellow bedroom, with its familiar air of modest privacy. There Gwendolen looked round as if taking leave of an entire life.

“I suppose I shall never see all this again,” she said; and then she dropped into a chair before the glass with a little groan, as if fatigue were bodily. Her face had grown very pale in the effort not to cry.

“You are not well, dear?” said Mrs. Davilow, alarm creeping into her tenderness.

“No; that chocolate has made me sick,” said Gwendolen, putting up her hand to be taken.

“I should be allowed to come to you if you were ill, darling,” said Mrs. Davilow timidly, pressing the hand to her bosom. Something in her told her to-day—more strongly than before—that her child loved her, and needed her.

“Oh, yes,” said Gwendolen, leaning her head against her mother’s, speaking as lightly as she could manage. “But you know I never am ill. I am as strong as possible; and you must not take to fretting about me, but make yourself as happy as you can with the girls. They are better children to you than I have been, you know.” She lifted her face with a smile that asked pardon and forbade questions.

“You have always been good, my darling. I remember nothing else.”

“Why, what did I ever do that was good to you, except marry Mr. Grandcourt?” said Gwendolen, starting up with a desperate resolve to be playful, as if play could nail down emotion. “And I should not have done that unless it had pleased myself.” She tossed her chin and reached for her hat.

“God forbid, child! I would not have had you marry for my sake. Your happiness by itself is half mine.”

“Very well,” said Gwendolen, arranging her hat with fastidious care, each pin pushed in as if it could fasten her feelings too. “Then you will please to consider that you are half happy, which is more than I am used to seeing you.” She turned again with her old playful smile.

Then, as if the words had opened a door and she must rush through before she lost courage, she said quickly, “Now I am ready; but oh, mamma, Mr. Grandcourt gives me a quantity of money, and expects me to spend it, and I can’t spend it; and you know I can’t bear charity children and all that; and here are thirty pounds. I wish the girls would spend it for me on little things for themselves when you go to the new house. Tell them so.”

She put the notes into her mother’s hands and looked away at once, moving toward the door, as if the sight of gratitude would undo her.

“God bless you, dear,” said Mrs. Davilow. “It will please them so that you should have thought of them in particular.”

“Oh, they are troublesome things; but they don’t trouble me now,” said Gwendolen, turning to nod playfully, as if she must not let the act look serious even to herself.

She went through the rest of her visit and all the good-byes with quiet propriety, holding herself together as one holds a full cup steady across a room. And when she rode away, the chestnut’s hoofs striking a clean rhythm on the road, the winter air sharp in her nostrils, she said to herself with sarcasm that was half a sob held back: “I think I am making a very good Mrs. Grandcourt.”

She believed her husband had gone to Gadsmere that day. She had inferred it, as she had long ago inferred who were the inmates of the place he had called “a dog-hutch of a place in a black country.” And the knowledge set her nerves on edge with a strange heat. Contradictions tugged at her: why should it sting her that he showed concern for those beings on whose account she herself carried remorse like a hidden bruise? Had she not, before marriage, determined inwardly to speak and act on their behalf? And since he had lately implied he wanted to be in town because he was making arrangements about his will, ought she not to be glad of any sign that a conscience stirred in him toward Gadsmere?

Yet now, as a wife, the thought of his being there was like red iron laid close to her skin.

She had brought on herself, in her own eyes, an indignity that she could not wash away: the humiliation of being doomed to terrified silence lest her husband should discover with what sort of consciousness she had married him. And after the moments of secret hatred toward this man who from the first had cowed her, there came back always that heavy spiritual pressure which made submission seem inevitable. Any effort at freedom threatened only fresh and worse humiliation. She dared nothing except sudden impulse; least of all did she dare to plan a vague future where the only certainty was indignity.

Even remorse could not quite blot out what still seemed the worst result of her marriage—that she should ever make a spectacle of herself. The humiliation was lightened by thinking that only Mrs. Glasher knew the fact that gave it its sharpest point. Gwendolen had never connected the interview at the Whispering Stones with Lush’s agency; her vague terror gave every threat a shadowy omnipresence, as if fatal power moved without channels and without hands. In her mind the secret lay with Mrs. Glasher alone; and in the horrible letter there were words implying that Mrs. Glasher would dread disclosure to the husband as much as the usurping Mrs. Grandcourt did.

Another thing, too, Gwendolen counted as more hidden from her husband than it truly was—her own suppressed struggle, the desperate rebellion that frightened her by its very strength. Grandcourt could not imagine how life felt to her except where it touched his own will; he had no vision of the shadowy powers that governed her. But here he had a sensibility that was like divination. Seeing only what concerned himself, he saw it with false proportions: he magnified her inward resistance, and the magnifying only increased his satisfaction in mastering it.

The Grandcourts had barely settled again into their white-and-gold rooms in Park Lane when the first invitation arrived—Lady Mallinger’s musical evening, neat as a visiting-card and yet heavy with all the unseen hands that pushed and pulled in Sir Hugo’s world. It was only the third night after their return; but for Gwendolen, the new ceilings and the pale crimson hangings were like a set hastily painted and already wearisome. Her thoughts kept circling back—like a refrain that would not be silenced—to a certainty: she would speak with Deronda again, and she would see the girl he had spoken of, the Miss Lapidoth who had “submitted to anything in the form of duty.”

That phrase—duty—lay in Gwendolen’s mind like a bitter spice too strong for the dish. It did not blend; it asserted itself. She repeated it with a kind of inward mockery, for she knew, even if she would not name it plainly, that her own submission had not the clean taste of obligation. It was submission to a yoke she had drawn over her own neck with an act she could not bear to look at, and the motives that had pulled it on were so selfish that they left no room for duty to take hold and lift.

Lady Mallinger’s drawing-rooms were already full of sound when the Grandcourts entered—first the measured stream of instrumental music, then that pause in which voices swelled up as if relieved from restraint. The air was warm with perfumes shaken from hair and fur, and with the faint resinous breath of polished wood: the scraped sweetness of violin-bow, the deeper, almost edible richness of old mahogany and beeswax, like a pantry warmed by a fire. Outside, far off, London rolled its iron wheels; inside, the acoustics were padded and gilded, the city’s harsher roar turned into a distant, dulled surf. Even so, the room had its own ecology of sound: the quick bright clink of bracelet against glass, the hush that people practiced as a kind of art, and under it the steady humming of many lives pressed together.

Klesmer sat already at the piano, his hands ready, his profile keen as a blade; and beside him stood Mirah Lapidoth—conspicuous not by boldness but by stillness, like a candle-flame that will not flicker. Klesmer, in his generous zeal for her, had chosen to accompany her in Leo’s “O patria mia,” a piece he said was more her own than the songs that had been worn smooth by a hundred fashionable throats.

Gwendolen, magnificent in pale green velvet, her diamonds like cold drops of poison, was ushered to a seat placed so that she could be seen and could see. On entering a room she had always possessed the hunter’s power—quick to distinguish faces and positions, to take the measure of a scene without betraying the act of measuring. She let her glance brush Mirah, and as she passed, she bowed to Klesmer. His answering smile flashed back on her with the cruelty of a memory: there had been a morning when it was her ambition to stand where this “little Jewess” stood, to be lifted above the crowd by talent rather than jewels. Now she was one of the crowd—silk, gems, trained grace—and all she could do was admire, or find fault, or sit with a face that said she was used to being there.

“He thinks I am in the right road now,” her resentment whispered, not loud enough to be heard, but sharp enough to sting her own heart.

She did not catch sight of Deronda at first. While she made her way through the proper interchange with Sir Hugo, her eyes traveled with practiced ease around the room, bowing here and there, careful not to let any anxious searching show itself—careful especially that her husband should not detect it and afterward brand it with that slow contempt of his as “damnably vulgar.”

But even the smoothest glance can stumble. Among the eyes that met hers and compelled a slight bow were those of Mr. Lush—the man she had pushed out of her mind as if will were a curtain. He stood near Grandcourt. Grandcourt, with a shoulder turned and his attention apparently for Lord Pentreath, let Lush hover at the edge of his importance like a servant who had once been an accomplice.

And then, for the first time, a sensation went through Gwendolen as sudden and disagreeable as tasting something rancid in a dish that looked perfect: Lush knew. He knew the old life, the hidden life—whatever there was that made her marriage feel like a locked room with no window. He had been absent, and in his absence her inner drama had shifted to other figures—Deronda, the girl singer, her own shame. Yet here Lush reappeared at her husband’s elbow, and in an instant her mind fabricated the certainty of his connection with the secrets that made her wretched.

She turned her head away with effort, continuing her survey as if she had seen nothing more noteworthy than a portrait. And then she found Deronda.

He stood not far from the door, with Hans Meyrick beside him, as if he had been careful to bring the young painter into Lady Mallinger’s orbit. Both had the look of men whose enjoyment is hitched to another’s success; they were anxious—anxious in that particular way artists and true listeners can be anxious—lest Mirah should be swallowed by talk, lest her voice should be treated like a decorative dessert set down among heavy roasts.

Deronda had come away from Lady Pentreath, who had spoken in her violoncello voice as if she were weighing an object she had bought: “Well, your Jewess is pretty—there’s no denying that. But where is her Jewish impudence? She looks as demure as a nun. I suppose she learned that on the stage.”

The word “Jewess” had struck him like a careless slap. In it he heard not merely ignorance but that fashionable habit of stamping human beings as if they were bales of imported silk with lettering that justified disdain. He winced the more because he knew how Mordecai would feel it—how that single word could carry a whole dominion of condescension, a dominant lexicon reducing a person to a label.

In this mood he saw the Grandcourts enter. Hans, delighted as always by a beauty he could frame into metaphor, leaned toward him. “That Vandyke duchess of a beauty!” he murmured.

Deronda’s response came with a sarcasm not quite good-natured. “I thought you could admire no style of woman but your Berenice.”

“That is the style I worship—not admire,” Hans returned, with his usual airy candor. “Other styles of women I might make myself wicked for, but for Berenice I could make myself—well, pretty good, which is something much more difficult.”

“Hush,” Deronda said, as if the music were about to begin—which it was.

He had never heard Mirah sing this “O patria mia.” He knew Leopardi’s ode—Italy as a mother in chains, hiding her face and weeping—and the few chosen words were filled, for him, with the greatness of all that lay unsaid: the untranslatability of grief that belongs to one’s native tongue and does not survive being carried into another. In Mirah’s singing, the syllables had the dark sweetness of something slowly reduced over fire—concentrated, essential; and the room itself seemed to alter its breath to receive it. The chatter stilled. Fans paused. Even the small noises—the rustle of silk, the click of a ring—became cautious, as if the listeners sensed that sound could bruise what was being offered.

Certain lines not in the song rang within Deronda nevertheless, as if they had been struck in his mind like a bell: “Non ti difende Nessun de’ tuoi! L’armi, qua l’armi: io solo Combatterò, procomberò sol io—” The heroic vow sounded to him not like vanity but like the pure, strange nourishment of unselfish love—love that people call “in vain” because they measure it by victory, not by what it reveals in the soul. And now that passion came to him in the image of a man who was dying away from battle, dying in a small room while his spirit demanded a battlefield.

Mirah was equal to every hope. When the applause rose, Klesmer’s praise—worth all the clapping—was given for her alone: “Good, good—the crescendo better than before.” But her chief anxiety, as always, was whether she had satisfied Mr. Deronda. She looked toward him, and he saw it; yet he remained where he was, watching as admirers gathered round her in little currents of compliment.

Presently those currents parted to let Gwendolen through. Mrs. Klesmer introduced her, and Gwendolen seated herself near Mirah on a red divan. The contrast between them—splendor and simplicity, the one armored with fashion, the other bare of it and therefore, in a way, more clothed—caught Klesmer’s amused eye. He lingered, smiling more with his gaze than his lips, as if he saw an odd duet beginning.

All the solicitude was on the side of the splendid one.

“You must let me say how much I am obliged to you,” Gwendolen began, her voice smooth, her manner carefully gracious. “I had heard from Mr. Deronda that I should have a great treat in your singing, but I was too ignorant to imagine how great.”

“You are very good to say so,” Mirah answered, her mind far less occupied with her own triumph than with studying this grand lady close at hand—this real creature of diamonds and trained ease, like someone who had stepped out of a drama Mirah had never been taught to read. There was in Gwendolen’s beauty, even under all its finish, a hint of tragedy—like a fine fruit with a bruise hidden on the side turned away.

“We shall all want to learn of you—I, at least,” Gwendolen went on. “I sing very badly, as Herr Klesmer will tell you.” She glanced up at Klesmer with an arch look and continued, “But I have been rebuked for not liking to be middling, since I can be nothing more. I think that is a different doctrine from yours?”

Klesmer answered quickly, with his brisk kindness. “Not if it means it would be worth while for you to study further, and for Miss Lapidoth to have the pleasure of helping you.” Then he moved away.

Mirah, taking everything with naïve seriousness, leaned toward Gwendolen. “If you think I could teach you, I shall be very glad. I am anxious to teach, but I have only just begun. If I do it well, it must be by remembering how my master taught me.”

Gwendolen had not expected such simple promptitude; it embarrassed her, because it was too real for the little play of phrases she had meant. She shifted, trying to change the subject, and her next question slipped into a tone that would have been rude to an equal, yet sounded, in her mind, like condescension made kindly.

“You have not been long in London, I think?—but you were perhaps introduced to Mr. Deronda abroad?”

“No,” Mirah said. “I never saw him before I came to England in the summer.”

“But he has seen you often and heard you sing a great deal, has he not?” Gwendolen asked—partly from an aching wish to hear anything about Deronda, partly from that helplessness which seizes even the ready talker when her mind is full and empty at once. “He spoke of you to me with the highest praise. He seemed to know you quite well.”

“Oh, I was poor and needed help,” Mirah answered, and at once her voice altered, warmed, as if gratitude itself were a hearth. “And Mr. Deronda has given me the best friends in the world. That is the only way he came to know anything about me—because he was sorry for me. I had no friends when I came. I was in distress. I owe everything to him.”

Gwendolen, who had once wanted to be a struggling artist herself, felt a prickle of humiliation she could not wholly understand. A question that would have been offensive to her, she had offered easily to this girl—this Jewess who might teach her singing. Yet Mirah’s reply did not plead; it only shone with a delicate insistence, as if she were guarding Deronda from any misunderstanding. There was in her gratitude a kind of strictness: she would not let anyone imagine a relation between herself and Deronda that was less purely generous than it was.

Deronda and Hans, watching from a distance, would have felt anger if they had known that Mirah had presented herself so simply as needy, to satisfy the curiosity of the fashionable world. But Mirah’s motive held a refinement she could not have explained: she would not allow anyone to place herself on equal terms with Deronda in imagination, as if his kindness were a casual acquaintance.

Gwendolen, however, heard only what pleased her most: that Deronda’s compassion had been ready, that he could bend down without despising. The thought soothed her with a sweetness that was almost pain. When Klesmer signaled he was about to play again, she moved away contentedly, without the least foreboding that this protégé would one day matter to her more than the possible improvement of her singing—if a Mrs. Grandcourt could ever have leisure and spirit for any lessons beyond those the world gave, charging dearly for every bitter mouthful.

Then, under the pretext of moving farther from the instrument, Gwendolen chose not to return to her former seat. With that alternation she had—careful for appearances, then suddenly reckless with impulse—she placed herself on a settee where she could have only one neighbor. It brought her nearer to Deronda.

He came up, naturally, in time to shake hands before the music began. He stood for a while by the empty end of the settee; then Klesmer’s playing rose—bass and treble rushing together like a tide—and in the storm of sound, in that brief license when art made all small social calculations seem ridiculous, Deronda sat down beside her.

But when the playing ended and talk burst forth like released steam, Gwendolen saw that Mr. Lush had placed himself within hearing, leaning against the wall close by them. His presence was like a coarse noise introduced into a delicate silence. She felt anger rise hot in her throat; yet she could not fling it out. She forced herself into a tone of polite indifference.

“Miss Lapidoth is everything you described her to be.”

“You have been very quick in discovering that,” Deronda said, with an irony that was more like a guard put up than a jest.

“I have not found out all the excellencies you spoke of—I don’t mean that,” Gwendolen hurried on. “But I think her singing is charming, and herself, too. Her face is lovely—not in the least common; and she is such a complete little person. I should think she will be a great success.”

The words grated on Deronda. He would not answer; his eyes fixed gravely ahead.

She knew he was displeased, and with Lush so near, blocking her as a wall blocks a voice, she could not say what she had come burning to say. The constraint stretched out, absurdly long—two people seated close, each locked in separate silence, while the room’s sounds flowed around them: laughter like broken glass, a low murmur like bees, the occasional hard edge of a man’s loud remark cutting through. At last Lush shifted from the wall and drifted away toward another group, as if his very leisure were a kind of insolence.

Gwendolen spoke at once, like someone snatching a moment before a door shuts.

“You despise me for talking artificially.”

“No,” Deronda said, looking at her coolly. “That is quite excusable sometimes. But I did not think what you were last saying was altogether artificial.”

“There was something in it that displeased you,” she insisted, her voice tightening. “What was it?”

“It is impossible to explain such things,” he answered. “One can never communicate niceties of feeling about words and manner.”

“You think I am shut out from understanding them,” Gwendolen said, a tremor betraying itself in spite of her effort. “Have I shown myself so very dense to everything you have said?”

Her eyes turned on him with a look that was like suppressed tears held down by pride, as one holds down a cry with one’s hand.

“Not at all,” Deronda said, and his voice softened. “But experience differs for different people. We don’t all wince at the same things. I have had plenty of proof that you are not dense.” He smiled at her.

“But one may feel things and not be able to do anything better for all that,” she said. She did not smile back. His words seemed to push her away into a cold distance. “I begin to think we can only get better by having people about us who raise good feelings. You must not be surprised at anything in me. I think it is too late for me to alter. I don’t know how to set about being wise, as you told me to be.”

“I seldom find I do any good by my preaching,” Deronda said, and there was sadness in it—his mind going back to the necklace, that unlucky interference which might lead only to his own pain, watching her hardened into another kind of gambling. “I might as well have kept from meddling.”

“Don’t say that.” Her words came hurriedly, as if she feared interruption, feared her own agitation would swell beyond control. “If you despair of me, I shall despair. Your saying that I should not go on being selfish and ignorant has been some strength to me. If you say you wish you had not meddled—that means you despair of me and forsake me. And then you will decide for me that I shall not be good. It is you who will decide; because you might have made me different by keeping as near to me as you could, and believing in me.”

As she spoke she did not look at him. She stared instead at the closed fan in her hand, as if the little carved handle were the only thing steady in the room. With the last words she rose and left him, returning to her former seat, which had been left vacant.

People settled into quiet again. Mirah’s voice began—Per pietà non dirmi addio—soft, searching, the melody seeming not a display but the shape of emotion itself, as if feeling had found a throat to pass through. In Deronda’s ear the strain became, for a moment, a continuation of Gwendolen’s pleading—a drawn-out, aching urgency, impossible to answer without cruelty, impossible to satisfy without betrayal of other claims.

He saw more clearly than ever the strange mixture in her: resolute pride and a precocious air of knowing the world, and yet a precipitate, almost guileless indiscretion. Sir Hugo’s hints had made him alert to dangers his own habit of pity might neglect; but it was plain as morning that Gwendolen’s reliance on him held no dream of trapping him, no notion that he might misread her. That trust, innocent in intention and terrible in consequence, wrestled with his sense of peril—and with the foreboding that her mind was fastening on him with an incompatible claim.

A collision seemed foreshadowed: on one side, Mordecai’s dying hand, grasping him with all the ideals and prospects it awakened; on the other, this fair creature in silk and gems, wounded in secret, dreading herself, stretching out her trust as if it were something she must lean on to keep from falling. It was as if he saw himself on a shore, arms reaching to him with cries, while the waves seized him and forced him toward a vessel already sailing for a far coast.

When Mirah’s song ended, he moved away, reproaching himself for exaggerating his own importance—accepting too readily Gwendolen’s view of him as if he could truly decide her fate.

Hans Meyrick came up with his irrepressible commentary. “What an enviable fellow you are,” he said. “Sitting on a sofa with that young duchess, and having an interesting quarrel with her!”

“Quarrel with her?” Deronda repeated, uncomfortable.

“Oh, about theology, of course; nothing personal,” Hans said, with airy assurance. “But she told you what you ought to think, and then left you with a grand air which was admirable. Is she an Antinomian? If so, tell her I am an Antinomian painter, and introduce me. I should like to paint her and her husband. He has the sort of handsome physique that the Duke ought to have in Lucrezia Borgia—if it could go with a fine baritone, which it can’t.”

Deronda devoutly hoped Hans’s version of what had been visible from afar was no more than the painter’s fancy, which turned even private pain into a scene.

Gwendolen, meanwhile, had her own afterthoughts. Had her husband watched her? Had his eyes extracted from her movements something to reprove—some failure of that perfect public equability which was her own ideal of dignity? Her conscience told her she had not kept it. Yet Grandcourt made no remark on her behavior.

Only when they were driving home, the carriage rocking with that subdued, expensive smoothness that seemed meant to deaden reality, did he speak.

“Lush will dine with us among the other people to-morrow. You will treat him civilly.”

Gwendolen’s heart began to beat violently, as if the words had struck it. The sentence she wanted to fling back—like a blow returned—rose in her throat: You are breaking your promise to me—the first promise you made me. But fear held her silent: fear of quarrel, as if she foresaw it might end not in harsh words but in throttling fingers.

After a pause she said, and the tone was more defeat than resentment, “I thought you did not intend him to frequent the house again.”

“I want him just now,” Grandcourt answered. “He is useful to me; and he must be treated civilly.”

Silence filled the carriage, but it was not quiet. It had its own sound—the tight, inward roar of a woman swallowing what she dared not say, and the steady, indifferent breath of a man who knew that his will set the household’s tune.

There may come a moment, even in a marriage that began with vows, when an excellent husband who once dropped smoking out of tenderness takes up his cigar again between himself and his wife, as if the air she must breathe were now his to flavor. Mr. Lush was, so to speak, a very large cigar. And if these are the sorts of lovers’ vows at which Jove laughs, he must have a merry time of it.

The hour had come when a secret, long kept warm in careful hands, must be set down plainly like a dish brought at last from the oven—steaming, fragrant, and too full of meaning to be tasted without trembling.

Daniel had been preparing everything with the same quiet exactness with which a good cook lays out knives, bowls, and linen before the guests arrive: nothing showy, nothing wasted, and yet the whole ordered to spare pain. A new lodging in Brompton had been found—near enough to the Meyricks for daily help, near enough that footsteps could pass between houses as easily as a spoon between cup and saucer. Mrs. Meyrick, who had been taken into confidence on all points save one, had moved about this business with a mother’s brisk tenderness and a Highland secrecy: she could keep a pot from boiling over, and she could keep a story from spilling out.

She had chosen the rooms with an eye for comfort—good bedding first, then warmth, then the small decent prettiness that makes a poor place feel less like exile. She had already pasted paper over an extra window to break the draught, as if she could paste over fate’s cold fingers too.

Yet her heart did not leap without reserve. The word “brother” had a music in it, but it could also bring a new key into the household—one that might drown the softer tunes she had been hoping to hear. She had pictured Mirah, day by day, relaxing her fierce clinging to Judaism in the gentle English air of affection and ordinary life—like strong tea gradually softened by milk. And she had seen, too, with a little private fondness, Hans’s hopes rising like bread in a warm kitchen.
