Now this brother—this Ezra—threatened to steep Mirah again in the darkest, most indelible dye of her inherited feeling.

Standing in the destined lodging, with its clean bareness and faint smell of paste and new-swept boards, Mrs. Meyrick could not help saying what sat on her palate like a taste she had never grown to like.

“I’m as glad as you are that the pawnbroker isn’t her brother,” she said. “There are Ezras and Ezras in the world; and it’s a comfort to think all Jews aren’t like those shopkeepers who will not let you get out of their shops. Besides, what he said about his mother and sister—bless him for that. I’m sure he’s good. But I never did like anything fanatical. I suppose I heard too much preaching in my youth and lost my palate for it.”

“I don’t think you’ll find that Mordecai obtrudes any preaching,” Daniel answered. “He isn’t what I call fanatical. I call a man fanatical when his enthusiasm is narrow—when it blinds him and makes him unjust to those not on his own track. Mordecai is an enthusiast in a wider sense—one of those minds that care most for general good. He’s not strictly orthodox; he has room in him for others. The people he lives with love him; they can’t understand his ideas, but they’re proud of him all the same.”

“Oh, well,” she returned, half yielding, half protesting, “I can live up to the level of the pawnbroker’s mother, and like a man for what I see good in him; and what I can’t see I’ll take on your word. According to your definition, one might be fanatical about common-sense; and my poor husband used to say the world would be a poor place if there were nothing but common-sense in it. Anyway, Mirah’s brother shall have good bedding—that I’ve seen to; and I’ll have this extra window pasted up to prevent draughts. It’s a comfort the people of the house are no strangers to me—no hypocritical harpies. When the children know, we can make the rooms prettier.”

“The next stage is to tell all to Mordecai, and persuade him to move,” Daniel said; and in his voice there was the same cautiousness with which one lifts a lid to see whether the simmering has gone too far.

“And you’ll tell Mirah before I tell my girls?” Mrs. Meyrick asked quickly.

He hesitated—because his whole care was to keep Mirah from any agitating suspicion until the moment could be made safe and right.

“No,” she decided for him, gently but firmly, as if she were choosing the proper moment to add spice. “Let me tell Hans and the girls the evening before; they’ll be away next morning.”

“Yes. That will be best. Only—do justice to my account of Mordecai… don’t assist their imagination by referring him to Habakkuk Mucklewrath.”

She laughed, and her laugh was like a kettle beginning to sing against anxiety. “Trust me. I shall have to persuade them so hard to be glad that I shall convert myself. When I’m frightened, it does me good to have somebody to be angry with for not being brave: it warms the blood.”

Daniel might have argued longer for Mordecai, but his mind was already deep in the more delicate work ahead—how to disclose the truth without wounding the Cohens, whose kindness had been given in daily portions like bread and broth, without fine words, but with the sustaining power of habit and affection. He could not forget Mordecai’s keen sensitiveness to any slight upon those who had sheltered him.

In the interval he had met Mordecai at the Hand and Banner; but now he wrote, asking leave to see him in his own home and sit with him in the workroom for an hour—carefully adding that if the family objected, Mordecai should accompany him elsewhere. He meant to set expectation stirring like yeast—enough to lift the mind, not enough to overflow it.

When he came the next evening he was received with the same friendliness as before, but heightened—women and children in a little extra finery, candles attended to, and on the elders’ faces a restraint of wondering. Even Cohen, who loved to feel there were mysteries just beyond his grasp—mysteries that proved he had a gentleman in his parlor—kept his curiosity within the decent bounds of silence.

“I suppose Mordecai is at home and expecting me?” Daniel said.

Little Jacob, who had been drinking in family whispers, trotted up and asked boldly, “What do you want to talk to Mordecai about?”

“Something very interesting to him,” Daniel said, pinching the boy’s ear with grave kindness, “but that you can’t understand.”

“Can you say this?” Jacob cried, and immediately poured out a string of Hebrew verses—throaty, nasal, and triumphant—nodding as if each syllable were a pebble flung to prove his strength.

“No, really,” Daniel answered, still keeping his face steady; “I can’t say anything like it.”

“I thought not,” Jacob said, and danced on his scarlet legs, plunging hands into deep knickerbocker pockets to draw out a miscellany of possessions and push them back again, a small pantomime of resource. Then, racing to the workroom door, he flung it open wide, planted his back against it, and called in his father’s borrowed phrase, “Mordecai, here’s the young swell!”

Hushes flew at him from mother and grandmother. Daniel went in and closed the door behind him.

In the workroom a bit of carpet had been laid down; a chair placed; the fire brightened; the candles set as if their small flames were meant to warm more than air. It had that mingled smell of a close room—woollen cloth, paper, dust held in by winter shutters—cut through by the sharper, comforting scent of coal and the faint animal sweetness of leather somewhere in the house. Outside, the street had its thin industrial murmur: wheels, distant shouting, a world that never fully rests. But in here, the fire made a softer sound—the steady crackle that lets the mind unclench.

Mordecai rose; and in his face Daniel saw an expectant solemnity, so intense it might have belonged to a man who had been promised revelation itself.

Neither spoke at once. Daniel drew the chair from the opposite side of the hearth and seated himself near, in his usual way of making his nearness feel like shelter.

Mordecai said at last, in a tone of fervent certainty, “You are coming to tell me something that my soul longs for.”

“It is true I have something very weighty to tell you—something I trust you will rejoice in,” Daniel said, guarding himself, for he felt that Mordecai’s longing might already have shaped the news into another form.

“It is all revealed—it is made clear to you,” Mordecai said, leaning forward, hands clasped. “You are even as my brother that sucked the breasts of my mother—the heritage is yours—there is no doubt to divide us.”

“I have learned nothing new about myself,” Daniel answered.

The disappointment fell like a sudden extinguishing. Mordecai sank back, closing his eyes, as if the day’s strain had snapped inside him; the reaction made him almost sick.

Daniel waited a moment, then added softly, “Except—that I had, some time ago, come into another sort of hidden connection with you, besides what you have spoken of as existing in your own feeling.”

The closed lids fluttered.

“I had made the acquaintance of one in whom you are interested,” Daniel went on, still trying to lead him gently, as one leads a fevered patient toward a draught he must drink.

“One who is closely related to your departed mother,” Daniel said; and seeing a shrinking movement, he added quickly, “whom she and you held dear above all others.”

Mordecai started and clutched Daniel’s wrist with a spasmodic grasp. Terror ran through him—swift, animal, voiceless. Daniel understood at once what he feared.

With a tremor in his clear tones he said, “What was prayed for has come to pass: Mirah has been delivered from evil.”

The grasp loosened, but Mordecai was panting, a tearless sob breaking in him like surf behind clenched teeth.

Daniel added, “Your sister is worthy of the mother you honored.”

He paused. Mordecai flung himself back, eyes closed again; his lips moved almost inaudibly in Hebrew for some minutes, the words flowing as if they had been stored up like grain in a bin against famine. Then the murmuring ceased, and silence came—full, sweet, and strange. In the uplift of his face there was something suffused, as if a long inward drought had been answered. Daniel, watching, could almost imagine Mordecai speaking with someone beloved. For the first time he thought he caught a family likeness to Mirah—something in the line of brow and the softened look, like the same recipe carried in two different hands.

When Mordecai was ready to listen, Daniel told the rest. He spoke of Mirah’s flight, keeping the father’s conduct as vague as truth allowed; laying the emphasis on her yearning for England as the place where her mother might be found. He did not tell of her purpose to drown herself, nor of his rescue—keeping that sharp, private anguish out of the story, as one keeps the bitterest spice from a dish meant to comfort the sick. He spoke instead of the home she had found with friends of his, the shelter given her, the effort she was making to secure her own maintenance—how dignity often demands dependence be carried on one’s own shoulders, unseen.

He dwelt most on Mirah’s feeling for her mother and brother, giving detail upon detail, because Mordecai’s mind fed on particulars the way a starving man feeds on bread.

“It was in search of you,” Daniel said at last, with a smile that trembled into warmth, “that I turned into this house. The name Ezra Cohen was just then the most interesting name in the world to me. I confess I had fear for a long while. Perhaps you will forgive me now for having asked that question about the elder Mrs. Cohen’s daughter. I cared very much what I should find Mirah’s friends to be. But I had found a brother worthy of her when I knew that her Ezra was disguised under the name of Mordecai.”

“Mordecai is really my name,” he said. “Ezra Mordecai Cohen.”

“Is there kinship between this family and yours?” Daniel asked.

“Only the kinship of Israel,” Mordecai answered. “My soul clings to these people who have sheltered me, given me succor out of the affection that abides in Jewish hearts, as sweet odor in things long crushed and hidden from the outer air. It is good for me to bear with their ignorance and be bound to them in gratitude, that I may keep in mind the spiritual poverty of the Jewish million, and not put impatient knowledge in the stead of loving wisdom.”

Daniel’s desire returned upon him with urgency—he could not bear that Mordecai should continue in cramped air and labor when he might have rest. He spoke as one pleads for a beloved elder, with a tenderness that did not weaken the claim in it.

“But you don’t feel bound to continue with them now there is a closer tie?” he said. “It seems right now—is it not?—that you should live with your sister. I have prepared a home to take you to in the neighborhood of her friends, that she may join you there. Grant me this wish. It will enable me to be with you often in the hours when Mirah is obliged to leave you—that is my selfish reason. But the chief reason is, that Mirah will desire to watch over you, and you ought to give her the guardianship of a brother’s presence. You shall have books about you. I shall want to learn of you, and to take you out to see the river and trees. And you will have the rest and comfort that you will be more and more in need of—nay, that I need for you. This is the claim I make on you, now that we have found each other.”

Mordecai listened without moving, eyes fixed with that look which made Daniel feel as if he stood before an inward tribunal where words were weighed for more than their surface meaning. When Daniel ceased, Mordecai said, with an almost reproachful emphasis,

“And you would have me hold it doubtful whether you were born a Jew! Have we not from the first touched each other with invisible fibres—have we not quivered together like the leaves from a common stem with stirring from a common root? I know what I am outwardly. I am one among the crowd of poor—I am stricken, I am dying. But our souls know each other. They gazed in silence as those who have long been parted and meet again, but when they found voice they were assured, and all their speech is understanding. The life of Israel is in your veins.”

Daniel sat perfectly still, his face tingling as if the air had changed. It was impossible to deny, impossible to assent. He waited, craving not metaphysics but an answer.

After a pause Mordecai said firmly, “What you wish of me I will do. And our mother—may the blessing of the Eternal be with her in our souls!—would have wished it too. I will accept what your loving kindness has prepared, and Mirah’s home shall be mine.” Then, with a shadow of sadness, “But I shall grieve to part from these parents and the little ones. You must tell them, for my heart would fail me.”

“I felt you would want me to tell them. Shall we go now—at once?” Daniel asked, relief loosening his breath.

“Yes; let us not defer it. It must be done,” Mordecai said, rising with the air of a man going to meet pain because duty commands it. Then, as if guarding a tender place, he added, “But do not dwell on my sister more than is needful.”

In the parlor Jacob was alert as a sparrow. Mordecai said, “Ask your father to come, and tell Sarah to mind the shop. My friend has something to say,” he added to the elder Mrs. Cohen. The word friend, applied to a gentleman like Daniel, always seemed part of Mordecai’s peculiarities; still, the women drew themselves up into their best manners, as if politeness were a shawl to be put on in cold weather.

When Cohen entered, a pen behind his ear, he rubbed his hands with loud satisfaction. “Well, sir! Glad you’re doing us the honor to join our family party again. We’re pretty comfortable, I think.”

He looked round with shiny gladness. The fire threw its rich light over the little group: Baby under a scarlet quilt, rocked by the young mother; Adelaide Rebekah on the grandmother’s knee; Jacob wedged between his father’s legs; and in the middle, the two contrasted figures—Daniel with his composed gentleness, and Mordecai a little backward in the shade, as if he would hide how every sound struck him. The room had its familiar domestic music: the faint creak of rocking, the soft cough of coal, the close human rustle of clothes. Outside, London’s ceaseless metallic undertone threatened the tenderness within, but for the moment the hearth held its own small kingdom of warmth.

“I have just been telling Mordecai of an event that makes a great change in his life,” Daniel began, “but I hope you will agree with me that it is a joyful one. Since he thinks of you as his best friends, he wishes me to tell you for him at once.”

“Relations with money, sir?” Cohen burst out, as if divination were a kind of trade and he must show his skill.

“No; not exactly,” Daniel said, smiling. “But a very precious relation wishes to be reunited to him—a very good and lovely young sister, who will care for his comfort in every way.”

“Married, sir?”

“No, not married.”

“But with a maintenance?”

“With talents which will secure her a maintenance. A home is already provided for Mordecai.”

Silence fell, heavy as a lid. Then the grandmother began in a wailing tone, “Well, well! and so you’re going away from us, Mordecai.”

“And where there’s no children as there is here,” said the mother, catching the wail as if it were a tune she could not keep from joining.

“No Jacob, and no Adelaide, and no Eugenie!” the grandmother wailed again.

“Ay, ay,” Cohen said decisively, as if business must be found even inside sorrow. “Jacob’s learning ’ill all wear out of him. He must go to school. It’ll be hard times for Jacob.”

In Jacob’s wide-open ears those words dropped like a sentence. Up till then Mordecai’s going away was a strange notion that might be revoked at any moment, like a threat adults forget; but “hard times for Jacob” made it real. He broke into loud lamentation. Adelaide Rebekah, as always, cried because her brother cried; Baby woke and added angry screams; the room’s acoustics suddenly changed, the hearth no longer a comforting crackle but a sharp chamber where grief echoed off plaster and furniture. Hushing rose from every side. Baby had to be lifted out of the cradle.

The crying pierced Mordecai. He opened his arms to Jacob, and in the midst of sobs and the child’s swivelling gaze—half tears, half curiosity—Cohen released him, and Jacob went to Mordecai. Mordecai clasped him and laid his cheek on the little black head without speaking, as if speech would break him.

Cohen, feeling the need to recover the dignity of the occasion and apologize for family weakness, squared his elbows, set a hand on each knee, and addressed Daniel with an elevated pitch.

“It’s not as we’re the people to grudge anybody’s good luck, sir, or the portion of their cup being made fuller, as I may say. I’m not an envious man, and if anybody offered to set up Mordecai in a shop of my sort two doors lower down, I shouldn’t make wry faces about it. I’m not one of them that had need have a poor opinion of themselves and be frightened at anybody else getting a chance. If I’m offal, let a wise man come and tell me, for I’ve never heard it yet. In point of business, I’m not a class of goods to be in danger. If anybody takes to rolling me, I can pack myself up like a caterpillar and find my feet when I’m let alone. And though, as I may say, you’re taking some of our good works from us, which is property bearing interest, I’m not saying but we can afford that, though my mother and my wife had the good will to wish and do for Mordecai to the last; and a Jew must not be like a servant who works for reward—though I see nothing against a reward if I can get it. And as to the extra outlay in schooling, I’m neither poor nor greedy—I wouldn’t hang myself for sixpence, nor half a crown neither. But the truth of it is, the women and children are fond of Mordecai. You may partly see how it is, sir, by your own sense. A Jewish man is bound to thank God day by day that he was not made a woman; but a woman has to thank God that He has made her according to His will. And we all know what He has made her—a child-bearing, tender-hearted thing is the woman of our people. Her children are mostly stout, as I think you’ll say Addy’s are, and she’s not mushy, but her heart is tender. So you must excuse present company, sir, for not being glad all at once. And as to this young lady—for by what you say ‘young lady’ is the proper term—” and here Cohen threw extra emphasis into look and tone, “we shall all be glad for Mordecai’s sake by-and-by, when we cast up our accounts and see where we are.”

Before Daniel could gather an answer to this mingled boast, apology, and bargaining with Providence, Mordecai cried out, his voice suddenly full.

“Friends, friends! For food and raiment and shelter I would not have sought better than you have given me. You have sweetened the morsel with love; and what I thought of as a joy that would be left to me even in the last months of my waning strength was to go on teaching the lad. But now I am as one who had clad himself beforehand in his shroud, and used himself to making the grave his bed, when the divine command sounded in his ears, ‘Arise, and go forth; the night is not yet come.’ For no light matter would I have turned away from your kindness to take another’s. But it has been taught us, as you know, that the reward of one duty is the power to fulfill another—so said Ben Azai. You have made your duty to one of the poor among your brethren a joy to you and me; and your reward shall be that you will not rest without the joy of like deeds in the time to come. And may not Jacob come and visit me?”

He turned this last question to Daniel.

“Surely that can be managed,” Daniel said. “It is no further than Brompton.”

The word visit slipped into Jacob’s mind like the smell of cakes into a child’s thoughts—holiday, permission, a loosening of rules. He began to see daylight. He danced away from Mordecai and planted himself in the middle of the hearthrug, hands in his pockets, taking survey as if the future had become a place he might stride into.

“Well,” the grandmother sighed, resignation settling on her like flour dust after kneading, “I hope there’ll be nothing in the way of your getting kosher meat, Mordecai. For you’ll have to trust to those you live with.”

“That’s all right, that’s all right, you may be sure, mother,” Cohen cut in quickly, anxious to stop inquiry on points where he did not know the gentleman’s position. Then, turning to Daniel with an amused enlightenment, he added, “So, sir, it was better than learning you had to talk to Mordecai about! I wondered to myself at the time. I thought somehow there was a something.”

“Mordecai will perhaps explain to you how it was that I was seeking him,” Daniel said, feeling the moment ripe for withdrawal, and he rose as he spoke—leaving behind him the firelit parlor, the mingled noises of family life, and a change begun that would reach, by quiet steps, into other rooms and other hearts.

It would have been easy—almost wickedly easy—to envy Daniel for the simple luxury of buying another man comfort, and then lingering over the fancy of it as if he were arranging a still life: the fine gray flannel shirts, newly aired, folded so their softness showed; the brown dressing-gown chosen for its humble likeness to a Franciscan frock; and, above that sober cloth, Mordecai’s worn, beautiful head and the long, fragile line of throat which seemed made for speech and prayer rather than for swallowing and breath.

Half Daniel’s pleasure lay in imagining Mirah’s eyes upon her brother—those eyes that could turn poverty itself into a kind of consecration—and in trying, by these preparations, to secure her joy from any jarring shock. Yet when the parcels were opened and the garments laid ready, doubt came like a thin cold draught under a door. Was he mistaking her? Was he putting the lower effect for the higher, as if tenderness must be bribed by cleanliness? Might she not feel her brother’s distinction more deeply if it came to her still wrapped in the visible memorials of hardship? The mind, after all, can be nourished by what the palate would reject; and Mirah’s reverence had never been dainty.

But there were also the Meyricks—good hearts, ready hands, and that quick recoil of taste which a lifetime of careful domestic sweetness can breed in those who have not been taught to read sanctity through alien signs. Daniel detected in himself a little prickle of pride: he wanted to get out of sight whatever might feed their ready repugnance toward this “too Judaic” brother. He wanted, too, to take away from Hans any cheap target for mockery. The air of a room, like the seasoning of a dish, can decide whether a guest will be met with appetite or aversion; and Daniel, with his own peculiar sensitiveness, was trying to quiet the harsh note before it could sound.

If he had been present late the same evening, he would have heard how loudly that note was already vibrating around Mrs. Meyrick’s fire, with all the familiar domestic sounds that made their little parlor a refuge: the quick purr and snap of coals as Mrs. Meyrick poked them into a blaze, the soft scrape of a chair-leg pulled closer, the hush that comes when a candle is snuffed and the fire becomes the chief light, and, beyond that, the steady, far-off city murmur—wheels and footsteps and distant calls—like a sea that never quite lets you forget it is there.

“Now, Kate, put out your candle,” Mrs. Meyrick said, briskly, as if coziness were an order to be obeyed, “and all come round the fire cosily. Hans, dear, do leave off laughing at those poems for the ninety-ninth time, and come too. I have something wonderful to tell.”

“As if I didn’t know that, ma,” said Kate, letting her impatience show itself in a composure that was only the prettier for being vexed. “I have seen it in the corner of your eye ever so long, and in your pretense of errands.”

The girls came up and set their feet on the fender, turning themselves toward the heat as creatures turn toward sustenance. Hans pushed his chair near and sat astride it, resting his fists and chin on the back, already braced for amusement.

“Well, then—if you are so wise,” Mrs. Meyrick said, with her clearest articulation, as if announcing news at the market, “perhaps you know that Mirah’s brother is found!”

“Oh, confound it!” Hans burst out, as if the words had been a sudden clatter in his ear.

“Hans, that is wicked,” Mab cried, pained and indignant at once. “Suppose we had lost you?”

“I cannot help being rather sorry,” Kate said, with that frankness which in her was less cruelty than an instinct for keeping life in proportion. “And her mother?—where is she?”

“Her mother is dead,” said Mrs. Meyrick, and the fire made a small sigh as a coal fell in.

“I hope the brother is not a bad man,” Amy said, in her quiet way, always anxious to keep kindness safe.

“Nor a fellow all smiles and jewelry—a Crystal Palace Assyrian with a hat on,” Hans added, in the worst humor, as if his imagination could only defend itself by ridicule.

“Were there ever such unfeeling children?” Mrs. Meyrick said, gathering her maternal dignity like a shawl about her shoulders. “You don’t think the least bit of Mirah’s joy in the matter.”

“You know, ma, Mirah hardly remembers her brother,” Kate insisted. “People who are lost for twelve years should never come back again.”

“They are always in the way,” Hans said, with the brutal exactness of a boy kicking at something he cannot name.

“Hans!” Mrs. Meyrick’s reproach had in it the tremor of fear—fear that he would grow into a man who could not be taught.

“If you had lost me for twenty years, I should have thought—”

“I said twelve years,” Hans broke in, as if the number mattered to his argument. “Anywhere about twelve years is the time at which lost relations should keep out of the way.”

“Well, but it’s nice finding people—there is something to tell,” Mab put in, clasping her knees and leaning forward, eager for story as for sweetmeat. “Did Prince Camaralzaman find him?”

Then Mrs. Meyrick, neat as ever in her narrative—never wasting words, never letting emotion blur the outline—told all she knew: how Mr. Deronda had discovered him, how strange and beautiful and grave he seemed, how Mirah was to be told. She ended with what struck her most.

“Mr. Deronda has the highest admiration for him—seems quite to look up to him. And he says Mirah is just the sister to understand this brother.”

“Deronda is getting perfectly preposterous about those Jews,” Hans said, with disgust. He rose, set his chair away with a bang, and the sound rang harshly in the little room, like a note that does not belong to the tune. “He wants to do everything he can to encourage Mirah in her prejudices.”

“Oh, for shame, Hans—to speak in that way of Mr. Deronda,” Mab cried; and Mrs. Meyrick’s face showed something like an under-current of feeling—pride, gratitude, and a little resentment—held down by her habit of quiet.

“And now we shall never be all together,” Hans went on, pacing with his hands thrust into the pockets of his brown velveteen coat, as if movement might shake off what he feared. “We must have this prophet Elijah to tea with us, and Mirah will think of nothing but sitting on the ruins of Jerusalem. She will be spoiled as an artist—mind that—she will get as narrow as a nun. Everything will be spoiled—our home and everything. I shall take to drinking.”

“Oh, really, Hans,” Kate said, sharp with the impatience that comes when one’s own nerves are tired of being pulled. “I do think men are the most contemptible animals in all creation. Every one of them must have everything to his mind, else he is unbearable.”

“Oh, oh, oh, it’s very dreadful!” Mab cried. “I feel as if ancient Nineveh were come again.”

“I should like to know what is the good of having gone to the university and knowing everything, if you are so childish, Hans,” Amy said, with a plainness that was like salt—necessary, a little stinging, but wholesome. “You ought to put up with a man that Providence sends you to be kind to. We shall have to put up with him.”

“I hope you will all of you like the new Lamentations of Jeremiah—‘to be continued in our next’—that’s all,” Hans said, seizing his wide-awake. “It’s no use being one thing more than another if one has to endure the company of those men with a fixed idea, staring blankly at you, and requiring all your remarks to be small foot-notes to their text. If you’re to be under a petrifying wall, you’d better be an old boot. I don’t feel myself an old boot.”

Then abruptly, as if the boy in him still wanted absolution from the woman who had borne him, he bent and kissed his mother’s brow in a hasty, desperate manner. “Good night, little mother.” And, condescendingly, on his way to the door, “Good-night, girls.”

“Suppose Mirah knew how you are behaving,” Kate called after him.

But the answer was only a slam—loud, final, and out of tune with the room’s soft fire-speech.

“I should like to see Mirah when Mr. Deronda tells her,” Kate went on, turning back to her mother as if to restore the severed thread. “I know she will look so beautiful.”

Yet Daniel did not tell her. On second thoughts, he wrote instead, and the letter came to Mrs. Meyrick the next morning, asking her to make the revelation without waiting for him. He did not confess the deeper reason—that he shrank from again going through a narrative in which he seemed to place himself at the center, dressing his actions in the showy garments of general beneficence. He said only that he wished to remain with Mordecai while Mrs. Meyrick brought Mirah on what should be understood as a visit, so that there might be a little interval before the change of abode which he expected Mirah herself would propose.

Still, under Daniel’s considerate arranging there lay an anxious curiosity, as persistent as the city’s low continuous roar. He wondered how far Mordecai—after years of solitude, his mind running in one deep channel cut by conviction and worn deeper by weakness—would be able to let his sister be dear to him simply as sister, not only as a pious duty reclaimed. Mordecai’s affection for the Cohens, and especially for little Jacob, had shown itself active, habitual, as if love too could become a daily bread; but those had been near him for years, kneaded into his routine. Mirah was a name, a prayer, a past.

It struck Daniel as noticeable that Mordecai asked no new questions about her. He maintained an unusual silence on all subjects, and seemed to submit to the changes gathering around him as a sick man submits to weather, not resisting, only feeling. He put on the new clothes obediently, as if clothing were merely another circumstance—yet afterward he said, with a faint smile that had tenderness in it, “I must keep my old garments by me for a remembrance.” The words were simple, but they had the weight of a people’s habit: to keep what is worn, what holds the body’s history, as if cloth itself could preserve a vanished voice.

When they were seated waiting for Mirah, Mordecai uttered no word. His eyelids were closed, but his hands betrayed him—restless, lightly opening and shutting, and his face had that nervous changefulness which comes when the mind, long driven forward in one direction, is suddenly compelled into a new, reopened channel. There are people who dread such meetings—imperious revivals of the past—as they dread a threatening illness. Joy may be there, but joy too can be terrible, like music suddenly made too loud for a weakened ear.

Daniel felt the infection of that excitement. When he heard the ring at the door—sharp in the stairwell, followed by the muffled footfalls—he went out, not knowing exactly why, only that he wanted to see and greet Mirah beforehand, to offer her some quietness before the storm of recognition.

He was startled to find her in the hat and cloak in which he had first seen her—the cloak that had once been wetted for a winding-sheet. It seemed an omen carried into ordinary daylight, as if memory could not help but dress itself. She had come down-stairs equipped in that way; and when Mrs. Meyrick, in a tone of gentle question, had said, “You like to go in that dress, dear?” Mirah had answered, “My brother is poor, and I want to look as much like him as I can, else he may feel distant from me”—imagining she should meet him still in a workman’s dress.

Daniel could find no remark that would not sound like self-justification. He felt, with a sudden shame, how his own fastidious arrangements might seem—like trying to sweeten a truth so it would be swallowed more easily by other people’s tastes.

They shook hands silently. Mirah looked pale and awed, as if her body had grown light with anticipation. When Daniel opened the door for her, Mordecai had risen. He stood with his eyes turned toward the entrance, an eager gaze fixed as if he were listening with his whole face.

Mirah took only two or three steps and then stood still.

They looked at each other motionless. It was less their own presence they felt than another’s: a mother’s call lingering in the air, the old language of the household that had once been theirs, sounds that carried a whole vanished room with them. They were meeting first in memories, compared with which touch was no union.

Mirah broke the silence first, from where she stood, her voice exactly as when she had once repeated their mother’s call, as if she were afraid to alter even a syllable.

“Ezra.”

Mordecai moved suddenly forward and laid his hand on her shoulders. He was a head taller, and he looked down at her with a tenderness that seemed to soften the sharpness of his illness.

“That was our mother’s voice,” he said. “You remember her calling me?”

“Yes,” Mirah answered, and her words came quickly now, warmed by the return of something long kept cold. “And how you answered her—‘Mother!’—and I knew you loved her.”

Then she flung her arms round his neck, clasped her little hands behind it, drew down his face, and kissed it with a childlike lavishness that had no thought but love. Her hat slipped backward and fell, and all her curls were suddenly free, dark and shining as if they held the light.

“Ah, the dear head, the dear head!” Mordecai murmured, low, loving, laying his thin hand gently on the curls as if blessing them.

“You are very ill, Ezra,” Mirah said then, sorrow entering with clearer sight. She looked at him now not only with memory but with observation.

“Yes, dear child, I shall not be long with you in the body,” he answered quietly, as if he were stating a known season.

“Oh, I will love you and we will talk to each other,” Mirah said, her words pouring out sweetly, spontaneous as bird-notes heard at dawn. “I will tell you everything, and you will teach me—you will teach me to be a good Jewess—what she would have liked me to be. I shall always be with you when I am not working. For I work now. I shall get money to keep us. Oh, I have had such good friends.”

Only then did she seem to remember there were others in the room. She turned with the prettiest unconscious grace, keeping one hand on her brother’s arm, and looked at Mrs. Meyrick and Daniel as if presenting them, as if gratitude itself were something that must be spoken aloud.

“See this dear lady!” she said. “I was a stranger, a poor wanderer, and she believed in me, and has treated me as a daughter. Please give my brother your hand,” she added beseechingly—taking Mrs. Meyrick’s hand and putting it into Mordecai’s, then pressing them both with her own and lifting them to her lips, as if sealing a covenant.

“The Eternal Goodness has been with you,” Mordecai said to Mrs. Meyrick. “You have helped to fulfill our mother’s prayer.”

Mrs. Meyrick’s happy emotion, in witnessing this meeting, had already won her. Mordecai’s face—so refined in its suffering, so gentle in its authority—seemed to her to have more dignity than she had felt obliged to believe possible from Daniel’s account. She could not answer much; her eyes said what her careful speech could not.

“I think we will go now, shall we?—and return later,” Daniel said, laying a gentle pressure on Mrs. Meyrick’s arm, and she immediately complied.

He was afraid—unreasonably, yet irresistibly—of any reference Mordecai might make to facts about himself which Daniel had kept back. And yet, as he led Mrs. Meyrick away, the uneasiness that had haunted him softened: he felt no fear now in leaving brother and sister alone together. Whatever was untranslatable between them—whatever words had died on their tongues over twelve years of separation—there was already a language in the room older than explanation, spoken in a voice that had once said, “Ezra,” and answered, “Mother.”

’Tis a hard bargain, this business of laying one’s life out beforehand with the neatness of a table set for guests who may never come, and trusting that foresight will keep every dish warm and every door bolted. The world has a trick of slipping in by the crack you forgot because it never occurred to you you had a hinge there at all.

Grandcourt’s consequence lay, as so many men’s does, in acres: the broad, quiet authority of inherited fields that do not argue, that go on yielding rent as patiently as wheat yields grain. Public matters reached him only when they threatened to graze that revenue—politics as a kind of distant thunder that might sour a harvest, but need not be listened to closely unless it broke over one’s own stack-yard. He could glance at newspapers as he might at a menu of foreign dishes he had no intention of tasting, and dismiss whole nations and whole movements with the same languid word, as if men were no better than bad soap that left one’s hands rough. He did nothing, said little; and his silence, like a cold draught in a warm room, unsettled weaker people into wondering whether they had been foolish to feel heat at all.

Within the narrower boundary of what he chose to care for, there was more skill—something of the diplomacy that conquers by waiting, by watching, by letting the other person move and then fastening the chain on the precise link that will hold. No turn of Gwendolen’s towards Deronda escaped him. He would have denied jealousy, because jealousy admits doubt, and doubt was not the temper in which he held his wife. It would not have stung him to learn that she liked another man’s company better than his. What he insisted on was that her liking should count for nothing against his resolve—that she should feel it as useless as a hand struggling inside an iron cuff.

The marriage, whatever half-idle whim had led to it, had become a new instrument in his hands: a fresh object on which to exercise will, a living creature to be trained into the exact posture he required. He had not repented. His taste was minute and tyrannical, like a fastidious palate that can detect one wrong spice and fling aside a whole dish. He wanted a wife whose rank he had raised, whose beauty drew eyes as a good vintage draws praise, whose nails and ears satisfied his small exactitudes, and whose spirit was sharp enough to answer—so long as the answer did not threaten him. He liked, even, that she should have fire in her, provided it burned under his grate. Love was not his need; command was.

So in London he had his satisfaction on every side. He had come up earlier than usual to consult lawyers—wills, mortgages, the transaction with his uncle about Diplow, that had been coaxed into agreement by the neat bait of ready money dangled as one offers a horse a bit of apple without seeming to entice. And with the business went the other indulgence: to show himself everywhere with the bride he had chosen against expectation. He carried his indifference as men carry a cane, needing the street and the passers-by to make the prop worth having. Splendid receptions, conspicuous rides and drives, her beauty beside him like a fine course served on plate—these enlarged his enjoyment of not caring. He wanted her sought after; he liked that men should hover, eager to talk and escort her, so long as it happened within his observation. A lofty coquetry on her part would not have offended him. What he could not bear were her ways with Deronda.

After Lady Mallinger’s musical evening, when he had marked the settee-dialogue as keenly as a servant who watches his betters, he showed his method: he named Deronda for invitation along with the Mallingers, careful that no one should suspect the name mattered. He said nothing directly to Gwendolen; pride would not risk a disgust too plainly spoken. But a few days later, without any decent preface, he remarked as if it were merely a general truth he had noticed in the world—

“Nothing makes a woman more of a gawky than looking out after people and showing tempers in public. A woman ought to have good manners. Else it’s intolerable to appear with her.”

The word “gawky” fell on Gwendolen as if it were a smear across her white glove. She knew the application, and felt a sudden cold of fear—not so much of his displeasure as of being made ridiculous in the eyes that still mattered to her. And the rebuke, hanging over her like a low ceiling, only tightened that inward strain with which she awaited any meeting with Deronda.

Her town life hurried on with the glitter and the changing scene of travel: engagements, toilettes, rooms full of voices and laughter, the soft whirl of wheels on the smoother streets. It was all a programme, carrying her forward even while some inner part of her sat still and despondent. And yet, as always with what is deeply felt, the rare moments when she could exchange a word with Deronda spread through her mind like some slow infusion—like a scent that will not be confined to the jar, but steals out and makes the whole room a place of remembered sweetness. Each slight communication grew large in her consciousness, and she imagined it large in his. Deronda did not avoid her; rather he tried, by every delicate means, to show that her confidence had not lowered his respect. And he liked being near her—how not? She was not merely a problem; she was a beautiful creature whose fate moved him, whose appeal had become to him like the pressure of a hand caught at the edge of a precipice. Yet when he dared to look at his own future, he saw it lying far away from her—far away from this splendid, sad-hearted woman who had turned to him as if his momentary warning had been the only firm ground under her feet.

One day, an incident touched that other name which was now always interwoven with Deronda’s in Gwendolen’s mind: Mirah. She had meant—out of a sort of obedience to Deronda’s counsel—to take singing lessons; but days slid past in the formless way of a life without work to mark its hours, and Grandcourt’s continual presence, his surveillance, lay on everything like damp mist: his negative mind clung to objects, spoiling their contact as fog spoils the smell of hay by flattening it into chill.

But one morning at breakfast, in a recurring fit of determination to assert the old spirit, Gwendolen began dallying prettily over her prawns, touching them with her fork as if the pearl-pink curve and the salted steam rising faintly from the dish were the whole point, and eating nothing.

“I think of making myself accomplished while we are in town,” she said, “and having singing lessons.”

“Why?” said Grandcourt, in his languid tone.

“Why?” she echoed with a little play of sauciness, her chin lifting. “Because I can’t eat pâté de foie gras to make me sleepy, and I can’t smoke, and I can’t go to the club to make me like to come away again. I want a variety of ennui. What would be the most convenient time—when you are busy with your lawyers and people—for me to have lessons from that little Jewess whose singing is getting all the rage?”

“Whenever you like,” he said, pushing away his plate, leaning back, and looking at her under his eyelids with that lizard-like stillness which made her feel as if he lay in sun and watched a fly. His fingers toyed with the ears of the tiny spaniel on his lap—one of the little dogs she had begun to dislike because they fawned on him as if his cold hand were their only warmth.

Then he added, still lazily: “I don’t see why a lady should sing. Amateurs make fools of themselves. A lady can’t risk herself in that way in company. And one doesn’t want to hear squalling in private.”

“I like frankness,” said Gwendolen, turning her eyes away while her pride swallowed the sting as one swallows a mouthful too hot, feeling it burn downwards. “That seems to me a husband’s great charm.” She lifted a prawn and stared at its boiled, ingenuous eyes, preferring that harmless fixedness to his. “But,” she went on, after the pause in which she forced her voice to keep its lightness, “I suppose you don’t object to Miss Lapidoth’s singing at our party on the fourth? I thought of engaging her. Lady Brackenshaw had her—you know. And the Raymonds, who are very particular about their music. And Mr. Deronda, who is a musician himself and a first-rate judge, says there is no singing in such good taste as hers for a drawing-room. I think his opinion is an authority.”

She meant it to fall like a small stone—little, but sharp.

“It’s very indecent of Deronda to go about praising that girl,” said Grandcourt, in the same indifferent tone.

“Indecent!” Gwendolen exclaimed, the blood springing to her face at first, then leaving it. “To go about praising.”

“Yes; and especially when she is patronized by Lady Mallinger. He ought to hold his tongue about her. Men can see what is his relation to her.”

“Men who judge of others by themselves,” Gwendolen said—and the words were out before she could catch them back. The moment they hung in the air, she felt as if she had touched something that would burn.

“Of course. And a woman should take their judgment—else she is likely to run her head into the wrong place,” he returned, feeling the pinchers close on the quick. “I suppose you take Deronda for a saint.”

“Oh dear no!” Gwendolen said, summoning that almost miraculous self-control which could make her voice high and hard and keep her hand steady when everything within shook. “Only a little less of a monster.”

She rose, pushed back her chair without hurry, and walked out with the careful carriage of someone determined that no one shall see she has been struck. In her dressing-room she turned the keys inside the doors and sat down, pale and still. Even the poisonous letter she had once read had hardly pierced her with a sharper pain than this: the emotion had reached that acute point where it is sensation—like a bruise you cannot reason away. Deronda, suddenly imagined as not what she believed, was a hideous apparition, dreadful before she could ask whether it were truth. And with it came the sickening perception of how little ground she had for her faith—how small her knowledge of his life—how childish her confidence. His former rebukes and severity seemed to curdle into something odious; poetry and lofty doctrine, all the fine language in the world, looked like a mask that might cover common habits. Even the grave beauty of his face seemed now an intolerable disguise.

It rushed through her like a fevered dream—then broke. A stream of sunlight, sudden through the grey sombre morning, poured into the room and wrapped her where she sat, warming her as if the world outside were insisting on itself. She moved, looked round: the dream proved nothing. She rose, stretching her arms upward and clasping her hands as she often did when feeling crushed, and walked about in the flood of sunbeams.

“It is not true! What does it matter whether he believes it or not?” she kept repeating. It was not faith restored; it was the gasp of a faith being smothered and refusing to die quietly.

How was she to go through the day in that state? Her imagination flung out wild actions—she would go to Lady Mallinger and question her about Mirah; she would write to Deronda, upbraid him for having made the world false and wicked and hopeless to her; to him she dared pour out all the bitter indignation she had no other outlet for. No—she would go to Mirah. That, at least, was practicable. She had the pretext: to ask her to sing on the fourth. What else would she say? How would she force the assurance she needed? She could not wait to foresee. If the thought maddening her had been a living thing, she would have wanted to seize it by the throat at once.

She rang, asked if Mr. Grandcourt were gone out; learning he was, she ordered the carriage and dressed quickly. Then she went down and walked about the great drawing-room—the gilded, painted prison—seeing herself in glass panels as if she were another woman, not noting anything, only feeling the hollow throb in her chest. He would find out where she had been. He would punish her—somehow. No matter. At this moment she could neither desire nor fear anything but certainty: certainty that she had not been fool enough to trust what was false.

She had Mirah’s address. Soon the carriage bore her through London’s roar and roll—iron tyres on stone, omnibuses groaning, the sharp cries of street-sellers, the ceaseless hiss and clatter that seemed to grind down thought as a mill grinds grain. Even inside the cushioned splendour, that city sound pressed upon her nerves, and she longed for the quieter, human noises of a home: a kettle’s small singing, a knife on a board, the gentle stir that belongs to rooms where life is made and mended. But she was heedless, as one is heedless of passages and lobbies when going to hear a verdict. Nothing existed until she was shown into a room where there were folding-doors—and from behind them she heard Deronda’s voice.

She knew it at once, as if she had seen him. The knowledge sent a shock through her; she unbuttoned her gloves and buttoned them again, bit her lip over the pretended difficulty, trying to give her hands something to do. Then the door opened and Mirah came in, perfectly quiet, with that sweet recognition which seemed to carry a softer air with it. There was relief in her face—the steady calm, the rich colour; it was like seeing a clear spring when one has been choking on dust. Gwendolen could smile back, though her own beauty under the plumed hat was pale and agitated.

Mirah drew her chair very near, as if she felt the talk must be subdued, and looked with placid expectation while Gwendolen began low, with something like bashfulness—

“Perhaps you wonder to see me—perhaps I ought to have written—but I wished to make a particular request.”

“I am glad to see you instead of having a letter,” Mirah said, still wondering at the changed manner of this woman whom Hans, with his rough play of fancy, had called the Vandyke duchess.

“I thought—at least I hoped—you would not object to sing at our house on the fourth—in the evening—at a party like Lady Brackenshaw’s. I should be so much obliged.”

“I shall be very happy to sing for you. At ten?” Mirah answered.

“At ten, please.” Gwendolen paused; her prepared errand was done, and yet she could not move. Deronda’s voice went on, close by, threading every silence. She must say it; she could contrive no other sentence.

“Mr. Deronda is in the next room.”

“Yes,” said Mirah, in her former tone. “He is reading Hebrew with my brother.”

“You have a brother?” Gwendolen said—though she had heard it before and had not cared then.

“Yes—a dear brother who is ill—consumptive. And Mr. Deronda is the best of friends to him, as he has been to me,” Mirah said, unable to mention those she loved without letting her love speak. There was, too, in the background of that room, a sense of the simple household labour by which sickness is borne: the careful quiet, the measured footsteps, the restraint of voices—an acoustic tenderness, as if the very air were trained not to jar.

“Tell me,” Gwendolen said, laying her hand on Mirah’s and speaking hardly above a whisper, “tell me—tell me the truth. You are sure he is quite good. You know no evil of him. Any evil that people say of him is false.”

It was the cry of a child for assurance; but Mirah received it with solemn indignation, as if someone had spoken blasphemy against the living.

With a sudden light in her eyes and a tremor in her voice, she said, “Who are the people that say evil of him? I would not believe any evil of him if an angel came to tell it me. He found me when I was so miserable—I was going to drown myself. I looked so poor and forsaken—you would have thought I was a beggar by the wayside. And he treated me as if I had been a king’s daughter. He took me to the best of women. He found my brother for me. And he honours my brother—though he too was poor—oh, almost as poor as he could be.” Her words came like warm bread broken in haste, offered with both hands. “And my brother honours him. That is no light thing to say”—here her tone deepened, and she shook her head with emphasis—“for my brother is very learned and great-minded. And Mr. Deronda says there are few men equal to him.”

There was in her, too, the flare of a people long forced to have their goodness measured in another’s language, their lives made small by other names; and the defiance in her gratitude would not help including Gwendolen, who had seemed to doubt.

But Gwendolen was like one parched with thirst, drinking. The fresh water ran through her as sufficient bliss. She did not notice Mirah’s anger. She hardly took in the details—only the great clearing certainty that Deronda and his life were no more like Grandcourt’s insinuation than dawn is like dawn muddied with street-gas. She pressed Mirah’s hand.

“Thank you, thank you,” she whispered hurriedly, and rose at once, as if she must escape even the sweetness that had saved her. “I must go—I shall see you—on the fourth—I am so much obliged.” She bowed herself out automatically, and Mirah, opening the door, wondered at what looked like a sudden retreat into chill loftiness.

Gwendolen had no feeling to spare for effusiveness. The passionate need to contradict Grandcourt’s estimate—so long the one point blunting her sensibility to everything else—was satisfied, and now she wanted only to be gone. Shame came back with the fear that Deronda might see her there, and with it the vision of what waited at home.

When the carriage drew up in Grosvenor Square, Grandcourt was arriving too, a cigar between his fingers. He threw it away and handed her out, accompanying her up-stairs. She turned into the drawing-room at once, so that he should not follow her farther and leave her no retreat. She sat down with a weary air, took off her gloves, rubbed her forehead, and tried to make his presence a cipher—something not to be read.

But he sat down also, not far off—just in front, so that not looking at him required the effort of a turned neck and an averted gaze.

“May I ask where you have been at this extraordinary hour?” he said.

“Oh yes; I have been to Miss Lapidoth’s, to ask her to come and sing for us,” Gwendolen answered, laying her gloves on the little table beside her and looking down at them as if the soft kid and its seams were worth more attention than his face.

“And to ask her about her relations with Deronda?” he added, the sneer in his low voice so cold it seemed to burn. In her ear it had the sound of something diabolically amused.

For the first time since their marriage she flashed out without the inward check that usually caught her anger by the throat. She turned her eyes full on him and said, biting out each word,

“Yes; and what you said is false—a low, wicked falsehood.”

“She told you so—did she?” he returned, with a sneer distilled to its last drop.

Gwendolen was mute. Her daring fury turned at once into the rage of dumbness. What proof had she? No proof that could live under his breath. All her reasons—strong, vivid within her—she saw them shrivelled, because they were only impressions, only the testimony of her own soul, which he would call folly. She turned her head away sharply, looking angrily toward the end of the room. She would have risen, but he was in her way.

Grandcourt felt the advantage and used it with that measured patience which presses hardest. “It’s of no consequence so far as her singing goes,” he drawled. “You can have her to sing, if you like.” Then, after a pause, he said in his lowest imperious tone, “But you will please to observe that you are not to go near that house again. As my wife, you must take my word about what is proper for you. When you undertook to be Mrs. Grandcourt, you undertook not to make a fool of yourself. You have been making a fool of yourself this morning; and if you were to go on as you have begun, you might soon get yourself talked of at the clubs in a way you would not like. What do you know about the world? You have married me, and must be guided by my opinion.”

Each slow sentence fell like a weight laid deliberately, not to strike her down at once, but to make rising impossible. The low tone carried its own argument, as if a physician, untroubled and exact, were telling her the course of a fatal disease. And then he allowed her to move, and never again referred to what had happened. He knew the force of his words.

If this white-handed man with the straight, perpendicular profile had been sent to rule a difficult colony, he might have won reputation among his contemporaries. He would have understood that extermination is often safer than persuasion when one’s object is security; and he would not have flinched from making things safe in that way.

Deronda, when he parted from Gwendolen, had kept back the words that rose and trembled at his lips—I shall not see you for a long while; I am going away. He would not give Grandcourt even the faintest excuse to imagine that his coming and going had any special weight in her mind. Yet Daniel himself was already moving under a weight that made every common act—promising, visiting, bowing, taking up his hat—feel like the outer skin of life, while something solemn and central pressed on within him, as if an old, half-buried experience had risen again and stood in the doorway, waiting to be named.

The message from Sir Hugo had been brief, jagged, and unlike him: Come immediately. Something has happened. Daniel went as a man goes through familiar rooms at night, guided by memory, yet aware that the house is altered. Even the street had a different character to his ear: the wheels, the calls, the opening and shutting of doors seemed to form a harsh chorus, a city-song too intent on commerce to be gentle. Underneath it he felt the craving for some steadier sound—wind in trees, a quiet human voice—something that would not be bought or sold. It was strange to notice this, and yet it was precisely in such moments that the world’s noise, with its perpetual insistence, made the inner life harder to hear.

He found Sir Hugo in his study, and the baronet’s greeting struck him at once as a thing changed. It was affectionate, yes, but grave; it was not the genial ease that usually filled the room like a warm fire. Daniel had come fearing distress—some blow to Sir Hugo, some misfortune to be met with cheerful resolution—and there was relief in finding no visible calamity, only an emotion held down, as if it were heavy.

“It is nothing to grieve you, sir?” Daniel said, and surprised himself by the steadiness he tried to keep, as he took the hand offered to him.

Sir Hugo looked at him with an unusual meaning, and his voice, when it came, seemed to have been softened by much thinking. “No, Dan—no. Sit down. I have something to say.”

Daniel obeyed. The chair, the table, the papers, the familiar objects had the sharp distinctness of things seen just before a storm breaks.

“It is not to grieve you, my boy—no,” Sir Hugo began again, as if reassuring himself while he reassured Daniel. “At least—if there is nothing in it that will grieve you too much. But I hardly expected that this—just this—would ever happen. There have been reasons why I have never prepared you for it. Reasons why I have never told you anything about your parentage. But I have striven in every way not to make that an injury to you.”

He paused. Daniel could not answer. It was not that he had a ready protest—You have never injured me—locked behind pride. It was that the words were too small for what he had lived with. Through all the years, that absence of knowledge had been like a dish set always covered on the table of his mind: the daily bread of affection and education served around it, yet the covered thing still there, never named, never offered. One learns, by necessity, to eat and be grateful; but the scent of what is withheld can mingle with every meal. He could not trust his voice.

Sir Hugo watched him, and the man who had delighted in Daniel’s noble look saw it now drained of color, the lips pressed together as if pain were being held in by force. A new anxiety softened Sir Hugo’s tone into almost a plea, as if he feared he might at last bruise what he had so carefully fostered.

“I have acted,” he said, “in obedience to your mother’s wishes. The secrecy was her wish. But now she desires to remove it. She desires to see you.” He drew out a letter and held it toward Daniel. “I will put this into your hands. You can look at it by-and-by. It will merely tell you what she wishes you to do, and where you will find her.”

The paper was foreign—its smoothness and faint, unfamiliar smell seemed to carry a hint of distance, of other rooms and voices, of another climate. Daniel took it and thrust it into his breast-pocket with instant relief at not having to read it there, under Sir Hugo’s eyes, while his own face betrayed whatever upheaval was passing within him. He felt as if a door had been opened on a corridor of his life he had never been allowed to enter.

The act of giving the letter shook Sir Hugo more than Daniel had expected. His composure, never theatrical, had been the habit of a man who believed that good intentions could set many things right. Now it wavered; he seemed to struggle for the right words, and for courage to say them.

Daniel’s whole soul, meanwhile, was possessed by a single question—one that had always been present like a faint ache, but now grew sharp and immediate. It was the hardest in the world to utter. Yet to delay was impossible. The moment had the solemnity of a vow: if he let it pass in silence, he felt he would lose the power to ask, and the answer would hover forever, unspoken, poisoning even gratitude.

For a little while his eyes were cast down, and the silence between them was full—so full that it was as if thoughts had become a palpable atmosphere. The ordinary noises outside, muffled by walls and curtains, beat on faintly, indifferent, while here, in a room made for comfort, two lives were poised over a truth.

At last Daniel lifted his eyes and looked at Sir Hugo. His voice, when it came, had a tremulous reverence in it, as if he feared that even a question might strike like a reproach against years of care. “Is my father also living?”

The answer came at once, low and emphatic, leaving no space for doubt. “No.”

In what followed, Daniel could not have distinguished joy from pain if he had tried. The word No fell like a stone into deep water: there was shock, a spreading circle of feeling, and then a strange hush. It altered retrospect, and yet did not complete it. Sir Hugo too seemed to receive a light thrown backward over his own acts—light that did not flatter him, but compelled him to see plainly.

After a silence in which Daniel felt like one whose old creed has fallen away before a new one can be embraced—left with bare longing and no form of faith to hold it—Sir Hugo spoke again. This time his voice had the tone of confession, stripped of all excuse.

“Perhaps I was wrong, Dan, to undertake what I did. Perhaps I liked it a little too well—having you all to myself. But if you have had any pain which I might have helped, I ask you to forgive me.”

Daniel’s answer came with the quiet truth of something long settled in the heart. “The forgiveness has long been there,” he said. “The chief pain has always been on account of some one else—whom I never knew—whom I am now to know. It has not hindered me from feeling an affection for you which has made a large part of all the life I remember.”

The words seemed to loosen what both had been holding. In one impulse they clasped hands—briefly, firmly—as if to seal, without further speech, the bond that secrecy had strained but never broken. The letter lay against Daniel’s breast like a warm weight, a summons, and beyond the study—beyond the city’s ceaseless, wearing din—there waited a voice that had withheld itself from him, and now called him by right.

“If some mortal, born too soon,”—so the old poet had imagined—“were laid away in some great trance… and could then record the words they spoke who kept watch by his bed.” Daniel Deronda, reading the lines again, felt the strange fitness of them to his own hour: the ages had been moving while he lay, not in a trance of sleep, but in a trance of ignorance; and now, at last, there was to be a watcher who would speak.

Sir Hugo had put a letter into his hand—quietly, as if passing a dish across a table whose fragrance must not be remarked on too eagerly.

TO MY SON, DANIEL DERONDA.

“My good friend and yours, Sir Hugo Mallinger, will have told you that I wish to see you. My health is shaken, and I desire there should be no time lost before I deliver to you what I have long withheld. Let nothing hinder you from being at the Albergo dell’ Italia in Genoa by the fourteenth of this month. Wait for me there. I am uncertain when I shall be able to make the journey from Spezia, where I shall be staying. That will depend on several things. Wait for me—the Princess Halm-Eberstein. Bring with you the diamond ring that Sir Hugo gave you. I shall like to see it again.—Your unknown mother,

LEONORA HALM-EBERSTEIN.”

The words were pale as water drawn from a deep well—no warmth, no savor, nothing that clung to the mind the way a remembered broth clings to the nostrils when one has been ill and starving. Yet the very bareness had weight. It left him no clue, and he could not press Sir Hugo for one: the baronet’s reticence had the air of a pledge, a sealed cask he must not broach before the owner came.

And with the discovery that all his lifelong conjectures had been mistaken, he found further guessing checked, as if the tongue, prepared for one familiar taste, were suddenly offered something unknown and was wiser to wait than to pretend a judgment. His imagination, swift as flame over dry twigs, ran along possibilities; but he would not let any one possibility become a favorite. He refused to season his mind with desire or repugnance in advance. Whatever the truth might be, he meant to meet it bravely, cleanly, without the cowardice of wishes.

In that mood he could not tell anyone the true reason for the absence he must announce in certain quarters. Least of all could he tell Mordecai; to say, “I am going to learn the truth about my birth,” would be to strike a match in tinder. Mordecai’s hope would flare into a dangerous brightness. So Deronda spoke of his journey as undertaken at Sir Hugo’s wish, and forced into his tone as much indifference as he could manage; he said he was uncertain how long he should be away, perhaps only a short time.

Mordecai’s eyes, after their first mournful searching, turned away as if to find some remedy in the ordinary.

“I will ask to have the child Jacob to stay with me,” he said, catching at that consolation with the eagerness of a man who clings to sound when sight is troubled.

“I will drive round and ask Mrs. Cohen to let him come,” Mirah answered—quick, affectionate, practical, as if she were already at the door with her bonnet strings in her fingers.

“The grandmother will deny you nothing,” Deronda said.

Then, because the strain between them all was too dear to be left without some play of light upon it, he added with a smile, “I’m glad you were a little wrong as well as I. You thought that old Mrs. Cohen would not bear to see Mirah.”

“I undervalued her heart,” Mordecai said, gently reproving himself. “She is capable of rejoicing that another’s plant blooms though her own be withered.”

“Oh, they are dear good people,” Mirah said; there was a small ripple of merriment in her smile, like a spoon’s faint clink against a cup—tenderness finding its way into sound. “I feel as if we all belonged to each other.”

Deronda, with the mischievousness that comes sometimes from love of one’s own claim, said, “What should you have felt if that Ezra had been your brother?” He was a little provoked that she had taken kindly, so quickly, to people who had caused him so much prospective annoyance on her account.

Mirah looked at him in mild surprise, then answered, “He is not a bad man—I think he would never forsake any one.”

But as she said it, the color rose suddenly and deeply in her cheeks. She glanced timidly at Mordecai, and turned away as if to busy her hands with some small task. The words had betrayed her: her father stood behind them like a shadow at midday. “If he should come and find us!”—that thought sometimes made the street daylight to Mirah as uncertain as a haunted forest where each corner might hide an apparition.

Deronda understood; he felt the blush as one feels a sudden hush in a room when a forbidden name is spoken. And how could he be slow to understand, now, when his own life was suddenly shot through with a like dread of painful conditions? That cold letter, announcing a mother and keeping her away, brought her nearer as a fact and remoter as an object of tenderness. For years he had nursed, without fully owning it even to himself, an image of a mother wronged by circumstance—a being whose life might have been the worse for lacking his care, whose dues of reverence or compassion might have gone unpaid. That image had mingled itself with his observation of women, coloring it as a warm sauce colors a plain dish. But now the handwriting itself, the actual words, had chilled his affections into a guarded neutrality. A veiled figure with enigmatic speech had thrust away the mother he had fashioned in longing.

So that when he set off to Genoa, the interest uppermost in his mind was scarcely his mother—rather Mordecai and Mirah, and all the new current of duty and feeling they had poured into him.

Sir Hugo, when they shook hands, had tried to cover seriousness with a flurry of talk, as if he were rattling the cutlery so no one should hear the heart beat.

“God bless you, Dan!” he said. “Whatever else changes for you, it can’t change my being the oldest friend you have known, and the one who has all along felt the most for you. I couldn’t have loved you better if you’d been my own—only I should have been better pleased with thinking of you always as the future master of the Abbey instead of my fine nephew; and then you would have seen it necessary for you to take a political line. However—things must be as they may.”

Deronda reached the Albergo dell’ Italia in Genoa on the appointed day, but there was no Princess Halm-Eberstein. The first night he lay listening to the hotel’s life—the corridor footsteps, the hollow closing of doors, the distant clatter of plates being carried away late from some Englishman’s supper—and in those sounds, as in a sort of acoustic map, he felt himself alone among strangers, suspended between what he had been and what he might become.

On the second day a letter came. Her arrival might be within a week, or it might be deferred a fortnight and more. Circumstances made it impossible to fix the journey more precisely. She entreated him to wait as patiently as he could.

Indefinite waiting—on a matter that would decide the very flavor of his being—was like being kept hungry with the promise of a meal whose hour kept shifting. He set himself, with that disciplined pride which was part of him, to seek amusement on philosophic grounds, as one might take a measured walk to quiet a fever. His former visit to Genoa had been cursory; now he wandered in the cooler hours, studying the city beyond the prescribed sights—turning into narrow lanes where laundry stirred like pale flags, and then emerging into open spaces where the sea-wind came salted and clean. He went often to the quay; and often he hired a boat so that, from the water, the superb curve of the harbor and the city’s rising terraces might enter him with their grandeur as bread enters a starving man.

Yet every sight, every subject, even the anticipated meeting with his mother, found itself drawn into a central union with Mordecai and Mirah. As his boat pushed and turned within view of the great harbor, he kept remembering another scene that had once stained that splendid quay—multitudinous Spanish Jews, centuries ago, driven destitute from their homes, allowed to land only for a brief rest, overspreading the stone with famine and plague. He saw them in imagination as if the air still held their voices: dying mothers with dying children at their breasts, fathers and sons staring at each other’s haggardness as if they had been thrust out of a hundred Hunger-towers into the pitiless midday. The thought returned in waves, and with it—inevitably—dreamy constructions about his own possible ancestry, weaving themselves into those historic memories which Mirah had already made vivid, and which Mordecai’s influence had rendered dominant.

He tried to seal his mind against those constructions. He had not yet fully admitted to himself that he wished the facts to verify Mordecai’s conviction. Wishing, on the question of parentage, seemed to him a mean thing—an anticipatory disowning. He repeated inwardly that he had no choice; his task was to accept what was. There had been resolved concealment; inference was untrustworthy; even his name might be false.

And yet—if Mordecai were wrong, if Daniel Deronda were bound by ties entirely aloof from the course of life his friend’s hope had marked out—Deronda would not say “I wish,” but he could not prevent himself from feeling where the sacrifice would fall. The thought pressed like a hand on his chest.

Across those importunate musings came another anxiety, one he did not banish but rather dwelt on with a mournfulness that seems, at times, the only atonement possible when one cannot help the suffering of another. He was anxious for Gwendolen.

It was not the exclusive passionate love some men and women are capable of; it was something distinct—neither friendship, nor merely benevolent regard. It was nearer than anything to the half-confessed phrase, “I should have loved her, if—”: the “if” covering both an inward history and an outward law. In Deronda’s case the “if” had reasons of both kinds. He had never been free, in his relations with Gwendolen, from a nervous consciousness that there was something to guard against—not only for her sake, but for his own: some precipitancy, some ruinous inroad of what is momentary upon what he had chosen as permanent, some spoiling of her trust. Now that trust haunted him like a sound. Her words—he must remain near her, must not forsake her—came back with the clearness and insistence of imagined noises in the night, arrows tipped with pity that pierce and will not be shaken out.

How could his feelings toward her ever be exactly like his feelings toward other women, even when there was one by whose side he desired to stand apart from them? Strangely, her figure entered into the pictures of his present and future; strangely, and now sadly, their lots had touched—hers narrowly personal, his possibly charged with far-reaching sensibilities and durable purposes, hardly more present to her than the reasons why men migrate are present to the birds that come as usual for crumbs and find them no more. Not that he imagined himself of supreme importance; but her insistence had laid hold of him. It was as though the sea had once lifted a swimmer and then withdrawn, leaving him with the memory of that support and the fear of the next undertow.

Day after day passed, and Italy itself seemed to carry in its air the knowledge that war had been declared against Austria, and that each day was a hurried step of crowded Time toward the world-changing battle of Sadowa. Genoa’s noons grew hotter; the outer roads converging on the city deepened with white dust. Oleanders in tubs along the wayside gardens looked more and more like fatigued holiday-makers, their flowers drooping as if thirst had made them human. Then evening would change her office—scattering abroad those whom midday had driven under shelter—and the paths would be sown with social sounds: the delicate tinkling of mule-bells, the whirr of thrummed strings, light footsteps and voices with pleasure in their haste. The encircling heights, crowned with forts and skirted with villas and gardens, seemed to wake from their long siesta and gaze down in renewed beauty. Strong color melted into moonlight, and the streets became a new spectacle—shadows lying still on cathedral steps or gliding across the façades of massive palaces. Later, as the moon descended, all sank into deep night and a silence that felt like a closed hand, until only the port lights of the great Lanterna shone in the blackness below, and the stars glimmered in the blackness above.

Deronda watched the revolving of the days as one watches a wonderful clock whose striking is made solemn by antique figures advancing and retreating in procession. His ear, always his most faithful sentinel, kept itself open for another signal—the knock, the message, the change. He began to sicken of occupation; all activity looked remote, as if he were a prisoner awaiting ransom. In letters to Mordecai and Hans he avoided writing about himself; yet he was sinking into that state of mind where every subject turns personal. The few books he had brought grew unreadable: the mind will not take ink when life is about to write its own sentence.

Many nights he watched from his open window, looking out on the double darkness—sea and sky, each faintly pierced. Sometimes he struggled under a heavy skepticism which made his lot, and the importance Mordecai gave it, seem no more lasting than a dream—mere shifts of mass and shadow in a universe indifferent to consciousness. Sometimes there came a reaction of feeling that made even disappointment, even sacrifice, seem like satisfied energy, and spread over his youth—whatever it was to be—the attraction of devoted service. Sometimes a sweet, irresistible hopefulness rose: that the best human possibilities might be granted him, personal love flowing in one current with larger duty. And sometimes, too—as no human creature escapes—there came rebellion against things in general because they were thus and not otherwise: a mood in which Gwendolen and her equivocal fate moved as busy images of what was amiss in the world, alongside the concealments that had been his own hardship, now taking the shape of an afflicting doubt about the mother who had announced herself coldly and still delayed.

At last she was come.

One morning, in his third week of waiting, there was a new kind of knock at the door—different in rhythm, carrying with it, like a footfall in a silent house, the certainty of meaning.
