A servant entered in Chasseurs livery and delivered, in French, the verbal message that the Princess Halm-Eberstein had arrived; she intended to rest during the day, but would be obliged if Monsieur would dine early, so as to be at liberty at seven, when she would be able to receive him.

She held the spindle as she sat, Errina with the thick-coiled mat  
Of raven hair and deepest agate eyes,  
Gazing with a sad surprise  
At surging visions of her destiny—  
To spin the byssus drearily  
In insect-labor, while the throng  
Of gods and men wrought deeds that poets wrought in song.

When Deronda presented himself at the door of his mother’s apartment in the Italia, something long-buried in him stirred awake—not tenderness exactly, but that earlier boyhood tremor, like the first thin cry of a kettle before water boils. Even the antechamber made him newly aware of sound: the hush was not natural quiet, but the manufactured stillness of thick curtains and trained servants, with the sea outside held back as if by a door’s consent. The two attendants looked at him with a marked surprise, as if expecting a physician with old hands and a leather case of tinctures, not this young man whose evening dress sat on him as easily as a well-cut jacket on a chef who knows his own worth.

But he scarcely saw them. The second door opened, and the room beyond—large, dimly mellowed, and arranged like a stage awaiting a single entrance—offered him at its far end a figure standing to receive him.

She was covered, save her face and part of her arms, in black lace that fell loosely from the summit of whitening hair and lengthened behind her in a train. The lace looked like sea-foam turned to mourning, light and intricate, yet weighted with intention. Her arms, bare to the elbow except for rich bracelets, were folded, and her head had that poised habit which makes a face seem handsomer than it is by giving it authority. Deronda had no interval for examining; he was already near, taking the hand she held out—cool, fine-boned, with a firmness that suggested not domestic caress but command—and lifting it to his lips.

She did not withdraw. She kept his hand in hers and looked at him as if measuring a story she had once rehearsed and now found altered by time. Her eyes were piercing; her face so mobile that even while she watched him, the shift of brow and nostril spoke like a dialect he could feel without knowing its words. Deronda dared no movement. His chief consciousness was his own strange helplessness: the long private imaginings, those ideal meetings with a mother made tender by absence, had been more vivid than this. He felt his color rise and fall with the quick shame of youth, while emotion itself—warmth, joy, grief—hung back, as if waiting for a cue. He could not even guess what language she would choose. It seemed impossible that she should speak plain English.

Suddenly she dropped his hand, placed both hers on his shoulders, and her face gave out a flash of admiration in which every worn line vanished, as if light had poured through her from some earlier hour.

“You are a beautiful creature!” she said, in a low melodious voice, the syllables edged with a foreign outline that made English itself seem like an adopted tongue. “I knew you would be.” Then she kissed him on each cheek, and he returned the kisses; yet it was like a ceremonial greeting between royalties, not the meeting of flesh that has remembered flesh.

She paused—lines returning to her face as if they belonged there and could not be kept away—and her tone cooled.

“I am your mother. But you can have no love for me.”

“I have thought of you more than of any other being in the world,” Deronda answered, his voice trembling with nervousness rather than tears.

“I am not like what you thought I was,” she said decisively, withdrawing her hands and folding her arms again, inviting him—almost challenging him—to look. He had often pictured a face akin to his own. He saw the likeness now, but set within differences more striking. Her beauty was worn, yet not softened by time; it had a strangeness in it, as if she were not wholly a human mother but a Melusina—half-bound to some world that keeps its own laws and does not ask ours.

“I used to think you might be suffering,” he said, anxious above all not to wound. “I used to wish I could be a comfort to you.”

“I am suffering. But with a suffering that you can’t comfort,” she replied, harder than before, moving to a sofa where cushions had been placed with the careful solicitude of servants accustomed to guarding a precious, temperamental instrument. “Sit down.” She pointed to a seat near. And then, noticing his distress, she added more gently, “I am not suffering at this moment. I am at ease now. I am able to talk.”

He sat and waited. Already she had thrown him to a distance—not by space, but by the air of inevitability around her, as if he had come not to a mother but to a Fate that had decided long ago and was only now explaining the decree.

“No,” she began. “I did not send for you to comfort me. I could not know beforehand—I don’t know now—what you will feel toward me. I have not the foolish notion that you can love me merely because I am your mother, when you have never seen or heard of me in all your life. But I thought I chose something better for you than being with me. I did not think I deprived you of anything worth having.”

“You cannot wish me to believe that your affection would not have been worth having,” Deronda said, because her pause seemed to demand answer.

“I don’t mean to speak ill of myself,” she flung out with proud impetuosity. “But I had not much affection to give you. I did not want affection. I had been stifled with it. I wanted to live out the life that was in me, and not to be hampered with other lives. You wonder what I was. I was no princess then.” She rose suddenly and stood again, and Deronda rose too without thinking; he felt as if the air itself had altered.

“No princess in this tame life that I live in now. I was a great singer, and I acted as well as I sang. All the rest were poor beside me. Men followed me from one country to another. I was living a myriad lives in one. I did not want a child.”

The words had the vehement edge of self-defence, spoken as if she were hurling them against a tribunal that had waited years for her confession. Deronda stood listening—his hand clutching his coat-collar as if he were keeping himself from sinking—while his blood moved in him with the bewildered commotion one might feel at witnessing a rite that sanctifies what one has been taught to call crime. What else was she going to tell him? Her face had that pale illumination of a performer in tragic passage, and she went on.

“I did not want to marry. I was forced into marrying your father—forced, I mean, by my father’s wishes and commands; and besides, it was my best way of getting some freedom. I could rule my husband, but not my father. I had a right to be free. I had a right to seek my freedom from a bondage that I hated.”

She sat again; her eyes and closed lips made that subtle movement which is like speech held back only because breath must be gathered. Deronda remained standing. After a moment she looked up with less defiance and more pleading.

“And the bondage I hated for myself I wanted to keep you from. What better could the most loving mother have done? I relieved you from the bondage of having been born a Jew.”

“Then I am a Jew?” The question burst from him with a deep-voiced energy that made her shrink back against her cushions. “My father was a Jew, and you are a Jewess?”

“Yes—your father was my cousin,” she said, watching him with a change as if she had seen something she might need to fear.

“I am glad of it,” he said, impetuously, in the veiled voice of passion.

He could not have imagined beforehand that the admission would come like that—hot and sudden, not as the quiet acceptance of a truth, but as opposition to her. Anger shook through him—anger at a mother who had borne him unwillingly, made herself a stranger by choice, and who now seemed to reveal herself under compulsion. That last suspicion flashed a light over her speech.

Her anger rose too, visibly physical. Her frame trembled; her pallor made her eyes look larger.

“Why do you say you are glad? You are an English gentleman. I secured you that.”

“You did not know what you secured me. How could you choose my birthright for me?” Deronda answered, throwing himself sideways into his chair as if the posture could help him hold down the surge inside him. He leaned his arm over the back and looked away.

The intolerance in him felt foreign, like a voice borrowed from someone harsher; and already he struggled to master it. With the anger came horror—horror lest he speak too hard in a moment that could never be called back. A pause fell. When she spoke again, her tone had hardened into a composed resistance, finely varied, like a singer controlling breath.

“I chose for you what I would have chosen for myself. How could I know that you would have the spirit of my father in you? How could I know that you would love what I hated?—if you really love to be a Jew.”

The bitterness made her words sound like enmity. Yet Deronda’s fuller self returned; his mind reached out, as it habitually did, to the life within the other person. He remembered the signs of suffering in her frame, the best years gone, the effort of speaking. His face regained its penetrative calm; and that calm, instead of soothing her, seemed to disturb her like an unwelcome mirror.

“Forgive me, if I speak hastily,” he said with diffident gravity. “Why have you resolved now on disclosing to me what you took care to have me brought up in ignorance of? Why—since you seem angry that I should be glad?”

“Oh—the reasons of our actions!” She gave a ring of sarcastic scorn. “When you are as old as I am, it will not seem so simple a question—‘Why did you do this?’ People talk of their motives in a cut and dried way. Every woman is supposed to have the same set of motives, or else to be a monster. I am not a monster, but I have not felt exactly what other women feel—or say they feel, for fear of being thought unlike others. When you reproach me in your heart for sending you away from me, you mean that I ought to say I felt about you as other women say they feel about their children. I did not feel that. I was glad to be freed from you. But I did well for you, and I gave you your father’s fortune. Do I seem now to be revoking everything?—Well, there are reasons. I feel many things that I cannot understand. A fatal illness has been growing in me for a year. I shall very likely not live another year. I will not deny anything I have done. I will not pretend to love where I have no love. But shadows are rising round me. Sickness makes them. If I have wronged the dead—I have but little time to do what I left undone.”

Every change of tone was as perfectly delivered as any trained actress could manage; and yet it was sincere—her nature turned feeling into representation at once, so that truth and performance were not enemies but twin threads, braided tightly. Deronda did not reflect on that. He heard only the purport: illness, approaching death, and an obligation to the dead. Compassion rose and forbade him to press her with questions while she sat silent, brow knit, head turned slightly away, eyes fixed as if on something in the air that only she could see.

She broke the silence abruptly, turning her eyes on him, speaking more quickly.

“Sir Hugo has written much about you. He tells me you have a wonderful mind—you comprehend everything—you are wiser than he is with all his sixty years. You say you are glad to know that you were born a Jew. I am not going to tell you that I have changed my mind about that. Your feelings are against mine. You don’t thank me for what I did. Shall you comprehend your mother, or only blame her?”

“There is not a fibre within me but makes me wish to comprehend her,” Deronda said, meeting her sharp gaze solemnly. “It is a bitter reversal of my longing to think of blaming her. What I have been most trying to do for fifteen years is to have some understanding of those who differ from myself.”

“Then you have become unlike your grandfather in that,” she returned, “though you are a young copy of him in your face. He never comprehended me—or if he did, he only thought of fettering me into obedience. I was to be what he called ‘the Jewish woman’ under pain of his curse. I was to feel everything I did not feel, and believe everything I did not believe.”

She spoke of it as of a house whose smells still clung to her hair and skin—old oil and wax and shut-up cloth, the sour breath of long fasts, the heavy sweetness of festival dishes that came to her not as comfort but as coercion. Her voice sharpened with remembered disgust.

“I was to feel awe for the bit of parchment in the mezuza over the door; to dread lest a bit of butter should touch a bit of meat; to think it beautiful that men should bind the tephillin on them, and women not,—to adore the wisdom of such laws, however silly they might seem to me. I was to love the long prayers in the ugly synagogue, and the howling, and the gabbling, and the dreadful fasts, and the tiresome feasts, and my father’s endless discoursing about our people, which was a thunder without meaning in my ears. I was to care forever about what Israel had been; and I did not care at all. I cared for the wide world, and all that I could represent in it.”

As she said “howling” and “gabbling,” Deronda’s mind—trained to attend—could almost hear the soundscape she described: a crowded room of male voices swelling and breaking, the clatter of benches, the insistent rhythm of words repeated until sense dissolves into sound. It came to him how such noise could become an enclosure, how a life might feel driven by it as surely as by walls. And yet in him, the same rituals were gathering another meaning, not from habit but from hunger: the desire to know the tongue of origins, to taste what had been withheld, to name himself with the old names rather than borrowed ones.

She continued, the words pressing forward as if they had waited years behind her teeth.

“I hated living under the shadow of my father’s strictness. Teaching, teaching for everlasting—‘this you must be,’ ‘that you must not be’—pressed on me like a frame that got tighter and tighter as I grew. I wanted to live a large life, with freedom to do what every one else did, and be carried along in a great current, not obliged to care. Ah!” Her tone cut more bitterly. “You are glad to have been born a Jew. You say so. That is because you have not been brought up as a Jew. That separateness seems sweet to you because I saved you from it.”

“When you resolved on that, you meant that I should never know my origin?” Deronda asked, the question coming out with the urgency of someone who has been fed on substitutes and has suddenly smelled the real broth.

“Yes, that was what I meant. That is what I persevered in. And it is not true to say that I have changed. Things have changed in spite of me. I am still the same Leonora”—she pointed with her forefinger to her breast—“here within me is the same desire, the same will, the same choice, but—” She spread her hands, palms upward, on each side as if showing emptiness. Her voice fell into muffled rapid utterance. “Events come upon us like evil enchantments: and thoughts, feelings, apparitions in the darkness are events—are they not? I don’t consent. We only consent to what we love. I obey something tyrannic.” Again the spread hands. “I am forced to be withered, to feel pain, to be dying slowly. Do I love that? Well, I have been forced to obey my dead father. I have been forced to tell you that you are a Jew, and deliver to you what he commanded me to deliver.”

“I beseech you to tell me what moved you—when you were young, I mean—to take the course you did,” Deronda said, trying to draw her away from the present’s heart-rending mixture of suffering and defiance. “I gather that my grandfather opposed your bent to be an artist. Though my own experience has been quite different, I enter into the painfulness of your struggle. I can imagine the hardship of an enforced renunciation.”

“No,” she said, shaking her head, folding her arms again with decision. “You are not a woman. You may try—but you can never imagine what it is to have a man’s force of genius in you, and yet to suffer the slavery of being a girl. To have a pattern cut out—‘this is the Jewish woman; this is what you must be; this is what you are wanted for; a woman’s heart must be of such a size and no larger, else it must be pressed small, like Chinese feet; her happiness is to be made as cakes are, by a fixed receipt.’”

The metaphor startled him with its domestic cruelty—happiness measured like ingredients, womanhood baked to a prescribed shape, any appetite beyond the recipe treated as sin. And behind it he felt another theme beating, older than their quarrel: how language itself, the naming and defining, can be a cage—how a dominant lexicon writes a person’s possibilities as if writing a menu that forbids hunger.

“That was what my father wanted,” she went on. “He wished I had been a son; he cared for me as a make-shift link. His heart was set on his Judaism. He hated that Jewish women should be thought of by the Christian world as a sort of ware to make public singers and actresses of. As if we were not the more enviable for that! That is a chance of escaping from bondage.”

“Was my grandfather a learned man?” Deronda asked, eager for particulars, fearing her fierce generalities would pass over the details that might anchor him.

She answered impatiently, lifting her hand. “Oh, yes,—and a clever physician—and good: I don’t deny that he was good. A man to be admired in a play—grand, with an iron will. Like the old Foscari before he pardons. But such men turn their wives and daughters into slaves. They would rule the world if they could; but not ruling the world, they throw all the weight of their will on the necks and souls of women. But nature sometimes thwarts them. My father had no other child than his daughter, and she was like himself.”

Her folded arms and set gaze were like armor, as if she expected mastery to strike again from the past.

“Your father was different. Unlike me—all lovingness and affection. I knew I could rule him; and I made him secretly promise me, before I married him, that he would put no hindrance in the way of my being an artist. My father was on his deathbed when we were married: from the first he had fixed his mind on my marrying my cousin Ephraim. And when a woman’s will is as strong as the man’s who wants to govern her, half her strength must be concealment. I meant to have my will in the end, but I could only have it by seeming to obey.”

Her voice changed; something like an involuntary tremor entered it.

“I had an awe of my father—always I had had an awe of him: it was impossible to help it. I hated to feel awed—I wished I could have defied him openly; but I never could. It was what I could not imagine: I could not act it to myself that I should begin to defy my father openly and succeed. And I never would risk failure.”

The last sentence fell with abrupt emphasis, like a knife set down on a board. She paused, and Deronda, listening, felt his own emotions re-arranging. The first repulsion at her frank coldness, the first indignation at what jarred his deepest instincts—these began to subside. In their place came his accustomed effort toward just allowance, and with it an unwilling admiration for a nature violently alive, whose errors lay along high pathways rather than low. Yet he could not be dispassionate. He trembled at what she might say next, feared the coercion that seemed to drive her to lay bare her mind, and still felt that terrible fascination which makes one listen even when every word burns.

He tried again to recall her to concrete things, as if particulars could be a rope thrown across a chasm.

“Where was my grandfather’s home?”

“Here in Genoa, where I was married; and his family had lived here generations ago. But my father had been in various countries.”

“You must surely have lived in England?”

“My mother was English—a Jewess of Portuguese descent. My father married her in England. Certain circumstances of that marriage made all the difference in my life: through that marriage my father thwarted his own plans. My mother’s sister was a singer, and afterward she married the English partner of a merchant’s house here in Genoa, and they came and lived here eleven years.”

As she spoke, the room seemed to fill with an older Genoa: merchants’ footsteps on stone, the salt-and-tar breath of the port rising into narrow streets, voices in shifting languages—Italian, English, Hebrew—each carrying its own music, each insisting on its own meanings that did not translate cleanly into the others. Deronda felt, almost physically, how a life might be torn between tongues, how memory itself can be eroded when the words that held it are forbidden or mocked.

“My mother died when I was eight years old,” she continued, “and my father allowed me to be continually with my Aunt Leonora and be taught under her eyes, as if he had not minded the danger of her encouraging my wish to be a singer, as she had been. But this was it—I saw it again and again in my father:—he did not guard against consequences, because he felt sure he could hinder them if he liked. Before my aunt left Genoa, I had had enough teaching to bring out the born singer and actress within me: my father did not know everything that was done; but he knew that I was taught music and singing—he knew my inclination. That was nothing to him: he meant that I should obey his will.”

Her voice had the old heat again.

“And he was resolved that I should marry my cousin Ephraim, the only one left of my father’s family that he knew. I wanted not to marry. I thought of all plans to resist it, but at last I found that I could rule my cousin, and I consented. My father died three weeks after we were married, and then I had my way!”

She uttered those words with a brief exultation, like someone remembering the first mouthful of forbidden fruit. Then her face changed; bitterness tightened her mouth.

“It has not lasted, though. My father is getting his way now.”

She looked at Deronda with renewed contemplation, as if he were both evidence and consequence.

“You are like him—but milder—there is something of your own father in you; and he made it the labor of his life to devote himself to me: wound up his money-changing and banking, and lived to wait upon me—he went against his conscience for me. As I loved the life of my art, so he loved me. Let me look at your hand again: the hand with the ring on. It was your father’s ring.”

Deronda drew his chair nearer and gave her his hand. Her own hand—much smaller—was of the same type: the same long, firm fingers, the same shape as if the family had carried its identity not only in faces and names but in the tools by which they might have worked, blessed, broken bread. Her fingers closed around his with a grip that felt less like a mother’s possession than like a musician’s recognition of an instrument.

As he felt her hand holding his, and saw the face that bore a likeness to his own—aged not by time’s gentle wearing but by intensity—something in him that was deeper than indignation asserted itself: that reverential tenderness which made him long to heal even what he could not approve. In his most fervent tone he said,

“Mother! take us all into your heart—the living and the dead. Forgive everything that hurts you in the past. Take my affection.”

She looked at him admiringly rather than lovingly; then she kissed him on the brow. The kiss was light, like a sign made for meaning, not for warmth.

“I reject nothing,” she said sadly, “but I have nothing to give.”

She released his hand and sank back on her cushions. Deronda turned pale with that pain which is less emotion than sensation—the sharp ache of tenderness repulsed, as if one had offered bread and found the other could not taste it. She saw the pain in his face, and said, still with melodious melancholy in her tones,

Among Deronda’s letters next morning there lay one from Hans Meyrick—four quarto pages in the small, careful hand that seemed hereditary in that house, as if even their flourishes were a family recipe.

Deronda opened it with the faint foreknowledge of what he should find there: an overflow of fancy, a peppering of jokes, and now and then—like a sharp herb in a rich sauce—some sentence that bit deeper than the writer intended.

Hans began, as usual, by turning public affairs into a private farce, tossing “time will show” in the air as lightly as if it were a catch to be made in play. He wrote of cattle plague and swindling telegrams, of compensation to farmers, and then—by some merry leap—of a murrain threatening to break out in the commercial class, the symptom to be the ready purchase of rejected pictures. He made his own ambition into a jest, imagining his “Berenice series” fetching a great price at the hands of men who deserved punishment for rewarding him by accident.

Then he passed into the subject Deronda could never read without a change in his pulse—Mirah and Mordecai, those lives that had come to hang upon his own conscience with a weight he never flaunted. Hans, in his bright way, called Mordecai “our Hebrew prophet,” and described sitting with him in the hours when Deronda used to be there, making studies of his head, getting credit as a learned young Gentile “who would have been a Jew if he could,” and agreeing with him—half in mockery, half in real admiration—that whatever was best must therefore be Jewish.

Hans’s letter ran on, nimble and various as a street musician’s medley: a picture of Jacob Cohen on Mordecai’s knee, stopping his ears with his palms to hear Hebrew through muffled hands, then being gently restrained; Jacob’s face darting through expressions as if he were trying on animals in a menagerie, owl and peccary most of all. Hans made sport of it, but even through the sport there came a kind of tenderness—an unwilling acknowledgment of the bond between the invalid dreamer and that too-quick child. And there, too, was Hans’s confession, thrown out as if it were no more than a flourish: that Mirah’s presence distracted him into longing, that if she were less of a heaven to look at he would have flung himself at her feet and demanded whether she meant him to live or die; that he lived on “Hope” as if on an estate in reversion, and kept away from the ugly two-faced god “Certainty.”

Deronda read the allegories with a patience sharpened by knowledge of Hans’s nature. The imagery was like a kitchen where everything fragrant was brought in at once—blossom and spice and smoke—so that what should have been nourishing became for the reader a little cloying. Yet, as always, the letter could not keep to jesting. Hans spoke of Mirah as seeming “a little sadder,” as if she were constantly trying to hide it; and he spoke too of watching “the slow death of this brother” whom she worshipped with such loving devoutness that Hans, half in envy, half in compassion, could almost wish himself in that place.

Then came more news: Rex Gascoigne in town with a neat sister; cousinship discovered between that sister and “your Vandyke duchess”; invitations jostling—one to a rectory in August, another to Topping Abbey where Sir Hugo meant Hans to paint his three daughters in a Gainsborough attitude on a bank. Hans turned even Sir Hugo’s kindness into a comic lecture on “the hinder wheel,” and then, with a careless drop of information as if it were nothing, mentioned that the duchess was gone yachting to the Mediterranean—adding a string of nonsense about whether Deronda would land from a yacht and continue a theological discussion with her.

At the close, Hans excused his “brevity,” boasted of the Klesmers’ splendid generosity—Mirah “rich with their oriental gifts”—and ended with his old devotion and his new Hebrew lore, offering to go below the triliteral roots if Mirah commanded, but declaring that while her brother lived she would not listen to a lover.

Deronda laid the letter down. Months earlier, this kind of romancing about Mirah would have fretted him, not least because it carried so little reverence for the strain Mirah lived under, so little fear of hurting what was delicate. But since March, the centre of his own life had shifted. Mirah was no longer so critically placed under the Meyricks’ roof and protection; and his own future, though still without any pictured certainty, had been altered and—only lately—crowned by the revelation of his birth. That knowledge, like a new light admitted into a familiar room, changed the look of every old object: even Hans’s extravagant “Hope” no longer seemed a mischievous insolence, but the bird-like skipping of a mind too restless to sit down with sorrow. Deronda found himself arguing, almost coldly, that Hans could not love with roots deep enough to make disappointment into grief: he was too excitable by novelty, too quick to turn everything—even pain—into imaginative material, to wear his feeling like a costume and drop it when another fancy offered a better colour.

“Already he is beginning to play at love,” Deronda said inwardly. “He is taking it as comedy. He knows there is no chance for him. And he never even considers that his outpourings may jar on me—never opens his eyes to any reason I could have to dislike them. Poor Hans! If we were under fiery hail together, he would howl like a Greek; and if I did not howl too, it would never occur to him that I was as badly off. And yet he is affectionate, tender-hearted in intention. He imagines other people’s feelings—only always in the shape most convenient to his own inclination.”

That touch of caustic thought cooled the slight heat his friend’s expansiveness had raised. The mention of Gwendolen—yachting with her husband—stirred a darker disturbance, the thought of his own strange parting from her returning like a sound heard at night when one would rather not listen. But it was not the duchess, nor Sir Hugo, nor Hans’s allegories, that held him. One sentence had lodged like a thorn.

“I wish I did not imagine that Mirah gets a little sadder, and tries all the while to hide it.”

Deronda could not dismiss that as mere romantic embroidery. Hans’s observation here ran counter to his own wishes; and because it ran counter, he was the more apt to credit it. A cause began to shape itself in his mind, anxiously, as if he were feeling along the edge of a wound.

Had something happened in his absence? Or was it only the slow growth of fear? Was there something in the new life arranged for Mirah—something that, while seeming a refuge, carried its own humiliations? Or—this struck him most sharply—had Mordecai, against his habitual reticence, spoken to her of those cherished hopes in which Deronda himself was made to figure? Had Mirah, with her quick sensitiveness, been hurt by finding that her brother’s will, his tenacity of vision, pressed upon Deronda’s friendship like a claim? Might she have feared that what looked like equal regard was, in truth, pity and self-suppression—Deronda lowering himself out of compassion? For beneath Mirah’s quiet renunciation there lay a hunger—no, a thirst—for the acknowledgment that meets one soul on level ground. And if that tribute of equality was sweet, then its withdrawal—or the suspicion that it had never been sincere—must bring a pain she would hide rather than display.

In that insight into Mirah’s nature Deronda was not mistaken. He understood, by an affinity of feeling, what protest lay latent in her gratitude—gratitude sharpened by the memory of a life in which people had thought any coarse charity enough for her. But he was wrong to imagine that Mordecai had broken his reserve. Mordecai had breathed to no one but Deronda the history of their relation, or his confidence about Deronda’s origin; not only because those subjects were sacred, but because he had discerned Deronda’s shrinking from any handling of his birth, and would not thrust speech where a silence was a protection.

Mirah herself had once let her own tendency betray her.

“Ezra,” she had said one day, with a half-smile at herself, “how is it? I am continually going to speak to Mr. Deronda as if he were a Jew.”

Mordecai smiled quietly. “It is because he treats us as if he were our brother. But he loves not to have the difference of birth dwelt upon.”

“He has never lived with his parents, Mr. Hans says,” Mirah continued—because to her, whose own life had been all torn from the natural shelters, such things were not idle curiosity but the search for some clue to every dear person’s wound or strength.

“Seek not to know such things from Mr. Hans,” Mordecai said gravely, and laid his hand on her curls in the familiar blessing-like gesture. “What Daniel Deronda wishes us to know about himself is for him to tell us.”

Mirah felt rebuked. Yet the rebuke from Mordecai did not humiliate her; it lifted her. It made her proud—proud of his dignity, proud of being near a soul that could command itself so.

And that pride, that reverence, ran deep. One day, calling at the Chelsea house on her way home, she found the little mother alone, and her heart—tired with holding itself in—turned to speech.

“I see no one so great as my brother,” Mirah said. “It is difficult to think that he belongs to the same world as those people I used to live amongst. I told you once they made life seem like a madhouse; but when I am with Ezra, he makes me feel that his life is a great good, though he has suffered so much. Not like me, who wanted to die because I had suffered a little—and only for a little while. His soul is so full, it is impossible for him to wish for death as I did.”

Her voice, always gentle, carried a dove-like melancholy—as if tenderness itself were weighted. She went on, trying to shape what she felt into something that could be shared.

“I get the same sort of feeling from him that I got yesterday, when I was tired, and came home through the park after the sweet rain had fallen and the sunshine lay on the grass and flowers. Everything in the sky and under the sky looked so pure and beautiful that the weariness and trouble and folly seemed only a small part of what is; and I became more patient and hopeful.”

Mrs. Meyrick, who had been stitching, let her work fall. She looked at Mirah more closely. At a little distance Mirah’s attitude—hands and feet crossed, her curls pressed flat as if she had smoothed herself into calm—might have been taken for serenity carved and coloured. But to Mrs. Meyrick’s motherly scrutiny there was in her face a new strain, as if patience and hopefulness now needed to be summoned like music to keep back an oppressive silence.

“Is there any fresh trouble on your mind, my dear?” she asked, with that quick, practical tenderness which does not pretend not to see.

Mirah hesitated. “I am too ready to speak of troubles, I think. It seems unkind to put anything painful into other people’s minds—unless one were sure it would hinder something worse. And perhaps I am too hasty and fearful.”

“Oh, my dear,” Mrs. Meyrick said, leaning forward, “mothers are made to like pain and trouble for the sake of their children. Is it because the singing lessons are so few, and likely to fall off when the season comes to an end? Success can’t come all at once.”

“No,” Mirah said, gently shaking her head. “I have been a little disappointed because so many ladies said they wanted me to give them—or their daughters—lessons, and then I never heard of them again. But perhaps after the holidays I shall teach in some schools. Besides—you know—I am as rich as a princess now. I have not touched the hundred pounds Mrs. Klesmer gave me. And I should never be afraid that Ezra would be in want of anything, because there is Mr. Deronda; and he said, ‘It is the chief honor of my life that your brother will share anything with me.’ Oh, no! Ezra and I can have no fears for each other about such things as food and clothing.”

“But there is some other fear on your mind,” Mrs. Meyrick said, her voice lower, as if making room for what must be spoken. “A fear of something that may disturb your peace. Don’t be forecasting evil unless it is what you can guard against. Anxiety is good for nothing if we can’t turn it into a defense. But there’s no defense against all the things that might be. Have you any more reason for being anxious now than you had a month ago?”

“Yes, I have,” Mirah answered, and the words came as if they had been held down and now rose against her will. “I have kept it from Ezra. I have not dared to tell him. Pray forgive me that I can’t do without telling you. I have more reason for being anxious. It is five days ago now. I am quite sure I saw my father.”

Mrs. Meyrick seemed to draw herself into a smaller space, folding her arms tight across her chest and leaning forward, as if bodily bracing against the impulse to fling hard words—like stones—at that distant figure.

“The year has changed him,” Mirah continued, her voice steady but thin. “He had already been much altered and worn in the time before I left him. You remember I said how he used sometimes to cry. He was always excited one way or the other. I have told Ezra everything that I told you, and he says my father had taken to gambling, which makes people easily distressed, and then again exalted. And now—it was only a moment that I saw him—his face was more haggard, and his clothes were shabby. He was with a much worse-looking man, who carried something, and they were hurrying along after an omnibus.”

“Well, child,” Mrs. Meyrick said, with anxious eagerness held in check by her effort to be calm, “he did not see you, I hope?”

Before Deronda was called again to his mother, a day slipped by in which she sent only a brief message: she was not yet well enough to see him. The delay had the strange effect of repeating itself in his nerves, like a refrain heard from a far room—now louder, now dying away—until, on the third morning, a note came with a quick, decisive stroke in the words: “I leave to-day. Come and see me at once.”

He was led into the same chamber as before, but it had been turned into a kind of twilight cell: blinds drawn, curtains thickened, daylight filtered and made solemn, as if even the sun had been asked to lower its voice. The house’s ordinary sounds—footsteps in a passage, a door’s soft click—seemed sharpened by the hush, and Deronda felt how silence itself can press upon the mind like a weight. There was no homely comfort of tea-service clinking, no friendly domestic stir—only that muffled quiet which, in great rooms, makes the heart listen too much.

The Princess was not there at first. Then she entered, and the dimness gathered around her as if it belonged to her. She wore a loose wrap of soft silk, dusky orange like the smoulder of an ember under ash, and black lace floated about her head. Her arms showed bare beneath wide sleeves, and in that sombre light her face looked more commanding than ever—eyes enlarged by shadow, lines more resolute, the whole countenance having the authority of someone who has long ago refused to plead.

One might have fancied her a woman who could brew marvels—philtres of youth or courage—yet would not spend the least drop on herself; as if she had tasted enough of all sweet potions and found them, in the end, thin.

She came straight to him, put her arms on his shoulders, and kissed him on both cheeks. Then she seated herself among her cushions with a composed firmness that differed from her former fitfulness, and with a gesture bade him sit near.

“You are quite relieved now, I trust?” he said.

“Yes, I am at ease again.” Her voice was steady, queenly rather than maternal. “Is there anything more that you would like to ask me?”

“Can I find the house in Genoa where you used to live with my grandfather?” Deronda asked.

“No,” she answered, with a slight, dismissing movement of her arm. “It is pulled down—not to be found. But about our family, and where my father lived at various times—you will find all that among the papers in the chest, better than I can tell you. My father, I told you, was a physician. My mother was a Morteira. I used to hear all those things without listening. You will find them all. I was born amongst them without my will. I banished them as soon as I could.”

He felt the words as one feels the cutting of a thread that had been held taut in hope. Yet he tried to keep his pain from showing.

“Anything else that I should desire to know from you,” he said quietly, “could only be what it is some satisfaction to your own feeling to tell me.”

“I think I have told you everything that could be demanded of me,” she said, her gaze fixed, coldly meditative, as if she were closing a case and sealing it.

To her, the confession had been a storm already spent. She had resolved not to be flung into that weather again; she would keep herself, now, in order. But to Deronda the moment was cruel in a different fashion: it was the end of a pilgrimage where he had expected—if not tenderness—at least some shrine-lamp of emotion to burn. Instead, he found a sacred place emptied.

All the womanly yearning she denied seemed to wake in him, and it trembled in his voice. “Then are we to part and I never be anything to you?”

“It is better so,” she said, and though her tone softened, it did not yield. “There could be nothing but hard duty for you, even if it were possible for you to take the place of my son. You would not love me. Don’t deny it.” She lifted her hand sharply, forbidding any protest. “I know what is the truth. You don’t like what I did. You are angry with me. You think I robbed you of something. You are on your grandfather’s side, and you will always have a condemnation of me in your heart.”

Deronda felt himself struck dumb—not because he had no answer, but because any answer seemed either false or a weapon. He rose, preferring to stand rather than sit under that command to be untender.

Then she looked up at him, and admiration—unexpected, almost alarming—came into her eyes.

“You are wrong to be angry with me,” she said. “You are the better for what I did.”

After a pause, she added, with abruptness, “And now tell me what you shall do?”

“Do you mean now, immediately,” he said, “or as to the course of my future life?”

“I mean in the future. What difference will it make to you that I have told you about your birth?”

“A very great difference,” Deronda answered, with an emphasis that surprised even himself. “I can hardly think of anything that would make a greater difference.”

“What shall you do then?” Her sharpness returned. “Make yourself just like your grandfather—be what he wished you—turn yourself into a Jew like him?”

“That is impossible. The effect of my education can never be done away with. The Christian sympathies in which my mind was reared can never die out of me.” His voice grew tenacious, like a hand tightening on a truth. “But I consider it my duty—it is the impulse of my feeling—to identify myself, as far as possible, with my hereditary people; and if I can see any work to be done for them that I can give my soul and hand to, I shall choose to do it.”

She watched him with a strange, searching attention, as if his face were written in a dialect she could not read but would master by force of staring. He bore her gaze, steadied by opposition which was not defiance but fidelity to the deepest part of himself.

She bent toward him. “You are in love with a Jewess.”

The color rose in his face. “My reasons would be independent of any such fact.”

“I know better. I have seen what men are.” Her tone was final, as if it pronounced sentence. “Tell me the truth. She is a Jewess who will not accept any one but a Jew. There are a few such,” she added with scorn.

To argue with certainty is to waste breath; it is like trying to soften iron by speaking warmly to it. And besides, this was a point on which Deronda felt a repugnance either to deny or affirm. He remained silent.

She took his silence for confession and went on: “You love her as your father loved me, and she draws you after her as I drew him.”

The comparison struck through him—filial imagination kindled, tenderness rose unbidden. His glance softened; she read it as assent.

“But I was leading him the other way,” she said, passion swelling. “And now your grandfather is getting his revenge.”

“Mother,” Deronda said, and the word itself was an appeal, “don’t let us think of it in that way. I will admit that there may come some benefit from the education you chose for me. I prefer cherishing the benefit with gratitude, to dwelling with resentment on the injury. I think it would have been right that I should have been brought up with the consciousness that I was a Jew; but it must always have been a good to me to have as wide an instruction and sympathy as possible. And now—you have restored me my inheritance—events have brought a fuller restitution than you could have made—you have been saved from robbing my people of my service and me of my duty: can you not bring your whole soul to consent to this?”

He paused, pleading with voice more than with argument. She listened as if the cadence itself worked on her—sound can sometimes enter where meaning is barred—yet she shook her head slowly.

He began again, more urgent, as if time were thinning. “You have told me that you sought what you held the best for me: open your heart to relenting and love toward my grandfather, who sought what he held the best for you.”

“Not for me, no,” she said, shaking her head with an absolute denial, folding her arms tightly, closing herself like a gate. “I tell you, he never thought of his daughter except as an instrument. Because I had wants outside his purpose, I was to be put in a frame and tortured. If that is the right law for the world, I will not say that I love it. If my acts were wrong—if it is God who is exacting from me that I should deliver up what I withheld—who is punishing me because I deceived my father and did not warn him that I should contradict his trust—well, I have told everything. I have done what I could. And your soul consents. That is enough. I have after all been the instrument my father wanted.—‘I desire a grandson who shall have a true Jewish heart. Every Jew should rear his family as if he hoped that a Deliverer might spring from it.’”

As she spoke these last sentences her eyes narrowed; she waved her head slowly up and down, the words coming in a new, reluctant chest-voice, as if she were quoting an old chant she hated yet could not forget.

“Were those my grandfather’s words?” Deronda asked, as if he had heard a key-note struck to something vast.

“Yes, yes; and you will find them written. I wanted to thwart him,” she burst out, the old fire flashing. Then, more slowly: “You would have me love what I have hated from the time I was so high”—she held her left hand a yard from the floor—“That can never be. But what does it matter? His yoke has been on me, whether I loved it or not. You are the grandson he wanted. You speak as men do—as if you felt yourself wise. What does it all mean?”

Her scorn came like a sudden harsh note in the chamber’s hush, and Deronda felt how words can bruise when the air is too still. Under the solemn urgency of parting he had to clutch at the mere fact of their relationship, lest his speech turn cruel.

“Mother,” he said, in a deep entreating tone, “don’t say that I feel myself wise. We are set in the midst of difficulties. I see no other way to get any clearness than by being truthful—not by keeping back facts which may—which should carry obligation within them—which should make the only guidance toward duty. No wonder if such facts come to reveal themselves in spite of concealments. The effects prepared by generations are likely to triumph over a contrivance which would bend them all to the satisfaction of self. Your will was strong, but my grandfather’s trust which you accepted and did not fulfill—what you call his yoke—is the expression of something stronger, with deeper, farther-spreading roots, knit into the foundations of sacredness for all men. You renounced me—you still banish me—as a son—” indignation moved in his voice despite him—“but that stronger Something has determined that I shall be all the more the grandson whom also you willed to annihilate.”

She watched him fixedly, and again admiration gathered on her face, as if strength—any strength—was the one thing she could still prize without surrender.

After a silence she said, low and persuasive, “Sit down again.” He obeyed and took his place beside her.

She laid her hand on his shoulder; it trembled, though she tried to hold it steady. “You rebuke me. Well—I am the loser. And you are angry because I banish you. What could you do for me but weary your own patience? Your mother is a shattered woman. My sense of life is little more than a sense of what was—except when the pain is present. You reproach me that I parted with you. I had joy enough without you then. Now you are come back to me, and I cannot make you a joy. Have you the cursing spirit of the Jew in you? Are you not able to forgive me? Shall you be glad to think that I am punished because I was not a Jewish mother to you?”

“How can you ask me that?” Deronda said, shocked into protest. “Have I not besought you that I might now at least be a son to you? My grief is that you have declared me helpless to comfort you. I would give up much that is dear for the sake of soothing your anguish.”

“You shall give up nothing,” she said hurriedly, agitation breaking through her command. “You shall be happy. You shall let me think of you as happy. I shall have done you no harm. You have no reason to curse me. You shall feel for me as they feel for the dead whom they say prayers for—you shall long that I may be freed from all suffering—from all punishment. And I shall see you instead of always seeing your grandfather. Will any harm come to me because I broke his trust in the daylight after he was gone into darkness? I cannot tell:—if you think Kaddish will help me—say it, say it. You will come between me and the dead. When I am in your mind, you will look as you do now—always as if you were a tender son—always—as if I had been a tender mother.”

The strange plea—half command, half beseeching—filled the room more than any loud cry could have done. Deronda’s compassion rose until it shut in speech; words felt poor and blunt. He put his arm around her and drew her head gently under his, as if sheltering her from the very air. They sat so for some moments, in that dense hush where even breathing seemed a kind of utterance.

Then she lifted her head and rose with a great sigh, as if she dismissed a multitude of thoughts in a single breath. Deronda stood before her, and felt the parting near like the approach of a cold dawn.

One of her swift changes came again.

“Is she beautiful?” she asked abruptly.

“Who?” he said, changing color.

“The woman you love.”

There was no time for careful explanation; he could only answer, “Yes.”

“Not ambitious?”

“No, I think not.”

“Not one who must have a path of her own?”

“I think her nature is not given to make great claims.”

“She is not like that?” The Princess drew from her wallet a miniature set round with jewels and held it out.

It was herself in the fire of youth: a face made for gaze and music, for the bright tyranny of applause. Deronda looked at it with admiring sadness; in that painted bloom he could almost hear the old theatre’s rustle—the eager coughs, the tuning strings, the roar that rises when a voice fills a hall like warmed wine poured into cold mouths. Yet all that brilliance was now in his mother’s hand like a relic of a life already entombed.

“Had I not a rightful claim to be something more than a mere daughter and mother?” she said. “The voice and the genius matched the face. Whatever else was wrong, acknowledge that I had a right to be an artist, though my father’s will was against it. My nature gave me a charter.”

“I do acknowledge that,” Deronda said, looking from the miniature to her face, which even in worn pallor had a force beyond what any pencil could catch.

“Will you take the portrait?” she asked more gently. “If she is a kind woman, teach her to think of me kindly.”

“I shall be grateful for the portrait,” Deronda said; then, compelled by honesty even in this hour, he added, “but—I ought to say, I have no assurance that she whom I love will have any love for me. I have kept silence.”

“Who and what is she?” The question fell like an order.

“She was brought up as a singer for the stage,” he said, reluctance tightening his throat. “Her father took her away early from her mother, and her life has been unhappy. She is very young—only twenty. Her father wished to bring her up in disregard—even in dislike of her Jewish origin, but she has clung with all her affection to the memory of her mother and the fellowship of her people.”

“Ah, like you,” the Princess said peremptorily. “She is attached to the Judaism she knows nothing of. That is poetry—fit to last through an opera night. Is she fond of her artist’s life—is her singing worth anything?”

“Her singing is exquisite. But her voice is not suited to the stage. I think that the artist’s life has been made repugnant to her.”

“Why, she is made for you then,” said the Princess. “Sir Hugo said you were bitterly against being a singer, and I can see that you would never have let yourself be merged in a wife, as your father was.”

“I repeat,” Deronda said, and his emphasis had the steadiness of someone bracing himself against a gust—“I repeat that I have no assurance of her love for me, of the possibility that we can ever be united. Other things—painful issues may lie before me. I have always felt that I should prepare myself to renounce, not cherish that prospect. But I suppose I might feel so of happiness in general. Whether it may come or not, one should try and prepare one’s self to do without it.”

“Do you feel in that way?” She laid her hands on his shoulders and studied his face, speaking slowly, with pauses, as if each thought were heavy to move. “Poor boy!—I wonder how it would have been if I had kept you with me—whether you would have turned your heart to the old things against mine—and we should have quarrelled—your grandfather would have been in you—and you would have hampered my life with your young growth from the old root.”

“I think my affection might have lasted through all our quarrelling,” Deronda said, sorrow deepening, “and that would not have hampered—surely it would have enriched your life.”

“Not then, not then—I did not want it then—I might have been glad of it now,” she said bitterly, “if I could have been glad of anything.”

“But you love your other children, and they love you?” he asked anxiously, as if clinging to any possibility of warmth in her world.

“Oh, yes,” she answered, as if it were a matter of course, folding her arms again. Then, in a deeper tone: “But I am not a loving woman. That is the truth. It is a talent to love—I lack it. Others have loved me—and I have acted their love. I know very well what love makes of men and women—it is subjection. It takes another for a larger self, enclosing this one”—she pointed to her bosom. “I was never willingly subject to any man. Men have been subject to me.”

“Perhaps the man who was subject was the happier of the two,” Deronda said, not smiling—only grieving, as one grieves over a hunger that has never even learned to name itself.

“Perhaps—but I was happy—for a few years I was happy. If I had not been afraid of defeat and failure, I might have gone on. I miscalculated. What then? It is all over. Another life! Men talk of ‘another life,’ as if it only began on the other side of the grave. I have long entered on another life.”

With the last words she raised her arms till they were bare to the elbow; her brow contracted into one deep fold; her eyes closed; her voice grew smothered. In her dusky, flame-coloured garment, with black lace like mourning smoke about her, she looked like a dreamed visitant from a region where the dead still remember the taste of earthly triumph and find it ashes.

Deronda’s feeling rose to a point where he was no longer master of himself. A sob broke from him—audible, helpless, like the voice of something young inside him that had at last understood.

She opened her eyes, and once more let her hands rest on his shoulders.

“Good-bye, my son, good-bye. We shall hear no more of each other. Kiss me.”

He clasped his arms round her neck, and they kissed each other—an embrace that was less reunion than final recognition.

Deronda did not know how he got out of the room. He went away with the sensation of having crossed an inner boundary: as if some boyish part of him, that had lived on yearning and unanswered questions, had been left behind in that darkened chamber. The anxious pilgrimage was ended; the shrine had not given him what he had once imagined, but it had given him something weightier—a tragic knowledge which would solemnize his life, and deepen forever the meaning of every bond he chose to make.

“The unwilling brain feigns often what it would not.” The line has the sound of oars in black water: a steady dip and lift that keeps time with thoughts one would rather not hear. And there are lives in which the mind, like a galley-slave, pulls at its own chain—pulls until the air is full of the creak of strained timber and the low slap of consequences against the hull.

There was once, in an older story, a woman carried away to the Maremma, to the flats where the very ground seems to breathe fever. Her removal was meant for punishment and became, by the strange justice of the elements, a kind of deliverance: the marsh that was to imprison her also took her husband’s triumph from him. That figure stands in an Italian poem asking only to be remembered kindly. But pity grows finer by comparison; and if one turns from that far-off legend to the young English wife now afloat on the Mediterranean, one feels how much crueller it is to be kept, not in a visible prison of stone and swamp, but in the invisible net of one’s own consent—knots tied by one’s own hand.

Grandcourt had brought Gwendolen yachting with no wish to cast her off. He wished, rather, to possess her more completely: to have her beyond the reach of drawing-rooms, beyond the reach of sudden visits and arranged encounters, beyond the reach of the one man whose name, once spoken in her mind, made her heart beat as if it had found its native measure. He liked the sea for himself—the dreamy absolutism of it, the way hours could be smoked away with nothing demanded but the turning of a glass and the giving of a brief order. There was no modern clatter of carriages, no fashionable music turned into a commodity, no thickened air of other people’s voices. The world fell silent except for wind and cordage and the obedient footfalls of men paid to be quiet. For a nature like his, that silence was not peace but power.

His reasons, stated plainly, did not sound like wickedness. He suspected opposition in her, a growing inward stiffening against his will; and what he would have named “jealousy” in another man he allowed himself only as a practical resolve—to end the “foolery” he believed had been planned with Deronda, and which he had interrupted in London as one snaps a thread between finger and thumb.

And, had he defended himself, he might have made the defense plausible. The marriage was a contract. All the visible advantages had been given to her: the rank, the wealth, the handsome provision for her mother—more, indeed, than she had dared to bargain for. He had paid; he expected the purchased thing.

Gwendolen knew it too. She could not sincerely take refuge in the notion that she had meant—without saying so—to rule. She had been indulged, spoilt, trained by the easy admiration of others into believing her whims were laws; yet she had, under all that, a root of conscience. It was bitter to feel it alive now, like a seed that has sprouted in darkness and hurts as it forces its way.

Set her, then, on that small moving island of planks, with the Mediterranean a blue division between her and the world she knew. Set her within the domain of the husband to whom she felt she had sold herself—and sold not only her youth and her smile, but her truthfulness, her sense of justice, the very inward voice that says No and means it. Those faculties seemed collared and dragged, compelled to look on, compelled to be silent.

And what, outwardly, had she to complain of? The yacht was a pretty toy, as if devised by those who think beauty can hush any pain. The cabin was fitted to perfection: cedar breathed its warm, clean resinous scent from panels and drawers; silk hangings held a faint sweetness like dried rose-leaves hidden among linen; cushions yielded with an inviting softness, and mirrors made the space seem larger, multiplying her own face back at her—her own eyes returned again and again, as if the glass had become an accomplice to her self-watching. The crew were picturesque, attentive, trained to make their presence part of the pleasure; one had ringlets, and bronze skin, and the show of fine teeth—an elegance even in service. Mr. Lush was gone back to England as soon as he had seen the yacht fairly launched into its private tyranny. The sea did not make Gwendolen ill, at least not often; and there were moments when the logic of rope and sail, the forecast of necessary adjustments, might have gratified her old relish for command—command without responsibility, imagination playing at rule.

The weather was fine. They coasted southward where cracked clay on the shore, seamed by heat and rain, can glow as if set with gems under purple shadows; where sky and water answer each other in blues so deep they seem to promise that sorrow has been outgrown, as childhood outgrows a fright. The air had salt in it, sharp and clean; it entered the lungs like a draught meant to revive.

But there are hungers no landscape feeds. There are paradises that, for a soul in moral revolt, become only perfumed prisons. The very ease oppresses; the sweet smell of cedar turns heavy, as if it had absorbed sighs. In the evening, when Gwendolen lay throned on cushions and watched the sea-sky soften into that tender glory which makes lovers believe the world was made only to hold their joy, she was not thinking of beauty. She was thinking—hoping—that Grandcourt would not pause near her; would not look at her; would not speak. And somewhere, under a smoky city sky, a woman counting the price of eggs for her dinner might be listening for a step that meant safety and happiness; somewhere, a couple might be bending cheek to cheek over work, counting their earnings with the quiet confidence of companionship—while Gwendolen, surrounded by luxuries, could have envied the homely clink of a pan, the familiar crackle of a hearth, the honest noise of a kitchen where speech is free and affection has a dialect.

Grandcourt did not conceive what was happening in her. He understood that she did not love him; but why should she? Love, to him, was not a necessary condition of possession. What lay entirely beyond him was the idea that she could feel repulsion toward him—personal repulsion, deeper than dislike, a moral nausea. He had been critical all his life; he knew what it was to be disgusted by other people—by their smirks, their vulgarities, their “odious familiarities,” their costumes and scents and foolish efforts to please. He understood her repulsion for Lush because it matched his own. But that his own person—Henleigh Grandcourt—could be the object of such shrinking loathing, he could not imagine. He had too long taken his own attractiveness for granted; too long set himself in flattering contrast to other men whom he assumed must be revolting. Moral repulsion—the resentment that makes even beauty hateful because it gives hateful things a kind of advantage—was as inconceivable to him as the existence of a language he could not buy.

Outwardly, nothing betrayed them. No observer could have found scandal—not the foreign maid who had escaped sea-sickness, not the valet with his seasoned eyes, not the deck-hands who saw in the pair a model of high-bred composure. Their companionship was chiefly silence—silence so well-bred it seemed an ornament. Grandcourt had no playful talk to invite refusal, no pleasantries to provoke quarrel. He could be punctiliously polite, arranging an extra wrap over her shoulders when the wind sharpened, handing her any object he noticed she wanted. She, with pride enough to hate vulgarity more than pain, could not accept or reject such politeness rudely.

He would put up his telescope and say, “There’s a plantation of sugar-canes at the foot of that rock; should you like to look?”

“Yes, please,” she would answer, forcing herself to be interested in sugar-canes—green spears rising by the shore, promise of sweetness made into commodity—anything outside the circle of her own misery.

Then he would pace and smoke, the soft scrape of his shoe and the faint click of his ring against the rail marking time like a metronome. Sometimes he would point at a sail on the horizon. At last he would sit and look at her with that narrow, immovable gaze, as if she were part of the yacht’s equipment—a chosen object, a possession that completed the elegance of his floating despotism. And she, feeling the look like a cold finger, would exert all her ingenuity not to meet his eyes.

At dinner he would remark that the fruit was getting stale and they must put in somewhere for more; or, seeing she did not drink wine, would ask if she preferred another kind. There was always something for a lady to answer suitably. And besides, quarrelling with him was impossible. One might as well argue with a coiled serpent displayed as an ornament: its stillness is not peace but readiness, and you cannot make it ashamed.

He took intense satisfaction in having her captive in this small world. It gave him a kind of royal publicity without society: everything familiar was swept away; every person, paid or bound, did what was expected, whatever private protest might be choking them. The protest, kept private, sharpened the flavor of command for him the way a bitter herb makes a rich dish more piquant.

To Gwendolen, who in her girlhood had scarcely glimpsed heroism except as a theatrical attitude, the medium thrust before her everywhere was this husband—this relation that turned the world into a distorted glass. Those closest to us are often our interpreters of life; and the dull, trivial sentences of some companion, their petty standards, their loveless ennui, can become for another a theory of existence—like looking through yellow, wavy panes that warp forms and make color an affliction. Grandcourt’s presence did that to her: it stained the far horizon, so that even the sea’s clean music—the wash against the planks, the sighing of rope, the brief cries of gulls—could not be heard as comfort, only as part of an enormous silence where her own thoughts sounded too loud.

Some wives are soothed by the hope of motherhood. For Gwendolen, the idea came not as deliverance but as a horror. To desire a child for herself would have been, she felt, consenting to the completion of her own wrong. She dreaded it, as one dreads an additional chain.

In those fluctuating stages of despair, hope came in strange forms—often, in the imagined benignity of accident. A sudden fall, a storm, a blow from the rigging: any event that would end this life without her choosing to end it. To dwell on accident was a refuge from darker temptation.

And temptation did not come as a neat thought she could dismiss. It came like an illness of the mind, a fevered hand reaching out. Hatred, especially hatred rooted in fear, grows in ways onlookers cannot measure by outward cause. It feeds inwardly, like a seed drawing nourishment from the very substance of the soul, until all currents run toward it. In Gwendolen’s secrecy there were “hidden rites” of vengeance—imagined annihilations, visions that rose unbidden and would not be spoken. Yet they did not soothe; they terrified her, because with the dread of Grandcourt had grown the dread of herself. She began to fear not only what he could do, but what she might do, impulsively, as if in a dream—waking at once to find effects real though the images had been false: a death under her hands; daylight instead of darkness; guilt instead of freedom; and forever after a white dead face that she fled and could not escape.

She could not separate any imagined act from the image of Deronda’s judgment. He had become, in her mind, the listener to whom she could not lie—not because he demanded confession, but because her better self had awakened under his regard. No flattery from him, no indulgence, no dependence she could seize on to soften his power: his very restraint had made his influence more binding. Whatever remedy existed seemed to lie in him, or in what she felt toward him; and yet that feeling itself was a torment, because it made her more conscious of what she had become. He stood in her imagination like an angel with terrible brows: not a comforter who would excuse, but one before whom she must be truthful or be nothing.

She remembered his words as one remembers a melody that haunts the ear even in sleep:

“Turn your fear into a safeguard. Keep your dread fixed on the idea of increasing your remorse… Take your fear as a safeguard. It is like quickness of hearing. It may make consequences passionately present to you.”

Yes—her fear was like quickness of hearing. In the great hush of the sea, every inward footstep sounded distinct. Temptation and dread met in her as two pale phantoms, staring, each seeing itself in the other and blocking the way. And behind them, her fuller self looked on and sobbed—sobbing without words, because there are feelings that lose their meaning when translated into the common coin of speech.

Often, in the night, inarticulate prayers—no more shaped than a cry—went out of her into the vastness. The silence around was broken only by Grandcourt’s breathing, the soft plash against the hull, the creaking of masts—sounds that in another life might have been lullaby, but now seemed to measure time in a sentence she must endure. And if she thought of definite help, it took the form of Deronda’s presence: his voice, his guidance, his sympathy that did not cheapen her by pretending her wrong was small. Sometimes, after a fierce, white-lipped temptation had visited her like a demon with murdering fingers, the better moment came: she would lie with wide-open eyes, tears rising—tears that felt like a blessing because they proved she was not all stone—and the thought would shape itself simply: I will not mind—if I can keep from getting wicked.

Days passed: light breezes about the Balearic Isles, then Sardinia, then a gentle persuasion northward toward Corsica. The routine of meals, the laying of the table, the opening of fruit, the tasting of wine offered and refused, the salt on the lips, the sun-warmed smell of deck-planks—these domestic details of floating life might have made a little idyll. But to Gwendolen the gentleness became nightmare, because it left her alone with herself. Even the sea’s music—so pure of the industrial roar that makes modern art a thin performance against machinery—could not cleanse her inward noise.

“How long are we to be yachting?” she ventured one day, after they had touched at Ajaccio and the simple act of going ashore—hearing other voices, other steps, other languages—had given her a moment’s relief, as if her mind had stepped into a different acoustical air.

“What else should we do?” Grandcourt answered. “I’m not tired of it. I don’t see why we shouldn’t stay out any length of time. There’s less to bore one in this way. And where would you go to? I’m sick of foreign places. And we shall have enough of Ryelands. Would you rather be at Ryelands?”

“Oh, no,” she said, indifferently—because every place, once she imagined herself in it with him, became the same prison, only with a different view.

“I only wondered how long you would like this.”

“I like yachting longer than anything else,” he said. “And I had none last year. I suppose you are beginning to tire of it. Women are so confoundedly whimsical. They expect everything to give way to them.”

“Oh, dear, no!” She let her scorn out in a flute-like tone—thin, high, controlled. “I never expect you to give way.”

“Why should I?” he said, in that inward voice of his, and looked at her while choosing an orange, as if even the fruit must be selected with the calmness of dominion.

She forced herself to imagine yachting stretched into an endless line she could not see the end of. But the next day a squall came in the night—“the devil’s own work,” Grandcourt called it—and for the first time the sea made her ill, shaking her as if to loosen her from herself.

In the morning he came down to her. She lay very white amid white drapery, her throat dry with that bitter taste which sickness leaves, as if the body itself had turned against all sweetness.

“There’s been the devil’s own work in the night,” he said. “The skipper says we shall have to stay at Genoa for a week while things are set right.”

“Do you mind that?” she asked. Even her languor could not prevent a faint lift of hope.

“I should think so. Who wants to be broiling at Genoa?”

“It will be a change,” she said, incautiously, because the word change sounded like water to a thirsty mouth.

“I don’t want any change. Besides, the place is intolerable; and one can’t move along the roads. I shall go out in a boat, as I used to do, and manage it myself. One can get a few hours every day in that way instead of striving in a damnable hotel.”

A few hours every day—alone. The phrase fell into her mind like the first smell of bread to a starving person: not because it was luxury, but because it was life. Instantly her imagination, wild and contradictory, began to play with freedom—running away, which she had so often argued down as a worse evil than endurance, now returning with new reasons; and, alongside it, that other visionary relief—the lawful wish that something outside her will might break the prison wall for her, as a night wind might blow down stones and save a captive from desperate deeds.

Expectation revived her. She moved and spoke with a cheerfulness that was almost alacrity; her senses, long dulled by inward dread, sharpened as if a door had opened. The evening air smelled of salt and distant land; the shore-breath carried hints—tar, citrus, smoke from kitchens—like fragments of other lives. She watched through the dimming lights to the moon’s sinking with less of her usual awe, even with a vague impression that the mighty frame of things might be preparing rescue for her. Hope, after long starvation, returned like the first honest hunger to a languishing patient.

She was waked next morning by the anchor dropping in Genoa’s harbor—a heavy chain running out with a harsh, metallic music that seemed to bind the yacht to earth. She woke from a dream strangely mixed: she was escaping over the Mont Cenis, and found it warmer even in moonlight on the snow—till suddenly she met Deronda, and he told her to go back.

Within an hour or two she met him.

Not on a mountain pass, but on the palatial staircase of the Italia, where she felt warm in her light woollen dress and straw hat, and Grandcourt stood by her side. The hotel air had its own mingled smells—polished stone holding coolness, flowers too lavishly arranged, coffee rising from below with that roasted bitterness that promises comfort but cannot give it to everyone. There were voices in the distance—Italian syllables running together like poured oil, English consonants striking sharper—each language carrying its own memory and power, each making its own kind of world in the ear.

Deronda started—surprise showing itself before he could recover the usual composure. He lifted his hat and passed on. The moment did not allow more; and the circumstances of their last parting made him doubtful whether Grandcourt would even permit a civil glance.

Grandcourt, on seeing Deronda there—Deronda, in Genoa of all places—felt at once the hot stir of suspicion. He tried immediately to conceive what arrangement could have brought this about: what message, what letter sent from Marseilles or Barcelona, what preconcerted flight of a man who seemed able to perch anywhere at will. Cool-headed as he was, he saw the improbabilities; he did not, even in anger, commit himself to inventions others might call preposterous. Yet Deronda’s presence remained—disgusting, insoluble. And that was enough.

A man out of temper does not wait for proofs before feeling the world in conspiracy. He kicks the dog because the rain falls. Grandcourt felt toward Gwendolen and Deronda as if he knew them to be leagued against him; and this meeting at Genoa seemed an event in league with them. What he took to be certain—and in this he touched truth—was that Gwendolen now counted on an interview whenever his back was turned.

When they were in their rooms, he sat over his coffee at an angle that allowed him to watch her. He could read her as far as his narrow alphabet allowed. He discerned something—some fresh ease in movement and speech, some peculiar meaning in her eyes as they fell on indifferent things—that he interpreted as secret delight. Her troubles had not marred her beauty. Mrs. Grandcourt was handsomer than Gwendolen Harleth: suffering had given variety to her expression, new play to features, new attitudes in repose and movement; she had gained that nameless something which sometimes makes a woman more interesting after marriage—less sure that the world will answer to her opinion, yet less shy, more deeply human.

This morning the voyage’s supposed benefits seemed suddenly to show themselves as elasticity. When she rose from the table and lifted her two heavily jewelled hands to either side of her neck—a gesture habitual with her—she could not conceal the look of expectation that makes the present bearable, as a man becomes more amiable when he knows he will soon go out. Grandcourt, with an instinct as narrowly correct as a dog’s, saw those signs and gave them one meaning: she was glad—glad because Deronda was near. He did not imagine what else might be in that glow: the desperate gratitude for a single sound in the world that spoke to her in a dialect of conscience, not in the cold dominant lexicon of possession.

Deronda met Gwendolen and Grandcourt on the staircase with an absent look that did not belong to indifference but to inward tumult. He had been summoned to the second interview with the Princess Halm-Eberstein; and within two hours of leaving her he learned she had quitted the hotel. The plain business of his journey—Mainz, the letter from Joseph Kalonymos, the family chest—lay ready like a packed valise at the foot of his mind. Yet he did not move toward it.

Some weight, not to be argued with, held him fast.
