He sat as if under a hand on his shoulder, living again—now with the painful sharpness that comes after the event—those scenes which were “past” only as the seed is past the tree: not ended, but on the point of leafing within him. Alone, he found tears coming, and let them. Compassion shook him for that strange mother’s life—so near his own blood and yet so remote in habit and speech, in the very air of the soul; a woman who had stepped across his path and vanished, leaving behind her a new map of the world. The certitude of ties altered the balance of his hopes and fears; it changed whom he belonged to. He felt as if he had followed, under cover of night, some band of wanderers by mistake, and then morning rose and showed the true tents of kinship pitched far off—calling him with a language he had not yet learned to speak aloud.

With this came a trembling imaginative nearness to the grandfather he had never seen: a man, he was told, of strong impulse and beloved thoughts—impulses, perhaps, that had not died but only slept, and were now stirring within Deronda like a long-inherited appetite. In all his meditation, Mordecai and Mirah were present also, clasping hands with him in that silent alliance by which the living fortify each other when words are too few or too worn. It was like the pressure of fingers in the dark—assurance without explanation.

The bell rang persistently as a signal; its metal insistence cut through the quiet like a nail on glass, and he thought, “I must look into Bradshaw; I must make my preparations and take the next train.” He thought it, as one thinks of eating when the body is numb; and he did nothing. Wishes went on ahead to Mainz, to the chest he was to possess; to London, to the lives that had grown round his heart. But other wishes clung to Genoa with a tenacity like the clinging of wet cloth, and held him there by that obscure compulsion which makes us linger where an interview has the air of final farewell, or where sorrow seems already in the room though not yet named.

He did not shape the thought formally—“I will stay because it is Friday, and I would hear the evening service, and perhaps I may see the Grandcourts again”—but his body obeyed that unspoken resolve. Instead of packing and ringing for his bill, he sat, and his mind went into the synagogue and saw faces that might have looked back on his grandfather; he heard in imagination the Spanish-Hebrew liturgy that had lasted through seasons of wandering generations, like a plant whose seed travels and takes root in foreign earth, making distant coasts kin to the exile’s first home. There was a continuity in that sound—older than any hotel, older than any passport—an acoustic homeland carried in the throat, surviving where dialects die and are replaced by the official tongue.

And his mind went, too, toward Gwendolen: toward the abruptness of their parting, toward the trouble he had seen in her and had not known how to ease. Something in him—half admitted—told him it would be hardness to go away at once without making some effort, in spite of Grandcourt’s probable dislike, to show her that his sympathy had not been a mere moment’s charity. Her voice, when she had spoken most hurriedly and in fear, returned to him with that peculiar force which belongs to phrases uttered at the edge of confession: she had named her mother—her mother’s presence—as if it were a medicine that could be had, if only the hand could reach it.

So he deferred departure, ate his dinner without taste—as if every dish were a wrong dish and every wine a thin shadow—rose quickly, and went to find the synagogue. The streets led him through mingled odors of Genoese evening: the salt of the harbor, damp stone, a breath of frying oil from low kitchens where families fed themselves with the faithful economy of garlic and herbs; and over it the unceasing surf of sound—heels on pavement, voices crossing in Italian and French and English, the clatter of cart-wheels, a far hammering from some workshop that made a harsh modern rhythm against the older human cadences. It seemed to him, with a sudden resentment, that such industrial clamor was always ready to drown what was most delicate in us—the thin thread of remembered prayer, the private tremor of pity.

In the synagogue the voices were fewer than his mind had peopled it with; sparse talithim moved and shook. Dark, keen faces bent and lifted with an easy familiarity in the utterance of awful things—Hebrew dyed with Italian, grave phrases slipping into the warmth of a local accent, as if sacred memory must be kneaded into the daily bread of speech to keep it from drying out. Deronda listened with a bodily attention—each rise and fall of the chant entering him like a scent enters the mind: not to be translated, only to be received. He thought how languages die—not in one dramatic silence, but by degrees, as if a hearth were allowed to go cold; and how with them die whole flavors of feeling, whole ways of naming the world. The dominant lexicon, the language of the street and the office, is always ready with its smooth conveniences; but it pushes aside what is peculiar, what is ancestral, what does not sell. Here, at least, the old words still had mouths.

Yet even among these prayers his thoughts divided; the information he had received earlier that the Grandcourts had gone out boating held a power over him. It made his mind swing, like a door that will not latch, between the liturgy and the quay. He could not keep still after the service. A mournful impatience—perhaps sharpened by his concern for Gwendolen—sent him quickly away through the evening air to his favorite walk by the water, with the dim hope that he might see them returning.

The sun had gone down behind a bank of cloud, and the light that remained was a faint yellow farewell, kissing the waves as they rose and fell restlessly under an active breeze. The strand was lively; voices clustered in knots, shifting, pressing forward; and the sea’s own sound—its broad breathing—was chopped and broken by the sharper noises of men. Deronda, moving slowly but with his senses strung tight, saw a group fix their attention on a sailing-boat advancing swiftly landward, pulled by two men.

There was clamor in various languages. Telescopes were lifted like accusing fingers. Loud statements flew before facts could arrive. Someone said it was the milord who had gone out; another, peering, declared the prostrate figure was miladi. A Frenchman without a glass made a joke—too ready, too polished—about an Englishman drowning his wife according to national practice; an English skipper answered with the blunt violence of our idiom, dismissing it as nonsense that had been through a mining operation and come out dirtier. Then, with a sudden plainness, the decision settled among them: the reclining figure was a woman.

Deronda’s heart leaped and fell in swift alternation. The oar-strokes seemed separated by visions—events possible, impossible—snatches of imagined struggle, a cry, a silence, the sudden white face of consequence. The boat drew near; the shapes grew human. Doubt ended. He saw Gwendolen.

She half raised herself on her hands by her own effort under a heavy covering of tarpaulin and pea-jackets. She was pale as one of the sheeted dead; shivering so that the motion shook her whole frame; her wet hair streamed; and there was in her eyes that wild, amazed consciousness of one who wakens in a world where judgment is impending, and the first faces seen are not friends but officers of fate. The first rower who sprang to land was wet through and ran off at once, as if the very sight of what had happened were intolerable.

Sailors pressed close and for a moment hindered Deronda from getting near. He could only watch as Gwendolen gave frightened glances from side to side and shrank, as if each touch might hurt, while rough bronzed arms helped her out with a tenderness that seemed all the more touching because it was unspoken. Her wet clothes clung about her limbs, heavy as soaked wool, making every step an effort; and she moved with the weakness of one who has fought with water and lost.

Suddenly her wandering eyes fell on Deronda. The change in her was instant, as if she had been looking for him in that crowd and had believed, with the irrational certainty of terror, that he must be there. She tried to stretch out her arms; the men, holding her for her own safety, kept them back; and she said in a muffled voice, the words coming as if forced up from under the sea, “It is come, it is come! He is dead!”

“Hush, hush!” said Deronda, with an authority that was not harsh but necessary, as one quiets a person on the edge of frenzy. “Quiet yourself.”

Then, turning quickly to the men supporting her, he said, “I am a connection of this lady’s husband. If you will get her on to the Italia as quickly as possible, I will undertake everything else.”

They obeyed, glad to have direction. He stayed behind long enough to catch the plain account from the remaining boatman. Grandcourt had gone down irrecoverably; his boat was left floating empty. The two men had heard a cry; they had come up in time to see the lady jump in after her husband, and had got her out fast enough to save her from much harm.

Deronda, with that dreadful piece of certainty lodged in him like a stone, hastened to the hotel. He made sure at once that the best medical help would be called and would not be delayed by ignorance or indifference. Then he telegraphed the event to Sir Hugo, begging him to come forthwith; and he also sent a message to Mr. Gascoigne at the rectory—the nearest known way, he thought, to carry the news to Gwendolen’s mother. For those words of Gwendolen’s, spoken long ago in agitation, returned now with the force of an inspiration: her mother’s presence might be help—might be the one familiar voice that could reach her through the roaring in her ears where the sea and guilt and grief were all one sound.

Deronda did not undress that night. The room allotted him had the faint, stale warmth of a place where other travellers had slept badly and risen early, and from the corridor there came at intervals the soft scuff of a slipper, a door-latch tried and let go, the hush of voices that meant to be mercifully inaudible. Beyond all that—the faintest undertone, as if the sea were still speaking through stone and timber, a long breathing that would not cease. He kept his coat on, as if any loosening of his own habit might admit the day’s calamity more freely into him.

Gwendolen had insisted on seeing him again before she would let her women undress her; and when he came she had been perfectly still—too still, as a flame is still when the air has been withdrawn from it. She had only whispered, with that eager control which was worse than sobbing, that he must promise to come when she sent in the morning. He had promised. And yet he lay down in his clothes with a foreboding that did not belong to imagination but to the trained dread of what follows a shock: fever, delirium, words flung out beyond recall. He spoke to her attendant, making it understood he would be within call, and that he was in communication with her friends in England—an authority he could assume the more readily because Grandcourt’s valet, the one old servant from the voyage, knew him and accepted his presence.

When at last weariness overcame the day’s various emotions, his sleep was broken by morning dreams—events knotted together, faces rising and sinking like things seen through water. He woke with his heart held in a grip, an image pressed on him by anxiety, and lay listening. No messenger. No quick steps. Only the hotel’s morning—somewhere a chair moved, somewhere a shutter tapped in the wind, and always the distant, tireless sea.

It was still early; he could not go asking questions. Later he learned she had been wakeful through most of the night, but without violent agitation, and had fallen asleep toward morning. He wondered at the force that dwelt in her—so alive to dread, and yet mastering herself as if concealment were a last necessity. For himself, he felt curiously dulled, as if what had passed between him and his mother had blunted the edge of immediate sensibility. He seemed to be living by claim and duty rather than by any overflow of tenderness. He had lately been absorbed in an experience far apart from Gwendolen’s lot; and now, though his care for her was urgent, it had the strange air of revisiting a former scene where he had once suffered, and not yet recovering the full inward response.

He set himself, with the practical steadiness that comes when the mind cannot rest, to obtain a formal statement from the fishermen who had rescued Gwendolen—something legally recognized, to guard her from conjecture and accusation. Few details emerged. The boat in which Grandcourt had gone out had been found drifting, the sail loose, and had been towed in. They thought it likely he had been struck overboard by the sail flapping while he put about, and that he could not swim. They had been near, but their attention was first arrested by a cry that seemed like a man in distress; then, as they hastened with their oars, they heard a shriek from the lady and saw her leap in.

When Deronda returned to the hotel, he was told Gwendolen had risen and desired to see him.

He was led into a room darkened by blinds and curtains, where the daylight was not allowed to enter frankly, but seeped in as a dim, chastened presence. The air carried that mingled odour of warmed cloth, extinguished candles, and the faintest medicinal sharpness—lavender and camphor—such scents as women summon about pain when they have no better defence. Outside, filtered through the curtains and the building’s thickness, the sea’s low thunder was like an acoustic memory that would not be silenced: a world insisting on its own continuance.

Gwendolen sat wrapped in a white shawl, facing the door as if she had been waiting and listening for his step. Her long hair was gathered up and coiled with care; the blue stars in her ears held their place with a strange pertinacity, as if vanity were a pin fastening her to the last shred of her former self. When he entered she rose impulsively to her full height, sheathed in white, her face and neck scarcely less white, save for a purple line beneath her eyes. Her lips were a little apart with the helpless look of one accused. She was like the unhappy ghost of that Gwendolen Harleth he had once seen at the gaming table—turning away with firm lips and proud self-possession from her losses. The sight pierced him; pity, and with it all their past, sprang back into living force.

“I beseech you to rest—not to stand,” he said, moving toward her.

She obeyed at once, dropping back into the chair as if her strength were only borrowed.

“Will you sit down near me?” she said. “I want to speak very low.”

He drew a small chair close beside her. The nearness, the quiet act of placing himself within the circle of her breath, seemed to touch her more than any words. She turned her pale face full upon his—so close now that he could see the slight trembling in her eyelids—and said, in the lowest audible tone, “You know I am a guilty woman?”

He himself grew paler. “I know nothing,” he answered, and dared not add more.

“He is dead.” The words came with the same undertoned decision.

“Yes,” Deronda said, suspended in mournful reluctance, as if speech might make the fact more final.

“His face will not be seen above the water again,” she whispered, her hands clenched. “Not by any one else—only by me. A dead face. I shall never get away from it.”

She spoke with desperate self-repression, looking away toward some point on the floor as if the scene lay there, fixed like a stain. Deronda’s mind caught at a hope—that she was speaking through an exaggerating medium of excitement and horror, that delirium might be shaping this confession. Yet he felt the conflict that held him silent: she was bent on confessing, and he dreaded the confession. Against his better will he shrank from the task laid on him. He was not a priest. He dreaded the weight of her soul flung upon his own with imploring dependence. Cowardly as the wish seemed, he wished she could bury her secret in herself.

She spoke again, hurriedly, fixing him with her glance.

“You will not say that I ought to tell the world? you will not say that I ought to be disgraced? I could not do it. I could not bear it. I cannot have my mother know. Not if I were dead. I could not have her know. I must tell you; but you will not say that any one else should know.”

“I can say nothing in my ignorance,” Deronda answered, in a low, mournful voice, “except that I desire to help you.”

“I told you from the beginning—as soon as I could—I told you I was afraid of myself.” The murmur was piteous, and he had to bend his ear to catch it. Her face afflicted him too much to look at steadily. “I felt a hatred in me that was always working like an evil spirit—contriving things. Everything I could do to free myself came into my mind; and it got worse—all things got worse. That is why I asked you to come to me in town. I thought then I would tell you the worst about myself. I tried. But I could not tell everything. And he came in.”

She paused; a shudder ran through her as if cold water had passed over her skin. Then she went on.

“I will tell you everything now. Do you think a woman who cried, and prayed, and struggled to be saved from herself, could be a murderess?”

“Great God!” Deronda’s voice broke, deep and shaken. “Don’t torture me needlessly. You have not murdered him. You threw yourself into the water with the impulse to save him. Tell me the rest afterward. This death was an accident that you could not have hindered.”

“Don’t be impatient with me.” The childlike beseeching in the words compelled him to look. Her poor quivering lips went on. “You said—you used to say—you felt more for those who had done something wicked and were miserable; you said they might get better—they might be scourged into something better. If you had not spoken in that way, everything would have been worse. I did remember all you said to me. It came to me always. It came to me at the very last—that was the reason why I—But now, if you cannot bear with me when I tell you everything—if you turn away from me and forsake me, what shall I do? Am I worse than I was when you found me and wanted to make me better? All the wrong I have done was in me then—and more—and more—if you had not come and been patient with me. And now—will you forsake me?”

Her hands, once clenched, lay now helplessly relaxed and trembling on the chair’s arms. Her lips stayed parted after she ceased speaking, as if she had no power to close them upon what she had uttered. Deronda could not answer; he was forced to look away. He took one of her hands and clasped it—an instinctive grasp, like that of two children who must walk through dark together. It was the only way he could say, I will not forsake you. And even as he did it he felt as if he were signing his name to a blank paper that might be filled with something dreadful.

That grasp was new to her: she had never had from any man a sign of tenderness that answered a need in her own being. She translated its powerful effect into a promise of inexhaustible patience and constancy. A stream of renewed strength came over her; she could go on, not in orderly narrative, but in that fitful, wandering confession where time collapses and all moments of guilt seem one.

“All sorts of contrivances in my mind—but all so difficult. And I fought against them—I was terrified at them—I saw his dead face”—her voice sank to a breath close to his ear—“ever so long ago I saw it, and I wished him to be dead. And yet it terrified me. I was like two creatures. I could not speak—I wanted to kill—it was as strong as thirst—and then directly I felt beforehand I had done something dreadful, unalterable—that would make me like an evil spirit. And it came—it came.”

She stopped, as if memory had entangled itself and could not find the strand to pull.

“It had all been in my mind when I first spoke to you—when we were at the Abbey. I had done something then. I could not tell you that. It was the only thing I did toward carrying out my thoughts. They went about over everything; but they all remained like dreadful dreams—all but one. I did one act—and I never undid it—it is there still—as long ago as when we were at Ryelands. There it was—something my fingers longed for among the beautiful toys in the cabinet in my boudoir—small and sharp like a long willow leaf in a silver sheath. I locked it in the drawer of my dressing-case. I was continually haunted with it and how I should use it. I fancied myself putting it under my pillow. But I never did. I never looked at it again. I dared not unlock the drawer: it had a key all to itself; and not long ago, when we were in the yacht, I dropped the key into the deep water. It was my wish to drop it and deliver myself. After that I began to think how I could open the drawer without the key: and when I found we were to stay at Genoa, it came into my mind that I could get it opened privately at the hotel. But then, when we were going up the stairs, I met you; and I thought I should talk to you alone and tell you this—everything I could not tell you in town; and then I was forced to go out in the boat.”

At the last words a sob rose for the first time, and she sank back. The recollection of that sharp disappointment—being shut out from speech with him—seemed for a moment to efface all that had followed. Deronda, not looking at her, spoke insistently, as if he could press her into safety by the sheer force of a question.

“And it has all remained in your imagination. It has gone on only in your thought. To the last the evil temptation has been resisted?”

Silence answered him. Tears rolled down her cheeks; she pressed her handkerchief to them and sat upright, summoning resolution. Then, leaning toward him again, she whispered:

“No, no; I will tell you everything as God knows it. I will tell you no falsehood; I will tell you the exact truth. What should I do else? I used to think I could never be wicked. I thought of wicked people as if they were a long way off me. Since then I have been wicked. I have felt wicked. And everything has been a punishment to me—all the things I used to wish for—it is as if they had been made red-hot. The very daylight has often been a punishment to me. Because—you know—I ought not to have married. That was the beginning of it. I wronged some one else. I broke my promise. I meant to get pleasure for myself, and it all turned to misery. I wanted to make my gain out of another’s loss—you remember?—it was like roulette—and the money burned into me. And I could not complain. It was as if I had prayed that another should lose and I should win. And I had won, I knew it all—I knew I was guilty. When we were on the sea, and I lay awake at night in the cabin, I sometimes felt that everything I had done lay open without excuse—nothing was hidden—how could anything be known to me only?—it was not my own knowledge, it was God’s that had entered into me, and even the stillness—everything held a punishment for me—everything but you. I always thought that you would not want me to be punished—you would have tried and helped me to be better. And only thinking of that helped me. You will not change—you will not want to punish me now?”

Deronda groaned, “God forbid!” but he sat motionless, as if movement would betray him into some wrong act—either too much comfort or too much recoil.

He dared not urge her again. He must let her mind go where it must. She left intervals unconsciously, not always distinguishing what she had spoken from what she had only seen inwardly. When she began again, it was as if she took up the thread from a different knot.

“That all made it so hard when I was forced to go in the boat. Because when I saw you it was an unexpected joy, and I thought I could tell you everything—about the locked-up drawer and what I had not told you before. And if I had told you, and knew it was in your mind, it would have less power over me. I hoped and trusted in that. For after all my struggles and my crying, the hatred and rage, the temptation that frightened me, the longing, the thirst for what I dreaded, always came back. And that disappointment—when I was quite shut out from speaking to you, and was driven to go in the boat—brought all the evil back, as if I had been locked in a prison with it and no escape. Oh, it seems so long ago now since I stepped into that boat! I could have given up everything in that moment, to have the forked lightning for a weapon to strike him dead.”

The fierceness she recalled crept into her undertone, like a knife’s cold edge in the voice. After a silence, she hurried on:

“If he were here again, what should I do? I cannot wish him here—and yet I cannot bear his dead face. I was a coward. I ought to have borne contempt. I ought to have gone away—gone and wandered like a beggar rather than stay to feel like a fiend. But turn where I would there was something I could not bear. Sometimes I thought he would kill me if I resisted his will. But now—his dead face is there, and I cannot bear it.”

Suddenly she loosed Deronda’s hand and sprang up, stretching her arms upward to their full length, and moaned as if the sound were torn from her body:

“I have been a cruel woman! What can I do but cry for help? I am sinking. Die—die—you are forsaken—go down, go down into darkness. Forsaken—no pity—I shall be forsaken.”

She dropped back into her chair and broke into sobs. For that moment Deronda had no place in her consciousness; she was alone with a vision that filled her. He was unmanned—more than he had been prepared for. Instead of his late experience having dulled him, it seemed to have made him more penetrable: her swift travel from bright rash girlhood into this agony of remorse—an agony he had watched grow while he stood helpless—pierced him the deeper because it came close upon another sad revelation of spiritual conflict. He rose, and as he watched that terrible outburst—made more awful by her instinct to keep the voice low, as if secrecy were still her only shelter—he felt that passionate pity which makes a man ready to renounce pleasure and live only for the stricken.

He turned his back and walked away a few paces, as if distance might give him a breath.

Presently there was stillness. Her mind opened to the fact that he had moved from her. When he turned and approached again, he saw her face lifted toward him, eyes dilated, lips parted: timid, forlorn beseeching—too timid to frame itself into words while he remained aloof. Was she forsaken—now—already? His eyes met hers fully for the first time since her first low question. His look, intense with mournfulness, seemed to say: I know it, and therefore I will not forsake you. He sat down beside her again, in the same attitude, without turning his face toward her and without taking her hand.

Once more she was pierced—not only by fear for herself, but by a compunction that reached beyond it. In a tone of loving regret she said, “I make you very unhappy.”

Deronda gave an indistinct “Oh,” shrinking together, shifting as if the words struck him physically. Then he gathered firmness enough to answer clearly: “There is no question of being happy or unhappy. What I most desire at this moment is what will most help you. Tell me all you feel it a relief to tell.”

Devotion lay in the words; yet they widened a spiritual distance between them—compassion that seemed to regard her from a height. She felt it, and speaking grew harder. An impulse rose in her to humble herself more, to kneel before him; but something in her—pride, fear, the strange checks of her mixed consciousness—held her motionless and silent.

Her stillness made him say at last, “Perhaps you are too weary. Shall I go away, and come again whenever you wish it?”

“No, no,” she said quickly, dread of his leaving bringing back her power. She leaned a little nearer, and her low-toned eagerness returned. “I want to tell you what it was that came over me in that boat. I was full of rage at being obliged to go—full of rage—and I could do nothing but sit there like a galley slave. And then we got away—out of the port—into the deep—and everything was still—and we never looked at each other, only he spoke to order me—and the very light about me seemed to hold me a prisoner and force me to sit as I did. It came over me that when I was a child I used to fancy sailing away into a world where people were not forced to live with any one they did not like—I did not like my father-in-law to come home. And now, I thought, just the opposite had come to me. I had stepped into a boat, and my life was a sailing and sailing away—gliding on and no help—always into solitude with him, away from deliverance. And because I felt more helpless than ever, my thoughts went out over worse things—I longed for worse things—I had cruel wishes—I fancied impossible ways of—I did not want to die myself; I was afraid of our being drowned together. If it had been any use I should have prayed—I should have prayed that something might befall him. I should have prayed that he might sink out of my sight and leave me alone. I knew no way of killing him there, but I did, I did kill him in my thoughts.”

She fell silent, overwhelmed by what no words could truly carry. The sea’s distant sound seemed to swell in the pause, a vast, indifferent ear.

“But yet, all the while I felt that I was getting more wicked. And what had been with me so much, came to me just then—what you once said—about dreading to increase my wrong-doing and my remorse—I should hope for nothing then. It was all like a writing of fire within me. Getting wicked was misery—being shut out forever from knowing what you—what better lives were. That had always been coming back to me then—but yet with a despair—a feeling that it was no use—evil wishes were too strong. I remember then letting go the tiller and saying ‘God help me!’ But then I was forced to take it again and go on; and the evil longings, the evil prayers came again and blotted everything else dim, till, in the midst of them—I don’t know how it was—he was turning the sail—there was a gust—he was struck—I know nothing—I only know that I saw my wish outside me.”

Her voice grew quicker, and sank even lower, as if shame pressed her down to secrecy.

“I saw him sink, and my heart gave a leap as if it were going out of me. I think I did not move. I kept my hands tight. It was long enough for me to be glad, and yet to think it was no use—he would come up again. And he was come—farther off—the boat had moved. It was all like lightning. ‘The rope!’ he called out in a voice—not his own—I hear it now—and I stooped for the rope—I felt I must—I felt sure he could swim, and he would come back whether or not, and I dreaded him. That was in my mind—he would come back. But he was gone down again, and I had the rope in my hand—no, there he was again—his face above the water—and he cried again—and I held my hand, and my heart said, ‘Die!’—and he sank; and I felt ‘It is done—I am wicked, I am lost!’—and I had the rope in my hand—I don’t know what I thought—I was leaping away from myself—I would have saved him then. I was leaping from my crime, and there it was—close to me as I fell—there was the dead face—dead, dead. It can never be altered. That was what happened. That was what I did. You know it all. It can never be altered.”

In the evening she sent for him again, as though the day could not close upon her without his presence to hold it in some shape that would not break her. The hour was near that in which, the night before, they had brought her in from the sea; and the room, with its blinds half-drawn and the windows open, had that subdued, salt-damp coolness which makes even a lamp-flame seem to breathe softly. Beyond, the sea lay in a long grey quiet, and from it came a low, incessant wash—like a careful hand forever smoothing a sheet—broken now and then by the creak of a rope, the faint clink of a ring, the far, thin call of some boatman. Those sounds, natural and ancient, should have been a kind of peace; yet to her they were as if the world insisted on continuing, indifferent to the one moment where her will had turned black.

She sat gazing fixedly outward, her cheek on her hand. She looked less shattered than when he had left her, but in her face there was a melancholy so deep that, as he drew near, it changed into an anxious timidity—as if she were afraid of her own voice and what it might carry into the air.

She did not put out her hand. “How long ago it is!” she said, and then, after a breath that trembled like a caught sob, “Will you sit near me again a little while?”

He placed himself at her side as he had done before, and because he saw that she turned to him with that look which means a wish to speak—something hovering on the edge of words—he waited. Again she looked toward the window, silent; again she turned with the same helpless expression, and still nothing came. Fear held her as if it had a physical grip. To ease her he averted his face, making a little space for her courage to enter.

Presently he heard her cry, imploring, as if the words were torn out of her—“You will not say that any one else should know?”

“Most decidedly not,” said Deronda. His voice, in the hush of the room, seemed to fall among the sea-sounds like a steady oar-stroke. “There is no action that ought to be taken in consequence. There is no injury that could be righted in that way. There is no retribution that any mortal could apportion justly.”

She was so still afterwards that it seemed she was holding her breath to keep herself together, before she whispered, “But if I had not had that murderous will—that moment—if I had thrown the rope on the instant—perhaps it would have hindered death?”

“No—I think not,” he said, slowly, as if he would not allow himself the comfort of easy assurance. “If it were true that he could swim, he must have been seized with cramp. With your quickest, utmost effort, it seems impossible that you could have done anything to save him. That momentary murderous will cannot, I think, have altered the course of events. Its effect is confined to the motives in your own breast. Within ourselves our evil will is momentous, and sooner or later it works its way outside us—it may be in the vitiation that breeds evil acts, but also it may be in the self-abhorrence that stings us into better striving.”

The sea breathed on, and the faint noises of the place—so much older than their misery—seemed to her like witnesses that could not be bribed into silence. She spoke again, hesitating, as if she feared he might suspect her even where she was trying to clear herself.

“I am saved from robbing others—there are others—they will have everything—they will have what they ought to have. I knew that some time before I left town. You do not suspect me of wrong desires about those things?”

“I had not thought of them,” said Deronda. “I was thinking too much of the other things.”

“Perhaps you don’t quite know the beginning of it all,” she said, slowly, as if each syllable were a step on ground that might give way. “There was some one else he ought to have married. And I knew it, and I told her I would not hinder it. And I went away—that was when you first saw me.” The words made a narrow bridge back into her past; her eyes did not leave the dim line of the water. “But then we became poor all at once, and I was very miserable, and I was tempted. I thought, ‘I shall do as I like and make everything right.’ I persuaded myself. And it was all different. It was all dreadful. Then came hatred and wicked thoughts. That was how it all came. I told you I was afraid of myself.”

Her fingers, lying on the chair-arm, moved as if they were feeling for some thread to wind round her and hold her in. “And I did what you told me—I did try to make my fear a safeguard. I thought of what would be if I—” She stopped, and when she went on her voice had that strange, strained clearness which comes when the mind is haunted and cannot sleep. “I felt what would come—how I should dread the morning—wishing it would be always night—and yet in the darkness always seeing something—seeing death.”

Outside, some distant sound—perhaps a shutter touched by wind—made a sharp little clap. She started, then went on hurriedly, as if she must pour the whole thing out before her courage failed. “If you did not know how miserable I was, you might—but now it has all been no use. I can care for nothing but saving the rest from knowing—poor mamma, who has never been happy.”

Silence fell, heavy as a closed door; then she said, with a repressed sob that seemed to shake her from within, “You cannot bear to look at me any more. You think I am too wicked. You do not believe that I can become any better—worth anything—worthy enough—I shall always be too wicked to—” Her voice broke helplessly, as if even language refused her at the end, leaving only that raw sound of a creature asking not to be cast out.

Deronda’s heart was pierced. He turned his eyes on her poor beseeching face and said, “I believe that you may become worthier than you have ever yet been—worthy to lead a life that may be a blessing. No evil dooms us hopelessly except the evil we love, and desire to continue in, and make no effort to escape from. You have made efforts—you will go on making them.”

“But you were the beginning of them.” She leaned forward, clasping her hands on the arm of her chair as if she would hold him there by the mere force of need; her face bore piteous traces of a whole life’s change crowded into twenty-four hours—this new terrible life lying on the other side of the deed that fulfills a criminal desire. “You must not forsake me,” she said. “I will bear any penance. I will lead any life you tell me. But you must not forsake me. You must be near. If you had been near me—if I could have said everything to you, I should have been different. You will not forsake me?”

“It could never be my impulse to forsake you,” said Deronda promptly—his voice and eyes having that ready tenderness which, without intending it, makes sympathy seem like a promise meant for one soul alone. And in that instant he was not himself quite free from a foreboding: he felt how words spoken to keep a despairing creature from sinking might bind him later as if they were vows. Strong pity would not hinder the rushing images of future difficulty. Yet he met her appealing eyes and spoke on, with the painful consciousness that to her ear his words might carry a pledge which one day would seem unfulfilled—an indefinite promise to an indefinite hope.

Anxieties, both immediate and distant, crowded on his thought; and under their pressure, after a moment’s silence, he said, “I expect Sir Hugo Mallinger to arrive by to-morrow night at least; and I am not without hope that Mrs. Davilow may shortly follow him. Her presence will be the greatest comfort to you—it will give you a motive to save her from unnecessary pain.”

“Yes, yes—I will try.” Her assent came quickly, as if she caught at any task that could be called duty. “And you will not go away?”

“Not till after Sir Hugo has come.”

“But we shall all go to England?”

“As soon as possible,” he said, not wishing to enter into particulars.

She looked toward the window again, and her face altered with an expression like a gradual waking—like someone who, after being stunned, begins to feel the bruises and remember the blow. The twilight was deepening; the sea-sound seemed louder by contrast, and every faint creak and distant call entered the room as if it had a right to be heard. Deronda could see a movement in her eyes and hands that belonged to returning perception.

“You will always be with Sir Hugo now!” she said presently, turning and looking at him. “You will always live at the Abbey—or else at Diplow?”

“I am quite uncertain where I shall live,” said Deronda, coloring.

The changed color warned her that she had spoken too rashly; she fell silent, as if she had put her foot upon a hidden sore. After a while she began again, looking away, her voice low and drained: “It is impossible to think how my life will go on. I think now it would be better for me to be poor and obliged to work.”

“New promptings will come as the days pass. When you are among your friends again, you will discern new duties,” said Deronda. “Make it a task now to get as well and calm—as much like yourself as you can, before—” He hesitated.

“Before my mother comes,” said Gwendolen.

“Ah! I must be changed.” Her hand went up, not quite touching her face, as if she dreaded the feel of her own skin. “I have not looked at myself. Should you have known me,” she added, turning toward him, “if you had met me now?—should you have known me for the one you saw at Leubronn?”

“Yes, I should have known you,” said Deronda, mournfully. “The outside change is not great. I should have seen at once that it was you, and that you had gone through some great sorrow.”

“Don’t wish now that you had never seen me; don’t wish that,” she said, imploringly; and as the tears gathered, her voice took on a childlike terror—of being erased, of being judged unworthy even of memory.

“I should despise myself for wishing it,” said Deronda. “How could I know what I was wishing? We must find our duties in what comes to us, not in what we imagine might have been. If I took to foolish wishing of that sort, I should wish—not that I had never seen you, but that I had been able to save you from this.”

“You have saved me from worse,” said Gwendolen, sobbing. “I should have been worse if it had not been for you. If you had not been good, I should have been more wicked than I am.”

“It will be better for me to go now,” said Deronda, worn in spirit by the perpetual strain—as if the room’s salt air and the sea’s tireless breath had been passing through him, taking strength away drop by drop. “Remember what we said of your task—to get well and calm before other friends come.”

He rose, and she gave him her hand submissively, as if obedience could keep him from vanishing. But when he had left her she sank on her knees, breaking into hysterical crying—the body at last uttering what the words had been forced to discipline. The distance between them was too great. She was a banished soul, beholding a possible life which she had sinned herself away from.

They found her crushed on the floor in that posture of grief which seemed natural enough in a poor lady whose husband had been drowned in her presence—while the sea outside went on murmuring its old speech, indifferent to the names and stories men give to their dead.

“Much adoe there was, God wot;
He wold love and she wold not.”

A year can be measured, if you like, by calendars and journeys—by how far the sun has paced along the hedgerows—but what grows within that span is not to be reckoned by miles any more than a field’s life is told by its acreage. One man goes away and comes back altered as if some secret ferment had worked through his blood; another stays at home where the same kettle sings, the same gate creaks, the same bees keep their old hours among peonies, and time merely lays a thinner glaze of habit over the days.

So it had been between the brilliant Gwendolen Harleth of the archery meeting and the Gwendolen who now moved somewhere far off, crushed into penitence; while at Pennicote, life kept to its familiar rounds, only with fewer guineas for trimming and fewer compliments to warm the drawing-room. The rectory was still a pleasant home. The red and pink peonies had flamed again on the lawn; the hollyhocks lifted their old spires along the hedge; and the rector’s days went forward with the wholesome regularity of a well-ordered kitchen, where the bread must be kneaded whether or not there is a grand guest expected.

He wrote his two ecclesiastical articles—peaceful authorship, done with windows open on fields and downs, not under the stale, thrice-breathed air of criticism. It was work that did not steal appetite, but rather seemed to make his dinner taste the better for a mind at ease; and it brought him no leanness of spirit—only that suffusive complacency which is like good broth: not showy, but nourishing.

Better still was the recovered delight in his favorite son. The loss of income was a real narrowing—fewer visits, fewer little indulgences—but this happiness outweighed it. Whatever hidden change disappointment had made in Rex, it showed itself less in gloom than in purpose. He came down to the rectory for the summer bringing Anna with him; and though he had nearly the old liveliness with his brothers and sisters, he kept the habits of the eager student—up early, and in the evenings shut away with his books as steadily as a baker turns back to his leaven.

“You don’t repent the choice of the law as a profession, Rex?” his father asked.

“There is no profession I would choose before it,” Rex said. “I should like to end my life as a first-rate judge, and help to draw up a code. I reverse the famous dictum. I should say, ‘Give me something to do with making the laws, and let who will make the songs.’”

“You will have to stow in an immense amount of rubbish, I suppose—that’s the worst of it,” the rector said, with the indulgent grumble that hides pride.

“I don’t see that law-rubbish is worse than any other sort. It is not so bad as the rubbishy literature that people choke their minds with. It doesn’t make one so dull. Our wittiest men have often been lawyers. Any orderly way of looking at things as cases and evidence seems to me better than a perpetual wash of odds and ends bearing on nothing in particular. And then, from a higher point of view, the foundations and the growth of law make the most interesting aspects of philosophy and history. Of course there will be a good deal that is troublesome, drudging, perhaps exasperating. But the great prizes in life can’t be won easily—I see that.”

“Well, my boy, the best augury of a man’s success in his profession is that he thinks it the finest in the world.” The rector’s eyes rested on him with that fatherly satisfaction which he carefully rationed, as one rations rich food that might turn to cloying. “But I fancy it so with most work when a man goes into it with a will. Brewitt, the blacksmith, said to me the other day that his ’prentice had no mind to his trade; ‘and yet, sir,’ said Brewitt, ‘what would a young fellow have if he doesn’t like the blacksmithing?’”

Rex was the romance of the rector’s later life: the son in whom a man comes to recognize something beyond his own measure, and therefore to picture a future eminence for him as easily as he pictures harvest when the wheat is still green. Only to his wife did he say with decision, “Rex will be a distinguished man, Nancy, I am sure of it—as sure as Paley’s father was about his son.”

“Was Paley an old bachelor?” Mrs. Gascoigne asked, with that domestic literalness which will put its finger on the wrong crumb.

“That is hardly to the point, my dear,” the rector said; and she felt she had spoken rather weakly.

This quiet trotting of time at the rectory was shared by the little household that had exchanged Offendene’s faded dignity for the low white house not a mile off, snugged in evergreens, known in the village simply as “Jodson’s.” Mrs. Davilow’s delicate face showed only a slight deepening of its mild melancholy; a few more silver lines ran through her hair; and the four girls had bloomed a little, as plants do when some taller growth is cut away and they find more light for themselves. The good Jocosa kept her useful neutrality toward splendor, as if splendour were a dish meant for those not “in a situation.”

On a July afternoon the low narrow drawing-room—widened in feeling by two quaint projecting windows—was full, for Rex and Anna were added to the usual group. The lattices stood wide open, letting in the scent of monthly roses and the soft murmur of the garden: bees worrying a flower, leaves whispering together, a far-off bird insisting on a phrase and then falling silent. Now and then, rare as a stone dropped in a well, came the sound of hoofs and wheels; the road’s brief disturbance made the following stillness clearer, as if quiet had a taste, and that taste could be rinsed and returned.

Anna, always a favorite with her younger cousins, had much to tell of her new London experience and acquaintances. When she had first visited alone, questions had pressed round her—questions that all edged towards Gwendolen’s house in Grosvenor Square, what Gwendolen had said, what other people had said, and whether Anna had seen her after she “knew about the yacht.” No—Anna had not. That answer left imagination to do what it pleased with the unknown vessel. All they had were two letters: one before the setting out, to say that Mr. and Mrs. Grandcourt were going yachting on the Mediterranean; another from Marseilles, briskly declaring that she was sure to like it, the cabins were very elegant, and she would probably not write again until she had filled a long diary with dittos. Besides, the movement had been mentioned in “the newspaper,” which to Isabel’s mind gave it a varnish of romance, and she threw in a corsair or two—an agreeable seasoning—so that the adventure might end well.

But when Rex was present, the girls, obeying instructions, never began that fascinating topic; and to-day the livelier talk had been of the Meyricks and their extraordinary Jewish friends. It startled these country minds, to whom “live Jews” seemed almost to belong to the pages of a book rather than to the pavement and the tea-table—some strange race out of Pliny that might sleep under the shade of its own ears. Bertha could not imagine what Jews believed now; she had a dim notion that they rejected the Old Testament because it proved the New; Miss Merry thought Mirah and her brother could “never have been properly argued with”; and gentle Alice, with the docility of inherited aversion, said she did not mind what they believed—she was sure she “couldn’t bear them.”

Mrs. Davilow corrected her, saying that great Jewish families in society were quite what they ought to be both in London and Paris, though she admitted that the commoner unconverted Jews were objectionable; and Isabel, book-devouring Isabel, asked whether Mirah talked just as they did, or whether one might be with her and not find out she was a Jewess.

Rex, who had no partisanship with Israelites—having made a troublesome acquaintance with the minutiae of their ancient history in the form of “cram”—amused himself by playfully exaggerating each speaker’s notion, while Anna begged them to see he was only joking.

The laughter was cut through by the entrance of a letter for Mrs. Davilow. A messenger had run with it in great haste from the rectory.

The air in the room seemed to tighten, as if the garden itself had hushed to listen. Mrs. Davilow read and re-read the enclosed telegram; her agitation held her silent, and all the young faces turned toward her, fear staining them as quickly as a spill of ink. No one dared speak. At last she looked up, remembering that their imaginations might run to something worse than the truth—something like her own first dread, which had made the words swim—and she said, with a sob that was half relief and half breaking, “My dears, Mr. Grandcourt—” She paused, as if the name itself were a weight in her mouth, and then began again: “Mr. Grandcourt is drowned.”

Rex started up as if something had been flung into the room. He could not help it; and Anna’s first look went to him, swift with a sister’s anxious tenderness. But Mrs. Davilow was reading what the rector had added on the paper enclosing the telegram, and Rex gathered himself.

“Can I do anything, aunt?” he said. “Can I carry any word to my father from you?”

“Yes, dear. Tell him I will be ready—he is very good. He says he will go with me to Genoa—he will be here at half-past six. Jocosa and Alice, help me to get ready. She is safe—Gwendolen is safe—but she must be ill. I am sure she must be very ill. Rex, dear—Rex and Anna—go and tell your father I will be quite ready. I would not for the world lose another night. And bless him for being ready so soon. I can travel night and day till we get there.”

Rex and Anna hurried away through sunshine that had suddenly become solemn, as if its warmth were now only the warmth that shines upon graves and weddings alike—impartial, relentless. They said nothing to one another. Anna’s mind clung to him with concern—would this news tear open what had been healing?—while Rex struggled with a crowd of thoughts that came upon him like a jangling of bells, rude, untimely, and against his will.

At the rectory gate he stopped.

“Nannie, I will leave you to say everything to my father. If he wants me immediately, let me know. I shall stay in the shrubbery for ten minutes—only ten minutes.”

He turned away into the green cover, where leaves whispered and a blackbird startled into a short, sharp flight—small natural sounds that ought to have soothed, but could not. There are moments when the mind, even in the presence of another’s death, makes egoistic escapes, picturing consequences for itself; and the very shame of it is like a bitter taste that will not be spat out. In Rex the shame rose instantly and spread an ugly light over the hurrying images that had thrust in with the thought, “Gwendolen is free.”

But no sooner did “Gwendolen free” rise than there rose also, like a wall built of stone and gold, “Gwendolen rich, exalted, courted.” In the earlier time, when both lives were fresh and untried, she had turned from his love with repugnance. What ground was there now to suppose her heart would be more open? The thoughts came like opposing chimes, each striking against the other, so that there was no clear music, only tumult.

During the last year he had worked himself into a calm resolve; and now three words—drowned, safe, Genoa—seemed enough to undo that hard-won order and fling him back into the wretched rise and fall of longing he believed hopeless. Worse, the longing’s very activity at such a moment felt like a kind of theft at a bedside.

Excuse him: it was not much more than eighteen months since he had been laid low by an archer who sometimes touches his arrow with a subtle, lingering poison. The disappointment of a youthful passion does not always leave its mark in one plain way: it may sharpen one nature and dull another, humble one and harden another, and leave a third apparently unchanged. Everything depends—not on the bare fact of disappointment, but on the nature that is struck and the force that stirs it.

In Rex’s well-endowed nature, brief as the hope had been, the passionate stirring had gone deep; the disappointment had been revolutionary, yet it had brought a beneficent new order which kept most of the old virtues. In certain respects he believed it had set the bias and color of his life. It was as if some strong flavor—once tasted—had made all the future meals remember the lost one, so that even the plain bread had a ghost of sweetness and pain.

Now, pacing between shrubs that smelt of crushed leaf and summer heat, he felt his inward peace no better than a city where the alarm-bell slackens work and makes tumult busy. His love had been sudden, clinging, penetrating: to have consciousness steeped in another’s personality, to have the strongest inclinations possessed by an image that keeps its dominion in spite of change and apart from worthiness—nay, to feel the passion cling faster for the tragic pangs inflicted by a cruel, reorganized unworthiness—this is a love that phlegmatic rationality stares at and calls unaccountable. Yet it exists, as undeniably as wind and wave, wrecking here, carrying to a triumphant voyage there. In a nature not brutish but capable of dignity, it may end not in mere appetite but in a devotedness that risks itself safely.

Rex had made up his mind to that companionship as if it had been some supremely dear creature stricken dumb and helpless, and he had turned all the future of tenderness into a shadow of the past. But he had also made up his mind that his life was not to be pauperized because he had renounced one kind of joy. He had begun again, counting what treasures remained. He had even felt a release of power that sometimes comes when you cease to be afraid of your own neck.

And now he was angry with himself that the sense of irrevocableness which ought, in reason, to have been as strong as ever, had been shaken by a change that could make no true change in his relation to Gwendolen.

He spoke the truth to himself roughly, as a man may swallow bitter medicine in one gulp.

“She would never love me; and that is not the question—I could never approach her as a lover in her present position. I am exactly of no consequence at all, and am not likely to be of much consequence till my head is turning gray. But what has that to do with it? She would not have me on any terms, and I would not ask her. It is a meanness to be thinking about it now—no better than lurking about the battle-field to strip the dead; but there never was more gratuitous sinning. I have nothing to gain there—absolutely nothing. Then why can’t I face the facts, and behave as they demand, instead of leaving my father to suppose that there are matters he can’t speak to me about, though I might be useful in them?”

That last thought—usefulness, plain duty—came like a firmer step on a slippery path. Rex turned and walked steadily into the house, and through the open door of the study.

There was his father, already packing a traveling-desk, the familiar implements of order laid out with the promptness of a man who has spent his life answering calls.

“Can I be of any use, sir?” Rex said, with rallied courage, as his father looked up.

“Yes, my boy; when I’m gone, just see to my letters, and answer where necessary, and send me word of everything. Dymock will manage the parish very well, and you will stay with your mother, or, at least, go up and down again, till I come back, whenever that may be.”

“You will hardly be very long, sir, I suppose,” Rex said, beginning to strap a railway rug. “You will perhaps bring my cousin back to England?”

He forced himself to speak of Gwendolen for the first time. The rector noticed the moment with satisfaction, as if a difficulty had been passed and a better tone secured between them.

“That depends,” he answered, as if this were a matter-of-course to be discussed like trains and luggage. “Perhaps her mother may stay there with her, and I may come back very soon. This telegram leaves us in ignorance which is rather anxious. But no doubt the arrangements of the will lately made are satisfactory, and there may possibly be an heir yet to be born. In any case, I feel confident that Gwendolen will be liberally—I should expect, splendidly—provided for.”

“It must have been a great shock for her,” Rex said, getting more resolute now the first twinge had been borne. “I suppose he was a devoted husband.”

“No doubt of it,” said the rector, in his most decided manner. “Few men of his position would have come forward as he did under the circumstances.”

Rex had never seen Grandcourt; no one in the family had talked to him about the man; he knew nothing of Gwendolen’s flight from her suitor to Leubronn. He only knew that Grandcourt, being very much in love with her, had made her an offer in the first weeks of her sudden poverty, and had behaved very handsomely in providing for her mother and sisters. That seemed natural—what Rex himself would have liked to do, had he possessed the power. Grandcourt had been a lucky fellow, and had had some happiness before he got drowned. Yet, even as he tightened the strap on the rug, Rex wondered—quietly, irresistibly—whether Gwendolen had been in love with the successful suitor, or had only forborne to tell Rex that she hated being made love to.

Sir Hugo was never a man to be hustled by other people’s urgency; and Daniel, for his part, would not let himself leave Genoa while the thought of his oldest friend—his first shelter and habit of home—was still only a promise on paper. Grandcourt’s drowning lay between them like a cold stone in the house, and, heavier still, that sudden opening of Daniel’s own life—the mother who had come and gone as if the air had shaped itself into a figure and then forgotten the trick—was not a thing to be told in letters without leaving the heart misheard.

So it was not until the fifth evening that Daniel stood waiting at the station, the telegram’s hour narrowing toward eight, then nine. The place had its own harsh orchestra—iron wheels clanging, porters calling, luggage thudded down with the blunt impatience of travel—yet beyond, the sea kept sending in its low breath, and a faint bell from somewhere in the town threaded through the racket like a remembered tune. Daniel found himself listening with that inward habit he had of taking the world in by its sounds as well as its sights: the difference between a noise that only bruised the mind and a sound that allowed it to be whole.

When Sir Hugo stepped down from the carriage at last, his familiar figure seeming to bring with it the smell of English cloth and old rooms and well-kept leather, Daniel felt the warmth of long gratitude rise with a force that for a moment drowned every new judgment. He had been wronged—yes, by a falsity, by a concealment that had made his boyhood a kind of hunger with no name for what it lacked. Yet the hand that had held him up had meant kindness; and Daniel’s nature, which could be unbending in principle, was tender in blame. Ignorant kindness might cut like cruelty; still, to rage at it as if it had been deliberate was only another form of ignorance. And after the last ten days—after the curtain had lifted on souls cramped by secrecy and power—he was less than ever willing to indulge that resentful appetite which looks so much like a love of punishment.

Sir Hugo’s hand closed on his.

“Well, Dan,” he said—nothing more, because the rest was crowded into the clasp and into their faces.

They gave brief orders to the courier, and Sir Hugo, who looked travel-worn but sound, proposed they should walk; there was no need to hurry to the hotel. The evening was mild, starlight still thin with the last sheen of day, and the air carried the briny dampness of the port. Carts rattled over the stones; a distant singer somewhere tried a phrase and let it drop; even the water made a small, ceaseless chafing against wood and rope that steadied the nerves more than silence could have done.

“I have taken my journey easily, and am in excellent condition,” Sir Hugo said. “I didn’t hurry in setting off, because I wanted to inquire into things a little; and so I got sight of your letter to Lady Mallinger before I started. But now—how is the widow?”

“Getting calmer,” Daniel answered. “She seems to be escaping the bodily illness one might have feared after her plunge and terrible excitement. Her uncle and mother came two days ago, and she is being well taken care of.”

“Any prospect of an heir being born?”

“From what Mr. Gascoigne said to me, I conclude not. He spoke as if it were a question whether the widow would have the estates for her life.”

Sir Hugo looked round at Daniel as they walked. “It will not be much of a wrench to her affections, I fancy, this loss of the husband?”

“The suddenness of the death has been a great blow to her,” Daniel said, quietly, stepping away from what Sir Hugo was trying to pull into light.

“I wonder whether Grandcourt gave her any notion what were the provisions of his will?”

“Do you know what they are, sir?” Daniel returned, unwilling to take up the role of interpreter of another person’s inwardness.

“Yes, I do,” Sir Hugo said sharply. “Gad! if there’s no prospect of a legitimate heir, he’s left everything to a boy he had by a Mrs. Glasher. You know nothing about the affair, I suppose; but she was a sort of wife to him for a good many years, and there are three older children—girls. The boy is to take his father’s name; he is Henleigh already, and he is to be Henleigh Mallinger Grandcourt. The Mallinger will be of no use to him, I am happy to say; but the young dog will have more than enough with his fourteen years’ minority—no need to have had holes filled up with my fifty thousand for Diplow that he had no right to. And meanwhile my beauty, the young widow, is to put up with a poor two thousand a year and the house at Gadsmere—a nice kind of banishment for her if she chose to shut herself up there, which I don’t think she will. The boy’s mother has been living there of late years. I’m perfectly disgusted with Grandcourt. I don’t know that I’m obliged to think the better of him because he’s drowned; though, so far as my affairs are concerned, nothing in his life became him like the leaving it.”

“In my opinion he did wrong when he married this wife—not in leaving his estates to the son,” Daniel said, the dryness in his tone like the edge of a knife used with restraint.

“I say nothing against his leaving the land to the lad,” Sir Hugo answered. “But since he had married this girl he ought to have given her a handsome provision, such as she could live on in a style fitted to the rank he had raised her to. She ought to have had four or five thousand a year and the London house for her life; that’s what I should have done for her. I suppose, as she was penniless, her friends couldn’t stand out for a settlement. It’s ill trusting to the will a man may make after he’s married. Even a wise man generally lets some folly ooze out of him in his will—my father did, I know; and if a fellow has any spite or tyranny in him, he’s likely to bottle off a good deal for keeping in that sort of document. It’s quite clear Grandcourt meant that his death should put an extinguisher on his wife, if she bore him no heir.”

“And, in the other case, I suppose everything would have been reversed—illegitimacy would have had the extinguisher?” Daniel said, and this time the contempt showed through.

“Precisely—Gadsmere and the two thousand. It’s queer. One nuisance is that Grandcourt has made me an executor; but seeing he was the son of my only brother, I can’t refuse to act. And I shall mind it less if I can be of any use to the widow. Lush thinks she was not in ignorance about the family under the rose, and the purport of the will. He hints that there was no very good understanding between the couple. But I fancy you are the man who knew most about what Mrs. Grandcourt felt or did not feel—eh, Dan?”

There was no jocoseness in Sir Hugo now; his voice dropped, as if the clang and shout around them ought not to overhear. Daniel felt that if he dodged, he would only set Sir Hugo’s imagination to work in a wrong direction.

“She was certainly not happy,” Daniel said gravely. “They were unsuited to each other. But as to the disposal of the property—from all I have seen of her, I should predict that she will be quite contented with it.”

“Then she is not much like the rest of her sex; that’s all I can say,” Sir Hugo answered with a small shrug. “However, she ought to be something extraordinary, for there must be an entanglement between your horoscope and hers—eh? When that tremendous telegram came, the first thing Lady Mallinger said was, ‘How very strange that it should be Daniel who sends it!’ But I’ve had something of the same sort in my own life. I was once at a foreign hotel where a lady had been left by her husband without money. When I heard of it, and came forward to help her, who should she be but an early flame of mine—who had been fool enough to marry an Austrian baron with a long mustache and short affection? But it was an affair of my own that called me there—nothing to do with knight-errantry, any more than you coming to Genoa had to do with the Grandcourts.”

The talk ran on the safer rail for a while—other people’s fates, the decent distance of scandal and law and property. Yet both of them were waiting, with an inward reluctance, for the subject that lay like a sealed packet between them. Daniel’s earlier letter—written after his first meeting with his mother—had been more like mist than sunlight; he knew it. He had been unable then to set down in ink what had shaken his blood and altered the language of his own being. Better to wait for Sir Hugo’s first opening.

They had nearly lost sight of the port when Sir Hugo turned, pausing as if for a last look at the masts and the dim play of lights over the water. The sea’s hush met the street’s receding clatter; it was as if the world offered a quieter chamber for what must now be spoken.

“And about the main business of your coming to Genoa, Dan?” he said, and there was a new gravity under the words. “You have not been deeply pained by anything you have learned, I hope? There is nothing that you feel need change your position in any way? You know, whatever happens to you must always be of importance to me.”

“I desire to meet your goodness by perfect confidence, sir,” Daniel answered. “But I can’t answer those questions truly by a simple yes or no. Much that I have heard about the past has pained me. And it has been a pain to meet and part with my mother in her suffering state, as I have been compelled to do. But it is no pain—it is rather a clearing up of doubts for which I am thankful, to know my parentage. As to the effect on my position, there will be no change in my gratitude to you, sir, for the fatherly care and affection you have always shown me. But to know that I was born a Jew may have a momentous influence on my life, which I am hardly able to tell you of at present.”

He forced the last words out with steadiness; not because he wished to wound Sir Hugo, but because he felt the future already pressing at him—asking not only what he would do, but in what tongue he would name himself. There are truths which, once spoken, change the room’s air; and Daniel felt Sir Hugo’s quick glance like a hand testing that altered atmosphere.

Sir Hugo turned and walked on again. For a few moments he was silent, and Daniel could almost hear the older man’s mind sorting its stored impressions, picking up fragments of half-remarked facts and trying to fit them into a shape that would not disturb his settled sense of the world.

At last Sir Hugo said, “I have long expected something remarkable from you, Dan; but, for God’s sake, don’t go into any eccentricities! I can tolerate any man’s difference of opinion, but let him tell it me without getting himself up as a lunatic. At this stage of the world, if a man wants to be taken seriously, he must keep clear of melodrama. Don’t misunderstand me. I’m not suspecting you of setting up any lunacy on your own account. I only think you might easily be led arm in arm with a lunatic, especially if he wanted defending. You have a passion for people who are pelted, Dan. I’m sorry for them too; but so far as company goes, it’s a bad ground of selection. However, I don’t ask you to anticipate your inclination in anything you have to tell me. When you make up your mind to a course that requires money, I have some sixteen thousand pounds that have been accumulating for you over and above what you have been having the interest of as income. And now I am come, I suppose you want to get back to England as soon as you can?”

“I must go first to Mainz,” Daniel said, catching at the practical, as if it were a rung of a ladder when the heart is dizzy. “To get away a chest of my grandfather’s, and perhaps to see a friend of his. Although the chest has been lying there these twenty years, I have an unreasonable sort of nervous eagerness to get it away under my care, as if it were more likely now than before that something might happen to it. And perhaps I am the more uneasy because I lingered after my mother left, instead of setting out immediately. Yet I can’t regret that I was here—else Mrs. Grandcourt would have had none but servants to act for her.”

“Yes, yes,” Sir Hugo said, and the flippancy that came back into his voice had the uneasy note of a man covering vexation with a thin cloth. “I hope you are not going to set a dead Jew above a living Christian.”

Color rose in Daniel’s face; it was as if, with that careless phrase, the power of a dominant vocabulary had tried to press down the truth he had only just dared to utter. He held back the retort that sprang to his lips—held it with the same discipline with which he had learned to bear the world’s clamor without letting it ruin the inner hearing.

They were turning in under the sign of the Italia, the hotel doors yawning bright and noisy, letting out a gust of warmed air thick with tobacco and roasted meat, and a burst of laughter that jarred after the sea’s steadier breath. Daniel went in beside Sir Hugo, carrying with him, under all the ordinary sounds of travel and society, the newly named fact of himself—still strange on the tongue, still untranslatable into the easy idioms of those he loved, yet irrevocable as blood.

When Deronda carried his letter into the banking-house in the Schuster Strasse at Mainz and asked for Joseph Kalonymos, he was led through the public hush into an inner room where the air changed—less of street-dust, more of paper and sealing-wax, that particular scent of money handled honestly and often. Beyond the door the city’s clatter thinned to a dull percussion, as if the walls had been built not merely to guard accounts, but to spare the mind from being rasped raw by noise.

At a table sat the white-bearded man Deronda remembered from the synagogue at Frankfort: the same old felt hat on his head, the same intent posture, as if every letter he touched had a pulse. Open envelopes lay in ordered disorder before him. Beside his chair was a packed portmanteau with a wrap and overcoat laid across it—travel already folded into readiness.

Kalonymos rose when Deronda entered, but he did not advance or offer his hand. He looked sharply, his small eyes bright and hard as dark stones set in the yellowed hollows of his face, and in German he said, “Good! It is now you who seek me, young man.”

“Yes; I seek you with gratitude, as a friend of my grandfather’s,” Deronda answered, the German coming to him without struggle, that generous tongue which makes room even for the stranger’s accent. “And I am under an obligation to you for giving yourself much trouble on my account.”

Kalonymos’ gaze held him a moment longer, as if testing whether gratitude had weight or was merely a polished phrase. Then his manner shifted: he put out his hand, and the grip was sudden, warm, decided. “So you are no longer angry at being something more than an Englishman?”

“On the contrary. I thank you heartily for helping to save me from remaining in ignorance of my parentage, and for taking care of the chest that my grandfather left in trust for me.”

“Sit down, sit down,” Kalonymos said quickly, in an undertone that matched the room’s guarded stillness. He seated himself again and motioned to a chair close by.

Then, with deliberation, he laid aside his hat. Under it was a thick mass of white hair. He stroked and clutched his beard while he examined Deronda’s face, searching in it for a remembered contour, a line of will, a likeness to a dead friend that might justify long vigilance and trouble.

To Deronda, that scrutiny had a strange sweetness in it. It was as though the man’s hand on his beard and his eyes on Deronda’s brow were touching a live wire running back through years and continents, binding him to a hope formed before he had breathed. The room, the sealed letters, the packed luggage, the muffled city outside—all the ordinary apparatus of a life spent in transactions—seemed suddenly to serve a mythic office: a guardian at a threshold, keeping safe a name and a story against the world’s forgetfulness.

Kalonymos spoke in Hebrew, quoting from the liturgy with the cadence of a remembered chant, and in the quiet the syllables sounded like something older than walls: “As thy goodness has been great to the former generations, even so may it be to the latter.”

After a pause he began again in German, briskly, as if time were a strict creditor. “Young man, I rejoice that I was not yet set off again on my travels, and that you are come in time for me to see the image of my friend as he was in his youth—no longer perverted from the fellowship of your people—no longer shrinking in proud wrath from the touch of him who seemed to be claiming you as a Jew. You come with thankfulness yourself to claim the kindred and heritage that wicked contrivance would have robbed you of. You come with a willing soul to declare, ‘I am the grandson of Daniel Charisi.’ Is it not so?”

“Assuredly it is,” Deronda said. “But let me say that I should at no time have been inclined to treat a Jew with incivility simply because he was a Jew. You can understand that I shrank from saying to a stranger, ‘I know nothing of my mother.’”

“A sin, a sin!” Kalonymos said, lifting his hand, his eyes closing in disgust as if at a taste gone rancid. “A robbery of our people—as when our youths and maidens were reared for the Roman Edom. But it is frustrated. I have frustrated it.”

He leaned forward, and the beard he had been grasping seemed to steady the flow of his speech, anchoring memory so it could not drift. “When Daniel Charisi—may his Rock and his Redeemer guard him!—when Daniel Charisi was a stripling and I was a lad little above his shoulder, we made a solemn vow always to be friends. He said, ‘Let us bind ourselves with duty, as if we were sons of the same mother.’ That was his bent from first to last—as he said, to fortify his soul with bonds. It was a saying of his, ‘Let us bind love with duty; for duty is the love of law; and law is the nature of the Eternal.’ So we bound ourselves. And though we were much apart in our later life, the bond has never been broken. When he was dead, they sought to rob him; but they could not rob him of me. I rescued that remainder of him which he had prized and preserved for his offspring. And I have restored to him the offspring they had robbed him of. I will bring you the chest forthwith.”

He went out for a few minutes. Deronda, left alone, listened to the building: the faint scratch of a pen somewhere, the soft shutting of a drawer, a footfall that did not hurry, the controlled acoustics of a place where even sound was disciplined. Out in the street, beyond the thick windows, there was a harsher rhythm—wheels over stone, a distant vendor’s call—life made noisy by the need to sell itself at every corner. Here, in this quieter chamber, the past could speak without being drowned.

Kalonymos returned with a clerk who carried a chest and set it down on the floor. The clerk drew off a leather cover and left without a word. The chest was not large, but its ornamental bracers and handles of gilt iron gave it weight beyond its size. The wood was beautifully incised with Arabic lettering, the curved lines like a script of flames arrested—beauty pressed into usefulness, as if even ornament had been taught to keep faith.

“So!” Kalonymos said, resuming his seat.

“And here is the curious key,” he added, taking it from a small leathern bag. He held it out, but his look stayed on Deronda with that wary, admonitory suspicion age often turns on youth. “Bestow it carefully. I trust you are methodic and wary.”
