“I shall be more careful of this than of any other property,” Deronda said, smiling as he put the key into his breast-pocket, feeling its cool metal settle there as if it had found the place prepared for it. “I never before possessed anything that was a sign to me of so much cherished hope and effort. And I shall never forget that the effort was partly yours. Have you time to tell me more of my grandfather? Or shall I be trespassing in staying longer?”

“Stay yet a while. In an hour and eighteen minutes I start for Trieste,” Kalonymos said, looking at his watch with exactness that made time itself seem an object he handled and arranged like letters. “And presently my sons will expect my attention. Will you let me make you known to them, so that they may have the pleasure of showing hospitality to my friend’s grandson? They dwell here in ease and luxury, though I choose to be a wanderer.”

“I shall be glad if you will commend me to their acquaintance for some future opportunity,” Deronda said. “There are pressing claims calling me to England—friends who may be much in need of my presence. I have been kept away from them too long by unexpected circumstances. But to know more of you and your family would be motive enough to bring me again to Mainz.”

“Good! Me you will hardly find, for I am beyond my threescore years and ten, and I am a wanderer, carrying my shroud with me. But my sons and their children dwell here in wealth and unity. The days are changed for us since Karl the Great fetched my ancestors from Italy to bring some tincture of knowledge to our rough German brethren. I and my contemporaries have had to fight for it too. Our youth fell on evil days; but this we have won; we increase our wealth in safety, and the learning of all Germany is fed and fattened by Jewish brains—though they keep not always their Jewish hearts.” He cut that last clause short, as if it left a bitter aftertaste. “Have you been left altogether ignorant of your people’s life, young man?”

“No,” said Deronda. “I have lately, before I had any true suspicion of my parentage, been led to study everything belonging to their history with more interest than any other subject. It turns out that I have been making myself ready to understand my grandfather a little.”

Kalonymos nodded, and Deronda felt he had struck the right path, the one that would lead back—without seeming to demand it—to what he most needed: not mere facts, but an image of the man whose thought had reached forward to him.

“So—you would perhaps have been such a man as he if your education had not hindered; for you are like him in features:—yet not altogether, young man.” Kalonymos’ eyes narrowed, measuring. “He had an iron will in his face: it braced up everybody about him. When he was quite young he had already got one deep upright line in his brow. I see none of that in you. Daniel Charisi used to say, ‘Better, a wrong will than a wavering; better a steadfast enemy than an uncertain friend; better a false belief than no belief at all.’ What he despised most was indifference. He had longer reasons than I can give you.”

“Yet his knowledge was not narrow?” Deronda asked, with that half-hidden thought that sometimes indecision is excused as breadth.

“Narrow? no.” Kalonymos shook his head, and a compassionate smile passed over his face, softening the sharpness. “From his childhood upward, he drank in learning as easily as the plant sucks up water. But he early took to medicine and theories about life and health. He traveled to many countries, and spent much of his substance in seeing and knowing. What he used to insist on was that the strength and wealth of mankind depended on the balance of separateness and communication, and he was bitterly against our people losing themselves among the Gentiles; ‘It’s no better,’ said he, ‘than the many sorts of grain going back from their variety into sameness.’”

As he spoke, Deronda seemed to feel that phrase on his tongue—grain, variety, sameness—and with it the sense of stored harvests and names for things that might vanish if one yielded too easily to the dominant speech of the world. A people could lose itself not only in marriage and custom, but in the very words by which it tasted bread, greeted morning, blessed the dead. To have one’s dialect thinned to an accent, one’s prayers turned into curiosities for others’ ears—there were power and violence in that, quieter than chains, but persistent.

Kalonymos went on, “He mingled all sorts of learning; and in that he was like our Arabic writers in the golden time. We studied together, but he went beyond me. Though we were bosom friends, and he poured himself out to me, we were as different as the inside and outside of the bowl.” His hand made a small shaping gesture, as if he could feel the vessel’s curve. “I stood up for two notions of my own: I took Charisi’s sayings as I took the shape of the trees: they were there, not to be disputed about. It came to the same thing in both of us; we were both faithful Jews, thankful not to be Gentiles.

“And since I was a ripe man, I have been what I am now, for all but age—loving to wander, loving transactions, loving to behold all things, and caring nothing about hardship. Charisi thought continually of our people’s future: he went with all his soul into that part of our religion: I, not. So we have freedom, I am content. Our people wandered before they were driven.” He paused, and through that pause Deronda heard again the controlled quiet of the room, as if even silence were a practiced craft. “Young man when I am in the East, I lie much on deck and watch the greater stars. The sight of them satisfies me. I know them as they rise, and hunger not to know more. Charisi was satisfied with no sight, but pieced it out with what had been before and what would come after. Yet we loved each other, and as he said, he bound our love with duty; we solemnly pledged ourselves to help and defend each other to the last. I have fulfilled my pledge.”

Kalonymos rose then, the movement decisive, like the closing of a ledger. Deronda rose also. The chest on the floor seemed to have altered the room’s meaning; it was no longer a place where letters were sorted, but a place where a life had been delivered into another’s hands.

“And in being faithful to him you have caused justice to be done to me,” Deronda said. “It would have been a robbery of me too that I should never have known of the inheritance he had prepared for me. I thank you with my whole soul.”

“Be worthy of him, young man.” Kalonymos’ voice sharpened, businesslike again, as if worthiness were a duty to be scheduled. “What is your vocation?”

The abruptness embarrassed Deronda. To call his law-reading a vocation felt like speaking a half-truth in a room where truth had been guarded at cost. “I cannot say that I have any.”

“Get one, get one. The Jew must be diligent.” Kalonymos put his hand on Deronda’s shoulder, the touch steadying, proprietary in the way of elders who believe they have earned the right to demand. He looked sharply into Deronda’s face. “You will call yourself a Jew and profess the faith of your fathers?”

Under that gaze Deronda grew slightly paler, not from fear, but from the weight of being asked to set his name aloud like a seal. “I shall call myself a Jew,” he said deliberately. “But I will not say that I shall profess to believe exactly as my fathers have believed. Our fathers themselves changed the horizon of their belief and learned of other races. But I think I can maintain my grandfather’s notion of separateness with communication. I hold that my first duty is to my own people, and if there is anything to be done toward restoring or perfecting their common life, I shall make that my vocation.”

As he spoke, it was as if the necessity of speech pressed a resolve into being—like dough that becomes coherent only under the hand’s demand. He felt, in the very forming of the words, that he had stepped into an identity that could not be translated into any other tongue without loss.

“Ah, you argue and you look forward—you are Daniel Charisi’s grandson,” Kalonymos said, and he added a benediction in Hebrew, the ancient sounds settling in the air with a tenderness that did not ask permission from modernity.

They parted. And almost as soon as Deronda was in London again, the aged man was once more on shipboard, with the sea’s vast hush under him and the cleaner, older music above—greeting the friendly stars without any eager curiosity, content to know their rising as one knows the return of a well-loved prayer.

There was another house besides the white one at Pennicote, another breast besides Rex Gascoigne’s, in which the tidings from Genoa fell like a stone dropped into a still pot—suddenly, sounding all the way down, and stirring what had seemed to have settled quiet at the bottom.

In the Meyricks’ little parlour, the day had been moving with its accustomed homeliness: the slight scent of last night’s extinguished fire still clung in the grate; and under it the room held the gentler smells of women’s work—warmed wool, a faint soapiness from washed hands, and the thin, clean odour of paper and ink that came of letters opened and folded often. All that was threaded through by the living sound that made the house happiest: the piano, and above it Mirah’s voice, guiding Mab through _Lascia ch’io pianga_. Mab, earnest and a little tragic in her imitation, had just reached one of those pleading turns where the air seems to ask for mercy with every note, when the latch-key clicked—then a sharp, crackling flourish, like the tearing of stiff brown paper that wraps sugar or dried figs, but louder and more imperious.

Hans came in with the _Times_ held up and shaken as if it were a flag. The paper’s harsh rustle cut straight across the music.

Mirah, who had been playing the accompaniment, started involuntarily. The sound, by that strange deceit of startled senses, had the weight of thunder to her. Mab let her voice die away with a groan of injury and cried—

“O-o-o, Hans! why do you bring a more horrible noise than my singing?”

Mrs. Meyrick, who sat near with her work and her quick eyes, looked up, all appetite for the world’s happenings awakened as it always was. She read news the way some people taste sauces—eager for everything, from great politics to the small garnish of weddings, which, she said, gave her the pleasant sense of finishing fashionable novels without the trouble of reading them, and of seeing the heroes and heroines made happy without knowing what poor creatures they were.

“What on earth is the wonderful news?” she said. “Anything about Italy—anything about the Austrians giving up Venice?”

“Nothing about Italy,” Hans returned, but with a tone that had an odd, anticipative tightness in it, as if he were holding a secret that pleased him too much to keep perfectly quiet—“but something from Italy.”

His mother’s mind, swift in anxiety, leapt at once to the name she most feared to hear connected with danger.

“Nothing bad?” she asked, the colour changing on her cheeks. Mirah’s heart clutched at the same thought before it had even taken words.

“Not bad for anybody we care much about,” Hans said quickly, and with his habitual twist, as if jesting were a cord to cling to when emotion pulled him. “Rather uncommonly lucky, I think. I never knew anybody die conveniently before. Considering what a dear gazelle I am, I’m constantly wondering to find myself alive.”

“Oh me, Hans!” Mab broke in, impatient as a child at a door kept shut. “If you must talk of yourself, let it be behind your own back. What _is_ it that has happened?”

Hans threw the paper before his mother and pressed a finger on the paragraph.

“Duke Alfonso is drowned, and the Duchess is alive, that’s all. But more than all is—Deronda was at Genoa in the same hotel with them, and he saw her brought in by the fishermen who had got her out of the water time enough to save her from any harm. It seems they saw her jump in after her husband—which was a less judicious action than I should have expected of the Duchess. However Deronda is a lucky fellow in being there to take care of her.”

At “Deronda,” Mirah’s breath seemed to stop. She sank back on the music-stool; her eyelids fell, and her hands clasped so tightly that the knuckles whitened. Mrs. Meyrick’s face softened with that ready pity which in her was as natural as the readiness with which she would cut bread for a hungry guest.

“Poor thing!” she said. “She must have been fond of her husband to jump in after him.”

“It was an inadvertence—a little absence of mind,” Hans answered, creasing his face roguishly and dropping into a chair near Mirah, as if the chair were an accomplice. “Who can be fond of a jealous baritone with freezing glances, always singing asides?—that was the husband’s _rôle_, depend upon it. Nothing can be neater than his getting drowned. The Duchess is at liberty now to marry a man with a fine head of hair, and glances that will melt instead of freezing her. And I shall be invited to the wedding.”

Mirah sprang up as if the words had struck her bodily. Her eyes—usually so gentle in their darkness—flashed with a sudden, fierce light; her face was pale, even to the lips that were commonly so rich in colour. She fixed Hans with a look that made him, for all his careless manhood, blush as if he had been a girl caught at some cruel trick.

“Mr. Hans,” she said, and her voice, shaken to its depth, had indignation in it like a sob turned to fire, “you ought not to speak in that way. Mr. Deronda would not like you to speak so. Why will you say he is lucky—why will you use words of that sort about life and death—when what is life to one is death to another? How do you know it would be lucky if he loved Mrs. Grandcourt? It might be a great evil to him. She would take him away from my brother—I know she would. Mr. Deronda would not call that lucky to pierce my brother’s heart.”

The room was struck silent, as if Mirah’s voice had stilled not only them but the very air. Hans sat transfixed, his usual quickness gone. Even when pain took him, his mind could not help producing a ludicrous shape for it, and he stammered, nervously—

“I am a fool and a brute, and I withdraw every word. I’ll go and hang myself like Judas—if it’s allowable to mention him.”

But Mirah’s anger had come like a jet from deep pain; it could not be soothed by his half-mocking penitence. She said no more. She sat down again at the piano and pushed the sheet of music before her with an air as if she meant to begin at once—only her hands trembled slightly, and the paper made a faint rasping sound under her fingers, a small, dry noise that seemed to accuse her of agitation.

It was Mab who spoke, and even her childish scorn had a seriousness in it, as if she felt the sanctity of names.

“Mirah is quite right to scold you, Hans. You are always taking Mr. Deronda’s name in vain. And it is horrible, joking in that way about his marrying Mrs. Grandcourt. Men’s minds must be very black, I think.”

“Quite true, my dear,” Hans said low, rising and turning away toward the back window, as if he could walk out of the shame in his own chest.

Mirah lifted her voice higher than usual, striving after firmness as after a straight seam when the cloth pulls.

“We had better go on, Mab; you have not given your full time to the lesson. Will you sing this again, or shall I sing it to you?”

“Oh, please sing it to me,” Mab answered, glad to slip back into the familiar track.

And Mirah sang _Lascia ch’io pianga_—but not now as a mere lesson. The melodious sobs and cries poured from her with a fuller, more urgent life, as if the old Italian plea were suddenly her own breath turned into sound. The piano, too, had that richer pressure which comes when a player’s heart is heavy and will have the keys give it speech. Hans, leaning against the mantel-piece, kept his eyes carefully away from his mother’s, and listened as one listens to the wind after having slammed a door in anger—ashamed to have made the peace of the house shake.

When Mirah had let her last note float away and had pressed the last chord, she rose quickly.

“I must go home now. Ezra expects me.”

She gave her hand silently to Mrs. Meyrick. She hung back a little, not daring to look at her, and—unlike her usual way—did not offer the kiss that had become a daily sweetness between them. But the little mother understood too much to rebuke. She drew Mirah’s face down to hers, and with a soft, steady touch said—

“God bless you, my dear.”

The words had the warmth of bread set down before one who is faint; and Mirah, with all her suffering, felt a new sharpness of compunction. She had been angry in Mrs. Meyrick’s house; she had rebuked Hans, who loved her; and mixed with jealousy and fear was the sting of thinking she had shown something like proud ingratitude, an unbecoming assertion of superiority. Her friend divined that self-reproach and met it with tenderness.

Hans had seized his wide-awake and stood ready at the door.

“Now, Hans,” Mab said, with what was really a sister’s tenderness cunningly disguised as severity, “you are not going to walk home with Mirah. I am sure she would rather not. You are so dreadfully disagreeable to-day.”

“I shall go to take care of her, if she does not forbid me,” Hans said, opening the door.

Mirah said nothing. The air outside had that cool edge which makes every sound sharper: distant wheels on the road, the brief cry of a bird, the click of their own steps on the paving. Hans walked by her side, unforbidden.

She had not courage to begin speaking again. She was aware that perhaps her words had been too severe, and yet behind them her heart held words far severer still. It was as if the crackle of that newspaper had burst open something in her that could not be folded down smooth again. And Hans, too, was busy with his own thoughts.

Mirah’s sudden flash of anger had waked in him a perception which made him feel dull not to have had it sooner. Suppose Mirah’s heart were preoccupied with Deronda in another character than that of benefactor to her and her brother? The supposition brought anxieties into Hans that, to do him justice, were not wholly selfish. He had long held, with a stubborn persuasion, that there was a serious attachment between Deronda and Mrs. Grandcourt. He had pieced together fragments of observation; he had gathered what his sisters had heard from Anna Gascoigne; and all had seemed to him to say plainly that Mrs. Grandcourt had a passion for Deronda, and that Deronda’s own austere self-repression covered a susceptibility which meant concealed love.

Many men, having such a belief, would have avoided every allusion that could irritate that susceptibility; but Hans’s talk naturally fluttered toward mischief, and he had a boyish taste for experimenting on live creatures—irritating his friends playfully to see what would stir. His experiments had ended by satisfying him that what he suspected was true.

Meanwhile, any susceptibility Deronda had shown about a lover’s attentions to Mirah, Hans had explained away by the alleged reason—her dependent position—for he credited his friend with unselfish anxiety for those he could rescue and protect. And Deronda’s insistence that Mirah would never marry one who was not a Jew necessarily seemed to exclude himself, since Hans shared the common opinion, undisturbed by anything he knew, that Deronda was Sir Hugo Mallinger’s son.

So Hans had thought himself clear about Deronda’s affections. Yet now—these events, which to him had looked like a step toward the union with Mrs. Grandcourt, had drawn from Mirah a betrayed passion which made him melancholy for her as well as for himself—though, on the whole, less melancholy than if he had imagined Deronda’s hopes fixed on her. It is not sublime, but it is common, that a man can bear more fortitude and milder jealousy at seeing the beloved object unhappy because his rival loves another, than at seeing her entirely happy in his rival. The mercurial Hans fluctuated between being wounded because Mirah was wounded, and being almost obliged to Deronda for loving somebody else.

He could not give Mirah any direct sign of how he understood her anger; and yet he longed that his speechless companionship might be eloquent in penitence and tender sympathy—an admissible form of wooing a bruised heart. Thus they went side by side in a companionship that seemed, for all its silence, like an agitated communication, as if two strings were vibrating together beyond the range of hearing, and the air between them were full of unheard sound.

At Mirah’s door Hans stopped. “Good-bye,” he said, holding out his hand with an appealing look.

Mirah met that look with melancholy gentleness and answered, quietly—

“Will you not come in and see my brother?”

Hans could not but read this as pardon. He did not understand how Mirah’s nature, wrought upon by early experience, could pass quickly from violent excitement into resolute acceptance of pain—as if pain were an old companion who, having been absent, had come back to sit in its accustomed chair.

“If you will let me,” Hans said; and they went in together. Half his grief was gone, and already his fancy was spinning a small romance: how his devotion might make him indispensable to Mirah in proportion as Deronda gave his devotion elsewhere. It seemed fair: his friend, Hans thought, was being provided for according to his own heart. And on the question of Judaism Hans felt thoroughly fortified. Who ever heard in tale or history that a woman’s love went in the track of her race and religion? Moslem and Jewish damsels were always attracted toward Christians; and now, if Mirah’s heart had gone too swiftly toward Deronda, here was another case.

Hans was accustomed to make merry with his own arguments, to call himself a Giaour, and antithesis the sole clue to events; but he believed a little in what he laughed at. His bird-like hope, built on the lightest principles, soared again in spite of heavy circumstances.

They found Mordecai looking singularly happy, holding a closed letter in his hand. His eyes glowed with a quiet triumph which, in his emaciated face, gave the impression of a conquest over assailing death—like a man who, with breath failing, yet holds up a cup of water to another’s lips.

After Hans’s greeting, Mirah put her arm round her brother’s neck and looked down at the letter without daring to ask about it, though she felt sure it was the source of his happiness.

“A letter from Daniel Deronda,” Mordecai said, answering her look. “Brief—only saying that he hopes soon to return. Unexpected claims have detained him. The promise of seeing him again is like the bow in the cloud to me,” he continued, turning to Hans; “and to you it must be a gladness. For who has two friends like him?”

While Hans answered, Mirah slipped away to her own little room—not to indulge in any outburst. If angels, once fancied to watch women at their toilette, had entered with her and let her shut the door, they would have seen only quiet, practical motions: she took off her hat and sat down, pressing her hands against her temples as if she had suddenly remembered a headache; then rose and dashed cold water on her eyes and brow and hair, until her backward curls held crystal beads and her face looked out again like a flower opened freshly after a shower. She sighed deeply—more than once—and put on her little slippers. Then she sat still for a couple of minutes which seemed to her long, as if full of things that were coming; and at last she rose with the air of one recollecting a duty and went down to make tea.

Something of her old life had returned. She had once been used to remembering she must learn her part, go to rehearsal, act and sing in the evening, hide her feelings from her father; and the more painful her life grew, the more she had been trained to hide. The force of her nature had found its chief action in resolute endurance; and to-day the violence of feeling which had broken out in anger had quickly transformed itself into a steady facing of trouble—the well-known companion of her young years.

Yet while she moved about and spoke as usual, a close observer might have discerned a difference between this apparent calm, born of restraining energy, and the sweet, genuine calm of the months when she had first felt a return of infantine happiness. Those whom fortune has indulged, who have always believed calamity to be what happens to others, feel a blind incredulous rage when their lot is reversed, and half believe their cries will alter the storm. Mirah felt no such surprise when familiar Sorrow came back from brief absence and sat down with her according to old use. But this habit of expecting trouble rather than joy hindered her from clinging persistently to any belief contrary to the probabilities which were not only suggested by Hans, but supported by her own private knowledge and long-growing presentiment.

An attachment between Deronda and Mrs. Grandcourt, ending in marriage, had the aspect of certainty to her feeling. There had been no fault in him: facts had ordered themselves into a tie between him and a woman who belonged to another world than hers and Ezra’s—nay, who seemed another sort of being than Deronda: something foreign that would disturb his life instead of blending with it. Well, well—if only it could have been deferred so as to make no difference while Ezra was there! Mirah did not know all the momentousness of the relation between Deronda and her brother, but she had seen and felt enough to forebode its incongruity with any close tie to Mrs. Grandcourt. That was the first clothing her mind gave to her mortal repugnance.

But beneath her habitual acts, her thoughts moved quickly and silently, like changing sensations. Soon the inward language said distinctly: the mortal repugnance would remain even if Ezra were secure.

“What I have read about and sung about and seen acted, is happening to me—this that I am feeling is the love that makes jealousy;” thus impartially Mirah summed up the charge against herself.

But what difference could her pain make to any one else? It must remain exclusively her own and hidden, as her early yearning and devotion to her lost mother had been hidden. And unlike that devotion, this new feeling seemed a misfortune of her nature: a discovery that what should have been pure gratitude and reverence had sunk into selfish pain; that the feeling she had delighted to pour out in words was degraded into something she was ashamed to betray—an absurd longing that she, who had received all and given nothing, should be of importance where she was of no importance—an angry feeling toward another woman who possessed the good she wanted.

Yet what vain reliance had lain darkly within her and now burned into sight as disappointment and jealousy? It was as if her soul had been steeped in poisonous passion in forgotten dreams of deep sleep, and now flamed out in this unaccountable misery. For with her waking reason she had never entertained what seemed the wildly unfitting thought that Deronda could love her. The uneasiness she had felt before had been vague, easily explained as regret that he was only a visitant in her and Ezra’s world—that his home-world, with its lights and lacqueys, was as different from hers as a portico is from the door of a tent, where the only splendour comes from inaccessible stars. But her pain was no longer vague. The image of Mrs. Grandcourt by Deronda’s side, drawing him farther and farther away, was as definite as pincers on her flesh.

In the Psyche-mould of Mirah’s frame there rested a fervid quality of emotion—sometimes rashly supposed to require the bulk of a Cleopatra. Her impressions had the thoroughness and tenacity that make the first selection of passionate feeling take on the character of a lifelong faithfulness. And now a selection had declared itself which gave love the cruel heart of jealousy. She had been used to strong repugnance toward objects around her and to walking inwardly aloof while they touched her senses; and now that repugnance concentrated itself on Mrs. Grandcourt, of whom she involuntarily conceived more evil than she knew.

“I could bear everything that used to be—but this is worse—this is worse,—I used not to have horrible feelings!” she whispered aloud to her pillow, as if the sound of her own words might keep her from drowning in them.

Strange that she should have to pray against any feeling concerned with Deronda.

But this conclusion had not come in an idle hour. It had been reached through an evening spent attending to Mordecai—whose exaltation, in the prospect of seeing his friend again, disposed him to speak much to her. Often his speech was broken by silences that seemed full of inward utterance, animating his eyes and moving his lips without sound, as if he listened to something beyond the room’s quiet noises—the small tick of the clock, the faint murmur of the kettle, the soft settling of coal ash—as if that humble domestic soundscape were only a threshold to greater voices.

One thought especially occupied him. Once, after a long silence, he said—

“Seest thou, Mirah, the _Shemah_, wherein we briefly confess the divine Unity, is the chief devotional exercise of the Hebrew; and this made our religion the fundamental religion for the whole world: for the divine Unity embraced as its consequence the ultimate unity of mankind. See, then—the nation which has been scoffed at for its separateness, has given a binding theory to the human race. Now, in complete unity a part possesses the whole as the whole possesses every part: and in this way human life is tending toward the image of the Supreme Unity. For as our life becomes more spiritual by capacity of thought, and joy therein, possession tends to become more universal, being independent of gross material contact; so that in a brief day the soul of man may know in fuller volume the good which has been and is, nay, is to come, than all he could possess in a whole life where he had to follow the creeping paths of the senses. In this moment, my sister, I hold the joy of another’s future within me: a future which these eyes will not see, and which my spirit may not then recognize as mine. I recognize it now, and love it so, that I can lay down this poor life upon its altar and say: ‘Burn, burn indiscernibly into that which shall be, which is my love and not me.’ Dost thou understand, Mirah?”

“A little,” Mirah had answered faintly, “but my mind is too poor to have felt it.”

“And yet,” Mordecai had said, rather insistently, “women are specially framed for the love which feels possession in renouncing, and is thus a fit image of what I mean. Somewhere in the later _Midrash_, I think, is the story of a Jewish maiden who loved a Gentile king so well, that this was what she did:—she entered into prison and changed clothes with the woman who was beloved by the king, that she might deliver that woman from death by dying in her stead, and leave the king to be happy in his love which was not for her. This is the surpassing love, that loses self in the object of love.”

“No, Ezra, no,” Mirah had said, with low-toned intensity, as if the story itself hurt her. “That was not it. She wanted the king, when she was dead, to know what she had done, and feel that she was better than the other. It was her strong self, wanting to conquer, that made her die.”

Mordecai had been silent a little, and then had argued gently, pressing the thought like a seal on wax.

“That might be, Mirah. But if she acted so, believing the king would never know.”

“You can make the story so in your mind, Ezra, because you are great, and like to fancy the greatest that could be. But I think it was not really like that. The Jewish girl must have had jealousy in her heart, and she wanted somehow to have the first place in the king’s mind. That is what she would die for.”

“My sister,” Mordecai had answered, “thou hast read too many plays, where the writers delight in showing the human passions as indwelling demons, unmixed with the relenting and devout elements of the soul. Thou judgest by the plays, and not by thy own heart, which is like our mother’s.”

Mirah had made no answer then. And now, making tea with hands that did not shake—measuring, pouring, listening to the small domestic sounds as if they were duties to hold on by—she felt how the very words about renouncing love and losing self had turned into a hard, bitter taste within her: she could not translate her own experience into the noble dialect her brother spoke. There was something in her that would not become pure by being named; and the name she feared most was the one she could not help hearing, again and again, like a refrain under every ordinary sound: Deronda.

Something Mirah had begun to watch for—as one listens for a familiar footfall in a house that has known both feasting and famine—came upon her again that morning, not like a single pang but like a sorrow returning with trunks and bundles, prepared to lodge.

She was turning out of Knightsbridge after singing at a charitable morning concert in a wealthy home, where Klesmer’s recommendation had won her the invitation and where the air still seemed sweet with violets and hot-house blossoms, mixed with the faint animal warmth of fur collars and the sharper tang of carriage-grease waiting at the curb. Outside, there had been the usual little crowd to stare at departing company, their voices a restless tide against the clatter of wheels. Mirah, in her simple black concert dress with a dust-cloak thrown over it, was not dressed to provoke notice. But it was not the eyes of strangers that tightened her breath: it was a sound.

Footsteps.

They kept an even pace with her own, neither hurrying nor lagging, as if they had learned her rhythm and meant to make it theirs. London’s din had its own ecology—iron rims on stone, the puff and hiss of horses, the barking of a newsboy—yet this steady accompaniment seemed to stand out as a single, obstinate note in the whole city’s chord, and it made her blood go cold. She felt dogged, and instantly, without looking, she knew whom she feared.

Her father.

The thought was so vivid that to turn her head felt like turning to meet a ghost. If it was he, he would claim her—claim recognition—force her to that encounter whose rush of shame and pity had been her nightly nightmare. She walked on, not quickening her pace—what was speed against fate?—and pictured what must happen as if certainty marched behind her. With the picture came a sting of regret: she had given her word to Mrs. Meyrick that she would use no concealment about him. It was that promise, bitter as an herb that nevertheless saves from poison, which urged her at last to do what she most dreaded. Better to choose the moment than to be seized by it.

She had reached the entrance of the small square where her home lay and had made up her mind to turn, when the embodied presentiment came closer, slid to her side, caught her wrist, and said, with that persuasive curl of accent which always tried to sweeten command into affection—

“Mirah!”

She paused without starting. It was the voice she expected, and the eyes were the eyes she expected. Her face was grave, as if she were looking at her executioner. His was arranged for soothing and propitiation. Once he had been handsome, bright with color; now he was sallow and deep-lined, wearing that impudent suavity which comes from courting favor while accepting disrespect. He was lightly made and active, with something of youth about him that made the signs of age seem almost like a disguise; and in truth he was hardly fifty-seven. His clothes were shabby as ever, and yet he carried his shabbiness with a jaunty air—the bushy grizzled curls, the small hands and feet, the light walk that gave him the look of a man who would always contrive a stage for himself.

His presence struck Mirah more keenly than before with the mingled anguish of shame and grief, repulsion and pity—more keenly now that she lived among people to whom he would be only a foreign, broken-down adventurer. Slowly, in a sad, trembling voice, she said,

“It is you, father.”

“Why did you run away from me, child?” he began at once, rapid and practiced, as if he were pouring out a speech he had rehearsed on lonely pavements. His quick gestures flickered like an abbreviated finger-language. “What were you afraid of? You knew I never made you do anything against your will. It was for your sake I broke up your engagement in the Vorstadt, because I saw it didn’t suit you, and you repaid me by leaving me to the bad times that came in consequence. I had made an easier engagement for you at the Vorstadt Theater in Dresden—I didn’t tell you, because I wanted to take you by surprise. And you left me planted there—obliged to make myself scarce because I had broken contract. That was hard lines for me, after I had given up everything for the sake of getting you an education which was to be a fortune to you. What father devoted himself to his daughter more than I did to you? You know how I bore that disappointment in your voice, and made the best of it: and when I had nobody besides you, and was getting broken, as a man must who has had to fight his way with his brains—you chose that time to leave me. Who else was it you owed everything to, if not to me? and where was your feeling in return? For what my daughter cared, I might have died in a ditch.”

He stopped, not from lack of invention but because he had reached a pathetic summit; and he sobbed suddenly, like a woman’s sob, pulling out an old yellow silk handkerchief. He truly felt himself ill-used: unscrupulous people keep a clear account of what is owing to them, with no reckoning on the other side.

Mirah, though the sob moved her by old habit into pity, had strength enough not to let him suppose she was deceived. For the first time in her life she forced accusing words through her filial tenderness.

“You know why I left you, father; and I had reason to distrust you, because I felt sure that you had deceived my mother. If I could have trusted you, I would have stayed with you and worked for you.”

“I never meant to deceive your mother, Mirah,” he said, putting back the handkerchief, and speaking in a voice that struggled as if more sobs would come to help his story. “I meant to take you back to her, but chances hindered me just at the time, and then there came information of her death. It was better for you that I should stay where I was, and your brother could take care of himself. Nobody had any claim on me but you. I had word of your mother’s death from a particular friend, who had undertaken to manage things for me, and I sent him over money to pay expenses. There’s one chance to be sure—he may have written me lies for the sake of getting the money out of me.”

Mirah could not bear to utter the only true answer—*I don’t believe you.* She only showed, by the direction of her steps, that she wished them to go on. To stand still here, where servants and coachmen and passing eyes made a constant little theatre, was unbearable. Even walking together, they were a spectacle: her quiet English-lady dress setting off her beauty like a plain dark frame, and beside her this shabby, eager, foreign-looking man, with his restlessness and his jaunty air, who made the square seem suddenly narrower, as if the city itself drew closer to listen.

“You seem to have done well for yourself, Mirah? *You* are in no want, I see,” he said, examining her with emphasis.

“Good friends who found me in distress have helped me to get work,” she answered, scarcely knowing what she said for the crowding of what she must say. “I give lessons. I have sung in private houses. I have just been singing at a private concert.” Then, with a meaning she wanted him to feel, she added, “I have very good friends, who know all about me.”

“And you would be ashamed they should see your father in this plight? No wonder. I came to England with no prospect, but the chance of finding you. It was a mad quest; but a father’s heart is superstitious—feels a loadstone drawing it somewhere or other. I might have done very well, staying abroad: when I hadn’t you to take care of, I could have rolled or settled as easily as a ball; but it’s hard being lonely in the world, when your spirit’s beginning to break. And I thought my little Mirah would repent leaving her father when she came to look back. I’ve had a sharp pinch to work my way; I don’t know what I shall come down to next. Talents like mine are no use in this country. When a man’s getting out at elbows nobody will believe in him. I couldn’t get any decent employ with my appearance. I’ve been obliged to get pretty low for a shilling already.”

London’s sounds seemed to take the words and make a rough chorus of them—the rattle of a cart, the rasp of a saw from some distant yard—no soft shelter anywhere, only the city grinding on. Mirah’s imagination was quick, and it showed her her father sinking to further degradation, each step downward like a stain spreading on cloth that cannot be washed clean.

Before she could reply to his glib string of sentences, he added, sharp as a knife laid suddenly on the table—

“Where do you live, Mirah?”

“Here, in this square. We are not far from the house.”

“In lodgings?”

“Yes.”

“Any one to take care of you?”

“Yes,” said Mirah again, and turned her face fully toward him, forcing herself to meet the keen look in his eyes. “My brother.”

His eyelids fluttered as if lightning had passed across them; his shoulders moved slightly. Then, after a pause just long enough for calculation, he said—

“Ezra? How did you know—how did you find him?”

“That would take long to tell. Here we are at the door. My brother would not wish me to close it on you.”

She was already on the step, but turned toward him as he stood below on the pavement. Her heart began to beat faster with the prospect of Ezra’s presence meeting this man—this father whose mere nearness could make Mirah feel the “stabbed heart of reverence,” the shame that comes because one has loved and cannot wholly stop loving. And now, even in the attitude of giving leave to the father she had been used to obey, seeing him there below her with a perceptible shrinking from the admission he had almost demanded, she felt that pang of sympathetic humiliation which belongs to an intensely filial nature.

“Stay a minute, *Liebchen*,” Lapidoth said, lowering his voice. “What sort of man has Ezra turned out?”

“A good man—a wonderful man,” Mirah answered with slow emphasis, struggling to master the agitation that made her voice tremble more as she went on. She felt urged—almost as if by a stern inward guardian—to prepare her father for the complete penetration of himself that awaited him. “But he was very poor when my friends found him for me—a poor workman. Once—twelve years ago—he was strong and happy, going to the East, which he loved to think of; and my mother called him back because—because she had lost me. And he went to her, and took care of her through great trouble, and worked for her till she died—died in grief. And Ezra, too, had lost his health and strength. The cold had seized him coming back to my mother, because she was forsaken. For years he has been getting weaker—always poor, always working—but full of knowledge, and great-minded. All who come near him honor him. To stand before him is like standing before a prophet of God—falsehoods are no use.”

She dropped her eyes on the last words, unable to endure the ignoble look of frustration gathering in his face. Yet he was quick—quick as a cook who, finding one dish spoiled, turns at once to another and disguises the lack with sauce. His invention never waited for feeling.

“Mirah, *Liebchen*,” he said, with the old caressing tone, “shouldn’t you like me to make myself a little more respectable before my son sees me? If I had a little sum of money, I could fit myself out and come home to you as your father ought, and then I could offer myself for some decent place. With a good shirt and coat on my back, people would be glad enough to have me. I could offer myself for a courier, if I didn’t look like a broken-down mountebank. I should like to be with my children, and forget and forgive. But you have never seen your father look like this before. If you had ten pounds at hand—or I could appoint you to bring it me somewhere—I could fit myself out by the day after to-morrow.”

The temptation struck Mirah like the scent of warm bread to one who has fasted: the instant desire to give, to relieve, to quiet trouble by a simple offering. But with it came the remembered taste of past bitterness—promises broken, lives strained thin as cheap cloth. She forced herself to look at him again.

“I don’t like to deny you what you ask, father; but I have given a promise not to do things for you in secret. It is hard to see you looking needy; but we will bear that for a little while; and then you can have new clothes, and we can pay for them.”

Now she understood, with a practical clearness, the wisdom that had made Mrs. Meyrick exact that promise: secrecy was the old door through which her father always entered and always escaped, leaving shame and confusion behind him like dirty footprints.

Lapidoth’s good humor gave way. A sneer tightened his mouth.

“You are a hard and fast young lady—you have been learning useful virtues—keeping promises not to help your father with a pound or two when you are getting money to dress yourself in silk—your father who made an idol of you, and gave up the best part of his life to providing for you.”

“It seems cruel—I know it seems cruel,” Mirah said, and the moment was to her worse than the hour when she had thought of drowning herself. The blood left her lips; her breath came thin. “But, father, it is more cruel to break the promises people trust in. That broke my mother’s heart—it has broken Ezra’s life. You and I must eat now this bitterness from what has been. Bear it. Bear to come in and be cared for as you are.”

“To-morrow, then,” Lapidoth said, almost turning away, as if her paleness and trembling meant the inconvenient world had taken her side. But he turned back at once, his hands feeling restlessly in his pockets, and his tone sliding again into appeal.

“I’m a little cut up with all this, Mirah. I shall get up my spirits by to-morrow. If you’ve a little money in your pocket, I suppose it isn’t against your promise to give me a trifle—to buy a cigar with.”

Mirah could not ask herself another question. She did what her pity and habit compelled: put her cold trembling hands into her pocket for her *portemonnaie* and held it out. He grasped it at once, pressed her fingers while he took it, and said in the old easy cadence, as if nothing had been torn or altered—

“Good-bye, my little girl—to-morrow then!”

And he left her.

He had not gone many steps before he opened the purse, searching every fold. He found two half-sovereigns, odd silver, and, pasted against the folding cover, a slip of paper on which Ezra had written, in beautiful Hebrew characters, the name of their mother, the dates of her birth, marriage, and death, and the prayer: “May Mirah be delivered from evil.” Mirah liked to have that inscription on many things she used—an intimate memorial clinging to daily habit, as if the dead could keep watch through the very objects her hands touched.

Lapidoth read it and had a quick vision of his marriage day: himself young, bright, unblamed, teaching many things, expecting to make money more easily by writing, very fond of Sara—his beautiful bride—who cried when he expected him to cry, and reflected each phase of his feeling with a mimetic readiness. But he had traveled far from that self; and the memory came without tenderness, as if words about nourishment lay on a tongue that can no longer taste. The shapes were there, the grain, the mere outline of what once had flavor; yet the savor—the compunction, the sweetness of regret—was gone.

The purse itself was handsome—a gift she had been unable to calculate about giving away. Presently his reverie slipped off like a cloak, and he was considering what the purse would fetch in addition to its contents, and what chance there might be of drawing more from his daughter without submitting to any penitential form of life under the eyes of that formidable son. On such a subject his susceptibilities remained lively enough.

Meanwhile Mirah went into the house, her power of reticence broken by pain too sharp to be carried alone. The noises of the street fell behind her; inside there was that quieter sound-world which Ezra guarded like a sanctuary—the faint turning of paper, the soft settling of a book, the breath between thoughts. She found him seated, quietly reading and sifting old manuscripts of his own, those pages he meant to consign to Deronda, as one might sort herbs carefully dried for a future healing.

In the reaction from her long effort to master herself, she sank before him and clasped his knees, sobbing out his name as if it were bread to keep her from starving.

“Ezra, Ezra!”

He did not speak at once. His alarm spent itself in searching for the cause—alarmed the more because this violent outburst was new in her. But Mirah’s longing was to speak, to pour out the reason and be relieved by truth spoken in the presence of truth.

Presently she raised her head, still sobbing, and said brokenly, “Ezra, my father! our father! He followed me. I wanted him to come in. I said you would let him come in. And he said No, he would not—not now, but to-morrow. And he begged for money from me. And I gave him my purse, and he went away.”

To her, the words were misery itself, every syllable salted with shame. To Mordecai, they were less grievous than what his imagination had prepared; and he answered gently, as he laid his hands tenderly on her head and took off her hat with the care of one who knows that even small acts can soothe an anguished spirit—

“Wait for calm, Mirah, and then tell me all.”

In a few minutes, under that quiet influence, she told him as exactly as she could what had passed—the footsteps, the grasp on her wrist, the request, her promise, the purse. Mordecai listened without interruption, his stillness like a deep place where turbulence can fall and lose its noise.

“He will not come to-morrow,” Mordecai said at last.

Neither spoke aloud what both thought: that he might watch for Mirah’s goings-out and beg again, as a hungry man watches a kitchen door.

After a silence, Mordecai added, and his voice had that cadence which made the small Brompton lodging seem for an instant linked to elder rooms where old griefs and hopes had been spoken in another tongue—

“Seest thou, our lot is the lot of Israel. The grief and the glory are mingled as the smoke and the flame. It is because we children have inherited the good that we feel the evil. These things are wedded for us, as our father was wedded to our mother.”

The place was Brompton, the world outside full of iron and commerce and the ceaseless buying and selling of every sound and every art; yet the words might have come from a Rabbi handing down sentences meant to be kept alive when languages perish and memories are worn thin by the dominant speech. “The Omnipresent,” a Rabbi had said, “is occupied in making marriages.” The levity of that saying lived only in the ear that heard it wrongly; for “marriages” meant all the strange joinings in the universe, the binding together of our good and evil, so that even in a plain room where paper rustled and a sister wept, the mingling went on—smoke and flame—inseparable.

Deronda had gone out from England as one goes from a familiar kitchen into a street full of unknown smells—aware of hunger, yet not knowing what food could satisfy it; aware of an inward longing, yet frightened by the chance that longing might be fed into something unmanageable. He had left with his will still held back, like a hand hovering over the seasoning: ready to give itself, yet afraid of spoiling the whole by one rash pinch. He came back as if he carried a title-deed written in his own blood and sealed by time—no mere liberty to drift, but a bond he could honor; and the bond, instead of tightening him into helplessness, gave him the strange ease of a purpose found.

There had always been, beneath his careful speech and his trained patience, a secret selection—quiet as a taste that returns again and again to the same bread though the table is spread with other things. Since the day he had left the little house at Chelsea, Mirah’s farewell—those few words and that look, tender as a hand laid on a bruise—had worked in him with the steadiness of daily nourishment. It did not intoxicate; it sustained. It had kept him from any self-indulgence in word or deed when circumstances had pressed him hard, and his habitual sympathy might have slid into weaker compliances. He could not, he thought, ever woo her; the very associations that had made her dear forbade it. Yet she had taken her place in him as a beloved type—so that other fascinations seemed thin, like dishes prettily served but without salt, without scent, without the slow warmth that rises from honest broth.

And poor Gwendolen’s dependence, however it stirred him, had roused in him not the heat of personal love but the stern ardor of pity—the kind of feeling that makes a man stand by a fireless hearth and give away his own cloak. Toward Mirah, unlike in everything, his tenderness flowed without being dragged, as a clear stream takes the deeper channel. His friendship with Mordecai had drawn Mirah nearer still, not by any open change, but by that inevitable closeness which comes when two lives are bound to the care of a third. He had watched his own feeling as one watches a craving it would be safer to starve; yet Hans’s pretensions had flung out the jealous flame, and when his mother, with her piercing imperiousness, accused him of being in love with a Jewess, any evasion felt like treachery. He had been forced, in one hour, both to name his love and to give shape to his resolve.

That new decisiveness acted on him like the sudden freeing of a wind that had long been held back by walls. Energy that had been spent in self-checking rushed forward; and as he travelled home from Mainz the remaining miles became an offence to his blood, as if the very rails were hindering him. It was as though, finding his ancestry, he had found an added soul: his judgment, once wandering in a wide impartiality that soothed itself by not choosing, now chose with that partiality which is man’s strength—the power to draw shoulder to shoulder with those whose inheritance is his own, and to turn sympathy into action. He longed to be again with Mordecai, to speak without that perpetual restraint, to agree, to dissent, to plan; and, all the while, to have Mirah’s presence without seeming to seek it—to see her with a new possibility before him, and test her words and looks by a new light.

Yet with all his impatience, there was in him a delicate fear. He was not greatly alarmed about Hans; but he had a presentiment that Mirah’s feeling toward himself had always flowed in a channel that would not easily be turned into love. To become a lover when a woman has been thinking of you as a grave protector—something like a judge, a guardian—seemed to him a violent transformation, and he shrank from startling her into pain.

Still, what could he do but go straight from the station to the small square in Brompton? He had promised to run down next day to the Abbey to see Lady Mallinger, and the sunset was already lowering into that London haze which drinks up the light and gives it back dimly, like a smoky lamp. Besides, he carried with him the precious chest, heavy not only with papers but with the sense of hands long dead that had packed and guarded them. He wished to deposit it with Mordecai at once—let him study its contents, alone and with him; and he knew that such swiftness of coming would gratify Mordecai’s heart. It gratified his own too. His nature rushed in one current: the eager affection that delighted in meeting the wishes of those he loved, and the imaginative need of a far-reaching relation that would make even daily acts part of a horizon.

He entered as noiselessly as possible, like one who comes into a sickroom, and, though his dress was only the drab contemporary cloth of a gentleman, there was a radiance in him—an added depth of color in the eyes, a quick returning glow under the skin—born of the thing he carried within, not of any thought about becomingness.

It was the evening of the same afternoon in which Mirah had had her interview with her father. The house held a hush that seemed to have thickened all day, as steam thickens under a lid. Papers Mordecai had been sifting lay scattered where they had fallen at the first shock of anxiety; neither he nor Mirah had had the will to stoop and gather them, as if even that small ordering would be a lie against disorder in the heart. They had sat still together—not counting minutes—while the mantel-clock ticked with that dry persistence which can make sorrow feel mocked, and the light sank away.

Mirah had not eaten; the very thought of food, that should have been comfort, had seemed to her like something belonging to other lives. She had thrown off her dust-cloak and sat close to her brother, her hand in his, while he leaned back with closed eyes and difficult breathing. To her he looked as he might look when the soul could no longer endure its narrow lodging. The fear of his death visited her again and again, and now her grief had a cruel doubling: the father’s shadow had returned, and with it the sense of being bereft not only of the dead but of the living—of losing one by death and one by disgrace.

She watched Mordecai’s emaciated face—so lately vivid with inner fire—now like a lamp turned low, as if a veil had been drawn over it. Her own cheeks were pallid; her eyes held that sorrowful brightness young tears leave behind; her curls were in the disorder of a child roused from sleep.

Then the door opened; no one entered at first; but a voice, known as one knows the sound of a loved foot on the stair, said, “Daniel Deronda—may he come in?”

“Come! come!” Mordecai answered, rising instantly, his face irradiated as if the name itself were light. He looked not surprised, but as if he had been expecting him all day. Mirah started up too, blushing with confused, half-alarmed expectation.

When Deronda came in, his presence was like clearness after rain—no matter what clouds might gather again, the beam of that moment warmed them. Mirah stood close by her brother’s left. Deronda held out his right hand to her, and at the same time laid his other hand on Mordecai’s shoulder; he stood thus a moment, holding them both, saying nothing, taking in their faces with anxious swiftness, until he asked Mirah, “Has anything happened?—any trouble?”

“Talk not of trouble now,” Mordecai said, saving her. “There is joy in your face—let the joy be ours.”

Mirah thought, with a quick ache, It is for something he cannot tell us. But they sat, Deronda drawing his chair close in front of Mordecai, as if he could not bear distance between them.

“That is true,” he said, his voice firm with restrained delight. “I have a joy which will remain to us even in the worst trouble. I did not tell you, Mordecai, the reason of my journey abroad, because—never mind. I went to learn my parentage. And you were right. I am a Jew.”

The clasping of the two men’s hands was like a flash—swift, involuntary, inevitable. It passed through Mirah as an electric shock—startling every nerve awake. But Deronda went on, not pausing for their amazement, speaking as if he were uttering what had long been prepared in Mordecai’s own mind as well as his.

“We have the same people. Our souls have the same vocation. We shall not be separated by life or by death.”

Mordecai’s answer came in Hebrew, loud only as a whisper, yet weighty as liturgy: “Our God and the God of our fathers.”

The feeling was too strong for his ready speech; the words that usually sprang winged and quick seemed pressed down by awe.

Mirah fell on her knees beside him and looked up at his illuminated face—so unlike the deathly look of moments ago. The movement was her one possible outlet: despair reversed into gladness so sudden and so solemn it felt like a rite. For that moment she thought of herself only through him—through what this meant to Ezra.

“And it is not only that I am a Jew,” Deronda continued, in one of those rare minutes when yearning and action are one, and the real seems to match the ideal. “I come of a strain that has ardently maintained the fellowship of our race—a line of Spanish Jews that has borne many students and men of practical power. And I possess what will give us a sort of communion with them. My grandfather, Daniel Charisi, preserved manuscripts and family records far back, hoping they would pass into the hands of his grandson. That hope is fulfilled, in spite of attempts to thwart it by hiding my parentage from me. I have the chest containing them, with his own papers; it is down below in this house. I mean to leave it with you, Mordecai, that you may help me study them. Some I can read easily—Spanish and Italian. Others are in Hebrew, and, I think, Arabic; but there seem to be Latin translations. I could only look at them hastily at Mainz. We will study them together.”

He ended with that bright smile which, shining out from his habitual gravity, seemed a revelation—the rare smile that has meaning because it is not cheap. But when his glance passed from Mordecai and rested on Mirah, it was like sunshine too direct: it made her shift as if she had been warmed and wounded at once. She had knelt under an impulse in which personal embarrassment had no place; now thoughts rushed in that were discordant—Mrs. Grandcourt; the altered aspect of Deronda’s life; her own position; and, as his eyes lingered, she colored and rose, taking her seat again with hands and feet crossed, trying to look quietly composed.

Deronda, keenly sensitive, imagined that the feeling he could not wholly hide had looked out too much and had repelled her. He was ready to believe that any sudden revelation might spoil her feeling toward him; and if Mirah could not love him, any advance from him would make her wretched in the very communion that must continue while Ezra lived. The fear pricked him sharply—fear born not of pride but of tenderness, the dread of being a claim upon her gratitude.

Mordecai, seeing only fulfillment, began to speak again, his voice enlarging as if his breath were freer.

“Daniel, from the first I have said to you: we know not all the pathways. Is there not a meeting among them, as in one soul when an idea is born and breathing draws the elements toward it and is fed and glows? All things are bound in that Omnipresence which is the place and habitation of the world; and events are of a glass whereby our eyes see some of the ways. And if it seems that erring and unloving wills have helped to prepare you, as Moses was prepared, to serve your people the better, that belongs to another order than the law by which our footsteps must be guided. For evil makes not a people’s good except by stirring the righteous will. Beneath all clouds with which our thought encompasses the Eternal, this is clear—that a people can be blessed only by counsellors, and by a multitude whose will moves in obedience to justice and love. See now: it was your loving will that made a chief pathway and resisted evil. In doing brotherhood to my sister, and seeking out her brother in the flesh, your soul has been prepared to receive with gladness the message—‘behold the multitude of your brethren.’”

“You and Mirah have been my teachers,” Deronda said. “If this revelation had come to me before I knew you, I think my mind would have rebelled. Perhaps I should have felt—‘If I could have chosen, I would not have been a Jew.’ What I feel now is—that my whole being consents to the fact. It has been the gradual accord between your mind and mine that has brought about that full consent.”

As he spoke, the first evening in the book-shop came back to him with vividness—the dusty air, the quiet murmurs of the place, the sense of being addressed from a height of prophetic certainty that had then made him struggle to keep aloof. Now, the delight of satisfying the eager watcher before him—like one who has long scanned the mountains for a signal-flame—made his fervor fuller.

“It is through your inspiration that I have discerned what may be my life’s task. You have given shape to what I believe was an inherited yearning—the effect of brooding passionate thoughts in many ancestors—thoughts that seem to have been intensely present in my grandfather. Suppose the stolen offspring of a mountain tribe brought up in a city of the plain; or one with an inherited genius for painting and born blind—the ancestral life would lie within as a dim longing for unknown objects and sensations, and the inherited frame would be like a cunningly wrought instrument never played on, quivering throughout with uneasy meanings that, under the right touch, give music. Something like that has been my experience. Since I began to read and know, I have longed for an ideal task in which I might feel myself the heart and brain of a multitude—a social captainship that should come as duty, not be striven for as personal prize. You have raised the image of such a task—to bind our race together in spite of heresy. You said to me, ‘Our religion united us before it divided us—it made us a people before it made Rabbanites and Karaites.’ I mean to try what can be done with that union. I mean to work in your spirit. Failure will not be ignoble; but it would be ignoble for me not to try.”

“Even as my brother that fed at the breasts of my mother,” Mordecai said, falling back with an exultant repose, like one who has finished his day’s labor and hears, through the quiet, the safe sounds of home.

For Mirah, Deronda’s outpouring had the force of a sudden dawn. His nearness to them, so frankly declared, was startling; it broke the old forebodings that had lain on her like night. She felt as if new facts might show themselves where she had expected only repetition of sorrow. Yet with the relief came another trembling awareness—an unspoken shifting of the air between her and Deronda, as if some note had been added to the familiar soundscape, and she did not know yet whether it would soothe or wound.

After a pause, Mordecai spoke again.

“It has begun already—the marriage of our souls. It waits but the passing away of this body; then they who are betrothed shall unite in a stricter bond, and what is mine shall be thine. Call nothing mine that I have written, Daniel; for though our masters taught rightly that all should be quoted in the name of him that said it—and their rule is good—yet it excludes not the willing marriage which melts soul into soul, and makes thought fuller as clear waters are made fuller, where fullness and clearness are inseparable. I have judged what I have written, and I desire the body I gave my thought to pass away as this fleshly body will pass; but let the thought be born again from our fuller soul which shall be called yours.”

“You must not ask me to promise that,” Deronda said, smiling with affectionate firmness. “I must be convinced first of special reasons in the writings themselves. I am too backward a pupil yet. That blended transmission will go on without any choice of ours; but what we cannot hinder must not become our rule for what we ought to choose. Our duty is faithful tradition where we can attain it. You would insist on that for any one but yourself. Do not ask me to deny my spiritual parentage when I am finding the clue of my life in the recognition of natural parentage.”

“I will ask for no promise till you see the reason,” Mordecai answered. “You have spoken truth: I would obey the Master’s rule for another. But for years my hope—nay, my confidence—has not been that the imperfect image of my thought, the ill-shaped work of a youthful carver who has seen a heavenly pattern and trembles in copying, should live; but that my vision and passion should enter into yours—yea, into yours. For he whom I longed for afar—was he not you whom I discerned as mine when you came near? Nevertheless, you shall judge. My soul is satisfied.”

He paused, then began, in a changed tone, “What moved your parents—” but checked himself and added, with a gentle restraint, “Nay, I ask nothing of others, unless it is your pleasure.”

“Some time—gradually—you will know all,” Deronda said. “But now tell me more of yourselves, and how time has passed since I went away. I am sure there has been trouble. Mirah has been in distress about something.”

He looked at Mirah; but she turned at once to her brother, silently begging him to answer for her. She could not bear that Deronda—on such an evening, when he had drawn himself so close and named himself one with them—should hear of the shame that clung about them, as if it might smear even his newly claimed heritage. To relieve her own overstrained heart, she rose and took up her hat and cloak, thinking to go to her room; perhaps they would speak more freely when she had gone.

Mordecai said, slowly, choosing his words as one chooses what may be spoken without profaning joy: “To-day there has been a grief. A duty which seemed far off has come back and turned its face upon us, raising no gladness—raising a dread we must submit to. But for the moment we are delivered from any visible yoke. Let us defer speaking of it—as if this evening deepening about us were the beginning of a festival in which we offer first fruits of our joy, and mingle no mourning with them.”

Deronda divined enough to be silent. He rose as Mirah rose.

“Are you going?” he said softly. “I must leave almost immediately—when Mrs. Adam and I have brought up the precious chest, and I have given the key to Mordecai—no, Ezra. May I call him Ezra now? I have learned to think of him as Ezra since I have heard you call him so.”

“Please call him Ezra,” Mirah answered faintly. His nearness made her timid in a new way. Was the difference in him—or only in herself, now shaken by the last hours’ violent alternations? The day’s distress had drained her; hunger and fatigue made her tremble. Deronda saw her pallor and the slight unsteadiness of her hands; he longed to show more feeling, to do something that would be like putting warm food before one who has forgotten to eat. But he dared not. She put out her hand, forcing a small smile; he took it gently, then opened the door for her. That was all.

Yet in him, when she had gone, the difficulty deepened instead of easing. Men shrink from approaching as lovers when their addresses may seem to have low motives, prompted by wealth or rank; but Deronda found a more delicate obstacle in the opposite case. For to reverential love, the loved woman always has a kind of wealth and rank that makes presumption possible in any station; and here, besides that awe, there was the peculiar tenderness of his position as benefactor. Mirah’s gratitude was strong; he knew she might feel bound, and any wish of his might seem to her like a claim. To be unable to satisfy it would be a pain renewed daily by the inevitable communion in their care of Ezra.

So he stood, with joy like newly kindled fire and fear like a cold draught crossing it—harder to bear because it was born of love itself—while outside the small square sank into evening, and the house held, with its scattered papers and its ticking clock, the sense of lives being written over by older scripts, in languages half-known and wholly felt.

It was not many days after her mother’s coming that Gwendolen consented to stay in Genoa. Her longing to quit that jewel-blue edge of the sea helped to brace her, as if flight itself were a kind of nourishment—bitter, medicinal, but sustaining. For what place, though it were a garden shaken with blossoms, may not the inward sense turn into a ring of punishment, where every flower seems to burn at the sole, and beauty is only a more delicate cruelty?

“I shall never like to see the Mediterranean again,” she said to her mother—said it with the shiver of one who smells a sweetness that has grown sickening, like orange-flowers clinging too closely to a room where one has wept.

Mrs. Davilow believed she understood, even in that mute injunction against naming the dead man. Formally she must wear calamity, but in truth she was living more than she had lived since her daughter’s marriage; for her darling had come back to her, not only with the old affection but with that new, conscious clutching at the near and tender—as we hold a cup of warm broth brought to us after faintness, knowing at last what it is to need.

“Are you there, mamma?” Gwendolen cried one night, suddenly, in the dark. A bed had been made for Mrs. Davilow in the same room.

“Yes, dear. Can I do anything for you?”

“No—thank you. Only I like so to know you are there. Do you mind my waking you?” There was humility in the question—something that would hardly have belonged to the spoilt girl she had been.

“I was not asleep, darling.”

“It seemed not real that you were with me. I wanted to make it real. I can bear things if you are with me. But you must not lie awake anxious about me. You must be happy now. You must let me make you happy now at last—else what shall I do?”

“God bless you, dear; I have the best happiness I can have, when you make much of me.”

But the next night, hearing her sigh and toss, Mrs. Davilow said, softly, as if offering a familiar domestic kindness—like warming a posset on the coals, or steeping a little balm for rest—“Let me give you your sleeping-draught, Gwendolen.”

“No, mamma, thank you; I don’t want to sleep.”

“It would be so good for you to sleep more, my darling.”

“Don’t say what would be good for me, mamma,” Gwendolen answered, with a sudden violence. “You don’t know what would be good for me. You and my uncle must not contradict me and tell me anything is good for me when I feel it is not good.”

Mrs. Davilow was silent. Poor child—pain makes irritability as naturally as hunger makes impatience.

Presently Gwendolen said, in another voice, like a confession forced up from deep within: “I was always naughty to you, mamma.”

“No, dear—no.”

“Yes, I was,” she insisted. “It is because I was always wicked that I am miserable now.” And she burst into sobs and cries.

Her resolve to keep all the facts of her married life and its end sealed within her reacted in these strange outcries, where the words were riddles but the anguish was plain. Yet dim lights were breaking on the mother’s mind. Hints had come from Sir Hugo to Mr. Gascoigne, and—shorn of what a man spares in repeating to a woman—from Mr. Gascoigne to herself.

Sir Hugo, while he attended to the decent business following his nephew’s death and to the chances of the sea yielding up what it had taken, thought it kindest to use his present intercourse with the rector to prepare him, gently, for the purport of Grandcourt’s will—so that the shock should not come afterwards, doubled by long-cherished illusion. He told the unpleasant truth by degrees: first only implying that the widow was not so splendidly provided for as expectation had painted; then, after vague mention of claims, letting fall the decisive fact—that the splendour had been bequeathed elsewhere, guided by a prior tie and by illegitimate children in default of a lawful heir.

Mr. Gascoigne was deeply wounded. He remembered, with a vividness sharpened by injury, the dead man’s cold pride and repellent manners toward him; remembered, too, that before the new occupant came to Diplow he had heard rumours—former entanglements, a dissipated taste for pleasure. Yet he had not foreseen that what respectable households imagine swept away into private rubbish-heaps could spring up again like a crawling infestation—live caterpillars set loose among their green leaves.

He did not utter those thoughts to Sir Hugo. He answered as a man of the world turned conscientious clergyman.

“When a young man makes his will in health,” he said, “he usually counts on living a long while. Probably Mr. Grandcourt did not believe that this will would ever have its present effect.”

After a moment he added, “The effect is painful in more ways than one. Female morality is likely to suffer from this marked advantage and prominence being given to illegitimate offspring.”

“Well, in point of fact,” Sir Hugo returned, in his comfortable way, “since the boy is there, this was really the best alternative for the disposal of the estates. Grandcourt had nobody nearer than his cousin. And it’s a chilling thought that you go out of this life only for the benefit of a cousin. A man gets a little pleasure in making his will if it’s for the good of his own curly heads; but it’s a nuisance when you’re giving the bequeathing to a used-up fellow like yourself, and one you don’t care two straws for. It’s the next worse thing to having only a life interest in your estates. No—I forgive Grandcourt for that part of his will. But what I don’t forgive him for is the shabby way he has provided for your niece—our niece, I will say—no better a position than if she had been a doctor’s widow. Nothing grates on me more than that posthumous grudgingness toward a wife. A man ought to have some pride and fondness for his widow. I should, I know. I take it as a test of a man, that he feels the easier about his death when he can think of his wife and daughters being comfortable after it.”

“It has certainly taken me by surprise,” said Mr. Gascoigne, “all the more because, as the one who stood in the place of father to my niece, I had shown my reliance on Mr. Grandcourt’s apparent liberality in money matters by making no claims for her beforehand. That seemed to me due to him under the circumstances. Probably you think me blamable.”

“Not blamable exactly. I respect a man for trusting another. But take my advice: if you marry another niece, though it may be to the Archbishop of Canterbury, bind him down. Your niece can’t be married for the first time twice over. And if he’s a good fellow, he’ll wish to be bound. But as to Mrs. Grandcourt—I can only say that I feel my relation to her all the nearer because I think she has not been well treated. And I hope you will urge her to rely on me as a friend.”

So spoke Sir Hugo, chivalrous in his disgust that the young and beautiful widow of a Mallinger Grandcourt should be left with only two thousand a year and a house set in a coal-mining district. To the rector that income looked less shabby in itself; but he had a keener sense than the baronet’s of the humiliation flung over his niece and over those nearest to her, by the conspicuous publishing of the dead man’s long bond with Mrs. Glasher. Like all men who are good husbands and fathers, he felt it through women’s minds—through the social sting that would smart in them. The first hearing was nothing to the pain of having to carry it to Mrs. Davilow, and of foreseeing what Gwendolen would feel when her mother judged it time.

For the good rector innocently believed his niece knew nothing of Mrs. Glasher. He argued from what maidens and wives were likely to know and suffer; he had observed women in general more than he had observed this particular woman.
