But Mrs. Davilow, with a mother’s slow, unwilling insight, began to see an explanation of much that had been inexplicable in her child—before and after the engagement. She suspected that, by some dreadful chance, Gwendolen had learned of that left-handed marriage and the children. She meant to wait for a moment of confidence—in the coming days, on the journey to England—when she might discover how much was clear to her daughter, and soften the approach of whatever must disappoint.

She was spared the contrivance. Gwendolen herself spoke.

“I hope you don’t expect that I am going to be rich and grand, mamma,” she said not long after the rector’s communication. “Perhaps I shall have nothing at all.”

She was dressed, and had been sitting long, very still—like a woman watching a pot whose simmering she dare not disturb, lest it boil over. Mrs. Davilow started.

“Oh yes, dear, you will have something. Sir Hugo knows all about the will.”

“That will not decide,” said Gwendolen, abruptly.

“Surely, dear. Sir Hugo says you are to have two thousand a year and the house at Gadsmere.”

“What I have will depend on what I accept,” said Gwendolen. “You and my uncle must not attempt to cross me and persuade me about this. I will do everything I can do to make you happy, but in anything about my husband I must not be interfered with. Is eight hundred a year enough for you, mamma?”

“More than enough, dear. You must not think of giving me so much.”

Mrs. Davilow paused, then ventured: “Do you know who is to have the estates and the rest of the money?”

“Yes,” said Gwendolen, waving her hand as if shutting a door. “I know everything. It is all perfectly right, and I wish never to have it mentioned.”

Her mother looked away and rose as if to fetch a trifle—a fan-screen—anything to fill the moment. A slight flush came on her delicate cheeks. Wondering, imagining, she could not meet her daughter’s eyes when she sat down again; she felt a sad constraint, as if they were in a room where some strong odour had been spilt and could not be named.

What wretchedness her child had lived through—wretchedness that must remain, as it always had remained, locked away from their mutual speech.

But Gwendolen watched her mother with that new divination which experience had given her—reading the tremor at the corners of her mouth, the effort to keep her breath steady, as one reads the state of a hearth by the sound of the coals. Tenderness rose in her, relenting against her own harshness.

“Come and sit nearer to me, mamma, and don’t be unhappy.”

Mrs. Davilow obeyed, but bit her lips in vain, trying to hinder the smarting tears.

Gwendolen leaned toward her caressingly. “I mean to be very wise; I do, really. And good—oh, so good to you, dear, old, sweet mamma, you won’t know me. Only you must not cry.”

Under that softness lay a fixed resolve. She meant to ask Deronda whether she ought to accept any of her husband’s money—whether she might accept what would enable her to provide for her mother. She felt strong enough for anything that would set her higher in Deronda’s mind, strong enough to renounce comfort if he judged it tainted. It was a strange hunger in her—a hunger not for bread, not for any rich dish of worldly ease, but for a rightness she could trust. Yet even that hunger had its senses: she craved the tone of his voice, the quiet air about him, the relief of a soundscape in which her own thoughts were not drowned by the grinding of fear.

Sir Hugo pressed an invitation on her with kind urgency: that she and Mrs. Davilow should go straight with him to Park Lane, and make his house their abode as long as mourning and other London details demanded. Town, he insisted, was just then the most retired of places. He would exert himself at once to have all articles belonging to Gwendolen removed from the house in Grosvenor Square.

No proposal could have suited her better. Park Lane would make it easier for her to have an interview with Deronda—if only she could get a letter into his hands asking him to come.

During the journey Sir Hugo, understanding that she knew the will’s purport, ventured to talk before her and to her about the future—touching lightly on prospects, shedding a decorous cheerfulness over her widowed position, as if the very management of tone were a form of kindness. To him it seemed almost graceful for a widow to recover spirits the sooner when she found her husband had dealt less handsomely by her: the testator’s fault had compromised grief by giving a testamentary reason for it, so that the world might suppose her sorrow sprang not from bereavement but from diminished means.

His own kindliness, fanned by favourable winds in his fortunes and by compassion for Gwendolen, made him quite fatherly; he called her “my dear,” and in speaking of Gadsmere to Mr. Gascoigne—its advantages and its drawbacks—he spoke of what “we” might do to make the best of that property. Gwendolen sat pale and silent while he conjectured that Mrs. Grandcourt might prefer letting Gadsmere rather than residing there; in which case, he thought, it might be leased on capital terms to one of the fellows engaged with the coal. He had seen enough of the place to know it was as comfortable and picturesque a box as any man need desire—provided his desires were circumscribed within a coal area.

“I shouldn’t mind about the soot myself,” said the baronet, with the serenity of the merely hypothetical. “Nothing is more healthy. And if one’s business lay there, Gadsmere would be a paradise. It makes quite a feature in Scrogg’s history of the county, with the little tower and the fine piece of water—the prettiest print in the book.”

“A more important place than Offendene, I suppose?” said Mr. Gascoigne.

“Much,” said Sir Hugo decisively. “I was there with my poor brother—it is more than a quarter of a century ago, but I remember it very well. The rooms may not be larger, but the grounds are on a different scale.”

“Our poor dear Offendene is empty after all,” Mrs. Davilow said. “When it came to the point, Mr. Haynes declared off, and there has been no one to take it since. I might as well have accepted Lord Brackenshaw’s kind offer that I should remain in it another year rent-free: for I should have kept the place aired and warmed.”

“I hope you’ve something snug instead,” said Sir Hugo.

“A little too snug,” Mr. Gascoigne returned, smiling at his sister-in-law. “You are rather thick upon the ground.”

At the mention of Offendene, Gwendolen’s glance changed. The conversation passed while the foreign train stood through one of those long, unaccountable pauses at a country station. Outside lay a dreamy, sunny stillness—hedgeless fields stretching to a boundary of poplars. The talk within the carriage—coal, leases, county histories—seemed to her like distant, meaningless murmurs, like the faint racket of machinery one hears across water, making the dreamland larger and more unreal, full of indistinct pits and a purgatorial Gadsmere she would never visit. But her mother’s words made it all dissolve.

Offendene and Pennicote rose before her under cooler lights. She saw the grey shoulders of the downs; the fields specked with cattle; the shadowy plantations and rutted lanes where barked timber lay like a wayside seat; the neatly clipped hedges on the road from the parsonage to Offendene; the avenue where her figure would be gradually discerned from the window; the hall-door opening; her mother, or one of those sisters who had once seemed troublesome, coming out to meet her. That brief experience of quiet home which had once been dullness to flee from now came back as a rest—like morning air and the unreproaching voice of birds after one has followed a lure through a long masquerade, entered with intoxicated belief in its fine disguises, and ended in shrieking fear lest one has become oneself one of the evil shapes that hiss, dropping their human mummery.

Her mind dwelt there, making Offendene the scene of many thoughts. Yet outwardly she gave no sign, any more than she did when Sir Hugo offered opinions on the telegraphic cable, or her uncle discussed the Church Rate Abolition Bill. What subjects will not conversation embrace in the long daylight journeying from Genoa to London? Even strangers, after glancing from China to Peru and emptying their mental stores with a liberality that threatens to leave nothing for the next meeting, are apt to grow excessively confidential. Sir Hugo and the rector were under a stronger pressure still: like acquaintances compelled to a long drive in a mourning-coach, they began by observing that the occasion was melancholy and then proceeded to enliven it by miscellaneous discourse.

“I don’t mind telling you,” Sir Hugo said to the rector, letting private details fall; while the rector, without saying so, did not mind telling the baronet of his sons and the difficulty of placing them in the world.

By dint of discussing all persons and things within driving-reach of Diplow, Sir Hugo worked himself into such a pitch of interest in that former home, such a conviction that it was his pleasant duty to regain and strengthen his personal influence in the neighbourhood, that he declared he meant to take his family there for a month or two before the autumn was over. Mr. Gascoigne cordially rejoiced.

So the journey went on and ended with mutual liking between the male fellow-travellers. Meanwhile Gwendolen sat by like one who has been into a spirit-world and come back with lips full of an experience she cannot utter—an experience that makes ordinary talk sound thin, as if the living had taken to chattering in a language that can no longer name what is real. Mrs. Davilow was chiefly occupied in imagining what her daughter felt, and in wondering at the meaning of that hinted doubt—whether she would accept her husband’s bequest.

For Gwendolen there stood before her an unsealed wall made of one immediate purpose, shutting out every other resolution. How was she to scale it? She must see and consult Deronda again, to secure herself against any act he would disapprove. Would her remorse have held its power—or would she have felt absolved by secrecy—if it had not been for that outer conscience which Deronda had become for her? It is hard to know how much we forgive ourselves when no ear listens, no voice answers, no human judgment makes the unseen judgment present and near. But when another’s opinion is the breathing-medium of all our joy, it presses on us with the authority of something larger than the world’s tolerance and stronger than our own excuses.

Deronda’s mission to her had begun with what she felt to be his judgment at the gaming-table. He might easily have spoiled it—so much of life is spent in marring our influence, turning another’s belief into a concluded unbelief they call knowledge of the world, when it is only disappointment in you or me. Deronda had not spoiled his mission.

But she had forgotten to ask his address. The only way to reach him was through Sir Hugo. She was not blind to the construction witnesses might put on her dependence on Deronda—on her seeking him more than he sought her. Grandcourt’s rebukes had schooled her pride. Yet the force, the tenacity of her nature had flung itself into that dependence; she could no more let go her hold on Deronda’s help because of watchers than if she had been in prison under sentence, needing one last appeal to save her life.

When she was in Park Lane, and knew the baronet meant to go down to the Abbey immediately—only to see his family for a couple of days and then return for needful business—she spoke to him without any air of hesitation, her mother present.

“Sir Hugo, I wish to see Mr. Deronda again as soon as possible. I don’t know his address. Will you tell it me, or let him know that I want to see him?”

A quick thought crossed Sir Hugo’s face, but it did not disturb his easy tone.

“Upon my word, I don’t know whether he’s at his chambers or the Abbey at this moment. But I’ll make sure of him. I’ll send a note now to his chambers telling him to come, and if he’s at the Abbey I can give him your message and send him up at once. I am sure he will want to obey your wish,” he ended, with grave kindness—treating it as if nothing could be more natural than that she should send such a message.

But Sir Hugo was convinced that Gwendolen had a passionate attachment to Deronda, sown long ago; and his former suspicion returned with more force—that her feeling might lead her into imprudences. Kind-hearted Sir Hugo was resolved to screen and defend her as far as he could. To him it made as pretty a story as one need desire: his favourite Dan and this fine creature formed for each other, and the unsuitable husband having made his exit in excellent time.

Indeed what vexed Sir Hugo now was a doubt whether the lofty, inscrutable Dan had not some scheme in his head which would prove dearer to him than the lovely Mrs. Grandcourt, putting that neatly-prepared marriage out of the question. Among the paradoxes of feeling, Sir Hugo—who had once cautioned Deronda against too much tenderness toward the bride—now felt irritated by the suspicion that Deronda had not fallen in love as he ought.

All this, of course, was premature, only a fortnight or so after Grandcourt’s death. But thinking has its own time, and it is rarely the time of events.

Sir Hugo sent the note to Deronda’s chambers. It found him there.

Deronda did not answer Gwendolen’s new summons without a stir of dread that was not vanity, but a fine, quick sympathy that shrank from being made the measure of another creature’s hope. He had learned—by that kind of knowledge which does not argue but simply feels, as one feels anger in a voice—that her inward life had fastened on his with a passionate need. It was as if her future hung, not in the general order of things, but on the steady holding of his hand at the brink of a precipice.

And yet there had come, since the first time he had saved her from that fatal glitter of the necklace, other bonds—love and duty twined elsewhere—binding his own life into shapes that could not be altered by any compassionate impulse, however strong. The impulse was still in him, living and tender: that old determining rush which, a year earlier, might have swept him into sheltering her forever from solitude. Now it could only quiver in him as yearning pity; and the certainty that he must keep himself asunder made the pity ache the more.

He waited in the back drawing-room—part of that white-and-crimson space whose very air seemed still to hold the memory of music, of a plaintive phrase once sung there, _Per pietà non dirmi addio_, that had melted into his consciousness with Mirah’s voice. The room was familiar to him in every line and ornament—Lady Mallinger’s gently smiling portrait, the lions on the pilasters with their urbane, almost human faces—yet everything looked like furniture of a former existence he had returned to visit, not to inhabit. It was strange to stand there with his hat in his hand, listening for the step of a young creature whose own life had been altered by tragedy into something wavering and uncertain, in which he still felt his own action tangled.

Gwendolen entered at last—changed. The mourning dress made the change more visible, but there was more than that: a quietness, a kind of satisfied hush on her face that he had not seen at Genoa. It was the satisfaction of finding him there. They clasped hands without a smile; remembrance and foreboding filled both their minds like a weight.

“It was good of you to come,” she said quickly. “Let us sit down.” She took the nearest chair at once, as if standing would make her courage evaporate. Deronda sat opposite her.

“I asked you to come because I want you to tell me what I ought to do,” she began, hastening on as if her words would fail her if she lingered. “Don’t be afraid of telling me what you think is right, because it seems hard. I have made up my mind to do it. I was afraid once of being poor; I could not bear to think of being under other people; and that was why I did something—why I married. I have borne worse things now. I think I could bear to be poor, if you think I ought. Do you know about my husband’s will?”

“Yes. Sir Hugo told me,” Deronda answered, already discerning the question behind her question.

“Ought I to take anything he has left me? I will tell you what I have been thinking.” Her eagerness trembled, as if she were trying to keep her thought from slipping back into terror. “Perhaps you may not quite know that I really did think a good deal about my mother when I married. I was selfish—but I did love her, and feel about her poverty; and what comforted me most at first, when I was miserable, was her being better off because I had married. The thing that would be hardest to me now would be to see her in poverty again; and I have been thinking that if I took enough to provide for her, and no more—nothing for myself—it would not be wrong; for I was very precious to my mother—and he took me from her—and he meant—and if she had known—”

She broke off. The reasons that crowded behind her words were like a swarm of stinging recollections she dared not let fly into speech. Her gaze dropped helplessly to her hands—bare now of all rings except the wedding-ring, that small circle seeming to tighten like a band of iron.

“Do not hurt yourself by speaking of that,” Deronda said, with a tenderness that was almost a command to spare herself. “There is no need. The case is very simple. I think I can hardly judge wrongly about it. You consult me because I am the only person to whom you have confided the most painful part of your experience: and I can understand your scruples.”

He waited, giving her silence as one gives a recovering patient air. That silence—made gentle by the tone in which he had spoken—was itself like a sustaining hand. She lifted her eyes at last, and he went on, slowly, with the careful pity of one who must be truthful.

“You are conscious of something you feel to be a crime toward one who is dead. You think that you have forfeited all claim as a wife. You shrink from taking what was his. You want to keep yourself from profiting by his death. Your feeling even urges you to some self-punishment—some scourging of the self that disobeyed your better will—the will that struggled against temptation. I have known something of that myself. Do I understand you?”

“Yes—at least, I want to be good—not like what I have been,” she said, low and urgent. “I will try to bear what you think I ought to bear. I have tried to tell you the worst about myself. What ought I to do?”

“If no one but yourself were concerned in this question of income,” said Deronda, “I should hardly dare to urge you against any remorseful prompting. But I take as a guide now, your feeling about Mrs. Davilow, which seems to me quite just. I cannot think that your husband’s dues even to yourself are nullified by any act you have committed. He voluntarily entered into your life, and affected its course in what is always the most momentous way. But setting that aside, it was due from him in his position that he should provide for your mother, and he of course understood that if this will took effect she would share the provision he had made for you.”

“She has had eight hundred a year,” Gwendolen said, clinging still to the limit she had privately argued for. “What I thought of was to take that and leave the rest.”

“I think it is not your duty to fix a limit in that way,” Deronda answered. “You would be making a painful enigma for Mrs. Davilow; an income from which you shut yourself out must be embittered to her. And your own course would become too difficult. We agreed at Genoa that the burden on your conscience is one what no one ought to be admitted to the knowledge of. The future beneficence of your life will be best furthered by your saving all others from the pain of that knowledge. In my opinion you ought simply to abide by the provisions of your husband’s will, and let your remorse tell only on the use that you will make of your monetary independence.”

As he finished, his hand moved almost unconsciously to take up his hat from the floor beside him; the action was slight, but Gwendolen’s whole being watched him as if her safety depended on his smallest motion. Her heart leapt with a sudden animal terror of being left. She started up too—without pausing to see that her rising looked like acquiescence in his departure; and Deronda, of course, rose also and came a little nearer.

“I will do what you tell me,” she said hurriedly; “but what else shall I do?”

The simplicity of the words betrayed her more than any confession could have done. They painted her helplessness to herself, and the sob she had been mastering broke through, and large tears gathered.

Deronda felt a crushing pain—pain that had to be governed, because consequences stood close and visible, and he must not, by softness, make the future harder. When she had wiped her tears away, he asked gently, “You will probably be soon going with Mrs. Davilow into the country?”

“Yes—in a week or ten days.” Her eyes moved vaguely toward the window as if she were trying to look into a future that had become indistinct. “I want to be kind to them all—they can be happier than I can. Is that the best I can do?”

“I think so. It is a duty that cannot be doubtful,” he said. He spoke with pauses, as if each sentence must carry its own weight and not topple into sentiment. “Other duties will spring from it. Looking at your life as a debt may seem the dreariest view of things at a distance; but it cannot really be so. What makes life dreary is the want of motive: but once beginning to act with that penitential, loving purpose you have in your mind, there will be unexpected satisfactions—there will be newly-opening needs—continually coming to carry you on from day to day. You will find your life growing like a plant.”

She turned her eyes on him as if she were listening for water in a drought—an intense, thirsty look that made him feel as though she were stretching her arms from a forsaken shore. His voice took an affectionate, almost imploring earnestness.

“This sorrow, which has cut down to the root, has come to you while you are so young—try to think of it not as a spoiling of your life, but as a preparation for it. Let it be a preparation. See—you have been saved from the worst evils that might have come from your marriage, which you feel was wrong. You have had a vision of injurious, selfish action—a vision of possible degradation; think that a severe angel, seeing you along the road of error, grasped you by the wrist and showed you the horror of the life you must avoid. And it has come to you in your spring-time. Think of it as a preparation. You can—you will—be among the best of women, such as make others glad that they were born.”

The words fell on Gwendolen as if some hand, at once firm and merciful, had touched the place where she was numb. A rush of mingled feeling swept through her with such strength that it seemed like the beginning of another life inside the old one—something newly alive, vaguely powerful, and yet helplessly dependent on the soul that had awakened it. Hope—moral recovery—has this divine pregnancy: it is not merely comfort, but energy.

But to her that new life was inseparable from Deronda. It was not that she suddenly thought he loved her in any ordinary way—such a thought would have toppled under its own improbability. Rather, he had become the air she breathed when she tried to be better. For the first time since that moment on the sea, a deep flush rose over her cheek and brow and throat, glowed for an instant, then faded gradually away. She could not speak.

Deronda stepped nearer and held out his hand. “I must not weary you.”

The sense that he was going startled her like cold water. She put her hand in his, still silent.

“You look ill yet—unlike yourself,” he said, and the solicitude in the words was not assumed.

“I can’t sleep much,” she answered, sinking back into her dispirited truth. “Things repeat themselves in me so. They come back—they will all come back.” A shudder ran through her, as if she felt the returning horror already at her shoulder.

“By degrees they will be less insistent,” he said. And still he could not drop her hand or step away suddenly, as if a clean break were possible. The pity held him physically.

“Sir Hugo says he shall come to stay at Diplow,” she said, snatching at the one thought that promised steadiness. “You will come too.”

“Probably,” he began; but the word sounded cold even to himself. “Yes, I shall come,” he added, correcting it, and then released her hand with a final friendly pressure that was like saying good-bye while refusing to utter the words.

“And not again here, before I leave town?” Her timid sadness made her look even paler.

What could he say? “If I can be of any use—if you wish me—certainly I will.”

“I must wish it,” she said with sudden, desperate frankness. “You know I must wish it. What strength have I? Who else is there?” The sob rose again.

Deronda’s face showed the pang he felt. “I will certainly come,” he said, with a misery that made the promise sound like something wrenched from him.

She saw the change in his face; but the relief of believing he would return was too great to yield to any other feeling. A steadier courage came back, lit by that hope he had breathed into her.

“Don’t be unhappy about me,” she said, with an affectionate reassurance that was almost childlike in its faith. “I shall remember your words—every one of them. I shall remember what you believe about me; I shall try.”

She held out her hand again, as if the earlier parting had not occurred. There was no smile—there had been no smile on her lips since her husband’s death. When she stood quiet, she looked like a melancholy statue of the Gwendolen whose laughter had once leapt out when others were grave.

Only by remembering the anguish that had altered the whole aspect of the world for her can one understand her behavior now—the unguarded openness, the importunate pleading dependence that did not stop to consider how it might appear to detached eyes. She clung to him as one clings in a burning house, not pausing to think what spectators infer from the embrace: he was the one figure she could see clearly through the smoke of her conscience. She identified him with the very struggle of renewal that had begun in her through his influence. Is it strange, then, that she read her own necessity into his feeling, and expected from him what she felt she must have?

Her imagination had not shaped itself into ordinary dreams of love-making and marriage; those images were too alien to her shame and effort. Love, if it had taken hold of her, demanded not flirtation but hard tasks—acceptance of rebuke, confession, endurance, self-change. She cried toward him as a child cries when its feet slip on a steep path—crying to be taken by the hand lest it lose itself.

That cry pierced Deronda. He alone knew the innermost nature of her trouble; to withdraw from her appeal would be to leave her in a loneliness that might be dangerous. Yet he foresaw, near or far, a coming wrench, and knew that every present strengthening of this bond would make the wrench harder. He was obliged to risk it.

He went more than once to Park Lane before Gwendolen left town; but those later interviews were in Mrs. Davilow’s presence, and thus less agitating, with a safer air, like conversation carried on in a room where the door stands open. Since she had resolved to accept her income, Gwendolen had formed a plan she liked to speak of: to place her mother and sisters with herself at Offendene again, and, as she said, to piece back her life to that time when they first went there, when everything had been happiness about her, only she had not known it. She had mentioned it to Sir Hugo, who meant to exert himself to get Gadsmere let at a rent that would more than pay for Offendene.

All this she told Deronda, and he willingly dwelt on any subject that offered her soothing occupation. He spoke nothing, and she asked nothing, of what chiefly occupied him. Her mind was fastened on his coming to Diplow before the autumn was out; and she no more thought of the Lapidoths—the little Jewess and her brother—as likely to alter her destiny than she thought of the great political and social ferment that alters the world while individual hearts burn in their own narrow fires. Poor Gwendolen’s memory seemed stunned; and everything outside the lava-lit track of her troubled conscience, and her effort to find deliverance from it, lay in dim forgetfulness.

“One day still fierce ’mid many a day struck calm.”

The day after he had stood on Mirah’s threshold and taken her purse as if it were a daughter’s natural tribute, Lapidoth let the thought of her fade behind the louder, rasping summons of chance. Money in his hand was never money for bread first: it was an entrance-fee to that heated chapel of hazard where every cough, every clink, every whispered “Try again” had the authority of a priest. He had walked away with thirty shillings that were meant to keep a modest household sweet and steady, and before the smell of Mirah’s room had left his coat—lavender, warm wood, the faint metallic breath of the piano wires—he was already hunting the sharper perfume of stale cigars and sour spirits that hung about the place with “PYRAMIDS” painted on the blind.

There, amidst the chafing murmur of men who had learned to keep their hope quiet, he doubled, trebled, and then watched the whole little store slide away as if a hand had brushed crumbs from a table. The coin had had a brief, bright ring; then only the duller world remained—hunger not as a bodily pang so much as a humiliating necessity that interfered with the true appetite. Lapidoth’s craving was not for meat or ale, but for the poised second before the ball fell, for the suspended breath of possibility. That longing, grown absolute, made other excitements—shame, affection, remorse—thin and easily blown out, like a candle in a draught.

Still, a man cannot gamble on empty stomach forever, and Lapidoth’s vagrant life required ready money even for the minimum that kept him from collapse. When he came out at last, Mirah’s purse lay flat in his pocket, its little clasp pressing a reproach into his thigh at every step. He stood a moment on the pavement balancing his next move with a practised quickness. He could pawn the purse; he could return it with a bold face and a tale about paying a score for food and lodging. In him there survived a sharp sensibility to his own “claims.” Children’s earnings, children’s shelter, children’s pity—these were, to his mind, only delayed repayments for what he had once been pleased to call devotion.

And yet he had shrunk, at first, from the thought of Ezra. Ezra’s very existence had the unpleasantness of a narrow place where one must hold one’s breath. But as the hours passed and the pocket grew light, Lapidoth’s dread altered its object: the possible opening of supplies—some generous friend of Mirah’s, some soft-hearted benefactor—began to shine in his imagination brighter than any fear of a son’s contempt. Luck had been against him lately. Luck must turn. Why should not the turn begin at his daughter’s door?

So he went, toward the little square in Brompton, with the plan of making his reappearance easy—watching for Mirah on the steps, catching her as she came or went, taking shelter in her startled tenderness before Ezra could be summoned. But evening had come down, and with it a hush that made the house-sounds clearer. As he drew near, he did not need to ask whether Mirah was within. Her voice floated out—warm, tremulous, alive with a young heart’s insistence—singing “Herz, mein Herz.” The song’s German syllables, with their intimate vowels and softened consonants, carried a whole old world in them, a world Lapidoth had used like a stage and then deserted. The melody sat on the air like a hand on a brow; it quieted the square’s small noises—distant wheels, a door-latch, the faint bark of a dog—and for an instant, even in him, it woke a confused sense of having once belonged to something tender.

Within, Mirah sat at the piano, her fingers resting after a phrase, while Ezra listened with his eyes shut, as if the sound were the one safe element left to him. Mrs. Adam opened the door and came in with a face of troubled respectability.

“A gentleman below says he is your father, miss.”

Mirah started up as if the words were a knife. “I will go down to him,” she said, and her eyes flew to Ezra.

“No, Mirah, not so,” Ezra answered, the decision in his voice like iron. “Let him come up, Mrs. Adam.”

Mirah stood, her hands twisting together until her knuckles whitened. The room, with its accustomed quiet—polished wood, the faint smell of lamp-oil and the clean starch of Mrs. Adam’s curtains—seemed suddenly too small for what was coming. Ezra had risen too, and Mirah saw in his face something she had never seen: his brow knit, his lips hardened, and in his eyes a severity that did not belong to illness but to judgment.

When Mrs. Adam admitted the visitor, she could not help one glance at the three, and the likeness that leapt out—shape and line—made her inwardly mutter, “Father, sure enough.” Yet it was as if the same mould had been used for two utterly different castings: the elder with his thin, restless elegance turned shabby; the younger with a worn intensity that made him look as if some inner fire had burnt away the ordinary coverings of comfort.

Lapidoth had arranged his face for sorrow before he entered, and he began with it. But there was a real twitch in him when he met Ezra’s gaze.

“Well, Ezra, my boy, you hardly know me after so many years.”

“I know you—too well—father,” Ezra said slowly, the word father pronounced as if it were an accusation.

Lapidoth’s mouth tightened, then loosened into the glibness that speech always restored in him. “Ah, you are not pleased with me. I don’t wonder at it. Appearances have been against me. When a man gets into straits he can’t do just as he would by himself or anybody else. I’ve suffered enough, I know.” He turned quickly toward Mirah, drawing her little purse from his pocket as if it were a prop in a play, and held it out. “Here’s your little purse, my dear. I thought you’d be anxious about it because of that bit of writing. I’ve emptied it—you’ll see—for I had a score to pay for food and lodging. I knew you would like me to clear myself, and here I stand—without a single farthing in my pocket—at the mercy of my children. You can turn me out if you like, without getting a policeman. Say the word, Mirah; say, ‘Father, I’ve had enough of you; you made a pet of me, and spent your all on me, when I couldn’t have done without you; but I can do better without you now,’—say that, and I’m gone out like a spark. I shan’t spoil your pleasure again.”

The practiced tears were already in his voice—those tears he could summon as other men might summon a bow.

“You know I could never say it, father,” Mirah answered. Her voice shook, not with persuasion but with anguish, for she felt the falseness in his speech like grit between her teeth, and yet could not wrench herself free of the old tenderness that had grown into her like scar tissue.

Mirah moved a step nearer Ezra, as if physical closeness might steady both of them. But Ezra’s pain had found its own hard line.

“Mirah, my sister, leave us!” he said, and the authority startled her.

She looked at him, faltering, beseeching. Awe held her, and yet she could not go without flinging one small shield between Ezra and the father. She came close, slipped her hand into Ezra’s thin trembling one, and whispered—low, but not so low that Lapidoth could not catch it—“Remember, Ezra—you said my mother would not have shut him out.”

“Trust me, and go,” Ezra returned.

Mirah obeyed, but she could not descend fully. A few steps up the staircase, she sat, heart beating so loudly she feared it would be heard, listening for sounds below—listening as if the fate of all their years would declare itself in the tone of a voice, the scrape of a chair, the sudden hush. The house itself became an instrument: boards creaked in their old speech; the distant street carried its soft, living rustle—footsteps that belonged to nobody, the far-off wheel on wet stone. Compared with the brutal roar of public rooms, those domestic sounds were mercy. She clung to them, as if they might keep violence out.

Lapidoth, left alone with his son, tried to adjust himself to the coming ordeal. He had long trained himself into a kind of spiritual callousness: the ability to see suffering as incongruous, as something that might be evaded by a laugh or dissolved by tears. Ezra looked like a man speaking out of a grave, and Lapidoth tried to treat it as one treats a gloomy sermon heard by chance—endurable because one can wait it out. But he had not guessed what sort of voice lived in Ezra, nor how long it had been gathering strength in silence.

“This home that we have here,” Ezra began, and his words came with measured force, as if every syllable cost breath, “is maintained partly by the generosity of a beloved friend who supports me, and partly by the labors of my sister, who supports herself. While we have a home we will not shut you out from it. We will not cast you out to the mercy of your vices. For you are our father, and though you have broken your bond, we acknowledge ours.”

Lapidoth made a slight movement, as if to seize on that concession, but Ezra went on, and the air in the room seemed to grow sharper.

“But I will never trust you. You absconded with money, leaving your debts unpaid; you forsook my mother; you robbed her of her little child and broke her heart; you have become a gambler, and where shame and conscience were there sits an insatiable desire; you were ready to sell my sister—you had sold her, but the price was denied you.”

Each charge fell not like a shouted insult but like a hard object placed deliberately on the table. Ezra’s voice did not rise; its restraint made it crueller.

“The man who has done these things must never expect to be trusted any more. We will share our food with you—you shall have a bed, and clothing. We will do this duty to you, because you are our father. But you will never be trusted. You are an evil man: you made the misery of our mother. That such a man is our father is a brand on our flesh which will not cease smarting. But the Eternal has laid it upon us; and though human justice were to flog you for crimes, and your body fell helpless before the public scorn, we would still say, ‘This is our father; make way, that we may carry him out of your sight.’”

Lapidoth had prepared himself for rebuke; he had not prepared himself for this—this voice that seemed to come from a depth he had never entered, and to strike, not around him, but through him. Something in him—some spring of hysterical excitability—was touched into violent action. He flung himself into a chair and cried aloud, burying his face against the table. It was, as ever with him, both involuntary reaction and conscious resource; tears had long been one of his easiest currencies.

Ezra sat down again and said nothing. The effort of speaking had shaken him. His thin hands trembled on the arms of the chair, and his face had the look of a man who has moved too near the edge of his strength. He stared before him without seeing, as if his own words had opened a door on a cold place and the draught was still passing over him.

Up on the stairs, Mirah heard the sobbing and could endure it no longer. The sound—raw, broken, too familiar—pulled her like a hook. She opened the door and came in. At once her fear turned toward Ezra: she went straight to him, took his trembling hand in both of hers, and he pressed it as if it were a support. He did not speak, scarcely even looked at her, but his fingers clung.

Lapidoth, face still hidden, knew she had entered by the faint rustle of her dress and the altered hush of the room’s breathing. After a moment he lifted his head, pressed his handkerchief to his eyes, and put out his hand toward her.

“Good-bye, Mirah,” he said hoarsely, with the plaintive tone that had so often served him. “Your father will not trouble you again. He deserves to die like a dog by the roadside, and he will. If your mother had lived, she would have forgiven me—thirty-four years ago I put the ring on her finger under the Chuppa, and we were made one. She would have forgiven me, and we should have spent our old age together. But I haven’t deserved it. Good-bye.”

He rose as he said the last word, as if the theatre required an exit. But Mirah caught his hand and held it fast. She was not weeping; she looked frightened, awe-struck, as if she had seen the blade of something that could not be blunted.

“No, father, no!” she cried. Then, turning to Ezra with a helpless urgency, “Ezra, you have not forbidden him?—Stay, father, and leave off wrong things. Ezra, I cannot bear it. How can I say to my father, ‘Go and die!’”

“I have not said it,” Ezra answered, and the effort to speak again drained him. “I have said, stay and be sheltered.”

“Then you will stay, father—and be taken care of—and come with me,” Mirah said. She drew Lapidoth toward the door as if to prevent any further clash of words, any further thunder that might split what little peace their house still held.

This, in truth, was what Lapidoth wanted: not repentance, but safety; not amendment, but warmth, and a roof without payment. For the moment, as Mirah’s dutiful hand guided him, a kind of comfort softened him, and he could almost imagine a different habit of life—almost, as one imagines a tune one will never learn.

Mirah led him downstairs to her own parlor. The room held the gentler odors of a woman’s care—clean linen, beeswax on furniture, the faint sweetness of something once stewed and now cooled, as if apples and clove had long ago breathed into the air and stayed there. Outside, the street murmured in its evening key: the distant drip from an eave, a carriage passing with a brief rush like wind over grain, then quiet again.

“This is my sitting-room when I am not with Ezra,” she said, “and there is a bedroom behind which shall be yours. You will stay and be good, father. Think that you are come back to my mother, and that she has forgiven you—she speaks to you through me.”

Her tones implored him, but she could not add the old caresses; something in her had learned fear. Lapidoth, quick to recover his balance when the pressure lifted, began to talk of her voice—how it had improved, how it carried, how such singing was not to be wasted. When Mrs. Adam entered to lay out his supper, he turned his attention to her too, speaking with a certain airy politeness meant to show that, whatever his clothes declared, he was not a common man.

Food was set before him—plain, warming, the sort of fare that makes a small room feel safer: bread with a firm crust, a modest portion of something hot whose steam rose as a comfort, and the domestic clatter of spoon against plate. Lapidoth ate moderately, as he always did; even his vices were not supported by hearty appetite. He accepted the shelter as if it were his due, and the house—its quiet, its soft lamp-light, its little careful economies—closed around him like a garment he had once worn and had the shamelessness to put on again.

But when night came, wakefulness brought back the stronger visions that ruled him. While the household settled into the low, breathing quiet of sleep—stairs creaking once, a door softly shutting, then only the faint, humane noises of a house at rest—Lapidoth lay and wondered what money Mirah might still have. He went back, not to the sound of Ezra’s terrible judgment, but to the remembered acoustics of roulette: the dry tick of the ball, the mutter of numbers, the soft scrape of coin, the thin laughter that snapped like grease-fire at a table edge. England, he thought, was a cursed country for most things. Ezra did pass across the gaming-table in his mind, and Ezra’s words were audible—yet he passed like a ghost, insubstantial, and the words had their heart eaten out by the glittering arithmetic of chance, by the imagined movements that seemed to weave themselves into the very tissue of Lapidoth’s consciousness.

It was a sour sort of home-coming for Deronda, to pass from the ordered hush of the Abbey—where even footsteps seemed to remember their manners—into Brompton, and to learn, before he had well set his hat down, that Mirah’s father was installed among the few rooms that had lately begun to feel like a refuge. The very word “father” had a homely sound, as if it must bring a loaf and a blessing; but this man’s nearness came like a stale breath in a pantry—something that tainted without touching, that made one keep turning to see whether the milk had turned, whether the bread would mold faster because he was there.

Mirah had done what she could do, and no more. She had spoken of Deronda because truth, to her, was like water: if you have any to give, you must not pretend the pitcher is empty. Yet she had ladled it out with trembling care, leaving the bottom unstirred. She told her father of Deronda’s friendship with Ezra—how it had begun in that grave companionship of studies, with old papers and older sorrows; how sympathy had sealed it. But she spoke lightly, as one might sift flour to keep stones from showing. She said nothing of the water that had almost closed over her, nothing of hands that had pulled her back from it. She named Mrs. Meyrick’s shelter as if that were the first warmth she had known, and let her father imagine that Deronda had come through those kind women’s doorway, not out of a night of terror.

She could not—she simply could not—let her father’s soul breathe across the most sacred part of her relation to Deronda. There are intimacies that live by their own language; and in Mirah’s mouth, any mention of them in his hearing would have been like putting a tender, untranslatable word into a stranger’s coarse dictionary.

Lapidoth, for his part, did not press. There were reasons why he was content to leave the tale in a mist: he had no appetite for what might condemn him afresh. But he had a keen appetite for another fact—that his children possessed a beneficent friend who seemed “high in the world,” a man whose name might be used like a credit at a shop-counter. That prospect seasoned everything. It was as if he had found, at the back of a cupboard, a jar labeled with a rich preserve, and meant to keep it from others while he considered the best hour to open it.

Ezra told Deronda first—Ezra, who had learned to speak of pain as if it were part of his duty, like reading by a failing lamp.

“I am become calm in beholding him now,” he said, with the quiet of one who has trained his nerves by long fasting from hope. “And I try to think it possible that my sister’s tenderness, and the daily tasting a life of peace, may win him to remain aloof from temptation. I have enjoined her, and she has promised, to trust him with no money. I have convinced her that he will buy with it his own destruction.”

Deronda’s first sensation was repulsion so bodily that it might have been a sudden smell of burning cloth. The man who had blighted wife and children was there, close among their poor furniture and their patience, as if he had a right to the little clean places their lives had made.

He did not meet Lapidoth until the third day after the father’s arrival. Lapidoth had delayed, like an actor waiting for costume. The new clothes for which he had been measured were not ready at first, and the old ones would not do to greet a “personage.” So he kept watch, listening at windows, catching glimpses of Deronda’s comings and goings. When at last he saw him clearly, he started at Deronda’s youthfulness. Mirah had not dwelt on that, perhaps from delicacy, perhaps because reverence makes us forget numbers. Lapidoth had imagined a grave, established patron—something nearer to a magistrate than a young man with a quick eye and a sensitive mouth. And this youthfulness immediately stirred a new conjecture in him: Deronda’s real motive must be love of Mirah.

Better still, then. A tie to Mirah promised softer indulgences than a tie to Ezra. Lapidoth, who could be docile where it served him, began at once to behave with winning amiability and to work himself into easy domestication—an art he had once practiced on audiences, now attempted on children. He listened to Mirah’s music, praising with the air of a man who understood the very grain of her voice. He submitted to the strict dislike of smoke in Mrs. Adam’s parlor, and carried his German pipe outside, pacing the square where the common London noise—wheels, cries, the thin clink of milk-cans—never let the air become truly still. Mirah supplied him with tobacco, and even that innocent act had in it a bitterness for her: to keep a man content by feeding a habit was like keeping a wasp quiet with jam.

He was too acute to remonstrate at once against the refusal of money. Mirah told him plainly that she must persist, having pledged herself to Ezra. Lapidoth smiled, shrugged, submitted. He could wait. A man who has lived by chances knows how to sit in ambush under politeness.

When Deronda came again, Lapidoth was prepared—new clothes on, his hair more carefully disposed, his face arranged into an expression meant to suggest injured merit and present gratitude. He was in the room with Ezra, who had set himself, as part of his severe discipline, to tolerate his father’s presence whenever it was imposed, as if endurance were a form of worship.

Deronda was cold—colder than he intended to be, and yet could not help. He felt the man as a stain that might spread by mere contact of air. But Lapidoth did not flinch. He asked leave to remain while they read from the old chest of papers, and—more than that—he made himself useful. There were German manuscripts that resisted Ezra’s laboring eyes; and Lapidoth, with his still-strong sight, bent over the crabbed lines and helped to decipher them. It was a strange thing, that the very fingers which had so often snatched and squandered could now trace meaning patiently, if meaning led to favor.

From this he took occasion to suggest that a transcription might be desirable. He offered his services to copy the manuscript, and to make copies in Roman characters of any papers needing them. Deronda, seeing at least the shape of grace in willingness to be employed, accepted the offer. He caught, too, a look of pleasure in Ezra’s face—pleasure not in the father, but in the possibility of easing the work, saving his eyes, shortening the long task.

Yet Ezra’s pleasure was quickly guarded.

“Let all the writing be done here,” he said, quietly but firmly. “For I cannot trust the papers out of my sight, lest there be an accident by burning or otherwise.”

It was the voice of a man who has learned that “otherwise” holds whole histories of betrayal. Poor Ezra felt as if he had a convict on leave under his care. Unless he saw his father working, it was impossible to believe in good faith.

And by this arrangement Ezra fastened on himself a burden—his father’s presence—made painful not only by the deepest, longest associations, but also by Lapidoth’s restless temperament. At first, restraint had sat on him like an ill-fitting coat. The more he became familiarized with his situation, the more he wriggled for relief: going out to smoke; drifting about the room with sudden talk; flinging himself back in a chair and falling silent, yet never still—his eyebrows rising and falling, his mouth twitching into little expressions, his hands making dumb gestures as if he were forever rehearsing speeches he did not quite deliver.

If Mirah were present he slid into old habits with her, gossiping of former doings and companions, repeating quirks and stories, and recounting the plots of the plays he used to adapt—as if he could at will command again that brisk vivacity which had once won applause and payments. The very cadence of his talk carried faint echoes of footlights and cheap music, as if a whole commercial art-world still rattled in his voice. Those echoes were a particular torment to Ezra: the sounds were not merely sounds, but reminders, like a tune that brings back a hunger you thought conquered.

Mirah, when she was at home, tried to relieve Ezra by drawing her father down into the parlor and keeping watch there. It was a vigilant domestic kindness—like standing between a well and a child who keeps edging toward the drop. What is duty made of, but one difficult resolve repeated until it becomes the day’s very bread? The resolve is simple; the consequences are not. The difficulty lies in the daily unflinching support of consequences that mar the blessed return of morning with the prospect of irritation to be swallowed, or shame to be borne in silence.

Such consequences were being borne by these two—Mirah and Ezra—as by many other heroic children of an unworthy father; and to Mirah at least there lay the dread that it might stretch onward through the solid part of life, not a sharp calamity but a constant, gnawing presence.

Meanwhile Lapidoth’s being there raised a new, impalpable partition between Deronda and Mirah. Each dreaded the soiling inferences of Lapidoth’s mind; each, watching the other’s increased reserve and diffidence, interpreted it mistakenly. Deronda held back lest his feeling should be made a lever for Lapidoth’s selfishness; Mirah held back lest any softness of hers should be read by her father as a marketable thing. Their very delicacy, which had made every small act between them a kind of offering, now compelled them into a caution that felt like a chill cloth laid over warmth.

It was not long, however, before light came to Deronda—light of a kind he had not dared to ask for, and yet could not help thirsting after, as one thirsts when the air is full of kitchen-smells and one has been long hungry.

As soon as he could after returning from the Abbey, he had gone to Hans Meyrick’s rooms. There were reasons of friendship—more than one—for telling Hans at once the cause of his journey and the change it had brought upon his intentions. Hans was not in; he was said to be in the country for a few days. Deronda left a note and waited a week, half expecting one in return. But no word came. Deronda, fearing some freak of feeling in that susceptible nature—fearing, too, that the deferred Abbey sojourn had pinched Hans’s pride or hope—made a second call.

He was admitted into the painting-room and found Hans in a light coat without a waistcoat, his long hair still wet from a bath, but his face looking worn and wizened—anything but country-bright. Palette and brushes were in hand; he stood before his easel as if caught in the act of diligent work. Yet the whole thing—the posture, the equipment—had the air of having been got up on short notice, like a hurriedly set table meant to prove that dinner was always in preparation.

“You don’t look much as if you had been in the country, old fellow,” Deronda said, as they shook hands. “Is it Cambridge you have been to?”

“No,” said Hans curtly; and he threw down his palette with the air of a man who has begun to feign and suddenly dislikes himself for it. He pushed a chair forward for Deronda, then flung himself into another and leaned back, hands behind his head.

“I’ve been to I-don’t-know-where—No man’s land—and a mortally unpleasant country it is.”

“You don’t mean to say you have been drinking, Hans,” Deronda said, alarmed by the look in him.

“Nothing so good. I’ve been smoking opium.” Hans spoke as if he were confessing to some foolish experiment with a kitchen-spice that had turned a whole dish bitter. “I always meant to do it some time or other, to try how much bliss could be got by it; and having found myself just now rather out of other bliss, I thought it judicious to seize the opportunity. But I pledge you my word I shall never tap a cask of that bliss again. It disagrees with my constitution.”

“What has been the matter? You were in good spirits enough when you wrote to me.”

“Oh, nothing in particular. The world began to look seedy—a sort of cabbage-garden with all the cabbages cut.” He forced a creasing smile. “A malady of genius, you may be sure; and, in fact, I was tired of being virtuous without reward, especially in this hot London weather.”

“Nothing else? No real vexation?”

Hans shook his head.

“I came to tell you of my own affairs,” Deronda said, “but I can’t do it with a good grace if you are to hide yours.”

“Haven’t an affair in the world,” Hans returned, flightily, “except a quarrel with a bric-à-brac man. Besides, as it is the first time in our lives that you ever spoke to me about your own affairs, you are only beginning to pay a pretty long debt.”

Deronda was sure Hans’s manner was artificial—like paint hastily laid on, not yet dry—but he trusted that frankness would return if he gave his own.

“You laughed at the mystery of my journey to Italy, Hans,” he began. “It was for an object that touched my happiness at the very roots. I had never known anything about my parents, and I really went to Genoa to meet my mother. My father has been long dead—died when I was an infant. My mother was the daughter of an eminent Jew; my father was her cousin. Many things had caused me to think of this origin as almost a probability before I set out. I was so far prepared for the result that I was glad of it—glad to find myself a Jew.”

“You must not expect me to look surprised, Deronda,” Hans said, changing his posture, crossing one leg and examining the heel of his slipper as if the truth were there to be studied. “You knew it?”

“My mother told me. She went to the house the morning after you had been there—brother and sister both told her. You may imagine we can’t rejoice as they do. But whatever you are glad of, I shall come to be glad of in the end—when exactly the end may be I can’t predict.” His tone sank low, as it always did when he was out of humor with his lot and determined to make no spectacle of it.

“I quite understand that you can’t share my feeling,” Deronda said. “But I could not let silence lie between us on what casts quite a new light over my future. I have taken up some of Mordecai’s ideas, and I mean to try and carry them out, so far as one man’s efforts can go. I dare say I shall by and by travel to the East and be away for some years.”

Hans said nothing. He rose, seized his palette, and began to work the brush over it, standing before the picture with his back to Deronda. The room filled with the small sounds of painting—the light scrape, the soft tap—sounds that ought to have soothed, but here only sharpened the sense of a barrier. Even silence has its acoustic, and theirs was like an irritating air, made worse by London’s distant grind outside, the ceaseless commercial roar that creeps through walls and leaves no place for clean feeling.

Presently Hans spoke low, still without turning.

“Excuse the question, but does Mrs. Grandcourt know of all this?”

“No; and I must beg of you, Hans,” Deronda answered, angered into firmness, “to cease joking on that subject. Any notions you have are wide of the truth—are the very reverse of the truth.”

“I am no more inclined to joke than I shall be at my own funeral,” Hans said. “But I am not at all sure that you are aware what are my notions on that subject.”

“Perhaps not,” said Deronda. “But let me say, once for all, that in relation to Mrs. Grandcourt, I never have had, and never shall have the position of a lover. If you have ever seriously put that interpretation on anything you have observed, you are supremely mistaken.”

Silence fell again, and each felt it as one feels a draught in a room: it searches you out and makes you shift.

“Perhaps I have been mistaken in another interpretation, also,” Hans said at last.

“What is that?”

“That you had no wish to hold the position of a lover toward another woman, who is neither wife nor widow.”

Deronda’s heart gave a quick, painful leap—the question naming what he had tried to keep unnamed even to himself, because names can be traded, and he was learning how easily language becomes a currency in the wrong hands.

“I can’t pretend not to understand you, Meyrick,” he said. “It is painful that our wishes should clash. I hope you will tell me if you have any ground for supposing that you would succeed.”

“That seems rather a superfluous inquiry on your part, Deronda,” Hans answered, irritation breaking through his guarded tone.

“Why superfluous?”

“Because you are perfectly convinced on the subject—and probably have had the very best evidence to convince you.”

“I will be more frank with you than you are with me,” Deronda said, heated and yet sorry for him. “I have never had the slightest evidence that I should succeed myself. In fact, I have very little hope.”

Hans looked round hastily, as if he had been struck by something he did not expect, then turned back to the picture.

“And in our present situation,” Deronda went on, stung by the suspicion of insincerity and giving his words an offended emphasis, “I don’t see how I can deliberately make known my feeling to her. If she could not return it, I should have embittered her best comfort; for neither she nor I can be parted from her brother, and we should have to meet continually. If I were to cause her that sort of pain by an unwilling betrayal of my feeling, I should be no better than a mischievous animal.”

“I don’t know that I have ever betrayed my feeling to her,” Hans said, with a quick defensive edge, as if to prove he too had tried to behave with honor.

“You mean that we are on a level, then; you have no reason to envy me.”

“Oh, not the slightest,” Hans returned, bitterly. “You have measured my conceit and know that it out-tops all your advantages.”

“I am a nuisance to you, Meyrick. I am sorry, but I can’t help it,” Deronda said, rising. “After what passed between us before, I wished to have this explanation; and I don’t see that any pretensions of mine have made a real difference to you. They are not likely to make any pleasant difference to myself under present circumstances. Now the father is there—did you know that the father is there?”

“Yes. If he were not a Jew I would permit myself to damn him—with faint praise, I mean,” Hans said, still without a smile.

“She and I meet under greater constraint than ever,” Deronda continued. “Things might go on in this way for two years without my getting any insight into her feeling toward me. That is the whole state of affairs, Hans. Neither you nor I have injured the other, that I can see. We must put up with this sort of rivalry in a hope that is likely enough to come to nothing. Our friendship can bear that strain, surely.”

“No, it can’t,” Hans burst out, impetuously. He flung down his tools, thrust his hands into his coat-pockets, and turned to face Deronda, who drew back a little, amazed at the sudden blaze. Hans went on, the words rushing as if they had been bottled too long.

“Our friendship—my friendship—can’t bear the strain of behaving to you like an ungrateful dastard and grudging you your happiness. For you are the happiest dog in the world. If Mirah loves anybody better than her brother, you are the man.”

He wheeled away and dropped into his chair, looking up at Deronda with an expression that seemed to dare him to deny what had been said.

A shock passed through Deronda—something like the sudden discovery of sweetness when one has expected only bitterness, and is afraid of being deceived by the palate.

“It is a good-natured fiction of yours, Hans,” he said, distrustful of delight because he was unused to it.

“I am not in a good-natured mood. I assure you I found the fact disagreeable when it was thrust on me—all the more, or perhaps all the less, because I believed then that your heart was pledged to the duchess. But now, confound you! you turn out to be in love in the right place—a Jew—and everything eligible.”

“Tell me what convinced you—there’s a good fellow,” Deronda said, almost pleading, like a man who has smelled bread and must know whether it is truly baking or only imagined.

“Don’t ask. Little mother was witness. The upshot is, that Mirah is jealous of the duchess, and the sooner you relieve your mind the better. There! I’ve cleared off a score or two, and may be allowed to swear at you for getting what you deserve—which is just the very best luck I know of.”

“God bless you, Hans!” Deronda said, and held out his hand.

Hans took it and wrung it in silence—hard, as if to press pain into loyalty and make it stay.

Deronda went again to Ezra Cohen’s lodging with a resolve that had the steadiness of hunger: not the coarse hunger that makes a man swallow without tasting, but that finer craving which sharpens the senses and will not be put off with trifles. Hans had spoken with honest bluntness—Mirah needed relief from jealousy—and the words had worked in Deronda like heat in dough, making what had been folded and hidden begin to rise and insist on its own shape.

If Mirah would take his love, he could meet the rest—her father’s perilous nearness, Ezra’s fragile peace, whatever disputes and humiliations might come—as a man meets weather when he has a roof to build for another. He had watched Lapidoth these days without seeing open signs of fresh turbulence; yet foreboding lingered with him like an undertone in music, something you might not name but could not stop hearing. He felt there would be a struggle, a mortification, some intolerable wrenching of domestic quiet; and that he might be called to save Ezra and Mirah from being helpless under it.

He did not know what was gathering in Lapidoth’s mind.

To Ezra, Lapidoth’s restlessness was a small daily torment—the shifting attention, the half-listening, the perpetual sense of a man only waiting for his own moment to escape. But to Lapidoth it was worse than torment: it was restraint, the clipped wing, submission made barely tolerable by the prospect of a later, better liberty. He had come at first meaning to wait for a chance of money—a real chance, some considerable sum from Deronda; meanwhile he watched with the stealthy curiosity of appetite, trying to learn where Mirah kept her keys, where she laid her earnings. The gambling desire in him was like a restless animal that never slept; it ran under every other thought and made a web of imagining that caught the world and dragged it into its service.

Yet Mirah, practical and clear-eyed, had defended the promise she had given Ezra. She kept by her only what she must spend at once, and carried the rest to Mrs. Meyrick’s care, as if her coins were loaves to be stored in a neighbor’s safe cupboard where a hungry hand could not reach. Lapidoth found himself supplied in kind—food, shelter, attendance—with the irritating completeness of a place arranged to defeat him, like an asylum where every sharp edge has been covered.

He felt injured by it. If he could once have taken what he wanted without being forced to ask, he would have called it no disgrace. People who boast their delicacy often draw their line of liberty with other people’s property in a way that is curiously precise until law begins; and Lapidoth’s mind made fine distinctions, as if a theft at home were only a kind of family tasting, like taking an extra slice from the tart before it is served. He had had of Mirah’s apple-tart when she brought it in with shy dutifulness; why should he not have of her other earnings? Still, he remained outwardly submissive; the strongest temptation in him was not to wrangle with Mirah, but to appeal to Deronda.

He had learned, as many clever men with nothing else to sell learn, that absence can be priced. He imagined his family would breathe more freely without him, and that Deronda might be willing to pay handsomely for the comfort of getting rid of him. Yet even his hardihood had a seam of fear: Deronda’s quiet authority, his look that seemed to see without staring, had kept Lapidoth from venturing too soon.

But this day Deronda came with a light in him that could not help showing itself—an amenity as unmistakable as the way a kitchen changes when the bread is nearly done, warm, expanded, ready to be broken and shared. Lapidoth was at a crisis of discontent and longing; Deronda’s new brightness fed his schemes, and his mind became so occupied that he could not even keep up his usual show of interest. Presently he went out, saying he would smoke and walk in the square.

The room grew easier at once, as if an ill-tuned instrument had been taken away and the remaining notes could ring true.

Mirah was not at home, but she was expected soon. Deronda’s eyes kept turning—half unconsciously—to the door, with a secret anticipation that made his pulse quicken. He fancied that when she came he would see on her face some sweetness of recognition that had been hidden from him before, as flavor is hidden until the right moment of heat brings it forth.

He sat with Ezra among the books and papers in that double room which was still too narrow for Ezra’s breath. The air lay heavy—London’s close heat, holding the smell of stone, dust, and old cloth—broken now and then by the faint drift of outdoor sounds: wheels on the square’s hard edge, a distant call, the thin song of a bird that persisted as if it would stitch something living into the city’s dull fabric. Deronda, sensitive to these small acoustics, felt how the room pressed on Ezra—not only with its walls but with that muffled urban roar which never fully ceased, a low industrial tide that modern life keeps rolling even into sickrooms.

“This little room is too close for you, Ezra,” he said, breaking off from the reading. “Our week’s heat is worse than Genoa’s, where one can sit in the shaded coolness of large rooms. You must have a better home now. I shall do as I like with you, being the stronger half.” There was play in his voice, but under it a firm tenderness.

Ezra answered, “I am straitened for nothing except breath. But you, who might be in a spacious palace with the wide green country round you, find this a narrow prison. Nevertheless, I cannot say, ‘Go.’”

“Oh, the country would be banishment while you are here,” Deronda said, rising and walking what little promenade the room allowed, fanning himself with his handkerchief. “This is the happiest room in the world to me. Besides, I will imagine myself in the East, since I am getting ready to go there some day. Only I will not wear a cravat and a heavy ring there.”

He paused, and with an emphatic gesture unfastened the cravat and slipped off the ring he had been wearing, laying both upon a small table behind Ezra—dark mahogany that showed the ring’s pale fire as plainly as a drop of oil on a cutting-board. “I’ve worn my memorable ring ever since I came home,” he went on, reseating himself. “But I’m such a Sybarite that I constantly put it off as a burden when I’m doing anything. I can understand why the Romans had summer rings—if they had them. Now then—I shall get on better.”

They returned to their work. Deronda read a piece of rabbinical Hebrew and Ezra corrected and commented, their voices making a kind of inward music against the city’s outer din. In that exchange there was also something more—the sense of a language carrying centuries in its consonants and breath, and of how easily, when no one listens, a tongue can die like a song drowned by machinery. Deronda felt the words in his mouth with care, aware how meaning is never fully carried over, how what Ezra heard in them could not be translated whole.

When Lapidoth re-entered, they scarcely noticed at first. He took a seat somewhat in the background. But his rambling eyes did not ramble long before they found the ring, detached and within reach, throwing back a small, tempting sparkle.

During his walk his mind had been busy with a fiction—an opening abroad needing ready money; he would communicate it to Deronda privately; Deronda would ask, inevitably, how much; and there lay the difficult art—ask too much and you risk refusal, ask too little and regret gnaws you. Lapidoth’s desire had no limit, and he had no measure of Deronda’s willingness.

Now, in the midst of that airy calculation, the ring lay before him, solid and immediate. Its value was far below the sums he had been balancing, but it was here, ready for a hand. Desire leapt, not yet into intention but into pictured act: pocket it, go out, and present restraint would be ended at once. He told himself it would be safe. Any property of Deronda’s, available without formal consent, was—so his mind argued—one with his children’s property; and no child would prosecute a father. He had never committed larceny; but larceny was what law punished, and this, he insisted inwardly, was no larceny—only taking from one who would have given more if pressed.

He rejected it—again. He would go below, he decided, and watch for Deronda’s departure; then ask to join him in his walk and boldly carry out the plan of a larger gift. He rose and stood looking out of the window; but what he saw, like a refrain repeating itself, was not the square—it was the short passage to the door by the table where the ring lay.

He meant to go down. And yet—without a distinct change of will, rather by the dominance of desire, like the drunkard’s thirst that overtakes resolution—when he passed the table his fingers fell noiselessly on the ring. The action was so quick it seemed to have happened before it was chosen. He found himself in the passage with the ring in his hand.

After that the rest followed as naturally as a man putting on his coat when he has decided to leave. He took his hat and quitted the house. The possibility of returning to throw himself again upon Ezra and Mirah receded, becoming a vague future that might never arrive. Before he was even out on the square, his haste had narrowed to one urgent line: sell the ring, get on shipboard, be free.

Deronda and Ezra were only just aware of his exit; nothing more.

By-and-by Mirah came in and made a real interruption—quiet footfall, the faint rustle of her dress, the cooler breath of outdoors following her as if she carried a small pocket of air with her. She had not taken off her hat, and there was a look on her face like someone who has been hurrying with an errand and does not know whether she brings help or trouble. When Deronda rose and advanced to shake hands, she said, with a confusion that was at once unaccountable and vexing to herself, “I only came in to see that Ezra had his new draught. I must go directly to Mrs. Meyrick’s to fetch something.”

“Pray allow me to walk with you,” Deronda said, urgency breaking through his usual restraint. “I must not tire Ezra any further; besides my brains are melting. I want to go to Mrs. Meyrick’s. May I go with you?”

“Oh—yes,” Mirah answered, blushing more, feeling something altered in him, as one feels a change in a room not by sight but by the way the sounds fall—his voice held a new warmth, a new nearness, as if it had moved closer to her ear. She turned away to pour out Ezra’s draught. Ezra, meanwhile, threw back his head with his eyes shut, still full of the ideas the reading had stirred—old words, old griefs, and the ache of meanings that cannot be laid into another language without losing their living pulse.

Deronda stood for a moment thinking of nothing but the walk with her, as if the world had narrowed to the short distance between Ezra’s lodging and the Meyricks’ door. Then Mirah turned round again with the draught; and suddenly he remembered his cravat. “Pray excuse my dishabille—I did not mean you to see it,” he said, and went to the little table to take up the cravat.

His hand found only the cloth.

A violent impulse of surprise seized him. “Good heavens—where is my ring gone?” He began searching on the floor, as if it must have rolled into shadow and lodged itself where the patterned carpet could hide its glint.

Ezra looked round the corner of his chair.

Mirah, quick as thought, went near where Deronda was seeking. “Did you lay it down?”

“Yes,” Deronda answered, still visited only by the idea that it had fallen. He moved small pieces of furniture, peered under edges, searched in places where reason said it could not be, but the eye still hopes.

Another explanation had come to Mirah like a chill. The color left her cheeks. She bent to Ezra’s ear and whispered, “Was my father here?”

Ezra bent his head in reply. Their eyes met—his full of terrible understanding, hers of dread that became certainty.

She darted back to Deronda, who still cast his eyes down in that hopeless exploration we persist in after we know we have already examined in vain. “You have not found it?” she said, hurriedly.

He met her frightened gaze and caught alarm from it. “I perhaps put it in my pocket,” he said, feeling there, trying—by that small feint—to spare her.

She watched him, and her voice sharpened with a painful clearness that would not let him pretend. “It is not there?—you put it on the table.” And immediately she rushed out of the room.

Deronda followed. She had gone into the sitting-room below, looking for her father, opening the bedroom door, glancing where his hat usually hung—searching with the swiftness of someone trying to outrun a shame that is already upon her. Then she turned, clasping her hands tight, lips pale, and stared out of the window as if the square might show him vanishing among strangers’ footsteps and wheels.

She looked up at Deronda. She could not utter a word. The look itself seemed her confession, her submission to humiliation in his presence—an unspoken “This is what I come from; this is what I cannot prevent.”

Deronda did not speak at once. He took her clasped hands between both his with a tenderness that was like reverence, as if he held something sacred and wounded. His voice, when it came, had the depth of a vow.

“Mirah—let me think that he is my father as well as yours—that we can have no sorrow, no disgrace, no joy apart. I will rather take your grief to be mine than I would take the brightest joy of another woman. Say you will not reject me—say you will take me to share all things with you. Say you will promise to be my wife—say it now. I have been in doubt so long—I have had to hide my love so long. Say that now and always I may prove to you that I love you with complete love.”

The change in Mirah did not come like a door flung open. It was gradual, as warmth spreads through a cold room, as broth turns from mere hot water into something that sustains. At first she felt only solemn comfort, attributing Deronda’s goodness to his feeling for Ezra—his loyalty to the house as a whole, not to her alone. But as his words went on, the assurance of an unhoped-for good took possession of her frame, and the shame that had made her white began to melt under a new radiance.

Her face glowed as he bent over her; yet her eyes kept their intense gravity—the same grave gratitude with which she had once acknowledged that he had thought her “worthy of the best.” When he had finished, she could say nothing. Speech, with its public weights and its imperfect translations, failed her. She only lifted her lips to his and kissed them—simply, as if that were the plainest “yes” she could give.
